name: Warren Buffett
domain: investing, capital allocation, valuing and buying businesses, moats, management and incentives, insurance float, temperament, and life lessons
sourcesLabel: shareholder letters, annual meetings, talks and interviews

sources.title: Warren Buffett at Florida: moats, circle of competence, and picking who to be
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett speaks with Florida University
sources.summary: Buffett tells UF MBA students that character and habits matter more than IQ, then explains how he picks businesses: simple, understandable, with a widening moat and honest management. He covers Long-Term Capital's collapse, avoiding macro forecasts, concentration, and his mistakes of omission.

principles.text: Character and habits are chosen; copy admired traits early, before the chains of habit get too heavy.
principles.quote: the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they're too heavy to be broken.

principles.text: Never risk what you have and need to gain what you don't need.
principles.quote: to make the money they didn't have and didn't need, they risked what they did have and did need. And that's foolish.

principles.text: Look for a castle with a durable moat run by an honest, able manager; widen the moat over time.
principles.quote: I want a business with a moat around it. I want a very valuable castle in the middle. And then I want the duke who's in charge of that castle to be honest and hard working and able.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; its size matters less than knowing its edges.
principles.quote: The important thing is not how big the circle is. The important thing is staying inside the circle.

principles.text: Focus on what is important and knowable; ignore macro and interest rate predictions.
principles.quote: what you really want to do in investments is figure out what's important and knowable. If it's unimportant or unknowable, you you forget about it.

principles.text: Buy a business you'd hold if the market closed for years; stocks are part ownership, not tickers.
principles.quote: I don't want to buy any stock where if they close the New York Stock Exchange tomorrow for 5 years, I won't be happy owning it.

sources.title: Warren Buffett at UGA 2001: choose character, stay in your circle of competence, buy wonderful businesses
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett speaks to University of Georgia students 2001
sources.summary: Buffett answers University of Georgia students on character and habits, circle of competence, intrinsic value as discounted cash, the cigar-butt mistake, mistakes of omission, market temperament, philanthropy, and why small businesses can beat scale.

principles.text: Hire for intelligence, energy and integrity; without integrity, you want them lazy and dumb.
principles.quote: we look for three things when we hire people we look for intelligence we look for for initiative or energy and we look for integrity

principles.text: Invest only in what you understand; knowing the edge of your circle of competence matters more than its size.
principles.quote: defining your circle of competence is the most important aspect of investing it's not how important how large your circle is

principles.text: A big industry does not mean profits for investors; autos, airlines and TVs destroyed capital despite transforming society.
principles.quote: understanding the economic characteristics of a business is different than predicting the fact that an industry is going to do wonderfully

principles.text: Intrinsic value is the discounted cash a business will give you over its life; investing is laying out money now to get more later.
principles.quote: the only reason for making an investment and laying out money now is to get more money later on right that's that's what investing is all about

principles.text: Prefer a wonderful business at a fair price to a fair business at a wonderful price; time favors great businesses.
principles.quote: I would rather buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price

principles.text: Temperament beats brains: detaching from the crowd is what makes you rich.
principles.quote: it doesn't take brains it takes temperament it takes the ability to sit there and look at something

sources.title: Warren Buffett at UNC 1996: character, circle of confidence, moats and why he ignores the market
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett | Lecture | University Of North Carolina | 1996
sources.summary: Buffett fields student questions on hiring and character, staying inside a circle of confidence, buying great businesses and rarely selling, moats and franchise value, ignoring market forecasts, his shareholder base, and mistakes of omission.

principles.text: Character traits are habits you can choose; form the good ones early, because habits harden.
principles.quote: the chains of habit are too like to be felt until they're too heavy to be broken

principles.text: Stay in your circle of confidence; knowing where its edges are matters more than its size.
principles.quote: the most important thing in terms of your circle of confidence is not how large the area of it is it's how well you've defined the perimeter

principles.text: Ignore market and rate forecasts; buy the right business at the right price with the right people.
principles.quote: all i know is if i buy the right kind of business the right price with the right people i'll do well over time

principles.text: A franchise is a moat around an economic castle; judge both castle size and moat durability.
principles.quote: franchise is basically like a moat around your economic castle now there's two things are important how big is the castle

principles.text: Selling a truly great business because the price looks high is almost always a mistake.
principles.quote: to sell off something that is a really wonderful business because the price looks a little high or something like that it's almost always a mistake

principles.text: Distrust accounting footnotes you can't understand; if you can't understand it, don't invest.
principles.quote: if it's written so you can't understand it i am very suspicious

sources.title: How Buffett picks people, stays in his circle of competence, and ignores the crowd
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett, Chairman, Berkshire Hathaway Investment Group | Terry Leadership Speaker Series
sources.outlet: Terry College of Business at the University of Georgia
sources.summary: At UGA's Terry College, Buffett explains how to choose a career, why character beats grades, how to value any business as discounted future cash, and why staying inside your circle of competence matters. He also covers his own mistakes (Berkshire, US Air, omissions), why temperament beats IQ, and why small businesses can beat giants.

principles.text: Work for someone you admire, not whatever looks best on your resume.
principles.quote: go to work for whomever you admire the most and I said you can't get a bad result you'll jump out of bed in the morning and you'll be having fun

principles.text: Hire for intelligence, energy and integrity; without integrity, you want them lazy and dumb.
principles.quote: we look for three things when we hire people we look for intelligence we look for for initiative or energy and we look for integrity and if they don't have the ladder the first two will kill you

principles.text: Intrinsic value is all the cash a business will give you from now to Judgment Day, discounted properly.
principles.quote: all the cash that a b a business would give you between now and Judgment Day discounted at the proper discount rate that number is what the intrinsic value of business is

principles.text: Define your circle of competence and stay inside it; its size matters less than knowing its edge.
principles.quote: defining your circle of competence is the most important aspect of investing it's not how important how how large your circle is you don't have to be an expert on everything but knowing where the perimeter of that Circle

principles.text: Prefer a wonderful business at a fair price to a fair business at a wonderful price; time rewards great businesses and punishes lousy ones.
principles.quote: I rather buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price

principles.text: His biggest mistakes are omissions: clear opportunities within his competence that he failed to seize.
principles.quote: the biggest mistakes I've made by far are mistakes of omission and not Co Mission I mean it's the things I knew enough to do they were within my circle of competence and I was sucking my thumb

sources.title: Warren Buffett at Georgetown 2013: temperament, circle of competence, and America's long-run optimism
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett | Lecture | Georgetown University | September 19, 2013
sources.summary: In a 2013 Georgetown conversation with Brian Moynihan, Buffett explains why temperament beats IQ in investing, why you only need to swing at a few pitches, and why he stays optimistic about America despite panics. He also covers the Giving Pledge, inequality, and the GEICO and Heinz deals.

principles.text: Investing success depends on temperament, not a sky-high IQ; ignore the crowd and judge the facts.
principles.quote: it doesn't take a high iq to figure out that they're cheap but it does take a temperament that's willing to step up and actually act

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; you only need to be right on a few businesses.
principles.quote: it's a terrible mistake to think you have to have an opinion on everything you only have to have an opinion on a few things

principles.text: Investing has no called strikes: wait for the right pitch and swing only when you understand the business and like the price.
principles.quote: in investing there's no called strikes

principles.text: Humans repeat the same mistakes: greed builds slowly, fear hits all at once, so panics will recur.
principles.quote: when they get fearful it happens all at once i mean when everybody wants when people get scared they all want to leave at one time

principles.text: Bet on America's long-run progress despite recessions and occasional panics.
principles.quote: don't ever worry about america it'll tell you you're in the right place

principles.text: Pick businesses with simple, durable, travelling products and think in per-unit economics, like Coca-Cola's penny.
principles.quote: i like products that travel well

sources.title: How Buffett built wealth: Graham's value investing, Berkshire, and loving the job
sources.originalTitle: The David Rubenstein Show: Warren Buffett on His Early Career in Finance
sources.summary: Buffett recounts his path from pinball machines to Ben Graham's partnership, the Buffett Partnership and Berkshire. He explains investing as assigning yourself the right story about what a business is worth, buying decent businesses at sensible prices, and why time and finding work you love matter more than money.

principles.text: Investing is valuing a business: write the story of what it is worth, then compare it to the price.
principles.quote: Investing is just about assigning yourself the right story.

principles.text: Buy decent businesses at sensible prices and back good people to run them.
principles.quote: We bought businesses that we thought were decent businesses at sensible prices and we had good people to run them.

principles.text: When fear drives a price far below intrinsic value, the gap is the opportunity.
principles.quote: So the Washington Post company, which was intrinsically worth $400 or $500 million, was selling for about 80 million in the market.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence: only value what you can write the story on.
principles.quote: If you ask me to write a story on, you know, what is some glamorous but nonprofit making business worth, I don't know how to write that story.

principles.text: Screen deals quickly and say no fast; most fail simple filters.
principles.quote: I can usually tell within two or three minutes whether a deal is likely to happen or not.

principles.text: Time is the scarce resource, not money. Find work you would do for free.
principles.quote: I think you should look for the job that you would want to hold if you didn't need a job.

sources.title: How Buffett reads Kraft Heinz, stock prices, and America's tailwind: CNBC interview, Feb 2019
sources.originalTitle: CNBC's Becky Quick interviews Warren Buffett (2/25/19)
sources.summary: In a long CNBC interview after his 2018 letter, Buffett explains why Berkshire overpaid for Kraft Heinz, why a good business can't fix a bad price, and why he shrugs off mark-to-market swings. He also covers buying stocks when cheaper, buybacks, index funds, IPOs, Bitcoin, and the American tailwind.

principles.text: Overpaying is permanent: a business earns what it earns regardless of the price you paid.
principles.quote: the business does not earn more just because you pay more for it

principles.text: Judge a business on returns to tangible assets, but your own cost basis includes any premium you paid.
principles.quote: we paid a hundred billion more than the tangible assets so for us it has to earn on 107 and not just on the seven billion that the business employees

principles.text: The market serves you; a price drop matters only if long-term business value changed.
principles.quote: the stock market is there not to instruct me it's there to serve me

principles.text: If you plan to keep owning a business, falling prices help you, especially when the company is repurchasing shares.
principles.quote: we're way better off you know if it's a if it's at a lower price when they're repurchasing share

principles.text: Whether stocks are expensive depends on interest rates; at very low long-term rates, stocks look cheap.
principles.quote: if you tell me that 3% long bonds will prevail over the next 30 years stocks are incredibly cheap

principles.text: Most people should own a low-cost S&P 500 index fund; just betting on America beat any political view.
principles.quote: you do not want to have a political view in investing

sources.title: Buffett on buying businesses, not stocks: the 2020 CNBC Omaha interview on markets, rates, and Berkshire
sources.originalTitle: Watch CNBC's full interview with Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett
sources.summary: In his annual post-letter CNBC interview, Buffett argues stocks are businesses to own for decades, so daily selloffs and virus headlines should not change decisions. He covers interest rates, reaching for yield, bad incentives (Wells Fargo), and why Berkshire's conglomerate structure works.

principles.text: Think of stocks as businesses you will own for decades, not tickers to trade on headlines.
principles.quote: people would be better off if they say, "I bought a business today, not a stock today." Because that gives you a different perspective on it.

principles.text: Nobody can predict the market; the real question is whether you are paying a sensible price for future earning power.
principles.quote: if you get your money's worth in terms of future earning power over the next 10 or 20 or 30 years, you're going to have made a good investment.

principles.text: Write down why a business is worth its total market price, rather than guessing short-term price moves.
principles.quote: You should say, I am buying the General Motors Company for $42 billion because, and you should get it on a piece of paper.

principles.text: A market drop is good news for a net buyer who holds for the long term; it only hurts those forced to sell.
principles.quote: how can it be bad news unless you have to sell stocks? Now, if you have to sell them for some reason, it's you're worse off if you don't have to sell them.

principles.text: Reaching for yield is foolish; adapt your spending to your income, not your income to your spending.
principles.quote: You should always adapt your consumption to your income. You shouldn't try and adjust your income to your consumption.

principles.text: Incentive systems drive behavior, so a dumb one produces bad behavior, and problems must be attacked the moment they appear.
principles.quote: you can cause people to do the wrong thing because they will do what they're incented to do.

sources.title: Warren Buffett at Fortune MPW 2014: good businesses, zone of reasonableness, ignoring macro noise
sources.originalTitle: Warren Buffett On Investment Strategy | Full Interview Fortune MPW
sources.summary: Buffett explains what makes a good business (high return on tangible assets, bought at a sensible price), why banks lose money copying competitors, and why the market sits in a "zone of reasonableness." He also covers owning stocks without anchoring to cost, admitting mistakes early, and ignoring politics and macro forecasts.

principles.text: A good business earns a high return on tangible assets; overpaying can turn it into a bad investment.
principles.quote: a good business is the one that earns a high rate of return on on tangible assets very simple

principles.text: Buying a bad business at a cheap price was an early mistake; it took decades to learn.
principles.quote: the big mistake which we made in the early years was to try and buy a bad business at a really cheap price and uh it took me about 20 or 30 years to figure out that wasn't a good idea

principles.text: Don't copy competitors; if the reason is that others are doing it, go back to square one.
principles.quote: if anybody comes to me and says we want to do this because the other guy is doing it you know I say go back to square one and come up with a better reason

principles.text: Markets sit in a broad zone of reasonableness; precise timing is impossible and unnecessary.
principles.quote: if you if you buy good businesses at reasonable prices and hold them you're going to make a lot of money

principles.text: A stock doesn't know what you paid; the only question is whether you can get more for your money elsewhere.
principles.quote: the stock doesn't even care that you own it you are nothing to the stock that's that stock is everything to you

principles.text: Don't let politics, Fed moves or macro forecasts change decisions on businesses meant to be held for decades.
principles.quote: the important thing is whether we get a good business with good management at a sensible price

sources.title: Berkshire 2025 annual meeting: Buffett on patience, float, currency risk, and handing the reins to Greg Abel
sources.originalTitle: Watch Warren Buffett preside over the full 2025 Berkshire Hathaway annual shareholder meeting
sources.summary: Buffett's last meeting as CEO, where he announces Greg Abel will take over at year end. He explains why he holds $335B in cash, why markets demand emotional control, why he distrusts currency debasement and earnings management, and what makes Berkshire's insurance float unique.

principles.text: Great opportunities arrive irregularly, so stay liquid and patient rather than forcing capital out on a schedule.
principles.quote: Things get extraordinarily attractive very occasionally.

principles.text: Investors must control their emotions; the market will not adapt to you, so you must adapt to it.
principles.quote: the world is not going to adapt to you. You're going to have to adapt to the world.

principles.text: Governments tend to debase currency over time, which is a core long-term risk to guard against.
principles.quote: the tendency of a government to want to debase its currency over time is there's no system that beats that.

principles.text: Surround yourself with people better than you, because you drift toward the company you keep.
principles.quote: you want to hang out with people that are better than you are

principles.text: Study balance sheets over many years before income statements, since they are harder to manipulate.
principles.quote: I spend more time looking at balance sheets than I do income statements.

principles.text: Don't make decisions to manage reported quarterly or annual earnings; focusing on a number tempts people to play games.
principles.quote: we don't do anything based on its impact on quarterly and annual earnings.

sources.title: Berkshire 2023 AGM morning: float, buybacks, Apple, Japan, and succession
sources.originalTitle: Berkshire's 2023 annual shareholder meeting: Watch the full morning session with Warren Buffett
sources.summary: Buffett opens the 2023 Berkshire meeting explaining operating earnings, retained earnings, and insurance float as a liability that works like free equity. He then covers Geico and reinsurance, Apple, the Japanese trading houses, buybacks, succession, and why he is still optimistic about America.

principles.text: Judge Berkshire by operating earnings; stock prices swing capriciously, but you should expect capital gains over time.
principles.quote: we expect to make capital gains over time why would we own the stocks otherwise uh doesn't always work out but overall it works out pretty well over time but in any day any quarter any year even occasionally over a five-year period uh the stock prices move around capriciously

principles.text: Float is a liability that finances assets like equity but costs nothing, and cannot vanish quickly; most insurers don't think of it this way.
principles.quote: float is another item that shows a it's a liability but hasn't cost us anything and it it can't disappear in a hurry and it finances the asset side in the same way as stockholders equity and nobody else thinks of it much that way

principles.text: Retain earnings and compound; Berkshire's size came from keeping the money, and the one dividend paid was a mistake.
principles.quote: the reason we've gotten to where we are is because we we kept the money we did pay a dividend in nineteen sixty seven ten cents to share it was a terrible mistake

principles.text: Buy back stock only when it's below intrinsic value and after funding the business; it's simple, not complicated.
principles.quote: if you've got ample capital and you don't see that you're going to use it all and your stock is attractive and it enhances the intrinsic value for the remaining shareholders it's an old-brainer and if it's if it's above the price of intrinsic value it's a no-brainer

principles.text: Concentration beats broad diversification when you know where your competence ends; an Apple stake is a business like any other.
principles.quote: if you know the edge of your own ability pretty well you should ignore most of the Notions of our experts about what I call diversification of portfolios

principles.text: Opportunities come from other people doing dumb things and from a short-term-focused world; don't play games you needn't play.
principles.quote: what gives you opportunities is other people doing dumb things

sources.title: Buffett at the 2024 Berkshire meeting: stocks as businesses, patient cash, and one-year insurance risk
sources.originalTitle: Watch Warren Buffett preside over the full 2024 Berkshire Hathaway annual shareholders meeting
sources.summary: Buffett fields shareholder questions on Apple, cash, succession, insurance, utilities and AI. He stresses owning stocks as businesses, swinging only at pitches he likes, compounding retained earnings, pricing insurance risk one year at a time, and being kind and lucky.

principles.text: Treat every stock as a business, not a ticker to trade or time.
principles.quote: when we look at Coca-Cola and American Express and apple we look at them as businesses

principles.text: Hold cash and wait; only act on opportunities you truly like, however big the pile gets.
principles.quote: we only swing at pitches we like

principles.text: Retained earnings plus a long runway compound into enormous wealth without any miracles.
principles.quote: the math of compounding and a long long Runway uh have done wonders

principles.text: Insurance means pricing uncertainty; limit commitments to a year so you can reprice or exit.
principles.quote: if there was no risk there'd be no insurance business and and we're in the business of evaluating it and we do it one year at a time

principles.text: Even for essential, low-return utilities, never invest where you can lose it all.
principles.quote: whether you earn X or go broke is not an equation that works

principles.text: Success is partly luck, so be kind and spread good fortune to others.
principles.quote: if you're lucky in life make sure bunch of other people are lucky

sources.title: How Buffett judged managers by return on equity, and bought stocks like whole businesses (1977 letter)
sources.summary: Buffett argues record EPS means little when equity compounds, so return on equity is the real measure. He explains buying marketable stocks as if buying whole businesses, why insurance magnifies manager quality, and why tailwind businesses beat headwind ones like textiles.

principles.text: Judge managers by return on equity capital, not record earnings per share, since retained equity compounds EPS automatically.
principles.quote: we believe a more appropriate measure of managerial economic performance to be return on equity capital.

principles.text: Buy stocks with the same four tests used to buy whole businesses: understandable, good prospects, honest management, attractive price.
principles.quote: We want the business to be (1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price.

principles.text: Welcome lower prices on stocks you own when the business still satisfies you; do not trade for short-term price moves.
principles.quote: In fact, if their business experience continues to satisfy us, we welcome lower market prices of stocks we own as an opportunity to acquire even more of a good thing at a better price.

principles.text: Minority stakes in outstanding businesses can be bargains unavailable through whole-company acquisition.
principles.quote: Our experience has been that pro-rata portions of truly outstanding businesses sometimes sell in the securities markets at very large discounts from the prices they would command in negotiated transactions involving entire companies.

principles.text: Prefer businesses with tailwinds over headwinds; good management cannot rescue a structurally poor industry.
principles.quote: One of the lessons your management has learned - and, unfortunately, sometimes re-learned - is the importance of being in businesses where tailwinds prevail rather than headwinds.

principles.text: In insurance, discipline means giving up volume when rates turn inadequate, even though institutions resist letting rivals take business.
principles.quote: Unusual managerial discipline will be required, as it runs counter to normal institutional behavior to let the other fellow take away business - even at foolish prices.

sources.title: Buffett's 1978 letter: buying small stakes in great businesses cheaply, and why textiles earn poor returns
sources.summary: Buffett explains how Berkshire's insurance float is put into concentrated stakes in outstanding businesses like SAFECO, bought below intrinsic value while corporations overpay for whole companies. He also shows why capital-intensive commodity businesses like textiles earn inadequate returns, and praises owner-minded managers.

principles.text: Commit heavily to stocks only when you understand the business, its prospects are good, management is honest and competent, and the price is attractive.
principles.quote: (1) businesses we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) priced very attractively.

principles.text: Don't try to forecast short-term stock prices; it can't be done reliably.
principles.quote: We make no attempt to predict how security markets will behave; successfully forecasting short term stock price movements is something we think neither we nor anyone else can do.

principles.text: Concentrate holdings: when convinced, buy meaningful amounts rather than a little of everything.
principles.quote: Our policy is to concentrate holdings. We try to avoid buying a little of this or that when we are only lukewarm about the business or its price.

principles.text: Buying a small piece of a great business below 100 cents on the dollar beats paying premiums for mediocre companies in negotiated deals.
principles.quote: We paid less than 100 cents on the dollar for the best company in the business, when far more than 100 cents on the dollar is being paid for mediocre companies in corporate transactions.

principles.text: Undifferentiated, capital-intensive businesses earn poor returns unless supply is tight, because prices track operating costs, not capital employed.
principles.quote: producers of relatively undifferentiated goods in capital intensive businesses must earn inadequate returns except under conditions of tight supply or real shortage.

principles.text: Prize managers who think and act like owners, regardless of age.
principles.quote: It is a real pleasure to work with managers who enjoy coming to work each morning and, once there, instinctively and unerringly think like owners.

sources.title: Buffett 1979 letter: ROE over EPS, inflation's misery index, and why turnarounds seldom turn
sources.summary: Buffett argues managers should be judged on return on equity capital rather than EPS growth, shows how inflation plus taxes can erase even a 20% return, and explains why a good business at a fair price beats a poor one at a bargain. He also covers underwriting discipline, avoiding long bonds, and candid owner reporting.

principles.text: Judge management by return on equity capital without undue leverage, not by steady EPS growth.
principles.quote: The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share.

principles.text: Rising EPS can be an illusion: retained earnings alone make a stopped clock look like a growth stock.
principles.quote: Thus, even a “stopped clock” can look like a growth stock if the dividend payout ratio is low.

principles.text: Turnarounds seldom turn; a good business at a fair price beats a poor business at a bargain price.
principles.quote: “turnarounds” seldom turn, and that the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price.

principles.text: Inflation plus the tax cost of cashing out can exceed a business's return, shrinking real capital.
principles.quote: When this index exceeds the rate of return earned on equity by the business, the investor’s purchasing power (real capital) shrinks even though he consumes nothing at all.

principles.text: Don't lock in a fixed price on money for decades in an inflationary world; avoid very long bonds.
principles.quote: our unwillingness to fix a price now for a pound of See’s candy or a yard of Berkshire cloth to be delivered in 2010 or 2020 makes us equally unwilling to buy bonds which set a price on money now for use in those years.

principles.text: Underwrite only business that makes sense, even if volume falls; don't lay off people over it.
principles.quote: if business makes sense, he writes it; if it doesn’t, he rejects it.

sources.title: Buffett's 1980 letter: retained earnings, inflation as a hidden tax, and GEICO
sources.summary: Buffett argues that the economic value of retained earnings depends on how they are used, not on accounting credit or ownership percentage. He explains why inflation turns ordinary corporate returns into negative real returns for owners, why GEICO is a rare franchise with a skilled manager, and why insurers should be wary of bond-driven price cutting.

principles.text: Retained earnings are worth what they earn when put to use, regardless of whether you own 1% or 100% or get accounting credit.
principles.quote: The value to Berkshire Hathaway of retained earnings is not determined by whether we own 100%, 50%, 20% or 1% of the businesses in which they reside. Rather, the value of those retained earnings is determined by the use to which they are put

principles.text: Prefer unrecorded earnings reinvested well by a good management over credited earnings reinvested poorly, even by yourself.
principles.quote: we would rather have earnings for which we did not get accounting credit put to good use in a 10%-owned company by a management we did not personally hire, than have earnings for which we did get credit put into projects of more dubious potential by another management - even if we are that management.

principles.text: Buybacks are the best use of capital when a fine business trades far below intrinsic value; markets often offer cheaper earning power than takeovers.
principles.quote: if a fine business is selling in the market place for far less than intrinsic value, what more certain or more profitable utilization of capital can there be than significant enlargement of the interests of all owners at that bargain price?

principles.text: Only gains in purchasing power are real earnings; inflation is a tax on capital that can make a decent return negative.
principles.quote: For only gains in purchasing power represent real earnings on investment.

principles.text: Turnarounds rarely work: when brilliant management meets a business with poor economics, the business's reputation usually survives intact.
principles.quote: with few exceptions, when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for poor fundamental economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.

principles.text: The best investments pair a hard-to-duplicate business advantage with management skilled in both operations and capital allocation.
principles.quote: GEICO represents the best of all investment worlds - the coupling of a very important and very hard to duplicate business advantage with an extraordinary management whose skills in operations are matched by skills in capital allocation.

sources.title: Berkshire 1981: Why buy 10% of a wonderful business over 100% at double
sources.summary: Buffett explains why he prefers fractional stakes in great businesses to costly control deals, why high-premium takeovers rarely work, and how rising passive interest rates erode the value of ordinary equity. He also covers insurance underwriting discipline and float-driven pricing pressure.

principles.text: Prefer a small slice of a wonderful business at a fair price over owning all of it at double.
principles.quote: we would rather buy 10% of Wonderful Business T at X per share than 100% of T at 2X per share.

principles.text: Acquisition premiums are driven by ego, size obsession and kiss-the-toad optimism, not by economics.
principles.quote: investors can always buy toads at the going price for toads. If investors instead bankroll princesses who wish to pay double for the right to kiss the toad, those kisses had better pack some real dynamite.

principles.text: Optimize for real economic benefit, not size or reported accounting numbers.
principles.quote: Our acquisition decisions will be aimed at maximizing real economic benefits, not at maximizing either managerial domain or reported numbers for accounting purposes.

principles.text: Buy fractional stakes in businesses with excellent franchises and competent, honest managers; don't plan to run them.
principles.quote: Currently, we find values most easily obtained through the open-market purchase of fractional positions in companies with excellent business franchises and competent, honest managements.

principles.text: High-return businesses should retain earnings; low-return ones should pay them out so owners can redeploy capital.
principles.quote: Logically, a company with historic and prospective high returns on equity should retain much or all of its earnings so that shareholders can earn premium returns on enhanced capital.

principles.text: Insurers desperate for cash flow price business at any price; discipline means turning down volume.
principles.quote: Such insurers necessarily fear a major decrease in volume more than they fear a major underwriting loss.

sources.title: Buffett 1982 letter: economic vs accounting earnings and why issuing undervalued stock destroys value
sources.summary: Buffett explains why look-through "economic" earnings matter more than reported accounting earnings, why commodity-like industries (including insurance) earn poor returns without differentiation or a cost edge, and why issuing undervalued stock for acquisitions hands over $2 of value for $1. He also lists his acquisition criteria and the owner-like managers he prizes.

principles.text: Accounting earnings are the start, not the end, of valuing a business; count retained earnings of partly-owned companies regardless of ownership percentage.
principles.quote: managers and investors alike must understand that accounting numbers are the beginning, not the end, of business valuation.

principles.text: Buy businesses where each retained dollar eventually becomes at least a dollar of market value; the manic auction market gives the value investor an edge.
principles.quote: it is our job to select businesses with economic characteristics allowing each dollar of retained earnings to be translated eventually into at least a dollar of market value.

principles.text: Price paid matters enormously: overpaying for an excellent company can wipe out a decade of good results.
principles.quote: For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments.

principles.text: Commodity businesses with overcapacity earn poor returns unless they have a wide, sustainable cost advantage.
principles.quote: For the great majority of companies selling “commodity”products, a depressing equation of business economics prevails: persistent over-capacity without administered prices (or costs) equals poor profitability.

principles.text: Only issue shares when you receive as much intrinsic business value as you give; size and activity are not progress.
principles.quote: we will not issue shares unless we receive as much intrinsic business value as we give.

principles.text: Managers should avoid the thrill of the chase in acquisitions, and judge dilution by intrinsic value, not near-term EPS.
principles.quote: For in many of these acquisitions, managerial intellect wilted in competition with managerial adrenaline

sources.title: Berkshire 1983 letter: Owner-partner principles, economic Goodwill vs book value, and the cost of hyperactive markets
sources.summary: Buffett restates Berkshire's manager-owner principles (partnership attitude, per-share intrinsic value, ignoring accounting optics, candor, no dilution). He explains economic Goodwill via See's Candies, contrasts book value with intrinsic value, and argues against stock splits and hyperactive trading.

principles.text: Treat shareholders as partners, and the company as a conduit through which they own the assets.
principles.quote: Although our form is corporate, our attitude is partnership.

principles.text: Judge performance by per-share gains in intrinsic business value, not by size.
principles.quote: We do not measure the economic significance or performance of Berkshire by its size; we measure by per-share progress.

principles.text: Accounting optics should never drive capital allocation; prefer more unreported earnings over fewer reported ones.
principles.quote: Accounting consequences do not influence our operating or capital-allocation decisions.

principles.text: Book value records what has been put in; intrinsic value estimates discounted future cash that can be taken out.
principles.quote: Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out.

principles.text: Franchise businesses needing few tangible assets are hurt least by inflation and create enduring economic Goodwill.
principles.quote: During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving.

principles.text: A great business is not automatically a good purchase; price paid determines the return.
principles.quote: A good business is not always a good purchase – although it’s a good place to look for one.

sources.title: Berkshire 1984 letter: buybacks, dividend policy, bonds as businesses, and dominant franchises
sources.summary: Buffett explains when retained earnings are justified, why buybacks below intrinsic value reveal pro-owner managers, and why he values even bonds like businesses. He also covers dominant newspaper economics, owner-style incentives for unconventional bets, and how insolvent insurers distort the industry.

principles.text: Retain earnings only if each retained dollar creates at least a dollar of market value for owners.
principles.quote: for every dollar retained by the corporation, at least one dollar of market value will be created for owners.

principles.text: Buybacks well below intrinsic value are the surest way to create value, and beat most acquisitions.
principles.quote: When companies purchase their own stock, they often find it easy to get $2 of present value for $1.

principles.text: A manager who ignores sensible buybacks reveals his true priorities, whatever he says publicly.
principles.quote: A manager who consistently turns his back on repurchases, when these clearly are in the interests of owners, reveals more than he knows of his motivations.

principles.text: Evaluate every investment, even bonds, as you would buying a business.
principles.quote: Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike.

principles.text: Dominant newspapers earn excellent returns regardless of quality, so management must impose its own standards.
principles.quote: While first-class newspapers make excellent profits, the profits of third-rate papers are as good or better - as long as either class of paper is dominant within its community.

principles.text: Insolvent insurers keep writing business at any price because cash arrives before losses are paid.
principles.quote: In most businesses, of course, insolvent companies run out of cash. Insurance is different: you can be broke but flush.

sources.title: Berkshire 1985 letter: textile exit, boat vs. rowing, option pitfalls, and buying Cap Cities and Scott Fetzer
sources.summary: Buffett explains why size dampens returns, why shutting down the textile business taught that business quality beats managerial brilliance, and how fixed-price options reward retained earnings rather than performance. He also covers buying at a discount to business value, Washington Post and Cap Cities, insurance as a commodity, and Berkshire's acquisition criteria.

principles.text: A good managerial record depends more on which business you are in than on how well you row; switch boats rather than patch leaks.
principles.quote: a good managerial record (measured by economic returns) is far more a function of what business boat you get into than it is of how effectively you row

principles.text: Capital spending that looks rational for each company in a commodity industry is irrational collectively, because everyone's costs and prices fall together.
principles.quote: Viewed individually, each company’s capital investment decision appeared cost-effective and rational; viewed collectively, the decisions neutralized each other and were irrational

principles.text: Judge earnings growth by the additional capital it required; adding earnings by retaining and adding capital at ordinary returns is no great achievement.
principles.quote: When returns on capital are ordinary, an earn-more-by-putting-up-more record is no great managerial achievement.

principles.text: Fixed-price, ten-year options ignore capital costs and individual performance; option holders have no downside, unlike owners.
principles.quote: No owner has ever escaped the burden of capital costs, whereas a holder of a fixed-price option bears no capital costs at all.

principles.text: Growth eventually dampens exceptional economics: high-return companies cannot keep reinvesting all earnings at high rates once they are large.
principles.quote: an iron law of business is that growth eventually dampens exceptional economics.

principles.text: The key to successful investing is buying shares in good businesses when market prices are at a large discount from underlying business values.
principles.quote: we had learned from Ben Graham that the key to successful investing was the purchase of shares in good businesses when market prices were at a large discount from underlying business values.

sources.title: Buffett 1986 letter: owner earnings, managing by not getting in the way, and commodity insurance
sources.summary: Buffett's 1986 shareholder letter covers hiring great managers and staying out of their way, capital allocation when good ideas are scarce, the Fechheimer deal and Berkshire's buying criteria, commodity insurance pricing, GEICO's cost moat, and the appendix on owner earnings versus the cash flow fallacy.

principles.text: Manage by hiring stars and staying out of their way; work only with people you like and admire.
principles.quote: They were managerial stars long before they knew us, and our main contribution has been to not get in their way.

principles.text: Capital allocation matters more the higher your returns and the more you retain.
principles.quote: the future results of a business earning 23% annually and retaining it all are far more affected by today’s capital allocations than are the results of a business earning 10% and distributing half of that to shareholders.

principles.text: Don't predict markets; be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.
principles.quote: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.

principles.text: Value businesses on owner earnings, not GAAP earnings or cash flow that ignores maintenance capex.
principles.quote: But you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting ( c) : though dentists correctly claim that if you ignore your teeth they'll go away, the same is not true for ( c) .

principles.text: A low-cost position is a moat around a valuable castle; keep widening it.
principles.quote: The difference between GEICO’s costs and those of its competitors is a kind of moat that protects a valuable and much-sought-after business castle.

principles.text: In commodity businesses, profits attract capacity; the fix is less supply, not better behavior.
principles.quote: What’s needed is not more statesmen, but less corn.

sources.title: Berkshire 1987 letter: great managers, Mr. Market, buying quality, and conservative debt
sources.summary: Buffett's 1987 letter shows how Berkshire judges businesses by return on capital, hands off great managers, and treats stocks as pieces of businesses while ignoring Mr. Market. It also covers commodity-like insurance economics, why it prefers a fine business at a fair price, capital allocation, and keeping debt low enough to be certain of surviving.

principles.text: Judge a business by growth in per-share business value, not book value, since the two are often unrelated.
principles.quote: What counts, of course, is the rate of gain in per-share business value, not book value.

principles.text: Treat market prices as Mr. Market's offers to serve you, never as guidance; know your business better than he does.
principles.quote: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful.

principles.text: Buy an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price.
principles.quote: Our goal is to find an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price.

principles.text: Investing success comes from business judgment plus emotional insulation from the market, not arcane formulas.
principles.quote: Rather an investor will succeed by coupling good business judgment with an ability to insulate his thoughts and behavior from the super-contagious emotions that swirl about the marketplace.

principles.text: Stable, unglamorous businesses with strong franchises produce the best returns; constant change invites major error.
principles.quote: Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix.

principles.text: Keep debt low enough that survival is certain, not just likely, rather than chase optimal returns with leverage.
principles.quote: But we do not wish it to be only likely that we can meet our obligations; we wish that to be certain.

sources.title: Berkshire 1988 letter: arbitrage, permanent holdings, owner-managers and why CEOs go unmeasured
sources.summary: Buffett reports a 20% gain in 1988 and explains why a growing capital base is Berkshire's main problem. He covers buying Borsheim's on a handshake, holding wonderful businesses forever, how he approaches arbitrage, and why efficient market theory fails. He also explains why GAAP is only a starting point and why CEOs escape the accountability faced by subordinates.

principles.text: A growing capital base is the main drag on returns; compounding gets harder each year.
principles.quote: The major problem we face, however, is a growing capital base. You’ve heard that from us before, but this problem, like age, grows in significance each year.

principles.text: With outstanding businesses and managers, the favorite holding period is forever.
principles.quote: In fact, when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever.

principles.text: Concentrate in a few companies you understand well and hold strong long-term convictions about.
principles.quote: We continue to concentrate our investments in a very few companies that we try to understand well. There are only a handful of businesses about which we have strong long-term convictions.

principles.text: CEOs escape the accountability that subordinates face: fuzzy standards, unmeasured boards, taboo criticism.
principles.quote: The supreme irony of business management is that it is far easier for an inadequate CEO to keep his job than it is for an inadequate subordinate.

principles.text: Never forecast the market, rates or the economy; invest on long-term business prospects of specific companies.
principles.quote: We do not have, never have had, and never will have an opinion about where the stock market, interest rates, or business activity will be a year from now.

principles.text: Efficient market theory is wrong because the market is often, not always, efficient; superior returns come from facts and discipline.
principles.quote: Observing correctly that the market was frequently efficient, they went on to conclude incorrectly that it was always efficient. The difference between these propositions is night and day.

sources.title: Berkshire 1989 letter: Cigar butts vs wonderful businesses, float-backed risk taking, and a no-leverage temperament
sources.summary: Buffett's 1989 letter defines intrinsic value, explains why high growth rates fade as the base grows, and lays out the economics of deferred taxes and look-through earnings. His "Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years" covers cigar-butt investing, the institutional imperative, and refusing leverage. He also explains why Berkshire writes insurance only at profitable prices.

principles.text: Intrinsic value is all future cash flows discounted at prevailing interest rates, which makes all businesses economic equals.
principles.quote: With perfect foresight, this number can be calculated by taking all future cash flows of a business - in and out - and discounting them at prevailing interest rates.

principles.text: Buy a wonderful company at a fair price rather than a fair company at a wonderful price.
principles.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.

principles.text: Cigar-butt bargains disappoint because low business returns erode the initial discount; time favors great businesses.
principles.quote: Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.

principles.text: Avoid leverage: a small chance of ruin is not worth a large chance of extra returns.
principles.quote: A small chance of distress or disgrace cannot, in our view, be offset by a large chance of extra returns.

principles.text: Take rational risks others avoid, indifferent to reported quarterly results, when aligned with owners.
principles.quote: We are willing to look foolish as long as we don't feel we have acted foolishly.

principles.text: Only partner with people you like, trust and admire; bad people don't make good deals.
principles.quote: We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person.

sources.title: How Buffett measures float, look-through earnings and margin of safety: 1990 letter
sources.summary: Buffett's 1990 letter explains look-through earnings, judging insurance by cost of float, why falling stock prices help permanent buyers, why debt-funded junk bonds fail, and what kind of business Berkshire wants to buy. It also covers managers over industry economics and bank leverage.

principles.text: Accounting earnings are a starting point; what matters is who owns retained earnings and how they are used.
principles.quote: We care not whether the auditors hear a tree fall in the forest; we do care who owns the tree and what's next done with it.

principles.text: Judge insurers by underwriting loss relative to float: a low cost of funds means a good business.
principles.quote: A low cost of funds signifies a good business; a high cost translates into a poor business.

principles.text: If you will be a lifelong buyer, welcome falling prices; optimism is the buyer's enemy.
principles.quote: It's optimism that is the enemy of the rational buyer.

principles.text: Margin of safety is the core of investing, and heavy debt violates it because business roads have potholes.
principles.quote: The roads of business are riddled with potholes; a plan that requires dodging them all is a plan for disaster.

principles.text: Superior returns come from outstanding operating managers, not just good industries.
principles.quote: Our extraordinary returns flow from outstanding operating managers, not fortuitous industry economics.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones; volatility is fine if long-term results are superior.
principles.quote: Charlie and I always have preferred a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.

sources.title: Berkshire 1991 letter: franchises vs businesses, See's lessons, and why Buffett concentrates in great companies
sources.summary: Buffett explains how look-through earnings, franchise economics (See's, media), owner-style manager compensation and cheap float drive Berkshire's value. He also sets his acquisition criteria, defends a concentrated hold-forever portfolio, and confesses the $1.4B Fannie Mae omission error.

principles.text: Judge your portfolio by look-through earnings a decade out; think about businesses, not stock prices.
principles.quote: The goal of each investor should be to create a portfolio (in effect, a "company") that will deliver him or her the highest possible look-through earnings a decade or so from now.

principles.text: A true franchise has needed product, no close substitute and no price regulation, so it can price aggressively and tolerate poor management.
principles.quote: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation.

principles.text: A mere business earns exceptional profits only as low-cost operator or under tight supply, and can be killed by bad management.
principles.quote: In contrast, "a business" earns exceptional profits only if it is the low-cost operator or if supply of its product or service is tight.

principles.text: Small changes in growth assumptions can cut a valuation by more than half, so expectations matter enormously.
principles.quote: Thus a seemingly modest shift in assumptions reduces the property's valuation to 10 times after-tax earnings (or about 6 1/2 times pre-tax earnings).

principles.text: Profit growth must be judged against the incremental capital needed to produce it; See's grew hugely on tiny reinvestment.
principles.quote: For an increase in profits to be evaluated properly, it must be compared with the incremental capital investment required to produce it.

principles.text: Seek great, understandable businesses with able managers; avoid trading portions of far-from-great businesses.
principles.quote: Charlie and I are simply not smart enough, considering the large sums we work with, to get great results by adroitly buying and selling portions of far-from-great businesses.

sources.title: Berkshire 1992 letter: good businesses at fair prices, margin of safety, and the cost of float
sources.summary: Buffett's 1992 letter covers value versus growth, the Williams discounted-cash-flow equation, margin of safety, acquisition discipline, the cost of insurance float, super-cat underwriting, stock option accounting, and low corporate overhead. He also accepts volatility for long-term returns and rejects market forecasting.

principles.text: Buy good businesses at fair prices rather than fair businesses at good prices.
principles.quote: And thereafter I revised my strategy and tried to buy good businesses at fair prices rather than fair businesses at good prices.

principles.text: Value and growth are joined at the hip; investing means paying no more than calculated value.
principles.quote: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value, constituting a variable whose importance can range from negligible to enormous and whose impact can be negative as well as positive.

principles.text: Growth only helps when each dollar invested creates over a dollar of long-term market value.
principles.quote: Growth benefits investors only when the business in point can invest at incremental returns that are enticing - in other words, only when each dollar used to finance the growth creates over a dollar of long-term market value.

principles.text: Insist on a margin of safety, and stay within businesses simple enough to understand.
principles.quote: We believe this margin-of-safety principle, so strongly emphasized by Ben Graham, to be the cornerstone of investment success.

principles.text: Success in investing comes from realistically defining what you don't know and avoiding big mistakes.
principles.quote: What counts for most people in investing is not how much they know, but rather how realistically they define what they don't know. An investor needs to do very few things right as long as he or she avoids big mistakes.

principles.text: Insurance float is only worth having if its cost beats the government's long-term bond rate.
principles.quote: (If, on average, we didn't beat the Government's rate, there would be no economic reason for us to be in the business.)

sources.title: Berkshire 1993: Concentration, Real Risk, and Holding Wonderful Businesses
sources.summary: Buffett's 1993 letter argues risk is loss of purchasing power, not beta, and that concentrating in a few understandable, moat-protected businesses beats diversification. It also covers float economics, super-cat discipline, tax-deferred compounding, Dexter Shoe, and governance.

principles.text: Real risk is failing to preserve purchasing power after taxes and inflation, not stock volatility (beta).
principles.quote: the real risk that an investor must assess is whether his aggregate after-tax receipts from an investment (including those he receives on sale) will, over his prospective holding period, give him at least as much purchasing power as he had to begin with, plus a modest rate of interest on that initial stake.

principles.text: If you understand business economics, concentrate on your best few ideas; conventional diversification hurts results and adds risk.
principles.quote: if you are a know-something investor, able to understand business economics and to find five to ten sensibly-priced companies that possess important long-term competitive advantages, conventional diversification makes no sense for you.

principles.text: Volatility is an opportunity: a manic Mr. Market periodically prices solid businesses irrationally low.
principles.quote: The more manic-depressive this chap is, the greater the opportunities available to the investor.

principles.text: Hold a piece of an outstanding business with the tenacity of an owner of the whole business.
principles.quote: An investor should ordinarily hold a small piece of an outstanding business with the same tenacity that an owner would exhibit if he owned all of that business.

principles.text: Brands, products and distribution create a protective moat; commodity-like businesses have no such defense.
principles.quote: The might of their brand names, the attributes of their products, and the strength of their distribution systems give them an enormous competitive advantage, setting up a protective moat around their economic castles.

principles.text: Avoid fast-changing industries you cannot evaluate; stick to easy-to-understand cases.
principles.quote: Why search for a needle buried in a haystack when one is sitting in plain sight?

sources.title: Berkshire 1994 letter: intrinsic value, capital allocation, aligned pay and the USAir mistake
sources.summary: Buffett's 1994 letter explains intrinsic value vs book value using Scott Fetzer, warns against dilution-focused acquisitions, and lays out symmetric manager compensation. It also covers insurance float, pricing rather than timing purchases, ignoring forecasts, and owning up to the USAir error.

principles.text: Intrinsic value, not book value, is what counts: discounted cash that can be taken out of a business over its life.
principles.quote: We define intrinsic value as the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life.

principles.text: Ignore macro forecasts; fear of unknowns shouldn't delay buying good businesses at sensible prices.
principles.quote: Fear is the foe of the faddist, but the friend of the fundamentalist.

principles.text: Price purchases rather than time them; don't scrap an informed decision over uninformed guesses.
principles.quote: We try to price, rather than time, purchases. In our view, it is folly to forego buying shares in an outstanding business whose long-term future is predictable, because of short-term worries about an economy or a stock market that we know to be unpredictable.

principles.text: Judge acquisitions by per-share intrinsic value, not near-term EPS dilution; most deals enrich the target and the bankers, not the acquirer's owners.
principles.quote: That happens because the acquirer typically gives up more intrinsic value than it receives.

principles.text: Real alignment means sharing downside as well as upside; charge managers for capital and credit them for releasing it.
principles.quote: In our book, alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable only if its cost is below the market cost of money; accept lumpy results rather than smoothing earnings.
principles.quote: An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.

sources.title: How Buffett buys businesses: Berkshire's 1995 letter on GEICO, float, moats and acquisitions
sources.summary: Buffett explains why he distrusts most acquisitions yet loves buying great businesses with great managers, using Helzberg's, R.C. Willey and the full GEICO purchase. He also covers insurance float economics, retail versus have-to-be-smart-once businesses, and his own mistakes.

principles.text: Compare every acquisition against buying small pieces of the best public businesses; this discipline stops expansion-driven deals.
principles.quote: Our practice of making this comparison - acquisitions against passive investments - is a discipline that managers focused simply on expansion seldom use.

principles.text: Having no strategic plan is an advantage: you aren't forced toward silly purchase prices.
principles.quote: Even so, we do have a few advantages, perhaps the greatest being that we don't have a strategic plan.

principles.text: Ignore sellers' projections; sellers know more and choose the timing, when the business is walking fine.
principles.quote: In any case, why potential buyers even look at projections prepared by sellers baffles me. Charlie and I never give them a glance

principles.text: Look for economic castles protected by unbreachable moats; rock-bottom operating costs widened GEICO's.
principles.quote: In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable "moats."

principles.text: Float is only valuable if it costs less than the market price of money; low-cost float acts like equity.
principles.quote: An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.

principles.text: Accept lumpy but higher long-term returns instead of smooth ones, since most managers opt for smoothness.
principles.quote: In other words, we prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%.

sources.title: Berkshire 1996 letter: inevitables, float, incentives, and investing simply
sources.summary: Buffett's 1996 letter reviews 36.1% net worth growth and explains intrinsic value, float cost, super-cat insurance discipline, and incentive pay. It also sets out his investing philosophy: own "Inevitables" with durable moats, stay inactive, avoid change, and admit mistakes like USAir.

principles.text: Buy an easily understandable business with earnings virtually certain to be higher in 5, 10, 20 years, at a rational price.
principles.quote: Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten and twenty years from now.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; knowing its boundary matters more than its size.
principles.quote: The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.

principles.text: Prefer certainty in stable, dominant businesses over hope in fast-changing industries.
principles.quote: Obviously many companies in high-tech businesses or embryonic industries will grow much faster in percentage terms than will The Inevitables. But I would rather be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable only if its cost is below the market cost of money; underwriting profit makes it free.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is an albatross if the cost of its float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones, and hold only shareholders who can tolerate volatility.
principles.quote: Charlie and I would much rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%.

principles.text: Design incentive pay to be tailored, simple, and tied to what participants control; shun lottery-ticket options.
principles.quote: Goals should be (1) tailored to the economics of the specific operating business; (2) simple in character so that the degree to which they are being realized can be easily measured; and (3) directly related to the daily activities of plan participants.

sources.title: Berkshire 1997 letter: waiting for the fat pitch, float, and why cash beats stock in acquisitions
sources.summary: Buffett explains why Berkshire's 34.1% gain was merely a "quack" in a bull market, how size erodes returns, and why savers should welcome falling prices. He details insurance float economics, super-cat discipline, GEICO's low-cost model, and confesses that stock-funded mergers have cost shareholders money.

principles.text: Judge results against peers and the index, not against a rising tide; bull markets flatter everyone.
principles.quote: In a bull market, one must avoid the error of the preening duck that quacks boastfully after a torrential rainstorm, thinking that its paddling skills have caused it to rise in the world.

principles.text: Wait for the fat pitch: don't swing at mediocre opportunities just to be active.
principles.quote: waiting for the fat pitch would mean a trip to the Hall of Fame; swinging indiscriminately would mean a ticket to the minors.

principles.text: Size is the enemy of returns; high past performance came from being small, not smarter.
principles.quote: We weren't smarter then, just smaller. At our present size, any performance superiority we achieve will be minor.

principles.text: Net savers should want lower stock prices, since they are buyers of the 'hamburgers'.
principles.quote: Prospective purchasers should much prefer sinking prices.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if its cost is below the market cost of money; a negative cost means you are paid to hold it.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Paying cash rather than issuing stock protects owners when your existing businesses are better than what you'd buy.
principles.quote: Because our roster is filled with .380 hitters, we have tried to pay cash for acquisitions, and here our record has been far better.

sources.title: Berkshire 1998 letter: intrinsic value, float economics, owner-style management and honest accounting
sources.summary: Buffett's 1998 letter separates book value from intrinsic value, explains how to judge insurance float, and describes how Berkshire lets managers run businesses like owners. He also attacks stock-option expensing and restructuring-charge games, admits his McDonald's sale was a mistake, and warns that Berkshire's size will cap future returns.

principles.text: Per-share intrinsic value is what counts, not per-share book value, which stock issuance at a premium can inflate without real gain.
principles.quote: it’s the per-share gain in intrinsic value that counts rather than the per-share gain in book value.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both; float is only worth having if it costs less than market money.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most important of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Spend on growth whenever each dollar creates more than a dollar of value, regardless of short-term earnings optics.
principles.quote: We simply measure whether we are creating more than a dollar of value per dollar spent — and if that calculation is favorable, the more dollars we spend the happier I am.

principles.text: Give managers an owner's mission and tell them to ignore how decisions will be counted, focusing on what counts.
principles.quote: Just run your business as if: 1) you own 100% of it; 2) it is the only asset in the world that you and your family have or will ever have; and 3) you can’t sell or merge it for at least a century.

principles.text: Stock options are a real expense; Buffett subtracts their cost from reported earnings when valuing investments and acquisitions.
principles.quote: When we consider investing in an option-issuing company, we make an appropriate downward adjustment to reported earnings, simply subtracting an amount equal to what the company could have realized by publicly selling options of like quantity and structure.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones; tolerating volatility is a structural advantage with strong capital.
principles.quote: As we’ve long said, we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.

sources.title: Berkshire 1999 letter: a "D" year, float economics, and why buybacks only work below intrinsic value
sources.summary: Buffett owns a poor 1999 as the worst year of his tenure, then teaches how to value insurance float, why managers run Berkshire companies like family assets, how to think about goodwill and acquisitions, circle of competence on tech, and strict rules for share repurchases.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float volume, its cost, and above all the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is worth having only if its cost is below what you would pay for money elsewhere.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; don't pretend to predict fast-changing industries.
principles.quote: If we have a strength, it is in recognizing when we are operating well within our circle of competence and when we are approaching the perimeter.

principles.text: Repurchase shares only with spare funds and when the stock trades below conservatively calculated intrinsic value.
principles.quote: There is only one combination of facts that makes it advisable for a company to repurchase its shares: First, the company has available funds — cash plus sensible borrowing capacity — beyond the near-term needs of the business and, second, finds its stock selling in the market below its intrinsic value, conservatively-calculated.

principles.text: Overpaying to buy back stock hurts the shareholders who stay.
principles.quote: But the continuing shareholder is penalized by repurchases above intrinsic value. Buying dollar bills for $1.10 is not good business for those who stick around.

principles.text: Give managers autonomy and ask them to run the business as their family's only asset for a century.
principles.quote: We simply ask our managers to run their companies as if these are the sole asset of their families and will remain so for the next century.

sources.title: Berkshire 2000 letter: buying whole businesses, float economics, Aesop's value formula, and bubble-era speculation
sources.summary: Buffett's 2000 letter explains why Berkshire prefers buying whole businesses to stocks, how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, and outlook), and the single value formula behind all investing. He also criticizes bubble speculation, earnings guidance, and corporate refusal to review failed decisions, while owning up to mistakes at GEICO and Dexter.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float generated, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both; float is only valuable if it costs less than other money.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: All assets bought for financial gain are valued by Aesop's formula: certainty, timing and amount of future cash, discounted at the risk-free rate.
principles.quote: How certain are you that there are indeed birds in the bush? When will they emerge and how many will there be? What is the risk-free interest rate

principles.text: Growth and value are not opposing styles; growth is just a component of value and can destroy it if it needs more cash than it returns.
principles.quote: Growth is simply a component  usually a plus, sometimes a minus  in the value equation.

principles.text: Speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest; easy money sedates rationality and bubbles transfer wealth rather than create value.
principles.quote: Nothing sedates rationality like large doses of effortless money.

principles.text: Prefer sellers who love their business and care who buys it; that attachment signals honest accounting, pride of product and loyal people.
principles.quote: We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him

principles.text: Acknowledge and analyze mistakes candidly; boardrooms rarely do post-mortems and instead bury blunders in 'nonrecurring' charges.
principles.quote: Agonizing over errors is a mistake. But acknowledging and analyzing them can be useful, though that practice is rare in corporate boardrooms.

sources.title: Berkshire 2001: Float economics, the three underwriting rules, and owning mistakes at General Re and Dexter
sources.summary: Buffett's 2001 letter covers a bad year: 9/11 losses and General Re's underreserving. It explains how to value an insurer by float, its cost and underwriting discipline, and gives candid mea culpas. It also covers owner-aligned management, buying from trusted managers, and his contempt for EBITDA and options.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by the amount of float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if its cost is below what you would pay to get funds elsewhere.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Insurance winners stick to underwriting discipline: stay in your circle of competence, cap aggregation, avoid moral risk.
principles.quote: What counts in this business is underwriting discipline. The winners are those that unfailingly stick to three key principles

principles.text: Predicting a danger is worthless unless you act on it; take action, not just forecasts.
principles.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn’t count; building arks does.

principles.text: Outstanding long-term results come mainly from avoiding dumb decisions, not from brilliant ones.
principles.quote: Just as is the case in investing, insurers produce outstanding long-term results primarily by avoiding dumb decisions, rather than by making brilliant ones.

principles.text: Align managers as true owners who bear downside and a cost of capital, not option holders who can reprice.
principles.quote: As they would not be if they had options, all of these managers are true owners. They face the downside of decisions as well as the upside. They incur a cost of capital.

sources.title: Berkshire 2002 letter: float, derivatives as time bombs, and governance reform
