sources.summary: Buffett reviews 2002: how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, durability), General Re's reserving and underwriting failures, why he calls derivatives "financial weapons of mass destruction," and why boards, audit committees and CEO pay were broken. Also covers buying to keep, hiring great managers, and refusing to buy stocks at poor prices.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if it costs less than other funds; otherwise the insurer is a lemon.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Insurers must underwrite with discipline, reserve conservatively, and avoid dangerous aggregation of risk.
principles.quote: they must: (a) underwrite with unwavering discipline; (b) reserve conservatively; and (c) avoid an aggregation of exposures that would allow a supposedly “impossible” incident to threaten their solvency.

principles.text: Accept lumpy returns if paid appropriately; prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%.
principles.quote: As long as we are paid appropriately, we love taking on short-term volatility that others wish to shed. At Berkshire, we would rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%.

principles.text: Buy good-to-great businesses run by great managers at a sensible price, and buy to keep rather than plan an exit.
principles.quote: Those attributes are two legs of our “entrance” strategy, the third being a sensible purchase price. Unlike LBO operators and private equity firms, we have no “exit” strategy – we buy to keep.

principles.text: Sit out when stocks aren't priced to offer high expected returns; inactivity can be part of good investing.
principles.quote: Unless, however, we see a very high probability of at least 10% pre-tax returns (which translate to 6½-7% after corporate tax), we will sit on the sidelines.

sources.title: Berkshire 2003 letter: owner-capitalism boards, float economics, and buying Clayton and McLane on trust
sources.summary: Buffett's 2003 letter explains how Berkshire judges itself against the S&P, why it prefers whole businesses when stocks are pricey, and how it buys companies on character and trust. It also covers director independence through real ownership, insurance float, avoiding derivatives, and owning up to mistakes.

principles.text: Judge performance by per-share intrinsic value gains versus the S&P; otherwise you add nothing an index fund doesn't.
principles.quote: Unless we achieve gains in per-share intrinsic value in the future that outdo the S&P’s performance, Charlie and I will be adding nothing to what you can accomplish on your own.

principles.text: Buy businesses with enduring economics, talented and honest managers, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: (1) have favorable and enduring economic charac-teristics; (2) are run by talented and honest managers and (3) are available at a sensible price.

principles.text: Idle capital is painful, but far better than doing something stupid.
principles.quote: Our capital is underutilized now, but that will happen periodically. It’s a painful condition to be in – but not as painful as doing something stupid.

principles.text: True director independence comes from real ownership: directors should win and lose big alongside shareholders.
principles.quote: You win, they win big; you lose, they lose big. Our approach might be called owner-capitalism.

principles.text: In insurance, a copyable product means managerial brains, discipline and integrity are the moat; float is only good if cheap.
principles.quote: The critical variables, therefore, are managerial brains, discipline and integrity.

principles.text: Never reach for yield by loosening credit standards or extending maturities; take risk only when paid for it.
principles.quote: Charlie and I detest taking even small risks unless we feel we are being adequately compensated for doing so.

sources.title: Berkshire 2004 letter: float, disciplined underwriting, and fractional ownership of businesses
sources.summary: Buffett's 2004 letter covers 21.9% compounded book value growth, how NICO and GEICO turn commodity insurance into float that can cost less than nothing, why he treats stocks as business ownership, and how director fees and unexpensed options distort incentives. He also admits mistakes and warns on the trade deficit.

principles.text: Judge long-term results against a low-cost index fund; otherwise management adds nothing.
principles.quote: Our shareholders can buy the S&P through an index fund at very low cost. Unless we achieve gains in per-share intrinsic value in the future that outdo the S&P, Charlie and I will be adding nothing to what you can accomplish on your own.

principles.text: Float is wonderful only if it doesn't come at a high price; underwriting profit makes it better than free.
principles.quote: Float is wonderful – if it doesn't come at a high price. Its cost is determined by underwriting results, meaning how the expenses and losses we will ultimately pay compare with the premiums we have received.

principles.text: In a commodity business, price for profit and accept shrinking volume rather than match the most optimistic competitor.
principles.quote: But we instead consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor. We never left customers – but they left us.

principles.text: Prefer simple propositions: many independent variables each likely to work still make success unlikely.
principles.quote: But if ten independent variables need to break favorably for a successful result, and each has a 90% probability of success, the likelihood of having a winner is only 35%.

principles.text: View stocks as fractional ownership of businesses, not tickers to trade on charts, brokers' opinions or near-term earnings.
principles.quote: Charlie and I ignore such distractions and instead view our holdings as fractional ownerships in businesses.

principles.text: Directors dependent on board fees are the least independent; where your treasure is, your heart is.
principles.quote: In our view, based on our considerable boardroom experience, the least independent directors are likely to be those who receive an important fraction of their annual income from the fees they receive for board service

sources.title: Berkshire 2005 letter: float, moats, the Gotrocks, and CEO option math
sources.summary: Buffett's 2005 letter covers insurance float, why acquisitions for stock cost shareholders, widening the moat over short-term earnings, and the cost of derivatives and delay. It also exposes how fixed-price options reward CEOs for retained earnings and explains how Wall Street "Helpers" shrink investor returns.

principles.text: Float is wonderful only if it doesn't come at a high price; its cost is set by underwriting results.
principles.quote: Float is wonderful – if it doesn’t come at a high price. Its cost is determined by underwriting results, meaning how the expenses and losses we will ultimately pay compare with the premiums we have received.

principles.text: Issuing stock for acquisitions means the acquirer's owners sell part of everything they own.
principles.quote: When a management proudly acquires another company for stock, the shareholders of the acquirer are concurrently selling part of their interest in everything they own.

principles.text: Widen the moat: when short-term and long-term conflict, long-term competitive position takes precedence.
principles.quote: We always, of course, hope to earn more money in the short-term. But when short-term and long-term conflict, widening the moat must take precedence.

principles.text: Act immediately on problems in personnel or operations; delay is costly.
principles.quote: When a problem exists, whether in personnel or in business operations, the time to act is now.

principles.text: Owners in aggregate can only earn what their businesses earn; frictional costs of Helpers reduce returns.
principles.quote: For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.

principles.text: Avoid significant debt: a string of great numbers multiplied by a single zero is zero.
principles.quote: a long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero.

sources.title: Berkshire 2006 letter: Buffett on float, incentives, temperament, newspapers and the 2-and-20 folly
sources.summary: Buffett's 2006 letter covers insurance float and disciplined super-cat pricing, buying businesses from owners who want a permanent home, simple performance-tied CEO pay, the decline of newspapers, truly independent directors, and the cost of Wall Street fees. It also describes the temperament he wants in a successor investor.

principles.text: Float is money you hold but don't own; its cost over time should be below industry norms, even zero or less, though bad years will come.
principles.quote: Simply put, float is money we hold that is not ours but which we get to invest.

principles.text: Only take insurance risk when paid appropriately; underpriced risk guarantees eventual losses, even if any single year looks fine.
principles.quote: Appropriate prices don’t guarantee profits in any given year, but inappropriate prices most certainly guarantee eventual losses.

principles.text: Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful, in insurance pricing as in markets.
principles.quote: Our behavior here parallels that which we employ in financial markets: Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.

principles.text: Great managers matter, but a business with eroding fundamentals eventually overwhelms even brilliant management; pick good businesses.
principles.quote: When an industry’s underlying economics are crumbling, talented management may slow the rate of decline. Eventually, though, eroding fundamentals will overwhelm managerial brilliance.

principles.text: Tie CEO incentives to results the CEO controls, not to unrelated Berkshire-wide outcomes or market swings.
principles.quote: We issue no lottery tickets that carry payoffs unrelated to business performance.

principles.text: A top investor needs temperament and risk sense, not just brains or a recent record: independent thinking, emotional stability, understanding of behavior.
principles.quote: Independent thinking, emotional stability, and a keen understanding of both human and institutional behavior is vital to long-term investment success.

sources.title: Berkshire 2007 letter: great, good and gruesome businesses, See's Candy economics, and Buffett's mistakes
sources.summary: Buffett explains what makes a great business (an enduring moat, low capital needs, not dependent on a superstar manager), contrasting See's Candy, FlightSafety and airlines. He owns up to unforced errors (Dexter, a TV station, US Air), shows why active management must trail index funds, and criticizes corporate accounting games.

principles.text: Seek businesses with an enduring moat protecting high returns on capital; a moat that must be rebuilt constantly is no moat.
principles.quote: A truly great business must have an enduring “moat” that protects excellent returns on invested capital.

principles.text: A business that needs a superstar manager to produce great results is not itself a great business.
principles.quote: But if a business requires a superstar to produce great results, the business itself cannot be deemed great.

principles.text: The worst business grows fast, needs heavy capital, and earns little; the best grows earnings with almost no new capital.
principles.quote: The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money.

principles.text: Redeploy a great business's surplus cash into other businesses rather than reinvesting where it was earned.
principles.quote: There’s no rule that you have to invest money where you’ve earned it.

principles.text: Active investors as a class must trail passive ones because of costs; beware advisers promising double-digit equity returns.
principles.quote: That means that the passive group – the “know-nothings” – must win.

principles.text: Prefer a partial stake in a great business over owning all of a mediocre one.
principles.quote: It’s better to have a part interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

sources.title: Berkshire 2008 letter: buying in fear, float, derivatives, and admitting mistakes
sources.summary: Buffett's 2008 letter covers Berkshire's four goals, insurance float that cost less than zero, and buying when pessimism reigns. He owns up to his own errors (ConocoPhillips, Irish banks), warns against derivatives, history-based models and Black-Scholes at long durations, and says he won't trade sleep for extra profit.

principles.text: When investing, pessimism is your friend and euphoria the enemy; buy quality when it is marked down.
principles.quote: When investing, pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable when underwriting is profitable, because the money is held and invested at negative cost.
principles.quote: This means that our $58.5 billion of insurance “float” – money that doesn’t belong to us but that we hold and invest for our own benefit – cost us less than zero.

principles.text: Keep ample liquidity; never risk sleep or survival for extra profit or rely on others' kindness.
principles.quote: We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow’s obligations. When forced to choose, I will not trade even a night’s sleep for the chance of extra profits.

principles.text: Be the buyer of choice by deserving it: keep promises, avoid leverage, give managers autonomy, hold through thick and thin.
principles.quote: That means we must keep our promises; avoid leveraging up acquired businesses; grant unusual autonomy to our managers; and hold the purchased companies through thick and thin (though we prefer thick and thicker).

principles.text: Be skeptical of history-based models; their assumptions can fail when current conditions differ from the past.
principles.quote: Investors should be skeptical of history-based models.

principles.text: Approval is not the goal of investing; applause can sedate the brain and block re-examining conclusions.
principles.quote: Approval, though, is not the goal of investing. In fact, approval is often counter-productive because it sedates the brain and makes it less receptive to new facts or a re-examination of conclusions formed earlier.

sources.title: Berkshire 2009 letter: float, inverted thinking, stock deals, and buying in a panic
sources.summary: Buffett restates how Berkshire measures itself, what it avoids (unknowable industries, dependence on outsiders, bureaucracy), how insurance float works, and why issuing undervalued stock is costly. He admits the GEICO credit card and NetJets blunders and urges buying big when fear is high.

principles.text: Avoid businesses whose long-term economics you can't evaluate, however exciting the growth.
principles.quote: Just because Charlie and I can clearly see dramatic growth ahead for an industry does not mean we can judge what its profit margins and returns on capital will be as a host of competitors battle for supremacy.

principles.text: Never depend on outsiders; hold liquidity that dwarfs any cash need, even at a steep cost.
principles.quote: We will never become dependent on the kindness of strangers.

principles.text: Insurance float is free money if you underwrite profitably; the industry usually pays to hold it.
principles.quote: If we do so, our float will be cost-free, much as if someone deposited $62 billion with us that we could invest for our own benefit without the payment of interest.

principles.text: Issuing undervalued stock to buy a business destroys value for your own shareholders.
principles.quote: You simply can't exchange an undervalued stock for a fully-valued one without hurting your shareholders.

principles.text: Fear is an investor's friend; when opportunities are huge, act big.
principles.quote: When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.

principles.text: Focus on what you pay for a business and what it earns over the next decade or two.
principles.quote: In the end, what counts in investing is what you pay for a business – through the purchase of a small piece of it in the stock market – and what that business earns in the succeeding decade or two.

sources.title: Berkshire 2010 letter: BNSF, intrinsic value, GEICO goodwill, float, culture, and leverage
sources.summary: Buffett's 2010 letter explains how to judge intrinsic value (investments, operating earnings, and how retained earnings get deployed), why capital-allocation flexibility and an owner-minded culture are Berkshire's edge, and how GEICO's goodwill far exceeds book value. It also covers insurance discipline and float, ignoring net income, and avoiding leverage.

principles.text: Set performance goals up front; otherwise management paints the bull's-eye around wherever the arrow lands.
principles.quote: Lacking such standards, managements are tempted to shoot the arrow of performance and then paint the bull’s-eye around wherever it lands.

principles.text: Value a company on what it has now plus what management will do with retained earnings.
principles.quote: This “what-will-they-do-with-the-money” factor must always be evaluated along with the “what-do-we-have-now” calculation in order for us, or anybody, to arrive at a sensible estimate of a company’s intrinsic value.

principles.text: Insurance discipline includes the willingness to walk away when the right premium can't be obtained.
principles.quote: The willingness to walk away if the appropriate premium can’t be obtained.

principles.text: Flexibility across industries and securities is a capital-allocation edge; when businesses are overpriced, buy securities and wait.
principles.quote: Often, businesses are priced ridiculously high against what can likely be earned from investments in stocks or bonds. At such moments, we buy securities and bide our time.

principles.text: Prefer being approximately right to being precisely wrong; students should learn to value businesses.
principles.quote: We would rather be approximately right than precisely wrong.

principles.text: Avoid leverage and hold ample liquidity so you can play offense when others scramble for survival.
principles.quote: The fundamental principle of auto racing is that to finish first, you must first finish.

sources.title: Berkshire 2011 letter: float, buybacks, intrinsic value, and why productive assets beat gold and bonds
sources.summary: Buffett's 2011 letter covers insurance float, price-disciplined share repurchases, intrinsic value, admitted mistakes (Energy Future Holdings, the housing call), succession, and a framework ranking currency, gold, and productive assets as investments. He argues low stock prices help net buyers and that fluctuation is not risk.

principles.text: Buy back stock only with ample funds and only when shares trade at a material discount to conservatively calculated intrinsic value.
principles.quote: Charlie and I favor repurchases when two conditions are met: first, a company has ample funds to take care of the operational and liquidity needs of its business; second, its stock is selling at a material discount to the company’s intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated.

principles.text: The first law of capital allocation: what is smart at one price is dumb at another.
principles.quote: The first law of capital allocation – whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases – is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another.

principles.text: If you are a net buyer of stocks, you benefit when prices fall; low prices are your friend.
principles.quote: If you are going to be a net buyer of stocks in the future, either directly with your own money or indirectly (through your ownership of a company that is repurchasing shares), you are hurt when stocks rise. You benefit when stocks swoon.

principles.text: Risk is the probability of losing purchasing power over your holding period, not volatility or beta.
principles.quote: The riskiness of an investment is not measured by beta (a Wall Street term encompassing volatility and often used in measuring risk) but rather by the probability – the reasoned probability – of that investment causing its owner a loss of purchasing-power over his contemplated holding period.

principles.text: Productive assets (businesses, farms, real estate) beat currency-based and non-productive assets like gold over the long run.
principles.quote: My own preference – and you knew this was coming – is our third category: investment in productive assets, whether businesses, farms, or real estate.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable when underwriting is disciplined, including a willingness to walk away from underpriced business.
principles.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. They simply can’t turn their back on business that their competitors are eagerly writing.

sources.title: Berkshire 2012 letter: float, buybacks, dividends vs sell-off, and staying in the game
sources.summary: Buffett reviews 2012 and explains why Berkshire measures itself on intrinsic value against the S&P. He covers insurance float as a revolving fund, price discipline in buybacks, why a sell-off policy beats dividends, and why timing the market is a mistake. He also admits capital-allocation errors.

principles.text: Judge management by growth in intrinsic value versus the S&P; otherwise investors should just buy a low-cost index fund.
principles.quote: It’s our job to increase intrinsic business value – for which we use book value as a significantly understated proxy – at a faster rate than the market gains of the S&P.

principles.text: Don't dance in and out of stocks on forecasts; the risks of being out of the game exceed the risks of being in it.
principles.quote: Charlie and I believe it’s a terrible mistake to try to dance in and out of it based upon the turn of tarot cards, the predictions of “experts,” or the ebb and flow of business activity.

principles.text: Good insurance requires walking away when the right premium can't be had; copying competitors' pricing spells trouble.
principles.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. They simply can’t turn their back on business that is being eagerly written by their competitors.

principles.text: Float is a revolving fund; if it is costless and long-enduring, its true liability value is far below the accounting figure.
principles.quote: If float is both costless and long-enduring, which I believe Berkshire’s will be, the true value of this liability is dramatically less than the accounting liability.

principles.text: Repurchase only when shares trade at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value; paying above it destroys value.
principles.quote: But never forget: In repurchase decisions, price is all-important. Value is destroyed when purchases are made above intrinsic value.

principles.text: Prefer a wonderful business at a fair price to a fair business at a wonderful price; bargain-hunting habits cause mistakes.
principles.quote: More than 50 years ago, Charlie told me that it was far better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than to buy a fair business at a wonderful price.

sources.title: Berkshire 2013 letter: Invest like you own a farm, ignore the macro chatter
sources.summary: Buffett's 2013 letter explains float, GEICO's cost-advantage moat, and Berkshire's flexible capital allocation. Its centerpiece is a lesson on investing: buy productive assets using future earnings, ignore market noise and price swings, and use a low-cost index fund if you are not an expert.

principles.text: Judge an asset by its future productivity, not by expected price changes; the latter is speculation.
principles.quote: Focus on the future productivity of the asset you are considering. If you don’t feel comfortable making a rough estimate of the asset’s future earnings, just forget it and move on.

principles.text: Focus on what the asset produces, not on daily price quotes.
principles.quote: Games are won by players who focus on the playing field – not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard. If you can enjoy Saturdays and Sundays without looking at stock prices, give it a try on weekdays.

principles.text: Macro opinions and market predictions are a waste of time and can blur the facts that matter.
principles.quote: Forming macro opinions or listening to the macro or market predictions of others is a waste of time. Indeed, it is dangerous because it may blur your vision of the facts that are truly important.

principles.text: Fear is an opportunity for investors with cash; euphoria is the enemy.
principles.quote: A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy.

principles.text: Non-experts should own a low-cost S&P 500 index fund rather than try to pick winners.
principles.quote: The goal of the non-professional should not be to pick winners – neither he nor his “helpers” can do that – but should rather be to own a cross-section of businesses that in aggregate are bound to do well. A low-cost S&P 500 index fund will achieve this goal.

principles.text: A low-cost operation creates an enduring moat, as GEICO shows.
principles.quote: GEICO’s cost advantage is the factor that has enabled the company to gobble up market share year after year. Its low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.

sources.title: Berkshire 2014 letter: wonderful businesses, float, conglomerate capital allocation, and volatility vs risk
sources.summary: Buffett's 50th-anniversary letter covers Berkshire's origins in a failed textile business, Munger's shift from cigar butts to wonderful businesses, insurance float economics, why the conglomerate form allocates capital efficiently, stock-acquisition discipline, a fortress balance sheet, and why diversified stocks beat dollar assets over decades.

principles.text: Buy wonderful businesses at fair prices, not fair businesses at wonderful prices; cigar-butt investing doesn't scale.
principles.quote: Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices.

principles.text: Volatility is not risk; for long-horizon investors, dollar-based assets are riskier than diversified stocks.
principles.quote: Volatility is far from synonymous with risk. Popular formulas that equate the two terms lead students, investors and CEOs astray.

principles.text: Float is a revolving fund, not just a liability, but its benefits can be drowned by poor underwriting.
principles.quote: But to think of float as strictly a liability is incorrect; it should instead be viewed as a revolving fund.

principles.text: Never issue shares in an acquisition worth more than the business received.
principles.quote: The intrinsic value of the shares you give in an acquisition must not be greater than the intrinsic value of the business you receive.

principles.text: Never risk what you need to chase what you want; keep ample real cash and avoid sudden-demand obligations.
principles.quote: In our view, it is madness to risk losing what you need in pursuing what you simply desire.

principles.text: A conglomerate can reallocate capital without taxes or friction, and can buy stock pieces of wonderful companies as an option.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, we can – without incurring taxes or much in the way of other costs – move huge sums from businesses that have limited opportunities for incremental investment to other sectors with greater promise.

sources.title: Berkshire 2015: float as a revolving fund, owning part of great businesses, and never betting against America
sources.summary: Buffett's 2015 letter explains why Berkshire's intrinsic value outruns book value, how insurance float and underwriting discipline create value, and why a partial stake in a wonderful company beats owning all of a mediocre one. It also covers honest accounting (stock comp, EBITDA, amortization), productivity and the long-run case for America.

principles.text: Under GAAP, winners are never written up, so intrinsic value diverges from book value; buy back shares at a discount to intrinsic value.
principles.quote: That’s why we would be delighted to repurchase our shares should they sell as low as 120% of book value. At that level, purchases would instantly and meaningfully increase per-share intrinsic value for Berkshire’s continuing shareholders.

principles.text: Prefer a partial stake in a wonderful business over full ownership of a so-so one.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, we much prefer owning a non-controlling but substantial portion of a wonderful company to owning 100% of a so-so business. It’s better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

principles.text: Float is a revolving fund, not strictly a liability; if costless and long-enduring it is worth far more than its accounting treatment.
principles.quote: But to think of float as strictly a liability is incorrect. It should instead be viewed as a revolving fund.

principles.text: Sound insurance requires willingness to walk away when the right premium can't be had; copying competitors is the classic failure.
principles.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. They simply can’t turn their back on business that is being eagerly written by their competitors.

principles.text: A durable low-cost advantage is a moat that competitors cannot cross, letting a company take share year after year.
principles.quote: The company’s low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.

principles.text: Stock-based compensation is a real expense; ignoring it, or leaning on EBITDA, misleads investors.
principles.quote: “Stock-based compensation” is the most egregious example. The very name says it all: “compensation.” If compensation isn’t an expense, what is it?

sources.title: Berkshire 2016 letter: float, repurchases, adjusted earnings, and the hedge-fund bet
sources.summary: Buffett explains why book value understates Berkshire's intrinsic value, how to judge buybacks by price versus value, how insurance float works, why "adjusted earnings" mislead, and why low-cost index funds beat high-fee managers. He also owns up to his Dexter Shoe and General Re mistakes.

principles.text: Buybacks only help continuing shareholders when shares are bought below intrinsic value; the result depends entirely on the price paid.
principles.quote: the question of whether a repurchase action is value-enhancing or value-destroying for continuing shareholders is entirely purchase-price dependent.

principles.text: Float is best seen as a revolving fund, not a typical liability; if it is costless and long-enduring, its true cost is far below its accounting liability.
principles.quote: But to think of float as a typical liability is a major mistake. It should instead be viewed as a revolving fund.

principles.text: A sound insurer needs four disciplines, the last being willingness to walk away when the right premium isn't available.
principles.quote: (4) be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can’t be obtained.

principles.text: Widespread fear is the investor's friend because it creates bargains; personal fear is the enemy and unwarranted.
principles.quote: First, widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases. Second, personal fear is your enemy.

principles.text: Active investors in aggregate must trail passive ones after costs, so most investors should hold low-cost index funds.
principles.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

principles.text: Treating stock-based compensation or recurring restructuring as non-costs is misleading, and chasing 'adjusted earnings' breeds a bad culture.
principles.quote: bad behavior is contagious: CEOs who overtly look for ways to report high numbers tend to foster a culture in which subordinates strive to be “helpful” as well.

sources.title: Berkshire 2017 letter: the Protégé bet, float, leverage aversion, and acquisition discipline
sources.summary: Buffett reviews 2017, warning about distorting GAAP rules and frenzied acquisition pricing, explaining insurance float and mega-cat preparedness, and settling his ten-year S&P 500 index fund bet against hedge funds. Core lessons: avoid leverage, ignore short-term price noise, favor big easy decisions, and bonds can be riskier than stocks over long horizons.

principles.text: Never risk what you have and need to obtain what you don't need; avoiding leverage lets you sleep well.
principles.quote: Both of us believe it is insane to risk what you have and need in order to obtain what you don’t need.

principles.text: Evaluate acquisitions on an all-equity basis and ignore forecast synergies; cheap debt and CEO enthusiasm inflate deal prices.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, in contrast, we evaluate acquisitions on an all-equity basis

principles.text: Seek durable competitive strengths, able management, good returns on tangible assets, growth, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: the key qualities we seek are durable competitive strengths; able and high-grade management; good returns on the net tangible assets required to operate the business

principles.text: Insurance float is money held for others that Berkshire invests; underwriting discipline can make its cost negative, but it carries oceans of risk.
principles.quote: The downside of float is that it comes with risk, sometimes oceans of risk.

principles.text: Never depend on the kindness of strangers; hold ample liquidity like Treasury Bills to withstand crises.
principles.quote: Charlie and I never will operate Berkshire in a manner that depends on the kindness of strangers

principles.text: Treat stocks as business interests; short-term prices are a voting machine, long-term a weighing machine.
principles.quote: “In the short run, the market is a voting machine; in the long run, however, it becomes a weighing machine.”

sources.title: Berkshire 2018 letter: five groves, float, buybacks, and the American Tailwind
sources.summary: Buffett explains how to value Berkshire as a forest of five asset groves rather than trees, why GAAP mark-to-market and book value mislead, how float and retained earnings fund growth, and why disciplined buybacks, minimal debt and a cash fortress matter. He closes with faith in American business.

principles.text: Ignore GAAP gains and losses on holdings; focus on operating earnings.
principles.quote: Our advice? Focus on operating earnings, paying little attention to gains or losses of any variety.

principles.text: Buy ably-managed businesses with durable economics at sensible prices, whole or in part.
principles.quote: our prime goal in the deployment of your capital: to buy ably-managed businesses, in whole or part, that possess favorable and durable economic characteristics. We also need to make these purchases at sensible prices.

principles.text: Repurchases only make sense below intrinsic value; blind buying of an overpriced stock destroys value.
principles.quote: Obviously, repurchases should be price-sensitive: Blindly buying an overpriced stock is value-destructive, a fact lost on many promotional or ever-optimistic CEOs.

principles.text: Don't risk what you have and need for what you don't have and don't need; use debt sparingly and keep a cash buffer.
principles.quote: Rational people don't risk what they have and need for what they don't have and don't need.

principles.text: Float is valuable only with disciplined underwriting; poor underwriting can drown its benefits.
principles.quote: Disciplined risk evaluation is the daily focus of our insurance managers, who know that the benefits of float can be drowned by poor underwriting results.

principles.text: Never play with numbers to meet Wall Street expectations; small fudges can lead to fraud.
principles.quote: Playing with the numbers "just this once" may well be the CEO's intent; it's seldom the end result.

sources.title: Buffett's 2019 letter: retained earnings, buying good businesses, float, and boards
sources.summary: Buffett explains why GAAP's unrealized-gain rule distorts results and urges focus on operating earnings. He champions retained earnings and compounding, acquisition criteria, insurance float and underwriting discipline, buybacks only below intrinsic value, and critiques board independence and deal-hungry CEOs.

principles.text: Focus on operating earnings and ignore short-term investment gains or losses, realized or unrealized.
principles.quote: Charlie and I urge you to focus on operating earnings – which were little changed in 2019 – and to ignore both quarterly and annual gains or losses from investments, whether these are realized or unrealized.

principles.text: Retained earnings compounding inside good businesses drive long-term value, even when not reported as earnings.
principles.quote: Overall, the retained earnings of our investees are certain to be of major importance in the growth of Berkshire’s value.

principles.text: Buy businesses with good returns on tangible capital, able and honest managers, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: First, they must earn good returns on the net tangible capital required in their operation. Second, they must be run by able and honest managers. Finally, they must be available at a sensible price.

principles.text: Acquisitions are like marriage: buyers are usually the ones surprised, so buy good businesses to begin with.
principles.quote: To achieve a reputation as a good manager, just be sure you buy good businesses.

principles.text: Float is valuable only if underwriting is disciplined; danger always lurks in insurance.
principles.quote: Disciplined risk evaluation is the daily focus of our insurance managers, who know that the rewards of float can be drowned by poor underwriting results.

principles.text: Repurchase stock only when below intrinsic value and ample cash remains; don't prop the price.
principles.quote: Berkshire will buy back its stock only if a) Charlie and I believe that it is selling for less than it is worth and b) the company, upon completing the repurchase, is left with ample cash.

sources.title: How Buffett owns businesses: 2020 letter on the PCC mistake, repurchases, float and partnership
sources.summary: Buffett's 2020 letter owns up to overpaying for Precision Castparts, explains why non-controlling stakes in great businesses beat controlling marginal ones, and shows how disciplined buybacks and retained earnings compound value. It also covers float, ultra-low bond yields, and treating shareholders as partners.

principles.text: Own businesses by durable strengths, management and price; control is unimportant.
principles.quote: owning a non-controlling portion of a wonderful business is more profitable, more enjoyable and far less work than struggling with 100% of a marginal enterprise.

principles.text: Treat marketable stock holdings as businesses; unrecorded retained earnings build real value.
principles.quote: What’s out of sight, however, should not be out of mind: Those unrecorded retained earnings are usually building value – lots of value – for Berkshire.

principles.text: Admit mistakes plainly: he overpaid for PCC by misjudging future normalized earnings.
principles.quote: I was wrong, however, in judging the average amount of future earnings and, consequently, wrong in my calculation of the proper price to pay for the business.

principles.text: Repurchase only below intrinsic value; most CEOs buy back more when prices are high.
principles.quote: American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Our approach is exactly the reverse.

principles.text: Conglomerates fail by using overvalued stock to pay control premiums for mediocre businesses.
principles.quote: Most of the truly great businesses had no interest in having anyone take them over.

principles.text: Equity investing is positive-sum; patience, diversification and low fees win, and investor expenses are Wall Street's income.
principles.quote: All that’s required is the passage of time, an inner calm, ample diversification and a minimization of transactions and fees.

sources.title: Berkshire 2021 letter: business-pickers, float, buybacks and patience with cash
sources.summary: Buffett's 2021 letter explains that Berkshire picks businesses with durable advantages and first-class CEOs rather than stocks, values insurance float as a sticky source of investable money, and buys back shares only when price is right. It also covers holding huge cash until opportunities meet criteria, and why owners like Paul Andrews choose Berkshire as a permanent home.

principles.text: Buy businesses with durable advantages and first-class CEOs for long-term performance, not timely market moves.
principles.quote: our goal is to have meaningful investments in businesses with both durable economic advantages and a first-class CEO.

principles.text: Think of yourself as a business-picker, not a stock-picker.
principles.quote: Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable when it costs less than nothing and is sticky enough to invest for the long term.
principles.quote: Of equal importance, float is very sticky. Funds attributable to our insurance operations come and go daily, but their aggregate total is immune from precipitous decline.

principles.text: Repurchases only make sense when the price/value equation is right; overpaying for your own shares destroys value.
principles.quote: I want to underscore that for Berkshire repurchases to make sense, our shares must offer appropriate value.

principles.text: Low long-term interest rates push up prices of all productive assets, so valuations depend heavily on rates.
principles.quote: Long-term interest rates that are low push the prices of all productive investments upward, whether these are stocks, apartments, farms, oil wells, whatever.

principles.text: Hold a large cash floor to stay financially impregnable and never depend on outside kindness; cash-heavy periods are unpleasant but not permanent.
principles.quote: We want your company to be financially impregnable and never dependent on the kindness of strangers (or even that of friends).

sources.title: Berkshire 2022 letter: business-pickers, compounding winners, and the American Tailwind
sources.summary: Buffett explains that Berkshire's results came from about a dozen good decisions compounding over decades, not constant activity. He covers owning businesses rather than stocks, buyback math, float, honest accounting, avoiding forecasts, and Charlie Munger's wisdom.

principles.text: Buy businesses with durable economics and trustworthy managers; don't try to be a stock-picker.
principles.quote: Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.

principles.text: A few big winners dominate results over time; the weeds wither as the flowers bloom.
principles.quote: The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom. Over time, it takes just a few winners to work wonders.

principles.text: Even a legendary record rests on few great decisions; most capital-allocation calls are mediocre.
principles.quote: Our satisfactory results have been the product of about a dozen truly good decisions – that would be about one every five years

principles.text: Markets are not efficient; stocks periodically trade at foolish prices, creating chances to buy wonderful businesses cheaply.
principles.quote: stocks often trade at truly foolish prices, both high and low. “Efficient” markets exist only in textbooks.

principles.text: Buybacks help continuing owners only when made below value; overpaying transfers wealth to sellers.
principles.quote: Just as surely, when a company overpays for repurchases, the continuing shareholders lose.

principles.text: Manipulating earnings to beat expectations needs only a desire to deceive, and is a shame of capitalism.
principles.quote: It requires no talent to manipulate numbers: Only a deep desire to deceive is required.

sources.title: Buffett's 2023 letter: wonderful businesses, permanent-loss avoidance, and fortress balance sheets
sources.summary: Buffett's 2023 shareholder letter, written after Munger's death, covers why Berkshire reports operating rather than GAAP earnings, why it buys wonderful businesses at fair prices, and why it never risks permanent loss of capital. It also covers the capital-intensity of BNSF, his utility mistake, insurance underwriting discipline, and why he trusts patient owners like his sister Bertie.

principles.text: Buy wonderful businesses at fair prices, not fair businesses at wonderful prices; Graham-style cheapness only works at small scale.
principles.quote: add to it wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices and give up buying fair businesses at wonderful prices. In other words, abandon everything you learned from your hero, Ben Graham. It works but only when practiced at small scale.”

principles.text: Never risk permanent loss of capital; a few good decisions plus avoiding serious mistakes is enough over a lifetime.
principles.quote: One investment rule at Berkshire has not and will not change: Never risk permanent loss of capital.

principles.text: Favor rare businesses that can deploy more capital at high returns; owning one and sitting tight can create enormous wealth.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, we particularly favor the rare enterprise that can deploy additional capital at high returns in the future. Owning only one of these companies – and simply sitting tight – can deliver wealth almost beyond measure.

principles.text: Repurchases only make sense at a discount to business value; at a premium they are stupid.
principles.quote: All stock repurchases should be price-dependent. What is sensible at a discount to business-value becomes stupid if done at a premium.

principles.text: You cannot reliably judge managers by sincerity; never deal with a rascal expecting to prevent cheating.
principles.quote: “Never deal with a rascal under the expectation that you can prevent him from cheating you.” Many bankers who thought they could “manage” the rascal problem have learned the wisdom of Mr. McCulloch’s advice – and I have as well.

principles.text: Insurance underwriters cannot be optimists, since P/C surprises are almost always negative.
principles.quote: our underwriters can be thin, fat, male, female, young, old, foreign or domestic. But they can’t be optimists at the office, however desirable that quality may generally be in life.

sources.title: Buffett's 2024 letter: mistakes, Pete Liegl, float, and why Berkshire stays in equities
sources.summary: Buffett's 2024 annual letter covers owning up to capital allocation and personnel mistakes, judging managers by character rather than schooling, the discipline of P/C insurance and float, and Berkshire's permanent preference for businesses over cash. It also celebrates 60 years of reinvestment, which produced record tax payments.

principles.text: Admit mistakes openly and correct them fast; delay is the cardinal sin.
principles.quote: The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes or what Charlie Munger called “thumb-sucking.” Problems, he would tell me, cannot be wished away. They require action, however uncomfortable that may be.

principles.text: One great decision outweighs many mistakes; winners compound while losses fade.
principles.quote: a single winning decision can make a breathtaking difference over time. (Think GEICO as a business decision, Ajit Jain as a managerial decision and my luck in finding Charlie Munger as a one-of-a-kind partner, personal advisor and steadfast friend.) Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom.

principles.text: Judge managers on innate ability and character, not pedigree or schooling.
principles.quote: One further point in our CEO selections: I never look at where a candidate has gone to school. Never!

principles.text: Never write underpriced insurance to stay in the game; underwriters should be nervous but not paralyzed.
principles.quote: We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide.

principles.text: Keep skin in the game; avoid one-sided compensation so managers share downside.
principles.quote: We do not use options or other one-sided forms of compensation; if you lose money, so do we. This approach encourages caution but does not ensure foresight.

principles.text: Hold the majority of capital in good businesses, not cash or fixed-coupon bonds, to guard against currency debasement.
principles.quote: Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned.

sources.title: How Buffett ran his partnership 1957-61: undervalued generals, work-outs, control, and beating the Dow
sources.summary: Buffett's early partnership letters lay out his method: buy undervalued securities with a margin of safety, split capital among generals, work-outs and control situations, and judge results against the Dow over years, not months. They show his temperament toward bull markets, the Sanborn Map and Dempster control cases, and his view of true conservatism.

principles.text: Judge performance over years against a stated yardstick; one year is far too short to mean anything.
principles.quote: My own thinking is much more geared to five year performance, preferably with tests of relative results in both strong and weak markets.

principles.text: A good investment record is mostly about doing better in down markets, not matching the Dow in up ones.
principles.quote: I would consider a year in which we declined 15% and the Average 30% to be much superior to a year when both we and the Average advanced 20%.

principles.text: Buy undervalued generals with a big excess of value over price; this gives a margin of safety and diversification.
principles.quote: This individual margin of safety, coupled with a diversity of commitments creates a most attractive package of safety and appreciation potential.

principles.text: True conservatism comes from correct facts and reasoning, not from agreement with the crowd or important people.
principles.quote: You will be right, over the course of many transactions, if your hypotheses are correct, your facts are correct, and your reasoning is correct. True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason.

principles.text: Do not forecast the market; focus on finding undervalued securities, and be wary when the public believes profits from stocks are inevitable.
principles.quote: I make no attempt to forecast the general market - my efforts are devoted to finding undervalued securities.

principles.text: While accumulating a position, you want the stock to stay dull or fall; patience in buying maximizes long-term profit.
principles.quote: Obviously during any acquisition period, our primary interest is to have the stock do nothing or decline rather than advance.

sources.title: How Buffett ran his partnership 1962-64: beat the Dow, buy cheap, compound, measure honestly
sources.summary: Buffett's partnership letters from 1962 to mid-1964 explain his three investing categories (generals, workouts, controls), why results should be judged against the Dow over three years or more, and how a wide margin of safety drove returns. Dempster Mill shows value buying and capital reallocation in practice. He also covers compounding, taxes, and alignment with partners.

principles.text: Judge performance against a pre-chosen benchmark, not by whether the year is up or down.
principles.quote: Whether we do a good job or a poor job is not to be measured by whether we are plus or minus for the year. It is instead to be measured against the general experience in securities as measured by the Dow- Jones Industrial Average

principles.text: Short-term results are noise; give any strategy at least three years.
principles.quote: While I much prefer a five-year test, I feel three years is an absolute minimum for judging performance.

principles.text: Buy at prices so attractive that a mediocre sale still works; never count on a great exit.
principles.quote: Never count on making a good sale. Have the purchase price be so attractive that even a mediocre sale gives good results.

principles.text: True conservatism comes from correct facts and reasoning, not from popular agreement.
principles.quote: You will not be right simply because a large number of people momentarily agree with you. You will not be right simply because important people agree with you.

principles.text: Don't predict the market; pick investments on value and limit permanent capital loss with a margin of safety and diversification.
principles.quote: I am not in the business of predicting general stock market or business fluctuations. If you think I can do this, or think it is essential to an investment program, you should not be in the partnership.

principles.text: Small differences in compounding rate become enormous over long periods.
principles.quote: It is obvious that a variation of merely a few percentage points has an enormous effect on the success of a compounding (investment) program.

sources.title: Buffett Partnership letters 1965-67: beating the Dow, concentration, and conservatism
sources.summary: Buffett's partnership letters from 1965-67 explain why he measures against the Dow, concentrates up to 40% in his best ideas, defines conservatism by facts and reasoning rather than convention, and values controlled businesses on assets and earning power. They also cover compounding, ignoring market forecasts, taxes, and the limits of size.

principles.text: Conservatism comes from correct facts and sound reasoning, not from doing what is conventional.
principles.quote: Truly conservative actions arise from intelligent hypotheses, correct facts and sound reasoning.

principles.text: Don't take comfort or discomfort from crowd agreement; understand the situation yourself.
principles.quote: A public opinion poll is no substitute for thought.

principles.text: Concentrate heavily in the best few ideas rather than owning dozens; over-diversification lowers expected results.
principles.quote: any portfolio encompassing one hundred stocks (whether the manager is handling one thousand dollars or one billion dollars) is not being operated logically.

principles.text: Accept bumpy short-term results for better long-term performance, but never risk permanent capital loss.
principles.quote: I am not willing to incur risk of substantial permanent capital loss in seeking to better long term performance.

principles.text: Focus on what a business will do, not when the market will recognize it; don't forecast the market.
principles.quote: we tend to concentrate on what should happen, not when it should happen.

principles.text: Maximize after-tax compounding by owning the best securities, not by minimizing taxes; don't confuse means with ends.
principles.quote: Means and end should not be confused, however, and the end is to come away with the largest after-tax rate of compound.

sources.title: How Buffett wound down his partnership: BPL letters, 1967-1970
sources.summary: Buffett's letters track BPL's results, then explain why he cut his goals in 1967 and liquidated in 1969 as bargains vanished and speculation grew. He covers quantitative versus qualitative investing, ignoring market price for controlled businesses, and a plain-spoken guide to tax-free bonds.

principles.text: Sure money comes from obvious quantitative bargains; the big money comes from rare high-probability qualitative insights.
principles.quote: So the really big money tends to be made by investors who are right on qualitative decisions but, at least in my opinion, the more sure money tends to be made on the obvious quantitative decisions.

principles.text: Stick with a method you understand even when the crowd profits from a style you don't.
principles.quote: I will not abandon a previous approach whose logic I understand (although I find it difficult to apply) even though it may mean foregoing large and apparently easy, profits

principles.text: Market quotes don't set the value of a business you control; operating performance does.
principles.quote: Market price is irrelevant to us in the valuation of our controlling interests.

principles.text: Over time the market weighs fundamentals; short-term moves are votes driven by psychology, and fundamentals are easier to judge.
principles.quote: I have always found it easier to evaluate weights dictated by fundamentals than votes dictated by psychology.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence and pass on what you can't analyze; just be right on what you do choose.
principles.quote: My approach to bonds is pretty much like my approach to stocks. If I can't understand something, I tend to forget it.

principles.text: He valued people and human consequences over a few extra points of return, even in a weak business.
principles.quote: I have no desire to trade severe human dislocations for a few percentage points additional return per annum.

sources.title: Buffett on Alphabet and what makes a good business (CNBC, July 2026)
sources.originalTitle: Buffett CNBC Interview Transcript: The Alphabet Bet (2026)
sources.summary: In a 2026 CNBC interview Buffett explains his giving plans, the Greg Abel succession, and why he initiated Berkshire's Alphabet stake. The core investing lesson: a good business earns far more than Treasuries, sustains high returns on capital for a long time, and must be bought on the right terms with the right manager.

principles.text: Buy a good business on the right terms, then get the right person to run it. Same test for stock or whole company.
principles.quote: We are always making the choice between whether we’ll buy marketable securities or the company. We look at it the same way.

principles.text: A good business earns far more than riskless Treasuries on the capital it uses.
principles.quote: So a good business is one that earns a lot more than the returns on essentially riskless investments, which you could define as Treasuries.

principles.text: The trick is finding businesses that sustain high returns on capital for a long period; duration drives compounding.
principles.quote: The trick in investing is to find businesses that are going to earn high returns on capital for an extended period of time

principles.text: Judge a business by the returns it actually earns, not by next-quarter guesses from Wall Street.
principles.quote: What’s more important is what a business is earning, but they ask all these questions about what will happen next quarter, and it’s ridiculous.

principles.text: Great businesses get attacked, so the question is how long the advantage lasts, not whether it was great yesterday.
principles.quote: if you have a wonderful business, you are going to be subject to attack. So it’s not a question of whether it was wonderful yesterday, it’s the question of how long it is going to be wonderful.

principles.text: Stay within what you understand; don't expect to profit from games you don't understand.
principles.quote: There are all kinds of games I don’t understand, sure. Why should I expect to make money in all kinds of things I don’t understand?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett tells UF MBA students that character and habits matter more than IQ, then explains how he picks businesses: simple, understandable, with a widening moat and honest management. He covers Long-Term Capital's collapse, avoiding macro forecasts, concentration, and his mistakes of omission.

chunks.heading: Picking people to bet on: the 10% classmate exercise
chunks.text:
Warren borrows Pete Kiewit's hiring test: look for integrity, intelligence and energy, and if a person lacks the first, "the latter two would kill them." Dumb and lazy is better than smart and energetic without integrity.

His exercise for students:
- Imagine buying 10% of one classmate's lifetime earnings (no rich fathers allowed). You would not pick the highest IQ, best grades, or even the most energetic.
- You would pick the person with leadership qualities: generous, honest, gives others credit for ideas.
- Then imagine going short 10% of another classmate. That person is egotistic, greedy, or slightly dishonest and cuts corners.
- None of the good qualities is forbidden to anyone. They are behavior, temperament and character, and all are achievable.
- Habits harden: "the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they're too heavy to be broken." Young people can choose their habits now. Ben Graham and Ben Franklin each picked the people they admired and copied them.
- "You already own 100%" of yourself, so be the person you would buy 10% of.

chunks.heading: Careers, money and living well
chunks.text:
- Take the job you would take if you were independently wealthy, not one that "looks good on your resume." Warren compares delaying a job you love for resume value to "saving up sex for your old age."
- He offered to work for Graham for free after Columbia; Graham said he was overpriced. He kept pestering him, sold securities in Omaha for 3 years, and kept sending ideas until he got the job.
- Chasing 10X or 20X wealth leads people to borrow money or cut corners they will regret.
- He argues that his life differs little from a student's except for travel (his private plane). He loved his work as much when he made a thousand dollars as he does now.
- On luck, the "ovarian lottery": before birth, imagine designing society without knowing which of 5.8 billion balls you draw (race, sex, health, IQ, country). He says you would want a system that produces abundant goods and services but does not abandon people who drew the wrong ball for it.
- His own ball: he is well wired for a market economy that pays him to allocate capital. Stranded on a desert island, the rice grower would be the most valuable person.
- If he lived again he would do almost the same, and work only with people he likes. Taking a deal with someone who makes his "stomach churn" is "like marrying for money."

chunks.heading: Long-Term Capital Management: why smart people go broke
chunks.text:
- Warren was involved in the 1998 rescue. He bid $250 million for the net assets plus $3.75 billion on top ($3 billion Berkshire, $700 million AIG, $300 million Goldman Sachs), with a short fuse because a fixed bid on about $100 billion of moving securities is risky. The Fed-orchestrated bank deal won instead.
- The 16 principals had enormous IQs, 350-400 years of combined experience in their field, and most of their very large net worth in the fund.
- Lesson: "to make the money they didn't have and didn't need, they risked what they did have and did need." That is foolish at any IQ or odds.
- He compares it to a gun with a thousand chambers and one bullet: no payment justifies pulling the trigger once.
- "You only have to get rich once" (Walter Gutman's title). Going from $100 million to $110 million versus $120 million changes nothing, while ruin means disgrace and losing other people's money.
- He rejects reliance on math models: beta "doesn't tell you a damn thing about the risk of the stock," and sigmas do not measure the risk of going broke. History does not give the probabilities of future financial events.
- Blind spots arise where you know a great deal about one thing. He cites Henry Kaufman: those going broke are the ones who knew nothing and the ones who knew everything.
- Warren never borrows money, even when he had $10,000, because it made no difference to his happiness.
- If he wrote a book it would be "Why Smart People Do Dumb Things."

chunks.heading: Businesses he likes: understandable, with a moat and honest management
chunks.text:
- "I like businesses I can understand." That cuts the field by about 90%, and a huge universe remains.
- He wants a valuable castle, an honest, hardworking and able duke in charge, and a wide moat. He wants businesses hard for competitors to attack.
- Moat examples:
  - GEICO: low cost, since people must buy auto insurance and judge mostly on price.
  - Coca-Cola: its moat is wider than 30 years ago.
  - Kodak: once as strong as Coke, but it let Fuji narrow the moat (for example by letting Fuji into the Olympics).
- "Share of mind" beats share of market. Kodak, Disney, See's and Coke own a favorable image in customers' heads. A parent choosing a video for the kids buys the Disney one without evaluating alternatives.
- His test: "Give me a billion dollars" (or ten billion) and ask how much you could hurt Wrigley or Coca-Cola. He believes you could not, so those are good businesses.
- He instructs his managers to "widen the moat." A See's clerk smiling at the last customer in a long line before Christmas widens it; a snarl narrows it. You cannot see it daily, but it shows up over ten years.
- He avoids tech businesses whose state in 10 years he cannot see (Oracle, Lotus, Microsoft), even though he calls Gates the best businessman he has met. Chewing gum is predictable; the internet will not change how people chew gum.
- On valuing internet companies: if he taught that exam, he would flunk anyone who gave a value, because he doesn't know how to do it.
- His test for ownership: be happy owning it if the stock exchange closed for 5 years, as you would with a farm or apartment house. "You're not buying a stock, you're buying a part ownership in a business." This is the most fundamental thing Graham taught him.

chunks.heading: Pricing power and the See's Candy purchase
chunks.text:
- 1972: See's sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 a pound, earning about 4 million pre-tax (two bits a pound). Berkshire paid $25 million, and the business needed little capital.
- Analysis: Warren and Charlie judged whether there was untapped pricing power, i.e. whether the $1.95 box could sell for $2 or $2.25. An extra 30 cents on 16 million pounds is about 4.8 million on a $25 million price. They hired no consultants; their consulting was buying a box of candy.
- They saw that Californians had a favorable image of See's, like the Valentine's gift that earns a kiss.
- Gifts are not price-dependent: a husband will not hand his wife a box and say "this year I took the low bid."
- He raises prices on December 26th. This year See's will sell about 30 million pounds and earn about $60 million (roughly $2 a pound), with the same formulas and still no capital needs. About $55 million comes in the three weeks before Christmas.
- Coke is global happiness; he says RC Cola could never build that image worldwide with any budget.

chunks.heading: Coca-Cola, Gillette and McDonald's
chunks.text:
- Coke's international growth will outpace the US for 20 years, so the Asian crisis is a short-term drag. Timing is tricky, but "you can figure out what will happen. You can't figure out when." Focus on what.
- Cola has no taste memory: you can drink one at 9, 11 and 3 and the 5 o'clock one tastes as good. Most foods "accumulate on you" (See's employees allowed unlimited candy eat the usual amount after a week). So people drink five a day.
- Prices: in 1936 he bought six bottles for a quarter and sold them at a nickel each. Now a 12 oz can costs not much more than 20 cents, only twice the per-ounce price of 1936.
- More than 1 billion 8 oz servings a day. Berkshire owns 8%; an extra penny per serving would be about $10 million a day for Coke, $800,000 a day for Berkshire.
- Coke went public in 1919 at $40, fell to $19 a year later, and survived the Depression, WWII and sugar rationing. One share bought at $40 with dividends reinvested is worth about $5 million. Being right about the business overrides timing.
- Procter & Gamble is a very good business, but he feels surer about Coke's unit growth and pricing power over 20-30 years.
- McDonald's has the strongest position in fast food, particularly abroad, but is tougher than Coke: people don't eat there daily, it doesn't win adult taste tests, and it leans on promotions (beanie babies). He prefers products that sell on their own, like Gillette's Mach 3. For Gillette: "a couple billion men with their hair growing on their faces" overnight.
- Berkshire owns Dairy Queen.

chunks.heading: Circle of competence, mistakes and how he analyzes deals
chunks.text:
- Define your circle of competence. "The important thing is not how big the circle is. The important thing is staying inside the circle." Thirty companies is enough if you know which ones.
- He buys with little analysis. He bought General Re (about $18 billion) without visiting the headquarters, and bought Executive Jet after owning a quarter share in the program for 3 years. H.H. Brown shoes came together in about 5 minutes after a phone call, because he knew Frank Rooney and the basic economics.
- His price rule: if the seller's price makes sense he buys; otherwise "I was happy the day before, so I'll be happy the day after without owning it." He does not negotiate much.
- Early research: "scuttlebutt" per Phil Fisher. He asked every CEO in an industry which competitor's stock he would buy and which competitor he would shoot with a silver bullet, then pieced the answers together.
- Cigar butts: Graham-style buying of stocks well below working capital gets "one free puff" and then must be repeated. "Time is the friend of the wonderful business. It's the enemy of the lousy business." A windmill company bought at a third of working capital made money once but not repeatedly.
- His biggest mistakes were omissions: businesses he understood and did not buy, such as healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan fight and Fannie Mae in the mid-80s. These cost billions and don't show up in GAAP.
- Commission mistakes: US Air preferred and Salomon were attractive securities in businesses he would not own the common stock of. Buying because the terms look good, when he doesn't like the business, is a mistake. He jokes that he has an 800 number for "aeroholics."
- Mistakes happen when he holds cash and hangs around the office; Charlie tells him to go to a bar.
- His first stock purchase, 2,000 dollars of his 10,000 dollars into a Sinclair station, lost money, and he puts the opportunity cost at about 6 billion.
- He prefers learning from others' mistakes and does not look back.
- Every purchase must be explainable in the mirror. A cocktail-party tip or a chart is not a reason.

chunks.heading: Macro, diversification, valuation and temperament
chunks.text:
- Focus on what is "important and knowable." Macro views are important but not knowable; Coke's business is knowable. Berkshire never buys or avoids a business over macro predictions. If Greenspan and Rubin whispered their plans in his ear it would not change what he pays. If he had avoided See's in 1972 over price controls, he would have missed $25 million turning into $60 million a year.
- Wall Street is stimulating; "Wall Street makes its money on activity. You make your money on inactivity." Brokers are like doctors paid per pill change. Thinking in a room alone beats being around constant price shouting. He aims for one good idea a year, then holds it.
- Buy with no price target. He didn't buy See's planning to sell at $50 million.
- Diversification: for non-professionals, he favors an index fund with very low cost and no trading. For someone willing to evaluate businesses, diversification is a mistake: "If you really know businesses, you probably shouldn't own more than six of them." "Very few people have gotten rich on their seventh best idea." Walter Schloss diversifies widely ("Noah, he's got two of everything") and does fine.
- Net savers should want lower prices: buyers of stocks over the next 10 years should hope stocks go down, like a hamburger eater. Graham's Intelligent Investor chapters 8 (market fluctuations) and 20 (margin of safety) are, to him, the two most important investing essays ever written.
- The stock doesn't know you own it, so feelings about your cost or the price are not reciprocated.
- Berkshire pays no dividend because each retained dollar has become more than a dollar, and he's wary of size: Berkshire's returns would be much higher at 1/100th of the size, and with roughly $75-80 billion to deploy he can only focus on very big companies.
- Japan: a 10-year yen loan at 1% means the hurdle is low, but he found few wonderful businesses there because returns on equity were low, and he avoids currency risk.
- Earlier returns: American business earning near 20% on equity is why large caps did so well, which he is skeptical will last.
- Real estate: he sees REITs as having high operating expenses and double-tax-like drag. Illiquid land valuations are often silly because you cannot sell 20% of the property at the quoted price. He would look at very big real estate deals.
- Utilities: he understands demand but not who will earn the profits after deregulation.
- Berkshire has 12 people at headquarters in 3,500 square feet, and about 45,000 employees. Partner Charlie Munger and he have never had an argument in 40 years.
- He judged turnover as a measure of shareholder quality: he wants Berkshire holders who plan to hold forever, like a church where the same people fill the seats each Sunday.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett answers University of Georgia students on character and habits, circle of competence, intrinsic value as discounted cash, the cigar-butt mistake, mistakes of omission, market temperament, philanthropy, and why small businesses can beat scale.

chunks.heading: Choosing people: character over grades
chunks.text:
- Warren frames a thought experiment: you may pick one classmate and receive 10% of their lifetime earnings, and you must also short one classmate and pay 10% of theirs.
- The winner is not the top-grades student. The qualities that matter are self-made: integrity, honesty, generosity, willingness to do more than your share.
- The one to short is the person who fails in character: claims credit for things they didn't do, cuts corners, can't be counted on.
- He hires for three things: "intelligence," "initiative or energy," and "integrity." If someone lacks integrity, "the first two will kill you," because "you want them lazy and dumb."
- Character is a choice built from habits: "the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they're too heavy to be broken." The time to form good habits is a student's age.
- Ben Graham and Ben Franklin decided in their teens what kind of person they admired and behaved that way. Warren says anyone can become the person they would buy 10% of.
- Career advice: work for whoever you admire most rather than padding a resume. Taking a job that "looks good" now and doing what you like "someday" is "saving up sex for your old age."

chunks.heading: Circle of competence and why industry growth is not investment return
chunks.text:
- Warren expects to make money only in businesses whose economics he can foresee 10 or 20 years out. Wrigley is the example: gum habits and brands (Doublemint, Spearmint, Juicy Fruit) won't change.
- Seeing that an industry will transform society does not tell you who wins. The auto industry had about 2,000 companies; roughly three survive, and Studebaker, Nash, Kelvinator and Hudson were all once in the Dow.
- Airlines: over 400 aircraft companies existed in the 1920s-30s, including in Nebraska. Warren says that if there had been a capitalist at Kitty Hawk "he should have shot Orville down." Aggregate airline earnings through 1991 were less than zero while passenger counts rose every year.
- TV sets and radios follow the same pattern: huge products, no lasting U.S. manufacturers.
- Coca-Cola, by contrast, now sells roughly 1.1 billion servings a day, 117 years after it began.
- On internet and tech: he enjoys using Amazon and the computer, but "unless I know who's going to win I'm not interested in investing."
- What matters is knowing the perimeter of your circle, not its size. He quotes Tom Watson Sr.: "I'm no genius, but I'm smart in spots and I stay around those spots."

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value and the bird in the bush
chunks.text:
- Intrinsic value is all the cash a business will deliver between now and Judgment Day, discounted at the proper rate.
- A bond prints its cash flows; a stock certificate does not. The analyst's job is to turn the stock into a bond by estimating what it will pay out.
- Applied to Coca-Cola at roughly $110-115 billion: would you lay out that sum for what the company delivers over the next two or three hundred years? Volume, analyst recommendations and chart shapes are irrelevant; only cash received matters.
- The same logic applies to farms, apartment houses and oil in the ground: you lay out cash now to get more cash later, and the questions are how much, when, and how sure.
- Berkshire at about $105 billion: can it distribute enough cash soon enough to justify the price at current rates? If you can't answer that, you are gambling, not investing.
- Aesop's "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush" is incomplete: how many birds are in the bush, when do they come out, and how sure are you? At 15% rates you need two birds in five years; at 3% you can wait 20 years.
- For many internet companies "there weren't any birds in the bush," so he stays away from them.

chunks.heading: Mistakes: cigar butts, omission, and the punch card
chunks.text:
- Buying Berkshire Hathaway was a mistake. Following Ben Graham's quantitative approach, he bought it below working capital per share, but it was a lousy textile business and 20 years later he was still running one.
- The "cigar butt" approach finds a soggy butt with one free puff left. It can make money but not big money. Now: "I would rather buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price."
- "Time is the friend of the wonderful business" and "the enemy of the lousy business." Compounding only works in good businesses.
- Other errors: a $2,000 stake in a Sinclair filling station at age 20 (opportunity cost he puts at about $6 billion), and a 1989 US Air preferred purchase that went into the red once his check cleared. He jokes about calling an "800 number" to talk himself out of airline stocks.
- His biggest mistakes are omission, not commission: things within his circle of competence he passed on while "sucking my thumb." He cites Fannie Mae, which he says could have been bought for practically nothing about 20 years earlier, costing Berkshire at least $5 billion.
- The punch card idea: imagine only 20 financial decisions in a lifetime. You would think hard about each and make fewer, bigger, better ones. Dabbling, especially in bull markets and with online trading, is the temptation to avoid.
