chunks.heading: When to sell and how he thinks about partners
chunks.text:
- Early on he had more ideas than money (stocks at two or even one times earnings), so he sold his least favorite holding to fund the next compelling one. Now Berkshire has more money than ideas, generating at least $5 billion a year, "a hundred million bucks every week."
- Berkshire's wholly owned businesses (See's Candy, the Buffalo News) are not for sale regardless of price, even at three times value. He compares selling to selling one of his children for a big check.
- He sells only if he gets really discouraged with management or the economics of the business change in a big way, not because a stock looks high.
- He tells shareholders his approach up front, treating them as partners for life. His analogy: for a marriage that lasts, "you look for low expectations."

chunks.heading: Market cycles and temperament
chunks.text:
- Per-capita U.S. GDP rose about 610% in the 20th century and grew in every decade, including the 1930s (up 13%) and the 1940s (up 36%).
- The Dow went from 66 to 71 between 1900 and 1921, then to 381 by September 1929, then fell to about 180 by 1948, then to near 1,000 by 1965, then went nowhere until 1982 (864 at the end of 1964, 865 at the end of 1981). It ended the century above 11,000.
- Of the 100 years, about 43.75 were huge bull markets and about 56.25 were stagnation, all during a growing economy.
- The cause is behavioral: investors look in the rearview mirror, see money made, and pile in, or see none and avoid stocks. They "get greedy when others get greedy" and fearful when others get fearful.
- Pension funds put 100%+ of new money into stocks in 1970 and a record-low 9% in 1978, when stocks were far cheaper.
- At 21 he couldn't sell Kansas City Life stock (under three times earnings, about a 35% earnings yield) even to the company's own agent.
- The edge: "it doesn't take brains, it takes temperament," the ability to detach from the crowd.
- Test for bubbles: ask whether you'd buy the whole business. A company selling for $10 billion must deliver several hundred million next year and growing after. Herb Stein: "anything that can't go on forever will end."

chunks.heading: Small business, scale and the Fed
chunks.text:
- Scale helps in some industries, but small players often win. Sam Walton beat Sears despite worse credit, supplier access and real estate, by inspiring hundreds of thousands of people.
- Berkshire has about 112,000 employees but only about 13.8 people at headquarters, and keeps units small for nimbleness and responsiveness to customers.
- Nebraska Furniture Mart: Rose Blumkin arrived from Russia in 1921 speaking no English, started the store in 1937 with $500, undersold Brandeis in court, sold to Warren at 89 with no audit ("I'd rather have your word"), and worked until 103. Her store does about $325 million from one Omaha location. Her focus was entirely the customer.
- Similarly, Bill Child built a Utah furniture business from $250,000 a year to roughly $400 million by thinking only about the customer. Shaw went from unknown to about 40% of the carpet business.
- On the Fed: he admires Alan Greenspan, whom he knew from the Cap Cities board. He argues the Fed's brake is stronger than its gas pedal, citing Volcker breaking inflation and Japan's zero rates failing to restart growth.
- Currency and economics have "hundreds of variables" whose weights change, so history "doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes."

chunks.heading: Philanthropy and luck
chunks.text:
- Warren plans to give 99%+ of his net worth to a foundation after he and his wife die, with few trustees chosen for high grade, because large boards homogenize to the lowest common denominator.
- He gives them no specific instructions: their judgment above ground will beat his instructions "from six feet underground." He wants big bets on intractable problems with no natural funding constituency, not an "eyedropper approach."
- He praises Bill Gates for treating giving rationally (saving the most lives per dollar, vaccines, AIDS in Africa).
- On luck: born in 1930, "the odds were 50 to 1 against me being born in the United States." Society, a capitalist market that pays well for his skill, made his wealth, so it should go back to society.
- On tax shelters: low-income housing credits are a congressionally intended benefit, which he distinguishes from aggressive shelters and evasion, which he says border on fraud.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett fields student questions on hiring and character, staying inside a circle of confidence, buying great businesses and rarely selling, moats and franchise value, ignoring market forecasts, his shareholder base, and mistakes of omission.

chunks.heading: The "circle of confidence" and how Warren buys a business
chunks.text:
- Warren operates inside a "circle of confidence." What matters is not its size but how well the perimeter is defined: "If you know where the edges are you're way better off than somebody that's got one that's five times as large but they get very fuzzy about the edge."
- He can understand simple businesses and not complicated ones, and he stays out of the rest. He does not try to pick winners among technology companies where "five guys are out in a garage someplace."
- His filter: a business he can understand, people running it he likes and trusts, and a price that makes sense relative to future economics. When he finds one he buys a lot and keeps it, because replacements are hard to find.
- He quotes Peter Lynch: "buy a business that's so good that any idiot can run it because sooner or later one will." He still wants a terrific manager on top of it.
- Any good investment idea can be put in one paragraph.
- Nebraska Furniture Mart example: Rose Blumkin arrived in the US unable to speak English, started the store with $500 after bringing over seven siblings and her parents from Russia, and was nearing 101. The store does about $230 million at one location, more than twice any other single-store furniture operation in the US, and earns roughly $22-23 million pre-tax. She cannot read, but computes room dimensions and prices in her head.
- Berkshire's total legal and accounting cost to buy the business was $1,400, on a one-page contract. There was no audit, and he never checked the real estate records on the 60 acres. "Anything she said was so."
- He does not need to be right on many companies: "I just have to be right on one decision a year."

chunks.heading: Predicting markets and treating stocks as pieces of businesses
chunks.text:
- Warren never thinks about what the stock market will do. He asks what the business will do over time.
- Test: if Walt Disney had offered him 5% of a private company for $4 million in 1966, or Roberto Goizueta had offered him a slice of a private Coca-Cola, he would have evaluated the company, not the market.
- He ignores forecasts, even from Alan Greenspan: "I'm not going to trade something I know how to do and give up something I know how to do because of some opinion about something I don't know how to do." He does not predict the stock market, interest rates, or business cycles.
- His formula: "If I buy the right kind of business at the right price with the right people I'll do well over time."
- "In stocks it's very hard to know when something will happen and it's very easy to know what will happen." He may not know whether the market will be higher in two years, but there will be intelligent things to do, and "if you see one the thing to do is to do it."
- Buying 100% of See's Candy (1972) and buying 6% of Coca-Cola use the same analysis: how strong is the hold on customers, and can prices be raised over time. For See's he asked whether Russell Stover could knock them out of the box.
- Owning all of a business has small advantages over owning a piece: you can change management and control the allocation and distribution of earnings. But being in a good business with good managers matters far more. He would rather own a part of a great business than all of a mediocre one.
- Berkshire's edge is mental flexibility: it is not committed to steel, shoes, or insurance per se, and can move capital to wherever it makes sense.

chunks.heading: Moats, franchise value and durability
chunks.text:
- Franchise test: if the store lacks your product and offers a substitute, will the customer walk across the street to buy yours, or pay a nickel more? If yes, it is a franchise, and it lives in people's minds.
- See's Candy sold at $1.95 a pound. The question was whether people would pay more as inflation went on. If a dominant share of customers perceive it as the best candy, the business does very well. Nobody takes the low bidder's chocolates home on Valentine's Day.
- Franchise value can come from taste, a mental association, service, or availability.
- His image: a moat around an economic castle. Two questions matter: how big is the castle, and how durable is the moat. Coca-Cola is a big castle; See's is a small castle, but still a castle with a moat.
- Moats are widened by service, employee training, and research, and you need one "to protect you from some guy that's going to come along and offer it a penny cheaper."
- You won't find it in carbon steel or integrated oil.
- Coca-Cola: 110 years old, 750 million eight-ounce servings a day, per-capita consumption rising in nearly every country, about 47% of soft drink consumption outside the US and 41% in the US, gaining share every year. Appeal is universal and the product is durable.
- Gillette: about 21 billion razor blades a year, 30% of them Gillettes but about 60% by value, with 90% share in some countries. About $20 a year per user, for a daily habit, and men rarely switch. Innovation in razors plus distribution plus mind position. Berkshire owned about 11% of Gillette (about two-thirds of its profits come from outside the US) and 7.7% of Coke (over 80% outside the US).
- He likes businesses where he knows what they will look like in 5, 10, 15 or 20 years.
- "You don't have to find very many." Ten good ideas in a lifetime is enough, and you could give half away.

chunks.heading: When to sell, how many bets, and mistakes
chunks.text:
- Selling a truly great business because the price looks a little high is "almost always a mistake." He learned this slowly and says he hasn't fully learned it.
- Most fortunes were made in a few securities, held for a very long time, that the buyer understood.
- Investing has no called strikes. Unlike his department-store days, where he had to match every competitor move (air conditioning, 18-month terms, an escalator), an investor can wait for the pitch he likes, then swing big.
- The ease of trading (buy at 10:00, sell at 10:05) causes people to do things that don't make sense.
- He rarely sells his best holdings because replacements are hard to find.
- Cash makes him worse: "I make more mistakes when I have a lot of cash around." His decision acuity fades with idle cash, because there is more compulsion to do something.
- His largest loss at the partnership and Berkshire was about 2% of net worth. Being careful and doing few things limits errors of commission.
- The big mistakes are omissions:
  - He started to buy Fannie Mae around 1988 but didn't follow through; Berkshire made about $5 million, versus roughly $1.5 billion if he had.
  - Disney in 1966: the entire company was selling for about $80 million, debt free. Five percent cost $4 million. They had 300 acres at Anaheim with Disneyland drawing about 9 million people a year, a film library, and had just spent $17 million on the Pirates ride. He bought 5% and sold it about a year later for $6 million. It would be worth about a billion now.
- US Air (1989) he calls "temporary insanity." He had cash, no one misled him, and the manager was excellent. But airlines have revenues set by market forces and costs that are not. Since Kitty Hawk, the airline industry as a whole has returned less than zero to owners. He jokes that he keeps an 800 number to call and say "my name is Warren, I'm an airaholic."

chunks.heading: Hiring and the character test: buy 10% of a classmate
chunks.text:
- Hiring at Salomon, Aug 1991: Salomon had about $150 billion in balance sheet assets, about $4 billion equity, with a large share of the other $146 billion due within weeks, and 8,000 employees. After the top management was forced out, Warren interviewed roughly a dozen candidates in one evening.
- He did not ask about grades, never looked at a résumé, and didn't ask about IQ, since everyone there was smart enough. He wanted Ben Franklin's qualities: willing to give others more credit than themselves, no corner-cutting, deliver what is promised and a little extra.
- He picked Deryck Maughan. The next day he tapped him on the chest ("you're it") and Maughan faced about 200 reporters for three hours with two minutes' notice. Maughan never asked what he'd be paid, worked 18-hour days for months, and showed uncanny judgment about what to bring to Warren.
- Classmate exercise: you get to pick one classmate and receive 10% of their lifetime earnings. You would not choose by grades, IQ, or looks, but by character: qualities anyone can acquire. Then imagine shorting 10% of another: the one who cuts corners and claims credit for others' work.
- Character determines output: some people have a 300-horsepower motor and get far less out of it; the best performers have the most efficient motors, not the biggest.
- Habits: Ben Graham wrote down at 12 the qualities he admired and disliked in others. These are habits you can choose. "The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken," so form the right ones early. Decide to be the person you'd buy 10% of.
- Work only with people you like and admire: "like marrying for money... crazy if you're already rich." Go to work for whomever you admire most. Admired managers: Tom Murphy (Capital Cities), Roberto Goizueta and Don Keough (Coca-Cola, took market value from about $5 billion to about $60 billion in 11-12 years), Bill Gates.

chunks.heading: Shareholder base and communication
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's A shares traded around $20,000-25,000 and Warren refuses to split the stock. A public company's owners are anyone with money, so the only tools are communications and policies. He wants partners with the same expectations, time horizon, and measures of success.
- Analogy: a sign reading "rock concert" draws one crowd and "ballet" another; both fine, but it's a mistake to advertise one and run the other.
- Not splitting screens out people who trade actively and buy because of a split or next quarter's earnings. Berkshire has by far the lowest turnover relative to capitalization on the NYSE, which he sees as a success. "If I was preaching at a church I would not measure my success by the turnover of the congregation."
- Writing as thinking: when he gets blocked writing the annual report, it's because he hasn't got the idea straight. "There's nothing like writing to force you to think."
- Footnotes: if he can't understand an accounting footnote, he assumes the company doesn't want him to, and "I won't invest in the company."

chunks.heading: Size, banks, foreign investing and inherited wealth
chunks.text:
- Size is a drag. Starting with $10,000, one cheap stock mattered. Now a $100 million position that gains 50% (about $32.5 million after tax) moves net worth only about 0.3%. Berkshire's universe is very small and its returns cannot match the past.
- When he started he went through Moody's and Standard & Poor's page by page and found insurers and a utility trading at about two times earnings, but he could only put $5-50 thousand in.
- Banking consolidation: it will continue because managers like to grow and trade rankings by asset size, but he sees no great economies of scale beyond a point. He would rather own 30% of the market in Rockford, Illinois (where Berkshire had a bank earning 2% on assets after tax, conservative) than 15% nationally. Acquired banks' shareholders do better than acquirers'. Wells Fargo's First Interstate-style deal was an exception that worked.
- Foreign companies: he'd buy Coke if it were domiciled in London or Amsterdam, but slightly prefers US domicile for governance, tax, and accounting familiarity. He'll look anywhere, but US equities are a $5 trillion market, and if he can't make money there, going a few thousand miles away is wishful thinking.
- Inherited wealth: leave children "enough money so they can do anything but not enough so they can do nothing." Inherited wealth is "a lifetime supply of food stamps given through a trust officer instead of a welfare officer."
- He credits society for much of what he earned; in Bangladesh or Peru the same talent would earn far less. The market pays disproportionately for some talents (Mike Tyson, a .360 hitter) and little for teachers and nurses, and those richly rewarded owe society a large claim on the proceeds.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At UGA's Terry College, Buffett explains how to choose a career, why character beats grades, how to value any business as discounted future cash, and why staying inside your circle of competence matters. He also covers his own mistakes (Berkshire, US Air, omissions), why temperament beats IQ, and why small businesses can beat giants.

chunks.heading: Picking people: the "10% of a classmate" test
chunks.text:
Warren asks listeners to imagine they could own 10% of one classmate's lifetime earnings, and must also short 10% of another's. He argues the winner is not the one with the highest grades.

- What separates big winners are self-made qualities: "Integrity, honesty, generosity, being willing to do more than your share."
- The short side fails on character, not grades: taking credit for work they didn't do, cutting corners, being unreliable.
- When hiring he looks for three things: intelligence, initiative or energy, and integrity. Without integrity, "the first two will kill you", because you want a dishonest person "lazy and dumb," not smart and energetic.
- Character is a habit pattern you choose. Warren quotes "the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they're too heavy to be broken," and notes people at 50 or 60 are often imprisoned by self-destructive habits.
- Ben Franklin and Ben Graham decided in their young teens whom they admired and why, then behaved that way.

chunks.heading: Work for someone you admire
chunks.text:
Warren's career advice is to go work for the person or institution you admire most, not for a resume line or slightly higher starting pay.

- He told a Harvard student planning a consulting stint to "round out" his resume: "Your plan sounds to me a lot like saving up sex for your old age."
- Following this advice, he says, means you "jump out of bed in the morning" and have fun.
- He jokes that Harvard's dean called later to say the students he spoke to were all becoming self-employed.

chunks.heading: Circle of competence
chunks.text:
Warren says he only expects to make money in businesses whose long-term economics he understands. That is different from knowing what a product does.

- Wrigley's gum is within his circle: he knows the Internet won't change which gum people chew, so he can roughly picture the business 10 years out.
- A big industry does not mean profitable investors. There were 2,000 auto companies at one point, and only three basically survived. Studebaker, Nash, Kelvinator and Hudson were once in the Dow and "got creamed."
- Easier than picking winners is identifying losers: in 1905 the smart move was to short horses (about 20 million then, about 4 million now).
- Airlines: over 4,100 airplane companies in the 1920s and 30s. "If there had been a capitalist at Kitty Hawk he should have shot Orville down." At the end of 1991 the industry's aggregate earnings since Kitty Hawk were less than zero, even as passengers grew every year.
- TV sets and radios: huge growth, almost no US manufacturers left or profitable.
- Coca-Cola, by contrast, now sells roughly 1.1 billion 8-ounce servings a day, a durable economic franchise.
- On the Internet and tech: he enjoys the technology and orders books from Amazon, but "I don't know who's going to win, and unless I know who's going to win I'm not interested in investing."
- The size of the circle doesn't matter; knowing its perimeter and staying inside it does. He quotes Tom Watson Sr.: "I'm no genius, but I'm smart in spots, and I stay around those spots."

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value
chunks.text:
Warren defines intrinsic value as all the cash a business will give you between now and Judgment Day, discounted at the proper rate.

- A bond has its cash flows printed on it; a stock certificate doesn't, so the analyst's job is to turn the stock into a bond by estimating future payouts.
- It applies equally to a farm, an apartment house, oil in the ground, a new carpet machine at Shaw, or the whole of Coca-Cola.
- It does not depend on analyst recommendations, trading volume or chart patterns.
- Esop's "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush" is incomplete: you need to know how many birds are in the bush, when you will get them, and how sure you are. At 15% rates you need two birds in 5 years to beat the one in hand; at 3% you can wait 20 years.
- Test for any stock: if you were buying the whole company at its market price, could it distribute enough cash soon enough to make sense at current interest rates? If you can't answer, you're gambling. He can't answer it for Internet companies, so he stays away.
- A hypothetical Internet company with 100 million shares at $100 is a $10 billion business, and would need to produce roughly $700-800 million next year and grow after that.
- Berkshire has never distributed anything to shareholders, but its ability to distribute rises as the value of its businesses rises.

chunks.heading: Mistakes: cigar butts, Berkshire and omission
chunks.text:
Warren is open about his errors and says the biggest are mistakes of omission, which never show up in conventional accounting.

- Cigar butts: following Ben Graham, he bought statistically cheap stocks with "one puff left." Berkshire Hathaway traded below working capital, so he bought it, and "20 years later I was still running a lousy business." Berkshire was a mistake as a platform; he'd have done better starting a fresh entity and buying better businesses.
- Quality over price: "I'd rather buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price." Time is the friend of a wonderful business and the enemy of a lousy one.
- US Air: he bought preferred in 1989 and the company went into the red as soon as his check cleared. He jokes about an 800 number to call at 3 a.m. to talk him out of airline stocks.
- A Sinclair filling station at about age 20: he put in $2,000 of roughly $10,000 and lost it all. At Berkshire's compounding, the opportunity cost is about $6 billion.
- Biggest mistakes: things within his circle of competence that he passed on while "sucking my thumb." Example: Fannie Mae, when it had troubles roughly 20 years earlier and could have been bought for practically nothing, cost Berkshire at least $5 billion. Microsoft isn't a similar regret because it was outside his circle.
- The "punch card" idea: imagine you got only 20 punches for the rest of your life, one per financial decision. You'd think hard, make fewer and bigger decisions, and probably not use all 20. He warns against dabbling, especially in bull markets and with online trading.

chunks.heading: Selling, holding and Berkshire's promises to partners
chunks.text:
Warren explains his approach to selling and says he treats shareholders as partners for life.

- Early on he had more ideas than money (he combed Moody's manual page by page, found stocks at one or two times earnings) and sold his least favorite holding to fund a new one. Now Berkshire has "more money than ideas," generating at least $5 billion of cash a year, about $100 million a week.
- Wholly owned businesses are not for sale at any price: Seas Candy, the Buffalo News and Borsheims won't be sold even at three times value. Selling would be "like selling one of my children."
- He puts this in the "economic principles of Berkshire" so partners know his thinking in advance and aren't disappointed.
- Stocks are sold mainly if management disappoints him badly or the business's economics change significantly, not simply because the price looks high.
- Marriage analogy: a lasting marriage depends on low expectations, so he wants partners to start with low expectations.
- Berkshire has 112,000 employees and, he says, only 13.8 people at headquarters; units are kept small for nimbleness and customer responsiveness.

chunks.heading: Market cycles, temperament and the Fed
chunks.text:
Warren says markets swing on human emotion while the economy keeps growing, and that temperament, not brains, produces investing results.

- US GDP per capita rose about 610% in the 20th century, up every decade including the 1930s. Yet the Dow went from 66 to 71 between 1900 and 1921, then to 381 by September 1929, back to about 180 by 1948, to about 1,000 by 1965, flat at 865 in 1981 versus 874 in 1964, then up enormously. By his count, about 43 and 3/4 years of big bull markets and 56 and 1/4 years of stagnation.
- Investors look in the rearview mirror: "I made money last year, so I'll borrow and make more." They get greedy when others are greedy and fearful when others are fearful.
- Pension funds put 10-plus percent of new money in stocks in 1970 but a record-low 9% in 1978 when stocks were far cheaper.
- At 21 he couldn't sell Kansas City Life stock to the company's own agent, though it traded under three times earnings (a roughly 35% yield) and its policies assumed 2% interest.
- "If you can detach yourself temperamentally from the crowd you get very rich and you won't have to be very bright." Bubbles end: quoting Herb Stein, "anything that can't go on forever will end."
- Fed: he likes Greenspan, but says the Fed's brakes are stronger than its gas pedal (Volcker broke inflation by braking). Japan shows zero rates don't guarantee stimulus. Economics has hundreds of changing variables, and "history doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes."

chunks.heading: Small business, philanthropy and taxes
chunks.text:
Warren says small companies can beat large ones in many fields, and describes his giving philosophy.

- Scale matters in some businesses, but Walmart beat Sears despite worse credit, supplier access and real estate, and Southwest Airlines didn't need to be biggest.
- Nebraska Furniture Mart: Rose Blumkin arrived from Russia in 1921 speaking no English, saved $500 by 1937, and built the largest home-furnishing store in the world on 72 acres doing about $325 million in one location. She relied on customer focus and low prices, never read a balance sheet, and worked until she was 103. Her word, he says, was worth more than an audit. Bill Child at Utah's furniture business and Shaw in carpet are other examples.
- Philanthropy: nearly all his net worth goes to a foundation after he and his wife die. He picked few, high-grade trustees (not 30), gave no specific instructions because their judgment above ground beats his from "6 feet underground," and wants them to take on hard problems that lack a natural funding constituency. He praises Bill Gates for aiming to save as many lives per dollar as possible.
- He credits luck: born in 1930 in the US, where odds were "50 to 1 against" it, wired for asset allocation in a society that pays for it, and says the money should go back to society.
- Taxes: legal benefits such as low-income housing credits are fine, aggressive shelters bought with shopped legal opinions are close to fraud, and Berkshire won't move to Bermuda to avoid taxes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2013 Georgetown conversation with Brian Moynihan, Buffett explains why temperament beats IQ in investing, why you only need to swing at a few pitches, and why he stays optimistic about America despite panics. He also covers the Giving Pledge, inequality, and the GEICO and Heinz deals.

chunks.heading: Warren's baseline: when to invest in a business, and why temperament beats IQ
chunks.text:
- Warren's best investment was a book: Ben Graham's *The Intelligent Investor*, bought in 1949. Aside from what he paid for his two marriage licenses, he calls it the best investment he ever made.
- He says you need "the right framework" and a sound investing philosophy. Graham's approach is simple, and Warren adopted it immediately, which most people don't.
- With the right philosophy you find opportunities over 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, and most often in panics. He says stocks sell at silly prices from time to time, and most stocks at one time or another sell at very silly prices.
- Spotting a cheap stock doesn't take a high IQ. It takes a temperament willing to step up and act.
- On IQ: "if you've got 160 IQ sell 30 points to somebody else because you won't need it." He figured out early that you don't have to be that smart, but you must have the right temperament.
- He says you must ignore what other people say and look at the facts, asking whether a stock selling at X is worth 2X. When you don't find such a case, you do nothing.
- He started young: he bought three shares of City Service preferred at 11, in spring 1942, after saving $120 over five years. He read every investment book in the Omaha public library, and his father's books on Saturday mornings in the investment office.
- He says he has as much fun working at 83 as ever: "working with people I love doing what I love."

chunks.heading: Circle of competence and the no-called-strikes advantage
chunks.text:
- Warren says the most important thing is to define which businesses you can reach an intelligent decision on and which are beyond your ability to evaluate. You don't need to be right about thousands of companies, only a few.
- Ted Williams, in *The Science of Hitting*, divided the strike zone into 77 baseball-sized squares. Swinging only at pitches in his sweet zone, Williams would hit .400. Forced to swing at low outside pitches in the zone, he'd hit .230. The key to hitting is waiting for the right pitch.
- Warren says investing is better than baseball because there are no called strikes. People can throw Microsoft or General Motors at him and he doesn't have to swing. He can watch thousands of companies and swing only at something he understands at a price he likes.
- "It's a terrible mistake to think you have to have an opinion on everything. You only have to have an opinion on a few things."
- His punch-card idea: if students got a card with 20 punches for all the investment decisions of their lives, they'd get very rich, because they would think hard about each one. Four or five right decisions would probably do it over time.
- He met Bill Gates on July 5, 1991, in Seattle. Gates said he needed a computer to do taxes and track his portfolio. Warren replied he had no income, Berkshire paid no dividend, and he held only one stock. He asked whether computers would change whether people chew gum, Gates said probably not, and Warren said "I'll stick to chewing gum and you stick to computers."
- He says there are all kinds of businesses he doesn't understand, but thousands of opportunities he does. He didn't try to predict that Amazon would win while ten others lost. He tips his hat to Jeff Bezos but says "I don't have to form an opinion on Amazon."
- He did form opinions on Bank of America and Coca-Cola.

chunks.heading: Valuing a brand: the Coca-Cola penny math, and products that travel
chunks.text:
- Warren points out Coca-Cola has been around since 1886, and about 1.8 billion eight-ounce servings are sold every day.
- One extra penny on each serving is $18 million a day. Over a year that is about $6.57 billion.
- His question: is Coca-Cola worth a penny more than "Joe's cola"? He says yes, and he has about 127 years of history behind that view.
- He likes decisions of that kind: simple, based on a durable product with a long record.
- On Heinz, he looks at people pouring ketchup on hamburgers and potatoes and doesn't think that will change.
- He prefers products that travel well. Soft drinks and ketchup travel. Candy bars don't: Cadbury bars sell poorly in the US and Hershey bars sell less well elsewhere.

chunks.heading: The GEICO story: patience, relationships, and buying the rest
chunks.text:
- At 20, Warren came to Washington on a Saturday because his Columbia professor Ben Graham was GEICO's chairman. The door was locked, a janitor let him in, and Lorimer Davidson spent four hours teaching him insurance. Warren says this help mattered enormously.
- He later sold 100 shares of GEICO to his aunt Alice, the first stock he ever sold.
- In 1976 GEICO was close to going broke after miscalculating its reserves. Warren came back and bought a third of the company in the market in a short period.
- By 1995 the company had repurchased shares, so Berkshire's third had become half. He visited Davidson, then 96 or 97, who held GEICO stock with a very low cost basis. Warren said an offer would trigger a big tax, whereas holding until death gives a stepped-up basis, so he wouldn't make it unless Davidson was comfortable. Davidson said "I've hoped for this all my life", and Berkshire bought the rest.
- Warren's lesson: "Nobody does it alone." He says "we all sit in the shade of trees that were planted by others," so it's obligatory to plant a few trees yourself if you've had good luck.

chunks.heading: How Warren finds deals: Iscar, Heinz and 3G
chunks.text:
- On deals, he says he loves not knowing what he'll do next. Playing golf where every drive went in the hole would make him give up the game; the rough makes it interesting.
- Iscar (2006): He received a letter out of the blue from Eitan Wertheimer, about a page and a half, saying that if the family sold, Berkshire was the only buyer they wanted. Warren emailed back, they came to Omaha quickly, and Berkshire paid $4 billion for 80% of a company he had never seen.
- Eitan insisted he visit Israel. Warren said he doesn't even go to Council Bluffs, Iowa, but agreed to visit after the purchase. The plants turned out to be the greatest operation he'd seen. His line: if he had visited first, "I'd pay more money."
- Heinz: He got to know Jorge Paulo Lemann through a board (Gillette). Last December, on a trip to Boulder, Colorado, Lemann explained the Heinz idea. Warren said "count me in."
- Lemann's 3G does the heavy lifting and runs the business. Afterward he sent Warren a one-page governance description of how the partnership would work and a short description of a fair deal. Warren didn't change a word. "Those are the kind of people you like to associate with."

chunks.heading: Panics, human behavior and how the next crisis gets handled
chunks.text:
- Warren says people will keep making the same mistakes, and it doesn't correlate with IQ. When greedy they build bubbles, like the housing bubble where a house worked like a margin account. When fearful, they all leave at once.
- He expects recessions periodically and occasional panics, though not all recessions come from panics. He says it will happen again in different circumstances, but "the human animal will keep behaving pretty much the way it has."
- His analogy: people think they're Cinderella at the ball. As the night goes on the music gets better and the drinks flow, they all think they'll leave at two minutes to twelve, and there are no clocks on the wall.
- On 2008: he says the panic was worse than anyone had seen and the country was "right on the edge of the cliff." He credits Bernanke, Paulson, Geithner and President Bush, who said "if money doesn't loosen up this sucker could go down."
- What stops a real panic is someone with the ability and the will saying "I'm going to do whatever it takes." He cites the Fed putting $85 billion into AIG, Paulson guaranteeing money market funds after about $300 billion left non-government funds in three days, and Bernanke's use of Section 13(3) and the Exchange Stabilization Fund.
- He doubts Bernanke and Paulson could do the same under Dodd-Frank, and says he isn't sure whether the new law is a plus or minus for the next panic. On derivatives and regulation, he says it is very hard to write rules that stop people acting foolishly after foolishness has been profitable for years.
- On the Fed's bond buying, he said the Fed had a $3.5 trillion balance sheet and called it "the greatest hedge fund in history," funded partly by currency that costs nothing and bank deposits at 25 basis points. He thinks it faces no pressure to deleverage and can pick its time, though it's an experiment at this scale.

chunks.heading: Optimism about America and the opportunity-versus-fairness tension
chunks.text:
- Warren says America works: the Dow went from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century despite two world wars, the Depression, the flu epidemic, the Cold War and the atom bomb. Stocks were around 100 when he bought his first in 1942, weeks after Pearl Harbor.
- Real GDP per capita has risen about sixfold since he was born in 1930. At 2% growth with 1% population growth, per-capita growth of 1% yields a 20% gain in a generation.
- He calls the baby born today in the US the luckiest person, probabilistically, ever. His advice: "don't ever worry about America."
- But he says the gains are unevenly shared. The Forbes 400's aggregate wealth went from about $300 billion to $2 trillion in 20 years, while median income in real purchasing power is about where it was in 1989.
- He argues markets get more specialized and will not pay well for a significant share of people, so government has to address it. He doesn't want equality of results but a satisfactory base level.
- His thought experiment: you are in the womb, a genie lets you design the economic, social and political system, but you then pull a random slip from a barrel of seven billion (male or female, black or white, strong or infirm, bright or not, US or Bangladesh). You'd want a system that produces lots of output, removes fear (of old age, health), and takes care of those who draw bad tickets.

chunks.heading: Giving it away: the Giving Pledge and swinging for the fences
chunks.text:
- The Giving Pledge came from Warren, Bill and Melinda Gates, and a dinner hosted by David Rockefeller with about 16-18 people (including Oprah and Mayor Bloomberg) talking about how they developed their philosophy of giving. The pledge now has about 115 people, and Warren has been "dialing for dollars." The letters are on givingpledge.org.
- He tells 70-year-olds: do you think your decision-making will be better at 95 "with some blonde on your lap" or now?
- He says nobody in the pledge group has given up anything that affects how they live. He admires more the person who drops a dollar in the collection plate, since that costs them real utility, whereas his stock certificates have none for him.
- He and his wife planned in their 20s to give back once they had everything they needed; he assumed she would outlive him, but she died in 2004. He applies Adam Smith's specialization of labor: go to those best at giving money away, as he goes to an obstetrician or a dentist.
- He picked the Gates Foundation because they were younger, energetic, smart and share the principle that "every human life has equal value." They also work for nothing.
- He tells the foundations of his three children to swing for the fences: if everything they do succeeds, they're doing the wrong things, since the important problems are the tough ones.
- His estate: all of it must be spent within 10 years after the estate is closed. He doesn't believe in controlling things from the grave or in picking some great-great-grandchild because of the name.
- He backs Tom Cousins' East Lake model (Atlanta), a holistic mixed-income community rebuild now replicated in New Orleans, Indianapolis and about 11 more towns, because it's high-quality, energetic people putting in their own money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett recounts his path from pinball machines to Ben Graham's partnership, the Buffett Partnership and Berkshire. He explains investing as assigning yourself the right story about what a business is worth, buying decent businesses at sensible prices, and why time and finding work you love matter more than money.

chunks.heading: Early life, partnerships and why Warren followed his hero
chunks.text:
- Warren always ran small businesses; the best was a pinball machine company (Wilson Coin Operated Machine Company, named after his high school). Barbers wanted newer flipper machines costing about $350, while obsolete machines cost $25. He stalled by saying he'd "take it up with Mr. Wilson," a mythical partner.
- He did not want college; his dad did. He attended Wharton two years, finished at Nebraska in three, and was rejected by Harvard after a 10-minute interview.
- He found Columbia in a library catalog, saw Graham and Dodd taught there, and wrote Dean Dodd: "I thought you guys were dead."
- He later worked for Ben Graham, his hero, for about a year and a half. He had read Graham's books so many times he "could have recited the words... better than he could have," so it was more inspiration than new learning.
- He left New York for Omaha because of family: two kids, grandparents alive, uncles and aunts, and a more pleasant life than commuting from White Plains. He rented a house for $175 a month and bought his current house in 1958.

chunks.heading: Starting the partnerships
chunks.text:
- On returning to Omaha he had about $175,000 and thought that was all he'd need for life.
- In May 1956 seven people put in $105,000 and Warren put in $100, giving $105,100. He handed them a short document called the "ground rules."
- Between May 1956 and January 1, 1962 he started 10 more partnerships. With no secretary or accountant, each purchase meant 11 tickets, 11 checks, 11 sets of books and 11 tax returns, all done himself, and he took physical delivery of stocks because it was other people's money.
- On January 1, 1962 he merged all 11 into Buffett Partnership and ran it through 1969, then dissolved it. At that point it held about $105 million; roughly $70 million was cash to distribute and the rest was in three stocks, mostly Berkshire Hathaway, distributed pro rata.

chunks.heading: Why the results came: businesses at sensible prices
chunks.text:
- His answer for success: studying companies, sticking to principles, and buying "decent businesses at sensible prices" with "good people to run them."
- At Berkshire the emphasis shifted over time from marketable securities to buying whole businesses.
- He is not against unfriendly deals ("there are managements that should be replaced") but Berkshire isn't interested in them.
- He screens inbound deal calls fast: he can usually tell within two or three minutes whether a deal will happen, because Berkshire's criteria are clear and there are "a half a dozen filters."

chunks.heading: Washington Post: assigning yourself the right story
chunks.text:
- The Post went public in 1971. In 1973, with the Nixon administration (through Nixon pal Bebe Rebozo) challenging the licenses of two Florida TV stations, the stock fell from $37 to $16.
- At $16 with about 5 million shares, the whole company sold for about $80 million, including the newspaper, four big TV stations, Newsweek and other assets, with little debt. Warren put its intrinsic value at $400-500 million.
- Berkshire bought most of its stock at the equivalent of about a $100 million market value. The business was worth four or five times the price, and Nixon "wasn't going to put him out of business."
- His advice to Bob Woodward, who asked what to do with his new money: "Investing is just about assigning yourself the right story." Imagine an editor asking what the Post is worth: you'd interview TV and newspaper brokers and owners and value each asset. "That's what I do."
- He only writes stories he can write. He can't value glamorous businesses that don't make money, but he can value something like an electric utility.
- He reads annual reports like novels and does the math in his head: "If you need to carry something out to four decimal places, forget it." Opportunities are fewer now than then.

chunks.heading: How Berkshire's big deals actually get done
chunks.text:
- **Precision Castparts (~$37 billion):** about $32-33 billion in cash plus about $4 billion of assumed debt. He met the CEO by accident when the CEO was calling on shareholders (a colleague already held the stock). After hearing him speak for 30 minutes, he had the colleague call the next day to say Berkshire would supply a cash bid if the CEO wanted one. He says that if he'd been out playing golf, it never would have happened.
- **No investment bankers for analysis.** Berkshire will pay commissions when a banker is involved in a deal, but doesn't hire them to analyze. In one deal he offered $35 a share; the target's banker spent a week and then pleaded for a higher price to justify the bill. Warren gave $35.05 so they "got the last nickel out of me."
- **Israeli company:** a letter arrived unsolicited from an Israeli company; Berkshire bought 80% for $4 billion and later the remaining 20%, without Warren visiting Israel.
- **BNSF:** the railroad business "had a bad century" but was rationalized and modernized, and is "not a great business but... a good business." In fall 2009 Berkshire already owned a fair amount. On a Thursday he said Berkshire would pay $100 per share if directors were interested; the board checked over the weekend and a contract was signed the following Sunday.

chunks.heading: Compounding, the U.S. economy and giving
chunks.text:
- He calls the U.S. the best place he knows to invest: "nobody has sold America short since 1776." With about 2% growth and just under 1% population growth, per-capita GDP adds roughly $18-19,000 per person (about $75,000 for a family of four) in one 25-year generation. Compounding an already prosperous economy means people live far better in 20 years.
- He says his life has been "a product of compound interest."
- He held off giving much away during the intermediate decades because he felt he was compounding fast enough to give away "billions instead of millions" later. His first wife died in 2004, ending the plan for her to handle his giving, so he chose to give to the Gates Foundation rather than do the work himself. He declined to have his name on it.
- He believes anyone making millions a year should pay at least 30% combined payroll and income tax, and says everyone in his office does except him.

chunks.heading: Bill Gates, Berkshire's culture and advice for young investors
chunks.text:
- He met Gates through Meg Greenfield's invitation and Gates's mother, Mary; they talked about 11 hours straight. He bought 100 shares of Microsoft just to keep track of the young founder.
- The first Berkshire annual meeting drew 12 people, including his aunt and uncle; now about 40,000 attend. He never imagined the scale and says he "put one foot in front of the other."
- Money has no utility to him; time does. He gets "to do every day what I love with people that I love," and likens Berkshire to a painting with an unlimited canvas and no finish line.
- Advice: "look for the job that you would want to hold if you didn't need a job." Marrying the right person matters more than earning X versus 120% of X. Don't worry about making the most money this week or next month. He offered to work for Graham for nothing, "and I meant it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a long CNBC interview after his 2018 letter, Buffett explains why Berkshire overpaid for Kraft Heinz, why a good business can't fix a bad price, and why he shrugs off mark-to-market swings. He also covers buying stocks when cheaper, buybacks, index funds, IPOs, Bitcoin, and the American tailwind.

chunks.heading: How Warren reads the Kraft Heinz write-down and what he paid for it
chunks.text:
- Warren says Kraft Heinz is still a great business on tangible assets: it uses about $7 billion of tangible assets and earned about $6 billion pre-tax (after depreciation, before amortization).
- Berkshire and certain predecessors paid about $100 billion more than the tangible assets, so for Berkshire the business has to earn on roughly $107 billion, not $7 billion.
- "The business does not earn more just because you pay more for it." If Berkshire had paid $7 billion for it, the earnings would be the same.
- Warren says Berkshire overpaid for Kraft (not for Heinz) and calls the $15 billion write-down fair. He does his own write-downs in his head, and the market had already marked it down further.
- The full company was valued at roughly $71-72 billion: about 1.2 billion shares at around $42 billion of equity, plus about $31 billion of debt. At that price, with earnings not expected to grow in 2019, he sees better places to put money.
- Debt of about $31 billion is higher than originally projected to the rating agencies, because the company paid out a lot and kept little to retire debt. Cutting the dividend from $250 million to $160 million saves about $1.1 billion a year, which helps only slowly.
- He has never sold a share and has no intention of selling or buying more. He would be happy to still be in it in 5 or 10 years and is happy to be George Paulo's partner.
- He is not on the board, and is reluctant to trade partly because purchases and sales must be reported within two days.

chunks.heading: Packaged-goods brands versus retailers
chunks.text:
- Warren says he and 3G misjudged the retailer-versus-brand fight. The retailers have gained ground and the weaker brands lose out; only the strongest brands can go toe-to-toe with Walmart or Costco.
- His example: Heinz dates to 1869 and Kraft to C.W. Post in 1895, with global distribution and a fortune spent on advertising, and sales of about $26-27 billion. Costco launched Kirkland in 1992 and did about $39 billion last year with only about 750 outlets, 50% more than all the Kraft Heinz brands combined.
- Private label is getting stronger and will keep getting bigger. Few new billion-dollar food brands are being created, and physical volume hasn't changed much, but the ability to raise prices has.
- He doesn't think the problem is Millennials changing habits, or under-investment in innovation: big food companies rarely produce new products that become big. Heinz ketchup has about 60% of its market and is very strong; Kool-Aid and Jell-O are old brands in secular decline.
- Amazon and Walmart fighting is "like the elephants fighting," and the mice get trampled. He doesn't see the retailers' position weakening.
- The 3G cost-cutting acquisition model works less well now because acquisition prices rose: "anything at a price can be good" and "if you pay too much you pay too much", especially if you borrowed to do it.

chunks.heading: Buying stocks and bad news on holdings
chunks.text:
- "The stock market is there not to instruct me, it's there to serve me." When a holding falls on bad news, the question is whether the long-term valuation has changed. Bad news about a fundamentally good business can be a buying opportunity (he cites American Express in the sixties, the partnership's best investment).
- A stock does not know you own it. Paying $10, watching it fall to $8, and waiting to get back to $10 is "nuts"; likewise selling half after it doubles.
- He prefers prices to fall when he is a long-term holder and a company is buying back shares: Berkshire is better off if Apple is cheaper while it repurchases. Apple has said it will go to cash neutral, about $130 billion away, and he expects mostly buybacks. At $200 that retires about 650 million shares; at $150 about 900 million.
- He would be buying Apple at lower levels. His average cost is about $141 and he has never sold a share himself; Ted or Todd trimmed about 3 million shares to fund another purchase, and Warren was not involved in that. He owns about 5% and likes the idea of drifting past 6% as Apple shrinks its share count.
- He generally avoids going over 10% of a company, because it complicates life, and with banks it makes Berkshire a bank holding company. Some banks he owns at 9-plus percent, so he leaves room for a year or two of buybacks.
- On a $4 billion one-day loss on a $173 billion equity portfolio: it doesn't bother him. If you like a business and it is cheaper, you'd want to buy more, like paying less for hamburger.

chunks.heading: Why Warren likes banks and how he thinks about valuing them
chunks.text:
- He added to JPMorgan, Bank of America, Bank of New York, PNC and US Bancorp. They are good businesses that are cheaper than other good businesses.
- JPMorgan earns roughly 15-17% on tangible equity, which is "incredible in the world of 3% bonds." His thought experiment: an FDIC-guaranteed deposit paying 15% by mistake and not redeemable would be worth well over 300 cents on the dollar, and more if the interest could compound.
- Bank of America's Brian Moynihan was the most underestimated bank executive in the country: he did what he said, beat his targets, and has repurchased shares smartly.
- Bank health: no FDIC-insured bank failed last year. The FDIC fund holds about $100 billion, all from banks, with no government money.
- Banks, like other US businesses, benefited from the tax cut, which could be reversed.
- He sold the short-lived Oracle position because he did not understand where the cloud business is going, after his IBM experience. He changed his mind on understanding it, not on valuation. He sold IBM at much higher prices than today and is not bothered that it has bounced.

chunks.heading: Stocks versus bonds, interest rates and finding deals
chunks.text:
- Whether stocks are expensive "depends on interest rates." If 3% long bonds prevail for 30 years, stocks are incredibly cheap. He would give enormous odds that the S&P outperforms 30-year bonds over 30 years.
- Given a choice of a 10-year bond or the S&P 500 held 10 years, he would "buy the S&P in a second."
- He doesn't understand why rates are so low worldwide so long into a recovery, and calls it a world not described in classical economics. Japan since 1990 is the possible precedent, though Japan has a declining population and no energy resources.
- Warren does not trade on Federal Reserve statements. Berkshire always spends more on the railroad and utility than depreciation and doesn't try to time in and out. He thinks Jay Powell is a terrific chairman.
- Why Berkshire didn't deploy more in Q4: it had a possible large deal in mind, which didn't come together. He prefers buying a whole business to buying stocks. Berkshire had about $112 billion in cash (including the $20 billion floor), and he says it would love to use it.
- Whole-business buying is harder because of competition from private equity, which he calls "private debt to a great extent," borrowing six or seven times EBITDA (a metric he doesn't use). A $1 trillion pool leveraged with $2 trillion of debt could buy $3 trillion of assets, plus corporate buyers. Deals in the 1970s leveraged buyouts were far more attractive.
- In the 2008 panic Berkshire spent about $16 billion in three weeks (roughly Sept. 15 to Oct. 7 or 8), when nobody else was spending, plus had $3 billion committed to Dow. It tried to buy Constellation Energy.
- Size is his constraint: investing $5 billion in a company at 10% of market cap needs a $50 billion company, and a 50% gain adds only about half a percent to Berkshire. There are perhaps a hundred stocks that can move the needle. He also faces far more competition and far more available data than in 1951, when he dug through manuals and visited the Interstate Commerce Commission and the insurance commissions.

chunks.heading: Reporting Berkshire: operating earnings, market value and the "groves"
chunks.text:
- Warren dropped book value as the lead metric because Berkshire is now overwhelmingly an operating company; market value is the more relevant measure over time. He kept both in the letter in a year when the change did not flatter him.
- He wrote the letter as if explaining to his sisters, Doris and Bertie, who hold nearly all their money in Berkshire, whether to sell their shares, since Berkshire may repurchase stock.
- He groups Berkshire's 80-90 businesses and close to 390,000 employees into "groves" (non-insurance businesses, equities, insurance, and cash and Treasuries) so the value of each can be judged, rather than looking at every tree.
- He won't name the diseased trees, for morale reasons; they are a tiny part of earnings and some are simply in industries in decline.
- BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy are the biggest redwoods, together earning about $8 billion after tax last year, about a third of operating earnings.
- Operating earnings were $24.8 billion, 41% above any prior year. GAAP earnings were about $4 billion because of a roughly $20.6 billion unrealized loss on the equity portfolio (new accounting rule: unrealized gains and losses now run through income) and a $3 billion Kraft Heinz write-down.
- He expects to make money on stocks over time but has no idea which years are up or down. Judge them over ten years. The $173 billion portfolio holds companies retaining earnings and shrinking share counts.
- Managers: Greg Abel and Ajit Jain each received about $18 million last year, mostly base salary with a discretionary bonus. Their pay is not deductible above $1 million, which he says doesn't bother him. Ted Weschler and Todd Combs each manage about $13 billion and are a tiny bit behind the S&P since arriving (they had clawback exposure on their pay), but are valuable on acquisitions and other work.

chunks.heading: Betting on America, politics and taxes
chunks.text:
- Warren bought his first stock on March 11, 1942 (three shares of City Service preferred for $114.75). A million dollars in the S&P 500 over that time, reinvested, would be $5.3 billion with no need to read a headline or an annual report: "all you had to do was believe in America." Household wealth is about $108 trillion.
- Most people should own an S&P 500 index fund because most people do not know how to pick stocks, and aggregate investors by definition get average returns before fees. His instructions for his widow's money: 90% in an S&P 500 index fund, 10% in governments.
- On politics: he has invested under 14 presidents, 7 Republican and 7 Democrat. He says do not look at investing through a political prism, because a staunch partisan would have missed a great deal over 77 years.
- He believes the rich are under-taxed relative to the general population, and thinks the Earned Income Tax Credit is the best way to help decent people without market skills. He would not move to avoid higher taxes: America is where people want to come.
- The deficit is about $1 trillion (about 5% of GDP) in a good year; a 2-3% deficit would not push debt-to-GDP up.
- He is wary of public pension liabilities in some states; corporate pensions are less of a problem now.
- On tariffs: a 10% tariff has had some effect on Berkshire companies, mostly pushing prices up; 25% would force big adjustments. He hopes sense prevails in trade talks with China and generally expects two smart countries with a lot at stake to reach a rational outcome.
- On new tech IPOs: he dislikes them because the sellers pick the time to sell to you, whereas he likes picking his own time to buy. If a company is worth $50 billion, you should expect it to earn about $5 billion pre-tax within five years, and few do.
- On Bitcoin: it has no unique value and produces nothing, "a delusion basically." He has no knowledge of the marijuana industry.

chunks.heading: Timeless investing fundamentals
chunks.text:
- Warren says the fundamentals won't change in the next 50 or 100 years: investing is laying out a dollar of purchasing power today to get more back in the future.
- You must learn how to value businesses, know which are within your circle of competence and which are outside, and know something about how markets operate. "You don't buy a business unless you can value it."
- Rose Blumkin, who founded Nebraska Furniture Mart, arrived in 1917 unable to speak English, started with $2,500 and built the country's largest home-furnishing store, and could not read or write. Berkshire bought about 80% of it in 1983 on a handshake and a one-page contract, valuing it at $60 million on a 100% basis, without an audit. He treated her word as good as the Bank of England's.
- He and Bezos and Dimon's health-care venture is long term, aimed at a medical system now costing about 18% of GDP versus 5% earlier. He calls it a tapeworm on the economy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In his annual post-letter CNBC interview, Buffett argues stocks are businesses to own for decades, so daily selloffs and virus headlines should not change decisions. He covers interest rates, reaching for yield, bad incentives (Wells Fargo), and why Berkshire's conglomerate structure works.

chunks.heading: Why he buys stocks as businesses, not tickers
chunks.text:
- Warren says people would be better off thinking "I bought a business today, not a stock today." That frames the decision as owning a farm or apartment house for 10, 20 or 30 years.
- The only real question is whether the 10 or 20 year outlook for American businesses changed in the last 24 to 48 hours. He says it hasn't.
- He bought his first stock on March 12, 1941, and it fell about 2% that day. He has been a net buyer of stocks every year since he was 11, under every one of 15 presidents in his lifetime (7 Republicans, 7 Democrats after Hoover).
- Holdings are long-term: American Express for 20 years, Coca-Cola for 40 years.
- If a stock drops and you like the business, he says that is "good luck basically." A price quote 2% lower on a house you like "really doesn't make any difference" unless you have to sell.
- On an 800-point Dow drop (roughly 3%): "I like to buy stocks." He can't think of a 3% decline that shouldn't have been bought. Anything Berkshire was buying the previous Friday, it would buy more eagerly today.
- The Corona virus (the Feb 2020 selloff) makes no difference to his investments. Even if global growth were down 1% instead of 0.1%, he would still buy a business he likes at a price he likes.

chunks.heading: Valuation discipline: write down what you are buying and why
chunks.text:
- He says you should be able to take a yellow pad and state: "I am buying the General Motors Company for $42 billion because..." (1.4 billion shares at $30 per share, used as an illustration).
- Example: American Express has about 815 million shares at roughly $126, so about $100 billion. The question is whether the company is worth more or less than $100 billion, not what the stock does tomorrow, next week or next month.
- Market prediction is not needed and not possible: "If you can predict the market, you don't need to read balance sheets." He says nobody he has met knows what the market will do.
- He can't predict what his businesses will earn in 6 or 12 months, but is confident American business will be "fabulously better" in 20 to 30 years.
- Example of buying at the bottom: in 1932 General Motors had 19,000 dealers, and in one month sold less than a tenth of a car per dealer. That was a terrific time to buy GM.
- He watches indicators like rail car loadings but says he doesn't use them for specific investment decisions. He believes he can make money predicting 10 years out, not next week.
- Trouble is always coming (1942, 1949, 2008). In 2008 he wrote in the New York Times that trouble was coming "but I said buy stocks." He would still say buy stocks "if you get enough for your money."

chunks.heading: Stocks versus bonds, interest rates and reaching for yield
chunks.text:
- Edgar Lawrence Smith's 1924 book set out to show bonds beat stocks in deflation, but concluded the opposite: with equal yields, stocks win because retained earnings build additional value. Warren says Berkshire's value comes from retained earnings, not dividends.
- Ben Graham told him "you get more trouble with a good idea than a bad idea because the good idea works." The 1920s boom took Smith's idea past its limiting condition (bonds and stocks yielding the same) as stock prices ran up five or six times.
- Three basic alternatives: short-term cash (an option to act later), long-term bonds, or long-term stocks. At the time, stocks were cheaper than bonds.
- A 30-year bond at 2% means paying 50 times earnings for earnings that can't rise for 30 years. A 10-year at about 1.4% is roughly 70 times earnings with no growth for a decade.
- About $13 trillion was at negative rates worldwide. He says even Keynes and Adam Smith never addressed it, and "we don't know what that means." Interest rates are "the basis of all value."
- Cheap rates and loose lending (weak covenants, leveraged loans) raise the price buyers will pay for whole businesses, since they can borrow a large share of the price. That is part of why whole-company purchases looked expensive to him.
- Reaching for yield is "really stupid, but it's very human." Insurers and savers who need 3% but earn 1% should "quit giving 3%" or learn to live on 1%. "You should always adapt your consumption to your income," not the reverse.
- Reaching-for-yield excess can take longer than you think (like late-1990s tech), "but eventually you get to midnight and everything turns to pumpkins and mice."
- Low rates hurt life and annuity insurers that promised returns. Property-casualty insurers don't promise returns but still earn less on float.
- He notes the federal deficit was about 4.5% in good times and that the US benefits enormously from low interest costs. At 5% on $20 trillion the interest bill would be a trillion.

chunks.heading: Banks, Wells Fargo and incentive systems
chunks.text:
- Banks are a good business if they "don't do dumb things on the asset side." The commercial banks Berkshire owns earn roughly 12% to 16% on tangible assets, versus a 2% long bond. He says a 3-4% return on tangible assets isn't likely.
- Steeper yield curves matter more than the absolute level of rates. American banks earn well at low rates; European and Japanese banks earn lower returns and use more leverage, which he dislikes.
- Bank of America buys back so much stock that Berkshire's ownership rises 7 or 8% a year "without us spending a dime," plus a dividend.
- He would not comment on why Berkshire sold down Wells Fargo (partly to stay under 10% to avoid Fed filings) or on specific positions, and says Berkshire doesn't give stock advice.
- Wells Fargo lesson: "dumbest incentive system you can think"; people "will do what they're incented to do," and Berkshire has made the same mistake. The bigger failure was ignoring the problem once management knew.
- Charlie Munger's version: "an ounce of prevention is worth a ton of cure." Attack problems immediately. Shareholders ended up paying billions for phony accounts that earned them nothing.
- Craft Heinz: it earns about $5 billion pre-tax after depreciation on about $7 billion of tangible assets with no working capital, so it's a valuable business. But "we paid too much" and it carries too much debt. He thinks it can pay down debt and keep the dividend.

chunks.heading: Running Berkshire: decentralization, conglomerate discount and capital allocation
chunks.text:
- Subsidiary managers run their own businesses. He hasn't been to the See's Candies factory in at least 10 years and doesn't pick the box contents. BNSF will spend about $3.5 billion on capital and he approves none of it.
- What headquarters controls: dividend policy of subsidiaries and the movement of capital between them. See's, bought in 1972, has sent several billion to other businesses. Moving capital inside one company avoids the taxes of selling one stock to buy another.
- Managers also save about 25% of their time by never dealing with Wall Street or bankers, and they "never have to finance their businesses."
- Old conglomerates had a bad name for good reason: dirty pooling, touting stock and chain-letter behavior in the late 1960s. Berkshire has never wanted to issue shares or tout them. He notes index funds are also conglomerates of 500 businesses.
- Breaking up Berkshire wouldn't create value: it would be very tax-inefficient (the General Utilities doctrine ended in 1986), and the businesses have real synergies. Berkshire also uses less leverage than a piece-by-piece buyer would, by design, since it has insurance promises out 50 or 100 years.
- Shareholder base: "you get the shareholders you deserve." Run a hamburger stand or a French restaurant, but be clear which and don't mix. There are about 1,600-odd thousand A shares and he doesn't recruit new holders.
- He expects directors to resist "Wall Streeters bearing fees." All his shares go to charity over about 15 years after his death, and he wants them kept in Berkshire.
- GEICO: Berkshire bought control in 1995 at about 2.5% market share; it reached about 13.7%, premiums rose from about $2.5 billion to $35 billion, and it is number two to State Farm. He credits Tony Nicely. BNSF paid a $5 billion dividend last year against a $35 billion purchase price.
- Precision scheduled railroading: Hunter Harrison made customers adapt to the railroad and improved margins. BNSF's margins improved but less than peers; it gained share instead, and he says Berkshire could adopt the method if needed.
- On the underperformance of Berkshire against the S&P: size is part of it. He expects Berkshire to be neither in the top 10-15% nor the bottom of stocks over the next 10 to 15 years, outperforming in down markets, with only a small edge at a $550 billion market value.

chunks.heading: Cash, buybacks and reserve
chunks.text:
- Berkshire holds more than $125 billion in cash and about $240 billion in stocks; roughly 80% is in equities counting operating businesses and about 20% in cash. He would rather have that 20% in good businesses, but whole companies were expensive.
- Cash exists for the "chief job": protecting people's money. Insurance obligations (workers' comp and auto claims) run out 50 years, and "every check clears under any circumstances." Berkshire holds Treasury bills, not commercial paper, and doesn't rely on bank lines. When people get terrified, "everything freezes."
- Buybacks: Berkshire bought $5 billion last year (about 1% of market cap). Blocks are hard to buy because holders are long-term. He invited holders with roughly $20 million or more to call his office, if Berkshire is buying at that price level; only blocks, and not tire-kickers.
- Banks and Apple can buy 4-5% or more a year without moving the market; Berkshire cannot.

chunks.heading: Apple, airlines and what he buys
chunks.text:
- Apple is Berkshire's third largest business (about 5.6% owned). He doesn't think of it as a stock or a tech company but as "a consumer product company that uses technology," compared to See's Candies for its pervasive usefulness. "I should have appreciated it earlier."
- Corona virus effects he noted: Dairy Queen franchises in China, Apple's supply chain, and others (Johns Manville, Shaw). He will weigh where those businesses stand in 5 to 10 years, not the quarter.
- Berkshire owns close to 10% of each of the four largest airlines, the largest in Delta (roughly 11%). Buying one outright would be unlikely due to regulation and complications with American Express's bank-holding status. Past 15% in any company, Hart-Scott-Rodino rules apply.
- Whole-business purchases looked expensive because of cheap debt, so he put money into pieces of companies via stocks.
- He doesn't invest in cryptocurrencies, which "basically have no value and they don't produce anything"; they "can't mail you a check." He doesn't own any and never will. He also doesn't buy ETFs; a pension fund Berkshire doesn't manage bought them.
- On sustainable investing, he doesn't screen on it when choosing stocks.
- Newspapers: Berkshire is financing Lee; the Times, Journal and Post each sold their smaller papers, and he stayed in.

chunks.heading: Boards, directors and independence
chunks.text:
- Berkshire looks for directors who are business-savvy, have a strong personal interest in Berkshire, and have integrity. They represent shareholders.
- He has served on 21 public company boards. Many "independent" directors are paid about $300,000 a year for a few days of work, and "who wouldn't want a job like that?" Headhunters and CEOs ask who "won't cause too much trouble." "To call them independent is ridiculous," and ignoring the compensation factor is "ridiculous."
- Succession: the board knows exactly what to do if he dies tonight. Greg Abel and Ajit Jain are vice chairmen and will take questions at the annual meeting.
- Todd Combs at GEICO: Bill Roberts took over less than two years earlier and asked to retire; Todd knows insurance, and the plan is to promote from within. Insurance is the only business he knows well. Underwriting needs rates that match risk (correlating risk and rate), such as pricing 16-year-old males differently from 80-year-olds.
- Most months neither Ted Weschler nor Todd Combs changes the portfolio. In many years leaving a portfolio untouched would beat tinkering.

chunks.heading: Charlie, politics and taxes (brief)
chunks.text:
- Charlie Munger is "the best partner anybody could possibly have" after 60 years, with "the best 30 second mind in the world." Charlie dislikes EBITDA as an earnings measure, and Warren dislikes GAAP net income swings from marketable securities.
- Political views: he votes mostly Democratic but not as a "card-carrying" one. He'd vote for Michael Bloomberg over Sanders. He favors a much higher earned income tax credit so full-time workers aren't left behind, but says "I don't think we should have killed the capital system in the process."
- He wouldn't cast a presidential vote based on the market's next 30-90 days.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains what makes a good business (high return on tangible assets, bought at a sensible price), why banks lose money copying competitors, and why the market sits in a "zone of reasonableness." He also covers owning stocks without anchoring to cost, admitting mistakes early, and ignoring politics and macro forecasts.

chunks.heading: Buying car dealerships: what makes a good business
chunks.text:
- Warren defines a good business as "one that earns a high rate of return on tangible assets." The best ones earn that return and also grow, but even non-growers are good businesses if they earn high returns on tangible assets.
- Price still matters: pay too much and "you can turn a good business into a bad investment." Pay an appropriate price and you can do all right.
- His early mistake was buying a bad business at a really cheap price. It "took me about 20 or 30 years to figure out that wasn't a good idea."
- Car dealerships, run well, can be very good businesses. There are almost no receivables, inventory is financed through floor plan, and real estate can be leased (Berkshire owns about 95% of its own real estate, so the capital tied up is still small).
- Van Tuyl Group, which Berkshire bought in October 2014, has 78 dealerships averaging over $100 million in volume each. That volume allows narrow margins while still earning a high return on capital.
- There are over 17,000 dealerships in the US, down from roughly 30,000 40 or 50 years ago. The average dealer now does far greater volume even though the country and the number of nameplates have grown. [Note: transcript reads "177,000" and "30,000"; the dealer count is left out as ambiguous.]
- Berkshire buys such businesses "to own a 100 years," so the question is whether they make money in 2024 or 2044, not what the Fed or politics does this year.

chunks.heading: Why big banks became a merely good business
chunks.text:
- Banks earn on assets, not on net worth. New rules require more net worth per dollar of assets, so with constant earnings on assets, returns on net worth fall.
- Fifteen or ten years earlier the better banks were "ungodly profitable" thanks to high assets-to-net-worth ratios. Some cheated with even more assets than regulators allowed, such as Citigroup's off-balance-sheet vehicles (the CIVs).
- Warren says a very profitable business "has been turned into a good business if executed well."
- Funding is cheap: he says Wells Fargo has roughly a trillion dollars of deposits costing around 10 basis points.
- Banks get into trouble on the asset side, not the liability side or the expense side. They "start copying what their dumb competitors are doing."
- He quotes John Stumpf of Wells Fargo: "I don't know why we keep looking for new ways to lose money when the old ones work so well."
- Copycat behavior is a danger in every business. When someone says "we want to do this because the other guy is doing it," Warren tells managers to "go back to square one and come up with a better reason."
- Example: a well-known property-casualty insurance CEO pitched a life insurance acquisition with weak reasons, then threw up his hands and said, "all the other kids have one."

chunks.heading: The stock market and the "zone of reasonableness"
chunks.text:
- Warren once used total market capitalization to GDP (later dubbed the "Buffett indicator") in a Sun Valley talk reprinted in Fortune about 15 years earlier. It showed how extreme things had become when the ratio went from a historical norm of around 40% to a very high level. [Note: he said "170% or something"; he was not precise.]
- It was never meant as fine-tuning. He says the market is not like pi: "there's a range of reasonableness," and most of the time stocks trade within it.
- That range shifts as earnings accumulate and interest rates change.
- He has spoken publicly about the market being outside the range only about five times in his life. The most recent was early October 2008, when he said stocks were cheap in a New York Times op-ed. He expects maybe one definitive call every five or ten years.
- "Anybody thinks they can pinpoint it, it's crazy."
- At the time of this interview (October 2014), he says stocks are in the zone of reasonableness.
- You don't need precision: "if you buy good businesses at reasonable prices and hold them you're going to make a lot of money," and that holds for stocks as a group and for individual companies.

chunks.heading: Ignore macro and politics when making business decisions
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie Munger have made stock and business decisions together for 55 years. They have never made decisions differently based on which party is in power, whether rates would rise or fall, or labor negotiations.
- "You don't want to give up what you know how to do because of opinions which you don't know whether are right or not and which are going to be transitory in any event."
- Each day you "do whatever makes the most sense." What matters is "whether we get a good business with good management at a sensible price."
- On Washington gridlock he is an optimist: "I always say buy stock in a business that's so good that an idiot can run it because sooner or later one will." The country has been through a civil war and much worse, and "the game isn't over."
- His concern is a situation where a significant portion of people involved "don't even really want to succeed, they want the other person to fail."

chunks.heading: The economy and America's long-run growth
