chunks.text:
- Since 2009 he sees steady growth of around 2% across Berkshire's 70-plus businesses (railroad freight loadings, autos, and so on). It neither accelerated nor decelerated much. Autos were better than he expected and housing worse.
- The 2008 crisis was unlike other postwar recessions: people were scared, and Treasury bill rates went negative, meaning investors accepted less than they would get "putting money under your mattress."
- Population grows a little under 1% a year, so 2% real growth means over 20% per capita real GDP gain in 20 years. Real GDP is about $54,000 per person, so that is roughly $10,000 more per person in one generation.
- Real GDP per capita has increased six-fold in his lifetime (born 1930). It isn't because Americans are smarter or work harder: "it's because we have a system that unleashes human potential."
- Housing: he expects a catch-up because household formation, which fell in the recession, resumes. "I have a lot of faith in hormones." Berkshire's Clayton Homes will build about 30,000 homes that year, and he is wrong on timing so far.
- On mortgages: a 30-year fixed mortgage is a one-sided instrument. If rates fall you refinance; if they rise you keep your low rate. "I can't get that one-sided an instrument at Berkshire."

chunks.heading: When to sell: recognizing bad businesses and mistakes
chunks.text:
- Warren says you usually throw in the towel too late. He bought into textiles in 1965 and left about 20 years later, "about 20 years too late." People tend to hold on to justify old decisions.
- A clear sign of a bad business: a good manager and bad results. "When a management with a reputation for excellence encounters a business with a reputation for bad economics, it's the reputation of the business that remains intact."
- Textile example: Berkshire made over half of men's suit linings in the US and was named Sears' supplier of the year, but when it asked to raise prices a quarter of a cent per yard, Sears said ten others would sell at the old price. No customer asks for a particular lining, so there was no connection to the consumer.
- Dexter Shoe: he paid over $400 million in Berkshire stock, it started losing money right after purchase, and it went to zero because of foreign competition. That stock would now be worth about $5 billion. He had forgotten that shoes would no longer be made in the US.
- If a good person runs a business and it isn't making money, "you're in the wrong business" and you must face it quickly.

chunks.heading: How to think about stock prices and holding or selling
chunks.text:
- Warren loves it when things he owns go down: it means he can buy more for less, like finding something cheaper at the grocery store.
- People wrongly treat a falling price as a referendum on themselves. "The stock doesn't care what you paid" and "doesn't even care that you own it." Waiting to get back to your cost before selling makes no sense.
- The only question is whether you can get more for your money somewhere else, though you shouldn't ask it that frequently.
- Investors have an advantage over Andrew Carnegie, who could not shift from steel to retailing. With negligible commissions you can rearrange your holdings at a moment's notice.
- "There is nothing about the price action of the stock that tells you whether you should keep owning." What matters is what you expect the company to do versus the current price, compared with other businesses you understand equally well.

chunks.heading: Crisis anecdotes: Lehman, Barclays, and AIG in 2008
chunks.text:
- During the Lehman weekend, Bob Diamond of Barclays called Warren asking what he would charge to guarantee counterparties' contracts for 30 to 60 days until a Barclays shareholder vote. Diamond wanted the indemnity unlimited, which Warren says was "not a great word in the fall of 2008." Warren asked for a faxed offer, but none arrived. He only heard the voicemail months later, in July 2009.
- On AIG, he reviewed property-casualty materials for about an hour and told AIG's advisers he couldn't come up with a number that would help. He needed to know there were no cross-guarantees with AIG Financial Products.
- Tim Geithner later asked whether AIG's value supported an $85 billion Fed loan. Warren said nobody could know that day, but if AIG had staying power, the underlying subsidiaries would probably bring $85 billion in a normal market. They have since proven worth much more.
- In his view, without the New York Fed's money AIG "would have been in bankruptcy within 48 hours." Nobody else would have lent on terms half as onerous.
- 2008 was "like the fog of war," with inaccurate and biased reports from every front. He credits Paulson, Bernanke, Geithner and President Bush for doing the right thing, even if what led up to the crisis can be criticized.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's last meeting as CEO, where he announces Greg Abel will take over at year end. He explains why he holds $335B in cash, why markets demand emotional control, why he distrusts currency debasement and earnings management, and what makes Berkshire's insurance float unique.

chunks.heading: Announcing the succession: Greg Abel becomes CEO at year end
chunks.text:
- Warren reveals at the end of the 2025 meeting (60th annual) that he will recommend to the board, meeting the next day, that Greg Abel become CEO of Berkshire at year end. Two of the 11 directors (his children Howard and Susie) know; the rest will hear it first at the board meeting.
- The board will digest it and act at the following meeting, a few months later. He expects them to be unanimously in favor.
- Warren would "still hang around" and could be useful in periods of great opportunity or trouble, but "Greg would have the tickets" and the final word on operations and capital deployment.
- He thinks the board would be more willing to give Greg authority on large acquisitions if they knew Warren was around.
- He has "zero" intention of selling a single Berkshire share; it will be given away gradually. Keeping every share is "an economic decision" because he thinks Berkshire's prospects are better under Greg than under him.
- Berkshire has a reputation as an asset, not a liability, when government is in trouble, and he sees that as hard to have.
- On what makes Greg suited: Greg described his first meeting with Warren during the MidAmerican deal. Warren went straight to the derivatives on the balance sheet and asked what the underlying risk was. Later he asked how much money MidAmerican was making during the energy crisis. The answer was no more than before, because the derivatives supported the business and were not speculative.

chunks.heading: Cash pile, patience and acting fast
chunks.text:
- Berkshire holds about $335 billion in Treasuries. Warren would rather have about $50 billion, but opportunities don't arrive on a schedule.
- He would spend $100 billion if something made sense, was understood, offered good value, and carried no worry of loss. Berkshire came close to spending $10 billion not long before.
- Investing $50 billion a year until cash reached $50 billion "would be the dumbest thing in the world." Berkshire has roughly $40 billion a year coming in.
- "Things get extraordinarily attractive very occasionally." The long-term trend is up, but nobody knows what the market or business will do next week. He has never found anyone worth listening to on the subject.
- Charlie said they made most of their money from eight or nine ideas over 50 years. Warren says if you think you can get an idea a day, "forget it."
- Passive investors can make a few simple investments and sit. Berkshire chose to be opportunistic and has made money by not being fully invested at all times.
- Patience and speed both matter: be patient waiting for the call, but act that same afternoon when a deal makes sense. "You have to be willing to hang up after 5 seconds and you have to be willing to say yes after 5 seconds." You can't be filled with self-doubt.
- Example: in 1966 he bought a business (Associated Cotton Shops) from Ben Rosner's partner's widow for $6 million. It had $2 million in cash, a $2 million Philadelphia property, and earned $2 million a year pre-tax. Rosner said he'd stay only until December 31; Warren told Charlie that if he quit, "you can throw away every book on psychology I've ever read." Rosner stayed on for years.
- Greg adds that being patient means doing the reading and work in advance so Berkshire is ready to act quickly.
- Warren says there's a big difference between a few good ideas and the market's spread of opportunities. In 2008-09 he said lots of things came along; he thinks something big will come within 5 years and that probability rises with time, "like death."

chunks.heading: Market temperament and volatility
chunks.text:
- Berkshire shares have fallen 50% three times since he took over, with nothing fundamentally wrong with the company each time.
- The Dow was 381 in September 1929 and fell to 42. When he was born (August 30, 1930) it was 240, and it later hit 41. The 2025 drop was "nothing" by comparison.
- "If it makes a difference to you whether your stocks are down 15% or not, you need to get a somewhat different investment philosophy because the world is not going to adapt to you."
- He expects a "hair curler" in the next 20 years. Surprises get bigger as systems get more sophisticated.
- The market is a good place if you have the right temperament and terrible if you get frightened when it falls and excited when it rises. "You got to check [emotions] at the door."
- He doesn't have emotions about stock prices: "those decisions get all the way to my brain." If Berkshire fell 50% next week, he'd see "a fantastic opportunity."
- Berkshire's best deals come when people are most pessimistic. "Everything isn't properly appraised," and the more other people misjudge, the better the opportunity.
- Quarterly earnings are never a factor in decisions. He never raised a board discussion about how a move would affect annual earnings, and he warns that focusing on a number tempts managers to play with the numbers.

chunks.heading: Insurance, GEICO and float
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's insurance advantages can't be replicated. Float is free money as long as the underwriting is profitable; cost of float including life insurance was negative 2.2% in the latest period, "like running a bank where people leave their money with you and you pay a minus 2.2%."
- Warren paid $50 million for half of GEICO in 1976. Berkshire now owns 100%, and 50% of the roughly $2 billion GEICO earned in Q1 is $1 billion, about 20 times the original investment in a quarter. GEICO also provides $29 billion of float.
- Ajit Jain says Todd Combs cut the workforce from over 50,000 to about 30,000 (a reduction of 20,000), worth at least $2 billion a year. GEICO caught up on telematics and matching rate to risk, and has posted a combined ratio starting with an 8 for seven straight quarters.
- Warren on how GEICO began in 1936: Lorimer Davidson (Warren says "Lauren"/"Larmer"), who came from USAA, bet that government employees were better-than-average drivers and priced to make money from the first year. Warren visited GEICO on a Saturday in January 1951, pounded on the locked door until a janitor let him in, and spent hours with Davidson, which changed his life.
- Auto insurance in 1950 cost about $40 a year; now it can reach $2,000 or more. Deaths per 100 million miles fell from about six to a little over one, yet premiums rose about 50 times. Homeowners' premiums in Nebraska doubled in 10 years after inflation and are still unprofitable.
- Self-driving cars: insurance will shift from driver error toward product liability. Ajit and Greg note accidents may fall, but repair costs per accident will rise with the technology.
- Warren said he'd rather have Ajit making property-casualty insurance decisions with $100 billion for 10 years than the top AI product. Berkshire is dabbling in AI but waiting to see; "we are not very good at being the fastest or first mover."
- Berkshire exited the private equity-style life and annuity space. Ajit says PE firms use leverage and credit risk that works only while the economy is good and spreads are low, and regulators could get cranky. Warren notes PE firms copy Berkshire's float model but without the CEO having all his money in the company forever.
- Berkshire and Zurich and Chubb announced a joint operation to write very large risks.

chunks.heading: Japan, currency and the dollar
chunks.text:
- Warren found the five Japanese trading companies by reading a thick handbook of Japanese companies, and bought them for about a year at "ridiculously low prices." Berkshire is near the 10% limit and the limit is being relaxed somewhat.
- He expects to hold them for 50 years or forever and won't sell: "we will not be selling any stock." Greg meets them a couple of times a year and hopes to do large things with them globally.
- Berkshire has about $20 billion in these positions, but he'd rather have $100 billion: "size is an enemy" of performance.
- He sets no policy on Japanese rate moves. Berkshire borrows in yen to match yen assets because funding is cheap and the holding is permanent, the first time it has done that, but it is not a policy.
- He says "turn every page" is one important ingredient in investing, and the people who do it won't tell you what they find.
- On the dollar: governments tend to debase currencies over time and no system has beaten that. Fiscal policy is "what scares me" about the US. The only large currency bet Berkshire made was after his Fortune article, when it was long 12 currencies for a couple of years and made several billion dollars. He wouldn't rule out doing it again.
- A country attracting investors should develop a reputation for a solid currency; Berkshire avoids anywhere with a real chance of runaway inflation.
- Fiscal deficits: a roughly 7% gap versus perhaps 3% that is sustainable. "If something can't go on forever, it will end" (Herbert Stein). He says it's a job he doesn't want but should be done.

chunks.heading: Balance sheets, capital intensity and the cathedral and casino
chunks.text:
- Warren spends more time on balance sheets than income statements. He likes to look at a balance sheet over an 8-10 year period first, since it's harder to play games with. Wall Street pays little attention to them.
- Charlie's rule: don't take a position until you can argue the opposing case better than the person who holds it.
- Asset-light businesses are better: "it's always better to make a lot of money without putting up anything than by putting up a lot of money." Coca-Cola's syrup business takes little capital; bottling takes real money. Apple has needed almost no capital and shrunk its share count. The Magnificent 7 are now more capital-intensive with AI spending, and he doesn't know whether that holds.
- Property-casualty insurance needs capital only as a guarantee fund, so the float can fund low-capital businesses.
- Money managers get rich by getting an override on other people's capital. If shareholders had paid 1% to manage Berkshire's assets last year, it would have been about $8 billion. He and Charlie put all their own money in and shared the losses.
- US capitalism is "a magnificent cathedral" attached to "a massive casino." The risk is the casino overtaking the cathedral, since people like the bells and drinks.
- Buybacks: Berkshire does none unless shares are almost certainly underpriced on conservative valuation. A 1% tax on buybacks means Berkshire pays more than a seller gets, and costs Apple about $1 billion a year on roughly $100 billion of repurchases.
- Earnings notes: Q1 underwriting income was down sharply from an exceptional prior year, with prices down and risks up. Of 49 non-insurance businesses tracked closely, 21 were up and 28 down.

chunks.heading: Utilities, wildfires and the BHE write-down
chunks.text:
- Warren says the mistake with PacifiCorp was not carving it into seven state companies; it came as one aggregate. Some states are now "rat poison," as Charlie would say, for utility investors.
- Value of Berkshire Hathaway Energy fell from roughly $87 billion to $48.8 billion in two years because of societal trend and a real estate ruling, not just PacifiCorp's liabilities. The Scott family sale and the Greg sale happened at different times. He says BHE "is worth considerably less money than it was two years ago."
- Greg on wildfire risk: it can be reduced, not eliminated. Berkshire hardens assets, and now de-energizes lines when fires approach, which went against how employees were trained to keep lights on. Berkshire cannot be the "insurer of last resort."
- The 2020 Oregon fire is the largest, about 60% of claims; Berkshire says it started from a lightning strike outside its territory.
- Warren on Berkshire's role: it won't take your money and attempt unsolvable problems; "it's easier to do stupid things with other people's money than your own."
- Grid: America needs a government-private partnership similar to the interstate highway system or World War II production, because 48 jurisdictions can't coordinate. Berkshire has capital and knowhow but no workable model yet; it's a "clear and present use of hundreds of billions."
- Greg: Berkshire respects state policy. In Iowa it invested $16 billion in renewables and retired five of ten coal units, and still needs the other five to keep the system stable.

chunks.heading: Management, hiring and life lessons
chunks.text:
- Greg's capital allocation approach: protect Berkshire's reputation, keep a "fortress" balance sheet and never depend on a bank, and use operating cash flow and float. He looks first at investing in existing businesses, then at buying whole companies, then at owning pieces through equities. He only invests if he can judge economics 5, 10 and 20 years out and understands the risk, whether it's 100% or 2% of a company.
- Greg manages with more engagement than Warren did: questions, linking managers (such as GEICO's tech transformation to others), while keeping autonomy. Warren says some managers need help and some should be left alone.
- Warren on culture: managers' behavior is contagious downward; if a boss games things, employees do too, and it's hard to rebuild. Quality falls more easily than it rises.
- Best manager he knew was Tom Murphy Sr., who "got the potential out of other people." Others he cites: Sandy Gottesman, Walter Scott, Bill Scott. Berkshire "held on to the human assets."
- Advice for young people: associate with people better than you; you go in the direction of those around you. Look for a job you'd hold if you didn't need the money. Be careful who you work for. Don't ignore a job's culture. Find the "sound" you're built for; he found investing at 7-8 years old. Spend time reading and you'll learn.
- A teacher trick: a Warren interview method with CEOs was to ask which competitor's stock they'd own if stranded on a desert island for ten years, and why. He asked it of coal companies 70 years ago. He used an hourglass for a 10-minute meeting.
- Setbacks: look at the bright side; he says people born now are very lucky.
- Warren says the most important trait is not getting rich once; "you only have to get rich once." Never do anything that risks what you've built, and avoid participating in stupid things around you.
- His reading as a boy: his dad's books on Saturdays, then every investment book in the Omaha library. He credits Ben Graham and David Dodd.

chunks.heading: Trade, tariffs and America
chunks.text:
- Warren's 2003 Fortune import certificates idea aimed to balance imports and exports, not tariffs as weapons. Charlie thought it "too Rube Goldberg."
- He says trade can be an act of war, and he thinks balanced, cooperative trade benefits everyone. "Trade should not be a weapon."
- In a world with 8 nuclear nations, some unstable, it's unwise for 300 million people to crow while billions are envious. "The more prosperous the rest of the world becomes, it won't be at our expense."
- He says the US's luckiest day for him was the day he was born. America has changed constantly and fixed things slowly (the Constitution's early flaws, the 19th Amendment in 1920), and he says not to get discouraged.
- Health care: he says it's about 20% of GDP and the JPMorgan/Amazon/Berkshire venture couldn't dent it. "The tapeworm won," because the system is entrenched and only government can change it.
- On DOGE and government waste: bureaucracy is contagious, and government has no checks. The real issue is currency and the fiscal gap.
- Ben Franklin question: Warren would tell Franklin to keep thinking, avoid lecturing the world, and build a system that doesn't invent things that can destroy the planet. Fundamental to a stable society is a currency that doesn't get debased.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett opens the 2023 Berkshire meeting explaining operating earnings, retained earnings, and insurance float as a liability that works like free equity. He then covers Geico and reinsurance, Apple, the Japanese trading houses, buybacks, succession, and why he is still optimistic about America.

chunks.heading: Why Warren expects Berkshire's operating earnings to hold up in 2023
chunks.text:
- Q1 2023 operating earnings were a little over $8 billion. Operating earnings are Berkshire's GAAP earnings excluding realized and unrealized capital gains.
- Warren expects capital gains over time ("why would we own the stocks otherwise"), but stock prices "move around capriciously" in any quarter, year or even five-year period. He judges the businesses, not the quotes.
- The post-pandemic period was "about as extraordinary as I've seen in business since World War II": government money chased scarce goods, buyers did not wait for sales, and backlogs were full. That period has ended.
- He expects a majority of Berkshire's operating businesses to report lower earnings in 2023 than in 2022. Some managers over-ordered inventory that arrived just as demand cooled, and now need sales.
- Two items push the other way:
  - Investment income: about $125 billion sat in very short-term investments earning roughly 4 basis points (about $50 million a year). Berkshire had just bought $3 billion of T-bills at about 5.9%, which means roughly $5 billion a year on the same cash.
  - Insurance underwriting: it does not correlate with the business cycle. It depends on events like hurricanes and earthquakes, so on probability the year should beat 2022. One massive quake or a hurricane in the wrong place could change that.
- He cautions that "nothing is sure" in forecasts, and Berkshire pays little attention to markets or forecasts.

chunks.heading: Retained earnings, net worth and per-share ownership
chunks.text:
- Berkshire retains all earnings, so operating earnings should be significantly higher in 5, 10 or 15 years. Warren calls this "no great triumph" because retention is what built the number from nothing. Historical growth rates cannot be repeated on today's capital base.
- Gaap net worth was about $504 billion at March 31. No other US company reports a larger number. This is not because Berkshire is the most valuable company; others used their cash to repurchase shares.
- The class A equivalent share count falls every year through buybacks. Owners' share of the businesses rises without them investing a dollar.
- Berkshire paid a dividend once, 10 cents a share in 1967, which Warren calls "a terrible mistake." He says he confessed to the board, and notes that retention produced the $500 billion of equity and over $30 billion of annual operating earnings.
- Cash and T-bills grew by roughly $6-7 billion in April. The pieces: about $400 million of stock buys, about $4 billion from net stock sales, and about $2.5 billion of operating earnings.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and Berkshire's underwriting position
chunks.text:
- Float was $165 billion. It is money from premiums paid in advance, shown as a liability for unpaid losses, but it is held by Berkshire and has cost essentially nothing in most years.
- Warren compares it to "a bank with no employees, no interest and no ability to withdraw the money in a hurry." He says it finances assets the way stockholders' equity does, but without the cost. Equity is expensive; long-term debt can be cheap for a while but can become expensive or unavailable.
- Float grew from "a pittance" in 1986 to $165 billion under Ajit Jain, who joined that year.
- Berkshire's insurers hold about 26% of the net worth of all US property-casualty companies. Berkshire carries about four times the usual stockholder capital behind each premium dollar. It also receives $25 billion or more a year in earnings from non-insurance businesses, and it pays no dividend and has no big debt maturities in its insurance operations.
- Buyers of large insurance liabilities have no comparable counterparty:
  - Lloyd's used Berkshire to resuscitate its market.
  - On the 2016 AIG deal, Berkshire assumed up to $20 billion of liabilities for about $10 billion upfront. It is not required to put the $10 billion into matching bonds; it goes into the general pool of assets. Ajit says actual payouts are 96% of projections so far, funding cost is "significantly less than four percent," and Berkshire earned a fee of about $1 million in 2015 dollars. He calls himself cautiously optimistic since the game is not over.
  - Warren says deals of this size are ones where "there isn't any other stop."
- Property catastrophe reinsurance: Ajit passed on weak pricing at the January 1 renewal, kept capital in reserve, then wrote a lot at April 1 when prices rose. The portfolio is heavily weighted to Florida. A big Florida hurricane could cost up to about $15 billion across units; with no loss, the book makes several billion.
- Berkshire thinks of insurance exposure as about 5% of capital of a little under $300 billion. When Ajit asked to raise exposure from $13 billion to $15 billion, Warren said yes in under 30 seconds.
- Ajit rates Berkshire Hathaway Specialty (started with four people and now about 1,500 worldwide) as roughly $12 billion of float built with essentially no underwriting loss. Warren says it is the one insurer started in the last ten years that he knows to be an "overwhelming success." He says the many tech-labeled insurance startups lost huge sums and consumed capital, and he would not want to own any of them.
- Geico: Ajit says the combined ratio was about 93 in Q1, flattered by prior-year reserve releases and seasonally good Q1 auto results. He expects just under 100 for the year, aiming for 96 by end of next year, and prioritizes profitability over growth. The telematics gap is a technology problem: more than 600 legacy systems being consolidated to 15-16.
- On automakers selling their own insurance (GM, Tesla), Ajit says insurance at point of sale is convenient but needs driver data, and margins are thin (about 4%). Warren notes GM has done insurance for decades and says it is hard to improve on matching price to risk. He points to State Farm, a mutual that "took twenty points out of the cost" in the 1920s, as the one big idea in auto insurance.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation, buybacks and why Berkshire holds cash
chunks.text:
- Warren's capital-allocation order: first do what the businesses need, then grow or buy more businesses, then consider dividends. Dividends are close to irrevocable ("you don't cut dividends"), so that decision is made carefully.
- On repurchases: if there is ample capital and the stock is below intrinsic value, it enhances value for the remaining owners. "It's no more complicated than if you and I and Charlie had a business and you wanted to sell your interest" for less than it is worth, without misleading you about it. Above intrinsic value, he says buying back is the wrong move whatever an investment banker says. Greg Abel understands capital allocation as well as Warren and will make these decisions in the same framework.
- Berkshire holds a lot of liquidity and avoids debt maturities and cashable insurance policies, so it never faces uncomfortable cash needs at inconvenient times. He frames the business model as being able to serve as a plus to the country in a crisis.
- Because Berkshire has no investor calls and makes no earnings promises, it can ignore Wall Street's quarterly expectations. Warren wants to own wonderful businesses "forever" and says "the world was made to order" for anyone thinking five, ten or twenty years out, since most others are short-term focused.

chunks.heading: Concentration and Apple
chunks.text:
- Warren rejects the claim that Apple is 35% of Berkshire's portfolio. Berkshire's assets are the whole enterprise: railroad, energy, See's, insurance, plus the securities. He says Berkshire "can't own more than 100%" of anything, and Apple is one more business.
- Apple's own buybacks lift Berkshire's ownership with no spending. Shares outstanding were about 15.7 billion and falling, Berkshire owned about 5.6-6%, and each extra tenth of a percent adds about $100 million to Berkshire's share of earnings.
- He calls Apple a better business than any Berkshire owns outright, including the railroad. His reasoning: consumers will pay about $1,500 for a phone and would give up a second car (about $35,000) before the iPhone. He says he does not understand the phone itself but understands consumer behavior. Berkshire's Apple stake is larger than its energy business.
- He says he made a mistake selling some Apple shares a couple of years back for tax-year reasons.
- Charlie's view: broad diversification "is an insane idea" if you only have a few good ideas. Own your best ideas rather than your worst; "know the edge of your own ability."
- Berkshire lost the Taiwan Semiconductor position (about $5 billion sold) over location. Warren calls TSMC a superbly managed company and "one of the best" but says he would rather deploy capital in the US, and feels better about capital in Japan than in Taiwan.

chunks.heading: Finding opportunities: Japan, value investing and the market environment
chunks.text:
- Charlie's description of the Japanese trading houses: five large, understandable companies earning roughly 14% on what Berkshire would pay, paying decent dividends, repurchasing shares, and owning many businesses Berkshire could understand. Berkshire could eliminate currency risk by financing in yen at about half a percent. "If you get 14 on one side and a half a percent on the other," it works. Warren says he bought for months before telling Greg, announced at 5%+ on his birthday, and now owns 7.4% of each, with a cap of 9.9% unless the company agrees. The yen issuance that was planned at 56 billion yen turned out to be about 164 billion yen. Warren says the position is ahead by "four or five billion" plus dividends, and Berkshire is the largest corporate borrower in Japan outside Japanese companies.
- Warren and Charlie both visited Japan; Greg joined for two days of meetings with the five companies.
- On whether value investing is harder now: Warren says to get used to making less, and that opportunities come from "other people doing dumb things," not from technology. He argues there are more big dumb things now because money is much easier to raise (for example, ten or fifteen dumb insurance startups in a decade). Small-capital investors have the advantage. He would "love to be born today" and start with little money.
- The T-bill market had a visible mispricing the week of the meeting (debt-ceiling doubts), which let Berkshire buy $3 billion at about 5.9%.
- Benjamin Graham: Warren says Graham did things for him without expecting anything in return. The Intelligent Investor (the 1949 book) has sold about 7.3 million copies and still ranks around #300-350 on Amazon, which Warren calls unmatched staying power. Charlie notes that over half of Graham's lifetime investment returns came from one stock, Geico, which Graham acknowledged; the Geico deal almost fell apart over a $25,000 difference in net worth.
- Warren's learning approach: he says he learns as he goes by watching consumer behavior across See's, apparel chains, auto dealerships (about 80), and Apple, and that early mistakes (department store business in 1966) taught him lessons. Charlie says he read "thousands and thousands of pages" of Moody's manuals in the past. Warren says he never looks at where managers went to school.

chunks.heading: Management, succession and Berkshire's long-term durability
chunks.text:
- Greg Abel will succeed Warren as CEO and handle capital allocation. Insurance stays with Ajit under a deliberately separated structure. Warren declines to name the next layer of successors now because "a lot can change." He calls the idea of an "executive bench" largely "baloney": few people can run the largest US company by net worth, and the key is a top capital allocator plus strong operating managers.
- The board's new-CEO job would be hard to judge at a business as strong as Berkshire, because "if they don't show up at the office it'll keep working for a long time." Warren relays Tom Murphy: "The secret of business is to buy a good business, and it's okay to inherit one too."
- Warren has 99% of his net worth in Berkshire, and an estimated $100 billion or more of philanthropy rides on it.
- Hiring and loyalty stories:
  - Ajit walked into Warren's office on a Saturday in 1986 with zero insurance experience; Warren recognized him quickly. Warren says if he could pick the best ten insurance managers in the world, he could not replace Ajit.
  - Ben Rosner, who left school after fourth grade, ran the retailer Berkshire bought; Warren says he knew retailing in tough neighborhoods better than anyone. Warren says Rosner was the kind of person who could not be replaced when he died.
  - Paul Andrews of TTI chose Berkshire as the owner for his business because a competitor would fire his people and private equity would plan its exit.
  - Charlie, on Louie Vincenti at Wesco: Berkshire bought Wesco for tens of millions and it became worth two or three billion, in part because Berkshire did not meddle.
- Protecting against a takeover after Warren's death: Warren says Greg and the directors will get a long honeymoon, and with no dividends and a trillion-plus market value in 12-15 years, a raider needs enormous borrowing capacity. He wants Berkshire regarded "as a national asset rather than a national liability."
- Berkshire's decisions are rational rather than emotional in business, but Warren concedes loyalty to managers sometimes delays replacing them. Charlie adds that Berkshire changes managers far less frequently than other conglomerates, which helps results.
- For estate planning: Charlie and Warren advise being transparent. Warren will not sign a will until his three children have read it and made suggestions. He says kids learn values from how parents live, and recommends writing your own obituary and reversing it.

chunks.heading: Warren's outlook on risk, society and the US
chunks.text:
- Warren will not bet against America. The country began with half of one percent of world population in 1790 and now has about a quarter of world GDP. He would pick the US and today as the best time and place to be born, and he points to personal examples like a recent root canal. He sees partisanship drifting toward "tribalism," which he says leads to mobs.
- Nuclear risk: he compares AI to the atom bomb, which could not be uninvented. Of AI he says "it can do all kinds of things, and when something can do all kinds of things I get a little bit worried." Charlie doubts the hype and prefers "old-fashioned intelligence."
- The US and China: Charlie says the tension was "wrongly created on both sides," and calls for more trade, citing Apple's China partnership as good for both. Warren says the two superpowers must understand the game and not push too far, comparing it to Cold War mutually assured destruction.
- Commercial real estate: the hollowing out of downtowns is "going to be quite significant and quite unpleasant." Buildings will remain, but owners will change. Warren notes the common standard that "a building is worth what you can borrow without signing your name." Rates have risen from the era of 2.5% loans; lenders will end up holding properties they do not want. Berkshire does not use commercial real estate heavily because it suits taxable investors better than corporations.
- Silicon Valley Bank: Warren says failing to cover all deposits would have been catastrophic. He says no official would go on TV and explain they were insuring only $250,000 and running the system.
- Energy transition: Greg says Berkshire Hathaway Energy has about $70 billion of known projects over the next decade, and the 2030 goal of cutting carbon 50% versus 2005. Pacific Corp's transmission plan started in the mid-2000s at about $6 billion and has cost about $7 billion for roughly a third of the build, with Greg describing multi-state transmission as the big bottleneck. Warren says World War II showed that the US can reorient industry quickly under unified authority, and doubts a peacetime 50-state system can do the same.
- BNSF: Warren says railroads will always have derailments (over 1,000 a year industry-wide) given weight, grades and 22,000 miles of track, and that BNSF must carry hazardous materials as a common carrier. Greg acknowledges BNSF breached a tribal-land easement on crude trains and says Berkshire is pursuing a resolution.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett fields shareholder questions on Apple, cash, succession, insurance, utilities and AI. He stresses owning stocks as businesses, swinging only at pitches he likes, compounding retained earnings, pricing insurance risk one year at a time, and being kind and lucky.

chunks.heading: How Warren treats stocks as businesses and why Apple is his largest holding
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie looked at marketable equities as businesses, whether the stock was Dairy Queen, Coca-Cola, American Express or Apple. They cannot buy 80-90% of every wonderful company, but they evaluate each stock as a business.
- He makes no attempt to predict markets or pick stocks. He spent years doing the wrong thing, fascinated by stocks, charts and moving averages, until he read *The Intelligent Investor*.
- The Graham lesson: treat the market as something there "to serve you," not to instruct you. Warren says the approach is "so simple that it's almost deceptive," and that investing needs the right mindset rather than ever more math or physics.
- Barring something dramatic that changes capital allocation strategy, Berkshire will keep American Express, Coca-Cola and Apple, and Apple will remain the largest common stock holding.
- He calls American Express "a wonderful business," Coca-Cola "a wonderful business," and Apple "an even better business." He says return on tangible equity at Coca-Cola, American Express and Apple makes utility returns look like "a whole different game."
- He is comfortable building cash under current conditions, given what is available in equity markets.

chunks.heading: Taxes, the fiscal deficit and why selling some Apple was acceptable
chunks.text:
- Warren says he does not mind paying taxes, and Berkshire pays 21% federal on the gains it realizes in Apple. That rate was 35% not long ago and 52% in the past.
- The government effectively owns a percentage of Berkshire's earnings and can change that percentage any year. He thinks current fiscal policy cannot continue and that higher taxes are quite likely.
- Berkshire sent over $5 billion to the US Treasury last year. He says that if 800 other companies did the same, no other person in the country would need to pay federal taxes of any kind. He hopes Berkshire stays in "the 800 club" and moves up.
- He frames the tax payment as appropriate for a company in a country that has been so generous to Berkshire's owners, and says shareholders shouldn't mind that Berkshire sold some Apple.
- Treasury market size is not his worry. He says he doesn't worry about the quantity of US debt but about the fiscal deficit, which the media ignores while fixating on the Fed. The risk is inflation and the future value of the dollar, as Paul Volcker understood. He sees no real alternative to the dollar as a reserve currency.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's economic goal, retained earnings and the cash pile
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's goal is to increase operating earnings and reduce shares outstanding. Warren says that is simple to describe, "not quite so simple to pull off."
- Operating earnings are the figure Berkshire uses because they strip out wild market swings. First-quarter operating earnings were $11.2 billion, helped by higher yields on short-term holdings. Investment income was certain to rise for the year.
- The earnings history he showed: $24 billion pre-pandemic, then a pandemic dip, then $27 billion, $30 billion and $37 billion. These figures are after depreciation, amortization and taxes. Warren says that works out to a little over $100 million per day to deploy, including weekends.
- Shareholders' equity was $574 billion (he also cites $571 billion) at March 31. Berkshire has retained earnings since taking control, apart from one 10-cent dividend decreed in about 1968 while he was "in the restroom."
- Compounding on a long runway is the mechanism, "without any Miracles." JP Morgan, second on equity, had $327 billion at year end and about $338 billion at quarter end. But it pays dividends and repurchases shares, so it does not plow back as Berkshire does.
- Cash and Treasury bills were $182 billion at quarter end, and he expected about $200 billion by the end of the next quarter. He says nobody at the table knows how to use it effectively right now. It would sit there at 5.4% or at 1%.
- "We only swing at pitches we like." He would not swing because he had passed on the last two pitches.
- Buying back stock adds slightly to value at current levels, but Berkshire can't repurchase in size because holders don't sell. The investors in the room don't think about selling, and "the people who check the price daily have not made the money" that those who forgot about it have.
- Large sums are hard to deploy. He says he could earn high returns on $10 million, and that something like Japan would have been better at a smaller size. He is not on "a hunger strike" and would do another Japan-style deal if one appeared.

chunks.heading: Japan, Costco, BYD and investing abroad
chunks.text:
- Warren says his primary investments will always be in the United States. He expects anything really big to be American, and says he doesn't pick up on other cultures well.
- The US went from about half a percent of world population to well over 20% of world output in a short time. He feels less likely to make a major mistake with your money in the US than in many other countries.
- Coca-Cola is the preferred soft drink in something like 170-180 of 200 countries, which he calls almost unmatched. American Express has strengthened dramatically over 20 years.
- The Japan commitment, made five years ago, was "overwhelmingly compelling." Berkshire bought as fast as it could over a year. He feels extremely good about the position.
- Charlie pounded the table with him twice, once for BYD and once for Costco. Warren says he should have been more aggressive in Costco. It was not fatal, but Charlie was "right big time" on both.
- Canada is comfortable: Berkshire would put big money there if an idea met its standards. He mentioned that a deal in a financial institution in Canada was done in a couple of days.
- India could be great, but the question is whether Berkshire has an advantage. He said a more energetic management could pursue it, since Berkshire's name is known worldwide.

chunks.heading: Recognizing a big investment: Apple, Geico and Occidental
chunks.text:
- Warren says Charlie and he decided very fast, but only after years of thinking about the parameters that enable the quick decision.
- Consumer behavior knowledge came from mistakes and small businesses. Berkshire's Baltimore furniture chain failed, but taught him how people behave. See's Candy was a study in consumer behavior, too. He did not learn how to run a department store or make candy.
- With Apple, he watched customers at the furniture store refuse to leave without one, even at prices with no profit, and he came to see it as "one of the great products maybe the greatest product of all time." People would give up a $30-35,000 second car before their iPhone, which costs a twentieth as much.
- He credits Tim Cook as a partner to Steve Jobs who did one thing extraordinarily well.
- The mental process resembles a "perceptive mass" crystallizing: many observations and knowledge then produce action, and "you can prepare yourself for it happening tomorrow."
- Geico: in 1950 Lorimer Davidson taught him in four hours on a Saturday what auto insurance was.
- Occidental: the original decision came over a weekend, then he kept buying as he learned more about the assets, the operations and the CEO's capital allocation. Berkshire holds options to buy more and intends to keep it. He does not know the price of oil.
- Paramount: he was 100% responsible for the decision, and Berkshire sold it all and lost a fair amount of money. He says he's smarter about the entertainment business now, but he paid for that knowledge.
- Warren sold shares for several reasons, including needing the money, but that rarely applies to Berkshire.

chunks.heading: Insurance: float, pricing and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- Insurance is the most important business at Berkshire. Ajit Jain joined in 1986 and Warren says Berkshire won't find another, but the structure he built means the business will still be very good.
- Contracts run mostly one year, so Berkshire can reprice or exit each year. Ajit said the one-year horizon is what lets Berkshire stay in climate-exposed lines. Prices need to go up a lot, and regulators who block exits make that harder. Warren says climate change "makes our business bigger over time" provided risks are priced correctly: "if there was no risk there'd be no insurance business."
- On hurricane risk, Warren prefers one very smart underwriter like Ajit over a thousand analysts of water currents.
- Inflation done right helped the risk bearer. Geico had about 175,000 policies at about $40 a car (roughly $7 million of volume) in 1950, and now writes about $40 billion.
- Geico's edge: lowest costs, with the underwriting expense ratio below 10%. It lagged in matching rate to risk and data analytics, and Ajit expected it to be among the best by end of 2025. Warren says it isn't a survival or profitability threat, and Geico had about 16 million policies without losing policyholders in March.
- Cyber insurance: Warren and Ajit see aggregation as the problem. A single event could link thousands of policies, and there is little data on loss costs. Ajit told underwriters to assume every cyber policy loses money, whatever the price. Warren said everyone will rush into fashionable lines because agents like them, and "as Charlie would say it may be rat poison."
- Florida: lawyers and fraud push losses up, and storms add more. Berkshire grew exposure last year and nothing bad happened. Ajit expects rates to rise and a workable balance in time.
- On autonomous cars, Warren says fewer accidents would lower insurance volume but be good for society. Ajit noted repair costs per accident have skyrocketed.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation, succession and management
chunks.text:
- Greg Abel will be CEO, and capital allocation, including the common stock portfolio, should rest with him. Warren says knowing businesses means you understand common stocks, and he would not split it among many managers. Greg said the capital allocation principles of today will continue.
- Greg sees equities as investing in a business, whether 1% or 100%, judged on economic prospects, sustainability, and what it looks like in 10 years, with excess cash in Treasuries to keep the "Fortress of a balance sheet."
- Warren says most of the job of the directors is picking the right CEO. The CEO must not be someone who wants to retire at 65. The other 1% is correcting a wrong pick, which is very hard.
- Managers now prefer to call Greg and Ajit, and Warren gets close to zero calls. He says Greg sees more of the managers, handles weak performers and delivers hard news well, as Charlie and he did not.
- Warren expects huge sums to be needed instantly maybe once every 10 years. In 2008-09 others had money but were paralyzed. Berkshire acted, and the government treated it as an asset. He wants Berkshire seen as an asset, not a supplicant.
- Tom Murphy was the best business manager he knew. The key is buying the right business: a great manager can't fix a terrible one, which is why he stayed too long in textiles, partly liking Ken Chace.
- Pilot: a couple of directors had doubts, but Warren says "all's well that ends well." He praises Adam Wright's story and the business, with over 800 locations on interstates averaging 10-12 acres.
- Tech Data: Berkshire bid in 2019 and the original bidder raised, and "we never make the same offer twice." Distribution is a decent business, not one to dream about, as TTI (Paul Andrews) shows. Berkshire won't pursue small acquisitions itself.
- Railroads: Warren bought BNSF in 2009 and says a 100%-owned rail is more tax-efficient than partial stakes. Greg said BNSF margins trail the other five Class I railroads because costs were not reset to demand after 2022. Fixes include yards, locomotive fleet and labor allocation. Railroads are essential and could not be built today.

chunks.heading: Utilities, energy and regulatory risk
chunks.text:
- Berkshire Hathaway Energy had severe earnings disappointment last year. Warren says utilities are asked to earn modest returns, and "whether you earn X or go broke is not an equation that works." He said Berkshire would invest $100 billion or more but will not "throw good money after bad."
- Greg: demand will double in Iowa by the mid-2030s and triple in Nevada, requiring a working regulatory compact. After wildfires, Berkshire changed its culture to prioritize de-energizing lines and speed shutoffs. Utah caps non-economic wildfire damages and created a fund, which Greg called the gold standard.
- Warren expects Utah to treat Berkshire fairly. Solar will not be the only source. Batteries run about four hours, and gas is needed for reliability, so Nevada's last two coal units retire and are replaced by a new gas unit.

chunks.heading: Temperament, heroes and life lessons
chunks.text:
- Warren advises thinking about how you'd like your obituary to read, then choosing your path. "Find the job you would like if you didn't need a job." He urges being kind: "you can be kind."
- He values a partner who never lies. Charlie never told him a half-lie or shaped a story. Warren says to surround yourself with trusted people, as he has since his 20s.
- Pick the right heroes by values and motivation. His father loved him even when he broke rules (the runaway-from-home story).
- He tells shareholders not to beat themselves up over the past. He believes the future can be changed and that "if you're lucky in life make sure a bunch of other people are lucky too."
- Luck matters: he was born male and American, and says anyone claiming to have done it all alone is delusional.
- Shareholders defer consumption for decades and then give it away. Ruth Gottesman gave $1 billion of Berkshire stock to Albert Einstein College of Medicine, making tuition free.
- Estate: he leaves his wife 90% in an S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short-term government bonds. He urges everyone to have a will (four presidents died intestate).
- Starting small: he'd read every page of manuals like Moody's, becoming deeply interested in obscure companies. With $1 million one could earn 50%, but "you have to be in love with the subject."
- AI: he compares it to the nuclear genie. He saw a deepfake of himself that he could not distinguish, and says scamming will be the "growth industry of all time."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett argues record EPS means little when equity compounds, so return on equity is the real measure. He explains buying marketable stocks as if buying whole businesses, why insurance magnifies manager quality, and why tailwind businesses beat headwind ones like textiles.

chunks.heading: Return on equity, not EPS, measures managerial performance
chunks.text:
- Warren says most companies define "record" earnings as a new high in earnings per share, but businesses routinely add to their equity base each year, so rising EPS alone proves little.
- A 10% increase in equity capital paired with a 5% increase in EPS is nothing noteworthy. Even "a totally dormant savings account" produces steadily rising interest earnings through compounding.
- He prefers return on equity capital as the measure of managerial economic performance. Exceptions: companies with unusual debt-equity ratios or important assets carried at unrealistic balance sheet values.
- 1977 example: operating earnings were $21,904,000, or $22.54 per share, a 19% return on beginning equity. That was slightly better than 1976 and above both Berkshire's long-term average and American industry's.
- Per-share operating earnings rose 37%, but beginning capital rose 24%, so the gain was "considerably less impressive than it might appear at first glance."
- Capital gains or losses realized directly by Berkshire or its insurance subsidiaries are excluded from operating earnings. Over the longer term, aggregate gains and losses still matter.

chunks.heading: Tailwinds versus headwinds: choosing the business
chunks.text:
- Warren contrasts textiles with insurance. In textiles, "even very good management probably can average only modest results." In insurance, some mistakes can be made and overall performance can still be quite satisfactory.
- A lesson learned, and sometimes re-learned: "the importance of being in businesses where tailwinds prevail rather than headwinds."
- Textile operations had another very poor year. Berkshire had mistakenly predicted better results in each of the prior two years. Marketing and manufacturing problems persisted, some from industry conditions and some self-made.
- Why Berkshire stayed in textiles despite poor expected returns on capital:
  - The New Bedford and Manchester mills were among the largest local employers, with an older workforce whose skills were non-transferable.
  - Workers and unions cooperated on cost structure and product mix.
  - Ken Chace's work after the 1965 change of control generated textile capital that financed the acquisition and expansion of the insurance operation.
  - At least modest profits seemed achievable with effort and imagination.
- Single-year snapshots mislead. Berkshire Fine Spinning and Hathaway Manufacturing merged in 1955. In 1948 their pro forma combined after-tax earnings were almost $18 million, with 10,000 employees at a dozen New England mills (versus IBM $28 million, Safeway $10 million, 3M $13 million, Time $9 million).
- In the decade after the merger, sales of $595 million produced an aggregate loss of $10 million. By 1964 only two mills remained and net worth had fallen to $22 million from $53 million.

chunks.heading: Insurance underwriting: the pricing cycle and managerial discipline
chunks.text:
- Berkshire entered insurance in early 1967 by buying National Indemnity and National Fire and Marine for about $8.6 million. Premium volume grew from $22 million in 1967 to $151 million in 1977, almost 600%, with no Berkshire shares issued.
- Growth came from National Indemnity's traditional liability lines, new startups (Cornhusker 1970, Lakeland 1971, Texas United 1972, Insurance Company of Iowa 1973, Kansas Fire and Casualty late 1977), cash purchases (Home and Automobile 1971, Kerkling/Central Fire and Casualty 1976, Cypress at yearend 1977), and added products, notably reinsurance.
- Mistakes were real: a surety operation started in 1969, Home and Auto's 1973 urban auto expansion into Miami, an unresolved aviation "fronting" arrangement, and California workers' compensation.
- The cycle: big rate increases in 1976 offset disastrous 1974-75 results. Because policies are typically one-year, repricing errors are fixed only at renewal, so the full earnings impact arrived in 1977.
- Costs in Berkshire's lines rise close to 1% per month from monetary inflation and "social inflation" (a broadening definition by society and juries of what is covered). Unless rates rise 1% per month, underwriting profits shrink. Rate increases had slowed sharply, and he expected margins to decline by the second half of 1978.
- Discipline: as markets loosen and rates become inadequate, Berkshire must accept reduced volume. "It runs counter to normal institutional behavior to let the other fellow take away business - even at foolish prices."
- National Indemnity's large volume gains came with excellent margins after competitors contracted or withdrew following 1974-75. Credit went to Phil Liesche, Roland Miller (underwriting) and Bill Lyons (claims).
- Reinsurance (George Young) had a combined ratio of 107.1, unsatisfactory but trending down, and generates unusually high investable funds relative to premium.
- Homestate operation (John Ringwalt): five companies, $23 million net premium versus $5.5 million three years earlier. All four full-year companies had combined ratios below 100; Cornhusker was 93.8 and had been below 100 in six of seven full years.
- Home and Auto (John Seward) was turned from red ink and possible extinction to sound, profitable and growing.
- Cypress Insurance (workers' comp, Milt Thornton) was bought for cash at yearend 1977, with about $12.5 million of volume not in 1977 results.

chunks.heading: Why people matter so much in insurance
chunks.text:
- Warren says insurers sell standardized policies anyone can copy, and their only product is a promise.
- Licensing is not difficult and rates are an open book. There are no important advantages from trademarks, patents, location, corporate longevity or raw material sources, and little consumer differentiation to insulate from competition.
- Annual reports commonly stress the difference people make; sometimes true, sometimes not. But the nature of insurance "magnifies the effect which individual managers have on company performance."

chunks.heading: Insurance float invested: results and the long-term scorecard
chunks.text:
- From 1975 to 1977, insurance investments at cost (excluding the Blue Chip Stamps stake) grew from $134.6 million to $252.8 million, driven by reserve growth from premium volume plus retained earnings.
- Pre-tax net investment income rose from $8.4 million in 1975 to $12.3 million in 1977. Realized pre-tax capital gains were $6.9 million, about a quarter from bonds.
- Unrealized stock gain at yearend 1977 was about $74 million, versus an unrealized loss of $17 million at the end of 1974. Warren says such single-date figures should not be taken too seriously.
- Most large positions will be held for many years, and "the scorecard on our investment decisions will be provided by business results over that period, and not by prices on any given day."
- He considers it as foolish to be mesmerized by near-term earnings when buying small pieces of a company as when buying a whole one.
- Largest holdings (cost / market, $000s): Washington Post Class B $10,628 / $33,401; GEICO convertible preferred $19,417 / $33,033; Interpublic $4,531 / $17,187; Capital Cities $10,909 / $13,228; GEICO common $4,116 / $10,516; Kaiser Aluminum $11,218 / $9,981; Knight-Ridder $7,534 / $8,736; Ogilvy & Mather $2,762 / $6,960; Kaiser Industries $778 / $6,039. Total equities: $106.9 million cost, $181.1 million market.

chunks.heading: How Warren selects stocks: buy pieces of businesses
chunks.text:
- He picks marketable equities the way he would evaluate buying a whole business. Four criteria:
  1. A business he can understand.
  2. Favorable long-term prospects.
  3. Operated by honest and competent people.
  4. Available at a very attractive price.
- He ordinarily makes no attempt to buy for short-term stock price behavior. If business results keep satisfying him, he welcomes lower prices on stocks he owns as a chance to buy "more of a good thing at a better price."
- Pro-rata slices of truly outstanding businesses sometimes sell in securities markets at very large discounts to what they would fetch in negotiated whole-company deals. So "bargains in business ownership, which simply are not available directly through corporate acquisition, can be obtained indirectly through stock ownership."
- When prices are right, Berkshire will take very large positions with no intent to control, and no expectation of sale or merger, betting that excellent business results translate over time into market value and dividends for minority and majority owners alike.
- These positions may barely affect reported operating earnings at first. Capital Cities: $10.9 million invested in 1977; attributable earnings about $1.3 million, but only the $40,000 annual cash dividend flows into operating earnings.

chunks.heading: Non-control can beat control: the Capital Cities case
chunks.text:
- Warren says Capital Cities has "both extraordinary properties and extraordinary management," skilled in both operations and the deployment of corporate capital.
- Buying such properties directly would cost roughly twice what Berkshire paid through the stock market, with no important advantages from direct ownership.
- Control would bring the opportunity and responsibility to manage operations and capital, but Berkshire could not match the management already in place.
- Conclusion: "we can obtain a better management result through non-control than control." He calls this unorthodox but believes it sound.

chunks.heading: Banking and See's Candies: high returns on little capital
chunks.text:
- Illinois National Bank earns about three times the asset return of most large banks while paying maximum rates to savers and holding low-risk, highly liquid assets.
- Gene Abegg founded it in 1931 with $250,000; first full-year earnings were $8,782. No new capital has been added. Since Berkshire's 1969 purchase, $20 million in dividends have been paid. 1977 earnings were $3.6 million, more than many banks two or three times its size.
- Abegg, 80, asked that a successor be brought in; Peter Jeffrey became President and CEO March 1, with Abegg staying as Chairman.
- Blue Chip Stamps: Berkshire owned about 36.5% at yearend 1977. Blue Chip earned about $12.9 million from operations plus $4.1 million in realized securities gains.
- See's Candies (Chuck Huggins), bought by Blue Chip at the start of 1972, grew pre-tax operating earnings from $4.2 million to $12.6 million with little additional capital, in an industry with practically no unit growth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains how Berkshire's insurance float is put into concentrated stakes in outstanding businesses like SAFECO, bought below intrinsic value while corporations overpay for whole companies. He also shows why capital-intensive commodity businesses like textiles earn inadequate returns, and praises owner-minded managers.

chunks.heading: 1978 results and how Warren reads consolidated accounts
chunks.text:
- Warren says full consolidation of Blue Chip Stamps (about 58% owned after the Diversified Retailing merger on Dec 30, 1978) mixes wholly and partly owned businesses and "tends to obscure economic reality more than illuminate it". It is a presentation never prepared for internal use and of no value in managing.
- He therefore reports segment by segment, and shows Berkshire's own share of each business's earnings. Berkshire owns about 58% of Blue Chip, which owns 80% of Wesco, so Berkshire's equity in Wesco's earnings is about 46%.
- Controlled businesses had about 7,000 employees and over $500 million in revenues.
- Operating earnings, excluding capital gains, were 19.4% of beginning shareholders' investment, near the 1972 record.
- Net worth per share roughly doubled over three years, about 25% compounded, helped by good operations and capital gains. Warren says neither the 25% nor the 19.4% is sustainable, as the insurance cycle turned down in 1979.
- He holds that capital gains or losses should not be used to judge a single year, but they matter in the long-term record.
- Table figures (pre-tax operating earnings, Berkshire share, after-tax) are "close approximations", not "holy writ". After-tax earnings from operations were $30.1 million in 1978 vs $23.1 million in 1977, plus $9.2 million of realized securities gains.

chunks.heading: Textiles: why undifferentiated, capital-intensive businesses earn poor returns
chunks.text:
- Textiles earned $1.3 million on about $17 million of capital employed, a low return despite plant carried on the books at a small fraction of replacement cost.
- Capital turnover is low because receivables and inventory are high relative to sales. Low turnover plus thin margins "inevitably produces inadequate returns on capital".
- Warren's rule: producers of undifferentiated goods in capital-intensive industries earn inadequate returns except under tight supply or real shortage. While excess capacity exists, prices reflect direct operating costs, not capital employed.
- Management is diligent (product differentiation, lower costs, better fabric mix), "The problem, of course, is that our competitors are just as diligently doing the same thing."
- He hopes not to buy many more businesses with such economics, but keeps supporting the mills because they are major community employers, management reports problems candidly, labor is cooperative, and the business should average modest cash returns. This is despite "more attractive alternative uses for capital".

chunks.heading: Insurance underwriting: cycles, reserving and honest costs
chunks.text:
- National Indemnity's segment run by Phil Liesche earned about $11 million underwriting profit on roughly $90 million of earned premiums. Warren credits the managers and founder Jack Ringwalt, whose philosophy "remains etched upon the company".
- Overall 1978 underwriting was good because the industry was "flying high". He expected the industry combined ratio to rise in 1979, possibly into an underwriting loss.
- Auto rates were only 3% higher in January 1979 than a year earlier, while repair and medical costs rose over 9%. In contrast, at yearend 1976 rates were up 22% against costs up 8%. Margins hold only if rates rise as fast as costs.
- Warren warns that self-delusion in reserving, especially in long-tail reinsurance and casualty lines, is easy and leads to inadequate industry rates. If major players don't know their true costs, the competitive "fall-out" hits even those who do.
- George Young's reinsurance unit generates large sums to invest relative to premiums (float), but underwriting is "not what it should be". Warren says Young would cut volume to get satisfactory underwriting.
- California workers' compensation volume was cut to about 25% of its level eighteen months earlier under Frank DeNardo.
- On expansion: "it is easier to buy one than create one", though some of his own insurance expansion efforts were lackluster or expensive failures. National Indemnity, bought in 1967, remains by far the best part.

chunks.heading: Four criteria for committing insurance capital to stocks
chunks.text:
- Warren commits a big percentage of insurance net worth to equities only when he finds (1) businesses he can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) priced very attractively. Usually a few names pass the first three; price (4) often prevents action.
- In 1971 equity holdings were only $10.7 million at cost, since few excellent companies were available at interesting prices. Pension managers that year put a record 122% of net funds into stocks; in 1974 they put in a record-low 21%; in 1978 only 9%, a new low.
- From end 1975 to end 1978 the equity portfolio grew from $39.3 million (market equal to cost) to $129.1 million cost and $216.5 million market. Realized gains of about $24.7 million brought combined gains to about $112 million pre-tax, while the Dow fell from 852 to 805. He calls it "a marvelous period for the value-oriented equity buyer".
- Policy is concentration: avoid "buying a little of this or that" when lukewarm about business or price; when convinced, buy worthwhile amounts.
- He makes no attempt to predict markets: "successfully forecasting short term stock price movements is something we think neither we nor anyone else can do."
- He prefers prices stay low, since he expects to be a net buyer in most years. Consistent attractive purchasing is worth more than selling chances from a short-term run-up.

chunks.heading: Buying parts of businesses cheaper than whole businesses
chunks.text:
- Warren finds small slices of "really outstanding businesses" in the stock market at prices "dramatically cheaper" than inferior businesses fetch in negotiated sales.
- Either corporations are making big mistakes buying whole businesses at negotiated and takeover prices, or Berkshire will profit by buying portions at the discounted market prices.
- SAFECO example: 953,750 shares, cost $23.9 million, market $26.5 million. He calls it probably the best-run large property and casualty insurer, with superb underwriting, conservative reserving and sensible investing, better than Berkshire's own operation or anything he could buy control of.
- Berkshire paid "substantially under book value", less than 100 cents on the dollar for the best company, when "far more than 100 cents on the dollar" is paid for mediocre companies. A new startup cannot be built at under 100 cents on the dollar either.
- Other large holdings (cost / market, $ thousands): Washington Post 10,628 / 43,445; GEICO preferred 19,417 / 28,314 plus common 4,116 / 9,060; Interpublic 4,531 / 19,039; Kaiser Aluminum 18,085 / 18,671; Knight-Ridder 7,534 / 10,267; ABC 6,082 / 8,626.

chunks.heading: Passive ownership and the value of retained earnings
chunks.text:
- With a minor stake Berkshire can't direct SAFECO, but Warren asks why he would want to, as the record shows they manage better than he could. Even with control of such a company, "the proper policy also would be to sit back and let management do its job". Passivity costs only excitement and prestige.
- SAFECO earnings attributable to Berkshire were $6.1 million, but only dividends (about 18% of earnings) hit reported operating earnings. He views the retained balance as "just as real in terms of eventual benefit" and possibly worth "more than 100 cents on the dollar" if reinvested well.
- He is glad when wholly owned businesses retain all earnings if they can reinvest at attractive rates, and sees no reason to feel differently about well-run companies he partly owns.
- The reverse: in low-capital-need industries, or where management has a record of low-return projects, earnings should be paid out or used to repurchase shares, "often by far the most attractive option for capital utilization".
- He says look-through retained earnings may be as significant long term as reported earnings, and hopes markets keep letting insurance subsidiaries buy underlying earning power cheaply.

chunks.heading: Managers who think like owners: banking and retailing
chunks.text:
- Illinois National Bank (Rockford, bought March 1969; Gene Abegg, Pete Jeffrey) earned about 2.1% of average assets, roughly three times major banks, with less asset risk. Since 1968: consumer time deposits quadrupled, net income tripled, trust income more than doubled, with costs tightly controlled. Berkshire must divest by Dec 31, 1980, most likely by spinning it off to shareholders.
- Cost insight: a manager of a high-cost operation is "uncommonly resourceful" at adding overhead; a manager of a tight operation keeps finding ways to cut costs even when already below competitors.
- Associated Retail Stores (about 75 popular-priced women's apparel stores; started 1931 with one store and $3,200; Ben Rosner and Leo Simon) has not grown and faces adverse trends, yet Rosner's merchandising, real estate and cost skills produced returns on necessary capital often near 20% after tax.
- Top managers Rosner (75), Abegg (81) and Louie Vincenti (73, Wesco) show an "almost passionately proprietary attitude". Warren says these unorthodox relationships have been rewarding financially and personally: managers who enjoy coming to work and "instinctively and unerringly think like owners".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett argues managers should be judged on return on equity capital rather than EPS growth, shows how inflation plus taxes can erase even a 20% return, and explains why a good business at a fair price beats a poor one at a bargain. He also covers underwriting discipline, avoiding long bonds, and candid owner reporting.

chunks.heading: Warren on accounting measures: operating ROE, not EPS, and why market-value net worth distorts
chunks.text:
- Warren measures a single year's operating performance as operating earnings (before securities gains or losses) divided by beginning shareholders' equity with all securities valued at cost. For 1979 this was 18.6% of beginning net worth.
- He argues measuring against equity with securities at market distorts the result: a large market decline shrinks net worth and makes mediocre operating earnings look unrealistically good, while strong investment success inflates the base and makes operations look worse.
- Insurance equity securities must now be carried at market value, which raises 1978 and 1979 net worth. Blue Chip Stamps still uses lower of cost or market, so the same stock bought at the same price by two subsidiaries can be carried at two different values.
- Earnings per share rose about 20% in 1979, but Warren calls it the wrong figure to focus on. Berkshire had far more capital in 1979, and its return on that capital fell short of 1978.
- "Earnings per share" rises constantly on a savings account or fixed-rate bond because interest is plowed back into the capital base: "even a 'stopped clock' can look like a growth stock if the dividend payout ratio is low."
- His primary test of managerial economic performance is a high earnings rate on equity capital employed, without undue leverage or accounting gimmickry, not consistent EPS gains. He thinks managements and analysts should de-emphasize EPS and its yearly changes.
- For long-term performance he does count realized and unrealized capital gains and uses market-value statements, since over years they matter as much as operating earnings. They are too capricious to judge a single year.

chunks.heading: Long-term results and the "investor's misery index"
chunks.text:
- Book value per share went from $19.46 (September 30, 1964) to $335.85 at yearend 1979 with equities at market, a 20.5% compound annual gain. This was achieved with low financial leverage, low insurance premium-to-capital leverage, and no significant share issuance or repurchase.
- He notes the 1964 book value probably overstated intrinsic value, since the textile assets weren't worth 100 cents on the dollar either as a going concern or in liquidation.
- Warren warns that a 20% compounded return no longer guarantees a good real return. At 14% inflation, after-tax purchasing power gain is "very close to zero," because most of the remaining six points goes to income tax when converting gains to cash.
- He defines the "investor's misery index": inflation rate plus the percentage of capital the owner must pay in taxes (ordinary income tax on dividends, capital gains tax on retained earnings) to move the business's earnings into his pocket. When it exceeds the business's return on equity, the investor's real capital shrinks even if he consumes nothing.
- A 3% savings bond, 5% passbook account or 8% Treasury note were each turned by inflation into instruments that chew up purchasing power; a business earning 20% can do the same under inflation not much worse than prevailing.
- He has no corporate solution: high inflation won't raise Berkshire's returns on equity. A commentator noted 1964 book value bought about half an ounce of gold, and 1979 book value buys about the same half ounce. The rub: "government has been exceptionally able in printing money and creating promises, but is unable to print gold or create oil."
- External conditions affecting currency stability may be the most important factor in whether shareholders earn real rewards.

chunks.heading: Easy businesses versus turnarounds: the Waumbec lesson
chunks.text:
- Warren says some businesses, like a network TV station, make it "virtually impossible to avoid earning extraordinary returns on tangible capital." Their assets sell at extraordinary prices (a thousand cents or more on the dollar), but "despite a fancy price tag, the 'easy' business may be the better route to go."
- He tried the other route with Waumbec Mills in Manchester, New Hampshire. The price was an extraordinary bargain by any statistical test: below working capital, with machinery and real estate effectively for less than nothing.
- It was still a mistake: "new problems arose as fast as old problems were tamed."
- His conclusion from operating and investment experience: "turnarounds" seldom turn, and the same energy and talent are better used "in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price."
- The textile business produces some cash but at a low rate relative to capital employed, which Warren attributes to the industry, not the managers.
- Some Waumbec pieces proved useful additions to the decorator line at New Bedford, the strongest franchise, and Manchester might run profitably on a reduced scale, but the original rationale did not prove out.
- Ben Rosner at Associated Retail Stores produces very large earnings relative to capital, realized in cash rather than receivables and inventories, in a low-growth market.

chunks.heading: Insurance underwriting discipline and the cycle
chunks.text:
- The industry combined ratio rose from about 97.4% to 100.7% in 1979; Berkshire's fell from 98.2% to 97.1%. Warren forecasts the industry averaging around 105 over the next five years.
- He disagrees with the conventional view that rates firm in 1981. High interest rates encourage writing business at underwriting loss levels once regarded as unacceptable, so he expects competition to create "a new threshold of tolerance for underwriting losses."
- National Indemnity's section under Phil Liesche earned an $8.4 million underwriting profit on about $82 million of earned premiums. Warren praises him for actually cutting volume when business doesn't make sense: "if business makes sense, he writes it; if it doesn't, he rejects it."
- Berkshire does not lay off people because of volume swings from this policy; he'd "rather have some slack in the organization" than keep everyone busy writing money-losing business. This discipline came from founder Jack Ringwalt.
- Cypress (workers' compensation) followed the same rule of sticking with business it understands and wants regardless of volume, and turned out to be "an absolute gem."
