- On reinsurance, he warns that capital inflows and softer prices on rising exposures may produce disastrous results for entrants, especially given the "long tail" that lets catastrophic loss experience fester undetected. Berkshire's reinsurance may shrink during the extended competition, since "it will be hard for us to be a whole lot smarter than the crowd."
- Insurance "tends to magnify, to an unusual degree, human managerial talent - or the lack of it," and has potential for terrible results in a single year, for example if auto accident frequency turns. Part of the 1979 reprieve was fewer accidents from changed driving habits after higher gas prices, a "dosage of serendipity" that won't last.
- He admits mistakes in the Homestate group, including data processing reorganization, and entered surety reinsurance late in the year, seeking long-term "partnership" relationships with quality client insurers.

chunks.heading: Bonds in an inflationary world: "Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be"
chunks.text:
- The insurance industry lost an extraordinary amount in bonds. Warren suggests the accounting convention of carrying bonds at amortized cost may have contributed, since market-value recognition might have focused attention earlier on the dangers of very long contracts.
- He points to an inconsistency: insurers shifted auto policies from one year to six months because they couldn't forecast costs a year out, then invested the proceeds by "selling the money at a fixed price for thirty or forty years."
- The very long-term bond is "the last major fixed price contract of extended duration still regularly initiated in an inflation-ridden world." Elsewhere, long contracts are indexed or reviewable annually. Lenders "slept through an economic and contractual revolution."
- Berkshire's insurers have not been net buyers of straight long-term bonds for years and never bought 30- or 40-year bonds, but Warren calls this mild caution "an improper response": "You do not adequately protect yourself by being half awake while others are sleeping."
- Specific mistakes: buying fifteen-year bonds, and, worse, not selling them at a loss when his views crystallized. He also notes that trying to be clever with sinking funds and special issues repeated the textile error of fighting a tide.
- Net fixed-dollar commitments in recent years went into convertible bonds. The conversion option effectively shortens the average life, because Berkshire can end the contract by converting to stock at a time of its choosing. Some converts looked exceptionally attractive with the same earnings-retention logic as the equity portfolio.
- He still allows that he could be too negative: inflation is man-made and perhaps "man-mastered," and rates might already compensate. His unwillingness to fix a price now for a pound of See's candy or yard of Berkshire cloth in 2010 or 2020 makes him equally unwilling to price money for those years. Of the fifteen-year bonds he says Berkshire "will annually pay a price in terms of earning power."

chunks.heading: Equity holdings and retained earnings
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's insurance equities (about $336.7 million market value vs $185.4 million cost at yearend 1979) performed well because the underlying companies did. Major positions included GEICO ($28.3M cost, $68.0M market), Washington Post ($10.6M cost, $39.2M market), Handy & Harman, SAFECO and Interpublic.
- Warren relies on retained earnings not reported in Berkshire's statements: he has faith that managements will turn a retained dollar into "a dollar or more of subsequent market value" for Berkshire.
- He expects portfolio underperformance relative to the market in 1980, "for the first time in recent years," but plans no changes to suit a specific year's market.
- He calls most holdings "splendid businesses, splendidly managed, purchased at highly attractive prices," and expects very large and growing underlying earning power from fractional ownership.
- On the planned sale of Illinois National Bank (required by the Bank Holding Company Act by end-1980), he warns the proceeds can't replace its earning power: "You simply can't buy high quality businesses at the sort of price/earnings multiple likely to prevail on our bank sale." The bank earned about 2.3% on average assets, over three times the average major bank.

chunks.heading: Shareholder communication and the right shareholder base
chunks.text:
- About 98% of shares are held by people who were also holders at the start of the year, and perhaps 90% of owners have Berkshire as their largest holding. So the annual report builds on prior years instead of restating, and provides what Warren would want if roles were reversed. Quarterly reports carry no narrative because owners and managers have very long time horizons.
- He believes the CEO owes owners direct reporting: "You would demand that in a private company; you should expect no less in a public company." The report should not be handed to a PR consultant. Owners deserve the same scope, balance and candor Berkshire expects from its operating managers.
- Companies "obtain the shareholder constituency that they seek and deserve." Short-term focus attracts short-term shareholders, and cynicism toward investors is returned.
- He cites Phil Fisher's restaurant analogy: a restaurant targeting one clientele gets loyal returning customers, but one vacillating "between French cuisine and take-out chicken" gets "a revolving door of confused and dissatisfied customers." A company can't simultaneously attract owners wanting high yield, long-term growth and "stock market pyrotechnics."
- Managements that court heavy trading are in effect asking existing owners to leave, since new owners can't be added without losing old ones. Warren wants very low turnover among owners who "understand our operation, approve of our policies, and share our expectations."

chunks.heading: Management structure: centralized capital allocation, delegated operations
chunks.text:
- Berkshire centralizes financial decisions "at the top (the very top)" and extremely delegates operating authority to key managers at each business. Headquarters uses about 1,500 square feet and "could just field a basketball team."
- He admits the approach "produces an occasional major mistake that might have been eliminated or minimized through closer operating controls," but says it removes layers of cost and speeds decisions. "Because everyone has a great deal to do, a very great deal gets done."
- Most importantly, it attracts and retains extraordinarily talented people "who simply can't be hired in the normal course of events" because working for Berkshire is "almost identical to running their own show."
- Warren notes sellers of businesses to Berkshire have almost without exception been honorable and fair. Thirteen businesses were acquired via negotiated cash purchases from private owners and six started, all from the original textile capital.
- Managers like Ben Rosner (76), Gene Abegg (82) and Louis Vincenti (74) keep achieving more each year. "We have placed much trust in them - and their achievements have far exceeded that trust."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett argues that the economic value of retained earnings depends on how they are used, not on accounting credit or ownership percentage. He explains why inflation turns ordinary corporate returns into negative real returns for owners, why GEICO is a rare franchise with a skilled manager, and why insurers should be wary of bond-driven price cutting.

chunks.heading: Operating results versus owner earnings: the "iceberg" of non-controlled holdings
chunks.text:
- Warren judges single-year managerial performance by operating earnings divided by beginning equity, with securities valued at cost. In 1980 operating earnings were $41.9 million (vs. $36.0 million in 1979); return on beginning equity was 17.8% (vs. 18.6%).
- Berkshire's insurance subsidiaries hold large stakes (under 20%) in companies that pay out little of their earnings. Accounting only counts dividends from such holdings, so undistributed earnings are ignored.
- In 1980 the retained portion of "our" earnings in those companies exceeded Berkshire's total reported operating earnings. Conventional accounting lets less than half of the earnings "iceberg" show above the surface.
- He argues "our economic well-being is determined by their earnings, not their dividends."
- The value of retained earnings depends on what they are used for and the earnings they later produce, not on whether Berkshire owns 100%, 50%, 20% or 1%: "It's the act that counts, not the actors." "If a tree grows in a forest partially owned by us, but we don't record the growth in our financial statements, we still own part of the tree."
- He would rather have unrecorded earnings put to good use in a 10%-owned company by a management he didn't hire than recorded earnings put into dubious projects, even by himself.
- Replacing the equity portfolio with long-term tax-free bonds would lift reported operating earnings by over $30 million a year; the idea "tempts us not at all."
- Example: Berkshire's insurers own about 3% of Kaiser Aluminum and 1 1/4% of Alcoa, worth about $13 million of 1980 earnings. That gives a larger economic interest in aluminum than in nearly any controlled business (perhaps 25% should be deducted for tax if converted to value and dividends).

chunks.heading: Reported earnings versus real earnings, and what retained earnings become
chunks.text:
- He explains that controlled businesses can have reported earnings worth far less than 100 cents on the dollar, because reinvested earnings may earn nothing close to a market return and assets deteriorate unless reinvested.
- Small fractions of businesses with extraordinary reinvestment opportunities can have retained earnings worth far more than 100 cents on the dollar.
- Long-term performance is measured including all realized and unrealized capital gains. Long-term return on equity considerably exceeds the average yearly return because retained earnings of non-controlled holdings are translated into market value gains.
- That translation is uneven, unpredictable in timing, and unlikely to be precisely dollar-for-dollar. "A silly purchase price for a block of stock in a corporation can negate the effects of a decade of earnings retention." With sensible purchase prices, market recognition of retained earnings almost certainly follows.
- Book value per share (insurance-held equities at market) rose from $19.46 to $400.80 in sixteen years, 20.5% compounded annually, "despite many mistakes." A competitive batting average is possible despite many managerial strikeouts.
- Warren's "commercial" on buybacks: if a fine business sells far below intrinsic value, repurchasing shares is the most certain and profitable use of capital. Corporate acquisitions usually require paying a full price or more, while the stock market's auction nature often lets well-run companies buy parts of themselves at under 50% of the price of acquiring equal earning power through a negotiated deal.

chunks.heading: Inflation as a tax on capital and the hurdle rate for owners
chunks.text:
- "Only gains in purchasing power represent real earnings on investment." Hamburger test: forgo ten hamburgers, receive dividends that after tax buy two, then sell for after-tax proceeds that buy eight. There is no real income, however much the investment appreciated in dollars: "You may feel richer, but you won't eat richer."
- High inflation acts as a tax on capital that makes much corporate investment unwise, measured by whether owners get a positive real return. The required "hurdle rate" of return on equity has risen sharply.
- Example: with 12% inflation, a business earning 20% on equity and distributing it all to owners in the 50% bracket leaves them with about 98% of their original purchasing power. They would be better off with stable prices and earnings of a few percent.
- Explicit income taxes alone can never turn a positive corporate return into a negative owner return. The inflation tax is not limited by reported income. At 16% inflation, owners of the 60%-plus of corporate America earning less than that would have negative real returns even with no income taxes on dividends and gains.
- Taxes are levied on nominal, not real, income, so owners pay tax on what would be deficits in constant dollars.
- At the inflation rates of the time, he believed individuals in medium or high tax brackets should expect no real long-term return from the average American corporation, even reinvesting all after-tax dividends.
- Berkshire has no corporate solution; "Inflation does not improve our return on equity."
- Truly indexed capital means return on equity rises with the price level without extra capital (including working capital); earnings increases from added investment don't count. A thrifty worker saving half his paycheck is not indexed, and neither is a high-saving company with flat return on equity. Few businesses come close, and Berkshire is not one.
- He reports that his short-term forecasts of stock or bond prices are useless: "The forecasts may tell you a great deal about the forecaster; they tell you nothing about the future."

chunks.heading: GEICO: a franchise with a fixable problem, not a turnaround
chunks.text:
- GEICO was Berkshire's largest non-controlled holding: 7.2 million shares, about 33% of the company, cost $47 million (about half invested in 1976, most of the rest in 1980), market value $105.3 million.
- Insurance regulators required the vote to sit with an independent party, so the stake didn't qualify for investee accounting. Dividends gave a little over $3 million a year in reported earnings, but Warren estimated his share of earning power at about $20 million, so undistributed earnings from this holding alone could equal about 40% of Berkshire's reported operating earnings.
- He is as comfortable with GEICO management retaining the estimated $17 million as if it were in his own hands. In two years GEICO's buybacks cut share equivalents outstanding from 34.2 million to 21.6 million.
- He calls GEICO "the best of all investment worlds": a very important, hard-to-duplicate business advantage plus a management skilled in both operations and capital allocation (Jack Byrne).
- Turnarounds: after tracking hundreds of cases, "when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for poor fundamental economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact."
- GEICO and American Express (after the 1964 salad oil scandal) are distinguished from true turnarounds. They were one-of-a-kind franchises with a localized, excisable cancer that needed a skilled surgeon. GEICO's low-cost design in a huge auto insurance market was intact, submerged under financial and operating troubles.
- Buying a similar $20 million of earning power in a first-class business would cost at least $200 million through a negotiated purchase of a whole company. Owning 100% adds options (leverage, changing managers, directing cash flow, selling), but buying minority pieces of already well-run businesses at prices far below the entire-business value suits Berkshire's insurance model.

chunks.heading: Insurance industry conditions: the bond-loss trap and "amateur night" reinsurance
chunks.text:
- The industry combined ratio rose from 100.6 in 1979 to an estimated 103.5 in 1980, with underwriting losses expected to mount significantly in 1981 and 1982. Warren recommended Chubb's annual report and Barbara Stewart's October 1980 analysis of competitive dynamics.
- Insurers may carry bonds at amortized cost regardless of market value. Many held long-term bonds worth two to three times net worth at cost; some large property-casualty companies had nominal or negative net worth at market values.
- Selling bonds forces recognition of losses and cuts stated net worth, so insurers become frozen in their investment posture, perhaps for a decade or more. For example, unwillingness to book losses may block a sensible shift from tax-exempt to taxable bonds.
- Policyholder and claimant money funds the bonds. If premium volume shrinks, liabilities shrink and bonds must be sold, turning unrealized losses into realized ones.
- The two options for a weak insurer: (1) price to exposure ("a dollar of premium for every dollar of expense cost plus expectable loss cost"), lose business, and be forced to sell bonds; or (2) "asset maintenance" underwriting, keeping terrible business to hold assets and praying. Warren says the second will be chosen, so no better day for underwriting comes while many large insurers do it. "Right behind having financial problems yourself, the next worst plight is to have a large group of competitors with financial problems that they can defer by a 'sell-at-any-price' policy."
- He says Berkshire's net worth relative to premium volume was the strongest among large stockholder-owned property-casualty groups. Capital and flexibility give "more staying power and more options," but not immunity. He admits the company also lost sums in bonds "because your Chairman was talking when he should have been acting," and that its asset and liability maturities were mismatched.
- Reinsurance has easy entry, large premiums paid in advance, and delayed loss reports and payments. Early on "the morning mail brings lots of cash and few claims," a feeling like an innocent receiving a first credit card. High interest rates are turning the market into "amateur night." A super catastrophe could cause a "bloodbath." Berkshire stayed active but expected no premium growth.

chunks.heading: Underwriting discipline and operating managers
chunks.text:
- National Indemnity (Phil Liesche, Roland Miller, Bill Lyons) had record underwriting margins relative to the industry on flat volume. Warren expected lower volume in 1981 but promised no complaints, layoffs or salary cuts, since the discipline set by founder Jack Ringwalt "if suspended, probably could not be fully regained."
- Cypress (Milt Thornton) runs a workers' compensation operation that far outpaces competitors: "admired and copied, but not matched." Frank DeNardo of the California workers' comp division died at 37; Warren praised him as someone who "instinctively thought like an underwriter."
- Homestate operations had serious problems; Insurance Company of Iowa lost money every year since 1973 and was folded into Cornhusker Casualty. Kansas (Floyd Taylor) was strong.
- Warren expected a significant decline in 1981 insurance volume and a poorer result, though better than the industry's.
- Textiles: Waumbec Mills was closed, and he called it a "costly mistake" not to face reality sooner. New Bedford dropped about a third of its looms and abandoned high-volume lines with no product differentiation, which could not earn adequate returns over a full cycle.
- Ben Rosner's Associated Retail Stores turned all of its excellent earnings into cash in a poor retail year; the 50th birthday was March 7, 1981.

chunks.heading: Financing, acquisition preferences and judging a seller
chunks.text:
- In August 1980 Berkshire sold $60 million of 12 3/4% notes due 2005, not for an immediate need but because opportunities would come, possibly when credit is extremely expensive or unavailable: "we want to have plenty of financial firepower."
- Acquisition preferences: businesses that generate cash, not consume it. With inflation, many companies must spend all internal funds just to maintain physical volume; Warren calls such operations "mirage-like" and stays wary of earnings that never convert into "no-strings-attached cash."
- Qualifying businesses are hard to find: of hundreds of acquisitions reported each year, only a handful would interest him. Policy is ample liquidity, moderate and properly structured debt, and abundant capital strength, even though this slightly reduces return on equity.
- On Gene Abegg, founder of Illinois National Bank, who died at 82: you learn a lot about a person when you buy a business and he stays on as an employee. A seller knows the business intimately and has many chances to mislead through omissions and ambiguities, and attitudes can change after the check clears. Gene "shot straight 100% of the time," laid out the negatives upfront, later told Warren about undisclosed valuable items, worked harder for Berkshire than for himself after selling at 71, and never delayed reporting a problem. He kept a fiduciary attitude toward other people's money, with enough cash on hand in the 1933 bank holiday to pay all depositors in full.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why he prefers fractional stakes in great businesses to costly control deals, why high-premium takeovers rarely work, and how rising passive interest rates erode the value of ordinary equity. He also covers insurance underwriting discipline and float-driven pricing pressure.

chunks.heading: Retained earnings only make sense when the business earns above the passive-return "crossbar"
chunks.text:
- Warren frames the case for equity as "value-added": equity should earn more than passive returns (bond interest) because it carries more risk and benefits from managerial skill.
- Decades earlier, a 10% return on equity made a "good" business, since long-term taxable bonds yielded 5% and tax-exempts 3%. American business then earned about 11% on equity and stocks sold at over 150 cents on the dollar of book value.
- In 1981, long-term taxable bonds yielded over 16% and tax-exempts 14%, while American business earned only about 14% on equity, before tax on the owner.
- Example for a 50% bracket investor: if a typical company pays out all earnings at 14% ROE, the return equals a 7% tax-exempt bond, which "might be worth fifty cents on the dollar."
- If all earnings are retained, earnings and price grow 14% a year, but a 20% maximum capital gains tax makes the net return worse than the passive after-tax rate.
- Conclusion: "companies achieving 14% per year gains in earnings per share while paying no cash dividend are an economic failure for their individual shareholders." The returns from passive capital outstrip the returns from active capital.
- Most American businesses were "bad" businesses economically, producing less after-tax for individual investors than the tax-exempt passive rate. American equity capital in aggregate produced no value-added.
- The crossbar rose faster than corporations jumped: ROE improved a few points in a decade, but passive rates rose much more. If inflation is tempered and passive returns fall, many "bad" businesses return to "good."
- Warren warns that old yardsticks (historic p/e ratios, valuation rules) are costly to retain when change is rapid: "facts do not cease to exist, either because they are unpleasant or because they are ignored."

chunks.heading: Retention policy: high-return businesses should retain, low-return businesses should pay out
chunks.text:
- Rational policy: a company with high historic and prospective ROE should retain most or all earnings so owners earn premium returns on added capital. A low-return company should pay a high dividend so owners can redeploy capital.
- Analogy: a holder of a 5% bond doesn't use the coupons to buy more 5% bonds at 100 cents when similar bonds sell at 40 cents. "Good money is not thrown after bad."
- He cites the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30): the high-earning servants keep and expand their capital, while the non-earning servant must hand his capital to the top performer.
- Inflation inverts this. It acts as a "gigantic corporate tapeworm": regardless of profits, more dollars are needed each year for receivables, inventory and fixed assets just to match the prior year's unit volume. The less prosperous the firm, the larger the share claimed.
- A business earning 8% or 10% on equity often has no leftovers for expansion, debt reduction or "real" dividends, so the low-return business must retain every nickel precisely because it is unattractive.
- Red flag: "Beware of 'dividends' that can be paid out only if someone promises to replace the capital distributed." Examples include dividend reinvestment plans with discounts that nearly force reinvestment, and issuing shares to Peter to pay dividends to Paul.
- Berkshire retains earnings "for offensive, not defensive or obligatory, reasons," yet only barely clears the after-tax passive crossbar with its historic 21% return. He admits its own value-added could turn negative.

chunks.heading: Non-controlled ownership earnings and buying fractions of businesses
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's share of undistributed earnings in companies it doesn't control is excluded from reported operating earnings. Warren believes they will become tangible value "just as surely as if subsidiaries we control had earned, retained - and reported - similar earnings."
- The translation into market gains is irregular. Market values track business values well over long periods but "in any given year the relationship can gyrate capriciously." Companies that employ retained earnings poorly see low or negative recognition; those with high returns on added capital see far more than dollar-for-dollar.
- In 1981 these unrecorded earnings exceeded reported operating earnings. Four positions (GEICO, General Foods, R. J. Reynolds, Washington Post) alone were expected to contribute well over $35 million of undistributed earnings in 1982.
- Non-controlled holdings have better underlying economics than controlled businesses because the area of choice is far wider. "Small portions of exceptionally good businesses are usually available in the securities markets at reasonable prices," while whole businesses are rarely for sale, and then at high prices.
- Current approach: open-market purchase of fractional positions in companies with "excellent business franchises and competent, honest managements." Berkshire never expects to run them but expects to profit.
- If these don't deliver full value, the mistake lies in one of three things: the management joined, the future economics of the business, or the price paid. Misjudging future economics is the most common error. Example: he volunteered a rosy view on aluminum, then revised it "approximately 180 degrees" (Berkshire held Alcoa).
- Lack of control is often an economic plus because mistakes in marketable securities can be corrected far faster than in controlled subsidiaries.
- GEICO accounted for over half of the $124 million (about 31%) net worth gain in 1981 (cost $47.1 million, market $199.8 million). He cautions that market gains outstripped underlying business value gains, and "such market variations will not always be on the pleasant side."

chunks.heading: Why acquirers overpay: toads, princes and the 2X takeover
chunks.text:
- Principle: "we would rather buy 10% of Wonderful Business T at X per share than 100% of T at 2X per share," regardless of the effect on reported earnings. Most managers prefer the reverse.
- Acquisition decisions aim at real economic benefit, not "managerial domain" or reported numbers. "Managements stressing accounting appearance over economic substance usually achieve little of either."
- Three usually unspoken motives behind high-premium takeovers:
  1. Animal spirits: leaders relish activity and challenge (Berkshire's pulse also quickens when an acquisition is in prospect).
  2. Size as yardstick: organizations measure and pay managers by size. A Fortune 500 manager knows his sales rank, not necessarily his profitability rank.
  3. The toad-to-prince fairy tale: managers assume their "kiss" will transform the target's profitability.
- Logic: investors can always buy toads at the going price. If they fund princesses paying double for the right to kiss the toad, "those kisses had better pack some real dynamite." Warren has "observed many kisses but very few miracles."
- Berkshire's own record: kisses on bargain toads "fell flat." Successes were princes when purchased, and some fractional interests in identifiable princes bought at toad-like prices.
- Warren won't pay a lot for what he is supposed to "bring to the party," because "we ordinarily don't bring a lot." He may pay a fairly fancy price for a business if he is reasonably confident of what he's getting, with prices that make sense even if the future resembles the past.
- In 1981 he came close to a major purchase but walked away because the price, given alternative uses of funds, would have left owners worse off: "The empire would have been larger, but the citizenry would have been poorer."
- Berkshire avoids small commitments: "If something's not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well."

chunks.heading: The two categories of dazzling acquisition records
chunks.text:
- Category 1: companies that bought businesses well adapted to inflation. Such businesses need two traits:
  1. Ability to raise prices easily, even with flat demand and unused capacity, without losing share or unit volume.
  2. Ability to absorb large dollar volume increases (often inflation-driven) with only minor additional capital.
- Managers of ordinary ability focused solely on these tests did excellently in recent decades. Few businesses have both traits, and competition to buy them became "fierce to the point of being self-defeating."
- Category 2: managerial superstars who can spot the prince disguised as a toad and peel away the disguise. Warren names Ben Heineman (Northwest Industries), Henry Singleton (Teledyne), Erwin Zaban (National Service Industries) and especially Tom Murphy (Capital Cities Communications), a "twofer" in both categories.
- These champions made few deals in recent years and often found repurchase of their own shares the most sensible use of capital.
- Warren says he does not qualify for Category 2, and Berkshire's actual Category 1 activity was "sporadic and inadequate." He invokes the Noah principle: "predicting rain doesn't count, building arks does."

chunks.heading: Property-casualty insurance: pricing discipline, the cycle and balance sheet strength
chunks.text:
- Because policies average a little under twelve months and prices are frozen for the contract life, a year's premiums written fix about half of next year's premiums earned. Pricing mistakes must be lived with for an uncomfortable period.
- Warren forecast that 1982 would be the worst underwriting year in recent history, locked in by pricing behavior. Industry premium growth was 3.6% written in 1981 and the combined ratio 105.7 (versus 103.1 in 1980 and 97.2 in 1977).
- An industry volume gain of at least 10% a year was needed to stabilize losses, since insurers expect incurred losses to rise about 10% annually. Each percentage point below 10% accelerates deterioration.
- Cost drivers: monetary inflation and "social" inflation (courts and juries stretching coverage). Results had worsened despite good luck (hurricanes staying at sea, less driving).
- Why insurers underprice: carriers holding bonds carried at "nonsensically high prices" must keep cash flowing by selling policies at nonsensically low prices. They fear a volume drop more than an underwriting loss. Others follow because "it's difficult to price much differently than your most threatened competitor," compounded by worship of size over profitability and fear that lost market share can't be regained.
- He rejects the notion of a regular underwriting cycle with a constant midpoint. He expects very large underwriting losses to be the norm, and the best future years may look substandard against the past decade's average.
- Berkshire's response: sacrifice volume, keep underwriting superior to the industry, expect continued low volume, and preserve financial flexibility. "At some point, should fear ever prevail throughout the industry, our financial strength could become an operational asset of immense value."
- He credits managers Phil Liesche, Bill Lyons, Roland Miller, Floyd Taylor and Milt Thornton for swimming against the tide. GEICO, by "extreme and improving operating efficiency," is in a more protected position and is "a brilliantly run implementation of a very important business idea."

chunks.heading: Measuring performance, inflation, and shareholder-designated contributions
chunks.text:
- Operating earnings were $39.7 million in 1981, 15.2% of beginning equity (securities at cost), versus 17.8% in 1980. The shareholder-designated giving program cut earnings by about $900,000.
- Over the 17 years under current management, GAAP book value rose from $19.46 to $526.02 per share, 21.1% compounded. Warren says this rate "is highly likely to drift downward" and hopes it stays significantly above the average large American corporation.
- Because GAAP ignores undistributed earnings of non-controlled companies, single-year return on equity is a weak measure. For long-term measurement, insurance-held equities are valued at market less a charge for taxes on unrealized gains.
- On inflation: he stays negative on the long-term trend ("Like virginity, a stable price level seems capable of maintenance, but not of restoration"). Apparently satisfactory long-term results are illusory as real investment results, and Berkshire "will continue to do a much better job of filling your wallet than of filling your stomach."
- Shareholder-designated contributions: owners, not officers, choose where corporate charitable funds go. 95.6% of 932,206 eligible shares responded, with no return envelope provided. $1,783,655 went to about 675 charities. The program runs only in years with adequate tax deductions (perhaps seven or eight years of ten).
- Practical lesson: shares held in nominee (broker) name missed the program, so Warren advises holding at least one share in your own name to be sure of receiving corporate news.
- Charlie Munger conceived the idea; he and Warren work "as partners in managing all controlled companies."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why look-through "economic" earnings matter more than reported accounting earnings, why commodity-like industries (including insurance) earn poor returns without differentiation or a cost edge, and why issuing undervalued stock for acquisitions hands over $2 of value for $1. He also lists his acquisition criteria and the owner-like managers he prizes.

chunks.heading: Why 1982 "accounting" earnings understated Berkshire's economic earnings
chunks.text:
- Warren reports 1982 operating earnings of $31.5 million, only 9.8% of beginning equity capital (valuing securities at cost). That compares with 15.2% in 1981 and a high of 19.4% in 1978.
- He blames three things: worse insurance underwriting, equity capital growing faster than the businesses Berkshire runs directly, and a growing commitment to partially-owned, nonoperated businesses.
- Accounting rules count only dividends from holdings below 20% ownership. Undistributed earnings of those companies are ignored.
- GEICO example: Berkshire owns about 35%, but because it assigned its voting rights it is treated as a sub-20% holding. Only $3.5 million of after-tax dividends hit reported earnings, while $23 million of Berkshire's share of GEICO's undistributed operating earnings was excluded.
- He notes the distortion cuts both ways. If GEICO had earned less but paid $1 million more in dividends, reported earnings would have been higher. If GEICO had earned $100 million more and retained it all, reported earnings would not have changed.
- He admits you should be suspicious of an executive abandoning a yardstick as results worsen: "most managers favor disposition of the yardstick rather than disposition of the manager." He compares it to drawing the bullseye around the arrow, and says he generally favors "pre-set, long-lived and small bullseyes."

chunks.heading: "Economic" earnings and the value of retained earnings
chunks.text:
- Warren prefers "economic" earnings, which include all undistributed earnings regardless of ownership percentage.
- The value of retained earnings to owners depends on how effectively they are used, not on the size of one's ownership stake. A holder of 0.01% of Berkshire benefits fully from its retained earnings, just like a 20% owner.
- A 100% owner of many capital-intensive businesses can be credited with retained earnings "with painstaking precision" and still get minor or zero economic value.
- "Accounting numbers are the beginning, not the end, of business valuation."
- Undistributed 1982 operating earnings from GEICO, General Foods, Washington Post and R. J. Reynolds came to well over $40 million (he had predicted over $35 million). That exceeds Berkshire's total reported earnings, which included only $14 million of dividends from these companies.
- He cautions against false precision: realizing retained earnings through market value is subject to "very substantial, but indeterminate" taxation, and the translation into market value is uneven and unpredictable in timing.
- His job is to pick businesses where each retained dollar becomes at least a dollar of market value. Some investees turned a retained dollar into two or more dollars of market value, and these overachievers have so far offset the laggards ("St. Offset").

chunks.heading: Partial vs. total ownership and the market as an auction
chunks.text:
- Partial stakes are bought in an auction market where prices are set by participants who sometimes behave like "an army of manic-depressive lemmings."
- This lets a value investor choose from nearly all major American corporations, many far better than any business that could be bought whole in a negotiated deal.
- Buying 100% of good businesses at reasonable prices is what "makes us dance," but it is "far more difficult" than buying fractional interests at attractive prices.
- He felt relief, not envy, at other companies' 1982 acquisitions: "managerial intellect wilted in competition with managerial adrenaline." He quotes Pascal on being unable "to stay quietly in one room."
- He says he almost starred in the "Acquisition Follies of 1982." A very large purchase Berkshire had firmly committed to fell through for reasons beyond its control, which he called the year's major accomplishment.
- The partial-ownership approach needs a moderately priced market. "A too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments."
- In 1972, at the two-tier market mania peak, the insurance subsidiaries held only $18 million of equities (about 15% of insurance investments), versus about 80% in 1982. There were as many good businesses in 1972, but prices "looked absurd."
- Higher prices would make Berkshire's results look good temporarily but hurt its long-term prospects.

chunks.heading: Long-term performance, market value vs. intrinsic value
chunks.text:
- 1982 net worth gain (insurance equities at market, less capital gains taxes payable) was $208 million, or 40% on a beginning base of $519 million.
- Over 18 years under present management, book value per share rose from $19.46 to $737.43, or 22.0% compounded annually. He warns it will fall: "Geometric progressions eventually forge their own anchors."
- Goal: a long-term return well above the average large American corporation, via partial or total ownership of well-situated businesses with price discipline.
- $79 million of the gain came from GEICO's higher market price. He says GEICO's market gain over two years exceeded its gain in intrinsic business value, which he expected as perception converged with reality.
- Market gains cannot favor Berkshire every year. In a down year net worth could shrink, and he would not be distressed: if the businesses still look attractive and cash is available, he would "simply add to our holdings at even more favorable prices."
- On GEICO management: "Let Jack Do It" (Jack Byrne) works as a corporate creed. Lou Simpson is called the best investment manager in property-casualty insurance.
- He jokes that "nostalgia should be weighted heavily in stock selection": the biggest unrealized gains were in Washington Post and GEICO, companies he connected with at ages 13 and 20. Cost vs. market: GEICO $47.1 million vs. $309.6 million; Washington Post $10.6 million vs. $103.2 million.

chunks.heading: Commodity economics and why insurance underwriting would not recover
chunks.text:
- Industries with substantial overcapacity and an undifferentiated "commodity" product are prime candidates for poor profits, unless prices or costs are administered (by government, collusion or cartel).
- Differentiation works with candy bars (customers buy the brand) but not sugar. In such industries only a producer with a "wide and sustainable" cost advantage does consistently well.
- His equation: "persistent over-capacity without administered prices (or costs) equals poor profitability." Overcapacity corrects slowly, and the rebound breeds enthusiasm for expansion that recreates overcapacity: "nothing fails like success."
- Long-term profitability is set by the ratio of supply-tight to supply-ample years. In textiles, the last tight period "lasted the better part of a morning."
- Insurance capacity can be created instantly by capital plus an underwriter's willingness to sign his name, and the product is largely undifferentiated, so it is a "textbook case" of overcapacity plus commodity.
- Industry combined ratios averaged 99.0 from 1950 through 1970 because regulator-negotiated bureau rates acted as quasi-administered pricing. That system has been undercut by new capacity that competes on price.
- Industry combined ratio was 109.5 in 1982 (est.), up from 106.0 in 1981. He says it is a "best case" figure, since weak managements may use reserving maneuvers: "weak managements ... weak accounting" ("It's difficult for an empty sack to stand upright").
- Premium growth under 10% a year means worsening underwriting, since insured losses rise by roughly 10% or more.
- Capacity will shrink only after a "megadisaster," not mere poor profits. When it does, a few firms with capital, willingness to commit it and in-place distribution will find big opportunities.
- Berkshire's insurance underwriting fell from above average to modestly below average in 1982; the biggest swing was in National Indemnity's traditional lines. Underwriting loss was $21.6 million pre-tax versus a $1.5 million profit in 1981.
- GEICO is the "high-profit exception": a wide, sustainable cost advantage. Berkshire's 35% interest represents about $250 million of premium volume, more than its own direct volume. Cypress (Milt Thornton) and Kansas Fire and Casualty (Floyd Taylor) have never had an underwriting loss since joining.

chunks.heading: Issuing stock: never give more intrinsic value than you get
chunks.text:
- Rule: "we will not issue shares unless we receive as much intrinsic business value as we give." Many managers issue "dollar bills in exchange for fifty-cent pieces."
- The trap: a seller of a whole business can demand full intrinsic value, but a buyer using its own stock gets only the market's valuation of it. If its stock sells at half of intrinsic value, it gives $2 to get $1. "Gold valued as gold cannot be purchased intelligently through the utilization of gold - or even silver - valued as lead."
- Rationalizations he rebuts:
  - "The target will be worth more": so will the business being traded away. If 2X is issued for X, the imbalance remains.
  - "We have to grow": existing owners' businesses shrink when shares are issued. His farm example: merging a neighbor's 60 acres with your family's 120 as equal partners grows your domain to 180 acres but cuts your family's ownership by 25%.
  - "51% stock and 49% cash for tax-free treatment": if full stock hurts, 51% hurts too ("a man is not charmed if a spaniel defaces his lawn... not a St. Bernard"). Sellers' wishes shouldn't set the buyer's interests.
- Three ways to avoid destroying value: (1) a true business-value-for-business-value merger, as intended for Berkshire-Blue Chip; (2) issue stock only when it sells at or above intrinsic value; (3) repurchase shares equal to those issued, turning a stock deal into a cash deal. He prefers repurchases that enhance wealth over "damage-repair" ones.
- He warns that projections can justify any price ("while deals often fail in practice, they never fail in projections"). Dilution should be judged on intrinsic business value, not near-term earnings per share.
- Describe a deal accurately: "Part of A sold to acquire B." Managers should ask whether they would sell 100% of their business on the same terms. His investment-company illustration: trading $2 of intrinsic value for $1 would never pass the SEC.
- "Double whammy": the merger itself destroys value, then the market rationally marks down a management with an anti-owner record. The highest price/value ratios go to managers who never issue shares on unfavorable terms.
- "We will not equate activity with progress or corporate size with owner-wealth."

chunks.heading: Acquisition criteria and how Berkshire is run
chunks.text:
- What Warren wants to buy:
  - Large purchases (at least $5 million of after-tax earnings)
  - Demonstrated consistent earning power ("future projections are of little interest"; no turnarounds)
  - Good returns on equity with little or no debt
  - Management in place ("we can't supply it")
  - Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it")
  - An offering price
- Unfriendly deals are excluded. He promises confidentiality and a fast answer, usually within five minutes. Cash is preferred; stock only on the terms described above.
- Headquarters has six people (including Warren, Mike Goldberg, Joan Atherton, Gladys Kaiser, Verne McKenzie, Bill Scott), who "outproduce corporate groups many times their number." A compact organization lets them manage the business "rather than managing each other." He finds a phone call with Charlie Munger more productive than "a half-day committee meeting."
- Retiring managers Phil Liesche (National Indemnity) and Ben Rosner (Associated Retail Stores) ran their businesses with the care of 100% owners; "no rules were necessary" because it was in their character. Attracting such managers is why "you need not worry about Berkshire's future."

chunks.heading: Buffalo News example of a franchise gaining readership
chunks.text:
- Sunday circulation of the Buffalo News reached 367,000 within six years of launching a Sunday edition, versus the rival Courier-Express's 272,000 as the only Sunday paper. That is a 35% gain, with little change in households.
- Only 14 U.S. cities have a daily paper with weekday circulation above the News. Warren credits Henry Urban, Stan Lipsey, Murray Light, Clyde Pinson, Dave Perona and Dick Feather.
- Earnings table notes: See's Candies pre-tax earnings were $23.9 million in 1982 (vs. $21.0 million), and Buffalo Evening News lost $1.2 million pre-tax.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett restates Berkshire's manager-owner principles (partnership attitude, per-share intrinsic value, ignoring accounting optics, candor, no dilution). He explains economic Goodwill via See's Candies, contrasts book value with intrinsic value, and argues against stock splits and hyperactive trading.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's operating philosophy: partnership, per-share value, and owner orientation
chunks.text:
- Warren describes Berkshire as a corporation in form but a partnership in attitude. He and Charlie Munger see shareholders as owner-partners and themselves as managing partners; the company is "a conduit through which our shareholders own the assets."
- All directors are major shareholders; for at least four of five, over 50% of family net worth is in Berkshire. "We eat our own cooking."
- The long-term goal is to maximize the average annual gain in intrinsic business value per share. Size is not the measure. He expects the rate to diminish as the capital base grows, but would be disappointed if it did not exceed that of the average large American corporation.
- Preferred route: directly own a diversified group of businesses that generate cash and earn above-average returns on capital. Second choice: own parts of similar businesses via marketable stocks held by the insurance subsidiaries. Price, availability, and insurance capital needs decide each year's allocation.
- "A managerial 'wish list' will not be filled at shareholder expense." Berkshire will not diversify by buying whole businesses at control prices that ignore long-term economics. It will only do with shareholders' money what it would do with its own.
- Candor: report the facts he would want to know if positions were reversed. "The CEO who misleads others in public may eventually mislead himself in private." Marketable-securities activity is discussed only as legally required, since good investment ideas are "rare, valuable and subject to competitive appropriation."

chunks.heading: Capital allocation rules: retention test, debt, share issuance, and not selling
chunks.text:
- Retained earnings test: retention must deliver at least $1 of market value per $1 retained, assessed on a rolling five-year basis. It has been met so far; Warren notes it gets harder as net worth grows.
- Accounting consequences do not drive decisions. With similar acquisition costs, he prefers $2 of earnings not reportable by Berkshire (from partial stock holdings) over $1 that is reportable. Whole businesses often sell for double the pro-rata price of small portions. Unreported earnings are expected to show up in intrinsic value through capital gains.
- Debt: rarely used, and structured as long-term fixed rate when it is. "We will reject interesting opportunities rather than over-leverage our balance sheet." This conservatism has cost results but fits obligations to policyholders, depositors, lenders, and equity holders.
- Share issuance: only when Berkshire receives as much business value as it gives, across mergers, offerings, stock-for-debt swaps, options, and convertibles. Issuing shares means selling small portions of the company, which must not be done inconsistently with the value of the whole.
- Selling: no interest in selling good businesses at any price, and reluctance to sell sub-par ones that still generate cash with good managers and labor relations. This hurts returns, but "gin rummy managerial behavior (discard your least promising business at each turn) is not our style."
- On fixing poor businesses with capex: "The projections will be dazzling - the advocates will be sincere - but, in the end, major additional investment in a terrible industry usually is about as rewarding as struggling in quicksand."
- Dilution check: Berkshire had 1,146,909 shares outstanding versus 1,137,778 at the start of fiscal 1965, so owners at that time hold .99% for every 1% they held then, even as all of today's assets were added.

chunks.heading: Book value versus intrinsic business value, and how to judge performance
chunks.text:
- 1983 book value rose from $737.43 to $975.83 per share (32%). Over the 19-year tenure, it grew from $19.46 to $975.83, or 22.6% compounded. Warren says that rate cannot be sustained at current size: "Those who believe otherwise should pursue a career in sales, but avoid one in mathematics."
- He does not take one-year figures seriously ("why should the time required for a planet to circle the sun synchronize precisely with the time required for business actions to pay off?"). He recommends at least a five-year test. Red lights should flash if the five-year average gain falls much below the return on equity of American industry in aggregate.
- Book value is an accounting concept recording contributed capital and retained earnings: "Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out." Intrinsic value is future cash output discounted to present value.
- Analogy: two children whose college costs are identical have the same book value of education, but the future payoff could range from zero to many times the cost.
- At the start of 1965, book value overstated intrinsic value because it was all textile assets earning inadequate returns. Now intrinsic value exceeds book value because (1) some stocks are carried at lower of cost or market (a $70 million pre-tax excess, about $50 million after tax, at end-1983), and (2) several businesses have economic Goodwill far above the accounting Goodwill.
- Warren's own shift: 35 years earlier he was taught to favor tangible assets and shun Goodwill-dependent businesses, which caused "many important business mistakes of omission, although relatively few of commission." Citing Keynes: "The difficulty lies not in the new ideas but in escaping from the old ones." He now strongly prefers businesses with large enduring Goodwill and minimal tangible assets.

chunks.heading: Economic Goodwill, See's Candies, and inflation
chunks.text:
- Economic Goodwill is the capitalized value of earnings on tangible assets far above market rates of return. Sources: consumer franchises where value to the buyer, not production cost, sets price; governmental franchises not subject to profit regulation (e.g., television stations); and an enduring low-cost-producer position.
- See's example: Blue Chip paid $25 million in 1972 against about $8 million of net tangible assets and about $2 million after-tax earnings. By 1983 See's earned $13 million after tax on about $20 million of net tangible assets, roughly 25%+ on tangibles with no leverage. Accounting amortization of the $17 million Goodwill (about $425,000 a year over 40 years) fell while economic Goodwill grew.
- Inflation comparison: a See's-type business needed only $8 million more capital to double earnings to $4 million, and could be worth about $50 million (over $3 of value per $1 invested). A mundane business earning 11% on $18 million of tangibles would need $18 million more and end up worth only about $36 million, a dollar-for-dollar result like a savings account.
- Conclusion: asset-heavy businesses are hurt most by inflation and earn low returns that barely fund their own inflationary needs. "During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving." He calls the traditional wisdom of tangible-asset inflation protection "long on tradition, short on wisdom."
- Spurious accounting Goodwill from silly acquisition prices might better be labeled "No-Will."
- Two perspectives: (1) when analyzing operating results, ignore amortization and look at earnings on unleveraged net tangible assets; (2) when evaluating acquisitions, ignore amortization and view Goodwill at full cost, including the full intrinsic value of consideration given. "A good business is not always a good purchase - although it's a good place to look for one."
- See's operations: product quality is "sacred" and raw materials are bought at the finest quality regardless of price. Non-raw-material costs per pound rose faster than inflation, which had to be reversed. Same-store poundage fell 0.8% in 1983 (about 8% cumulative since 1979), so the 1984 price increase was kept modest, and profits were expected to be flat. Sales were $133.5 million with $13.7 million after-tax profit in 1983. Warren notes: "In candy, as in stocks, price and value can differ; price is what you give, value is what you get."

chunks.heading: Nebraska Furniture Mart and how Warren appraises a business
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart in 1983, with 10% left to family members in management and 10% optioned to young family managers. Mrs. Blumkin (90) stayed as Chairman and worked the floor seven days a week.
- She started in 1937 with $500, beat entrenched competitors who pressured suppliers, won Fair Trade lawsuits, and once sold carpet to the judge. The single 200,000 sq ft store does over $100 million in sales and sells more than all other Omaha competitors combined.
- Appraisal test: "how I would like, assuming I had ample capital and skilled personnel, to compete with it." He would "rather wrestle grizzlies than compete with Mrs. B."
- Why it works: brilliant buying, expense ratios competitors "don't even dream about," and passing savings to customers. "It's the ideal business - one built upon exceptional value to the customer that in turn translates into exceptional economics for its owners."
- Louie Blumkin is regarded as the shrewdest furniture and appliance buyer in the country. Warren emphasizes character and work ethic of the family above business ability, and says he had admired the business for decades before the deal closed quickly.

chunks.heading: Buffalo News: measuring newspaper franchise strength
chunks.text:
- Warren considers a paper's penetration ratio (percent of households buying daily) the best measure of franchise strength. High penetration in the area retailers care about makes a paper an efficient buy for advertisers.
- The News ranked number one in weekday penetration among the 100 largest US papers and number three on Sunday. Average Sunday circulation was 376,000, against 270,000 for the Courier-Express in 1976.
- Three reasons: a stable population (low migration), a reputation for editorial quality and integrity, and a 50% news hole versus a high-30s average for comparable papers. Page for page, readers get over 25% more news, and Berkshire will keep it despite pressure for margins.
- The 1983 after-tax margin somewhat exceeded the 10% target, helped by a tax loss carry-forward and a newsprint cost drop he called an "unanticipated fluke" that would reverse.
- Preprint growth (revenue from $3.6 million to $8.1 million) is economically worse than ROP advertising: lower profitability, more competition, and less news space.
- He credits Henry Urban for not flinching through litigation and losses after the Sunday paper launched, an introduction many in the industry questioned. Without Sunday, the News would not have survived long term.

chunks.heading: Insurance, GEICO, and the long lead-time of underwriting
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's own insurance operations had a 121 combined ratio in 1983 against an industry 111 (worst in a long time). GEICO wrote at 96 after a large voluntary accrual for policyholder dividends. Warren says his own decisions of a few years earlier produced the poor results: "I made some serious mistakes a few years ago that came home to roost."
- Insurance has long lead times: policy and personnel changes take years to show. That is how Berkshire made so much in GEICO, since the outcome could be foreseen well before it appeared.
- He expects poor industry experience for years, with the combined ratio averaging no better than 1981-83 levels. Given pessimism on inflation, industry premiums must grow about 10% a year just to stabilize loss ratios.
- GEICO: Berkshire owns roughly one-third, giving a $270 million share of premium volume, about 80% larger than its own. He credits "a truly exceptional business idea and an exceptional management," discipline on full loss reserves, and Lou Simpson as "the class of the field among insurance investment managers."
- New focus: reinsurance where the buyer's overriding concern is the seller's long-term creditworthiness, such as structured settlements (lifetime periodic payments) and loss-reserve transfers. Berkshire's financial strength is the selling point. It "front ends" no profit on these and expenses overhead currently.
- Tax detail: the special GEICO distribution (a proportional tender) was treated as a dividend, taxed at an effective 6.9% for corporations versus 28% on capital gains.
- Undistributed earnings of non-controlled holdings are expected to be reflected in market prices dollar-for-dollar over time. Berkshire's experience had been "far more than a dollar of market value gain for every dollar of earnings retained." Year-end common stocks: $566 million cost, $1.306 billion market, with GEICO at $398 million and R.J. Reynolds, General Foods, and Washington Post among top holdings.

chunks.heading: Stock splits, shareholder quality, and the cost of market activity
chunks.text:
- Warren opposes splitting Berkshire's stock. The goal is a price "rationally related" to intrinsic value, which requires rational shareholders. "Manic-depressive personalities produce manic-depressive valuations."
- He attracts the right owners through consistent communication of business and ownership philosophy and then lets self-selection work, like an opera versus a rock concert audience. Over 95% of shares were held by those who were holders five years earlier, and the holding is typically at least double the size of the holder's next largest.
- A split would draw buyers who "prefer paper to value" (feeling wealthier with nine $10 bills than one $100 bill). "People who buy for non-value reasons are likely to sell for non-value reasons."
- "A hyperactive stock market is the pickpocket of enterprise." Example: a company earning 12% on equity with 100% annual turnover and 1% commissions each way loses 2% of net worth a year, or 1/6 of earnings, to transfer costs.
- At 100-million-share days and 15 cents per share each way, the "chair-changing tax" is about $7.5 billion a year, roughly the combined 1982 profits of Exxon, GM, Mobil, and Texaco. Investment management fees of over $2 billion equal the earnings of the five largest banks. "These expensive activities may decide who eats the pie, but they don't enlarge it."
- Berkshire's spread is about 2% with roughly 3% annual true turnover, so owners pay about 6/100 of 1% of market value yearly for transfer privileges.

chunks.heading: Acquisition criteria
chunks.text:
- Warren repeats Berkshire's criteria: (1) large purchases, at least $5 million of after-tax earnings; (2) demonstrated consistent earning power ("future projections are of little interest to us, nor are 'turn-around' situations"); (3) good returns on equity with little or no debt; (4) management in place; (5) simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it"); (6) an offering price stated up front.
- No unfriendly takeovers. He promises confidentiality and a fast answer, customarily within five minutes. Cash is preferred; stock only when Berkshire gets as much intrinsic value as it gives.
- Sellers are invited to check references from past deals: "For the right business - and the right people - we can provide a good home."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains when retained earnings are justified, why buybacks below intrinsic value reveal pro-owner managers, and why he values even bonds like businesses. He also covers dominant newspaper economics, owner-style incentives for unconventional bets, and how insolvent insurers distort the industry.

chunks.heading: Why earnings and book value must be judged against the capital that produces them
chunks.text:
- Warren says an economic gain "must be evaluated by comparison with the capital that produces them." Berkshire's 1984 net worth gain was $152.6 million ($133 per share), which he calls "mediocre" because it was only 13.6% on the capital base.
- The 20-year compounded gain in book value was 22.1% a year ($19.46 in 1964 to $1,108.77 in 1984).
- The measure that counts is the gain in per-share intrinsic business value. It is subjective, so he uses book value as a useful but somewhat understated proxy.
- A growing capital base drags on returns. To earn even 15% a year for the next decade, Berkshire would need about $3.9 billion of aggregate profits. That takes "a few big ideas - small ones just won't do." He and Charlie Munger had none at the moment but had found that they "pop up occasionally."
- He regards any single year's realized capital gains or losses as meaningless. The aggregate of realized and unrealized gains over a period of years is "very important."
- On GEICO, the stock's carrying value barely moved in 1984 while its intrinsic value rose substantially. He would far rather have business value rise by X with market value falling than have intrinsic value rise only X/2 with market value soaring. "We look to business performance, not market performance. If we are correct in expectations regarding the business, the market eventually will follow along."

chunks.heading: Share repurchases: when they create value and how they signal management's character
chunks.text:
- Buybacks at prices well below intrinsic value immediately raise per-share intrinsic value. Companies "often find it easy to get $2 of present value for $1." Corporate acquisition programs almost never do as well, and often fail to get $1 of value for each $1 spent.
- The second, subtler benefit is the signal. Repurchases when market value is well below business value demonstrate a management that acts for shareholder wealth rather than for expanding its own domain. Investors raise their estimates of future returns and prices move closer to intrinsic value. That repricing is rational: you should pay more for a business in the hands of a manager with demonstrated pro-shareholder leanings.
- The key word is "demonstrated." A manager who consistently skips clearly beneficial repurchases reveals his motives, however often he says "maximizing shareholder wealth." The market discounts assets lodged with him: "His heart is not listening to his mouth - and, after a while, neither will the market."
- Warren endorses only buybacks driven by price/value relationships. He calls "greenmail" repurchases "odious and repugnant," because the extortionist and the insiders both exploit an unconsulted third party, the innocent shareholder who funds the payoff.
- Berkshire's three largest holdings (GEICO, Washington Post, General Foods) all repurchased heavily at bargain prices. Exxon, the fourth largest and a recent position, also did. He likes owning businesses with excellent economics and shareholder-conscious managers.
- Tax and accounting detail on proportionate redemptions:
  - Berkshire sold shares back to GEICO (1983 tender, 350,000 shares, $21 million) and General Foods (1984, $21,843,601) so its ownership percentage stayed exactly unchanged (General Foods at 8.75%). The tax code treated these as dividends, taxed at the 6.9% inter-corporate rate.
  - He viewed the economic substance as dividend income. The receipts were far below the earnings retained for Berkshire's account.
  - To avoid a qualified opinion, Berkshire accepted the auditor's New York office view and recorded them as stock sales.
  - He considers such repurchases "at least equally favorable for shareholders who do not sell."

chunks.heading: Dividend policy and capital allocation: retain only if a dollar retained creates at least a dollar of market value
chunks.text:
- He says dividend policy is "often reported to shareholders, but seldom explained," yet capital allocation "is crucial to business and investment management." A payout target such as "40% to 50% of earnings" is given without any analysis of why it suits owners.
- Not all earnings are equal. In asset-heavy businesses, inflation makes some reported earnings "ersatz" or "restricted." If distributed, the business loses ground in unit volume, competitive position or financial strength. Restricted earnings are seldom worthless to owners but "often must be discounted heavily." Consolidated Edison is his example of retention regardless of return: its stock sold at one-fourth of book value, so each retained dollar became 25 cents of market value, yet its slogan was "Dig We Must."
- For unrestricted earnings, the only valid reason to retain is "a reasonable prospect - backed preferably by historical evidence or ... a thoughtful analysis of the future - that for every dollar retained by the corporation, at least one dollar of market value will be created for owners." That requires incremental earnings at or above what investors can get elsewhere.
- Bond illustration: take a risk-free perpetual 10% bond with a cash-or-reinvest coupon option.
  - If market rates are 5%, take more bonds, which are worth well over 100 cents on the dollar.
  - If market rates are 15%, take cash.
  - Owners should reason the same way about retained earnings, estimating the likely return on reinvestment.
- Managers reason correctly at the subsidiary level (move cash from a 5%-return unit to a 15%-return unit) but often impose a historical or industry payout pattern on parent-company shareholders. They rarely supply owners the same analysis they demand from subsidiaries.
- A great core business can camouflage poor allocation. Returns on incremental capital look good because the core absorbs small amounts at very high returns, like a Pro-Am golf team's best-ball score hiding hopeless amateurs. Many companies burn retained earnings on high-priced acquisitions with "inherently mediocre economics." Better to retain only what the high-return business can use and pay out the rest or repurchase stock. Such managers "should be held to account for those allocation decisions."
- Dividends should be steady and reflect long-term expectations, not wiggle with each quarter. "If earnings have been unwisely retained, it is likely that managers, too, have been unwisely retained."
- Berkshire's own application:
  - It has earned well over market rates on retained earnings and so retains everything.
  - It would have been disastrous to pay out early earnings. The original cornerstone businesses had, respectively, survived but earned almost nothing (textiles), shriveled while incurring large losses (department stores), and shrunk to about 5% of their sales volume (trading stamps).
  - Only by redeploying into better businesses did it overcome those origins.
  - If prospective returns fall below the one-dollar-per-dollar threshold, it will distribute unrestricted earnings. It judges history with a five-year rolling average.

chunks.heading: Treating bonds as a "business": the WPPSS investment and the inflation warning
chunks.text:
- Berkshire applies the same business-valuation lens to marketable stocks and to bonds. If it can buy small pieces of businesses with satisfactory economics at a fraction of per-share business value, "something good is likely to happen to us - particularly if we own a group of such securities." Academics reply that it works in practice but "will never work in theory."
- From October 1983 to June 1984 Berkshire's insurers bought Washington Public Power Supply System Projects 1, 2 and 3 bonds, even though the same issuer had defaulted on $2.2 billion of Projects 4 and 5 bonds.
- The math:
  - A $139 million yearend cost was compared with a $139 million operating business.
  - The bond "business" earned $22.7 million after tax in cash, a 16.3% after-tax return on unleveraged capital.
  - A comparable business at those earnings (about $45 million pre-tax) might sell for $250-$300 million, double what Berkshire paid.
  - Downside: a small risk the "business" is worth nothing within a year or two, and a possible interruption of interest.
  - Upside is capped at about $205 million face value, only 48% above cost.
- A 12% zero-coupon bond bought for $10 million grows to $300 million by 2015, the same as a $10 million business earning 12% on equity and retaining everything.
- Example of bond-buying errors: in 1946, 20-year AAA tax-exempt bonds yielded just under 1%, a "business" earning 1% on book that could never earn more, bought at 100 cents on the dollar, while good businesses were available near book value earning 10%-15% after tax. Ben Graham's line, from the last chapter of "The Intelligent Investor," which Warren calls by far the best investing book: "Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike."
- Inflation view:
  - He dislikes most long-term bonds, "as sound as a dollar," and views the long-term outlook for dollars as dismal.
  - He expects substantial inflation and sees a small but real chance of runaway inflation because of the huge deficit.
  - In runaway inflation a diversified stock portfolio would lose real value, but outstanding bonds would suffer far more. An all-bond portfolio carries an "unacceptable 'wipe out' risk."
  - Bond purchases must clear a special hurdle: decidedly superior to other business opportunities, so such occasions are rare.

chunks.heading: Temperament, concentration and unconventional decisions
chunks.text:
- Warren says Charlie and he cannot get 50 such decisions a year; "in any given year we run a risk that we will look extraordinarily foolish." The intelligent-but-might-look-like-an-idiot decision is one most managers avoid, because success earns a pat on the back and failure a pink slip. "Failing conventionally is the route to go; as a group, lemmings may have a rotten image, but no individual lemming has ever received bad press."
- Berkshire's equation differs: with 47% of the stock, Charlie and he "don't worry about being fired" and are rewarded as owners, not managers, so they behave with Berkshire's money as with their own.
- They concentrate insurance-company investments in a few securities they have thought hard about and bought at attractive prices. This is appropriate only because of exceptional financial strength; most insurers could not withstand a big error. Billy Rose on over-diversification: "If you have a harem of forty women, you never get to know any of them very well." Concentration should produce superior long-term results, tempered by size, and a "really bad year" is inevitable.
- Doing nothing is hard. It had been over ten years since equity investments meeting both qualitative and quantitative standards were this difficult to find, and "we find doing nothing the most difficult task of all." He cites "masterly inactivity" as a strategy easier for historians to commend than for participants to follow.
- Secrecy on trading: Berkshire will not comment on its securities activity to anyone. In WPPSS it tried to buy nearly all it could from October 1983 to June 1984 but got under 3% of bonds outstanding; a few coat-tail riders "easily could have cost us $5 million." Any change in position would be disclosed only long after completion.
- Subsequent event: Berkshire agreed to buy three million Capital Cities Communications shares at $172.50, contingent on Capital Cities acquiring ABC. Warren calls Tom Murphy and Dan Burke "tops in both ability and integrity."

chunks.heading: Business quality: Nebraska Furniture Mart, See's and the dominant newspaper
chunks.text:
- Nebraska Furniture Mart (Mrs. B, Rose Blumkin, age 91):
  - Sales rose $14.3 million to $115 million, from one Omaha store, the largest volume of any single home-furnishings store in the US.
  - Levitz ran a 44.4% gross margin and 35.6% operating expenses. NFM's margin is a bit over half that, with operating expenses about 16.5% of sales. NFM saves customers at least $30 million a year versus typical markups while earning excellent returns on capital.
  - The Blumkin family's four "secrets": (1) energy and application; (2) realistically define their area of competence and act decisively within it; (3) ignore enticing propositions outside it; (4) behave in a high-grade manner with everyone. Mrs. B's version: "sell cheap and tell the truth."
  - Buying 90% for $55 million: no audit, no inventory count, no receivables check, no title check. "We gave Mrs. B a check for $55 million and she gave us her word."
  - It all began with a $500 investment in 1937.
- See's Candies:
  - 1984 sales were $135.9 million, after-tax profit $13.4 million, 24.8 million pounds, 214 shops. Per-pound price was up only 1.4%, and 1985 prices were expected up 6%-7%.
  - Same-store volume fell 1.1%, creating cost pressure. Quantity is held level only by adding shops.
  - The Christmas four weeks produce 40% of volume and about 75% of profits.
  - Competitors add preservatives or freeze product to smooth production. See's refuses, "opting, in effect, for production headaches rather than product modification."
  - Success is credited to an exceptional product and an exceptional manager, Chuck Huggins.
- Buffalo Evening News (a dominant newspaper):
  - Total hours (excluding the newsroom) fell about 2.8% and overall costs rose only 4.9%. The 50.9% news hole (versus a typical 35%-40%) and a maintained newsroom staff are deliberate.
  - Advertising is usually 70%-80% of revenue and responds to useful circulation. Concentrated local circulation matters because "wasted" circulation raises costs without adding revenue. Penetration was number one on weekdays among the top 100 papers.
  - "The economics of a dominant newspaper are excellent, among the very best in the business world." Third-rate papers earn as well or better than first-class ones while dominant. Once dominant, the paper itself, not the marketplace, determines quality, so "management must impose its own" standards. Typical news-cost differences are about three points against pre-tax margins "often ten times that amount."
- GEICO: its low-cost auto and homeowners business has a "major, sustainable competitive advantage," which is "a rare asset in business generally" and almost non-existent in financial services. GEICO earned superior profit nowhere else but its core. Berkshire owned 36% and its share of GEICO's $885 million direct volume was $320 million. Lou Simpson has the "rare combination of temperamental and intellectual characteristics" for long-term investing, generating the industry's best returns "with below-average risk."

chunks.heading: Insurance economics: pricing cycles, reserving errors and financial strength
chunks.text:
- Industry premiums must grow about 10% a year to keep the combined ratio stable (loss costs grow roughly 10% from volume, inflation and expanding judicial coverage). Since 1979 premiums rose 30% versus the 61% that 10% a year would give. The 1984 industry combined ratio was 117.7, not the 1979 level of 100.6.
  - Getting back to 100 would need five years of 15% premium growth. He expects several years above 10% followed by competitive pricing and combined ratios of 108-113.
  - Year-to-year change in industry premium volume is "the key index" to underwriting profitability.
- Berkshire's own 1984 combined ratio was a "humbling 134," the third year in a row far worse than the industry.
- Reserving errors:
  - Insurer statements are "at best, only a first rough draft of earnings and financial condition." The charge includes paid losses, estimates for reported-unsettled and incurred-but-not-reported losses, and revisions of prior years' estimates.
  - Example: a 1979 claim reserved at $10,000 but settled in 1984 for $100,000 charges $90,000 to 1984 earnings though it was a 1979 expense.
  - Berkshire reported underwriting results that were later corrected unfavorably each year since 1981: 1983 was reported as a $33.2 million loss and corrected to $51.0 million. 1984's reported $45.4 million loss was $27.6 million on 1984 business plus $17.8 million of 1983 correction.
  - Causes: juries and courts making the "deep pocket" pay, publicity about giant awards, and ceding insurers' mistakes in reinsurance, which Berkshire inherits since reserves are set on their data.
  - Consequences: management acted with less urgency, and Berkshire overpaid taxes on overstated earnings.
  - The "rented suit" story: a brother pays the funeral bill, then keeps getting $15 bills, because "We buried Dad in a rented suit." He uses it to illustrate lingering reserve liabilities, saying the record "should make us humble, and you suspicious."
- The "walking dead":
