  - Insolvent insurers can be "broke but flush," because premium cash arrives long before losses are paid. Some take optimistic reserve views, and some hide losses, and external auditors cannot effectively police this. "The corpse is supposed to file the death certificate."
  - They keep writing business at almost any price, like an embezzler hoping the next batch covers earlier shortfalls, since penalties are no greater for a $100 million shortfall than $10 million.
  - Berkshire suffers from their sell-at-any-price competition and from state guarantee fund assessments when insolvency surfaces.
- Financial strength as a competitive weapon:
  - He argues the promise should be appraised "against the possibility of adversity, not prosperity." Berkshire believes it is almost certainly the strongest property/casualty operation in the country and intends to stay so.
  - This matters for structured settlements and loss-reserve assumptions, where claimants need confidence in decades of payments. Funds held against assumed liabilities grew from $16.2 million to $30.6 million.
  - Weakened competitors let Berkshire raise prices significantly in the last half of 1984 with little business lost. Its plan is to build insurance capital with retained earnings as industry premiums rose, probably over $15 billion in 1985 versus under $5 billion in 1983.

chunks.heading: What Berkshire wants to buy, and how it runs its annual meeting
chunks.text:
- The standing "business wanted" ad lists:
  - Large purchases (at least $5 million of after-tax earnings).
  - Demonstrated consistent earning power; projections and turnarounds are of no interest.
  - Good returns on equity with little or no debt.
  - Management in place ("we can't supply it").
  - Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it").
  - An offering price.
- No unfriendly takeovers; complete confidentiality and an answer typically within five minutes. Cash preferred. Stock is considered only when Berkshire receives as much intrinsic business value as it gives.
- Annual meeting: Warren and Charlie answer every question about the business "no matter how long it takes," except matters where candor could cost money, mainly securities activity. He contrasts it with meetings that become "theatrics, spleen-venting and advocacy of issues."
- 97.2% of eligible shares took part in the shareholder-designated contributions program ($3,179,000 to 1,519 charities).
- He notes: "Managers who put their trust in capitalism seem in no hurry to put their trust in capitalists."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why size dampens returns, why shutting down the textile business taught that business quality beats managerial brilliance, and how fixed-price options reward retained earnings rather than performance. He also covers buying at a discount to business value, Washington Post and Cap Cities, insurance as a commodity, and Berkshire's acquisition criteria.

chunks.heading: 1985 results and why Berkshire's returns will fall
chunks.text:
- Net worth rose $613.6 million, or 48.2%, in 1985. Per-share book value went from $19.46 to $1643.71 over 21 years, 23.2% compounded.
- Warren says neither figure can be repeated. One cause is a market offering little opportunity: "we cannot find significantly-undervalued equities to purchase for our insurance company portfolios."
- The second and "far more telling" cause is size. "An iron law of business is that growth eventually dampens exceptional economics." No high-return company he knows of has kept earning 20% or more on equity for ten years while reinvesting all earnings once it passed $1 billion of equity. To sustain returns, such companies had to shed capital through dividends or buybacks.
- Berkshire needed $3.9 billion of profits over ten years to earn 15% annually. The figure is now $5.7 billion, up 48% in line with the capital base.
- Berkshire's advantages: no pressure from quarterly or annual figures, freedom to enter any business that makes sense, and "we love our work." Hitting 15% will still take far more luck than 23.2% did.

chunks.heading: Market price versus business value, and who the shareholders are
chunks.text:
- Berkshire historically sold modestly below intrinsic value. The discount has disappeared and a premium occasionally appears. That helped holders but hurts new buyers, who must see the premium maintained to match the business's results.
- Warren prefers a price that consistently approximates business value, so all owners prosper as the business prospers. "In the end, investor gains must equal business gains." Long over- or undervaluation distributes the gains unfairly depending on how "lucky, shrewd, or foolish" each owner is.
- Berkshire's shareholders are almost all individuals, not institutions, and have been "rational, interested, and investment-oriented." Institutions with large staffs are not a stabilizing force: "stocks heavily owned and constantly monitored by institutions have often been among the most inappropriately valued."
- He uses Ben Graham's story of the prospector who yells "Oil discovered in hell" and then follows the crowd, to illustrate herd behavior among professionals.

chunks.heading: Reading earnings and selling securities
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie focus on segment-level earnings and never prepare consolidated figures for internal use. Investors need segment data too.
- Realized gains are "meaningless as a measure of how well we have done in the current year." They are like a graduation: all growth since purchase is booked in the year of sale.
- The General Foods sale produced $338 million of the $488 million realized gain. Purchased in 1980 far below business value, it paid off through four factors: a bargain price, fine economics, an able shareholder-oriented management, and a buyer paying full value. Only the last produces reported earnings, but the first three are the key. "We devote our attention to attractive purchases, not to the possibility of attractive sales."
- Special distributions (Washington Post, General Foods) are sales of shares back to the company, sized to keep Berkshire's ownership percentage unchanged. They are taxed like dividends, which is favorable for corporate holders. Warren agrees only when management proposes it and the buyback is below intrinsic value.

chunks.heading: The textile failure: a business with bad economics
chunks.text:
- Buffett Partnership bought control of Berkshire 21 years ago with $22 million net worth, all in textiles. The previous nine years produced $10 million of aggregate losses on $530 million of sales.
- Warren closed the business in 1985 and says he should be "faulted for not quitting sooner." He wrote in 1978 that textiles "should average modest cash returns relative to investment"; he was "very wrong." He "ignored Comte's advice" and "believed what I preferred to believe." The 250 textile mills closed since 1980 processed the same information "more objectively."
- Good managers (Ken Chace, Garry Morrison) and a cooperative union could not fix it. In a commodity business with world excess capacity, each firm's cost-cutting capex looked rational but neutralized itself as savings became industrywide price cuts, "just as happens when each person watching a parade decides he can see a little better if he stands on tiptoes."
- Burlington Industries spent about $3 billion of capex from 1964 to 1985 (more than $200 per share on a $60 stock). Its stock was about at its 1964 price after a 2-for-1 split, while the CPI more than tripled. "A textile company that allocates capital brilliantly within its industry is a remarkable textile company - but not a remarkable business."
- Lesson: "A good managerial record ... is far more a function of what business boat you get into than it is of how effectively you row." In a chronically leaking boat, "energy devoted to changing vessels is likely to be more productive than energy devoted to patching leaks."
- He won't close sub-normal businesses just to add a fraction of a point to returns, but won't fund one with unending losses in prospect.
- Machinery cost $13 million, had $866,000 book value and $30-50 million replacement cost. It sold for $163,122 gross, with a net below zero. Modern looms bought for $5,000 sold for $26 scrap. Book value and replacement value mislead; two paper routes or one See's store have more economic goodwill than that equipment.
- He cites Charlie's habit of studying mistakes: "All I want to know is where I'm going to die so I'll never go there."

chunks.heading: Incentive compensation and stock options
chunks.text:
- NFM, See's and the Buffalo News grew pre-tax earnings from about $8 million to $72 million in 15 years while needing only about $40 million more capital. The average American business needs about $5 of added capital per $1 of added pre-tax earnings, which would have meant over $300 million.
- Earnings growth from retained earnings alone is no achievement. A savings account at 8% quadruples its earnings in 18 years. With a $100,000 account and a 25% payout ratio, it reaches $179,084 in ten years and earnings rise from $8,000 to $13,515.
- Ten-year fixed-price options let managers profit from retained earnings, ignore the carrying cost of capital, and are "blind to individual performance," so "a managerial Rip Van Winkle" could collect. Owners bear capital costs and downside; option holders do not. "I'll be happy to accept a lottery ticket as a gift - but I'll never buy one."
- Managers would never give outsiders such options. Warren says options should go only to those with overall responsibility, include a retained-earnings or carrying-cost factor, and be priced at true business value.
- Berkshire instead pays bonuses for results in each manager's own unit, regardless of Berkshire's stock price. Bonuses are uncapped, sometimes five times salary or more, and age and seniority don't matter. Many managers buy Berkshire stock and so "walk in the shoes of owners."

chunks.heading: Insurance: a commodity business and the lay-off game
chunks.text:
- Premiums grew 20.9% in 1985 but the industry combined ratio was about 118. Losses grew 16% in 1984 and 17% in 1985, partly from reserve corrections and "judicial inflation."
- The profit upturn will be short. Commodity businesses profit only when prices are fixed or capacity is short, and in insurance capacity is "an attitudinal concept": capital can be raised instantly. About 15 insurers raised over $3 billion in 1985. Price-cutting will follow, and the fault will lie with the capital-raisers.
- Berkshire's strong capital is now a competitive advantage. Premium volume more than tripled. It is willing to risk $10 million of its own money on one event if the price is right and the risk is uncorrelated with others, while few insurers will risk half that.
- Large insurers wrote big gross lines but kept small net lines. One 1984 example: the issuer kept about 40% of $6 billion in premiums with an underwriting loss under $200 million (combined ratio well under 110), while reinsurers lost over $1.5 billion (over 140). Berkshire never played the "lay it off at a profit" game.
- A National Indemnity ad for policies with minimum $1 million premiums drew 600 replies and about $50 million in premiums. It is long-tail, so results are unknown for at least five years.
- Combined ratio improved from 134 to 111, still reflecting past under-reserving. Warren says "except for" should be excised from business vocabulary: count "the runs scored against you in all nine innings." "The real mistake is not the act, but the actor." Learn lessons from others' experience.
- Fireman's Fund: from September 1, 1985 Berkshire takes a 7% share of its business for four years, receiving $92.7 million of unearned premium and paying $29.4 million of expenses. Berkshire holds the float for investment but has no role in underwriting or specific investment decisions.

chunks.heading: Buying stocks and businesses: Washington Post, Cap Cities, Scott Fetzer
chunks.text:
- Washington Post: bought in 1973 at no more than one-quarter of per-share business value (about $100 million market versus $400-500 million value). Warren says the edge was attitude from Graham, not insight, and he credits academics preaching efficient markets as an advantage. The stock fell 25% by 1974 before Kay Graham's buybacks and management paid off. A $10.6 million cost became $221 million, versus perhaps $40-60 million in a typical media stock. With a $1.8 billion valuation now, such returns are impossible.
- Cap Cities/ABC: 3 million shares at $172.50, a full price. Warren calls Tom Murphy and Dan Burke the best managers of any public company. Berkshire gave Tom the vote on its shares and accepted sale restrictions, as at GEICO and Washington Post, to shield management from "revolving-door capitalists." Warren says there will be "no surprises."
- Scott & Fetzer: about $320 million plus $90 million of existing debt, 17 businesses on $700 million of sales, World Book 40% of sales. Warren wrote Ralph Schey on October 10, met him October 22 and signed within a week.
- Warren's acquisition ad: (1) at least $10 million after-tax earnings, (2) consistent earning power, no turnarounds or projections, (3) good returns on equity with little debt, (4) management in place, (5) simple businesses, (6) a stated price. No unfriendly takeovers, a fast answer (customarily five minutes), and cash preferred. Berkshire also buys large non-controlling blocks only when the economics and the people are right.
- Berkshire has "no master strategy" and no planners: it waits for something sensible and acts. Beatrice was a short-term arbitrage "parking place for money" when Berkshire has "more money than ideas."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1986 shareholder letter covers hiring great managers and staying out of their way, capital allocation when good ideas are scarce, the Fechheimer deal and Berkshire's buying criteria, commodity insurance pricing, GEICO's cost moat, and the appendix on owner earnings versus the cash flow fallacy.

chunks.heading: Compounding, owner-minded managers, and why Warren's job is attracting them
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie Munger say they have only two jobs: attract and keep outstanding managers, and allocate capital.
- Most managers came with the companies Berkshire bought, already stars in their fields. Warren's main contribution is "to not get in their way." He compares it to managing a golf team where Jack Nicklaus and Arnold Palmer would get no swing directives.
- The highest compliment he pays a manager is that they "think like owners" and love the work. Several are independently wealthy and keep working for the thrill of outstanding performance.
- He endorses David Ogilvy: "If each of us hires people who are smaller than we are, we shall become a company of dwarfs. But, if each of us hires people who are bigger than we are, we shall become a company of giants."
- Span of control: with able managers of high character running businesses they are passionate about, a dozen or more can report to you "and still have time for an afternoon nap." One deceitful, inept or uninterested manager can overwhelm you. Charlie and Warren could handle double the number of managers, if they had the same rare qualities.
- Policy: work only with people they like and admire. Working with people who make your stomach churn is "like marrying for money - probably a bad idea under any circumstances, but absolute madness if you are already rich."
- 1986 results: net worth up $492.5 million, or 26.1%. Per-share book value rose from $19.46 to $2,073.06 over 22 years, 23.3% compounded. Net worth rose 10,600% while shares outstanding rose less than 1%.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation: why it matters more at Berkshire, and why 1986 was hard
chunks.text:
- Capital allocation matters more at Berkshire than at most companies for three reasons: it earns more than average, it retains all earnings, and most operations need little incremental capital to stay competitive and grow.
- A business earning 23% and retaining everything is far more affected by today's allocation decisions than one earning 10% and paying out half. At a company adding only about 5% to net worth a year, allocation errors change the economics much more slowly.
- Berkshire's retained earnings, plus those of major investees GEICO and Capital Cities/ABC, must be deployed productively or "the economics of Berkshire will deteriorate very quickly."
- In 1986 Warren admits his performance lagged his managers'. He bought one business (Fechheimer, about 2% of net worth) and found no new ideas in marketable equities. The main moves were paying off debt and stockpiling funds.
- Size drag: Warren still hopes for 15% return on equity, but that requires net worth to grow $7.2 billion in ten years. That is only possible with "a few very big (and good) ideas."
- He expects roughly one operating-business acquisition every couple of years, and it must be large to matter.

chunks.heading: What Berkshire wants to buy: the acquisition "ad" and the Fechheimer case
chunks.text:
- The 1986 purchase of Fechheimer Bros. came from the annual "ad" describing what Berkshire wants. Chairman Bob Heldman, a long-time shareholder, wrote on January 15, 1986.
- Fechheimer is a uniform manufacturer and distributor founded in 1842. It was sold in a 1981 leveraged buyout, with management keeping equity. Debt was paid down and equity value rose, and the venture capitalists wanted to sell. Berkshire bought about 84% on a valuation of $55 million for the whole business.
- The purchase resembled Nebraska Furniture Mart: sellers wanted money for other uses, the family wanted to keep running the business, several generations were active, and they wanted a buyer who "would not re-sell, regardless of price."
- Warren and Charlie had not visited Cincinnati, and See's manager Chuck Huggins, after 15 years, had never visited Omaha. Warren says they judge "the economic characteristics of the business - its competitive strengths and weaknesses - and the quality of the people," not plant inspections.
- The acquisition criteria, as restated:
  1. Large purchases (at least $10 million of after-tax earnings, raised from $5 million).
  2. Demonstrated consistent earning power. Future projections and turnarounds are of no interest.
  3. Good returns on equity with little or no debt.
  4. Management in place ("we can't supply it").
  5. Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it").
  6. An offering price stated up front.
- Terms: no unfriendly takeovers, complete confidentiality, an answer customarily within five minutes. Cash is preferred. Stock is issued only when Berkshire receives as much intrinsic business value as it gives.
- Not interested in: new ventures, turnarounds, auction-like sales, and "I'm-sure-something-will-work-out-if-you-people-get-to-know-each-other" deals.
- Also interested in large negotiated, non-controlling stakes (as with Cap Cities) when comfortable with the economics and the people's ability and integrity. The preference is for commitments of many times $50 million.

chunks.heading: Moats and franchise economics: Buffalo News, See's, NFM, GEICO
chunks.text:
- GEICO's low costs: underwriting plus loss-adjustment expense was 23.5% of premiums in 1986 (24.1% in 1985). Many major insurers run about 15 points higher. Warren calls this gap "a kind of moat that protects a valuable and much-sought-after business castle," and says chairman Bill Snyder keeps widening the moat by cutting costs further.
- GEICO's combined ratio was 96.9 with 16% premium growth, and it repurchased shares, ending the year with 5.5% fewer outstanding.
- Lou Simpson's GEICO equity portfolio beat the S&P 500 every year from 1980 to 1986. 1986: 38.7% vs 18.6%. Warren credits buying "undervalued common stocks that, individually, were unlikely to present him with a permanent loss and that, collectively, were close to risk-free."
- The Buffalo News: a 50% news hole versus about 40% at comparable papers (30 ad pages become 30 pages of news instead of 20). It has the highest weekday penetration among the top 50 US papers and 83% Sunday penetration, against about 63% for the rival Courier-Express a decade earlier. Ad rate increases were well below industry levels. Warren says he would keep the news-hole ratio even if margins shrink.
- See's: over 12,000 tons sold a year. Same-store pounds were flat after six years of decline. It held margins with minimal price increases, and Warren expects only modest increases that match cost increases. Its "personality" comes from taste, moderate price, total control of distribution and service.
- Nebraska Furniture Mart: 1986 sales rose 10.2% to $132 million (from $44 million ten years earlier) from a single store whose reach widens because of "rock-bottom everyday prices" and the broadest selection. Mrs. B, 93, works seven days a week.
- World Book and Kirby: unit volume rose for four straight years. World Book is priced under 5 cents per page, and over half its salespeople are teachers or former teachers.

chunks.heading: Taxes and who captures the benefit: franchise strength decides
chunks.text:
- The 1986 tax law cut the corporate rate from 46% to 34% by 1988. Warren asks whether companies keep the benefit or pass it to customers. His answer: it depends on franchise strength and whether profits are regulated.
  - Regulated utilities: tax changes flow into prices.
  - Price-competitive industries with weak franchises: the market "regulates" profits, so tax changes eventually affect prices more than profits.
  - Unregulated businesses with strong franchises: the company and shareholders keep the benefit. His analogy is the best local brain surgeon or lawyer, whose fees won't fall because the tax rate does.
- Shareholders' take on a dollar of per-share business value fell from 80 cents to 72 cents as the top personal capital gains rate rose from 20% to 28%.
- Corporate capital gains rose from 28% to 34%. This hurts because most of Berkshire's expected value gain comes from capital gains. Cap Cities, GEICO and Washington Post were over $1.7 billion (close to 75% of net worth) and yielded only about $9 million a year in income. Unrealized gains were $1.2 billion, and about $73 million would move from GAAP net worth to deferred taxes once the accounting rule changed.
- Insurer-specific hits: dividends taxed on 20% (up from 15%), tax-exempt interest on bonds bought after August 7, 1986 only 85% exempt, and reserves discounted for tax. Warren guesses these cut insurance earning power by at least 10%. A one-time "fresh start" benefit was expected at $30-$40 million.
- Repeal of the General Utilities Doctrine creates a double tax on corporate liquidations. Warren says this reduces what sellers can realize and that investors and managers have not yet fully grasped it.
- He doubts the scheduled 1988 rates are sustainable and expects higher tax rates or higher inflation within about five years, possibly both.

chunks.heading: Insurance: commodity pricing, float, and discipline
chunks.text:
- Combined ratio: losses plus expenses over premiums. Below 100 is an underwriting profit. With float income, a combined ratio of about 107-112 typically produces break-even.
- Warren says industry revenues must grow close to 10% a year just to hold profitability, because social and judicial inflation (bigger verdicts, expanded coverage) outruns general inflation of 2-4%.
- Industry premium growth was 22.6% in 1986, and the combined ratio improved from 116.5 to 108.5. Quarterly premium growth slowed from 27.1% to 18.7%. He predicted that profits would be fleeting and that improvement would end by late 1988 or early 1989.
- The commodity cycle: profits come only under shortage. Insurers then raise capital, new entrants rush in, "capacity soars, competitive juices flow, and prices fade." Appeals for "statesmanlike" pricing are like asking corn growers to market with more statesmanship: "What's needed is not more statesmen, but less corn."
- Berkshire's approach: always willing to write at adequate prices, and its volume swings widely because competitors come and go. National Indemnity monthly volume went from $5 million (late 1984) to about $35 million (early 1986) to about $20 million and falling. No layoffs when volume falls, so employees don't chase volume out of fear.
- Combined ratio fell from 111 to 103. Warren admits three straight years of reserve underestimation, and calls "reserve strengthening" a euphemism for "correction of previous untruths."
- Warren says Berkshire's edges are attitude, capital, and developing personnel, plus a long-term edge in investing float. Insurance is "a treacherous business and a wary attitude is essential."

chunks.heading: Investing temperament, "owner earnings," and the cash flow fallacy
chunks.text:
- When no stocks meet his tests, he doesn't buy. In 1986 he found none, and insurance money went into about $700 million of mediocre tax-exempt bonds (8 to 12 years), the least objectionable option. He stresses that this is not a market prediction: "we have no idea - and never have had" where the market goes.
- Fear and greed: "we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful." Euphoria was prevailing. Because of transaction and management costs, stockholders as a whole must underperform the businesses they own. If American business earns about 12% on equity, investors must earn significantly less: "Bull markets can obscure mathematical laws, but they cannot repeal them."
- Long bonds are avoided over fear of higher inflation. Arbitrage is limited to a few large, publicly announced deals, never "betting on the come," as an alternative to Treasury bills with higher risk.
- Holdings at yearend 1986 included Capital Cities/ABC (cost $515.8 million, market $801.7 million), GEICO (cost $45.7 million, market $674.7 million) and Washington Post (cost $9.7 million, market $269.5 million). Warren expects to hold these three permanently, even if overpriced, just as he wouldn't sell See's or the Buffalo News at a price far above value. He favors a "'til-death-do-us-part policy" over the "portfolio restructuring" mentality.
- Owner earnings = reported earnings + depreciation, depletion, amortization and other non-cash charges, minus the average annual capital expenditures needed to fully maintain long-term competitive position and unit volume (plus any extra working capital needed). He calls it the relevant figure for valuation. The capex term is a guess: "I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong" (Keynes).
- Scott Fetzer example: Berkshire paid $315 million for net assets carried at $172.4 million, a $142.6 million premium. Purchase-price adjustments cut 1986 GAAP net income from $40.2 million (old basis) to $28.6 million (new basis) with identical economics and cash. Warren says Scott Fetzer's maintenance capex is close to the old depreciation of $8.3 million, so owner earnings are far better shown by the higher "old" figure. That is why Berkshire reports business-unit earnings before purchase-price adjustments.
- The "cash flow" fallacy: Wall Street cash flow adds earnings plus depreciation but ignores capital spending. Warren says it is meaningless for manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies and utilities, whose capex is always significant. Investment bankers use it to "justify the unjustifiable," such as junk bond debt service or foolish stock prices. For many businesses (the oil industry is the example) GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings.
- On accounting: it is the language of business and the starting point, but "accounting is but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it." The accountant's job is to record; the evaluation falls to investors and managers.
- Intrinsic value: business value is a "soft number," and two well-informed observers could differ by more than 10%. Book value has been a conservative proxy for Berkshire's business value.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1987 letter shows how Berkshire judges businesses by return on capital, hands off great managers, and treats stocks as pieces of businesses while ignoring Mr. Market. It also covers commodity-like insurance economics, why it prefers a fine business at a fair price, capital allocation, and keeping debt low enough to be certain of surviving.

chunks.heading: Per-share business value, not book value, is what counts
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's net worth rose $464 million, or 19.5%, in 1987. Per-share book value grew from $19.46 to $2,477.47 over 23 years, a 23.1% compounded annual rate.
- Warren says the rate of gain in per-share business value is what matters, not book value. The two can be almost unrelated: LTV and Baldwin-United published year-end book values of $652 million and $397 million just before going bankrupt, while Belridge Oil sold to Shell in 1979 for $3.6 billion against a $177 million book value.
- At Berkshire, business value has moderately outpaced book value over the last decade, because it owns remarkable businesses run by remarkable managers.
- He ignores GAAP figures and focuses on the future earning power of both controlled and non-controlled businesses. He sets his own idea of business value, independent of the accounting values on the books for controlled companies and of the prices a "sometimes foolish" market puts on partially owned ones.
- GAAP quirk: controlled companies show full earnings in the income account but are never written up on the balance sheet. The three permanent stocks are marked to market on the balance sheet but only their small dividends reach income. They were worth over $2 billion and produced only $11 million of reported earnings, versus well over $100 million of look-through earnings.

chunks.heading: Judging managers by returns on underlying capital
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's seven largest non-financial units (Buffalo News, Fechheimer, Kirby, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Scott Fetzer Manufacturing Group, See's Candies, World Book) earned $180 million before interest and taxes in 1987.
- Net interest expense was only $2 million, so pre-tax earnings on equity were $178 million on historical-cost equity of just $175 million. After-tax earnings of about $100 million equal roughly a 57% return on equity.
- Benchmark: per Fortune, only six of the 1,000 largest industrial and service companies averaged over 30% ROE in the prior decade. The best was Commerce Clearing House at 40.2%.
- Managers should be judged on returns on the underlying assets, not on what Berkshire paid. Those units are carried about $222 million above their historical accounting values, but "what we pay for a business does not affect the amount of capital its manager has to work with."
- Three inferences: business value is far above book value; so little capital is needed that the units can grow while sending almost all earnings out for redeployment; and the managers are extraordinary.

chunks.heading: How Warren and Charlie manage managers
chunks.text:
- With such managers, Warren and Charlie "have little to do with operations." They hold no corporate meetings, set no corporate budgets and do no performance reviews. "What can we tell the Blumkins about home furnishings, or the Heldmans about uniforms?"
- Their contribution is "informed applause," based on long careers observing business performance and managerial behavior.
- They reject flexible operating budgets. At the Buffalo News the news hole is about 50% of the paper. Cutting it to a typical 40% would save about $4 million a year in newsprint, and "that interests us not at all," even if margins shrink.
- Neither cut essential activities when profits fall nor add unneeded people (a staff economist, a corporate strategist, an institutional ad campaign) when money is rolling in. "That kind of yo-yo approach is neither business-like nor humane."
- When a unit stumbles, they call a fixer. Harry Bottle was named "Man of the Year" for turning around Dempster Mill in 1962. In 1987 Charlie made him CEO of K & W Products after it stumbled in 1985-86; profits rose over 300% and receivables and inventories fell 20%.

chunks.heading: Boring franchises beat exciting change
chunks.text:
- "Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix." Investors give the highest P/Es to exotic businesses promising feverish change, letting them fantasize about future profitability instead of facing today's realities.
- The best returns usually come from companies doing something quite similar to what they did five or ten years ago. Constant change brings many chances for major error and makes it hard to build a fortress-like franchise.
- Fortune's test: only 25 of 1,000 companies averaged over 20% ROE from 1977 to 1986 with no year below 15%. 24 of the 25 beat the S&P 500. Most used very little leverage ("Really good businesses usually don't need to borrow"), and most sold mundane, non-sexy products, apart from one high-tech company and several ethical-drug makers.
- Berkshire's managers get extraordinary results from ordinary things done exceptionally well. They protect their franchises, control costs, look for new products and markets that build on existing strengths, and don't get diverted.
- Examples:
  - Mrs. B (Rose Blumkin), 94, started Nebraska Furniture Mart 50 years earlier with $500. NFM sold $142.6 million in 1987, up 8%, and customers saved about $30 million versus buying elsewhere. Her maxim: "Sell cheap and tell the truth."
  - Chuck Huggins at See's: volume near 25 million pounds, about 85% of profit earned in December. When 14 candy items were cut, hundreds of customers complained; Chuck restored the two badly missed ones and answered every letter honestly.
  - Ralph Schey runs 19 Scott Fetzer businesses. Pre-tax earnings rose 10% in 1987 while average capital employed fell significantly.

chunks.heading: Mr. Market and investing as business analysis
chunks.text:
- When buying stocks, Warren and Charlie act as if buying into a private business. They weigh the business's economics, its managers and the price, with no set time or price to sell. "We view ourselves as business analysts - not as market analysts, not as macroeconomic analysts, and not even as security analysts."
- Ben Graham's Mr. Market: a manic-depressive partner who quotes a buy-sell price daily. Transactions are strictly at your option, so his wild swings help you. "Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful."
- "If you aren't certain that you understand and can value your business far better than Mr. Market, you don't belong in the game."
- Success comes from good business judgment plus insulating your thoughts and behavior from market emotions, not from "arcane formulae, computer programs or signals." Graham: "In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine."
- Judge holdings by operating results, not price quotes. Delayed recognition can be an advantage, giving a chance to buy more at a bargain.
- Selling: sell when the market overvalues a business, or to fund a more undervalued idea. Don't sell just because of appreciation or holding time ("You can't go broke taking a profit" is perhaps "the most foolish" Wall Street maxim).
- Hold while the business's return on equity is satisfactory, management is competent and honest, and the market does not overvalue it.
- Goal: "an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price." Making "silk purses out of silk" works; sow's ears fail. Warren took about 20 years to learn this, after "bargains" like short-line farm implement makers, third-place department stores and New England textiles.
- Permanent holdings, which Warren would hold even if far overpriced: Capital Cities/ABC (3,000,000 shares, cost $517.5 million, market $1,035 million), GEICO (6,850,000 shares, cost $45.7 million, market $756.9 million), Washington Post (1,727,765 shares, cost $9.7 million, market $323.1 million). He prefers a return of X with people he admires over 110% of X with people he doesn't.
- Washington Post bought in 1973 at $5.63 per share earned $10.30 per share after tax in 1987. GEICO bought at an average $6.67 earned $9.01.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation and control versus minority stakes
chunks.text:
- Control's first advantage: you allocate capital. Many CEOs rose through marketing, production, engineering or politics and never learned it, "as if the final step for a highly-talented musician was not to perform at Carnegie Hall but, instead, to be named Chairman of the Federal Reserve."
- It matters because a CEO retaining earnings equal to 10% of net worth will, after ten years, have deployed more than 60% of all capital in the business.
- Staffs, consultants and investment bankers more likely accentuate the problem than solve it. Plenty of unintelligent allocation explains the amount of "restructuring."
- Second advantage is tax: as a corporate holder, a given business result can deliver Berkshire results up to 50% better from an 80%-or-greater holding than from a lesser one.
- Management changes, "like marital changes, are painful, time-consuming and chancy," so the power to effect change is somewhat illusory.
- Offsetting benefit: the market occasionally sells non-controlling pieces of extraordinary businesses at prices far below those paid in control transactions.

chunks.heading: Insurance: commodity economics, float and discipline
chunks.text:
- Combined ratio below 100 means an underwriting profit. With float, a ratio of 107-111 typically produces overall break-even, excluding earnings on shareholder funds.
- Industry revenues must grow about 10% a year to hold its own, because social and judicial inflation (courtroom costs, verdicts, expanded coverage) outruns general inflation. Premiums grew 22% in 1985-86 but only 8.7% in 1987; "the party is over." Policies run one year, so earnings lag price changes.
- Insurance is a commodity business: hundreds of competitors, easy entry, an undifferentiable product. Only a low-cost operator or protected niche sustains high profits, except in shortages. Typical managers hate shortages yet are the only time commodity businesses earn good returns, and they rush to add capacity (Disraeli: "What we learn from history is that we do not learn from history.").
- Berkshire differentiates in two ways: financial strength (which matters most when buyers remember Ben Franklin's line that "it is hard for an empty sack to stand upright") and total indifference to volume. It will write five times or one-fifth as much next year, pricing on exposure, not competition.
- Three conditions allow this: market share doesn't drive profitability ("survival of the fattest" doesn't apply); distribution channels are easily entered, so low volume this year doesn't preclude high volume next; idle capacity, mostly people, isn't intolerably costly.
- A broker who lost the business on price in 1987 bought more Berkshire stock instead. Berkshire's 1987 combined ratio was 105 (103 in 1986), but profits improved because it had far more float.
- Be suspicious of insurers' reported earnings. Long-tail lines (product liability, D&O) make reserves unknowable, and the dishonest exploit this ("long-tail insurance is heaven"). Warren proposes auditor opinion wording admitting they can't judge loss reserves.
- Tax changes hurt: the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and the 1987 Bill (dividends-received credit cut from 80% to 70%) penalize insurers owning stocks indirectly.

chunks.heading: Market turmoil, bonds, arbitrage, debt and acquisition criteria
chunks.text:
- The Dow rose just 2.3% in 1987 despite a manic run and October crash. Warren blames professionals focusing on "what they expect other money managers to do in the days ahead." Portfolio insurance, with $60-90 billion poised on a hair trigger, is "an exotically-labeled version" of a stop-loss order. He compares it to selling a farm piece by piece when a neighbor sells lower.
- Volatility helps the true investor who sticks to his "investment knitting", unless forced by financial or psychological pressure to sell at bad times. Berkshire found little to buy and held no non-permanent, non-arbitrage stock position over $50 million.
- Bonds: about $900 million in medium-term tax-exempts as a parking place; aversion to long-term bonds because "bonds are no better than the currency in which they are denominated." He fears the trade deficit will pressure the US to inflate, though timing is unpredictable. Exception: Washington Public Power Supply Systems bonds, bought where he saw a specific edge (amortized cost $240 million, market $316 million, $34 million tax-exempt income).
- Arbitrage: few large, publicly announced deals, no greenmail situations; estimated average pre-tax returns of at least 25%, with bad experiences able to change that. Also bought Texaco bonds after bankruptcy (carried at $104 million, market $119 million) and $700 million of Salomon 9% convertible preferred (convertible at $38 after three years), based on trust in John Gutfreund.
- Debt: Berkshire wants to meet obligations with certainty and seeks "acceptable long-term results under extraordinarily adverse conditions, rather than optimal results under a normal range of conditions." Leverage risks what is important for returns that are unimportant.
- It finances in anticipation of need, since tight money creates the best acquisition chances. It raised $250 million of debentures at slightly over 10%, earning about 6.5% on the proceeds, costing about $160,000 per week. "If you want to shoot rare, fast-moving elephants, you should always carry a loaded gun."
- Warren never comments on rumors, true or false, since denying some and refusing comment on others would comment on all.
- Acquisition criteria:
  - Large purchases (at least $10 million of after-tax earnings)
  - Demonstrated consistent earning power (no projections or turnarounds)
  - Good ROE with little or no debt
  - Management in place
  - Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it")
  - An offering price
- No unfriendly takeovers. Complete confidentiality, and an answer "customarily within five minutes." Cash preferred, stock only when Berkshire gets as much intrinsic value as it gives.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett reports a 20% gain in 1988 and explains why a growing capital base is Berkshire's main problem. He covers buying Borsheim's on a handshake, holding wonderful businesses forever, how he approaches arbitrage, and why efficient market theory fails. He also explains why GAAP is only a starting point and why CEOs escape the accountability faced by subordinates.

chunks.heading: Valuing the Business: Intrinsic Value, Book Value, and the Growing-Capital Problem
chunks.text:
- Warren says what counts is intrinsic business value, "the figure, necessarily an estimate, indicating what all of our constituent businesses are worth." Berkshire's intrinsic value significantly exceeds book value.
- 1988 net worth gain was $569 million, or 20.0%. Per-share book value went from $19.46 to $2,974.52 over 24 years, 23.0% compounded.
- He warns against extrapolating the past: doing so is like judging "a 42-year-old center fielder on the basis of his lifetime batting average."
- Headwinds he lists: a less attractive stock market, higher corporate tax rates on investment income, a richly priced market for acquiring businesses, and weaker industry conditions at Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO and Washington Post.
- The main problem is a growing capital base. Four years earlier a 15% annual return over the next decade needed $3.9 billion of profits; now it needs $10.3 billion.
- The offset is the "Sainted Seven" (Buffalo News, Fechheimer, Kirby, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Scott Fetzer Manufacturing Group, See's, World Book). They earned about 67% on average equity capital with no financial leverage.
- Their results come from an exceptional franchise plus exceptional management. His and Charlie's contribution "is to leave these managers alone." The open question is whether they can effectively deploy the cash these businesses generate.

chunks.heading: Accounting, GAAP, and What Owners Need to Know
chunks.text:
- Warren treats GAAP "as a beginning rather than an end" of a CEO's duty to inform owners. A subsidiary manager who gave his boss only barebones numbers would be in hot water, so a CEO shouldn't do it to shareholders.
- Reporting should help financially literate readers answer three questions: (1) approximately how much is the company worth, (2) how likely is it to meet its obligations, (3) how good a job are managers doing given the hand they were dealt.
- Many managements see GAAP "not as a standard to be met, but as an obstacle to overcome." Earnings smoothing and the "big bath" quarter are "white lie" techniques. Some managers use GAAP to defraud: "It has been far safer to steal large sums with a pen than small sums with a gun."
- Consolidation is mandated, but he argues the more diverse the businesses lumped together, the less useful the statements. Charlie and he "constantly study" segment data and prepare consolidated figures only for outside requirements.
- Berkshire added supplementary four-segment statements: finance operations, insurance, manufacturing/publishing/retailing, and all other. They are meant to give owners information "in a form that we would wish to get it if our roles were reversed."
- Deferred taxes: Berkshire books 28% on $1.2 billion of older unrealized appreciation and 34% on $600 million built since. A 1990 rule would require 34% on everything, cutting earnings by $71 million. Neither rate reflects reality since Berkshire has no plans to sell the stocks holding its gains.
- Shareholders can take a "faith" approach (Warren and Charlie have most of their money in Berkshire, gains and losses are shared proportionally) or an "analysis" approach. "In our own investing, we search for situations in which both approaches give us the same answer."

chunks.heading: Managers, Family Businesses, and the Borsheim's Purchase
chunks.text:
- Warren does not retire superstars by age. Mrs. B (Rose Blumkin) turned 95; she started Nebraska Furniture Mart at 44 with $500 and has been boss for 51 years. "Superb managers are too scarce a resource to be discarded simply because a cake gets crowded with candles."
- He is skeptical of newly minted MBAs: records look terrific but candidates are "too often short on personal commitment to the company and general business savvy."
- Examples of managers: Stan Lipsey at the Buffalo News improved margins even after Warren predicted they'd fall; the paper keeps its newshole near 50% (49.5% in 1988) regardless of margins. Chuck Huggins runs See's, which sold a record 25.1 million pounds and earned 90% of annual profit in December ($29 million of $32.5 million pre-tax). Ralph Schey runs 19 businesses at Scott Fetzer.
- Fechheimer's Heldman family made a fairly large acquisition that Warren and Charlie "okayed the deal without even looking at it." Furniture retailing and uniform manufacturing are not inherently attractive, so "only exceptional managements can deliver high returns."
- In early 1989 Berkshire bought 80% of Borsheim's, an Omaha jeweler run by the Friedman family (relatives of Mrs. B). He admits he blundered in 1983 by not asking Mrs. B "Are there any more at home like you?"
- The cornerstone is Mrs. B's creed, "Sell cheap and tell the truth." Fundamentals: single-store operations with huge inventories, daily top-management attention to detail, rapid turnover, shrewd buying, and very low expenses.
- Jewelry buyers cannot judge quality or price, so: "If you don't know jewelry, know the jeweler."
- Berkshire bought Borsheim's with no audit, inventory count or receivables check. Ike Friedman "simply told us what was so" and a one-page contract was signed.
- Warren and Charlie stay on the sidelines; the Friedmans keep operating as before.

chunks.heading: Insurance: Pricing Discipline, Float, and Industry Economics
chunks.text:
- The combined ratio is losses plus expenses over premiums; below 100 means an underwriting profit. With float counted, a ratio of 107-111 typically breaks even. The 1988 industry combined ratio was 105.4.
- He expects industry incurred losses to grow about 10% a year, so underwriting losses will mount if premiums lag, and may be obscured by under-reserving.
- Industries with inadequate prices get blamed by customers, while highly profitable ones don't. Breakfast cereal earns more than double the return on capital of auto insurance, yet "not a peep" is heard on price hikes. Cereal makers sell at about five times book; most insurers sell near book.
- California's Proposition 103 would force auto rates below cost. Warren argues that below-cost prices must eventually be subsidized by taxpayers. Most insurers have commodity economics and little "economic goodwill" to lose, but GEICO, a low-cost producer with high returns, has a lot at risk, and so does Berkshire (44% owner).
- Berkshire "will not write policies at rates that carry the expectation of economic loss." Volume will stay low. Its 1988 combined ratio was 104 and reserve development was favorable for a second year.
- Low volume with high float means better profits than the industry: he expects float-to-premium at least three times a typical property/casualty company in 1989-1990.
- He expects to be "deluged with insurance business" at some point, likely after a catastrophe or when other insurers recognize they're under-reserved, as in 1985. Meanwhile: retain talent, protect capital, avoid major mistakes.

chunks.heading: Investing Approach, Holdings, and Bonds
chunks.text:
- Criteria for choosing among stocks, bonds, cash and arbitrage: highest after-tax return by "mathematical expectation," limited to alternatives Berkshire thinks it understands. The goal is to maximize eventual net worth, not reported earnings.
- Holdings over $100 million at cost/market (000s): Capital Cities/ABC $517,500 / $1,086,750; Coca-Cola $592,540 / $632,448; Freddie Mac preferred $71,729 / $121,200; GEICO $45,713 / $849,400; Washington Post $9,731 / $364,126.
- Cap Cities, GEICO and Washington Post are permanent holdings. Coca-Cola and Freddie Mac were major 1988 buys that he expects to hold long. "Our favorite holding period is forever." He rejects "cutting the flowers and watering the weeds" (Peter Lynch's phrase).
- He concentrates in a few companies he understands: "Too much of a good thing can be wonderful" (Mae West). New commitments reflect long-term business views: "We do not have, never have had, and never will have an opinion about where the stock market, interest rates, or business activity will be a year from now."
- Long-term bonds: he stays averse until he's enthused about long-term stability in the purchasing power of money, which he doesn't expect.
- Exceptions: WPPSS bonds, bought around 17% after-tax yield when unrated and stigmatized, now rated AA-; carried at $247 million, worth about $352 million. He hopes to find "some other large stigmatized issue" misappraised by the market.
- Texaco bankruptcy bonds sold for about $22 million pre-tax profit. The $700 million Salomon 9% convertible preferred is mostly valued for its fixed-income traits; the conversion option may add value, but he has no insight into investment banking profitability.
- He sold about $100 million of tax-exempt bonds bought after August 7, 1986; the remaining $800 million is mostly grandfathered fully tax-exempt.

chunks.heading: CEO Accountability and Board Dynamics
chunks.text:
- "The supreme irony of business management is that it is far easier for an inadequate CEO to keep his job than it is for an inadequate subordinate."
- A secretary who can't type 80 words per minute is gone quickly because the standard is clear. CEO standards are fuzzy or waived: "the boss shoots the arrow of managerial performance and then hastily paints the bullseye around the spot where it lands."
- The CEO's boss, the board, seldom measures itself or is held to account. Even if a takeover follows a hiring mistake, outgoing directors typically benefit. Board criticism of the CEO is viewed as "the social equivalent of belching."
- He praises his permanent-holding managers (Tom Murphy and Dan Burke, Bill Snyder and Lou Simpson, Kay Graham and Dick Simmons) for loving their businesses, thinking like owners, and showing integrity and ability.

chunks.heading: Arbitrage and Efficient Market Theory
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's insurance units use arbitrage as an alternative to cash when they "have more cash than good ideas." It also "cools any temptation" to relax standards for long-term investments. 1988 pre-tax gain: about $78 million on average invested funds of about $147 million.
- Four questions for any arbitrage: (1) how likely is the promised event, (2) how long is money tied up, (3) what chance of something better (e.g. a competing bid), (4) what happens if the event fails.
- Arcata example: KKR offered $37.00 plus two-thirds of any extra government payment for redwood lands. Warren bought about 400,000 shares near $33.50 and later raised to 655,000 shares (over 7%), buying near $38.00, leaning toward "a whole lot" rather than "zero" on the redwood claim. KKR's financing wobbled, but a rival group paid $37.50 plus half of any recovery. Berkshire received $24.6 million on a $22.9 million cost (about 15% annualized over roughly six months), then about $19.3 million more ($29.48 per share) after the claim settled for $519 million.
- Rockwood cocoa example (age 24, Graham-Newman): the company distributed cocoa beans to shareholders at 80 pounds per share to avoid LIFO tax. Warren bought shares, sold beans, and profited with only subway tokens as expense. Rockwood stock rose from 15 to 100 around the tender.
- Berkshire's style: only a few, usually very large, publicly announced deals per year; no rumors or guessing takeover candidates; "What's the sense in getting rich just to stare at a ticker tape all day?" RJR Nabisco: 3,342,000 shares at year-end, cost $281.8 million, eventually a $64 million pre-tax profit.
- He expects to sit out 1989 arbitrage because of takeover-field excesses: "the less the prudence with which others conduct their affairs, the greater the prudence with which we should conduct our own."
- On efficient market theory: the market is frequently efficient, not always, and "the difference between these propositions is night and day." Graham-Newman's 1926-1956 unleveraged arbitrage averaged 20% a year; 1956-1988 returns at Buffett Partnership and Berkshire averaged well over 20%. The market returned just under 10%, so $1,000 becomes $405,000 at 10% versus $97 million at 20%.
- Caveat: arbitrage is not a guaranteed 20%. "An investor cannot obtain superior profits from stocks by simply committing to a specific investment category or style. He can earn them only by carefully evaluating facts and continuously exercising discipline."

chunks.heading: Shareholder Policy, Acquisition Criteria, and Dave Dodd
chunks.text:
- Warren does not want to maximize Berkshire's share price. He wants it to trade in a narrow range around intrinsic value, since both big over- and undervaluation produce investor results that diverge from business results.
- He wants little trading and long-term owners with no timetable or price target: "At what other organization - school, club, church, etc. - do leaders cheer when members leave?"
- Acquisition criteria: (1) purchases of at least $10 million after-tax earnings, (2) demonstrated consistent earning power (no projections or turnarounds), (3) good returns on equity with little or no debt, (4) management in place, (5) simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it"), (6) an offering price stated up front.
- No unfriendly takeovers. Confidentiality promised, an answer usually within five minutes, cash preferred, stock only when Berkshire gets as much intrinsic value as it gives. Favorite deal: the Blumkin-Friedman-Heldman mold, where owner-managers take cash but stay on as significant owners running the business. He also wants large non-controlling stakes and convertible preferreds, like Salomon.
- Warning: "if you advertise an interest in buying collies, a lot of people will call hoping to sell you their cocker spaniels."
- S&P raised Berkshire to AAA, which only 15 other U.S. industrial or property-casualty companies hold. He promises bondholders the same respect as shareholders and no "event risk."
- Warren credits David Dodd (died at 93; co-author of Security Analysis with Ben Graham) for principles that were "simple, sound, useful, and enduring." Berkshire's prosperity is "the fruit of their intellectual tree."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1989 letter defines intrinsic value, explains why high growth rates fade as the base grows, and lays out the economics of deferred taxes and look-through earnings. His "Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years" covers cigar-butt investing, the institutional imperative, and refusing leverage. He also explains why Berkshire writes insurance only at profitable prices.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value, book value, and the limits of compounding
chunks.text:
- Warren reports a 44.4% gain in net worth for 1989 ($1.515 billion). Book value per share grew from $19.46 to $4,296.01 over 25 years, a 23.8% compound annual rate.
- He says book value is not what counts. Intrinsic value does: "all future cash flows of a business - in and out - and discounted at prevailing interest rates." Valued this way, businesses "from manufacturers of buggy whips to operators of cellular phones, become economic equals."
- Berkshire's intrinsic value compounded faster than book value. At the start, book value was tied up in a textile business worth less than its carrying value, whereas most businesses are now worth more than carrying value.
- Much of the past gain was a "double-dip": gains in the portfolio companies' intrinsic value, plus the market re-rating their prices up toward that value. That catch-up is over, so he expects a "single-dip" going forward.
- "In a finite world, high growth rates must self-destruct." He cites Carl Sagan's bacteria that double every 15 minutes. From a $4.9 billion base, averaging 15% will be much harder than averaging 23.8% from the original $22 million.
- Many holdings were priced high relative to intrinsic value at year-end. Warren says he will keep most of them anyway ("'til-death-do-us-part"). He says a roughly 10% yearly drop in the portfolio's aggregate value would reduce net worth, and he expects a decline in at least one of the next three years.

chunks.heading: Taxes, deferred liabilities, and why Warren holds long
chunks.text:
- The 1989 tax charge was about $712 million: about $172 million paid currently and $540 million deferred, mostly on unrealized stock gains. He reserved 34%. Pre-1987 gains of about $1.2 billion carry reserves booked at the old 28% rate.
- A deferred tax liability of over $1.1 billion on unrealized gains is not like a trade payable, nor is it a meaningless fiction. He calls it "an interest-free loan from the U.S. Treasury that comes due only at our election." It can only finance the particular appreciated stocks. It works like a transfer tax paid only if Berkshire moves from one asset to another. In 1989 Berkshire sold small holdings, incurring about $76 million of tax on $224 million of gains.
- Illustration: $1 doubled each year for 20 years, taxed at 34% on each sale, ends at about $25,250. One investment that doubles 20 times, taxed once at the end, ends at about $692,000 (from $1,048,576 pre-tax). The difference is only the timing of tax payments, roughly 27:1 in tax collected.
- He says Berkshire does not hold long because of this arithmetic. It might earn more after tax by moving often, and he and Charlie did that years ago. He now prefers to stay put because splendid business relationships are rare and enjoyable. Giving them up for unknown, likely average people would be "akin to marrying for money - a mistake under most circumstances, insanity if one is already rich."

chunks.heading: Look-through earnings and retained earnings of investees
chunks.text:
- GAAP does not let Berkshire report its share of retained earnings at its major investees. In 1989 it received about $45 million after tax in dividends from five investees, but its share of their retained earnings was about $212 million. This excludes large capital gains at GEICO and Coca-Cola. With that $212 million distributed and taxed, operating earnings would have been close to $500 million rather than about $300 million.
- Warren thinks retained earnings may be worth more than distributed ones. They are deployed by "talented, owner-oriented managers who sometimes have better uses for these funds in their own businesses than we would have in ours." He says he would not make this generous judgment about most managements.
- Berkshire's earning power is best measured by "look-through" earnings: reported operating earnings plus its share of investees' retained operating earnings, excluding capital gains. For intrinsic value to compound at about 15% a year, look-through earnings must grow at about that pace.
- Berkshire's results are presented by business rather than under GAAP purchase-price accounting, which he says is more useful to investors and managers. Goodwill amortization and other purchase-price adjustments are shown separately instead of being charged to the businesses.

chunks.heading: The operating businesses and the managers behind them
chunks.text:
- The "Sainted Seven Plus One" (Borsheim's, Buffalo News, Fechheimer, Kirby, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Scott Fetzer, See's, World Book) earned 57% after tax on average equity, with no net leverage (cash equivalents matched funded debt). Warren says most managers "have no need to work for a living; they show up at the ballpark because they like to hit home runs." He compares his lineup to the 1927 Yankees.
- **Borsheim's and Nebraska Furniture Mart share one formula:**
  1. Unparalleled depth and breadth of merchandise at one location.
  2. The lowest operating costs in the business.
  3. The shrewdest buying, helped by huge volume.
  4. Gross margins, and so prices, far below competitors'.
  5. Friendly personalized service with family on hand.
- Borsheim's expense ratio is about one-third that of comparable jewelers. Sales are more than twice what they were four years ago. It was bought without an audit, and every surprise was positive: "If you don't know jewelry, know your jeweler." NFM's carpet department held a 75.3% consumer share in Omaha in Q4 1989, over six times its nearest competitor.
- **See's Candies:** pounds sold rose 8% on a record 1988, with excellent same-store gains. Advertising rose from $4 million to $5 million, and newspaper advertising more than tripled. Chuck Huggins runs over 27 million pounds of candy a year through 225 shops plus mail and phone orders.
- **Buffalo News:** it ranks first among major metro papers in household penetration and has a news hole of 50.1%. It set its seventh straight profit record. Erie County population fell from 1,113,000 (1970) to 966,000 (1988), yet Sunday circulation rose from the 207,500 the Courier-Express sold in 1975 to 292,700. Warren says high penetration lets retailers "talk to the entire community through a single megaphone." He believes publisher Stan Lipsey adds at least five points of margin versus an average manager.
- **Mrs. B (Rose Blumkin)** left NFM at age 96 after disagreeing over the carpet department, where sales fell 17% in three years while other departments rose 24%. Warren says the family was right. At 96 she started a new carpet and furniture business.
- Fechheimer and Ralph Schey's group (World Book, Kirby, Scott Fetzer) run so well that Warren and Charlie have never visited Fechheimer's plants. Kirby's international share of unit sales rose from 5% to 20%. Warren says buying Ralph was as important as buying Scott Fetzer's businesses, since his capital management funds other Berkshire commitments.

chunks.heading: Insurance: commodity pricing, capacity, and writing CAT covers
chunks.text:
- Property-casualty combined ratio: below 100 means an underwriting profit. With float included, a ratio of 107-111 is about breakeven. Industry incurred losses grow about 10% a year (11% over 25 years), and premium growth must match to hold the ratio steady. 1989 premiums grew an estimated 2.1% with a 110.4 combined ratio.
- The "underwriting cycle" was a lag effect from the cartel era. Today hundreds of sellers offer a commodity-like product at independent prices, which "is certain to cause subnormal profitability in all circumstances but one: a shortage of usable capacity." Capacity "primarily depends on the mental state of insurance managers," and shortages come only when insurers are frightened. He compares the industry to steel: needing better profits has nothing to do with getting them.
- Warren will write no insurance carrying "a mathematical expectation of loss." Premium volume may fall to $150 million in 1990, from a high of $1 billion in 1986.
- After Hurricane Hugo (over $4 billion insured loss) and the California earthquake, CAT cover capacity ran short. Berkshire advertised up to $250 million of coverage in trade publications and booked a substantial amount in ten days. CAT premiums usually run 3% to 15% of coverage, a level Berkshire had thought inadequate.
- Berkshire keeps the risk rather than laying it off. Its edge is about $6 billion of regulatory net worth, plus "we simply don't care what earnings we report quarterly, or even annually, just as long as the decisions leading to those earnings (or losses) were reached intelligently." A full $250 million loss would cost about $165 million after tax: "a blow only to our pride, not to our well-being." Most managers avoid this posture, but Warren says "We are willing to look foolish as long as we don't feel we have acted foolishly."
- Berkshire adds capacity when it is short and backs off when it is abundant. It holds unusually large float relative to premiums, which should keep underwriting results tolerable for a few years.

chunks.heading: Marketable securities: Coca-Cola, convertible preferreds, and arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Selection criteria: the highest after-tax return by "mathematical expectation," limited to investments Berkshire understands, aiming to maximize eventual net worth and not reportable earnings. There is no bias among five categories: long-term stocks, medium-term bonds, long-term bonds, cash equivalents, and arbitrage.
- Warren raised Coca-Cola from 14,172,500 to 23,350,000 shares (cost $1,023,920,000, market $1,803,787,000 at year-end). He sold Cokes in 1936 and noticed the product for 52 years but bought no shares until summer 1988, having instead put money into "street railway companies, windmill manufacturers, anthracite producers, textile businesses, trading-stamp issuers." His praise for Roberto Goizueta, CEO since 1981, is that he has a "perfect" mesh of marketing and finance. Warren says he should have bought earlier and resolves to react faster to the next glaringly attractive idea.
- Other year-end holdings: Capital Cities/ABC (cost $517.5 million, market $1.69 billion), GEICO (cost $45.7 million, market $1.04 billion), Washington Post (cost $9.7 million, market $486 million), Freddie Mac.
- Arbitrage: Warren did little in 1989 because deals made no economic sense and arbitraging them "comes too close to playing the greater-fool game." He will do it only "when we like the odds."
- Bonds: Berkshire sold low-coupon WPPSS issues bought at big discounts, some of which had roughly doubled and paid 15%-17% tax-free. It also sold medium-term tax-exempts for about $51 million of pre-tax profit.
- Berkshire bought three convertible preferreds in 1989:
  - **Gillette:** $600 million, 8 3/4% dividend, convertible at $50.
  - **USAir:** $358 million, 9 1/4%, convertible at $60.
  - **Champion:** $300 million, 9 1/4%, convertible at $38.
  - All have mandatory redemption in ten years, and Berkshire's voting rights are unrestricted on an as-converted basis.
- Berkshire understands Gillette's economics ("go right out and get" the new Sensor razor), and has no ability to forecast airlines, paper, or investment banking. In those it structures investments differently, as "agnostics, not atheists." He wants to link only with people he likes, admires and trusts. Returns will be mediocre if industry economics are bad, and these are not a substitute for buying wonderful businesses or 80%+ of a fine company, "our favorite form of capital deployment."

chunks.heading: Zero-coupon bonds, EBDIT, and Wall Street excess
chunks.text:
- Berkshire issued $902.6 million principal of zero-coupon convertible debentures at 44.314% of face (about $400 million raised), due in 15 years. This is equivalent to a 5.5% semiannual-compounded rate, and each bond converts at $9,815 per share, a 15% premium. Berkshire deducts the accrued 5.5% for tax, creating positive cash flow, so its effective cost is well below 5.5%.
- Warren calls Series E savings bonds and stripped Treasury coupons benign zeros, since they remove reinvestment risk for long-term holders. But "what the wise do in the beginning, fools do in the end": junk issuers use zero and PIK bonds because "it is impossible to default on a promise to pay nothing."
- Debt standards slid: first free cash flow had to cover interest and some principal, then deals were priced so all cash went to interest, then "EBDIT" replaced real cash flow, and finally EBDIT was measured against cash interest only. He calls ignoring depreciation "delusional": at 95% of businesses, capital spending roughly equal to depreciation is as real an expense as labor.
- His advice: "Whenever an investment banker starts talking about EBDIT... zip up your wallet." Test a deal by asking the promoter to take zero-coupon fees. Bankers should act as gatekeepers, like a responsible bartender. He notes that savings and loans that booked unreceived interest on zeros pushed the cost onto taxpayers. He says Berkshire has owned some zeros and might buy more if the market becomes sufficiently distressed, but never new issues from weak credits.

chunks.heading: Mistakes of the first 25 years
chunks.text:
- **Cigar butts:** Warren bought Berkshire because the price looked cheap, though the textile business was unpromising. A "cigar butt" with one puff left gives you a profit only if you are a liquidator. The low business return erodes the bargain, and "never is there just one cockroach in the kitchen." "Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre." Hochschild Kohn, bought at a discount to book value, was sold three years later for about what he paid. His conclusion: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price."
- **Jockeys and horses:** good managers do well in good businesses but "not on broken-down nags." A management with a reputation for brilliance meeting a business with a reputation for bad economics leaves the business's reputation intact.
- **Avoid dragons:** after 25 years he and Charlie have not learned to solve difficult business problems; they avoid them. They look for "one-foot hurdles" and not seven-footers. Exceptions are a marvelous business with a one-time, solvable problem (American Express, GEICO).
- **Institutional imperative:** rationality wilts under four forces: (1) institutions resist change, (2) projects expand to soak up available funds, (3) the leader's craving gets quick support from studies prepared by subordinates, and (4) peer behavior is mindlessly imitated. Berkshire is organized to minimize this, and Warren favors investees that are alert to it.
- **People:** "We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person." Going into business only with people he likes, trusts and admires will not make a poor business prosper, but it lets an owner accomplish wonders in businesses with decent economics.
- **Unseen mistakes:** the worst were purchases he understood but did not make, on which Berkshire paid a huge cost for "thumb-sucking." Missing opportunities outside one's circle of competence is no sin.
- **Conservatism on leverage:** higher leverage would likely have beaten 23.8%. But he rejects 99:1 odds: "A small chance of distress or disgrace cannot... be offset by a large chance of extra returns." He and Charlie "enjoy the process far more than the proceeds."

chunks.heading: What Warren looks for in acquisitions
chunks.text:
- **Criteria:**
  1. Large purchases (at least $10 million of after-tax earnings).
  2. Demonstrated consistent earning power (no projections, no turnarounds).
  3. Good returns on equity with little or no debt.
  4. Management in place.
  5. Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it").
  6. An offering price.
- No unfriendly takeovers. He promises confidentiality and an answer within five minutes, prefers cash, and would issue stock only when Berkshire gets as much intrinsic value as it gives. Auction-like sales, new ventures and turnarounds are out: "Please include me out."
- His favorite form is the Blumkin-Friedman-Heldman mold: owner-managers who want cash but wish to remain significant owners and keep running the company. He also wants negotiated large, non-controlling blocks like those in Capital Cities, Salomon, Gillette, USAir and Champion.
- Harry Bottle turned around K&W Products (quadrupling profits), then bought a product line at a bankruptcy auction for a pittance. Berkshire's NYSE listing narrowed dealer spreads from 3% or more to under 1%.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1990 letter explains look-through earnings, judging insurance by cost of float, why falling stock prices help permanent buyers, why debt-funded junk bonds fail, and what kind of business Berkshire wants to buy. It also covers managers over industry economics and bank leverage.

chunks.heading: Value comes from owned earnings, not reported earnings: "look-through" results
chunks.text:
- Warren says GAAP earnings understate what Berkshire owns because investee profits are recorded only to the extent of dividends received. Example: Berkshire's 17% share of Capital Cities/ABC earnings was over $83 million in 1990, but only about $530,000 ($600,000 of dividends less roughly $70,000 of tax) hit reported earnings.
- His view: "The way they are accounted for is of no importance, but their ownership and subsequent utilization is all-important." He says he doesn't care whether auditors hear a tree fall in the forest; he cares who owns the tree and what's done with it.
- Retained earnings can be more efficient than dividends. When Coca-Cola repurchases shares, it raises Berkshire's ownership of "the most valuable franchise in the world" without the dividend tax Berkshire would pay if it received cash and bought shares itself.
- Look-through earnings method for 1990: take about $250 million (Berkshire's share of investee retained operating earnings), subtract $30 million (incremental tax had it been paid as dividends), and add the $220 million to reported operating earnings of $371 million. Result: about $590 million.
- Berkshire aims for 15% annual growth in look-through earnings and intrinsic value (Warren notes this gets harder as the equity base, then $5.3 billion, grows).
- Accounting numbers are "a beginning, not an end" in calculating true economic earnings. He warns earnings "can be as pliable as putty when a charlatan heads the company reporting them" and that some American fortunes were made by "monetization of accounting mirages."
- Appendix A reprints Ben Graham's 1936 satire "U.S. Steel Announces Sweeping Modernization Scheme" (plant written down to minus $1 billion, wages paid in option warrants, inventory carried at $1, a $1 billion contingency reserve), producing a pro-forma $49.80 per share against a reported loss of $2.76.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value, book value and what shareholders actually earn
chunks.text:
- Per-share book value grew from $19.46 to $4,612.06 over 26 years, 23.2% compounded. Net worth rose $362 million (7.3%) in 1990. Warren calls the long record "meaningless in forecasting future results."
- A shareholder's return matches the company's only if he sells at the same price-to-intrinsic-value relationship at which he bought. Example: buy at a 10% premium, intrinsic value compounds at 15%, sell at a 10% premium, and you earn 15%. Buy at a premium and sell at a smaller one and you do worse.
- Charlie Munger and Warren want Berkshire to trade consistently near intrinsic value and dislike "value-ignoring volatility." In 1989 book value rose 44% while the stock rose 85%; in 1990 book and intrinsic value rose slightly while the stock fell 23%.
- Intrinsic value is an estimate; Warren says he and Charlie might differ by 10% in appraising it. It substantially exceeds book value.
- Much of the excess value was created by the operating managers: "Our job is merely to identify talented managers and provide an environment in which they can do their stuff." His own contribution is compared (with the granddaughter and Beemer the Clown story) to a four-year-old who waves a wand and says "Gee, I'm really good at this."

chunks.heading: Excellent businesses run by excellent managers, in prosaic industries
chunks.text:
- The non-insurance operations earned 51% after tax on average equity in 1990, which would have ranked about 20th on the 1989 Fortune 500. Leverage didn't produce it: facilities are mostly owned, and the small debt is basically offset by cash. On return on assets the group would rank in Fortune's top ten.
- The returns came from furniture retailing, candy, vacuum cleaners and steel warehousing, not from spectacular industries like cigarettes or network television. Warren's conclusion: "Our extraordinary returns flow from outstanding operating managers, not fortuitous industry economics."
- Managers deployed capital only with good reason. Net worth of these businesses rose just $47 million on $133 million of earnings, and over the past five years they sent well over 80% of earnings to Warren and Charlie for reallocation.
- Low operating cost is the competitive weapon at Borsheim's and Nebraska Furniture Mart:
  - Borsheim's operating costs run about 18% of sales versus about 40% at the typical fine-jewelry competitor. Sales rose 18% in 1990. Volume is believed to be second only to Tiffany's New York store. Mail assortments (about 1,500 in 1990) went to customers on an honor system with no losses from dishonesty to date.
  - Nebraska Furniture Mart: 1990 sales of $159 million, up 4%; operating costs 15% versus about 40% for Levitz and 25% for Circuit City. Low costs mean low prices, big volume and the broadest selection, so customers drive 130 miles from Des Moines.
  - "What works with diapers works with diamonds": he compares this to Wal-Mart's roughly 15% operating costs.
- Warren admits a "counterrevelation": after years of scorning corporate synergy claims, a See's candy cart at NFM outsold some See's stores.
- At See's, quality and service fanaticism (Chuck Huggins, 19 years running it) mattered. A 5% price increase lifted dollar sales when volume slipped; 263 customers rallied to save the Albuquerque store from a bad lease.
