chunks.heading: Media businesses and the erosion of pricing power
chunks.text:
- Warren was surprised by how vulnerable newspapers and media were to the early recession. He judges that media businesses will remain "economic marvels" relative to American industry but "considerably less marvelous" than he, the industry or lenders thought only a few years earlier.
- Their past excellence came from pricing power, not physical growth. Now ad dollars grow slowly, retailers using little media advertising have taken share, and the number of print and electronic ad channels has multiplied, dispersing ad dollars and weakening pricing power. That "materially" reduced the intrinsic value of Capital Cities/ABC, Washington Post and the Buffalo News.
- Buffalo News earnings fell 5% in 1990, with a steeper decline late in the year, and he promised they would fall substantially in 1991 as newsprint prices and labor costs rose. Despite the squeeze, he keeps the news hole at least 50% (52.3% in 1990): "Cutting product quality is not a proper response to adversity."

chunks.heading: Insurance: float, cost of funds and super-cat pricing
chunks.text:
- Float is funds of others that insurers temporarily hold and can invest. A typical property-casualty insurer breaks even at a combined ratio of about 107-111 because of float income. Long-tail lines (malpractice) generate large float; crop hail generates almost none.
- Warren's preferred yardstick is underwriting loss divided by average float, a rough "cost of funds developed from insurance." A cost below what the government pays on long-term bonds means a good business. In 1990: about $1.6 billion average float ($1,637.3 million), a $26.65 million underwriting loss, cost of funds about 1.63%, versus an 8.24% long-term Treasury yield. Berkshire's float cost was below government bond yields in 19 of its 24 insurance years.
- Qualifications: true cost isn't known until claims settle decades later, and shareholders bear a tax penalty (about one percentage point added to the cost of float for the average insurer, and roughly that for Berkshire) because they fund the insurer and are taxed twice on its investment income.
- GEICO (48% owned) typically underwrites at a profit, so its policyholders effectively pay interest on the float; its edge is operating efficiency and careful risk classification.
- Pricing principle: long-tail lines may be profitable at 110-115 combined ratios, but pricing to those targets is dangerous. Aiming for 100 can itself lose heavily; "aiming for 110-115 is business suicide." Prices need a margin of safety against social trends that spring expensive surprises.
- Industry behavior: losses grow about 10% a year (11% over 25 years) while premiums lagged in 1990, so the 1991 combined ratio would rise about two points. "The most important thing to do when you find yourself in a hole is to stop digging." Berkshire would write huge amounts of business once managements got scared enough to raise prices.
- Super-cat reinsurance: Berkshire was likely the largest US seller. Illustrative contract: $10 million of coverage for roughly a $3 million premium, with $100 million of annual super-cat premiums leading to either a profit near $100 million or a loss well over $200 million. Combined ratio would be near zero or near 300%, concentrating rather than spreading risk.
- Warren's stance: "Charlie and I always have preferred a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%." He expects satisfactory results over a decade, terrible results in occasional years, and will write it only at prices commensurate with risk, letting volume fall when competitors get optimistic. He confesses insurance mistakes made before Mike Goldberg arrived: "there is no statute of limitations on stupidity."

chunks.heading: Buying Wells Fargo and thinking about banks and market prices
chunks.text:
- Warren dislikes banking because with assets twenty times equity, small mistakes on a fraction of assets can wipe out much of the equity. Most bank losses came from the "institutional imperative": executives mindlessly imitating peers (follow-the-leader lending "with lemming-like zeal"). He wants only well-managed banks at fair prices, never poorly managed ones that look cheap.
- Wells Fargo purchase: Berkshire raised its stake to just under 10% (the most allowed without Federal Reserve approval) for $290 million, less than five times after-tax earnings and less than three times pre-tax earnings. The bank had $56 billion of assets, earned over 20% on equity and 1.25% on assets, and Carl Reichardt and Paul Hazen were "the best managers in the business." A 10% stake equated to buying a $5 billion bank outright for roughly twice $290 million, and without a Reichardt to run it.
- The stress test he applied: Wells earned well over $1 billion pre-tax after expensing over $300 million of loan losses. If 10% of its $48 billion in loans soured and lost 30% of principal (including foregone interest), the bank would roughly break even.
- Stock fell almost 50% within a few months in 1990 on real-estate and earthquake fears, which he welcomed since it let Berkshire buy more at "panic prices."
- Principle on prices: people who will be perpetual buyers should welcome falling prices, as with food or newsprint. "We will be buying businesses - or small parts of businesses, called stocks - year in, year out." Falling prices help, rising prices hurt. "It's optimism that is the enemy of the rational buyer."
- But unpopularity alone isn't a reason to buy; contrarianism is as foolish as following the crowd. "What's required is thinking rather than polling" (Bertrand Russell: "Most men would rather die than think. Many do.").
- Holdings table (12/31/90, cost to market): Capital Cities/ABC $517.5M to $1,377M; Coca-Cola $1,024M to $2,172M; GEICO $45.7M to $1,111M; Washington Post $9.7M to $342M; Wells Fargo $289M to $289M. He neither bought nor sold five of the six major holdings that year: "Lethargy bordering on sloth remains the cornerstone of our investment style."
- Qualities he admires in managers (Reichardt/Hazen like Murphy/Burke): mutual trust, paying good people well while hating excess headcount, attacking costs in good times and bad, and sticking to what they understand. He quotes Thomas Watson Sr.: "I'm smart in spots - but I stay around those spots."

chunks.heading: Junk bonds, debt and margin of safety
chunks.text:
- Warren criticizes 1980s manufactured junk bonds. Salesmen claimed academic data showed higher yields had more than offset higher defaults, but the data came from "fallen angels" (once investment-grade bonds whose managers wanted to regain status), a different universe from new issues, like "checking the historical death rate from Kool-Aid before drinking the version served at Jonestown."
- The "debt as dagger on the steering wheel" thesis: huge debt makes managers careful, but a pothole causes a fatal crash: "a plan that requires dodging them all is a plan for disaster." Example: a Tampa TV station bought with so much debt that interest exceeded gross revenues.
- Beware past-performance "proofs": "If history books were the key to riches, the Forbes 400 would consist of librarians." Wall Street's enthusiasm for an idea is proportional "not to its merit, but rather to the revenue it would produce."
- He cites Graham's The Intelligent Investor: the three words are "Margin of Safety," still right 42 years after he read them.
- Berkshire never buys new-issue junk, but with the market in disarray bought RJR Nabisco bonds: $440 million at yearend 1990 (market value up more than $150 million after yearend), because the credit was better than perceived, asset sales were at good prices, equity was added and management was competent.
- He will look at any investment category so long as he understands the business and believes price and value differ significantly.

chunks.heading: Convertible preferreds, mistakes and commodity businesses
chunks.text:
- Preferreds held: $700 million Salomon, $600 million Gillette (converting to 12 million common shares April 1), $358 million USAir, $300 million Champion International. At yearend 1990 he valued Salomon and Champion at about cost, Gillette somewhat above, and USAir substantially below.
- He calls USAir an "unforced error": he bought just as the airline hit industry and merger-integration (Piedmont) trouble. Lesson: "In a business selling a commodity-type product, it's impossible to be a lot smarter than your dumbest competitor."
- Valuation point: most of a convertible preferred's value comes from fixed-income characteristics. The security can't be worth less than as a non-convertible preferred and may be worth more with the conversion option; valuing it at the common-equivalent value is wrong.
- Gillette CEO Colman Mockler is described as a gentleman with "integrity, courage and modesty." Gillette's success came from devotion to quality and constantly improving a product already best in class.

chunks.heading: Acquisition criteria and how Berkshire treats sellers
chunks.text:
- Criteria: large purchases (at least $10 million after-tax earnings); demonstrated consistent earning power (not projections or turnarounds); good return on equity with little or no debt; management in place; simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it"); an offering price. No unfriendly takeovers; complete confidentiality; an answer customarily within five minutes; prefer cash, but will issue stock only when receiving as much intrinsic value as given.
- Favorite deal shape: the Blumkin-Friedman-Heldman mold, where owner-managers want cash for themselves or family but remain significant owners and keep running the business. Also interested in large, non-controlling negotiated blocks.
- Appendix B (seller letter): sellers sell only once, often under broker pressure, so mistakes are irreversible. Price matters but isn't the only factor, and a great business becomes more valuable over time, so the owner can wait and choose the buyer.
- Typical buyers are (1) industry operators who will eventually want "hands-on help," or (2) leveraged financial maneuverers who change accounting before flipping. Berkshire is different: it buys to keep, has no operating staff at the parent, runs businesses autonomously (managers often haven't visited Omaha or met each other), and has no one waiting for a chance to run an acquisition. It wants the operating family to keep 20%, since it needs 80% for tax consolidation.
- Warren's involvement is limited to capital allocation and selection and compensation of the top manager. Cash payment, no brokers, no financing contingency, no re-trading. He is candid that the seller would be no richer afterward; only the form of wealth changes.
- He also notes that advertising an interest in buying collies draws people hoping to sell cocker spaniels, and says of turnarounds and auctions: "When the phone don't ring, you'll know it's me."

chunks.heading: Succession and corporate-governance attitudes
chunks.text:
- His wife Susan was nominated to the board. She would inherit his stock and effectively control the company, and shares his view that neither Berkshire nor its businesses should be sold just because a very high bid arrives. Both estate plans aim at preserving Berkshire's character and returning the fortune to society.
- If he died, none of his stock would be sold, a controlling shareholder and manager with similar philosophies would follow, and Charlie would sell the corporate jet, The Indefensible, adding $1 million a year to earnings.
- Charitable giving: 97.3% of eligible shares took part in shareholder-designated contributions ($5.8 million to 2,600 charities). He insists managers not use company money for personal-interest charities: "they should use their own money, not yours."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains how look-through earnings, franchise economics (See's, media), owner-style manager compensation and cheap float drive Berkshire's value. He also sets his acquisition criteria, defends a concentrated hold-forever portfolio, and confesses the $1.4B Fannie Mae omission error.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's 1991 results and the limits of size
chunks.text:
- Net worth rose $2.1 billion, or 39.6%, in 1991. Per-share book value grew from $19 to $6,437 over 27 years, a 23.7% compound annual rate. Equity capital was $7.4 billion.
- Warren says Berkshire cannot keep that pace, because "the universe of opportunities that can significantly influence the company's performance constantly shrinks."
  - On $20 million of capital, a $1 million profit idea added five percentage points to the year's return.
  - Now it takes a $370 million idea (over $550 million of pre-tax profit) to add the same five points.
  - "There are many more ways to make $1 million than to make $370 million."
- He and Charlie Munger target a 15% average annual increase in intrinsic value. Keeping book value on that pace requires earning $22 billion over the next decade.
- Most of 1991's gain was a one-time re-rating. Coca-Cola and Gillette supplied nearly $1.6 billion of the $2.1 billion because their price-earnings ratios rose far faster than earnings.
  - He calls this a "double-dip" of earnings growth plus market reappraisal. The reappraisal was warranted but "can't recur annually: We'll have to settle for a single dip in the future."
  - Berkshire's Coke stake alone is now worth more than the $3.4 billion net worth it had when it loaded up on Coke three years earlier.

chunks.heading: Look-through earnings and thinking like a business owner
chunks.text:
- Look-through earnings are Berkshire's reported operating earnings, plus the retained operating earnings of major investees that GAAP does not reflect, less an allowance for the tax Berkshire would owe had those earnings been distributed.
  - For these to support 15% intrinsic value growth, they must grow about 15% a year. Since 1965 they have grown about 23%, nearly matching book value.
  - In 1991 they fell 14% to $516 million (from $602 million). Causes: declining media earnings, the Gillette preferred's conversion to common on April 1, a break-even result at Wells Fargo, and lower insurance profits.
- Warren says individual investors should compute their own look-through earnings: total the underlying earnings attributable to the shares in the portfolio.
  - The goal is a portfolio (in effect a "company") that delivers the highest possible look-through earnings "a decade or so from now."
  - This forces long-term thinking about business prospects rather than short-term stock market prospects.
- His scoreboard analogy: "in the long run, the scoreboard for investment decisions is market price. But prices will be determined by future earnings. In investing, just as in baseball, to put runs on the scoreboard one must watch the playing field, not the scoreboard."

chunks.heading: Franchise versus business, and why media lost its franchise
chunks.text:
- An economic franchise comes from a product or service that:
  1. is needed or desired,
  2. is thought by customers to have no close substitute, and
  3. is not subject to price regulation.
- The proof is the ability to regularly price aggressively and earn high returns on capital. Franchises can tolerate mismanagement: inept managers reduce profitability but cannot inflict mortal damage.
- "A business" earns exceptional profits only if it is the low-cost operator or supply is tight. Tight supply rarely lasts, even low-cost status faces constant attack, and a business can be killed by poor management.
- Newspapers, TV and magazines were franchises and could "both price aggressively and be managed loosely." Choices for information and entertainment multiplied while demand could not expand ("500 million American eyeballs and a 24-hour day are all that's available"), so they now behave more like ordinary businesses.
- Valuation math (deliberately oversimplified):
  - Old view: earnings grow 6% a year forever with no extra capital, discounted at 10%. That supports $25 million for $1 million of after-tax earnings (about 16x pre-tax).
  - New view: $1 million is "normal earning power" that "bobs around" cyclically. At the same 10% rate that is worth $10 million, or 10x after-tax (about 6.5x pre-tax).
  - "Dollars are dollars" whether from media or steel mills. Media earned a premium multiple only because they were expected to grow without much capital, and when that expectation changes, valuations "must change dramatically."
- Warren says the intrinsic value of Berkshire's media holdings (Buffalo News, Washington Post, Capital Cities/ABC) fell materially. Cyclical weakness hurts current look-through earnings but not intrinsic value; secular decline does.
- Berkshire does not sell businesses or "permanent" holdings merely because the money could be used better elsewhere. He is most comfortable with Cap Cities and Washington Post because both have strong managements, stayed out of the late-1980s irrational media auctions, and carry little debt. Most other media companies carry debt of five or more times current net income.

chunks.heading: See's Candy: twenty years of franchise economics
chunks.text:
- Blue Chip Stamps bought See's on January 3, 1972. The asking price was $40 million, but $10 million was excess cash, so the true price was $30 million. Warren and Charlie, "not yet fully appreciative of the value of an economic franchise," looked at $7 million of tangible net worth and said $25 million was their limit. The sellers accepted.
- Results over the 20 years:
  - Candy sales rose from $29 million to $196 million; pre-tax profit from $4.2 million to $42.4 million.
  - See's now operates on only $25 million of net worth, so $18 million of reinvested earnings was added to the $7 million base.
  - Roughly $410 million of pre-tax profit was distributed to Blue Chip/Berkshire to deploy elsewhere.
- Profit growth must be judged against the incremental capital needed to produce it; See's needed very little.
- The one insight at purchase: See's had untapped pricing power. They were also "lucky twice over": the $25 million insistence did not derail the deal, and they found Chuck Huggins, whom they put in charge immediately.
  - His pay arrangement was a handshake deal conceived in about five minutes and never put in writing; it is unchanged to this day.
- 1991: dollar sales flat, pounds down 4% (all in the last two months, which produce over 80% of annual profit), yet profit rose 7% and pre-tax margin hit a record 21.6%.
- He says See's taught Berkshire to evaluate franchises, and "We've made significant money in certain common stocks because of the lessons we learned at See's."

chunks.heading: Buying whole businesses: H.H. Brown, management and compensation
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought H.H. Brown (work shoes and boots; about $25 million pre-tax earnings, close to 2,000 employees) after Frank Rooney, the founder's son-in-law and former CEO of Melville, mentioned it to a friend of Warren's. The investment bank hired to sell it never contacted Berkshire.
  - Warren notes that in four major purchases with banker-represented sellers, the bank contacted Berkshire only once.
  - A deal was done quickly; "With Brown, we didn't even need to take five" minutes.
- Why he wanted it: Frank's willingness to stay as CEO. Managers like him have no financial need to work but love the game. "Managers of this stripe cannot be 'hired' in the normal sense of the word. What we must do is provide a concert hall in which business artists of this class will wish to perform."
- Shoes are a tough business (about 85% of the billion pairs bought in the US are imported; heavy inventory and receivables), so only outstanding managers prosper.
- Brown's compensation: key managers get a $7,800 annual salary plus a percentage of profits after a charge for capital employed.
  - They "truly stand in the shoes of owners." Most companies "talk the talk but don't walk the walk," with systems "long on carrots but short on sticks" that treat equity capital as cost-free.
  - "Managers eager to bet heavily on their abilities usually have plenty of ability to bet on."
- Berkshire's acquisition criteria:
  1. Large purchases (at least $10 million of after-tax earnings).
  2. Demonstrated consistent earning power (no interest in projections or turnarounds).
  3. Good returns on equity with little or no debt.
  4. Management in place ("we can't supply it").
  5. Simple businesses ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it").
  6. An offering price.
- Terms: no unfriendly takeovers, complete confidentiality, an answer usually within five minutes, cash preferred. Stock is considered only if Berkshire receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
- His favorite deal shape (Nebraska Furniture Mart, Fechheimer, Borsheim's): owner-managers want cash for family or inactive shareholders but want to stay significant owners and keep running the business.
- On unsolicited pitches: "if you advertise an interest in buying collies, a lot of people will call hoping to sell you their cocker spaniels." Of new ventures, turnarounds and auction-like sales: "When the phone don't ring, you'll know it's me."
- He also seeks large negotiated minority stakes like Capital Cities, Salomon, Gillette, USAir, Champion and American Express.
- Managing the managers: Berkshire's operating managers are so strong that Warren could take the Salomon interim chairmanship without Berkshire missing a beat. His job is "merely to treat them right and to allocate the capital they generate."

chunks.heading: Insurance: float and the cost of funds
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's insurance business has changed so that combined ratios, its own or the industry's, are "largely irrelevant." What counts is the "cost of funds developed from insurance," i.e. the cost of float.
- Float is loss reserves plus loss adjustment expense reserves plus unearned premium reserves, minus agents' balances, prepaid acquisition costs and deferred charges on assumed reinsurance. Its cost is the underwriting loss.
- 1991: average float of $1,895 million, underwriting loss of $119.6 million, a cost of 6.31%. That was below the 7.40% year-end long-term government bond yield, and Berkshire has beaten the government rate in 20 of its 25 insurance years, often by a wide margin. Growth in float counts as favorable only because the cost has been satisfactory; the challenge is to garner float "at a reasonable cost."
- Industry view: Warren expects industry incurred losses to grow close to 10% a year (11% over the last 25 years). Premiums grew only 3.1% in 1991.
  - The industry's combined ratio failed to worsen as expected, but he is skeptical because insurers tend to under-reserve in bad times. Managements that paper over problems with accounting "achieve the same result as the seriously-ill patient who tells his doctor: 'I can't afford the operation, but would you accept a small payment to touch up the x-rays?'"
  - A combined ratio of roughly 107-111 typically produces break-even once float income is counted.
- Super-cat reinsurance: Berkshire is perhaps the world's largest writer.
  - About $100 million of annual premiums could produce anything from a $100 million profit to a $200 million loss. It is priced expecting to pay out about 90% of premiums over the long term.
  - A one-year accounting cycle is ill-suited because GAAP bars reserving in quiet years for certain losses in other years.
  - 1991's underwriting profit from this business was about $11 million. The biggest catastrophe was a September typhoon in Japan (insured loss of about $4-5 billion), triggering payments on only about 25% of Berkshire's policies.
  - In the 1980s "innocents" who did not understand the risks supplied much of this cover; "Berkshire itself was an innocent all too often when I was personally running the insurance operation." He expects innocents to return after a few quiet years and prices to "plunge to silly levels."
  - Berkshire's advantage is financial strength: when "the big one" comes, many reinsurers will find it hard to write checks.

chunks.heading: Concentrated, patient investing and admitted mistakes
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's "Rip Van Winkle approach": of eight large holdings, one was new (Guinness) and six of the other seven were unchanged in share count. "The stock market serves as a relocation center at which money is moved from the active to the patient."
- What he looks for: "large businesses with understandable, enduring and mouth-watering economics that are run by able and shareholder-oriented managements," bought at a sensible price and then validated by business performance.
  - "Charlie and I are simply not smart enough, considering the large sums we work with, to get great results by adroitly buying and selling portions of far-from-great businesses."
  - Calling actively trading institutions "investors" is "like calling someone who repeatedly engages in one-night stands a romantic."
- His Omaha test: with only private Omaha companies to choose from, he would assess each business's long-term economics, assess the people running it, and buy into a few of the best at a sensible price, not an equal part of every business in town. Berkshire should do the same with public companies.
- He endorses Keynes's 1934 view: put "fairly large sums into enterprises which one thinks one knows something about and in the management of which one thoroughly believes"; spreading across businesses you know little about does not limit risk.
- Mistake of omission, Fannie Mae: in early 1988 Berkshire decided to buy 30 million shares ($350-400 million). After buying about 7 million shares the price rose, he stopped in frustration, then sold the 7 million because of his "distaste for holding small positions." By year-end 1991 the gain forgone was about $1.4 billion. He notes the error was not repeated with Coca-Cola, whose price also climbed during its buying program.
  - He says his worst mistakes are typically omissions on businesses he could understand, not missed technology or merchandising stories (Xerox, Apple, Wal-Mart) that Berkshire cannot spot early.
- USAir: the airline preferred is carried at a low value because the industry may stay unprofitable; the industry has lost money in aggregate since Kitty Hawk, and bankrupt carriers selling assets to fund losses push fares below solvent carriers' costs. This is a "burn-the-furniture-to-provide-firewood" dynamic, and he calls running an airline the toughest job in corporate America.
- Charity: managers should not spend company money on personal-attachment giving; "they should use their own money, not yours."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1992 letter covers value versus growth, the Williams discounted-cash-flow equation, margin of safety, acquisition discipline, the cost of insurance float, super-cat underwriting, stock option accounting, and low corporate overhead. He also accepts volatility for long-term returns and rejects market forecasting.

chunks.heading: Book value growth, the 15% goal, and why results are lumpy
chunks.text:
- Per-share book value rose 20.3% in 1992. Since present management took over 28 years earlier, it went from $19 to $7,745, or 23.6% compounded annually.
- Warren's stated goal is to grow per-share intrinsic value at 15% a year. He uses book value as a "conservative, but useful, proxy."
- He says the path cannot be smooth. Since 1979 GAAP has required insurers' stock holdings to be carried at market, so ordinary equity swings make annual results "gyrate."
- He lists three things to remember when comparing Berkshire with the S&P 500:
  - Early on, the textile business was a drag. More recently the operating businesses have usually earned well above the S&P.
  - Berkshire's returns are after corporate tax, while the S&P figures are pre-tax. An 18% S&P gain delivers a corporate holder well short of 13%. He calls this a structural disadvantage with "no antidote."
  - He and Charlie Munger are "virtually certain" the S&P's next-decade return will be far below the last decade's. They are "dead certain" that Berkshire's growing capital base will shrink its historical edge. Stocks "cannot forever overperform their underlying businesses."
- Short-term market forecasts are "poison" to be "kept locked up in a safe place, away from children and also from grown-ups who behave in the market like children."
- Volatility is accepted and welcomed because it comes from concentrated holdings and from super-catastrophe insurance. "A tolerance for short-term swings improves our long-term prospects." In baseball terms, the yardstick is "slugging percentage, not batting average."

chunks.heading: Look-through earnings and capital allocation
chunks.text:
- Look-through earnings are: reported operating earnings, plus retained operating earnings of major investees not shown under GAAP, minus an allowance for the tax Berkshire would pay if those earnings were distributed. Warren thinks this portrays Berkshire's earnings better than the GAAP figure.
- 1992 look-through earnings were $604 million, against $516 million in 1991. The undistributed investee earnings were $298 million, less $42 million hypothetical tax, plus $348 million of reported operating earnings.
- For 15% intrinsic-value growth they must exceed $1.8 billion by 2000. He does not promise it. "When we allocate capital today, we are thinking about what will maximize look-through earnings in 2000."
- Long-term focus is no excuse for poor short-term results. "If plantings made confidently are repeatedly followed by disappointing harvests, something is wrong with the farmer." For some industries "there simply is no good long-term strategy."
- Be suspicious of managers who pump up short-term earnings with accounting maneuvers or asset sales. Be equally suspicious of those who miss for years and blame their long-term focus.
- Shares are issued only when Berkshire receives as much value as it gives. In a bank-merger anecdote, the acquiree's owner demanded a swap valuing his business at over twice the acquirer's and then asked that they never again make a deal "this dumb."

chunks.heading: Buying businesses: good businesses at fair prices
chunks.text:
- Acquiring a business with excellent economics and managers he likes, trusts and admires is the most exhilarating activity. The search attitude should be like looking for a spouse: "active, interested and open-minded," but not "in a hurry."
- He criticizes managers who pay dearly to "kiss corporate toads" and then announce a big "restructuring" charge. "The CEO receives the education but the stockholders pay the tuition."
- His own early toads were cheap and still croaked. A golf pro's line, "Practice doesn't make perfect; practice makes permanent," led him to change strategy: buy "good businesses at fair prices rather than fair businesses at good prices."
- Central States Indemnity was bought in December 1992 as a prototype:
  - Berkshire bought 82%. The company insures monthly payments for credit-card holders who become disabled or unemployed.
  - Annual premiums are about $90 million and profits about $10 million.
  - It is run by Bill Kizer, a friend of 35+ years. The Kizer family keeps 18% and continues to run it.
- It resembles Berkshire's first insurance deal, National Indemnity, bought from Jack Ringwalt 26 years earlier. Both sellers chose Berkshire as the home for their company.
- Subsidiaries make small add-on acquisitions, which Warren calls "low-risk and high-return" since they extend managers already known to be outstanding. There were five in 1992. H. H. Brown bought Lowell Shoe, which has $90 million in sales and makes Nursemates.

chunks.heading: Value, growth, and the equity-investing creed
chunks.text:
- The 1977 creed is unchanged except for one word. Buy businesses that:
  - (a) he can understand;
  - (b) have favorable long-term prospects;
  - (c) are operated by honest and competent people;
  - (d) are available at "an attractive price," previously "a very attractive price."
- He calls the value/growth split "fuzzy thinking." "The two approaches are joined at the hip." Growth is always a component of value, and its effect can be negative as well as positive. "Value investing" is redundant, since investing means seeking value at least equal to the price paid. Paying more in the hope of selling higher is speculation.
- Low price-to-book, low P/E and high dividend yield do not determine whether something is a value purchase. The opposite traits are not inconsistent with one.
- Growth helps only when incremental capital earns enticing returns, that is, when each dollar used to finance growth creates more than a dollar of long-term market value. The airline industry is his example: "The more the industry has grown, the worse the disaster for owners."
- Value is the discounted cash flows, in and out, over the remaining life of the asset, per John Burr Williams. The formula is the same for stocks and bonds, but with equities the analyst must estimate the "coupons," and management quality can swing them dramatically.
- Buy whichever investment is cheapest on that calculation, whether or not it grows, has smooth earnings, or looks cheap on P/E or book. When bonds calculate as more attractive, buy bonds.
- Best business: one that can employ large amounts of incremental capital at very high returns. Worst: one that consistently needs ever more capital at very low returns. Most high-return businesses need little capital, and their owners benefit if they pay out earnings or buy back stock.
- To avoid errors in estimating cash flows, he does two things:
  - Stick to businesses he understands, meaning simple and stable. "What counts for most people in investing is not how much they know, but rather how realistically they define what they don't know."
  - Insist on a margin of safety. If calculated value is only slightly above price, he is not interested. He calls this Ben Graham's principle "the cornerstone of investment success."
- "An investor needs to do very few things right as long as he or she avoids big mistakes."

chunks.heading: Portfolio activity, General Dynamics, and fixed income
chunks.text:
- Holdings over $100 million at year-end 1992, with cost and market in millions:
  - Coca-Cola: $1,024 cost, $3,911 market
  - GEICO: $46 cost, $2,226 market
  - Capital Cities/ABC: $518 cost, $1,524 market
  - Gillette: $600 cost, $1,365 market
  - Freddie Mac: $414 cost, $784 market
  - Wells Fargo: $381 cost, $486 market
  - General Dynamics: $312 cost, $451 market
  - Washington Post: $10 cost, $397 market
  - Guinness: $333 cost, $300 market
- In 1992 Berkshire added to Guinness and Wells Fargo, more than doubled Freddie Mac, and started General Dynamics. "We like to buy. Selling, however, is a different story."
- General Dynamics began as an arbitrage. After announcing a Dutch tender for about 30% of its shares, Warren bought expecting a small profit by tendering. Then he studied CEO Bill Anders: a clear, rational strategy, urgency, and remarkable results. Warren dropped the arbitrage idea and became a long-term holder, buying 14% of the post-tender shares in a month. A tender swells trading volume, which helped him build the position.
- He has made arbitrage commitments like this perhaps half a dozen times in recent years, with decent returns.
- On fixed income:
  - Berkshire realized $80 million of gains from fixed income in 1992, and losses have been negligible: "thrills but so far no spills."
  - Negotiated preferred purchases have been inferior to secondary-market purchases, as he expected. The secondary market, "periodically ruled by mass folly," constantly sets a clearing price, and shares worth x have sold for 1/2x or less. Corporations and controlling holders pick when to issue, so they rarely offer bargains. "It's rare you'll find x for 1/2x here."
- He admits USAir was a mistake: "it was I who happily jumped into the pool; no one pushed me." He expected a tough industry but not "prolonged kamikaze behavior." A competitively beset business needs far more managerial skill, and the reward is "simply survival, not prosperity."
- He says he cannot forecast the economics of investment banking, airlines or paper.

chunks.heading: Insurance: float, cost of float, and super-cat
chunks.text:
- Float is loss reserves, loss adjustment expense reserves and unearned premium reserves, less agents' balances, prepaid acquisition costs and deferred charges on assumed reinsurance. The cost of float is the underwriting loss. What counts is "the cost of funds developed from insurance."
- 1992 numbers:
  - Underwriting loss: $108.96 million.
  - Average float: $2,290.4 million.
  - Cost of float: 4.76%, against a 7.39% long-term Treasury yield.
  - In 21 of 26 insurance years Berkshire's float cost less than the government's rate. "If, on average, we didn't beat the Government's rate, there would be no economic reason for us to be in the business."
- Industry combined ratio was an estimated 114.8 in 1992, with about four points from Hurricane Andrew. A ratio of 106-110 typically means break-even once float income is counted. Below 100 is an underwriting profit.
- Andrew exposed weak reinsurance protection: "It's only when the tide goes out that you learn who's been swimming naked."
- Super-cat policies, sold to other insurers, usually trigger only when both of these happen:
  - the client's loss exceeds its retention;
  - industry-wide insured losses pass a minimum, usually $3 billion or more.
  - Many cover only a second or later event, or one type such as earthquake.
- Berkshire lost about $125 million to Andrew, roughly equal to its 1992 super-cat premiums, so the line lost only about $2 million. One policy would pay $100 million on a specified catastrophe. Warren targets a 10% margin over time but expects "enormously profitable or enormously unprofitable" years.
- On pricing and underwriting:
  - Warren warns that past experience cannot be simply extrapolated, citing possible global warming, growth of insured values in coastal areas, and rare events like the 1812 New Madrid quake.
  - Berkshire rejects more than 98% of the business it is offered, and Ajit Jain is "simply the best in this business."
  - "A fool and his money are soon invited everywhere."
- Super-cat premiums are recognized only when a loss occurs or the policy expires, because nine of the ten largest US insured losses came in the second half of a year.
- Berkshire was second in US property-casualty net worth, behind State Farm. Insurance is expected to be the main earnings source "for decades to come."

chunks.heading: Accounting honesty: stock options, retiree health, and overhead
chunks.text:
- Stock options are compensation, so they are an expense:
  - "If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it? And, if expenses shouldn't go into the calculation of earnings, where in the world should they go?"
  - Costs arise when something of value is delivered, not only when cash moves.
  - Imprecision is no excuse, since 747 lifespans, loan losses and insurance reserves are also estimates.
  - He offers to buy any restricted option from an executive who claims it is worthless, and to sell insurance in exchange for options on a company's stock.
  - He faults accountants and the SEC for letting executives "muscle" them.
- On post-retirement health benefits:
  - He calls the new rule requiring recognition of present-value liabilities a good change. Berkshire avoids acquiring companies with these liabilities.
  - In 1982 he nearly bought a company burdened by them. Another buyer appeared, the company went bankrupt, and workers' health promises became "largely worthless."
- Lincoln's riddle: "How many legs does a dog have if you call his tail a leg? Four, because calling a tail a leg does not make it a leg."
- Corporate overhead:
  - Berkshire's was $4.2 million in 1992, under 1% of operating earnings, with no legal, HR, PR, investor-relations or strategic-planning departments.
  - If a business spends 10% on headquarters while a peer spends 1%, shareholders lose about 9% of value. He sees no correlation between high corporate costs and good performance.
  - He admires the Wal-Mart, Nucor, Dover, GEICO, Golden West Financial and Price Co. models.

chunks.heading: Managers, owner policies, and temperament
chunks.text:
- He prizes managers working past retirement age:
  - Rose Blumkin ("Mrs. B"), 99, works seven days a week. She sold her building to Nebraska Furniture Mart and signed a non-compete at 99.
  - Ralph Schey's Scott Fetzer earned a record $110 million pre-tax on only $116 million of equity, without leverage. It shrank inventory and fixed assets and sent Berkshire over 100% of its earnings in seven years.
- Operating managers' own charitable gifts go through the shareholder-designated program or their own money. Warren says if employees "wish to give to their alma maters... they should use their own money, not yours."
- Berkshire's shareholder-designated contributions were $7.6 million across 2,810 charities, with 97% of eligible shares taking part.
- No stock split. Warren believes the policy helps assemble shareholders who "think and behave like rational long-term owners." Trading frictions are minimal, and a split would modestly degrade the shareholder base.
- Aversion to debt, especially short-term. The 5½% zero-coupon convertible debentures were called because the rate stopped being attractive and the conversion option disadvantages owners. Of the $476 million, $405 million was redeemed in cash and 6,106 shares were issued.
- He accepts board seats, including at USAir, when large owners should "do their bit," though five outside boards is more than he thinks advisable for an active CEO.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1993 letter argues risk is loss of purchasing power, not beta, and that concentrating in a few understandable, moat-protected businesses beats diversification. It also covers float economics, super-cat discipline, tax-deferred compounding, Dexter Shoe, and governance.

chunks.heading: How Warren values businesses, measures risk, and why he holds Coke-type franchises
chunks.text:
- **Book value vs. intrinsic value.** Book value is "the capital, including retained earnings, that has been put into a business." Intrinsic value is "a present-value estimate of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life."
- At most companies the two are unrelated. At Berkshire, book value (14.3% growth in 1993, $19 to $8,854 over 29 years, 23.3% compounded) is a useful tracking device, though well below intrinsic value.
- Berkshire's long-standing goal is 15% annual growth in per-share intrinsic value. He says the growing capital base makes it "an ever-more difficult target to hit."
- Look-through earnings must reach about $1.85 billion by 2000 to hit the goal. He "paints first and shoots later" rather than centering the target on wherever the arrow landed.

chunks.heading: Market price vs. business value: Mr. Market and the voting machine
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's market price rose 39% in 1993 while book and intrinsic value rose about 14%. Over time price and value "arrive at about the same destination," but in the short run they often diverge sharply.
- From 1991 to 1993, Coke and Gillette grew operating earnings per share 38% and 37%, but their stocks rose only 11% and 6%. What counts over time is the earnings performance of the businesses.
- Coke IPO'd in 1919 at $40 and fell more than 50% to $19.50 by end-1920. A single share with dividends reinvested was worth over $2.1 million at end-1993.
- He quotes Ben Graham: "In the short-run, the market is a voting machine... but in the long-run, the market is a weighing machine."
- A wildly fluctuating market means "irrationally low prices will periodically be attached to solid businesses." The true investor welcomes volatility and is "totally free to either ignore the market or exploit its folly."
- After buying, he would not be disturbed if markets closed for a year or two. He needs no daily quote on a 7% Coke stake, any more than on 100% of See's or H. H. Brown.

chunks.heading: Redefining risk: against beta, for business economics
chunks.text:
- Risk, in dictionary terms, is "the possibility of loss or injury." He rejects the academic definition of risk as relative volatility ("beta"): "It is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong."
- Beta logic is absurd: Washington Post, bought in 1973 after a sharp drop, became "riskier" at the lower price, though someone offered the whole company at a vastly reduced price would see it as safer.
- The real risk is whether aggregate after-tax receipts, including sale proceeds, give at least as much purchasing power as the initial stake plus a modest interest rate.
- Five factors determine it:
  1. The certainty with which the business's long-term economics can be evaluated.
  2. The certainty with which management can be evaluated, both on realizing the business's potential and on employing its cash flows wisely.
  3. The certainty that management will channel rewards to shareholders rather than itself.
  4. The purchase price.
  5. The levels of taxation and inflation.
- These can't be pulled from a database, but like Justice Stewart on obscenity, "I know it when I see it."
- Coke sells about 44% of all soft drinks. Gillette has more than 60% of the blade market by value. Both have increased share, and brand power, product attributes and distribution give them "a protective moat around their economic castles."
- Their stocks have betas similar to run-of-the-mill companies with no advantage, which shows beta can't capture business risk.
- He quotes Peter Lynch: commodity-business stocks should carry the warning "Competition may prove hazardous to human wealth."

chunks.heading: Staying in the circle of competence and concentrating
chunks.text:
- He can usually tell a "Barbie" (Monopoly, Barbie) from a "pet rock" (hula hoops) in consumer businesses. In many industries he and Charlie cannot, even after years of study.
- Fast-moving technology industries don't lend themselves to reliable long-term evaluation. They didn't foresee what would happen in TVs or computers 30 years ago. His stance: "Why search for a needle buried in a haystack when one is sitting in plain sight?"
- Charlie and he concluded that "it's just too hard to make hundreds of smart decisions." They need to be smart only a few times and will "settle for one good idea a year."
- Concentration may lower risk because it raises the intensity of thought and the comfort level required before buying.
- For a know-something investor who can find five to ten sensibly priced companies with durable advantages, conventional diversification "is apt simply to hurt your results and increase your risk." He can't see why anyone puts money into a 20th favorite rather than adding to top choices. Quoting Mae West: "Too much of a good thing can be wonderful."
- Wide diversification is right in two cases:
  - Risky-but-favorable bets such as arbitrage or venture capital. Act like a casino with a roulette wheel: want lots of action, but refuse any single huge bet.
  - The know-nothing investor who regularly buys an index fund can outperform most professionals. "When 'dumb' money acknowledges its limitations, it ceases to be dumb."

chunks.heading: Holding great businesses and the power of deferred taxes
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's 1993 holdings were nearly unchanged from the prior year: Coke (93.4M shares, cost $1.02B, market $4.17B), GEICO (cost $46M, market $1.76B), Gillette, Cap Cities/ABC, Wells Fargo, Freddie Mac, Washington Post, General Dynamics, Guinness.
- Rule: hold "a small piece of an outstanding business with the same tenacity that an owner would exhibit if he owned all of that business." Understandable, durably wonderful businesses "are simply too hard to replace."
- CEOs would never sell a crown-jewel subsidiary, yet move around their personal portfolios on slogans like "You can't go broke taking a profit." He asks whether a CEO would tell his board that about a star subsidiary.
- In 1938 Fortune said investors looking at Coke were "looking too late." Coke sold 207 million cases then and about 10.7 billion in 1993 (50-fold). $40 invested in 1919 became $3,277 by 1938, and a fresh $40 in 1938 grew to $25,000 by end-1993.
- He keeps a buy-and-hold policy even as if tax-exempt, but notes taxes are due only on realization.
- Li'l Abner example: doubling $1 for 27.5 years, taxed at 35% each year, needs 7.5 extra years beyond 20 to reach $1M (about $22,370 after 20 years). One investment held through the same doublings yields about $200M pre-tax, or about $130M after a $70M tax. A single investment compounding internally beats a succession of investments at the same rate.
- Cap Cities: bought 3M shares in 1986 at $172.50, sold a third at $630 in 1993. After 35% capital gains tax, the realized profit was $297M, versus only $152M of hypothetically taxed look-through retained earnings over eight years. He views look-through earnings as conservative.
- Berkshire paid about $390M in 1993 federal income taxes (about $200M on operating earnings, $190M on gains). He has "absolutely no complaint," noting the market economy rewards them far more than others of equal benefit.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and super-cat underwriting
chunks.text:
- Float is premiums prepaid plus funds earmarked for incurred-but-unpaid claims. Berkshire computes it as loss reserves, loss adjustment reserves and unearned premium reserves, minus agents' balances, prepaid acquisition costs and deferred charges on assumed reinsurance.
- Falling interest rates cut the value of float. The industry once broke even at a combined ratio of 107-111, but a company writing at the same ratio now has a "far less attractive business."
- Float should be valued at the risk-free long-term interest rate, and underwriting results separated from investment results when judging managers.
- Berkshire's cost of float is its underwriting loss or profit. Average float in 1993 was $2,624.7M, at a negative cost (a $31M underwriting profit), versus a 6.35% long-bond yield.
- He tempers enthusiasm because the profit partly reflects a quiet super-cat year. A year without losses doesn't validate the business:
  - An event that occurs 25 times a century, priced at 5-for-1 odds, gives many winning years and even a straight six or seven, but "you also will eventually go broke."
  - Berkshire thinks it gives about 3.5-for-1, but no one can calculate true super-cat odds, and it will take decades to know.
- Hurricane Andrew cost about $125M in 1992. A similar storm after expansion could cost $600M. Losses in a bad year could be three or four times 1993's earnings from super-cat. The LA quake would have been a different story at 7.5 instead of 6.8.
- Advantages: Ajit Jain, and a net worth ten to twenty times that of main competitors. Super-cat can't be diversified or laid off, so capital determines limits offered. The four largest reinsurers buy meaningful coverage from Berkshire, because "the test of a reinsurer is its ability and willingness to pay losses under trying circumstances."
- About $5B of new reinsurance capital has arrived. If prices deteriorate, he'll accept much-reduced volume rather than chase business.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions, managers, and why owners sell to Berkshire
chunks.text:
- Dexter Shoe: founded in 1956 by Harold Alfond with $10,000; produces over 7.5M pairs a year with 77 retail outlets. Berkshire issued 25,203 shares. Combined shoe sales in 1994 are expected to exceed $550M, with pre-tax earnings possibly above $85M, and 7,200 employees.
- Berkshire's path was H. H. Brown (1991), Lowell (end of 1992), then Dexter, after Frank Rooney vouched for it. Frank's H. H. Brown earnings were up 35% over its 1992 high.
- No grand plan: "usually poison for a corporate giant's shareholders if it embarks upon new ventures pursuant to some grand vision." Berkshire focuses on "the economic characteristics of businesses that we wish to own and the personal characteristics of managers," then hopes to find both together.
- Pitch to private owners:
  - A tax-free swap into a diversified group of terrific businesses.
  - Easier gifting and liquidity.
  - Owner-oriented treatment, with no restricted stock or options for Warren, so his gain-loss equation matches other owners'.
  - Promises of no change of control or culture for decades.
  - Managers keep running the business: "we do not tell .400 hitters how to swing."
- He refuses marginal deals just because Berkshire is long on cash: "There's no use running if you're on the wrong road."
- Manager examples:
  - Mrs. B turned 100 and founded Nebraska Furniture Mart with $500 in 1937. Berkshire bought control without audits, real estate checks or warranties, because "her word was good enough."
  - Kay Graham at Washington Post: Berkshire paid about $10M in 1973 and now has a stake worth over $400M paying $7M a year in dividends. He judged her character and shareholder treatment on a dual-class company.
  - Don Keough and Roberto Goizueta took Coke from $4.4B to $58B of market value in under 13 years. His observations of Keough as a neighbor contributed to the record $1B Coke investment in 1988-89.
  - Susan Jacques went from a $4/hour job to president and CEO of Borsheim's in 11 years.

chunks.heading: Corporate governance and shareholder-oriented capital allocation
chunks.text:
- Three board situations:
  1. No controlling shareholder: directors should act as if for a single absentee owner. They should be relatively few (ten or fewer), mostly outsiders, chosen for business savvy, interest in the job and owner-orientation (not prominence or diversity). They should evaluate the CEO without him present.
  2. Controlling owner who also manages (Berkshire now): directors can only persuade, and should resign if serious problems persist.
  3. Controlling owner not in management (Berkshire after Warren): the best structure. Directors take complaints to one interested owner, who can fix mistakes quickly.
- After his death the stock goes to Susie, or to a foundation, with no consequential stock sales needed. She and son Howard are on the board, and most other directors are significant owners.
- Philanthropy: "the company's money is the owners' money." Shareholders direct $10 per share ($9.4M in 1993, 97% participation, 3,110 charities) rather than the CEO. He has "yet to find a CEO who believes he should personally fund the charities favored by his shareholders."
- Overhead is under half of charitable contributions ($4.9M overhead, of which $1.4M is the corporate jet).
- Disclosure standard: give shareholders the information he and Charlie would want if positions were reversed, which is why he presents earnings by business excluding purchase-price accounting charges.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1994 letter explains intrinsic value vs book value using Scott Fetzer, warns against dilution-focused acquisitions, and lays out symmetric manager compensation. It also covers insurance float, pricing rather than timing purchases, ignoring forecasts, and owning up to the USAir error.

chunks.heading: Performance, scale, and the "happy zone"
chunks.text:
- 1994: net worth up $1.45 billion, or 13.9%. Per-share book value went from $19 to $10,083 over 30 years, 23% compounded.
- Warren and Charlie "make few predictions," but one is confident: future performance "won't come close to matching the performance of the past."
- The formula is unchanged: "the purchase at sensible prices of businesses that have good underlying economics and are run by honest and able people."
- "A fat wallet... is the enemy of superior investment results." Net worth was $11.9 billion versus about $22 million when he and Charlie took over.
- Berkshire now considers a security only if it can deploy at least $100 million in it. Charlie's rule: "If something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well."
- Warren cites Ted Williams: to be a good hitter you need a good ball to hit. Swinging outside the "happy zone" turns a .344 hitter into a .250 hitter. Berkshire waits for opportunities well within its own happy zone.

chunks.heading: Ignoring forecasts, pricing instead of timing
chunks.text:
- Berkshire ignores political and economic forecasts, "an expensive distraction."
- Over 30 years, nobody foresaw Vietnam's escalation, wage and price controls, two oil shocks, a presidential resignation, the Soviet collapse, a 508-point one-day Dow drop, or T-bill yields swinging between 2.8% and 17.4%.
- None of it dented Ben Graham's principles. Deferring capital deployment out of fear of unknowns would have been costly.
- The best purchases usually came when worries about some macro event peaked: "Fear is the foe of the faddist, but the friend of the fundamentalist."
- "We try to price, rather than time, purchases." It is folly to skip an outstanding business with a predictable long-term future over short-term worries about an unpredictable economy: "Why scrap an informed decision because of an uninformed guess?"
- The same logic applies to whole businesses and stock-market pieces. National Indemnity (1967), See's (1972), Buffalo News (1977), Nebraska Furniture Mart (1983) and Scott Fetzer (1986) were bought because they became available at acceptable prices, not because of the Dow or the Fed.

chunks.heading: Book value versus intrinsic value
chunks.text:
- Book value is easy to calculate but of limited use. What counts is intrinsic value, "impossible to pinpoint but essential to estimate."
- Definition: "the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life." It is subjective and shifts with cash flow estimates and interest rates, but it is "the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments and businesses."
- In 1964 book value was $19.46, but the figure overstated intrinsic value because everything was tied up in sub-profitable textiles. Today many controlled businesses are worth far more than carrying value, so book value is a "significantly understated" tracking measure. In 1994 both rose about 13.9%.
- College analogy: cost (including foregone earnings) is "book value." Intrinsic value is the discounted excess lifetime earnings. Book value is meaningless as an indicator of intrinsic value.

chunks.heading: Scott Fetzer: a case study
chunks.text:
- Bought at the start of 1986 for $315.2 million against $172.6 million of book value. The $142.6 million premium reflected a belief that intrinsic value was close to double book.
- 22 businesses then and now; main units World Book, Kirby and Campbell Hausfeld. No additions or disposals, no leverage, no sale-leasebacks, no receivable sales.
- Excess cash let it pay $125 million of dividends in 1986 on $40.3 million of earnings. Earnings rose to $79.3 million in 1994; book value ended 1994 at $94.0 million.
- Return on equity would have ranked 4th on the 1993 Fortune 500, and first excluding three companies whose earnings came from bankruptcy debt forgiveness. It was double the number 10 company's.
- Not from a cyclical peak, monopoly or leverage, but from CEO Ralph Schey's management.
- Accounting lesson: the purchase premium is written off through annual charges (to $54.2 million by 1994). Warren says these charges have no effect on cash or taxes and are not, in his view, an economic cost. Carrying value fell to $148.2 million, less than half the purchase level, while earnings roughly doubled.
- Ralph's formula: "in investing it is not necessary to do extraordinary things to get extraordinary results" (Ben Graham, 45 years earlier), and it holds in management too. Handle the basics, set the right goals, don't get diverted.
- Berkshire looks at performance, not the calendar. Many managers are over 65, and Warren (71) and Charlie (64) keep George Foreman's picture on their desks.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation and acquisitions
chunks.text:
- Managers must act to increase per-share intrinsic value, including in share repurchases.
- Focusing on immediate EPS (or book value) dilution is dangerous. Analogy: an MBA student "merging" with a day laborer share-for-share would boost near-term earnings, which is silly. Differences in prospects, non-operating assets or capital structure matter more.
- Berkshire has rejected deals that would have raised near-term earnings but cut intrinsic value per share. Advice from Wayne Gretzky: "Go to where the puck is going to be, not to where it is."
- Most big acquisitions enrich acquiree shareholders, the acquirer's management and bankers, but usually reduce acquirer shareholders' wealth because it gives up more intrinsic value than it gets. Quote from John Medlin: "you are running a chain letter in reverse."
- A good business throws off more cash than it can use. Asking planners, consultants or bankers whether to acquire "is like asking your interior decorator whether you need a $50,000 rug."
- CEOs are selected partly for "animal spirits and ego." Advisors urging deals is not a push they need. A CEO friend's rationale: "Aw, fellas, all the other kids have one."
- Berkshire's system: managers first reinvest earnings in their businesses; surplus goes to Omaha for Warren and Charlie to deploy into whole or partial businesses they understand, with good sustainable economics, run by managers "we like, admire and trust."

chunks.heading: Compensation and alignment
chunks.text:
- Pay managers on results of the unit they control, not Berkshire as a whole. Ralph is paid on Scott Fetzer. Tying him to Berkshire would be "capricious."
- Hold out large carrots tied directly to controllable results. Charge managers a high rate for incremental capital and credit them equally for capital released.
- The bonus is symmetrical: returns above the hurdle raise it, sub-standard returns cost the manager, so it pays well to send unused cash to Omaha.
- "Alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside." Many plans are "heads I win, tails you lose."
- Typical options flaw: no periodic increase in strike price for retained earnings, so a ten-year option, low payout and compounding can enrich a manager who merely "tread water." Low dividends even raise the option holder's profit.
- Ralph's arrangement was worked out in about five minutes, without lawyers or consultants, and has never changed. Other units' deals are similarly simple.
- Warren and Charlie, as the only people responsible for the whole business, are the only ones who logically should be paid on the whole. They don't want it, and would be happy in their jobs unpaid. Their pledge: no compensation giving more upside than downside, and personal fortunes stay overwhelmingly in Berkshire shares.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and super-cat
chunks.text:
- Float is "money we hold but don't own," arising from prepaid premiums and the delay before claims are resolved. An underwriting loss is the cost of float. The business is valuable when float costs less than alternative funding.
- Average float rose from $17.3 million (1967) to $3,056.6 million (1994). Underwriting was profitable in 1993 and 1994, so float cost was negative. Warren cautions the insurance business "is not as good as it currently looks."
- Super-cat policies are few, large and non-standardized, requiring judgment (manager Ajit Jain). Berkshire's financial strength means buyers are certain it will pay after a mega-catastrophe, and it can write amounts others won't. Example: a $400 million short-term California earthquake policy written immediately; quotes up to $500 million the same day.
- Berkshire accepts lumpy results: insurers who "smooth" earnings follow sub-optimum strategies. They expect higher long-term returns from accepting volatility rather than pursuing predictability.
- Worst-case super-cat loss estimated at about $600 million after tax, slightly above annual earnings from other sources. Shareholders uncomfortable with that should sell now.
- Pricing on garden-variety policies fell as new capital chased premiums, so 1995 volume would probably be lower.

chunks.heading: Investing approach, look-through earnings and mistakes
chunks.text:
- The big investment idea "can usually be explained in a short paragraph": a business with enduring competitive advantages, run by able, owner-oriented people, bought at a sensible price.
- "Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count." If one easy-to-understand, enduring factor drives value, the payoff equals that from a complex analysis.
- Consider adding to existing holdings first. In 1994 Berkshire added to Coca-Cola and American Express. Long familiarity with a company helps.
- Partial ownership analogies: Coke sold about 280 billion servings and earned under a penny on each, giving Berkshire's 7.8% stake about $200 million of "soft-drink earnings." Gillette's 7% market share was about $250 million of sales. Wells Fargo's 13% was a $7 billion "Berkshire Bank" earning about $100 million. "It's far better to own a significant portion of the Hope diamond than 100% of a rhinestone."
- Look-through earnings = operating earnings + retained investee earnings − hypothetical tax (14% rate). 1994: $1,030 million versus $841 million in 1993. Target intrinsic value growth is 15%, implying about $1.85 billion of look-through earnings by 2000.
- Amex: about 40% of Buffett Partnership capital in the mid-1960s after the salad-oil scandal; Berkshire owns just under 10% at a $1.36 billion cost.
- Mistakes: selling 10 million Cap Cities shares at $63 (price $85.25 at year-end, about $222.5 million forgone). Top "mistake du jour": the $358 million USAir preferred, an "unforced error" from sloppy analysis. Warren missed the rule that in an unregulated commodity business a company must lower costs to competitive levels or face extinction. Written down to $89.5 million (25 cents on the dollar), with the lesson: "You don't have to make it back the way that you lost it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why he distrusts most acquisitions yet loves buying great businesses with great managers, using Helzberg's, R.C. Willey and the full GEICO purchase. He also covers insurance float economics, retail versus have-to-be-smart-once businesses, and his own mistakes.

chunks.heading: Two paths to ownership: negotiated whole-company purchases and stock-market part-interests
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie Munger want a collection of companies, wholly or partly owned, with excellent economics and outstanding managers.
- His favorite deal is a negotiated purchase of 100% of such a business at a fair price. He is almost as happy when the market offers a modest percentage of an outstanding business at a pro-rata price well below what buying 100% would cost.
- This "double-barrelled approach" is an advantage over capital allocators who stick to a single course. His joke: being eclectic "doubles your chances for a date on Saturday night."
- Berkshire's marketable securities per share went from $4 (1965) to $159 (1975), $2,443 (1985) and $22,088 (1995), a 33.4% yearly growth rate. Per-share operating earnings excluding investment income went from $4.08 (1965) to $(6.48) (1975), $18.86 (1985) and $258.20 (1995), 14.7% yearly.
- None of this came from a master plan. He says they had no road map in 1965 and have none now.
- 1995 results: net worth rose $5.3 billion (45.0%), per-share book value 43.1%, and since 1964 book value per share grew from $19 to $14,426 (23.6% compounded). He gives the market's help most of the credit: "a rising tide lifts all yachts."
- Size is the main disadvantage: early on Berkshire needed good ideas, now it needs "good big ideas," and finding them gets harder in direct proportion to financial success.
- His best hope is to double per-share intrinsic value every five years on average, and he says they may fall far short.

chunks.heading: Why most acquisitions hurt the buyer, and how Berkshire tries to avoid that
chunks.text:
- Warren believes most deals do damage to the acquirer's shareholders. Sellers' projections have "more entertainment value than educational value."
- He and Charlie never glance at seller-prepared projections. His story: a man tells a vet his horse sometimes walks fine and sometimes limps; the vet says "when he's walking fine, sell him." Sellers pick the time to sell, when the business is walking fine.
- The seller knows far more about the business than the buyer.
- Berkshire's advantages:
  - It has no strategic plan, so no pressure to proceed in an ordained direction, which "almost invariably" leads to silly prices.
  - It mentally compares every acquisition with dozens of other opportunities, including buying small pieces of the best businesses via the stock market. Managers focused on expansion seldom use this discipline.
- He cites Peter Drucker: "Dealmaking beats working... Dealmaking is romantic, sexy. That's why you have deals that make no sense."
- Diversification-by-consultant anecdote: a company with a glamorless but leading product bought many businesses after costly studies. Result: "When we started, we were getting 100% of our earnings from the original business. After ten years, we were getting 150%."
- Berkshire stock is useful currency for sellers who want to defer taxes indefinitely. Managers get extraordinary autonomy, and the "we are buying to keep" promise is credible given the ownership structure.
- Criteria offered in the letter: a business earning $25 million or more pre-tax, with good economics and excellent management. Discussions are confidential.
- He says most owners who care about their people are less likely to hold unpleasant surprises than a seller simply auctioning the business.

chunks.heading: Helzberg's and R.C. Willey: finding deals "by walking around," and retail's risks
chunks.text:
- Helzberg's Diamond Shops: Barnett Helzberg, who owned four Berkshire shares, stopped Warren on a New York street in May 1994. The company had 134 stores in 23 states and sales of $10 million (1974), $53 million (1984) and $282 million (1994). Average store sales of about $2 million, far above competitors' similar-size stores, drive the profits.
- Warren says he would not have bought without CEO Jeff Comment: "Buying a retailer without good management is like buying the Eiffel Tower without an elevator." The deal was a tax-free stock exchange, the only kind that interested the seller. Barnett shared part of his proceeds with associates, which signaled to Warren that Berkshire would be treated right.
- R.C. Willey: Irv Blumkin of Nebraska Furniture Mart introduced CEO Bill Child. Warren wrote a letter stating his idea of value, they quickly agreed on a number, and the deal closed by mid-1995. Bill took over the business in 1954 when sales were about $250,000. 1995 sales were $257 million, with over 50% of Utah's furniture business and a sixth major store about to open.
- Retail is tough: he has watched many retailers enjoy terrific growth and high returns on equity and then "nosedive," often to bankruptcy. A retailer must stay smart every day because competitors copy and top whatever you do ("to coast is to fail").
- Contrast with "have-to-be-smart-once" businesses (e.g., an early network TV station), which could survive a shiftless nephew running them. For a retailer, that nephew is "an express ticket to bankruptcy."
- Management principle: managers operate autonomously with no second-guessing. Warren wants to behave toward managers as he likes owners to behave toward him, and he rejects the attitude of the alumnus telling the coach "I'm 100% with you - win or tie."
- How many reports can he handle? "If I have one person reporting to me and he is a lemon, that's one too many," while with managers like these the number can be almost unlimited.
- He says many managers don't have to work for a living but perform for the same reason wealthy golfers stay on the tour, and that no key manager has left Berkshire to join another employer between 1965 and 1995.

chunks.heading: GEICO: the history, the moat, and the lesson of selling a wonderful business
chunks.text:
- Warren studied under Ben Graham at Columbia in 1950-51, then found Graham was chairman of GEICO. On a Saturday in January 1951 he took a train to Washington and pounded on the locked door. Lorimer "Davy" Davidson spent about four hours teaching him how insurance works and what lets one company excel.
- Davy's key point: GEICO's direct marketing gave it an enormous cost advantage over agent-based competitors, who couldn't give up their distribution.
- In 1951 he bought 350 GEICO shares in four purchases for $10,282, more than 50% of his net worth at the time of the last purchase. By year-end the stake was worth $13,125, over 65% of his net worth.
- He sold in 1952 for $15,259 to switch into Western Insurance Securities (about one times earnings). The GEICO shares he sold grew to about $1.3 million over the next 20 years. The lesson: "the inadvisability of selling a stake in an identifiably-wonderful company."
- In the early 1970s GEICO under-estimated claims costs, underpriced policies and nearly went bankrupt. Jack Byrne became CEO in 1976 and took drastic remedial steps. Berkshire bought heavily in the second half of 1976. By year-end 1980 it had invested $45.7 million for 33.3% of the company. The stake rose to about 50% by 1995 because GEICO repurchased shares.
- In 1995 Berkshire agreed to pay $2.3 billion for the half it didn't own: "a steep price," but it buys full ownership of a growing enterprise that is exceptional for the same reasons as in 1951.
- Key people: Tony Nicely (insurance operations, 34 years at GEICO, "brains, energy, integrity and focus") and Lou Simpson (investments: 22.8% annual return versus 15.7% for the S&P, 1980-95; concentrated, conservative approach like Berkshire's). Lou's presence also means a professional would be available to manage investments if something happened to Warren and Charlie.
- The moat: rock-bottom operating costs. Underwriting and loss adjustment expenses fell to 23.6% of premiums in 1995. Warren says "I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable 'moats,'" and GEICO's moat widened.
- GEICO insured about 3.7 million cars and was the seventh largest US auto insurer. The deal added nearly $3 billion of float.

chunks.heading: Insurance float: how it works and when it is valuable
chunks.text:
- Float is "money we hold but don't own." It arises because premiums are prepaid and claims take time to be reported and resolved.
- Underwriting loss is the cost of float. An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds, and has negative value if the cost is above market rates.
- Berkshire's float grew at 20.7% compounded from 1967. Average float was $17.3 million (1967 profit year), $237 million (1980), $1,637 million (1990) and $3,607 million (1995). The cost of float was less than zero in 1993, 1994 and 1995 (underwriting profits), against a 5.95% long-term government bond yield at year-end 1995.
- Profitability depends on three things: what assets earn, what liabilities cost, and leverage. Berkshire's liabilities cost very little because float came on advantageous terms; for many other insurers the cost exceeds the float's worth, making leverage a disadvantage.
- Warren's equity-equivalence argument: replacing $3.4 billion of float with $3.4 billion of equity would have meant more shares, equal assets and lower earnings, since the float actually threw off profits.
- The float he calls "free": nearly all of the table's float growth was developed internally, whereas GEICO's float was bought at a very substantial price.

chunks.heading: Super-cat and large-risk insurance: pricing discipline, volatility, and alignment
chunks.text:
- Berkshire sells policies that insurers and reinsurers buy against mega-catastrophes. Warren expects large profits in most years and occasionally a huge loss, so measuring attractiveness takes many years. He cautions that three good years (1993-95) will be "at least partially offset" by some terrible year.
- Ajit Jain also writes one-off large-risk coverage: Mike Tyson's life (declining fight by fight), Lloyd's against over 225 "names" dying during the year, and the launch and one-year orbit of two Chinese satellites. Policies offered carried up to $1 billion of potential loss; the largest accepted coverage was $400 million.
- Why clients come to Berkshire: unmatched financial strength, the fastest quotes, and the largest limits. Competitors lay off much of their business via reinsurance, which reduces flexibility and reaction time.
- Warren and Charlie accept volatility: "we prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%." Most managers opt for smoothness, which leaves Berkshire a competitive advantage. They still monitor aggregate exposure so the worst case stays at a level they are comfortable with.
- Many primary insurers writing many small property policies face an uncapped aggregate risk that could blow through their reinsurance covers. Berkshire's worst case is large but capped.
- He will not knowingly write business at inadequate rates, even as super-cat prices weaken. Berkshire learned this in the early 1970s: "A bad reinsurance contract is like hell: easy to enter and impossible to exit." Berkshire "paid a heavy tuition" for his education in reinsurance, and GEICO had a similar disaster in the early 1980s.
- Alignment: Lloyd's problems show that people writing insurance must share the downside as well as the upside with those supplying capital. The joke he tells: the CEO saying things could be worse, "It could be my money." Warren's version: "At Berkshire, it's our money."
- Other insurance results: National Indemnity's traditional business had a combined ratio of 84.2 (three-year average 85.6, run by Don Wurster); the homestate operation under Rod Eldred had 81.4 (three-year 82.4); California workers' comp under Brad Kinstler lost renewals rather than accept inadequate rates and still earned an underwriting profit; Central States Indemnity under John Kizer grew premiums 23% and underwriting profit 59%.

chunks.heading: Convertible preferreds, mistakes, and the Gillette lesson
chunks.text:
- Berkshire made five private convertible preferred purchases during 1987-91 (Champion, First Empire, Gillette, Salomon, USAir). They were valued mainly as fixed-income securities, with the conversion option as a "kicker."
- Warren admits he got three predictions wrong or only partly right. Returns "moderately" beat medium-term fixed income only because of one issue (Gillette). They did not produce returns like those from wonderful businesses. His claim that it was almost impossible to lose money on them gave him "well-deserved heartburn."
- Gillette was his biggest mistake of a kind never shown on financial statements. Berkshire paid $600 million in 1989 for preferred convertible into 48 million split-adjusted shares; buying common directly with the same money could have meant about 60 million shares, possibly at a 5%+ discount (the common then traded around $10.50). He estimates he would have been better off at year-end 1995 by about $625 million minus roughly $70 million of extra dividends. He chose preferred because he was "far too clever."
- Champion: he and Charlie have never had a conviction about the paper industry, and in 54 years of investing he cannot recall owning a paper producer's common stock.
