They converted ahead of a call and sold the shares back to the company at a modest discount, for a gain of about 19% after tax over six years.
- First Empire: to be called March 31, 1996, and Berkshire will convert and keep the common because he is "comfortable owning stock in well-run banks" and thinks highly of CEO Bob Wilmers.
- Salomon: he took the position expecting no special insight into investment banking and later served as interim chairman, giving the holding far more management time than its economic significance. The Dow doubled after the purchase, and the brokerage group did equally well, so he grades his decision to value the conversion option "very poor." The 9% dividend remains attractive, 20% of the issue is redeemed each year from 1995-99 ($140 million taken in 1995), and he thinks the conversion right may still prove valuable.
- USAir: results improved, but the company is a weak credit. The preferred was carried at 60% of par; unpaid dividends compound at 5% over prime.
- Net: leaving Gillette aside, the preferreds as a group earned after-tax returns no better than the medium-term fixed-income issues they replaced.

chunks.heading: Common stock holdings, "Rip Van Winkle" patience, and costly sales
chunks.text:
- Year-end 1995 holdings (cost / market): Coca-Cola 100 million shares ($1,298.9 million / $7,425 million), Gillette ($600 million / $2,502 million), Capital Cities/ABC 20 million shares ($345 million / $2,467.5 million), GEICO ($45.7 million / $2,393.2 million), American Express ($1,392.7 million / $2,046.3 million), Wells Fargo ($423.7 million / $1,466.9 million), Freddie Mac ($260.1 million / $1,044 million). Total common stocks: cost $5,745.1 million, market $22,000.3 million.
- Five of the six top positions were left untouched in 1995, which he calls "Rip Van Winkle mode." The exception was American Express, where Berkshire raised its stake to about 10%.
- Disney: he first became interested in 1966, when its market value was under $90 million against about $21 million pre-tax earnings in 1965 and more cash than debt, "a company selling at only five times rides" (Pirates of the Caribbean cost $17 million). Buffett Partnership bought at a split-adjusted 31 cents per share and he sold in 1967 at 48 cents; the stock was $66 in 1996.
- Cap Cities/ABC: the Disney deal let holders swap for one Disney share plus $65 per Cap Cities share, with options for all stock or all cash. Berkshire sought stock. He had sold one-third of the Cap Cities holding two years earlier for $635 million versus the $1.27 billion those shares would bring in the merger.
- Capital Cities CEO Tom Murphy: "as fine an executive as I have ever seen." He cites Murphy's favoring owners when personal interests diverged and says he likes managers "whom I would love to have as a sibling, in-law, or trustee of my will." His advice: "If Murph should elect to run another business, don't bother to study its value - just buy the stock."
- The Disney-Cap Cities deal began with a chance meeting with Michael Eisner in Sun Valley on July 14, 1995, which Warren says is the deal's timing, not its logic: a deal that "makes so much sense" would likely have happened anyway.

chunks.heading: Operating-business trends, honest reporting, and the B-share recapitalization
chunks.text:
- Charlie's dictum: "Just tell me the bad news; the good news will take care of itself." Warren applies it by reporting three declining businesses:
  - Shoes: a cyclical downturn, not a secular one; competitors earned marginal profits or worse, so Berkshire's relative position held or widened.
  - Buffalo News: still strong, but newspapers have "lost still another notch" from their once bullet-proof franchise and he expects gradual erosion over time.
  - World Book: facing CD-ROM and on-line competition; profitable but trending the wrong way, so it changed distribution, expanded electronic products and cut overhead.
- 1995 earnings: operating earnings $814.7 million pre-tax ($600.2 million after tax); total earnings across all entities $1,008.8 million pre-tax ($725.2 million after tax). Headquarters staff grew only from 11 to 12 despite 11,000+ new employees from three acquisitions.
- Recapitalization: Class A common remains; a new Class B has 1/30th of an A share's economic rights, 1/200th of the vote, no participation in the shareholder-designated charity program, and no conversion back to A. At least $100 million of B shares were to be offered for cash.
- Purpose: to make expense-laden "clone" unit trusts holding only Berkshire stock unmerchandisable. Warren fears brokers selling them to unsophisticated buyers drawn by Berkshire's record and publicity, a recipe for disappointed investors.
- Valuation candor: at $36,000 per share and a $43 billion market cap, "Berkshire is selling at a price at which Charlie and I would not consider buying it." He adds that over the past five years the stock "outperformed the business" and warns that this cannot persist.
- Shareholder philosophy: he wants shareholders of any size who are knowledgeable, share the long-term perspective and understand the limits imposed by a large capital base. He would ideally want the market price to track intrinsic value precisely, so every owner benefits in proportion to the business's progress.
- Tripling a $1,000 stake would require turning $43 billion into $129 billion (roughly General Electric's market cap), which Berkshire cannot come close to doing.
- Communication: Berkshire has no investor relations department and does not use analysts to disseminate "guidance." The annual meeting is its direct owner communication channel, and 1995's drew about 3,200 in the main room plus overflow, with Warren and Charlie answering questions for around five hours.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1996 letter reviews 36.1% net worth growth and explains intrinsic value, float cost, super-cat insurance discipline, and incentive pay. It also sets out his investing philosophy: own "Inevitables" with durable moats, stay inactive, avoid change, and admit mistakes like USAir.

chunks.heading: Scale, float and the "free money" engine
chunks.text:
- Warren reports a 1996 net worth gain of $6.2 billion (36.1%). Per-share book value grew 31.8%, and has compounded from $19 to $19,011 over 32 years, or 23.8% a year.
- He says book value only roughly tracks progress: "what counts at Berkshire is intrinsic value, not book value."
- He tracks two value indices per share. Investments (including cash) went from $4 in 1965 to $22,088 in 1995 and $28,500 in 1996. Pre-tax operating earnings excluding all investment income went from $4.08 to $258.20 in 1995 and $421.39 in 1996.
- Growth in those indices was 29.0% and 63.2% in 1996.
- He warns the past growth rates "cannot be matched nor even approached." Fewer than ten American businesses have more equity capital, and "an abundance of funds tends to dampen returns."

chunks.heading: Float, super-cat insurance and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
**Float**
- Float is "money we hold but don't own." Premiums arrive before losses are paid.
- An underwriting loss is the cost of float. The insurance business has value only if its cost of float is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds. Otherwise it is "an albatross."
- Berkshire's float grew from $17.3 million in 1967 to $6,702 million in 1996, a 22.3% compound rate. Its cost of float was below zero in more years than not, so Berkshire was in effect "paid for holding money."
- Float is a major part of intrinsic value that book value does not show.

**Super-cat**
- Berkshire sells mega-catastrophe cover to insurers and reinsurers. In 1996 it wrote an Allstate Florida hurricane contract. It also wrote a California Earthquake Authority layer of about $1 billion, effective April 1, 1997 and triggered if the Authority's aggregate losses exceed about $5 billion by March 31, 2001.
- Warren estimates the after-tax worst-case loss at probably no more than $600 million, under 3% of book value and 1.5% of market value.
- The business will have a "truly terrible year": "not a possibility - it's a certainty. The only question is when it will come."
- He prices so that about 90% of premiums are eventually paid out in losses and expenses.
- He distrusts computer models: "the precision they project is a chimera." Models can lull decision-makers into false security. He cites portfolio insurance in 1987.
- You do not need precision to underwrite sensibly: "you need not know a man's precise age to know that he is old enough to vote." He adds that in insurance "virtually all surprises are unpleasant."
- Berkshire's three advantages in super-cat:
  - Buyers know it will pay in the worst case. Berkshire never lays off risk, partly because it doubts it could collect from others.
  - After a mega-cat, long-standing clients get first call on its capacity. Reinsurers already pay stand-by fees to lock that in.
  - It offers dollar coverage sizes no one else matches, from a single phone call.
- Ajit Jain runs it. Warren says he has made "all too many" bad reinsurance deals himself, as in the 1970s.

**Volatility**
- "Charlie and I would much rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%."
- He wants shareholders who can tolerate volatility. If a crash would make you panic-sell, you should not own stocks or Berkshire.
- He quotes Robert Woodruff of Coca-Cola on when to sell Coke: "I don't know. I've never sold any."
- He says "Selling fine businesses on 'scary' news is usually a bad decision."

**Reverse engineering**
- He quotes Charlie Munger: "All I want to know is where I'm going to die so I'll never go there."
- If a consequence cannot be tolerated, even a remote one, Berkshire avoids planting its seeds. That is why it does not borrow big amounts and caps super-cat losses at a level that will not dent intrinsic value.

chunks.heading: GEICO: low cost, a moat, and focused incentives
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought the 49% of GEICO it did not own for $2.3 billion in 1996. Warren first liked the company in 1951, when the whole business was valued at $7 million.
- The flywheel is low cost, then low prices, then good policyholders, then referrals. GEICO gets more than one million referrals a year, producing over half of new business, which cuts acquisition costs further.
- Voluntary auto policies grew 10% in 1996. The previous best year in 20 had been 8%, achieved once.
- The goal is to widen the price advantage over customers, not the profit margin. Scale and higher penetration should widen "the protective moat surrounding our economic castle."
- Bonuses for dozens of top executives, starting with Tony Nicely, rest on only two variables:
  - growth in voluntary auto policies;
  - underwriting profit on seasoned auto business (policies on the books more than a year).
- The profit-sharing plan uses the same two yardsticks. In 1996 it paid a record 16.9% ($40 million), against a prior five-year average under 10%. The plan went "off the chart" and Warren's fix was: "Enlarge the chart." He adds: "we never greet good work by raising the bar."
- Warren's incentive principles:
  - goals tailored to the specific business's economics;
  - simple, easily measured goals;
  - goals directly tied to participants' daily activities.
- He shuns "lottery ticket" pay such as Berkshire options, whose value is outside the manager's control.
- Lou Simpson's investment pay is tied to four-year investment results, not to underwriting or company-wide results. Warren calls it foolish to let great work on one side be cancelled by bad work on the other. In 1996 Lou's equities beat the S&P 500 by 6.2 points.
- Smaller primary units had combined ratios well under 100:
  - National Indemnity traditional business: 74.2 (3-year average 83.0).
  - Homestate: 87.1 (3-year 83.2).

chunks.heading: Buying businesses: the 1996 acquisitions and how deals arrive
chunks.text:
- Warren seeks "excellent business economics and an outstanding manager."
- Kansas Bankers Surety cost $75 million, placed with 80%-owned Wesco. It came from a chance remark at a birthday party on January 26. Warren got the financials on February 12 and bid $75 million on February 13. He says he treasures managers like Don Towle who think of the company as "his."
- FlightSafety International cost about $1.5 billion. It trains pilots at 41 locations with 175 simulators, which can cost as much as $19 million each. About half of revenue is corporate pilot training. It was suggested by a Berkshire shareholder, and Warren says that in "about 60 seconds" he knew Al Ueltschi was his kind of manager.
- The consideration was about 51% cash, 41% Class A and 8% Class B. The structure encouraged tax-indifferent holders to take cash, to limit new Berkshire shares.
- Warren keeps managers past 70, saying "We never fool with success." He says "It's difficult to teach a new dog old tricks."
- He invites owners of large businesses with good economics to call. His requirements are on page 21 of the report.

chunks.heading: Investing philosophy: inactivity, Inevitables and the circle of competence
chunks.text:
**Inactivity**
- "We continue to make more money when snoring than when active."
- Buying stocks is the same art as acquiring subsidiaries: buy at a sensible price a business with excellent economics and able, honest management, then monitor whether those qualities persist.
- Concentration is a natural result. He compares it to owning 20% of the future earnings of several college basketball stars. Selling winners because they dominate the portfolio would be like the Bulls trading Michael Jordan.

**Predictability**
- He favors businesses unlikely to change much, seeking operations "virtually certain to possess enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now." In fermenting industries, "we applaud the endeavor but prefer to skip the ride."
- See's candy: the reasons people buy boxed chocolates, and from See's, are unchanged since the 1920s.
- Coca-Cola: he read the 1896 annual report. Sales that year were $148,000. Syrup sales were 116,492 gallons, against about 3.2 billion gallons in 1996.
- He calls Coke and Gillette "The Inevitables." Dominance is near-certain for an investment lifetime, and he would rather "be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one."
- He warns that for every Inevitable there are dozens of "Impostors." General Motors, IBM and Sears all once looked invincible.
- He adds "Highly Probables" because they can find so few Inevitables.

**Risks to a great holding**
- Overpayment: in 1996 he says the risk "may now be quite high" for nearly all stocks, Inevitables included. Even an outstanding company may take years to catch up with a price paid in an overheated market.
- Loss of focus: management buying so-so businesses (Coke once grew shrimp, Gillette once explored for oil) or boredom and hubris that lets attention wander.

**Advice for your own portfolio**
- Most investors should hold a low-fee index fund, which will beat most professionals after fees.
- Costs matter. Equity mutual fund expenses of about 100 basis points can cut investor returns by 10% or more over time.
- Intelligent investing "is not complex, though that is far from saying that it is easy." You need to evaluate selected businesses inside your circle of competence: "The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."
- You do not need beta, efficient markets, modern portfolio theory, option pricing or emerging markets. Business schools need only two courses: How to Value a Business, and How to Think About Market Prices.
- The goal is to buy, at a rational price, part of an understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher in five, ten and twenty years. Buy a meaningful amount when you find one.
- "If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes."
- Portfolio value follows aggregate earnings upward over time.

chunks.heading: Look-through earnings and retained earnings
chunks.text:
- Reported earnings understate economic progress. Berkshire books only dividends from investees, but their undistributed earnings are worth more to Berkshire because investees can reinvest at high rates.
- Look-through earnings equal operating earnings, plus Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings, less a hypothetical tax on those. The tax rate used is 14%, the rate Berkshire pays on dividends.
- 1996 look-through earnings were about $1,522 million: reported operating earnings of $954 million, plus $661 million of undistributed investee earnings, less $93 million of hypothetical tax. Warren says the figures are approximate, built on judgment calls.
- Largest undistributed earnings shares:
  - Coca-Cola: $180 million, 8.1% owned.
  - American Express: $132 million, 10.5% owned.
  - Wells Fargo: $84 million.
  - Freddie Mac: $77 million.
  - Gillette: $73 million.
- 12/31/96 market values:
  - Coca-Cola: 200 million shares, cost $1,298.9 million, market $10,525.0 million.
  - Gillette: 48 million shares, cost $600 million, market $3,732 million.
  - American Express: cost $1,392.7 million, market $2,794.3 million.
  - Total common stocks: cost $7,910.2 million, market $27,750.6 million.
- Berkshire's own reporting shows purchase-accounting adjustments separately, to show business earnings as if never purchased. He says this is more useful to investors and managers than GAAP. He wants to give shareholders the financial information "that we would wish you to give us if our positions were reversed."

chunks.heading: Mistakes, fairness and alignment with owners
chunks.text:
**USAir**
- In 1989 he invested $358 million in a 9.25% USAir preferred, beguiled by its history of profits and by the apparent protection of a senior security.
- He admits his analysis was "superficial and wrong." The company's revenues faced deregulated, fierce competition while its costs were a holdover from regulated days. USAir lost $2.4 billion in 1990-1994.
- Berkshire wrote the position down 75% to $89.5 million. He tried to sell at half of face value, and again in 1996 for about $335 million, and failed both times. He calls that lucky.
- The saving feature was a penalty-dividend clause: unpaid dividends accrued at prime plus five points, compounding at 13.25% to 14%. USAir paid $47.9 million in the second half of 1996.
- The preferred was then probably worth par, and Berkshire had collected $240.5 million in dividends over the years.
- Quips: "If history supplied all of the answers, the Forbes 400 would consist of librarians." And on airlines: "Start as a billionaire and then buy an airline."

**Price versus value and fairness**
- When a stock over- or underperforms the business, buyers or sellers get "outsized benefits at the expense of those they trade with." He wants market price and intrinsic value kept roughly in sync, as fairness in a family partnership would require.
- Over time shareholders' gains must match the company's business gains.
- He wants long-term owners. Berkshire probably ranks first among large US companies in the share held by long-term owners.
- In 1996 intrinsic value rose sharply, largely from GEICO, while the share price was flat. He says price versus value was then "more appropriate."

**Class B shares**
- In May 1996 he sold 517,500 Class B shares for $565 million net. Each is 1/30 of a Class A.
- The goal was to head off unit trusts marketed as Berkshire look-alikes. They would have used a non-repeatable record to lure small investors, charged high fees and driven a speculative bubble.
- He built the offering to deter flippers: a 1.5% commission, the lowest he had seen, and an open-ended size. About 40,000 shareholders were added. Salomon earned perhaps a tenth of what a standard deal would have paid, yet he was glad to pay it.
- He says he is happy to pay fees "commensurate with performance."

**Costs and owner orientation**
- Headquarters expense is under two basis points of net worth.
- "We are here to make money with you, not off you."
- He keeps the shareholder-designated contributions program: 97.2% of eligible shares participated, and $13.3 million went to 3,910 charities. He counts it as a shareholder benefit, not an expense.
- Berkshire paid $860 million in income taxes in 1996. He calls large tax payments "entirely fitting" because "Berkshire prospers in America as it would nowhere else."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why Berkshire's 34.1% gain was merely a "quack" in a bull market, how size erodes returns, and why savers should welcome falling prices. He details insurance float economics, super-cat discipline, GEICO's low-cost model, and confesses that stock-funded mergers have cost shareholders money.

chunks.heading: Performance is measured against the S&P, not in absolute terms
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's 1997 net worth gain was $8.0 billion, a 34.1% rise in per-share book value. Over 33 years, book value per share grew from $19 to $25,488, a 24.1% compounded annual rate.
- Warren refuses to call 34.1% a triumph in a bull market. His analogy is the "preening duck that quacks boastfully after a torrential rainstorm"; a right-thinking duck compares itself to the other ducks on the pond.
- The passive S&P Index nearly matched Berkshire in 1997. His verdict: "Quack."
- Berkshire is at a structural disadvantage in booms. The Index and mutual funds bear no tax cost, while Berkshire paid or accrued $4.2 billion of federal income tax in 1997, about 18% of beginning net worth.
- The yardstick is a modest advantage over the Index over time, not every year. He rejects the Cubs-fan attitude: "Everyone has a bad century now and then."
- What counts is per-share intrinsic business value, not book value. The two usually move roughly in tandem.

chunks.heading: Size erodes returns: "We weren't smarter then, just smaller"
chunks.text:
- In 1951, in Ben Graham's class at Columbia, an idea giving a $10,000 gain improved his yearly performance by 100 percentage points. In 1997, an idea producing $500 million of pre-tax profit adds one percentage point to Berkshire's performance.
- His 1950s annual results beat any later decade by nearly thirty percentage points. "We weren't smarter then, just smaller." Charlie Munger's experience was similar.
- "For anyone deploying capital, nothing recedes like success." Any performance superiority at Berkshire's size will be minor.
- Berkshire's offsets are its businesses' long-term prospects and managers who are wealthy and "motivated by the joy of accomplishment, not by fame or fortune."

chunks.heading: Waiting for the fat pitch (Ted Williams discipline)
chunks.text:
- Prices were high for both businesses and stocks, so fresh money earns little in prospective earnings. He has no view on whether prices will fall.
- Ted Williams, in The Science of Hitting, split the strike zone into 77 cells. Swinging only at his best cell meant batting .400; reaching for the worst cell (low outside corner) meant .230.
- The business pitches Warren sees in 1997 are "just catching the lower outside corner." Swinging locks Berkshire into low returns.
- The catch: letting them all go gives no assurance that better ones come. Perhaps past low prices were the aberration. He adds that standing with the bat on his shoulder "is not my idea of fun."
- Default use of new money when the favorite commitment is unavailable ("a well-run and sensibly-priced business with fine economics"): very short-term, highest-quality instruments.

chunks.heading: Unconventional, non-business commitments and their risk
chunks.text:
At yearend 1997 Berkshire held three non-traditional positions. Warren says these carry no certainty of profit, unlike a wonderful business bought at a good price, where "we are going to make money -- the only question being when." With alternatives, "we think that we are going to make money" and will sometimes realize substantial losses.

- **Oil derivatives:** contracts for 14.0 million barrels remained of a 45.7 million barrel position set up in 1994-95. Contracts for 31.7 million barrels settled in 1995-97 for a pre-tax gain of about $61.9 million. Unrealized gain was $11.6 million. Oil had seemed "modestly underpriced" at purchase; he now has no opinion.
- **Silver:** 111.2 million ounces bought, with a 1997 pre-tax gain of $97.4 million. Bullion inventories had fallen and he and Charlie concluded a higher price was needed to balance supply and demand. Inflation expectations play no part in the valuation. He had bought silver 30 years earlier, expecting US demonetization.
- **Zero-coupon Treasuries:** $4.6 billion at amortized cost, with a $598.8 million unrealized pre-tax gain. Zeros move sharply with rates: losses if rates rise, outsized gains if they fall.
- On the macro bet: "you pay Charlie and me to use our best judgment -- not to avoid embarrassment." Skin in the game: the Munger family has over 90% of its net worth in Berkshire and the Buffetts over 99%.

chunks.heading: Savers should want lower prices (market fluctuations)
chunks.text:
- The hamburger test: if you will buy beef or cars for life and don't produce them, you want lower prices. Likewise, a net saver in stocks should want lower stock prices. "Only those who will be sellers of equities in the near future should be happy at seeing stocks rise."
- Berkshire shareholders are automatic savers because Berkshire retains all earnings and uses them to buy businesses and securities. The cheaper the buys, the better.
- Investees that repurchase shares benefit more when prices are low. Repurchases by Coca-Cola, The Washington Post and Wells Fargo at very low past prices helped Berkshire far more than today's repurchases at loftier prices.
- About 97% of Berkshire shares are held at yearend by the same investors who held them at the start, so they are savers.
- Reframe the headline "Investors lose as market falls" as "Disinvestors lose... but investors gain." There is a buyer for every seller. Low prices in the 1970s and 1980s rewarded permanent holders; few such opportunities appeared in recent years.

chunks.heading: Valuing the stock market and Graham's margin of safety
chunks.text:
- He does not predict the market but values it roughly. At the 1996 annual meeting (Dow 7,071, long-term Treasuries at 6.89%), he and Charlie said the market was not overvalued if (1) interest rates stayed put or fell and (2) American business kept earning its high returns on equity. Rates fell and ROE stayed high.
- Returns on equity are "not a sure thing to remain at, or even near, their present levels."
- His 1979 Forbes article: "You pay a very high price in the stock market for a cheery consensus." In 1979 skepticism prevailed and pessimism drove prices to attractive levels. In 1997 there is a "very cheery consensus."
- Lower rates make each dollar of earnings more valuable, but price levels "have materially eroded the 'margin of safety' that Ben Graham identified as the cornerstone of intelligent investing."
- Look-through earnings are his better measure of economic progress. They equal reported operating earnings, plus Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings, less a hypothetical tax (14%, the rate Berkshire pays on dividends). 1997: $1,292 million reported plus $743 million undistributed investee earnings, less $105 million tax, totals $1,930 million.
- He prefers investees retaining earnings because they can often reinvest at high returns. Coca-Cola ($216M), American Express ($161M) and Wells Fargo ($103M) were the largest contributors to undistributed earnings.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and its cost
chunks.text:
- Float is "money we hold but don't own." Premiums arrive before losses are paid, sometimes years later, and the insurer invests the money.
- The cost of float is the underwriting loss. An insurance business is valuable if its cost of float is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds, and "a lemon" if above market rates.
- Berkshire's float formula: net loss reserves, loss adjustment reserves, funds held under reinsurance assumed and unearned premium reserves, minus agents' balances, prepaid acquisition costs, prepaid taxes and deferred charges on assumed reinsurance.
- Float grew from $17.3 million (1967) to $7,093.1 million (1997), a 21.7% compound rate. Underwriting profits in each of the last five years (1993-97) made the cost of float negative: "we have been paid for holding money."
- Accounting irony: float is a balance sheet liability, yet worth more to Berkshire than an equal amount of net worth.
- Reserve estimation gives insurers "enormous latitude," so outsiders struggle to know true float cost. Errors can be huge, and "virtually all surprises in insurance are unpleasant ones." Berkshire reports conservatively.
- Warren says understanding float is necessary to judge Berkshire's intrinsic value. Float was expected to dip in Q1 1998 as large contracts expired.

chunks.heading: Super-cat insurance and catastrophe-bond mispricing
chunks.text:
- Super-cat policies are bought by insurers and reinsurers to limit mega-catastrophe losses. It is the most volatile insurance line. Most years show large profits with an occasional huge loss: "a truly terrible year in the super-cat business is not a possibility -- it's a certainty. The only question is when."
- 1997 was lucky (no huge insured catastrophes), so premiums dropped to the bottom line. Super-cat underwriting earned $283.0 million pre-tax.
- Warren criticizes "catastrophe bonds" sold to "innocents" who rely on salespeople. A true bond obliges the issuer to pay; these lay a provisional promise to pay on the purchaser. The label is meant to dodge insurance licensing laws and to make buyers assume less risk.
- Dice example: a 1-in-36 chance of a 12, with a $50 million payout against a $1 million annual premium, is underpriced. There is a 75.4% chance of going a decade without paying, so it looks like easy money until you go broke.
- Catastrophe odds are fuzzy and hired "experts" are paid up front regardless of accuracy. "an expert can invariably be found" to say 1 in 100 instead of 1 in 36, and he probably believes it, which makes him "less reprehensible -- but more dangerous."
- Inflows from such investors hurt pricing, so Berkshire wrote less in 1998. Its worst-case after-tax loss was about $600 million (the California Earthquake Authority policy maximum), around 1% of market value. Warren would take more exposure at appropriate prices.
- Ajit Jain built the business from scratch and has "the discipline to walk away from business that is inadequately priced."

chunks.heading: GEICO: low cost, shared gains and incentives that fit
chunks.text:
- CEO Tony Nicely lifted voluntary auto policy growth from 10% in 1996 to 16% in 1997. New voluntary auto policies rose from 617,669 (1996) to 913,176 (1997); policies in force reached 2,949,439.
- Underwriting profit was 8.1% of premiums, above the 4% target. GEICO deliberately cut average rates to pass low-cost benefits to customers.
- Warren welcomes tougher industry competition, since "a tough market helps the low-cost operator." Marketing spend for 1998 was set above $100 million, up 50%, against a 3% market share in a roughly $115 billion industry.
- Compensation: GEICO's 10,500 associates got a 26.9% profit-sharing contribution ($71 million), driven by two variables, policy growth and profitability of seasoned business (policies over a year old, past acquisition-cost losses). Executive cash bonuses used the same variables.
- "We distribute merit badges, not lottery tickets": no Berkshire subsidiary ties pay to Berkshire's stock price, which employees cannot meaningfully affect. Bonuses track each unit's own business performance.
- Lorimer Davidson, then at GEICO, spent a Saturday in early 1951 teaching a 20-year-old stranger about GEICO and insurance, shaping Warren's whole understanding of the field.
- Other primary units posted a combined 15.0% underwriting profit (National Indemnity traditional business 32.9%).

chunks.heading: Acquisitions: criteria, referrals and why not to issue stock
chunks.text:
- Criteria for Star Furniture and International Dairy Queen: "understandable; possess excellent economics; and are run by outstanding people."
- Sourcing trick: after buying into an industry, he asks new partners, "Are there any more at home like you?" The Blumkins (Nebraska Furniture Mart) named three furniture retailers, leading to R.C. Willey and Star Furniture years later.
- Star was agreed in a single two-hour meeting with Melvyn Wolff, with no need to check leases or employment contracts: "I knew I was dealing with a man of integrity and that's what counted." Wolff and his sister funded special payments to all employees from their own proceeds.
- International Dairy Queen (5,792 stores in 23 countries) deal: sellers could pick cash or Berkshire stock of slightly lower value, tilting them toward cash. Only 45% of shares chose cash.
- The confession: in stock-only mergers, Berkshire shareholders are "slightly worse off" than if he hadn't done them: "when I've issued stock, I've cost you money." Issuing shares dilutes ownership of every wonderful business Berkshire already owns.
- Baseball analogy: it's a bad trade to give up a .380 hitter to get a .350 hitter. Berkshire's roster is full of .380 hitters, so it is "almost impossible for us to 'trade up.'" Cash deals (National Indemnity, See's, Buffalo News, Scott Fetzer, GEICO) did far better.
- A takeover premium only makes sense if (a) the acquirer's stock is overvalued relative to the target's or (b) the combination earns more than the two apart. Synergies are usually unrealistic and costs are often "illusory"; serial share-issuers tacitly concede overvaluation. When a CEO wants a foolish deal, staff and advisors will produce supporting projections: "Only in fairy tales are emperors told that they are naked."
- On options: when buying an option-issuing company, Berkshire replaces options with equivalent cash compensation so the true cost hits earnings. He calls the standard accounting that ignores option cost "dead wrong."

chunks.heading: Operating subsidiaries and capital allocation within Berkshire
chunks.text:
- Operating pre-tax earnings per share grew from $1.09 (1967) to $717.82 (1997), 24.2% a year. Pre-tax operating earnings rose from $1 million to $888 million.
- Subsidiaries like Buffalo News, See's and Scott Fetzer pay 100% of earnings to Berkshire, while public peers retain two-thirds or more. Berkshire redeploys the cash elsewhere. These three alone paid $1.8 billion, so their records understate their contribution.
- Warren wants executives he likes, trusts and admires. The US Airways and Salomon episodes show it: he calls his US Airways record "unblemished by success", saying he was wrong to buy and wrong to try repeatedly to sell at 50 cents on the dollar. The recovery coincided with Stephen Wolf becoming CEO and with Warren and Charlie leaving the board. US Airways stock rose from $4 to $73.
- Convertible preferred outcomes: Gillette $600 million became $4.8 billion; First Empire $40 million became $236 million.
- Roberto Goizueta at Coca-Cola: Warren calls the 100+ letters from him "a guidebook for success in both business and life." Roberto relabeled Warren's "focus" for his own "obsession." Goizueta prepared Doug Ivester's succession long before it seemed necessary.
- Amex: on the verge of selling at the Perc conversion in 1994, he was persuaded by Hertz CEO Frank Olson on a golf course that the corporate card was a terrific franchise. Berkshire turned buyer, ending with 10% and a $3 billion gain. He credits "110% luck, the balance skill."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 1998 letter separates book value from intrinsic value, explains how to judge insurance float, and describes how Berkshire lets managers run businesses like owners. He also attacks stock-option expensing and restructuring-charge games, admits his McDonald's sale was a mistake, and warns that Berkshire's size will cap future returns.

chunks.heading: Why book value overstated 1998 progress
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's net worth rose $25.9 billion in 1998, lifting per-share book value 48.3%. Over 34 years it grew from $19 to $37,801, or 24.7% compounded annually.
- Most of the 1998 gain came from issuing shares in acquisitions. Berkshire stock sells at a large premium to book value, so issuing shares for cash or in a merger instantly raises per-share book value without any earnings.
- Intrinsic value does not rise in these deals, because what Berkshire gives and gets is roughly equal. Warren and Charlie Munger stress that "it's the per-share gain in intrinsic value that counts rather than the per-share gain in book value."
- Intrinsic value still far exceeds book value.
- He tracks two components of value: per-share investments (including cash) and pre-tax operating earnings per share with all investment income excluded.
  - Investments per share: $53 (1968), $465 (1978), $4,876 (1988), $47,647 (1998), a 25.4% compound rate over 1968-1998.
  - Operating earnings per share: $2.87, $12.85, $145.77 and $474.45, an 18.6% compound rate over the same period.
  - Operating earnings per share fell 33.9% in 1998 on a pro-forma basis because of General Re's underwriting loss. Investments per share rose 25.2%.

chunks.heading: Size limits future returns; a 15% target
chunks.text:
- Warren says future gains "will fall far short of those achieved in the past" because the $57.4 billion net worth, the largest of any American corporation, is too large for outsized returns. Anyone who believes otherwise "should consider a career in sales but avoid one in mathematics."
- He and Charlie will try to raise intrinsic value at an average of 15% a year, "a result we consider to be at the very peak of possible outcomes." Some years will fall short, including negative years.
- Compounding 15% for five years means adding about $58 billion of net worth. That requires "big ideas: Popcorn stands just won't do," so they hunt "elephants" even though markets are unfriendly to the search.
- He promises to keep at least 99% of his net worth in Berkshire.
- Capital allocation is a waiting game. "In allocating capital, activity does not correlate with achievement," and frenetic behavior in investments and acquisitions is often counterproductive. He and Charlie "mainly just wait for the phone to ring."
- Berkshire held more than $15 billion in cash equivalents at yearend. "Cash never makes us happy," but it is better in Berkshire's pocket than someone else's, and he saw nothing on the horizon to buy.
- He admits his 1998 portfolio moves cut the year's gain. Selling McDonald's was "a very big mistake," and Berkshire "would have been better off" had he "snuck off to the movies during market hours."
- Berkshire does not comment on specific holdings, since discussing them would make the shares worth less. He warns that media speculation about its investment moves is usually wrong.

chunks.heading: How to evaluate an insurer: float and its cost
General Re: why Berkshire is a better home for a reinsurer
chunks.text:
- Berkshire completed the $22 billion acquisition on December 21, 1998. General Re owns General Reinsurance Corporation, the largest U.S. property-casualty reinsurer, and 82% of Cologne Re (including stock it has an arrangement to buy). Together they operate in 124 countries.
- Warren says Berkshire "can add absolutely nothing" to the managers' skills. He expects earnings a decade out to be materially higher than without the merger, because of the freedom Berkshire can offer.
- Reinsurers sell absorption of volatility, yet a public reinsurer is graded by owners and rating agencies on the smoothness of its own results. That pushes it to lay off business (retrocessions) or decline good business that adds volatility.
- Berkshire "happily accepts volatility" if it carries the expectation of higher profit. Its capital, "a Fort Knox," means lumpy earnings cannot hurt its credit ratings.
- "We prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%."
- Berkshire will manage General Re's investment portfolio but not Cologne Re's, and will not be involved in underwriting. He asks the company to keep its underwriting discipline while retaining more business, broadening products and expanding geographically, especially internationally.
- After the merger, General Re dropped about 250 stock positions, incurring $935 million of taxes. This reflects a principle: "We don't back into decisions."

chunks.heading: GEICO: spend on growth when each dollar buys more than a dollar of value
chunks.text:
- Warren's formula: "Combine a great idea with a great manager and you're certain to obtain a great result." The idea is low-cost direct auto insurance and the manager is Tony Nicely.
- Direct writing needs a large front-end investment and first-year business is unprofitable. Berkshire leaves that cost out of compensation so staff pursue new business aggressively.
  - 50% of bonuses and profit sharing is tied to earnings of the "seasoned" book (policies older than one year).
  - The other 50% is tied to growth in policyholders.
- Marketing spend rose from $33 million in 1995 to $143 million in 1998, and is at least $190 million planned for 1999. Telephone counselors grew from 652 to 2,162.
- The test: "We simply measure whether we are creating more than a dollar of value per dollar spent — and if that calculation is favorable, the more dollars we spend the happier I am." Companies focused on quarterly earnings would shy away from such spending.
- Results:
  - Voluntary auto policies in force rose from 2,949,439 (1997) to 3,562,644 (1998).
  - Profit margin was 6.7% in 1998, "better than we wished." Accident frequency and severity fell, so GEICO cut rates 3.3% and will cut more. The target margin is 4%, possibly lower.
  - Profit sharing was $103 million, or 32.3% of salary, for all 9,313 associates with over a year of service.
  - Market share rose from 3% to 3½%. About 40% of people who check rates save money. Shareholders get a special discount (usually 8%) in 40 states.
- Claims handling also counts. New York's Insurance Department found GEICO had the lowest complaint ratio of the five largest auto insurers, under half the average of the other four.

chunks.heading: Managing managers: "run it as if you own 100%"
chunks.text:
- Warren says telling outstanding CEOs how to run their companies "would be the height of foolishness." Most would not work for Berkshire with much backseat driving, and about 75% are independently wealthy.
- Berkshire removes the ritual of the CEO job. Managers control their own schedules, with no board meetings, press interviews, banker presentations, analyst calls, or concern with financing, credit ratings or "Street" earnings expectations.
- The simple mission is to run the business as if:
  1. you own 100% of it;
  2. it is the only asset you and your family will ever have;
  3. you can't sell or merge it for at least a century.
- Managers should not let accounting considerations affect decisions. "We want our managers to think about what counts, not how it will be counted."
- This works because Berkshire's shareholders have the longest horizon in the public-company universe. A majority of shares are held by people who expect to die still holding them.
- Current results still matter, but not at the expense of building competitive strengths.
- Managers are motivated mainly by a vision of how far their business can go, not just pay. Example: Scott Fetzer earned a record $96.5 million after tax on $112 million of net worth with no leverage beyond a conservative finance-subsidiary debt.
- Corporate overhead is tiny: 12.8 people at headquarters, and about $3.5 million after-tax, under one basis point of assets managed.

chunks.heading: Executive Jet (NetJets): buying a franchise from a founder-operator
chunks.text:
- Executive Jet Aviation sells fractional shares of jets and operates the fleet. Rich Santulli created the industry in 1986.
- An owner buys a fraction, say 1/8, which entitles them to 100 flying hours a year (averaged over five years), and pays a monthly management fee plus a fee per hour flown. A plane is available on a few hours' notice at 5,500 U.S. airports.
- Warren became a customer first. Frank Rooney, manager of H.H. Brown, recommended it, and Rich sold him a quarter of a Hawker 1000 (200 hours) in about 15 minutes. His family flew 900 hours on 300 trips and loved it, and he did a testimonial ad before there was any thought of buying the company. Rich called last May and they made a $725 million deal, half cash and half stock.
- The business has over 1,000 customers and 163 aircraft, including 23 "core" aircraft EJA owns or leases to guarantee service at peak demand. About 650 pilots train twice a year at FlightSafety International, another Berkshire company. In 1997 EJA took 31% of all corporate jets ordered worldwide.
- Competitive advantages:
  - Scale: planes positioned throughout the country improve service and cut dead-head costs.
  - Brand neutrality: it offers planes from Boeing, Gulfstream, Falcon, Cessna and Raytheon, while its two competitors are owned by manufacturers and sell only their own. Warren compares it to a physician who can recommend any medicine.
- Whole-plane ownership only makes sense at 350-400 hours a year, so Warren and Rich believe fractional ownership's potential "has barely been scratched."
- He sold the Berkshire plane and now flies on NetJets for business and personal trips.

chunks.heading: Accounting honesty: options, restructurings and merger games
chunks.text:
- Options: existing rules ignore the cost of stock options in earnings. Warren calls that treatment "outrageous." Paying GEICO's $190 million ad bill in ten-year at-the-market options would plainly be a cost.
  - Options "if properly structured" can be a fine way to motivate managers but are usually "wildly capricious" in rewards, inefficient motivators and "inordinately expensive for shareholders."
  - When evaluating an option-issuing company, he and Charlie subtract what the company could have realized by selling options of like quantity and structure. This often cuts reported per-share earnings 5%, sometimes 10%, and has changed portfolio decisions.
  - He rebuts the usual objections: employee options are sometimes repriced (raising cost), and non-transferability lowers value to the employee but not cost to the employer, like a restricted company car.
  - For General Re, Berkshire replaced the stock option plan with a cash plan tied to operating results. The economics match, but the pro-forma showed $63 million more compensation expense.
  - His unanswered questions: "If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it? And, if expenses shouldn't go into the calculation of earnings, where in the world should they go?"
- Restructuring charges: costs that belong to many years get dumped into one bad quarter, so Wall Street ignores it and later results beat expectations. He illustrates with golf scores of 140, 80, 80, 80, 80 instead of 91, 94, 89, 94, 92.
  - Special charges in 1998 totaled $72.1 billion across 1,369 items, versus $324 billion of 1997 earnings for the Fortune 500.
- Merger accounting: acquirers sometimes raise loss reserves at deal time to release them as "earnings" later. Berkshire leaves acquired reserves exactly as found. "If we are to disappoint you, we would rather it be with our earnings than with our accounting."
- He disagrees with the premise that a CEO's job is always to maximize the stock price, and says "bad accounting drives out good."
- He praises SEC chairman Arthur Levitt's campaign against "earnings management."
- Disclosure: Berkshire aims to give owners the information it would want in their position and to release it to everyone at once. It treats a B-share holder as equal to a large institution and refuses "earnings guidance," pointing to public documents.

chunks.heading: Taxes and Berkshire's tax position
chunks.text:
- Berkshire and General Re owed $2.7 billion of federal income tax on 1998 earnings. Warren says Berkshire has prospered in America "as we would have in no other country," and is glad to write large checks rather than receive them.
- Capital gains get no special treatment for a corporation. It pays 35%, which is 75% higher than an individual pays on the same long-term gain.
- The dividends-received exclusion is 70% for most corporations but 59.5% for Berkshire's equity holdings, because almost all are in its insurance companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett owns a poor 1999 as the worst year of his tenure, then teaches how to value insurance float, why managers run Berkshire companies like family assets, how to think about goodwill and acquisitions, circle of competence on tech, and strict rules for share repurchases.

chunks.heading: Why 1999 was Warren's worst year, and what he blames
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's 1999 net worth gain was $358 million, or 0.5% per share, the worst absolute performance of his tenure and the worst relative to the S&P. Over 35 years per-share book value grew from $19 to $37,987, 24.0% compounded.
- He puts the blame on himself: "My 'one subject' is capital allocation, and my grade for 1999 most assuredly is a D."
- The cause was the equity portfolio. Several large investees lagged the market on disappointing operating results. He still likes the businesses but says a quick recovery is "no sure thing."
- Relative results are what concern him: "Over time, bad relative numbers will produce unsatisfactory absolute results."
- Stock and business can diverge. In 1998 the stock outperformed the business. In 1999 the business did much better than the stock. Over time the stock must roughly match the business.
- He and Charlie expect intrinsic value gains over the next decade to "modestly exceed" the S&P's. He backs this with over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire. He and his wife have never sold a share.
- Large superiority over the S&P is a thing of the past. Businesses and stocks were cheaper then, and the capital base was much smaller, allowing a wider range of opportunities.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value versus book value
chunks.text:
- Intrinsic value is "a key, though far from precise" measure used in buying businesses and stocks.
- He splits Berkshire into two parts: per-share investments (including cash) and pre-tax operating earnings per share with all investment income excluded.
  - Investments per share: $45 (1969), $577 (1979), $7,200 (1989), $47,339 (1999). Growth was 25.4% annually over 1969-1999.
  - Operating earnings per share excluding investment income: $4.39, $13.07, $108.86, then a 1999 loss of $(458.55), caused mainly by a huge General Re underwriting loss.
- Book value was $57.8 billion, which he says intrinsic value "far exceeds."
- The goodwill amortization charge (about $500 million a year) widens the gap between book and intrinsic value. This is accounting, unrelated to true economic goodwill, which "increases in most years."
- See's and Buffalo News are worth fifteen to twenty times their carrying values. The goal is to keep widening that spread at every subsidiary.
- Look-through earnings give a better picture than reported earnings. They are operating earnings, plus Berkshire's share of investees' retained operating earnings, less an allowance for tax (14% here).
  - 1999 figures: $707 million of undistributed investee earnings, minus $99 million hypothetical tax, plus $1,318 million reported operating earnings, for $1,926 million.
- He prefers investees retaining earnings when they can reinvest at high rates of return: "why should we want them paid out?"

chunks.heading: Managers: autonomy, no contracts, owner mentality
chunks.text:
- Many Berkshire managers are independently wealthy and work because they love their businesses. There are no contracts.
- There are no budgets to approve, no show-and-tell presentations and no capital expenditure dictums from Omaha. Managers are asked to run the company "as if these are the sole asset of their families and will remain so for the next century."
- Warren and Charlie treat managers the way they would want to be treated in their position.
- R. C. Willey example: Bill Child built the business from $250,000 of sales in 1954 to $342 million in 1999 while keeping stores closed on Sundays for religious reasons.
  - Warren was skeptical of taking a no-Sunday policy to Boise, but told Bill to follow his business judgment and convictions.
  - Bill insisted on buying the land and building the store himself (about $9 million). Berkshire would buy it at his cost if it succeeded, and owe him nothing if it failed.
  - The store succeeded. Berkshire paid Bill his cost, and he refused interest on the capital tied up for two years.
  - Warren says he has never heard of a manager at another public company behaving similarly.
- Chuck Huggins at See's: Berkshire paid $25 million in 1972 and the business has earned $857 million pre-tax since, with little additional capital. 1999 operating margin was a record 24%.

chunks.heading: How to evaluate an insurance company: float and its cost
chunks.text:
- Three determinants: (1) the amount of float, (2) its cost, and (3) "most critical of all," the long-term outlook for both.
- Float is "money we hold but don't own." Premiums arrive before losses are paid, sometimes years later, and the insurer invests the money.
- An underwriting loss is the cost of float. The business has value if cost of float is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds. It is "a lemon" if cost exceeds market rates.
- Caution: loss costs must be estimated, so insurers have "enormous latitude" in reporting results. Reserving errors, usually innocent but sometimes not, can be huge and flow straight into earnings. In 1999 several insurers made reserve adjustments that "made a mockery" of previously reported earnings.
- Berkshire float: $20 million (1967), $1,508 million (1987), $22,754 million (1998), $25,298 million (1999), with GEICO at $3,444 million, General Re $15,166 million, other reinsurance $6,285 million and other primary $403 million.
- In 1999 Berkshire had a $1.4 billion underwriting loss, a float cost of 5.8%. About $400 million of that loss came from business expected to deliver exceptional float for the next decade. Cumulative results through 1998 were an underwriting profit.
- Ajit Jain, super-cat reinsurance: he has the intelligence to rate risks, the realism to skip those he can't evaluate, the courage to write huge policies at an appropriate premium, and the discipline to reject even small risks when the premium is inadequate. His business holds $6.3 billion of float with an underwriting profit over his tenure. Warren notes it is volatile and Berkshire has benefited from good luck.
- General Re: 1999 business was badly underpriced. Incentive compensation at General Re and Cologne is now tied to float growth and cost of float, "the same variables that determine value for owners."
- The "other primary" insurers delivered a $192 million underwriting profit over five years.

chunks.heading: GEICO: spending on growth, compensation design, economics
chunks.text:
- GEICO policies in force rose from 2,011,055 (1993) to 4,328,900 (1999). New auto policies rose from 346,882 to 1,648,095. Tony Nicely was handed the keys in 1996 and asked to run it as if he owned 100%.
- Marketing spend: $33 million in 1995, $242 million in 1999, with $300-$350 million planned for 2000. Counselors grew from 652 to 2,631. Warren would "happily commit $1 billion annually" if the business could be handled smoothly and the last dollar produced new business at an attractive cost.
- Acquisition costs are rising: media rates up and diminishing returns on ads, partly offset by a better closure ratio. GEICO's renewal operating costs are the lowest among broad-based national auto insurers. Competitors "may copy our model, but they will be unable to replicate our economics."
- Customer value: each household sends about $1,100 a year. In 1999 GEICO added 766,256 customers and gained $590 million of cash from operating earnings and float growth. He notes "no Internet economics here." Market share rose from 2.7% to 4.1% in three years.
- Referrals are the best source of new business. He guesses about $50 million a year of advertising could hold the policy count, but advertising beyond that is an optional investment he considers "the best investment Berkshire can make."
- Compensation uses only two variables: percentage growth in policyholders and earnings on "seasoned" policies (more than one year old). New-business costs are excluded so associates aren't penalized for growth. 1999 profit sharing was 28.4% of salary ($113.3 million).
- Warren predicted auto insurer margins would fall about three percentage points in 2000. Rate increases are slow because of regulation and contract terms, and reserve releases from earlier overestimates have largely dried up.

chunks.heading: Aviation, furniture and how Berkshire finds acquisitions
chunks.text:
- FlightSafety: capital-intensive (a simulator can cost up to $15 million, with 222 owned). One trainee at a time per simulator, so operating margins must be high to earn a reasonable return. 1999 capex was $215 million.
- EJA (NetJets): customers own the aircraft, so modest pre-tax margins can still produce good returns on equity. Customers own over $2 billion of planes, with $4.2 billion on order. Recurring revenue rose 46%. Scale matters: "Buy a fraction, get a fleet." EJA sells planes from five suppliers, while its largest rivals are tied to manufacturers' own aircraft. About 65% of new owners come from referrals. Everyone, including Warren, pays the same price ("most favored nations").
- Warren's acquisition strategy is "simply to wait for the phone to ring," typically because a prior seller recommended Berkshire to a friend.
- He mocks auction "books" projecting earnings precisely for years while the authors won't forecast their own firm's next month. On Scott Fetzer, which a bank failed to sell in 1985, he wrote to CEO Ralph Schey and had a deal within a week. Charlie told the banker: "I'll pay $2.5 million not to read it."
- Furniture chain: Nebraska Furniture Mart (1983), R. C. Willey (1995), Star Furniture (1997), Jordan's (1999). Jordan's has the highest sales per square foot of any major US furniture operation. The Tatelmans paid employees 50¢ per hour worked, $9 million from their own pockets.
- MidAmerican Energy: about $2 billion for an 11% fixed-income security plus common and exchangeable preferred. This gives Berkshire just under 10% of the votes but about 76% of the equity, structured around the Public Utility Holding Company Act. Walter Scott and family invest about $280 million in cash alongside. Warren says more utility commitments, possibly large, may follow.
- Jordan's and MidAmerican were both bought for cash, issuing no Berkshire shares, which Warren and Charlie "vastly prefer."

chunks.heading: Acquisition accounting, goodwill and deal structure
chunks.text:
- Pooling versus purchase: managements like pooling because it avoids a goodwill account and its annual charge. Warren agrees with the FASB that most mergers are purchases ("ask employees severed from their jobs which company was the conqueror").
- He argues goodwill amortization is usually spurious because economic goodwill often grows. Depreciation and similar charges describe something that truly occurs. See's economic goodwill has grown for 78 years.
- His proposed rule: record the purchase at fair value, create the goodwill asset, don't amortize it, and write it down only if it becomes impaired. Apply it retroactively. He predicts managers would then choose cash or stock on real shareholder consequences, not reported earnings.
- Tax structure: Berkshire bought Jordan's assets for cash, so goodwill is tax-deductible over 15 years. This raises cash but lowers reported earnings. A stock purchase for cash gives no deduction.
- A stock-for-stock deal is the worst for the acquirer, often with no tax basis step-up. Berkshire has done some inefficient structures at sellers' insistence, but never to make its figures look better.

chunks.heading: Circle of competence, market valuation and buybacks
chunks.text:
- Berkshire owns no tech stocks. Warren and Charlie can't tell which firms have durable competitive advantage. Predicting long-term economics in fast-changing industries is beyond their perimeter. "If we have a strength, it is in recognizing when we are operating well within our circle of competence and when we are approaching the perimeter."
- If others claim predictive skill and the market validates it, "we neither envy nor emulate them."
- Price versus business: "If the choice is between a questionable business at a comfortable price or a comfortable business at a questionable price, we much prefer the latter. What really gets our attention, however, is a comfortable business at a comfortable price." In 1999 he felt better about the businesses than their stocks, so he didn't add.
- Market expectations: he never forecasts the market, but sees profits tracking GDP at about 3% real growth plus 2% inflation (the TIPS spread), so roughly 5%. Valuations are unlikely to climb much beyond that, so equity returns will be far below what investors expect. He expects a severe adjustment, especially in speculative sectors. "Fools give you reasons, wise men never try."
- Buyback conditions: repurchase only when (1) funds exceed the business's needs (maintenance and value-creating growth spending) and (2) the stock trades below conservatively calculated intrinsic value. Shareholders must also have the information to estimate that value.
- In the 1970s Warren looked for heavy repurchasers as a sign of undervaluation and shareholder-oriented management.
- Now buybacks are often to prop up the price. "Buying dollar bills for $1.10 is not good business for those who stick around."
- Repurchasing to offset option exercises is "buy high, sell low." Issuing and repurchasing decisions should each stand on their own.
- Math: repurchasing 2% of shares at a 25% discount to intrinsic value adds at most about ½% to per-share value.
- Berkshire will buy only below intrinsic value, never to stem a decline, and won't talk the stock up or down. A continuing holder should want the stock to fall and trade enough volume for Berkshire to buy a lot.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2000 letter explains why Berkshire prefers buying whole businesses to stocks, how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, and outlook), and the single value formula behind all investing. He also criticizes bubble speculation, earnings guidance, and corporate refusal to review failed decisions, while owning up to mistakes at GEICO and Dexter.

chunks.heading: Where the money comes from: businesses over stocks, and why
chunks.text:
- Warren says Berkshire would rather buy whole businesses than marketable stocks, and has said so since publishing its economic principles in 1983.
- Part of the reason is personal: he loves working with Berkshire's managers, who are "high-grade, talented and loyal," and finds their behavior "more rational and owner-oriented" than at many public companies.
- The bigger reason is tax. Owning 80% or more of a business is far more profitable, proportionately, than owning a minority stake.
- Wholly owned earnings of $1 million after tax:
  - Upstreamed dividends carry no tax.
  - Retained earnings add to the tax cost basis, so a later sale at $1 million above cost would bring no capital gains tax.
- A 10% stake in a business earning $10 million after tax, where Berkshire's $1 million share is taxed twice:
  - About $140,000 if distributed (a 14% rate on most dividends).
  - At least $350,000 if retained and later realized as a capital gain (usually about 35%, sometimes nearly 40%).
- His summary: the government is a "partner" twice on a stock investment but only once when Berkshire owns at least 80%.
- Warren said the equity portfolio looked only mildly attractive. Most holdings were "fully priced," with no "bargains," and he expected only moderate returns.
- The long-term outlook for equities in general was "far from exciting."
- Negotiated acquisitions were the most promising use of capital, but he said they "will at best provide us only reasonable returns." Really juicy results come only "when capital markets are severely constrained and the whole business world is pessimistic. We are 180 degrees from that point."

chunks.heading: Valuation: Aesop's bird in the hand, and why "growth vs. value" is a false split
chunks.text:
- Warren values every asset bought for financial gain with one formula, which he attributes to Aesop in about 600 B.C.: "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush."
- Three questions fill it in:
  - How certain are you that there are birds in the bush?
  - When will they emerge, and how many?
  - What is the risk-free rate? Berkshire uses the yield on long-term U.S. bonds.
- Answering these gives the maximum value of the bush and the maximum number of birds in hand worth offering for it. "Don't literally think birds. Think dollars."
- The formula applies to farms, oil royalties, bonds, stocks, lottery tickets and plants. The steam engine, electricity, the automobile and the Internet did not change it "one iota."
- Dividend yield, price-to-earnings, price-to-book and growth rates matter only as clues to the amount and timing of cash flows.
- Growth can destroy value if it needs early cash inputs larger than the discounted value of later cash.
- Warren calls "growth" and "value" styles contrasting approaches a display of ignorance: "Growth is simply a component... in the value equation."
- Precision is foolish. He works with a range of possibilities, and the range is often too wide to conclude anything.
- Occasionally even very conservative estimates show a price "startlingly low in relation to value." He jokes about this as the IBT, "Inefficient Bush Theory."
- An investor needs a general understanding of business economics and independent thinking, not "brilliance nor blinding insights."
- Berkshire keeps estimates conservative and sticks to industries where business surprises are unlikely to "wreak havoc on owners."
- He admits many mistakes, such as misjudging the future economics of "trading stamps, textiles, shoes and second-tier department stores."

chunks.heading: Speculation, the bubble and "value creation"
chunks.text:
- Where no one can form a conviction about the birds, as with new businesses and rapidly changing industries, any capital commitment "must be labeled speculative."
- Warren defines speculation as focusing "not on what an asset will produce but rather on what the next fellow will pay for it." It is "neither illegal, immoral nor un-American," but Berkshire does not play: "We bring nothing to the party, so why should we expect to take anything home?"
- The line between investing and speculation blurs when most participants have recently won. "Nothing sedates rationality like large doses of effortless money."
- His Cinderella image: everyone plans to leave "just seconds before midnight," but "they are dancing in a room in which the clocks have no hands."
- A December 1999 Paine Webber-Gallup survey had investors expecting 19% a year over the next decade. Warren called that irrational, since for American business as a whole "there couldn't possibly be enough birds in the 2009 bush."
- On "value creation": value is "destroyed, not created, by any business that loses money over its lifetime, no matter how high its interim valuation may get." What actually happens is wealth transfer, often on a massive scale.
- Promoters "merchandising birdless bushes" moved billions from the public to themselves. For many, an IPO rather than profits was the real goal, and the "business model" was "the old-fashioned chain letter," with investment bankers as "eager postmen."
- Two lessons for investors:
  - Many on Wall Street, "a community in which quality control is not prized," will sell investors anything they will buy.
  - Speculation "is most dangerous when it looks easiest."
- Berkshire does not try to pick the few winners from an ocean of unproven enterprises: "We're not smart enough to do that, and we know it."

chunks.heading: How Berkshire buys businesses
chunks.text:
- Warren's technique "is simplicity itself: We answer the phone." Owners and managers increasingly want to join Berkshire, and calls were coming more often.
- Cases from 2000:
  - CORT (rent-to-rent furniture): a stranger's fax on Nov 23, 1999 led to a meeting with the CEO on Nov 29. Warren saw the right ingredients: "a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price... that made sense." Wesco paid about $386 million in cash.
  - Ben Bridge Jeweler: bought by phone, half cash and half stock, on a recommendation from Barnett Helzberg, who had sold Helzberg Diamonds in 1995. Same-store sales rose 9%, 11%, 13%, 10%, 12%, 21% and 7% over seven years. The family feared a jewelry chain would arrive with "ideas about synergy and cost saving," so Warren told Ed and Jon Bridge they would stay in charge.
  - Justin Industries (boots and brick): bought for $570 million in cash. Acme Brick makes over a billion bricks a year at 22 plants, about 11.7% of national output. 75% of Texans name Acme as a brick brand, against 16% for the runner-up.
  - Shaw Industries: the largest carpet maker, about $4 billion in sales, with Berkshire owning 87.3%. Founders Bob Shaw and Julian Saul kept at least 5%.
  - Benjamin Moore: after meeting the CEOs in late August, Warren and Charlie made a $1 billion cash offer on the spot. The deal closed in December.
  - Johns Manville: about $1.8 billion in cash. The LBO deal collapsed on Dec 8, Berkshire called the trust on Monday with an all-cash offer with no financing contingencies, and a contract was signed a week after the trustees voted tentatively.
- The eight acquisitions cost about $8 billion, 97% cash and 3% stock. They added about $13 billion in sales and 58,000 employees, with no debt incurred and Berkshire's share count up only 1/3 of 1%.
- Asbestos: Shaw's deal with an asbestos-burdened partner died when Warren refused to write an uncapped policy: "we would never issue a policy that lacked a cap."
- Why 2000 was a good buying year:
  - Managers and owners expected near-term slowdowns. Several targets will see earnings decline from 1999-2000 peaks. "The declines make no difference to us."
  - Junk bond markets dried up, so leveraged "financial" buyers could not borrow what they wanted and bid less aggressively. Berkshire analyzes purchases on an all-equity basis, "which means we became considerably more competitive."
- Berkshire is often "the buyer of choice." Warren values an owner who cares whom he sells to, because that signals honest accounting, pride of product, respect for customers and loyal associates. Owners who auction off their company "often dress it up for sale," especially "financial owners."
- Berkshire's pitch to the "painter" of a "business Rembrandt" is a permanent home. Promises such as keeping a business headquartered in Fort Worth or unmerged "can take those promises to the bank." "We'll leave the auctions to others."

chunks.heading: Managers: autonomy, retention and the lean home office
chunks.text:
- At most large companies, talented divisional managers yearn to be CEO. At Berkshire, "our all-stars have exactly the jobs they want," so they focus on the long-term value of businesses they "own" and love.
- In 36 years, no manager of a significant subsidiary has voluntarily left for another business.
- Warren spends his time allocating capital rather than supervising. "I wouldn't be good at that anyway."
- The home office has 13.8 people, up one in a year when acquisitions more than doubled the workforce to about 112,000.
  - They cover a $40 billion revenue run-rate, more than 300,000 owners, a 4,896-page tax return, and checks to 3,660 shareholder-designated charities.
  - Charlie cites Franklin: "A small leak can sink a great ship."
- Ralph Schey ran Scott Fetzer for 15 years after Berkshire bought it in 1985 (he was then 61), and distributed $1.03 billion to Berkshire against a $230 million net purchase price. Warren puts him in Berkshire's Hall of Fame.
- Warren occasionally moves managers between businesses. Brad Kinstler went from Cypress to Fechheimer and is "hitting home runs." He says Berkshire should try it more often.
- Warren admits Dexter was a mistake: he overpaid in 1993 and compounded it by paying in Berkshire shares. All remaining Dexter goodwill was written off.
- Warren's example of the high cost of keeping production at home: the shoe businesses' attempt to keep most production in domestic factories "has cost us dearly."

chunks.heading: Insurance float: how to judge an insurer, and Berkshire's float
chunks.text:
- Warren says to evaluate an insurer on three determinants:
  - The amount of float.
  - Its cost.
  - Most critical, the long-term outlook for both.
- Float is "money we hold but don't own," because premiums arrive before losses are paid, sometimes years earlier. The underwriting loss is the cost of float.
- An insurance business has value if its float costs less than the money it would otherwise have to raise. It is "a lemon" if float costs more than market rates.
- Caution: loss costs must be estimated, so insurers have "enormous latitude" in reporting results, and income statements and balance sheets "can be minefields." Surprises in insurance "almost always are unpleasant."
- Berkshire's yearend float ($ millions):

| Year | GEICO | General Re | Other Reinsurance | Other Primary | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1967 | | | | 20 | 20 |
| 1987 | | | 701 | 807 | 1,508 |
| 1997 | 2,917 | | 4,014 | 455 | 7,386 |
| 1999 | 3,444 | 15,166 | 6,285 | 403 | 25,298 |
| 2000 | 3,943 | 15,525 | 7,805 | 598 | 27,871 |

- Over the years the cost of float has been close to zero, with the worst year at 19% (1984). 2000 had a $1.6 billion underwriting loss, a 6% float cost.
- Two features distort Berkshire's results and are rare elsewhere:
  - Big loss-heavy contracts that other insurers offload, which penalize current earnings but give usable float for many years. Of the underwriting loss, $400 million (27.8%) in 1999 and $482 million (34.4%) in 2000 came from this business. "Pain-today, gain-tomorrow" is welcome when priced properly.
  - Retroactive reinsurance, which assumes past losses with a cap on exposure (always required). Under GAAP, a "deferred charges" asset is set up and amortized as annual underwriting losses for years, often decades. Warren still expects it to be "decent business."
- He expects float cost to be "very attractive" but rarely back to no-cost. Benefits depend on cost and "how effectively we deploy it."
- Ajit Jain, who wrote nearly all the retroactive business, brought in a $2.4 billion premium for a retroactive policy on a U.K. company. Other policies: disability cover on A-Rod's $252 million contract for the Texas Rangers, and the $1 billion Grab.com prize (a $170 million present value).
- Why Berkshire wins these: "Charlie and I... like any proposition that makes compelling mathematical sense, regardless of its effect on reported earnings." Other CEOs avoid the risk of a horrible quarterly number.
- General Re repriced or dropped severely unprofitable business, and Warren expects its float cost to fall materially if there is no mega-catastrophe in 2001.

chunks.heading: GEICO, a low-cost model, and learning from mistakes
chunks.text:
- Warren was wrong that extra 2000 advertising would pay off. Inquiries did not rise proportionally, the conversion rate fell for the first time in years, and per-policy acquisition cost jumped.
- GEICO's new policies fell from 1,648,095 in 1999 to 1,472,853 in 2000. Policies in force rose to 4,696,842.
- His four explanations:
  - Frequency was pushed too hard, with diminishing returns: "The third ad in an hour on a given cable channel is simply not going to be as effective as the first."
  - Much low-hanging fruit may have been picked, though reluctance toward direct buying will ebb.
  - Stricter underwriting and rate increases cut conversion. Some prospects will switch to save $200 but not $50.
  - State Farm was slow to raise prices.
- State Farm lost 18% of premiums on auto in 2000 (including rebates), against 4% at GEICO. GEICO's float cost was 6.1%, and Warren estimates State Farm's at about 23%. The industry leader tolerating such a loss makes the economics hard for others.
- He urges business schools to study State Farm, because it succeeded without outside capital, stock options or lavish salaries.
- GEICO nonetheless has "much the better business model" with lower operating costs. In a commodity-like product, being the low-cost producer is "all-important," so GEICO will inevitably gain share. He first became enamored with it in 1951, as a 20-year-old student.
- Tony Nicely, GEICO's CEO, "never engages in wishful thinking," cut ineffective advertising, filed aggressively for price increases and reads loss reports daily. GEICO's profit-sharing targets only policy growth and the underwriting results of seasoned business, and it paid 8.8% ($40.7 million) despite the tough year.
- Post-mortems: "Agonizing over errors is a mistake. But acknowledging and analyzing them can be useful." Warren and Charlie have almost never seen a candid post-mortem of a failed decision, especially an acquisition, in boardrooms. The exception is The Washington Post Company, which reviews acquisitions three years later. Elsewhere, blunders are buried in "nonrecurring" restructuring charges, and "CEOs invoke the concept of the Virgin Birth."

chunks.heading: Honest reporting, look-through earnings and what Warren distrusts
chunks.text:
- Full reporting means giving owners what he and Charlie would want if positions were reversed: the important facts on current operations, plus the CEO's frank view of long-term economics. They have "no interest in pictures of personnel, plants or products," are "very suspicious" of vague accounting, and don't want public-relations prose.
- EBITDA makes them "shudder: does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures?" FlightSafety spent $272 million on simulators in 2000 and will spend a similar amount this year. Depreciation is a real cost, "every bit as real as payroll or raw materials."
- Reported earnings understate economic progress, so Berkshire uses look-through earnings:
  - Reported operating earnings, plus
  - its share of investees' retained operating earnings, less
  - an allowance for the tax that would be paid if those earnings had been distributed.
- 2000 look-through earnings were $2,415 million: $740 million of undistributed investee earnings, minus $104 million of hypothetical tax (at 14%), added to $1,779 million of reported operating earnings.
- Fair reporting means telling all owners at the same time. Berkshire posts financials on the Internet after the close on Friday, so shareholders have the weekend before markets open.
- He praises SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt for ending selective disclosure to analysts and large holders ("hints, winks and nods"), which gave speculators an edge. Reform came "because of coercion rather than conscience," which Warren says is shameful.
- He calls it "deceptive and dangerous" for CEOs to predict growth rates.
