  - A 15% annual EPS growth rate is sustained by very few large companies. He would bet a "very significant sum" that fewer than 10 of the 200 most profitable companies in 2000 will reach it over 20 years.
  - Predictions corrode CEO behavior: uneconomic operating moves, then accounting games that snowball from fudging into fraud. "More money... has been stolen with the point of a pen than at the point of a gun."
  - Charlie and Warren are wary of CEOs who woo investors with fancy predictions, since they may be prophets, congenital optimists or charlatans.
- On media rumors: a Wall Street Journal and CNBC report said Berkshire was buying Conseco and Finova bonds. Berkshire had bought Finova debt, in far smaller amounts than reported, and had never bought Conseco. Conseco stock still jumped on heavy volume. Warren's point is that outlets should label such items "rumors" rather than hiding behind phrases such as "sources say."

chunks.heading: Long-run goals, compounding and Ben Graham
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's 2000 net worth gain was $3.96 billion, or 6.5% per share. Over 36 years, book value per share grew from $19 to $40,442, or 23.6% compounded annually.
- Warren and Charlie aim to beat the S&P 500 modestly over time, and note that a small annual edge, sustained, becomes a large long-term gap. The plan needs a few good businesses each year, existing businesses gaining in value, and no material increase in shares outstanding.
- Intrinsic value, not book value, is the real yardstick, and he believed intrinsic value gained moderately more than book.
- Berkshire holds "awash in liquid assets" and is "eager and ready for even larger acquisitions."
- Dec 31, 2000 stock holdings (market value): Coca-Cola $12,188 million (cost $1,299 million), American Express $8,329 million, Gillette $3,468 million, Wells Fargo $3,067 million, Washington Post $1,066 million; total common stocks $37,619 million against $10,402 million cost.
- In 2000 Berkshire sold nearly all its Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae shares, took 15% positions in several mid-sized companies, bought a few high-yield bonds ("the category is not labeled junk without reason") and added to high-grade mortgage-backed securities.
- Ben Graham: Warren entered his Columbia class exactly 50 years earlier. In the prior decade he had "loved" analyzing and trading stocks but got average results. "A few hours spent at the feet of the master proved far more valuable... than had ten years of supposedly original thinking." His debt to Graham is "incalculable."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2001 letter covers a bad year: 9/11 losses and General Re's underreserving. It explains how to value an insurer by float, its cost and underwriting discipline, and gives candid mea culpas. It also covers owner-aligned management, buying from trusted managers, and his contempt for EBITDA and options.

chunks.heading: Relative performance, and the "Ground Rules"
chunks.text:
- Warren has judged results against general securities experience since forming his first partnership on May 5, 1956. His "Ground Rules" said: "Whether we do a good job or a poor job is to be measured against the general experience in securities."
- The benchmark started as the Dow Jones Industrials and moved to the S&P 500 once that index became widely used. In 2001 Berkshire beat it by 5.7 percentage points, even though book value fell 6.2% (a $3.77 billion loss in net worth).
- Per-share book value grew from $19 to $37,920 over 37 years, a 22.6% compounded annual rate. Intrinsic value grew somewhat faster than book value over that span.
- He answers "you can't eat relative performance" this way. If you expect the S&P 500 to deliver reasonably satisfactory results over time, small annual advantages over it must be rewarding for long-term investors. See's loses money in the summer months, yet it is a profitable business across the year, and variable absolute returns can work the same way.
- Another Ground Rule still holds: "I cannot promise results to partners."
- He expects Berkshire's future record to fall well short of the past. Valuations were lower then, and he worked with far less money. A good $10 million idea (Washington Post in 1973, GEICO in 1976) once moved the needle. Today ten such ideas, each tripling, would add only ¼ of 1% to net worth. Berkshire now needs "elephants."

chunks.heading: Owner-orientation, incentives and shareholder abuse
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie promise that shareholders' results will parallel theirs. They take no cash compensation, restricted stock or option grants that would make their results better than shareholders'.
- He keeps well over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire. He and his wife have never sold a share and don't intend to.
- He is disgusted by CEOs and promoters who caused billions in shareholder losses and left rich. Some urged investors to buy while quietly dumping their own shares. These leaders see shareholders "as patsies, not partners."
- His illustration of the attitude: a CEO at a party is asked what he wants and answers, "Reprice my options."
- At MiTek, 55 managers bought 10% of the company, each putting in at least $100,000 of cash. Many borrowed to do it.
  - Warren says these managers are real owners, unlike option holders. They face downside as well as upside, incur a cost of capital, and can't "reprice" their stakes. "What they paid is what they live with."
- All 2001 acquisitions were paid in cash, so existing shareholders gave up no interest in the companies they already owned. The formula: raise the value of the excellent businesses already owned, add businesses of similar quality, and issue shares "only grudgingly."
- Berkshire completed 37 years without any operating-business CEO choosing to leave for another employer.

chunks.heading: How Warren finds and buys businesses
chunks.text:
- Deals often start with the seller's own letter or call.
  - MiTek: its CEO, Gene Toombs, mailed Warren a "connector plate" (a part used in roofing trusses) along with a letter. A one-minute call showed Warren he was "our kind of manager" in "our kind of business." A cash offer to the U.K. parent followed, and a deal came quickly.
  - Larson-Juhl: owner Craig Ponzio called on December 3rd. Warren had never heard of the company, a maker of custom picture frames. Ponzio had grown sales from $3 million to $300 million since buying it in 1981. He was "straightforward in describing the business, cared about who bought it, and was realistic as to price."
  - The Larson-Juhl deal was agreed in 90 minutes in Omaha and signed within ten days. The company serves about 18,000 framing shops in the U.S. and leads in Canada and much of Europe.
- XTRA (truck-trailer leasing): Warren approached it after Julian Robertson announced he was liquidating Tiger Fund. The deal came about 18 months later, when Robertson decided to sell. Warren calls trailer leasing cyclical but expects "decent returns over time."
- Fruit of the Loom was bought out of bankruptcy.
  - It failed from too much debt and poor management. Warren's offer carried no financing conditions, though it had to stay open for months.
  - He insisted on one unusual condition: John Holland, who had run it in its best years and returned after bankruptcy, had to stay as CEO. In Warren's view, "John and the brand are Fruit's key assets." Holland cut employment from a bloated 40,000 to 23,000.
  - Warren had earlier bought the company's public and bank debt at about 50% of face value. Interest on the senior debt kept being paid, so he earned a current return of about 15%. He expected to recover roughly 70% of face value, which indirectly lowered his purchase price for the whole company.
- The 1955 P&R deal shows the kind of bargain he admires. Union Underwear (Fruit of the Loom) cost $15 million, and it held $5 million of cash and earned about $3 million pre-tax. Of the remaining $12.5 million owed, $9 million was paid in non-interest-bearing notes, payable from half of earnings above $1 million.
- He quotes Horace, from the frontispiece of *Security Analysis*: "Many shall be restored that now are fallen and many shall fall that are now in honor." His appreciation for it keeps growing. Acme Boot, once the world's largest bootmaker, ended up as remnants bought by H.H. Brown for $700,000.

chunks.heading: Insurance economics: float, cost of float, underwriting
chunks.text:
- Three things determine an insurer's value: (1) the amount of float it generates, (2) its cost, and (3) most critical, the long-term outlook for both.
- Float is "money we hold but don't own." Premiums arrive before losses are paid, sometimes years earlier. An underwriting loss is the cost of float.
- An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds. It is "a lemon" if the cost exceeds market rates.
- Berkshire's float rose from $20 million in 1967 to $35.5 billion in 2001 (GEICO $4,251 million, General Re $19,310 million, Other Reinsurance $11,262 million, Other Primary $685 million).
- Berkshire's float cost was below zero in about half its years. In 2001 it was 12.8%, the worst since 1984, after 6% in 2000.
- With short-term funds earning under 2%, float costing 4% is no longer tolerable. Every insurance operation except retroactive reinsurance must now earn an underwriting profit to count as a good business. Retroactive reinsurance has desirable economics even though it runs an underwriting loss of about $425 million a year.
- GEICO made a $221 million underwriting profit in 2001, so Berkshire was paid to hold $4.25 billion of float. Premiums rose 6.6%. Policies in force fell 0.8%.
- Warren and GEICO's CEO would like to spend more than the $219 million marketing budget but "cannot see how to do so effectively." GEICO's operating costs are far below its competitors'.
- The other primary insurers wrote $579 million of premium (up 40%), grew float 14.5% to $685 million, and made a $30 million underwriting profit.

chunks.heading: The three underwriting rules, and Warren's 9/11 mistake
chunks.text:
- Size and brand name don't decide an insurer's profitability. Underwriting discipline does. The winners stick to three rules:
  1. Accept only risks you can properly evaluate (your circle of competence) that carry an expectancy of profit after weighing remote loss scenarios. Ignore market share, and be "sanguine about losing business" to competitors offering foolish prices or terms.
  2. Limit business so that no single event or related events can create an aggregation of losses that threatens solvency. Search "ceaselessly" for correlation among seemingly unrelated risks.
  3. Avoid moral risk: "trying to write good contracts with bad people doesn't work."
- General Re broke all three rules in 2001. It misjudged its costs by under-reserving, and it was "overly-competitive" in chasing and retaining business. If "winning" means market share rather than profit, "trouble awaits." "'No' must be an important part of any underwriter's vocabulary."
- Both Warren and the industry priced from experience rather than exposure. They ignored large-scale terrorism, so a huge risk was assumed without premium.
  - Experience is a useful starting point, for example how many 6.0+ California earthquakes occurred in a century. At times, though, it is dangerous.
  - Late in a bull market, directors and officers liability losses look rare, but exposure is exploding through "ridiculous public offerings, earnings manipulation, chain-letter-like stock promotions." Priced on exposure, the correct rate on excess D&O might be five or more times the rate that experience dictates.
- He admits he saw the terrorism risk before September 11th but didn't act. "I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn't count; building arks does."
- He still takes more risk than any other insurer knowingly takes. Berkshire is willing to lose $2 billion to $2½ billion in one event, as it did on September 11th, if it is paid properly for the risk. Its tolerance for huge losses is a competitive advantage, backed by liquid resources, non-insurance earnings, a favorable tax position and a shareholder base that accepts earnings volatility.
- He will cap total exposure "no matter what the competition does." For example, Berkshire won't cover many towers in one city without excluding losses from a nuclear blast and the fires that follow.
- Ajit Jain (18 associates) writes huge, fast, disciplined policies. Warren has known the details of nearly every policy since 1986 and never saw Ajit break a rule.
  - Examples written and retained: $578 million of property cover for a South American refinery above a $1 billion loss; $1 billion of third-party terrorism liability for large international airlines; £500 million on a North Sea oil platform above £600 million; and Sears Tower cover above $500 million.
  - His insight: "insurers produce outstanding long-term results primarily by avoiding dumb decisions, rather than by making brilliant ones."
- On reinsurance chains: a weak link in a "daisy chain" of retrocessionaires can sink everyone. Stress-test every participant under a mega-catastrophe in a bad economy. "You only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out." Berkshire retains its risks and depends on no one.

chunks.heading: Reserves, accounting language, and "EBITDA"
chunks.text:
- "Bad terminology is the enemy of good thinking." Warren objects to "EBITDA," "pro forma," "loss development" and "reserve strengthening" as terms that make investors accept flawed concepts.
- Loss reserves are a liability for losses that have occurred but are unpaid, including IBNR (incurred but not reported) losses. Accurate estimates are vital, because otherwise managers don't know their true costs against the premiums they charge.
- GEICO nearly failed in the early 1970s by severely under-reserving. It believed its product cost less than it did, so it underpriced and sold more at larger losses.
- General Re recognized $800 million of costs from earlier years in 2001. The under-reserving hid its true costs, led to inadequate pricing, produced overstated profits, caused incentive pay it should not have paid, and brought income taxes earlier than needed.
- "The losses didn't 'develop' – they were there all along. What developed was management's understanding of the losses." A forthright label would be "loss costs we failed to recognize when they occurred" (or "oops").
- Insurance accounting is "a self-graded exam." Companies in trouble seldom grade tough, and under-reserving is common among companies struggling to survive. Surprises in insurance rarely help earnings, so conservatism is essential.
- He opposes discounting reserves to present value. Reserves can't be precisely established, since judicial broadening of policy language and medical inflation keep pushing them up, and discounting would give companies inclined to fudge a new tool.
- On EBITDA, FlightSafety spends $162 million on 27 simulators in 2002 against annual depreciation of $95 million. Those who think EBITDA equals true earnings "are welcome to pick up the tab."
- Goodwill amortization will end under new GAAP rules. That raises reported earnings "though not our true economic earnings."

chunks.heading: Operating businesses and mistakes
chunks.text:
- Dexter shoes: three costly decisions, all his own. He bought it, paid for it with stock, and procrastinated when change was obviously needed. He wrongly concluded Dexter could cope with brutal low-cost foreign competition. The shoe operations lost $46.2 million pre-tax in 2001. Dexter went under the management of Frank Rooney and Jim Issler at H.H. Brown.
- R.C. Willey: the "closed on Sunday" policy defied conventional retailing wisdom, and Warren was skeptical it would work in Boise or Las Vegas. Chairman Bill Child put up $11 million of his own money for the Boise store, selling it to Berkshire at cost, without interest, only if it succeeded.
  - The store succeeded. The Henderson (Las Vegas) store now outsells every other store in the chain and runs at twice Warren's expectation.
  - Berkshire people now say "What does Bill think?" about retailing questions. Warren keeps the planned Kansas City Nebraska Furniture Mart (450,000 sq ft) open Sundays.
- Retailing in 2001: jewelry same-store sales fell 7.6%, pre-tax margin was 8.9% against 10.7%. Home-furnishings margin was 9.1% pre-tax.
- Shaw, Johns Manville and Benjamin Moore together earned about $659 million pre-tax in their first year. Berkshire swapped 4,740 A shares for Shaw's 12.7% minority interest.
- NetJets accounts for about half the industry by value of customers' planes. Scale (300+ planes) lowers positioning costs, but under current conditions the edge "will at best produce modest profits." It lost a small amount in 2001.
- Warren also notes Lou Simpson's independent $2 billion GEICO portfolio, whose results have recently beaten his own.

chunks.heading: Investing outlook, junk and distressed debt, and capital sourcing
chunks.text:
- Warren's own equity results have been poor for several years. Berkshire's larger holdings have done poorly as a group (Coca-Cola, Gillette, American Express, Wells Fargo and others, with $28.7 billion of market value on $8.5 billion of cost).
- He likes the businesses, but doesn't think the equity holdings "as a group" are undervalued. He is "decidedly lukewarm" on stocks over the next decade, expecting only moderate returns because prices were still high after the bubble. The NASDAQ peaked at 5,132 on March 10, 2000 (recently 1,731), the day Berkshire hit $40,800, its lowest price since mid-1997.
- "The market outperformed business for a very long period, and that phenomenon had to end." A market that only keeps pace with business may disappoint investors who are new to the game.
- Junk bonds are unsuitable for the general public. Berkshire has never bought a newly issued junk bond, and losses in the field are often disastrous. Warren has made money in distressed debt for 50 years, in situations including Washington Public Power System, Chrysler Financial, Texaco and RJR Nabisco.
- FINOVA: Berkshire bought 13% of about $11 billion of debt at roughly two-thirds of face value. He expected bankruptcy but judged that liquidating the assets would pay creditors above his cost.
  - Berkshire and Leucadia proposed a prepackaged plan: creditors get 70% of face value plus full interest, and a new 7½% note for the other 30%.
  - To fund the 70% payout, a jointly owned entity (Berkadia) borrowed $5.6 billion through FleetBoston and re-lent it to FINOVA with a priority claim on its assets. Berkshire guaranteed 90% of the borrowing and earns 90% of the roughly two-point spread.
  - He pulled a follow-on offer after September 11th, because the aircraft assets and other receivables FINOVA held were impaired.
- "Debt is a four-letter word around Berkshire." Berkshire borrowed almost nothing from banks for three decades. When it needed $10 million in 1969 (Illinois National Bank), the Boston bank flew people to Omaha and said "we'll work out the details later." In 2001 FleetBoston did the same for a $6 billion loan, which 17 banks oversubscribed.

chunks.heading: Charity and culture
chunks.text:
- Operating subsidiaries make their own charitable decisions, but former owner-managers must give to personal charities from their own funds, not company money.
- At the parent level, Berkshire gives only what shareholders designate. A fixed per-share amount goes to up to three charities of each registered A-share holder's choice. In 2001 that was $16.7 million, directed by 5,700 holders. Cumulative shareholder-directed gifts total $181 million.
- Warren compares it to paying a dividend that the shareholder then donates, but more tax-efficient. Berkshire follows owners' wishes, including for Planned Parenthood or Metro Right to Life, as long as the charity qualifies under 501(c)(3).
- Berkshire never considers religion, gender, race or sexual orientation in hiring or buying. Doing so would be wrong and "idiotic," because able and trustworthy people come from "a very wide spectrum of humanity."
- It is "not our style to tamper with successful business cultures," so acquired subsidiaries keep their existing employee-match programs.
- Headquarters has 14.8 employees, in 5,246.5 square feet, for a workforce of 110,000.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett reviews 2002: how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, durability), General Re's reserving and underwriting failures, why he calls derivatives "financial weapons of mass destruction," and why boards, audit committees and CEO pay were broken. Also covers buying to keep, hiring great managers, and refusing to buy stocks at poor prices.

chunks.heading: Float: the core of Berkshire's insurance economics
chunks.text:
- Float is "money we hold but don't own": premiums arrive before losses are paid, sometimes years earlier, and the insurer invests the money meanwhile.
- Warren evaluates an insurer on three things: (1) the amount of float, (2) its cost, and (3) "most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both."
- The cost of float is the underwriting loss. An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is below what the company would otherwise pay for funds. It is "a lemon" if the cost exceeds market rates for money.
- Falling interest rates turned formerly tolerable underwriting losses into burdens that push many insurers deep into the lemon category.
- Berkshire's cost has often been below zero (it was paid to hold other people's money). It is not automatic: 2001 cost 12.8% (about half from World Trade Center losses), and 1983-84 were worse.
- Float grew from $20 million (1967) to $1.5 billion (1987), $7.4 billion (1997) and $41.2 billion (2002), up $5.7 billion that year. 2002 float cost about 1%.
- 2002 float by segment: General Re $22.2 billion, Other Reinsurance $13.4 billion, GEICO $4.7 billion, Other Primary $0.9 billion.
- 2002 absorbed $1.75 billion (about 4.6% of float) in charges: a $1.31 billion General Re reserve correction and the "desirable" annual retroactive-insurance charge.
- Warren warns that cheap float needs a caveat: 2002 had no megacatastrophe, and float cost will spike when one arrives.

chunks.heading: Underwriting discipline, reserving and catastrophe aggregation
chunks.text:
- Three rules for low-cost float: (a) "underwrite with unwavering discipline"; (b) reserve conservatively; (c) avoid aggregating exposures so that a supposedly "impossible" event threatens solvency.
- General Re broke all three after the 1998 merger. Warren admits: "I was dead wrong." He had studied it for decades and saw no slippage at merger time, but it was grossly mispricing business and had accumulated nuclear, chemical and biological risk that would have been fatal in a large terrorist attack. The World Trade Center loss alone would have threatened an independent Gen Re.
- The fix under Joe Brandon and Tad Montross: write only properly priced business "whatever the effect on volume"; judge themselves only on underwriting profit, not size; cut the NCB aggregation to a tolerable level.
- On reserving: "any insurer that has no idea what its costs are is heading for big trouble." Casualty managers tend naturally to under-reserve, and overcoming that takes a particular mindset that has "nothing to do with actuarial expertise." Reinsurers find it harder than primary insurers. Warren promises it is the top priority but cannot guarantee success.
- Financial strength matters most in reinsurance. Gen Re's three largest competitors were downgraded from AAA, leaving Gen Re alone at AAA across the board. One major reinsurer had all but stopped paying valid claims.
- "'Cheap' reinsurance is a fool's bargain." Paying today for a promise decades away is dangerous unless the reinsurer is the strongest around.
- GEICO case: in 1981-83 it wrote $3,051,000 of commercial umbrella and product liability premium and ceded $2,979,000 to reinsurers, keeping $72,000. Losses from the line total $94.1 million (about 130,000% of net premium), including $90.3 million of uncollectable reinsurance receivables.

chunks.heading: Retroactive insurance and tolerating volatility
chunks.text:
- In retroactive insurance, Berkshire assumes another insurer's obligation to pay up to a specified cap for losses already incurred, often decades old, in exchange for a large upfront premium that is less than expected losses.
- Why Warren accepts the gap: payments are capped, and Berkshire uses the money for a decade or more until losses are paid. About 80% of the $6.6 billion of asbestos and environmental reserves come from capped contracts.
- Accounting: premium and reserve are booked immediately, with the difference recorded as an asset, "deferred charges, reinsurance assumed" ($3.4 billion at yearend 2002), then amortized through income. These charges ($440 million in 2002) create an intentional, desirable underwriting loss.
- Ajit Jain's reinsurance unit built $13.4 billion of float from a standing start in 1986 with about 20 people, and posted a $534 million 2002 underwriting profit after a $428 million retroactive charge.
- Warren states that Berkshire assumes far larger risks than any other insurer, so single events can swing quarterly or annual results. He is untroubled: "As long as we are paid appropriately, we love taking on short-term volatility that others wish to shed. At Berkshire, we would rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%."
- Smaller insurers grew float 38% and earned a $32 million underwriting profit (4.5% of premiums). California workers' comp had reserving problems, so Warren will keep it small until it is fixed.

chunks.heading: Acquisition criteria and why Berkshire "buys to keep"
chunks.text:
- Three-legged "entrance" strategy: good-to-great economic characteristics, great managers, and a sensible price. There is no exit strategy, unlike LBO and private-equity operators: "we buy to keep." That makes Berkshire usually the first, and sometimes the only, choice for sellers and their managers.
- 2002 purchases: Albecca/Larson-Juhl (custom picture frames), Fruit of the Loom (about 33.3% of US men's and boys' underwear), CTB (poultry, hog, egg and grain equipment) and Garan (children's apparel, Garanimals). The last two earn over $60 million pre-tax combined, in tough industries but with competitive strengths that earn decent returns on capital.
- The Pampered Chef: Doris Christopher started in 1980 with $3,000 borrowed against a life insurance policy (the only capital ever put in), did $50,000 in year one, and now does over $700 million a year through 67,000 consultants. Warren says it took him "about ten seconds" to decide to partner with her and CEO Sheila O'Connell Cooper.
- Non-insurance earnings: a decade earlier, pre-tax non-insurance earnings were $272 million a year; by 2002 Berkshire earned that amount monthly.
- Warren says Berkshire's "income" of about $500 million pre-tax in 2002 was helped by two favorable breaks: no megacatastrophe, and bond-market conditions favoring its finance strategies, which will fade within a year or two.

chunks.heading: Managers: hands-off management and capital allocation
chunks.text:
- No subsidiary CEO has left Berkshire for another employer in 38 years, though many have no financial need to work. Six managers are over 75, and Warren hopes for more: "It's hard to teach a new dog old tricks."
- His job: "stay out of their way and allocate whatever excess capital their businesses generate. It's easy work."
- The Eddie Bennett parable: a batboy who joined the pennant-winning White Sox (1919), Dodgers (1920) and Yankees (1921), then collected a $700 World Series share in 1927. Lesson: "to be a winner, work with winners." Warren hands bats "to many of the heaviest hitters in American business."
- Cost-consciousness is cherished at Berkshire. Warren's model is the widow who placed the obituary "Fred Brown died, golf clubs for sale."
- Shaw's earnings grew from $292 million to $424 million on productivity gains and expense control, even though carpet prices rose only 1%. Berkshire's home and construction businesses earned $941 million pre-tax.
- MidAmerican Energy (80.2% equity, 9.9% voting due to PUHCA) bought Kern River (about 900 million cubic feet a day, $1.2 billion expansion) and Northern Natural Gas (16,600 miles). Once the expansion is done, MEHC will carry about 8% of US gas. Warren funded it with $1,273 million of junior debt and $402 million of common-equivalent stock.
- HomeServices became the second largest US residential brokerage, taking part in $37 billion of transactions (up 100%), and is a cyclical business Warren is happy to keep buying into at sensible prices.

chunks.heading: Derivatives as "financial weapons of mass destruction"
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie view derivatives as "time bombs, both for the parties that deal in them and the economic system," and as "financial weapons of mass destruction, carrying dangers that, while now latent, are potentially lethal."
- Accounting problem: parties book large profits and losses without any cash changing hands. With no real market, firms use mark-to-model, which can degrade into "mark-to-myth." Marking errors are not symmetrical; they favor traders chasing bonuses and CEOs wanting to report impressive earnings.
- Illustration: General Re Securities held 14,384 contracts with 672 counterparties after ten months of winding down, and its $6.5 billion of receivables remained. It lost $173 million pre-tax in 2002. Berkshire could not sell it and is liquidating.
- Parallels with reinsurance: both are "like Hell, easy to enter and almost impossible to exit," and both generate earnings that are often wildly overstated because they rest on estimates that are not exposed for years.
- Systemic risks: collateral triggers on credit downgrades can spiral a firm into a liquidity crisis; counterparty receivables form a daisy chain that correlates in a crisis; risk is concentrated among a few dealers who trade with one another. LTCM in 1998 required a Fed-orchestrated rescue. Total-return swaps "make a joke of margin requirements."
- Principle: when a chain-reaction threat exists, "it pays to minimize links of any kind." Berkshire wants to be "a fortress of financial strength" for owners, creditors, policyholders and employees.

chunks.heading: Investing: patience, price discipline and junk bonds
chunks.text:
- Equities: Warren did little in 2002. Major holdings (Coca-Cola, American Express, Gillette, Wells Fargo, Moody's, Washington Post) had higher earnings and lower valuations, yet he was not inclined to add because they were not yet undervalued. Total common stocks: $9,164 million cost, $28,363 million market.
- He calls the market's excesses "The Great Bubble" and warns that "the hangover may prove to be proportional to the binge."
- His hurdle: "Unless... we see a very high probability of at least 10% pre-tax returns (which translate to 6½-7% after corporate tax), we will sit on the sidelines." In 61 years of investing, about 50 offered such opportunities. "Occasionally successful investing requires inactivity," even with short-term money earning under 1% after tax.
- Berkshire-managed equity gains outweighed losses about 100 to one over 38 years, because Warren buys conservatively financed businesses with strong competitive strengths run by able, honest people at sensible prices.
- Junk bonds and loans: commitments rose sixfold to $8.3 billion. Both stocks and junk bonds require a price-value calculation and scanning hundreds of securities for the few with good reward/risk, but junk issuers are marginal, overleveraged, in low-return industries, and sometimes run by managers whose interests oppose the debtholders'. Warren expects occasional large losses there.
- Berkshire's book value grew from $19 to $41,727 per share (22.2% compounded) over 38 years. He cautions the 32.1-point outperformance in 2002 is "aberrational" and that the goal is only a few points of average annual advantage.

chunks.heading: Corporate governance, audit committees and honest accounting
chunks.text:
- Directors should behave "as if there was a single absentee owner," removing mediocre CEOs regardless of likability and slapping the hands of overreaching ones. The failure came from "boardroom atmosphere," not weak laws.
- Real independence requires being business-savvy, interested and shareholder-oriented, not just formally independent. Warren served on 19 public boards over 40 years with about 250 directors, and most lacked at least one of these qualities. He admits he too stayed silent when collegiality trumped independence.
- Mutual fund boards are the 62-year case study: they have only two key jobs, choosing the best manager and negotiating the lowest fee, and have failed at both. A director whose income depends on board fees will not offend the CEO.
- The fix is concentrated owners: twenty or fewer large institutions could reform a company by withholding votes. The acid test is CEO pay. Directors should shout "Less!" for anything short of exceptional performance.
- Berkshire practice: pays directors a pittance, provides no D&O insurance so directors share in any disaster, and will choose directors who hold millions of dollars of Berkshire stock they bought themselves.
- Audit committees "can't audit." Warren's four questions for auditors, with answers reported to shareholders: Would the auditor have prepared the statements differently? Would an auditor-investor have received what he needs to understand performance? Would the auditor run internal audit differently as CEO? Is the auditor aware of any actions that shifted revenues or expenses between periods? Ask at least a week before earnings.
- Option expensing: Arthur Andersen's standards group backed expensing in 1992 and was overruled by rainmaker partners; FASB voted 7-0 for it and the Senate voted 88-9 against; 498 of 500 S&P companies chose not to expense.
- Three tips for investors: beware weak accounting ("There is seldom just one cockroach in the kitchen"); EBITDA treats depreciation as not a real expense, though the cash is paid up front; unintelligible footnotes signal untrustworthy management; and be suspicious of managers who trumpet earnings projections, since "Managers that always promise to 'make the numbers' will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2003 letter explains how Berkshire judges itself against the S&P, why it prefers whole businesses when stocks are pricey, and how it buys companies on character and trust. It also covers director independence through real ownership, insurance float, avoiding derivatives, and owning up to mistakes.

chunks.heading: How Berkshire thinks about intrinsic value, book value and benchmarks
chunks.text:
- Warren says per-share intrinsic value is what counts, not book value. Book value is "a slightly understated gauge" of long-term intrinsic value growth.
- 1964-2003: per-share book value grew from $19 to $50,498, 22.2% compounded annually. Net worth rose $13.6 billion in 2003, up 21% per share.
- Book is less useful for judging a single year versus the S&P 500, because equities fell from an average of 114% of net worth in the 1980s to 50% in 2000-03.
- The benchmark that matters is the S&P 500, which shareholders can buy cheaply through an index fund. Unless per-share intrinsic value outdoes the S&P, "Charlie and I will be adding nothing to what you can accomplish on your own."
- He says Berkshire's freedom is a rare advantage: no historical industry commitments and no shareholders pressuring management "to dance to Wall Street's tune". Mistakes there are "unforced errors".
- He expects future performance to "fall far short" of the past, hoping only for results "modestly above average. That's what we're being paid for."
- He warns that growth-rate tables can be distorted by choosing tiny or buoyant base or terminal years. He shows operating earnings per share from several base years: $2.69 in 1968 growing to $3,531.32 in 2003, 22.8% compounded.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation: businesses versus stocks
chunks.text:
- When valuations are similar, Warren strongly prefers owning businesses to owning stocks. For most of Berkshire's history stocks were much cheaper, so he tilted heavily toward equities.
- Today few stocks can be bought in large enough size to move Berkshire's needle, and significantly undervalued ones are hard to find.
- His acquisition criteria: businesses that (1) have favorable and enduring economic characteristics, (2) are run by talented and honest managers, and (3) are available at a sensible price. For businesses that qualify, "the bigger the better".
- Policy: buy stocks aggressively if they become significantly cheaper than whole businesses, and load up on bonds if they become attractive (as in 2002).
- Idle capital is "a painful condition to be in - but not as painful as doing something stupid."
- On asset managers: "when one tells you that increased funds won't hurt his investment performance, step back: His nose is about to grow." Managers often profit more from gathering assets than from managing them well.
- Default position when nothing is exciting: U.S. Treasury bills and repos. He never "reaches" for yield by lowering credit standards or extending maturities. "Charlie and I detest taking even small risks unless we feel we are being adequately compensated."
- He avoids macro forecasting: "the cemetery for seers has a huge section set aside for macro forecasters."
- In 2002 Berkshire bought about $8 billion of junk bonds when they were cheap. By 2003 he judged the sector unattractive: "Yesterday's weeds are today being priced as flowers." Berkshire also took a currency position (about $12 billion of foreign exchange contracts), as a partial offset to its dollar cash.

chunks.heading: Case studies in buying businesses: Clayton Homes and McLane
chunks.text:
- **Clayton Homes.** The lead came from University of Tennessee finance students who gave Warren Jim Clayton's autobiography.
  - He already knew Clayton as the "class act" of manufactured housing, from a failed junk-debt purchase in Oakwood Homes, which went bankrupt.
  - He offered based on the book, his read of CEO Kevin Clayton as "able and a straight-shooter", public financials, and the Oakwood lesson.
  - The industry's flaw was a model built on retailers and manufacturers unloading terrible loans on naive lenders, worsened by securitization. The fix is significant down payments and shorter loans.
  - Clayton later agreed to buy Oakwood's assets, which probably returns a small profit on Berkshire's discounted Oakwood debt.
- **McLane.** Wal-Mart sold this distributor (about $23 billion of sales, roughly 1% pre-tax margin) because it was off its mainstream path.
  - One two-hour meeting with Wal-Mart's CFO, then a handshake. Money changed hands 29 days later with no due diligence: "We knew everything would be exactly as Wal-Mart said it would be - and it was."
  - Rival retailers had shunned McLane because Wal-Mart owned it, so independence can win accounts.
- He credits Goldman's Byron Trott, who has helped on three deals, for understanding Berkshire and for earning his fee.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and why management is the moat
chunks.text:
- Float is money held that belongs to others: premiums are paid upfront, and claims can take years to be reported and settled. It is "wonderful - if it doesn't come at a high price."
- The cost of float is the underwriting result. The industry regularly loses money on underwriting. Berkshire had five terrible years when float cost over 10%, but operated at an underwriting profit in 18 of 37 years.
- Float grew from $20 million in 1967 to $171 million in 1977, $1,508 million in 1987, $7,386 million in 1997 and $44,220 million in 2003. In 2003 it came at no cost, with a $1.7 billion pre-tax underwriting profit.
- Insurance has no moat in product: "Insurers sell a non-proprietary piece of paper containing a non-proprietary promise." No patents, installed base, real estate or brand protect it. The critical variables are "managerial brains, discipline and integrity."
- General Re was fixed after discipline was restored in underwriting and reserving. Gen Re and National Indemnity were the only AAA-rated major reinsurers, and Berkshire retains virtually all risks it assumes.
- Ajit Jain (staff of 23) writes jumbo, catastrophe-type risks, so results are lumpy and an occasional horrible year is expected. Example: a $1 billion policy on PepsiCo's contest, with present-value exposure of $250 million, retained entirely.
- GEICO under Tony Nicely: premiums rose from $2.2 billion to $8.1 billion and personal-auto share from 2.1% to 5.0%, with strong underwriting.
- Long-tail insurers can report almost any earnings the CEO wants by misstating liabilities. Warren admits he missed Gen Re's under-reserving, which cost Berkshire inaccurate reporting and taxes paid early.

chunks.heading: Derivatives, accounting and an admitted mistake
chunks.text:
- Gen Re Securities was being unwound at a cost: pre-tax losses of $173 million in 2002 and $99 million in 2003. It started with 23,218 contracts ("tickets") with 884 counterparties, and still had 7,580 with 453 counterparties at yearend 2003.
- He argues disclosures cannot reveal derivatives risk: "the more you know about derivatives, the less you will feel you can learn from the disclosures." He quotes Darwin: "Ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge."
- His confession: he and Charlie knew at the Gen Re merger that the derivatives business was unattractive, with illusory reported profits and risks that could not be measured or limited. Trouble there would correlate with trouble elsewhere, just when Berkshire's capital would be best used elsewhere. Charlie would have closed it quickly; "I, however, dithered", probably costing about $100 million pre-tax.
- 1974 precedent: after an insurance fraud of uncertain cost, Berkshire held extra cash and so could not buy as much of the then very cheap stocks.
- "Every tub on its own bottom": Berkshire borrows and re-lends to Clayton at its cost plus one percentage point, so a subsidiary pays an appropriate rate and is not subsidized. "Having a rich daddy can lead to sloppy decisions." Clayton also began retaining loans rather than securitizing, avoiding front-ended income under GAAP. Receivables are financed almost entirely with debt, as a bank would.
- He is wary of Berkshire's wider use of leverage and notes limited circumstances where it uses debt. AAA fixed-income arbitrage was financed with borrowed money only because there was no credit risk and exceptional liquidity.

chunks.heading: Boards, independence and CEO pay
chunks.text:
- CEO pay is "the acid test" of reform. Negotiations over stock options turn "play-money" because the CEO cares far more than the committee. Consultants avoid offending "actual and potential" clients.
- Statutory "independent" directors have failed at mutual funds: they routinely rehire incumbent managers however poor, approve excessive fees, and sign on with a new manager when a management company is sold at a huge price.
- Two key board jobs: obtain or retain an able and honest manager, and compensate that manager fairly.
- Suggested annual-report declarations: (1) directors looked at other management companies and believe theirs is among the better ones; (2) they negotiated a fee comparable to what other clients with equivalent funds would negotiate. If directors won't say this, "If you don't know whose side someone is on, he's probably not on yours."
- Rules treating a director earning 100% of income from board fees as independent are "nonsense". Large dependence on fees can compromise independence.
- Low-cost index funds (such as Vanguard's) are the best choice for most who want to own equities.
- Berkshire's approach, "owner-capitalism": all eleven directors and their families each own over $4 million of stock bought in the market (no options or restricted shares). Director fees are nominal, there is no D&O insurance, so "You win, they win big; you lose, they lose big." "Who ever washes a rental car?"
- Directors need business savvy (the rarest quality), a shareholder orientation and genuine interest; without savvy, they could be "replaced, without loss, by a potted plant."
- The board's main job is choosing a successor; four internal candidates have been identified. Warren has over 99% of his net worth in Berkshire.

chunks.heading: Portfolio habits, Berkshire's businesses and other lessons
chunks.text:
- Major holdings (market value, 12/31/03): Coca-Cola $10,150M (200M shares), American Express $7,312M, Gillette $3,526M, Wells Fargo $3,324M, Moody's $1,453M, Washington Post $1,367M. Last changes: Coca-Cola 1994, Amex 1998, Gillette 1989, Washington Post 1973, Moody's 2000. "Brokers don't love us."
- He is neither enthusiastic nor negative: these are excellent businesses whose prices now reflect that. He says his big mistake was not selling several larger holdings during "The Great Bubble".
- Realized gains are "meaningless for analytical purposes"; he decides on selling regardless of when earnings are reported. Berkshire should be seen "as an unfolding movie, not as a still photograph."
- Manufacturing, service and retailing earned 20.7% on average tangible net worth, but only 9.2% on carrying value after goodwill paid.
- Mrs. B's lesson at Nebraska Furniture Mart: "If you have the lowest price, customers will find you at the bottom of a river." Borsheim's runs a gross margin 20 points below rivals.
- NetJets: dominates fractional ownership (70% of net sales among four competitors). He accepts a European loss because forsaking Europe means second-tier status.
- Taxes: Berkshire will pay $3.3 billion for 2003, 2.5% of all U.S. corporate income tax. Corporate taxes fell to 7.4% of federal receipts, from 32% in 1952.
- Books recommended: *The Intelligent Investor* (revised by Jason Zweig), his favorite on investing; also *Bull!*, *The Smartest Guys in the Room* and *In an Uncertain World*.
- He ended the shareholder-designated gifts program ($197 million given since 1981) because boycotts hurt independent Pampered Chef associates: "nothing charitable in harming decent, hard-working people."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2004 letter covers 21.9% compounded book value growth, how NICO and GEICO turn commodity insurance into float that can cost less than nothing, why he treats stocks as business ownership, and how director fees and unexpensed options distort incentives. He also admits mistakes and warns on the trade deficit.

chunks.heading: How Berkshire's insurance float works and why it is worth owning
chunks.text:
- Float is "money that doesn't belong to us but that we temporarily hold." It arises because premiums are paid upfront while protection is delivered over a year or more, and because claims (asbestos is his example) can take many years to be reported, negotiated and settled.
- Berkshire's float grew from $20 million at the 1967 purchase of National Indemnity (NICO) to $46.1 billion at the end of 2004, through internal growth and acquisitions.
- Warren says "Float is wonderful – if it doesn't come at a high price." Its cost is the underwriting result: expenses and losses compared with premiums received.
- When there is an underwriting profit, float is "better than free" because Berkshire is "actually paid for holding other people's money." That happened in about half of Berkshire's 38 years in insurance.
- The property-casualty industry as a whole almost always runs an underwriting loss, which can make float expensive, "sometimes devastatingly so."
- In 2004 Berkshire earned an underwriting profit of $1.551 billion, so it was paid more than $1.5 billion to hold an average of about $45.2 billion. The profit split was GEICO $970 million, B-H Reinsurance $417 million, Other Primary $161 million and General Re $3 million. Float rose $1.9 billion.
- He expected 2005 pricing to be less attractive but still saw a decent chance of no-cost float again, absent a mega-catastrophe.
- On commutations (insureds unwinding reinsurance contracts), he agrees only when the economics favor Berkshire after weighing what it could earn on the money returned.

chunks.heading: Why insurance is a bad commodity business and how to get an edge anyway
chunks.text:
- Insurers earn poor returns because the product is commodity-like: standard policy forms, many suppliers (including mutuals with limited profit goals), and customers who don't care who the insurer is. Warren's contrast: customers say "I need some Gillette blades" or "I'll have a Coke" but never "I'd like a National Indemnity policy, please." Price competition is fierce, "Think airline seats."
- He names two ways Berkshire gets durable advantage:
  - Discipline in pricing, which means being willing to lose volume (NICO).
  - Being the low-cost operator with a "foot-to-the-floor" strategy (GEICO).
- Reinsurance should not be a commodity because a policy is just a promise and promises vary in quality. At the primary level, state guaranty assessments cover 60% of industry volume (personal lines and workers' comp), so who makes the promise matters little. Reinsurance carries far more solvency risk: when a reinsurer fails, staggering losses hit the primary companies it dealt with, and GEICO lost tens of millions from careless reinsurer selection in the early 1980s.

chunks.heading: National Indemnity: pricing for profit and accepting shrinking volume
chunks.text:
- NICO had no apparent advantage when bought in 1967. It was a specialist in commercial auto and general liability, little known, had no informational edge (it has never had an actuary), wasn't low-cost, and sold through general agents. Still, for almost all of 38 years it has been a star. Warren says without it, "Berkshire would be lucky to be worth half of what it is today."
- Its edge is a managerial mindset most insurers can't replicate. NICO "consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor." Written premiums fell from $366.2 million in 1986 to $54.5 million in 1999 even though billions of premium were available had it cut prices. In his words: "We never left customers – but they left us."
- Why other companies can't copy it:
  - The "institutional imperative" rejects extended volume declines. No CEO wants to tell shareholders business will keep shrinking.
  - Bad pricing doesn't show up for years, so optimistic reserving overstates earnings. He cites this as the self-deception that nearly destroyed GEICO in the early 1970s.
  - Fear of layoffs makes employees rationalize inadequate pricing to keep the organization and distribution system intact.
- Berkshire's fix is a promise that no one at NICO will be fired because of declining volume, however severe. NICO isn't labor-intensive and can live with excess overhead, but "it can't live with underpriced business."
- The no-layoff policy requires care about overstaffing in good times. Tom Murphy of Cap Cities taught Warren to treat a request to hire a $20,000 assistant as a $3 million decision, because the person will likely cost that much over a lifetime and is rarely dismissed. ("More people, more toilet paper.")
- Don Wurster, who has run NICO since 1989, "will accept a walk rather than swing at a bad pitch," like Barry Bonds. He has built $950 million of float that is almost certain to be negative-cost. With insurance prices falling, his volume will drop, and Warren says he will "applaud him ever more loudly."
- Warren believes extraordinary business ability is largely innate. NICO has had four CEOs since 1940 and only one graduated from college.

chunks.heading: GEICO: the low-cost model, a near-failure, and the turnaround
chunks.text:
- History of low-cost insurers:
  - Around 1900 the industry was a cartel with "bureau" rates and high agent commissions.
  - State Farm (1922) used captive agents, lowered acquisition costs, and captured about 25% of personal lines.
  - Allstate (1931) followed the same model.
  - Leo Goodwin started GEICO in 1936 with $200,000 and eliminated the agent entirely, because most consumers know what they need in an auto policy. Warren calls this "a powerful insight."
- From 1936 to 1975 GEICO grew from nothing to a 4% market share, the fourth largest auto insurer. After Lorimer Davidson retired as CEO in 1970, successors under-reserved for losses. That gave faulty cost information, then inadequate pricing, and GEICO was near failure by 1976.
- Jack Byrne saved it with major price increases. Policyholders fled, share fell to 1.8% by 1980, and unwise diversification kept share at only 1.9% in 1993. Tony Nicely then took over, and GEICO should reach about a 6% share in 2005.
- 2004 benefits to each constituent:
  - Customers saved about $1 billion versus what they would otherwise have paid.
  - Employees earned a $191 million profit-sharing bonus averaging 24.3% of salary.
  - Berkshire got excellent returns.
- New Jersey re-entry:
  - GEICO left in 1976 and avoided New Jersey and Massachusetts as hard jurisdictions.
  - After 2003 reform legislation, it was licensed in August 2004.
  - It had 140,000 policyholders (about 4% of the market) by the letter, with word of mouth driving inquiries and a closure rate well above the national one.
- Warren claims GEICO offers the lowest price more often than any other national insurer serving all segments, though not for everyone. Berkshire shareholders get an 8% discount in most states.

chunks.heading: Catastrophe risk and being able to pay
chunks.text:
- The largest insured loss to date is the World Trade Center at about $35 billion. Hurricane Andrew cost insurers about $15.5 billion in 1992. Four 2004 Florida hurricanes cost about $25 billion in insured losses, and Charley and Ivan could have done at least three times the damage had they landed slightly differently.
- Warren treats a $100 billion industry loss as a real possibility that many insurers call "unthinkable" and won't plan for. Berkshire's share would probably be 3% to 5%, and its investment and business earnings would comfortably exceed that: "When 'the day after' arrives, Berkshire's checks will clear."
- The 2004 hurricanes cost Berkshire $1.25 billion, yet the reinsurance operations did well.
- General Re: Joe Brandon restored underwriting discipline that "had lost its way." Good current results were offset by adverse development on years before he took over.
- Ajit Jain at NICO's reinsurance operation underwrites huge risks no one else will take, and Warren calls his value "enormous."

chunks.heading: Capital allocation, the "simple propositions" rule, and cash
chunks.text:
- Business-owner mindset for managers: "Run your business as if it were the only asset your family will own over the next hundred years." After they fund their businesses, they send excess cash to Omaha for Warren to deploy.
- He admits he did that job poorly in 2004. He hoped for several multi-billion acquisitions, "struck out," and found few attractive securities, leaving $43 billion in cash equivalents, "not a happy position." He buys only at prices offering "a reasonable return on our investment."
- The "mono-linked chain" rule, drawn from the failed MidAmerican zinc recovery project (initiated 1998, operational 2002, written off in September 2004 with a $579 million loss):
  - If one key variable has a 90% chance of going your way, success is 90%.
  - If ten independent variables each have 90% odds, the chance of a winner is only 35%.
  - Mining prospects "tease" developers: every solved problem is followed by another.
  - His conclusion: "a chain is no stronger than its weakest link," so look for "mono-linked chains" and "stay with simple propositions."
- Debt: Berkshire typically shuns it but borrows to fund profitable interest-bearing receivables. Examples:
  - Clayton Homes: borrowing of $2 billion at the start of 2004 grew to $7.35 billion by January 2005, relent to Clayton at a one-point markup. Receivables should hover near $9 billion.
  - MidAmerican: Berkshire holds $1.478 billion of its junior debt at 11% interest, so partners aren't diluted when acquisitions need funding.

chunks.heading: How Warren views stocks, markets and investor mistakes
chunks.text:
- He looks at holdings as "fractional ownerships in businesses," not stocks to trade on "chart patterns, brokers' opinions, or estimates of near-term earnings." This has been his approach since reading Ben Graham's The Intelligent Investor at 19, when "the scales fell from my eyes."
- The "Big Four" (American Express, Coca-Cola, Gillette, Wells Fargo):
  - Cost: $3.83 billion, bought between May 1988 and October 2003, with a weighted purchase date of July 1992.
  - 2004 results: Berkshire's share of their earnings was $1.2 billion, about 31.3% of cost, and distributions were $434 million, about 11.3% of cost.
  - His verdict: "satisfactory, though far from spectacular."
  - Market values diverged from business results. Market gains far outstripped business performance in the Bubble and the reverse followed.
- His admitted error: he "talked when I should have walked" during the Bubble, clucking about valuations but not acting. He also notes huge positions make it hard to dance in and out of holdings.
- Why investors do badly even in a good market (S&P averaged 11.2% over 35 years after the 1960s):
  - High costs from excess trading or expensive management.
  - Decisions based on tips and fads instead of "thoughtful, quantified evaluation of businesses."
  - A start-stop approach that enters after advances and exits after declines.
- His advice: "excitement and expenses are their enemies." If trying to time markets, "be fearful when others are greedy and greedy only when others are fearful."
- The index fund benchmark: shareholders can buy the S&P at very low cost, so unless Berkshire beats it in per-share intrinsic value, Charlie and he add nothing. 2004 book value rose 10.5% against the S&P's 10.9%.
- Book value vs intrinsic value: book is a slightly understated gauge of the long-term rise in intrinsic value. It matters less for single years because equities fell from an average 114% of net worth in the 1980s to under 50%.
- Realized gains are "meaningless for analytical purposes," and the timing of realizing gains does not depend on reporting preferences.

chunks.heading: Delegation, managers and Lou Simpson
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie "truly hand over the baton." Lou Simpson manages about $2.5 billion of equities at GEICO, usually buying $200-$300 million positions in companies smaller than those Warren focuses on. Warren learns of the trades about ten days after month end and sometimes silently disagrees, "But he's usually right."
- Lou's record at GEICO equities from 1980-2004 was an average annual gain of 20.3% against 13.5% for the S&P, a 6.8-point edge. Warren says he is "a cinch" for the investment Hall of Fame.
- Press stories saying "Buffett buys" are usually wrong because the SEC filings are Berkshire's, and the buyer is often Lou.
- Manager examples he praises:
  - Kevin Clayton, a "prototype Berkshire manager," running Clayton Homes (11,837 employees versus 7,136 at purchase) after the Oakwood Homes acquisition.
  - Bill Child and Scott Hymas at R. C. Willey: Warren thought out-of-state expansion and a second Las Vegas store were mistakes, but each Las Vegas store does about 26% more volume than any other chain store. He jokes that "the opinion of someone who is always wrong has its own special utility."
  - The Bridges at Ben Bridge: same-store sales up 11.4% in 2004 and 8.8% average over a decade.
  - Gene Toombs at MiTek, building a "mini-Berkshire" through bolt-on acquisitions.

chunks.heading: Operating businesses: economics worth noting
chunks.text:
- The manufacturing, service and retailing group earned 21.7% on average tangible net worth in 2004 (20.7% in 2003) with little leverage, but only 9.9% on carrying value because of premiums paid over net worth (goodwill). Pre-tax earnings were $2.481 billion on revenue of $44.142 billion.
- Cost pressure: MiTek's steel costs were up 100% year over year (665 million pounds a year), and Shaw faced more than $300 million in fiber cost increases. Shaw still earned 25.6% on tangible equity, though margins narrowed with a lag in price increases.
- FlightSafety is capital-intensive: 283 simulators cost $1.2 billion, so up to $3.50 of capital produces $1 of annual revenue. That demands high margins and utilization. Return on tangible equity rose to 15.1% from 8.4%. Founder Al Ueltschi's standard: a flunked pilot "belongs in the back of the plane, not the cockpit."
- NetJets:
  - Warren compares choosing a flight provider to picking a brain surgeon: "you simply want the best."
  - U.S. contracts grew from 3,877 to 4,967 (about 1,200 when Berkshire bought it in 1998), and it took about 70% of net new business among the four dominant firms.
  - Europe was costlier than expected (contracts rose from 364 to 693) but is essential, and a significant European loss is expected in 2005.
- Manufactured housing: sales of fewer than 135,000 homes in 2004, versus about 40% of 1995-99 volume levels, because of "irresponsible financing and naïve funders." Berkshire's funding gave Clayton an advantage once securitization dried up.
- Derivatives (Gen Re Securities wind-down):
  - Contracts fell to 2,890 from a peak of 23,218. "Like Hell, derivative trading is easy to enter but difficult to leave."
  - Marks are fuzzy over decades-long contracts and feed annual bonuses, so "phantom profits" get recorded.
  - Rapid growth in financial institutions can mask major problems, and the real test is performance in no-growth mode: "You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out."

chunks.heading: Currencies and the trade deficit
chunks.text:
- Berkshire held about $21.4 billion in foreign exchange contracts across 12 currencies, a change for him: he never traded currencies before March 2002.
- His reasoning is not doubt about America, which he calls the strongest economy. It is that trade practices will pressure the dollar for years.
- Key figures: the 2004 current-account deficit was $618 billion, versus $263 billion in 1999 (the year before a Congressional study). Wealth is transferring abroad at about $1.8 billion a day, and foreigners own a net of about $3 trillion of the U.S.
- A decade out at the current pace, net foreign ownership would be about $11 trillion. At 5% that is $0.55 trillion yearly, about 3% of a roughly $18 trillion GDP, a "Sharecropper's Society."
- Budget deficit vs current-account deficit: the budget deficit only redistributes a pie Americans own, but persistent trade deficits send ownership abroad.
- He distinguishes "true trade" ($1.15 trillion of goods and services exchanged) from the $618 billion of "pseudo-trade," where wealth is exchanged for product.
- Caveats: "macro-economics is a tough game in which few people, Charlie and I included, have demonstrated skill," and it makes him uneasy that many pundits predict a weak dollar. He cites Keynes: "it is better for reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally." Berkshire manages as if he owned 100% of it, so a dollar-only policy wasn't right. A prompt policy fix would probably cost Berkshire losses on its contracts, but he'd welcome it since most assets are dollar-based.
- A 2004 profit example: Level 3 euro bonds bought in 2001 at 51.7% of par and sold at 85% in December 2004. About $85 million of the $163 million gain came from improved credit, and $78 million from the euro rising from 88 cents to $1.29.

chunks.heading: Governance, incentives and stock options
chunks.text:
- Two reforms he regrets not adopting earlier: regular director meetings without the CEO present (he has sat on 19 boards), and a whistleblower line to him and the audit committee, useful in a 180,000-employee company.
- The three questions institutional owners should ask: is it the right CEO, is he overreaching on pay, and will proposed acquisitions create or destroy per-share value? He criticizes checklist "independence" tests.
- On independence, he cites Matthew 6:21 ("where your treasure is, there will your heart be also"). His $8 billion Coca-Cola stake dwarfs any business Berkshire does with Coke, so his loyalty is to Coke's owners.
- The Berkshire board standard: each director's family owns at least $4 million of stock, none acquired via options or grants, fees are a tiny portion of income, and there is no directors' liability insurance. "Board members travel the same road as shareholders."
- He argues the least independent directors are often those who get a big share of income from board fees. His example: a multi-billion acquisition offer above the long-run stock price was killed by directors earning about $100,000 a year, who then voted themselves a fee increase.
- Stock options should be expensed. He does not oppose options themselves, and says a successor's pay might include options with an appropriate strike price, a price escalation reflecting retained earnings, and a ban on quickly selling shares. CEOs resist expensing because it would make pay more rational and might lower the stock price.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2005 letter covers insurance float, why acquisitions for stock cost shareholders, widening the moat over short-term earnings, and the cost of derivatives and delay. It also exposes how fixed-price options reward CEOs for retained earnings and explains how Wall Street "Helpers" shrink investor returns.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value, acquisitions and what Berkshire buys
chunks.text:
- Warren writes the letter to give shareholders what they need to estimate intrinsic value. He calls the calculation "all-important" but "necessarily imprecise and often seriously wrong," and the more uncertain a business's future, the more likely the estimate is "wildly off-base."
- Berkshire is easier to value than most companies: relatively stable earnings streams, great liquidity, minimum debt.
- By 2005 Berkshire owned 68 distinct businesses, so consolidated statements no longer suffice. He groups them into four clusters (insurance, regulated utilities, finance, manufacturing/service/retailing) and asks whether Berkshire ownership adds value over owning the 68 directly. Shareholders must answer that themselves.
- Two value measures, per share (A shares):
  - Investments: $4 (1965) to $74,129 (2005), 28.0% compounded.
  - Pre-tax operating earnings: $4 (1965) to $2,441 (2005), 17.2% compounded (30.2% over 1995-2005).
- Be suspicious of growth rates: check why the start and end years were picked. A poor base year gives a "breathtaking, but meaningless" rate. 1965 was an abnormally good base year, so the 17.2% is not flattered.
- Book value rose from $19 to $59,377 over 41 years, 21.5% compounded; 2005 gain was $5.6 billion, or 6.4% per share.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions, stock issuance and "buy to keep"
chunks.text:
- Existing businesses will produce only "modest growth"; satisfactory gains need major acquisitions.
- None of the 2005 deals involved issuing Berkshire shares. When a management buys a company with stock, its shareholders "are concurrently selling part of their interest in everything they own." He did this a few times and "on balance, my actions have cost you money."
- Berkshire has no "exit strategy": "We buy to keep." It has an "entrance strategy" of six criteria plus a price giving a reasonable return.
- 2005 deals:
  - Medical Protective (106-year-old malpractice insurer, bought June 30). Malpractice is a graveyard for many insurers, but Berkshire's underwriting discipline and financial strength help.
  - Forest River (RVs, $1.6 billion sales, 60 plants, 5,400 employees). A two-page fax arrived June 21, he made an offer the same afternoon he got figures, and they shook hands June 28. Owner Pete Liegl, 61, once sold to an LBO operator who meddled, left, watched the firm go bankrupt, and bought it back. Warren says he won't tell Pete how to run it.
  - Business Wire. President Cathy Baron Tamraz wrote after reading a WSJ piece; Warren liked "We run a tight ship... No secretaries or management layers here. Yet we'll invest big dollars to gain a technological advantage." Founder Lorry Lokey, 78, serves 25,000 clients in 150 countries.
  - Applied Underwriters (81% bought; payroll plus workers' comp). Founders Sid Ferenc and Steve Menzies keep 19%; 400 of 479 employees are in Omaha.
  - PacifiCorp via MidAmerican: Berkshire buys $3.4 billion of MidAmerican stock, supplemented by $1.7 billion of borrowing. Regulated utilities offer "the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns," not outsized profits.
- Bolt-ons also continue, such as Shaw spending about $550 million on two purchases.

chunks.heading: Insurance float, underwriting discipline and catastrophe risk
chunks.text:
- Float is money Berkshire holds but doesn't own, arising from premiums paid up front and claims that take years to be reported and settled. It grew from $20 million (1967) to $49 billion.
- Float is "wonderful" only if cheap. Its cost is the underwriting result. Berkshire earned an underwriting profit in about half of 39 years, making float "better than free." The industry almost always runs an underwriting loss, which can make float "devastatingly" expensive.
- 2005 float was costless despite $3.4 billion of hurricane losses (Katrina about $2.5 billion; Rita and Wilma about $0.9 billion), thanks to GEICO and other units. Underwriting profit was $53 million versus $1,551 million in 2004; float rose from $46.1 billion to $49.3 billion.
- Mega-cat stance: because nobody knows whether storm frequency or intensity has changed, he follows Pascal's wager logic. Write mega-cat only at much higher prices and with aggregate exposure that wouldn't cause distress if storms get worse. Cut back in 2004 when prices didn't move. Berkshire keeps the ability and appetite to be the world's largest writer if prices are right.
- Reserving lesson: "Surprises in insurance are far from symmetrical. You are lucky if you get one that is pleasant for every ten that go the other way." Insurers react to looming losses with optimism. He added about $125 million to MedPro's reserves right after buying it.
- "Underwriting discipline trumps all other goals" is the attitude shared by all Berkshire insurers. Financial strength is itself a selling point, since doctors want claims that take years to settle not to boomerang if the insurer fails.
- Other primary insurers earned a $324 million underwriting profit on $1,270 million of volume.

chunks.heading: GEICO and low-cost compounding
chunks.text:
- GEICO improved productivity 32% in two years: employment fell 4% while policy count grew 26%. Lower unit costs let it offer more value to customers.
- Policies in force grew 12.1%; U.S. private-passenger auto share rose from about 5.6% to 6.1%, each share point being $1.6 billion of sales. Underwriting profit was $1,221 million.
- Advertising went from $31 million (1996) to $502 million (2005), and he can't wait to spend more. It works because "more people can save money by insuring with us" than with any other national carrier, and quote-to-sale conversion hit a record.
- The simple formula (low costs, low prices, steady gains in profitable business) impressed him 55 years earlier; at 21 he wrote about it as "The Security I Like Best" when its market value was $7 million.
- Brand strength is not quantifiable but grew significantly.

chunks.heading: Moat-widening, management and CEO pay
chunks.text:
- Every day each business's competitive position weakens or strengthens. Delighting customers, eliminating unnecessary costs and improving products and services builds strength; indifference and bloat erode it. Daily effects are imperceptible, cumulative effects "enormous."
- "Widening the moat" is essential. When short-term and long-term conflict, widening the moat must take precedence. Bad decisions made to hit earnings targets leave damage no later brilliance can fix; auto and airline managers inherit this.
- Berkshire's managers are passionate and usually ran their businesses before Berkshire arrived; Warren's job is to "stay out of the way."
- "It's hard to overemphasize the importance of who is CEO." Jim Kilts transformed Gillette after capital-allocation blunders (the Duracell acquisition cost shareholders billions without showing in accounting); Warren says he earned every penny of his pay. It's difficult to overpay a truly extraordinary CEO of a giant enterprise, but "this species is rare."
- The yardstick ignored in acquisitions: whether business value received equals what was given up.
- Fixed-price options: a CEO with ten-year fixed-price options is rewarded for skipping dividends and buying back stock or wasting retained earnings. Fred Futile example: $1 billion earnings on $10 billion of net worth, 100 million shares, p/e of 10, all earnings used for buybacks gives 158% appreciation and about $158 million to the CEO with no business improvement. Retained earnings deployed at a 5% return still pay him $63 million.
- Remedy: options with strike prices adjusted for retained earnings, which boards almost never issue.
- Comp committees ratchet up pay through comparative data ("all the other kids have one"). Hank Greenberg's rule for a .246 hitter asking for a bonus: "Ask for a uniform."

chunks.heading: Friction costs, the Gotrocks family and Dow math
chunks.text:
- Owners in aggregate can earn only what their businesses earn, less frictional costs. One investor selling high means another buys high.
- Gotrocks parable: a family owning all American business earns about $700 billion a year. Brokers, then managers, consultants, and finally hedge/private-equity "hyper-Helpers" take slices. Frictional costs may reach about 20% of corporate earnings, so equity investors might earn only about 80% of what they would by doing nothing.
- Contingent-fee deals (heads the Helper takes winnings; tails the family loses and pays fixed fees) are especially costly.
- "Fourth Law of Motion: For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases."
- The Dow went from 65.73 to 11,497.12 in the 20th century, 5.3% compounded; matching that would require about 2,011,011 by 2099.
- Portfolio outlook: expect "no miracles." Holdings (American Express, Coca-Cola, P&G, Wells Fargo, Moody's, Anheuser-Busch, Wal-Mart, etc.) aren't bargains; they may double in ten years as per-share earnings grow 6-8% a year and stock prices match.

chunks.heading: Derivatives, debt, currency and acting promptly
chunks.text:
- Gen Re Securities: losses of $104 million in 2005 and $404 million cumulative while unwinding. Contracts fell from 23,218 to 741. One had a term of 100 years.
- Derivative danger: long or multi-variable contracts are hard to mark to market, invite "imagination" in valuation, and let two firms each book profit on the same trade, with compensation flowing from assumed numbers. Total derivatives are a multiple of 1998 levels; Berkshire is "a canary in this business coal mine." The time to fix levees was before Katrina.
- His mistake: he wasted years trying to sell the unit instead of closing it. "When a problem exists, whether in personnel or in business operations, the time to act is now." Charlie calls the dithering "thumb-sucking."
- Debt policy: Berkshire shuns debt except short-term repos on liquid government securities, borrowing against understood receivables (Clayton's manufactured-home loans, with a one-point markup; he prefers "better profits to better cosmetics" over securitizing), and MidAmerican's non-guaranteed utility debt, which is safe because of diversified, stable earnings.
- Why conservative: investors, directors and long-term insurance claimants depend on Berkshire, and he promised "total security, whatever comes." "A long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero."
- Currency bet: long-term positions are marked to market daily, costing $955 million pre-tax in 2005 (though $2.0 billion ahead overall). Rising U.S. rates create negative carry, so he favors foreign-currency-exposed equities. He sees the U.S. current-account deficit worsening and warns that the problem will address Americans "in an unpleasant way" if they don't address it first.

chunks.heading: Operating businesses, succession and temperament
chunks.text:
- Non-insurance group: $46.9 billion revenue, $2.6 billion pre-tax earnings, 22.2% on average tangible net worth with little leverage; only 10.1% on carrying value because of goodwill from premium purchase prices.
- Examples: Fruit of the Loom's men's and boys' underwear share rose from 44.2% to 48.7% of mass-market sales. R. C. Willey's never-on-Sunday approach beat seven-day competitors (Boise up 21% after 10%). See's: Chuck Huggins' 34-year tenure produced more than tenfold profit growth in a slow industry.
- Admitted misses: NetJets U.S. fell far into the red and he was "dead wrong" saying it would earn money in 2005. Managed commitment to service and safety stays.
- Succession: operations "won't miss a beat" if he dies; three capable younger CEO candidates exist and the board has unanimously chosen a successor. Someone else will handle marketable securities, as at GEICO for 26 years. The board must be willing to tell him if he declines, and he wants them to, since all his shares go to philanthropy.
- Lucky-in-America mindset: he credits birth in America, good parents and a "business gene" and tap-dances to work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2006 letter covers insurance float and disciplined super-cat pricing, buying businesses from owners who want a permanent home, simple performance-tied CEO pay, the decline of newspapers, truly independent directors, and the cost of Wall Street fees. It also describes the temperament he wants in a successor investor.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's 2006 Results and the Scale of the Business
chunks.text:
- Net worth rose $16.9 billion in 2006, lifting per-share book value 18.4%. Since present management took over 42 years earlier, book value grew from $19 to $70,281, a 21.4% compound annual rate.
- Warren believes this is a record one-year gain for an American business, excluding merger effects. Exxon Mobil earns more, but pays most of it out as dividends and repurchases rather than building net worth.
- He admits luck helped: after hurricane losses in 2004 and 2005, "Mother Nature... went on vacation" and super-cat red ink turned "very black."
- GEICO under Tony Nicely: policies rose 42% (5.7M to 8.1M) from yearend 2003 to 2006 while full-time-equivalent employees fell 3.5%, a 47% productivity gain.
  - That kept GEICO a low-cost producer even as ad spend rose to $631 million (from $238 million in 2003 and $31 million in 1995).
- Berkshire had 217,000 employees and revenues approaching $100 billion. Warren and Charlie grew skeptical of big organizations, which become "slow-thinking, resistant to change and smug."
  - Only one of the ten largest non-oil companies by market cap in 1965 (GM, Sears, DuPont, Kodak among them) was still on the 2006 list.
- His job model: work through great managers who run their own shows. His only tasks are to cheer them on, "sculpt and harden our corporate culture," and make major capital-allocation decisions.

chunks.heading: Yardsticks for Intrinsic Value
chunks.text:
