- No single statistic captures value. Succession depth, for example, matters but can't be proven with numbers.
- Two statistics matter most:
  - Per-share investments (including cash, excluding the finance operation): $4 in 1965, $159 in 1975, $2,407 in 1985, $21,817 in 1995, $80,636 in 2006. That is 27.5% compounded from 1965, but 12.6% from 1995.
  - Per-share pre-tax earnings from non-insurance businesses: $4 (1965), $4 (1975), $52 (1985), $175 (1995), $3,625 (2006). That is 17.9% compounded from 1965 and 31.7% from 1995. Non-insurance earnings rose 38% in 2006.
- Investment growth slowed because Berkshire shifted from buying marketable securities to buying operating businesses, which accelerated earnings growth.
- Large further gains will require "major, and sensible, acquisitions," which won't be easy. Berkshire's advantage is increasingly being "the buyer of choice" for business owners and managers.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions: ISCAR, TTI and Tuck-Ins
chunks.text:
- Warren began 2006 by closing about $6 billion of deals pending at yearend 2005: PacifiCorp, Business Wire and Applied Underwriters.
- ISCAR (Israel, cutting tools):
  - The deal began with a 1¼-page letter from chairman Eitan Wertheimer on October 25, 2005. It described generational-transfer concerns and said Berkshire would be "the ideal home."
  - A few hours in Omaha with Eitan, CEO Jacob Harpaz and CFO Danny Goldman convinced Warren they could be trusted to run the business with the same energy after a sale.
  - Berkshire bought 80% for $4 billion; the Wertheimer family kept 20%. Warren first had to learn tax and jurisdictional issues, having never bought a business based outside the U.S.
  - ISCAR sells small consumable tools used with expensive machine tools. "It's a business without magic except for that imparted by the people who run it": it makes money because it enables customers to make more money.
- TTI (Fort Worth electronic-components distributor):
  - Founder Paul Andrews, Jr., 64, owned about 80% and built sales from $112,000 to $1.3 billion over 35 years.
  - He saw how a founder's death disrupts a private company and wanted an owner he chose rather than a trust officer's or lawyer's auction.
  - He rejected a "strategic" buyer (which would chase "synergies" and dismantle his work) and private equity (which would load debt and flip it). He and Warren met the morning of November 15 and made a deal before lunch.
- Tuck-ins at Fruit of the Loom, MiTek, CTB, Shaw and Clayton:
  - Fruit bought Russell for about $1.2 billion including debt, and agreed to buy VF Corp.'s intimate apparel business, adding about $2.2 billion of sales and 23,000 employees.
  - Warren likes placing acquisitions under managers who have already proven themselves at Berkshire. MiTek's Gene Toombs made 14 acquisitions that beat his predictions.
- Berkshire still needs "elephants" to use its flood of incoming cash, so Warren and Charlie ignore "mice." He asks for acquisition leads "day or night."

chunks.heading: Insurance, Float and Super-Cat Risk
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought National Indemnity and National Fire & Marine from Jack Ringwalt on March 9, 1967 for $8.6 million.
  - Warren made the deal in minutes, waiving audit and due diligence so Jack had no chance to reconsider. Jack arrived late because he was hunting for a parking meter with time left, which told Warren he was "my kind of manager."
  - Float then was $17 million. At yearend 2006 it was $50.9 billion, with about $7 billion more coming from the Equitas contract.
- Float is "money we hold that is not ours but which we get to invest." Cost of float over time should be well below the industry's, "perhaps even falling to less than zero," but there will be bad years.
- 2006 underwriting profit was $3,838 million versus $53 million in 2005 (Gen Re $526M, B-H Reinsurance $1,658M, GEICO $1,314M, other primary $340M). Warren warns, "you won't soon see another like it."
- Super-cat: he doesn't know whether 2004-05 were aberrations or a warning about climate change, and says it would be "a huge mistake to bet that evolving atmospheric changes are benign." Katrina is nowhere near a worst case.
- Pricing discipline:
  - Berkshire is willing to lose $6 billion in a single event if paid appropriately for the risk.
  - It won't take even small exposures at prices that don't reflect loss probabilities: "Appropriate prices don't guarantee profits in any given year, but inappropriate prices most certainly guarantee eventual losses."
  - Rates fell as capital flooded super-cat, so Berkshire sharply cut wind exposure: "Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful."

chunks.heading: Equitas and Retroactive Reinsurance Accounting
chunks.text:
- Lloyd's began around 1688 at Edward Lloyd's coffee house. Passive "names" had unlimited liability "down to the last cufflink," but three centuries of retained cufflinks made the warning feel perfunctory.
- Asbestos and environmental claims from the 1980s caused Lloyd's to implode. In 1996 Equitas received £11.1 billion to pay all pre-1993 claims, pooling the misery and cutting syndicate squabbling.
- Berkshire's deal: Equitas pays $7.12 billion in cash and securities, and Berkshire pays all future claims and expenses up to $13.9 billion, which is $5.7 billion above Equitas's own estimate. Warren and Ajit Jain judged "the odds are in our favor," and "should we be wrong, Berkshire can handle it."
- Accounting (laid out in debits and credits because Warren dislikes opaque footnotes):
  - No profit or loss is booked at inception. Underwriting losses follow annually as the Deferred Charges for Reinsurance Assumed (DCRA) asset is amortized.
  - Retroactive contracts always produce underwriting losses. They are worth it only if investment income on the cash exceeds those losses.
  - Annual DCRA charges had been about $300 million and will rise to about $450 million after Equitas. Other insurance operations must earn at least that in underwriting gains for float to be cost-free, a hurdle Warren expects to clear in most years.
- Berkshire is the reinsurer of choice because some obligations (lifetime indemnity and medical payments to injured workers) can run 50 years or more, and no one else offers equal certainty.

chunks.heading: Operating Businesses, Newspapers and Compensation
chunks.text:
- The manufacturing, service and retailing group earned 25% on average tangible net worth with little leverage. Because many units were bought at premiums to net worth, the return on carrying value is 10.8%.
- Business-quality lessons:
  - "If you want to get a reputation as a good businessman, be sure to get into a good business." When fundamentals erode, talented managers only slow the decline.
  - Newspapers were once near-monopolies: for most of the 20th century they were the primary source of news and the easiest way to find jobs or grocery prices. The leading paper in a city took share of both readers and advertisers ("Survival of the Fattest") and gained pricing power in both. Warren warned of change in 1991. If cable, satellite and the internet had come first, newspapers "probably would never have existed."
  - The Buffalo News still has the highest market penetration of large U.S. papers, but profit margins will slide and "the days of lush profits... are over." Fixed costs are high, and non-economic buyers value local prominence. Berkshire will keep the paper unless it faces an irreversible cash drain.
- MiTek: Berkshire paid $420 million in 2001, lending $200 million at 9% and buying $198 million of stock at $10,000 a share. Fifty-five employees bought 2,200 shares for $22 million at the same price. Five years later, sales tripled and the stock was valued at $71,699 a share, and the debt was repaid.
- NetJets: revenue from flight operations is up 596% since 1998. Europe cost a cumulative $212 million pre-tax loss by mid-2006 before turning profitable. Worldwide pre-tax earnings were $143 million in 2006.
- Compensation:
  - Warren is a one-man compensation committee for about 40 CEOs, spending virtually no time on it; no CEO has voluntarily left in 42 years.
  - Incentives are tied only to results the CEO controls. A .300 hitter gets paid as one even if Berkshire performs poorly, and a .150 hitter gets nothing just because others did well. Berkshire's $61 billion of equities can swing 10% a year, and operating executives' pay shouldn't depend on that.
  - Excessive pay persists because CEO perks get copied ("All the other kids have one") and consultants pick favorable peer groups. Reform will come only if a few large institutional shareholders demand it.
- Real estate: slowing housing reflected weak lending, such as "optional" contracts and teaser rates. "A rolling loan gathers no loss," but unpaid payments add to principal, leaving borrowers a larger bill later.

chunks.heading: Investments, Currencies, Derivatives and Wall Street
chunks.text:
- Warren expected Berkshire's major holdings to grow earnings 6% to 8% a year. In 2006 American Express, Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble and Wells Fargo grew per-share earnings 18%, 9%, 8% and 11%.
- Currencies: direct foreign-exchange gains reached $2.2 billion since 2002, including $186 million in 2006, with the largest from the euro ($839.2 million). Berkshire nearly closed the position once interest-rate differentials turned negative in 2005, and shifted to foreign equities and U.S. companies with large foreign earnings.
- Trade deficit view:
  - He supports real trade, but the U.S. ran $0.76 trillion of "pseudo-trade" (imports with no exports exchanged, about 6% of GDP).
  - That means transferring assets or IOUs abroad, like a rich, self-indulgent family selling off assets to consume more than it produces. The U.S. "investment income" account turned negative in 2006 for the first time since 1915, creating "reverse compounding."
  - Americans will still live better in 10-20 years, but must ship part of production abroad as annual "tribute." He expects political backlash and thinks a "soft landing" is wishful thinking.
- Derivatives: Berkshire selectively writes a few, large contracts when they are mispriced; it had 62 outstanding, managed personally by Warren, with no counterparty credit risk, producing pre-tax profits in the hundreds of millions. This contrasts with the Gen Re derivatives wind-down: contracts fell from 23,218 to 197, with cumulative pre-tax loss of $409 million.
- The Gotrocks family and "2-and-20":
  - Investors keep paying ever-higher fees to "helpers" and holding unrealistic return expectations (pension plans use assumptions out of reach).
  - Under 2-and-20, a 10% gross return nets investors 6.4 points after 3.6 points go to the manager. On a $3 billion fund that is $108 million to the manager, while an index fund might have returned 15% for a token fee.
  - Adage: when someone with experience proposes a deal to someone with money, the person with money gets the experience and the experienced person gets the money.
- Walter Schloss:
  - Managed a partnership from 1956 to 2002, taking nothing unless investors made money, with one file cabinet, no secretary, and no inside information. His approach, per his son Edwin: "We try to buy stocks cheap."
  - Built his record across about 1,000 mostly lackluster securities, so a few big winners did not explain it. It could not be luck.
  - Efficient market theory was taught as scripture while Walter's record contradicted it, yet business schools made no attempt to study it. "If you are in the shipping business, it's helpful to have all of your potential competitors be taught that the earth is flat."

chunks.heading: Succession, Boards and Giving
chunks.text:
- Berkshire has three outstanding CEO candidates, all much younger than Warren. The investment side is less prepared: Lou Simpson is only six years younger. Warren plans to hire a younger investor (possibly several candidates) as future chief investment officer.
- Qualities sought in an investment successor:
  - Genetic wiring to recognize and avoid serious risks, including never-before-seen ones. Models commonly used by financial institutions can't spot certain perils, and "a single, big mistake could wipe out a long string of successes."
  - Temperament: "Independent thinking, emotional stability, and a keen understanding of both human and institutional behavior is vital to long-term investment success."
  - Retention: Berkshire on a resume makes someone marketable, so they need a person like Lou Simpson, who stayed despite being able to earn far more elsewhere.
- Board criteria: owner-oriented, business-savvy, interested and truly independent. Fees of $150,000 to $250,000 undermine true independence. Warren says to select for business judgment and to ask "Does he think like an intelligent owner?" rather than "stocking Noah's ark." Susan Decker (Yahoo! CFO, age 44) joins; Kim Chace steps down.
- Philanthropy: most of Warren's shares go to five foundations. Proceeds from remaining shares are to be spent within ten years of his estate closing, a roughly 25-year horizon. He prefers prompt spending by capable, motivated people over perpetual foundations whose vigor may fade, because future rich donors can fund the best organizations through a "market test of ideas."
- Foundation sales won't hurt the stock: annual volume is only 15% of shares, and the foundations would add at most three points. Berkshire should sell near intrinsic value, neither at a large discount nor a premium. Dividend, buyback and issuance decisions follow the usual rule: what is likely to deliver the best result for shareholders over time.

chunks.heading: Overhead, Taxes and Culture
chunks.text:
- Berkshire expected to pay about $4.4 billion of federal income tax on 2006 earnings, roughly half a day of U.S. government spending. The tax return ran 9,386 pages.
- World Headquarters has 19 employees in 9,708 square feet (plus 655 for Charlie in Los Angeles), with home-office payroll of $3,531,978: "We're careful when spending your money."
- Executives spend differently when it's not their own wallet. At Salomon, once free haircuts ended, one top executive cut his barber visits from weekly to every three weeks.
- Blue Chip Stamps (bought 1970): sales fell from $126 million to $25,920 in 2006, a reminder that a seemingly sure thing can fail.
- Warren feels fortunate: born in America, good parents, health, and a "business" gene that pays disproportionately, along with jobs they love. He is 76 and credits "Cherry Coke and hamburgers" for his health.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains what makes a great business (an enduring moat, low capital needs, not dependent on a superstar manager), contrasting See's Candy, FlightSafety and airlines. He owns up to unforced errors (Dexter, a TV station, US Air), shows why active management must trail index funds, and criticizes corporate accounting games.

chunks.heading: How Warren defines a great business: the moat and the "savings account" test
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie look for a) a business they understand, b) favorable long-term economics, c) able and trustworthy management, and d) a sensible price tag.
- He likes to buy the whole business or, where management is a partner, at least 80%. When control purchases of quality aren't available, he is happy to buy small stock-market portions of great businesses: "It's better to have a part interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone."
- A great business needs an enduring "moat" protecting excellent returns on invested capital. Competitors will repeatedly assault any "castle" earning high returns, so a formidable barrier is essential.
  - Low-cost producer moats: GEICO, Costco.
  - Powerful worldwide brand moats: Coca-Cola, Gillette, American Express.
  - Business history is full of "Roman Candles", companies whose moats proved illusory.
- He rules out industries prone to rapid, continuous change. "Creative destruction" is good for society but precludes investment certainty: "A moat that must be continuously rebuilt will eventually be no moat at all."
- He also rules out businesses that depend on a superstar manager. "If a business requires a superstar to produce great results, the business itself cannot be deemed great." A medical partnership led by the area's best brain surgeon loses its moat when the surgeon goes; the Mayo Clinic's moat endures even though you can't name its CEO.
- He wants long-term competitive advantage in a stable industry. Organic growth is a bonus; without it, he takes the earnings and buys similar businesses elsewhere. "There's no rule that you have to invest money where you've earned it."
- Three kinds of "savings accounts":
  - **Great:** pays an extraordinarily high rate that rises over the years.
  - **Good:** pays an attractive rate that is also earned on added deposits.
  - **Gruesome:** pays an inadequate rate and requires you to keep adding money at those returns.

chunks.heading: See's Candy: the prototype dream business
chunks.text:
- See's operates in an unexciting industry: per-capita U.S. consumption of boxed chocolates is low and flat, many once-important brands disappeared, and only three companies earned more than token profits over 40 years. Warren believes See's accounts for nearly half the industry's earnings.
- Purchase in 1972 (by Blue Chip Stamps): $25 million for a company with $30 million of sales and under $5 million of pre-tax earnings. Capital required was $8 million, so it earned about 60% pre-tax on invested capital.
- Capital needs were low because the product sold for cash (no receivables) and the production and distribution cycle was short (little inventory).
- Results by 2007: sales of $383 million and pre-tax profit of $82 million, with $40 million of capital needed. Volume grew from 16 million to 31 million pounds, only about 2% a year.
- Only $32 million was reinvested since 1972. Cumulative pre-tax earnings were $1.35 billion, all sent to Berkshire except that $32 million, and redeployed into other businesses.
- Typical companies growing earnings from $5 million to $82 million need about $400 million of capital. Earning $82 million on $400 million is not shabby, but it is "vastly different" for the owner from See's. Others in this camp: Microsoft, Google.
- Durable advantage was built by the See's family over 50 years and strengthened by Chuck Huggins and Brad Kinstler. Brad, moved from running Fechheimer and Cypress Insurance, raised See's profits more than 50% in two years.
- Warren calls himself a "one-price" guy, citing See's, where he nearly walked from the deal.

chunks.heading: Great vs. good vs. gruesome: FlightSafety and airlines
chunks.text:
- **FlightSafety (good, not great):** it has a durable advantage ("Going to any other flight-training provider than the best is like taking the low bid on a surgical procedure"), but growth demands heavy reinvestment.
  - 1996 purchase: $111 million pre-tax operating earnings, $570 million net fixed assets.
  - Since then depreciation totaled $923 million, capex $1.635 billion (mostly simulators costing over $12 million each; 273 in use).
  - 2007 pre-tax operating earnings were $270 million, up $159 million on an incremental investment of $509 million: "good, but far from See's-like".
  - Its "put-up-more-to-earn-more" profile is the norm for corporations, including Berkshire's regulated utilities.
- **Gruesome:** "The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines."
  - Durable advantage has been elusive since the Wright Brothers; a farsighted capitalist at Kitty Hawk "would have done his successors a huge favor by shooting Orville down."
  - Investors poured money into a bottomless pit, "attracted by growth when they should have been repelled by it."
  - Warren's own error: buying U.S. Air preferred in 1989. The dividend stopped soon after; he got lucky selling in 1998 for a hefty gain; the company then went bankrupt twice.

chunks.heading: Warren's confessed mistakes: See's near-miss, the TV station, Dexter
chunks.text:
He stresses these were "unforced errors"; no consultant, board or banker pushed him.
- **Almost blowing See's:** the seller asked $30 million and Warren was adamant at $25 million. The seller caved. Otherwise the $1.35 billion would have gone to someone else.
- **Passing on the Dallas-Fort Worth NBC station:** Tom Murphy of Capital Cities offered it for $35 million (a forced divestiture tied to a newspaper purchase).
  - TV stations were See's-like: little capital needed, good growth, cash-rich.
  - Murph, a friend he admired, "whispered 'buy'", but Warren didn't listen.
  - In 2006 the station earned $73 million pre-tax, at least $1 billion cumulatively since, with a capital value of about $800 million.
  - His explanation: "my brain had gone on vacation and forgot to notify me."
- **Dexter (worst deal to date):** a shoe business bought in 1993 for $433 million in Berkshire stock (25,203 A shares).
  - The competitive advantage vanished within a few years.
  - Paying in stock compounded the error: the cost to shareholders was about $3.5 billion, not $400 million. He gave away 1.6% of a wonderful business, then valued at $220 billion, for a worthless one.
  - He expects more mistakes. Quoting Bobby Bare on acquisitions: "I've never gone to bed with an ugly woman, but I've sure woke up with a few."
- General Re (merged 1998): he missed that its Tiffany reputation "outlived its factual underpinnings"; the 1998 company wasn't the 1968 or 1978 one.

chunks.heading: Managers, deal-making style and the Marmon purchase
chunks.text:
- **Berkshire's managers:** many have no financial need to work (they sold for large sums) and run their businesses because they love it. They have the job they want for the rest of their working lives, unlike managers elsewhere who see a division as a way station. Their scorecard is long-term performance, not getting Warren's job: "a here-today, here-forever mindset." He calls this rare, hard-to-replicate structure a real advantage.
- **Hiring:** Warren and Charlie "are not big fans of resumes"; they focus on "brains, passion and integrity."
  - Susan Jacques started at Borsheims 25 years earlier as a $4-an-hour saleswoman and became CEO in 1994 without a managerial background: "She's smart, she loves the business, and she loves her associates. That beats having an MBA degree any time."
  - Cathy Baron Tamraz, who began as a cab driver, grew Business Wire's earnings.
- **Marmon:** the largest cash purchase in Berkshire's history, signed Christmas Day 2007.
  - Berkshire buys 60% now for $4.5 billion and nearly all the rest within six years at a price tied to an earnings formula.
  - Marmon: about 125 businesses in nine sectors, $7 billion of sales, about 20,000 employees; Union Tank Car and its Canadian counterpart own 94,000 leased rail cars with an original cost of $5.1 billion.
  - Price was set from Marmon's financial statements alone, with no advisors and no nit-picking. "With the Pritzkers, as with Berkshire, a deal is a deal": the seller could trust the business, and Berkshire would close on the dot however chaotic the markets.
  - Warren's interest began in 1954 when Jay Pritzker's cocoa-bean tender for Rockwood Chocolate impressed him.
  - Byron Trott of Goldman Sachs, "the rare investment banker who puts himself in his client's shoes," facilitated it.
- **Richline:** a small jewelry-supplier combination (Dennis Ulrich) bought below Berkshire's normal earnings threshold; Warren bet on the manager building a large, high-return operation.

chunks.heading: Insurance, float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's value has two buckets: investments ($141 billion at yearend, excluding finance and utility operations) and earnings from non-insurance, non-investment businesses (66 companies).
- Float of $59 billion funds the investments. It is "free" as long as underwriting breaks even (premiums equal losses plus expenses). Underwriting is volatile, but Berkshire has been profitable over its history, and Warren expects breakeven or better, making the investments an unencumbered source of value.
- Per-share investments grew from $4 (1965) to $90,343 (2007), 27.1% a year, but the pace slowed as funds went into operating businesses. Per-share pre-tax earnings of non-insurance businesses grew from $4 to $4,093, 17.8% a year, accelerating to 23.5% over 1993-2007.
- Warren warns the past record "can't be duplicated or even approached" because the asset base is too large.
- Insurance results: float grew from $18.5 million (1967) to $58.7 billion (2007); underwriting profits were $3.4 billion in 2007 and $3.8 billion in 2006.
- He warned that 2007 benefited from a second straight catastrophe-light year, that prices were falling, and that industry margins would fall about four points in 2008. He expects lower insurance earnings for a few years.
- GEICO: the widest moat of any Berkshire insurer. Market share rose from 2.5% (1995) to 7.2%, while ad spend rose from $31 million to $751 million; it is expanding into motorcycles (2.1% to 6%), ATVs, RVs and commercial auto. CEO Tony Nicely has been with the company since age 18.
- General Re (CEO Joe Brandon, with Tad Montross) restored underwriting discipline and holds $23 billion of float. Ajit Jain's reinsurance unit takes one-of-a-kind mammoth transactions; the Equitas deal moved capped liabilities for a single $7.1 billion premium.
- Reserving is an "honor system": the $56 billion loss reserve (about $3 billion discounted) is a guess that is "sure to be wrong." Payments can run 50 years or more. He tells the "rented suit" funeral story about hidden, unknown liabilities and says he believes reserves are adequate but has "been wrong several times in the past."

chunks.heading: Evaluating investments, sales and derivatives
chunks.text:
- Warren measures stock holdings by the same two tests as owned businesses, not by yearly price moves: (1) improvement in earnings, allowing for industry conditions; (2) the more subjective test of whether the "moat" has widened.
- In 2007 American Express, Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble grew per-share earnings 12%, 14% and 14%; Wells Fargo's slipped, though he believes its intrinsic value still rose slightly.
- Start-ups are "not our game": Amex and Wells Fargo date from 1850 and 1852, P&G from 1837, Coke from 1886.
- **PetroChina sale:** bought 1.3% in 2002-03 for $488 million, valuing the company at about $37 billion; Charlie and Warren thought it worth about $100 billion. By the second half of 2007 the market valued it at $275 billion, roughly their view of its worth against other giant oil companies, so they sold for $4 billion and paid $1.2 billion of tax.
- **Derivatives:** 94 contracts.
  - 54 contracts cover defaults in high-yield bond indices; premiums received were $3.2 billion, losses paid $472 million, and the worst-case further payout is $4.7 billion.
  - Index put options on the S&P 500 and three foreign indices have 15- or 20-year terms, exercisable only at expiration (2019-2027); premiums received were $4.5 billion against a recorded $4.6 billion liability.
  - He sees both as profitable in aggregate and notes Berkshire holds the money, so there is no counterparty risk.
  - Mark-to-market accounting may swing quarterly earnings by $1 billion or more; he and Charlie won't mind, trading short-run earnings volatility for long-run net-worth gains, as in catastrophe insurance.
- **Currencies:** the only direct position in 2007 was the Brazilian real; direct currency positions earned $2.3 billion pre-tax over five years. In 2001-02 Berkshire bought €310 million of Amazon 6 7/8 bonds due 2010 at 57% of par (cost $169 million), which were priced as junk but weren't; "you can occasionally find markets that are ridiculously inefficient." About $118 million of the $246 million gain came from the falling dollar.
- Trade deficit view: a falling dollar hasn't fixed it (U.S. deficit with Germany rose from $36 billion to $45 billion as the euro rose; with Canada from $50 billion to $64 billion). Roughly $2 billion a day of "force-fed" dollars goes abroad. He favors reducing the imbalance sooner rather than later, without singling out countries or industries.

chunks.heading: Housing and lending bubble; pension and accounting games
chunks.text:
- **Lending folly:** "weakened lending practices" and the belief that house prices would rise forever (HPA) made borrower income and cash equity seem unimportant. "You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out." Clayton Homes' $11 billion portfolio of 300,000 borrowers performed in line with prior years.
- **Pension return assumptions:** the average S&P company assumed 8% (2006). With about 28% in bonds and cash earning no more than 5%, the rest must earn 9.2% net of fees.
  - The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century, only 5.3% a year. Matching that this century would require the Dow near 2,000,000 by 2099; a 10% annual return would imply about 24,000,000.
  - Dividends are about 2%; subtracting costs of 0.5%, equities would give about 7% even with 5.3% appreciation.
  - CEOs choose high assumptions to report higher earnings, with the cost landing after they retire. Charlie's line: "If you've hit three balls out of bounds to the left, aim a little to the right on the next swing."
- **Active vs. passive:** all investors earn the average return minus costs; index investors have very low costs, so active investors, with high transaction, management and advisory costs, must lose as a group. "The passive group – the 'know-nothings' – must win." "Beware the glib helper who fills your head with fantasies while he fills his pockets with fees."
- **Stock options:** CEOs lobbied the Senate to 88-9 to override FASB's push to expense options; only 2 of the S&P 500 chose the preferred route to expensing in six years, and some backdated grants.
- **Public pensions:** huge promises, inadequate funding, long fuse; politicians promise early retirement and generous COLAs that will be hard to keep.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's operating model, succession and temperament
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie view Berkshire's four sectors (insurance, regulated utilities, manufacturing/service/retail, finance) as separate businesses because their balance sheets differ.
- Manufacturing, service and retailing earned 23% on tangible net worth with minor leverage, but 9.8% on carrying value because of large premiums paid, reflected in goodwill.
- MidAmerican: Berkshire owns 87.4% with Walter Scott, Dave Sokol and Greg Abel; major moves are made only when all are unanimous. Warren agreed to buy at $35.05 a share in 1999 (he had decided the business was worth $35.00, then "caved" to give the bankers a nickel); 2007 earnings were $15.78 a share, or $15.01 normalized, so he was glad he wilted.
- Housing-linked units (Shaw, Acme Brick, Johns Manville, MiTek) saw pre-tax earnings fall 27%, 41%, 38% and 9%. Warren calls the setbacks minor and temporary since competitive positions and CEOs remain strong.
- Tuck-in acquisitions (Shaw, MiTek, Acme) continue.
- Succession: three internal CEO candidates are identified and the board knows its pick; four candidates for the investment role have been identified, all wealthy or well-off and motivated by more than compensation.
- Warren's attitude: he and Charlie, 84 and 77, say they "tap-dance to work" because they love the work and are helped by talented associates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2008 letter covers Berkshire's four goals, insurance float that cost less than zero, and buying when pessimism reigns. He owns up to his own errors (ConocoPhillips, Irish banks), warns against derivatives, history-based models and Black-Scholes at long durations, and says he won't trade sleep for extra profit.

chunks.heading: Surviving the 2008 crisis: Berkshire's four goals and what stays constant
chunks.text:
- **Performance in 2008:** Book value fell 9.6% (a $11.5 billion drop), the worst year for Berkshire and the S&P 500 in the 44-year record. Warren notes book value has compounded at 20.3% annually since 1965, from $19 to $70,530 per share.
- **Four goals in good years and bad:**
  1. Maintain a "Gibraltar-like" financial position with huge excess liquidity, modest near-term obligations and dozens of sources of earnings and cash.
  2. Widen the "moats" that give operating businesses durable competitive advantages.
  3. Acquire and develop new and varied streams of earnings.
  4. Expand and nurture the cadre of outstanding operating managers.
- **No market forecasting:** The S&P gained in 75% of the 44 years, and Warren guesses a similar share of the next 44 will be positive. He says neither he nor Charlie can predict winning and losing years, and "we don't think anyone else can either." He was certain the economy would be in shambles in 2009, but says that tells nothing about whether stocks rise or fall.
- **Long-run optimism:** The real U.S. standard of living rose nearly seven-fold in the 1900s while the Dow went from 66 to 11,497, despite two world wars, a dozen panics and recessions, a 21.5% prime rate in 1980 and the Depression. "America's best days lie ahead."
- **Liquidity over profit:** He sold part of Johnson & Johnson, Procter & Gamble and ConocoPhillips to fund purchases rather than lean on credit. "We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations. When forced to choose, I will not trade even a night's sleep for the chance of extra profits."

chunks.heading: Buying when others are fearful: 2008 capital allocation
chunks.text:
- **Principle:** "When investing, pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy." He recalls Ben Graham's line "Price is what you pay; value is what you get," and says he likes buying quality merchandise marked down, "whether we're talking about socks or stocks."
- **Falling prices are welcome** if funds are available to increase positions.
- **Fixed-income deals:** $14.5 billion of securities issued by Wrigley, Goldman Sachs and General Electric. High current yields made them satisfactory on their own, and each carried a substantial equity participation as a bonus.
- **Three large insurance-portfolio investments** on terms unavailable in normal markets, expected to add about $1.5 billion pre-tax to annual earnings, plus the Marmon acquisition (64% owned, remainder to be bought over six years) and several tuck-in acquisitions.
- **Risk repricing:** The investment world went "from underpricing risk to overpricing it." Good-grade municipal and corporate bonds offered yields that would have seemed unthinkable earlier, while Treasuries paid a pittance. He calls the late-2008 Treasury bond "bubble" nearly as extraordinary as the Internet and housing bubbles.
- **Cash is not safe:** Holding cash equivalents or long-term governments at present yields "is almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long," because purchasing power erodes.
- **Against applause:** "Approval... is often counter-productive because it sedates the brain." He warns: "Beware the investment activity that produces applause; the great moves are usually greeted by yawns."
- **Operating businesses over securities:** Berkshire's focus remains the earnings segment. "We like buying underpriced securities, but we like buying fairly-priced operating businesses even more."

chunks.heading: Admitting mistakes: ConocoPhillips and the Irish banks
chunks.text:
- **ConocoPhillips:** He bought a large stake when oil and gas prices were near their peak, did not anticipate the second-half collapse, and says the terrible timing "has cost Berkshire several billion dollars." He still thinks the odds are good that oil sells far higher than the then-current $40-$50, but admits "so far I have been dead wrong."
- **Irish banks:** He spent $244 million on two Irish bank stocks that "appeared cheap to me." They were written down to $27 million, an 89% loss, and fell further afterward. He calls them "unforced errors."
- **Errors of omission:** He admits "sucking my thumb when new facts came in that should have caused me to re-examine my thinking and promptly take action."
- **Unrealized declines:** Holdings that fell with the market did not bother him. Investments per share fell from $90,343 to $77,793, caused by market prices rather than sales.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- **Float:** $58.5 billion of money held and invested for Berkshire's benefit. With a sixth straight underwriting gain, the float cost less than zero; Berkshire was paid $2.8 billion to hold it in 2008.
- **Industry contrast:** Over 25 years to 2007, insurers' return on net worth averaged 8.5% versus 14.0% for the Fortune 500. Most insurers eventually book substantial underwriting losses. Warren expects Berkshire to average an underwriting profit, because its managers run entrenched, valuable franchises, while acknowledging it will have terrible years too.
- **GEICO (Tony Nicely):** Market share grew from 2.0% in 1993 to 7.7%, making it the number three auto insurer. Policies per employee rose from 299 to 439 in five years. It grows because it saves drivers money, and efficiency is the key to low cost. It also expanded in motorcycles (+23.4%), RVs, ATVs and commercial autos.
- **General Re:** Culture had deteriorated (loose underwriting, reserving and expenses) in a problem Warren says he failed to detect at the 1998 purchase. Joe Brandon and Tad Montross restored discipline. In reinsurance, "a promise is no better than the person or institution making it," and General Re is the only reinsurer backed by an AAA corporation.
- **Ajit Jain's reinsurance division:** 31 employees writing very large, unusual risks with speed. Year-end float by unit: General Re $21.1B, BH Reinsurance $24.2B, GEICO $8.5B, Other Primary $4.7B.
- **Manager quality:** He credits managers who excel "to a degree Charlie and I never dreamed possible," even without a favorable industry tailwind.

chunks.heading: Tax-exempt bond insurance and the flaw in back-tested models
chunks.text:
- **BHAC:** Berkshire Hathaway Assurance Company was activated in 2008 to insure municipal bonds. The monolines had drifted into ever-riskier mortgage-related business under competitive pressure ("I was Snow White, but I drifted").
- **A mistake that worked out:** Berkshire offered to take over about $822 billion of insured bonds from the three largest monolines at a 1.5% rate. They refused, and Warren later saw the offer was severely underpriced. Berkshire instead wrote about $15.6 billion of secondary-market "second-to-pay" insurance, averaging 3.3% rates, plus $3.7 billion of primary business for a $96 million premium.
- **Why the business is dangerous:** Historic low default rates reflect uninsured bonds. Local holders of uninsured bonds (as in 1975 New York City) feel pressure to make sacrifices. If everything is insured, cities will prefer pain for a "far-away bond insurer" over tax increases. Losses would also be highly correlated, much like natural-catastrophe insurance, where a string of loss-free years can precede a devastating one. Pension underfunding adds to the fiscal stress.
- **Lesson on models:** History-based models failed on mortgages because they ignored that house prices had skyrocketed and lending standards had deteriorated, so the "past" universe differed from the "current" one. "If merely looking up past financial data would tell you what the future holds, the Forbes 400 would consist of librarians." His advice: "Beware of geeks bearing formulas."

chunks.heading: Lending discipline: Clayton Homes and the housing crisis
chunks.text:
- **Clayton:** The largest manufactured-home company (27,499 units, about 34% of the industry) with 198,888 borrowers who kept paying through the housing crash. Median FICO was 644 versus a national 723, and about 35% were below 620. Delinquency was 3.6% and foreclosures 3.0% of originated loans.
- **Why it worked:** Borrowers compared full-bore payments to actual, not hoped-for, income. They did not rely on refinancing or teaser rates, and did not assume they could always sell at a profit. "Lending 101."
- **Industry folly:** Both the 1997-2000 manufactured-housing bust and the 2004-07 conventional boom involved "borrowers who shouldn't have borrowed being financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent," relying on house-price appreciation.
- **Foreclosure driver:** Most foreclosures happen because borrowers can't make the monthly payment, not merely because homes are worth less than the mortgage.
- **Policy lessons:** Require a real down payment of at least 10%, payments the borrower's verified income can handle, and purchases motivated by enjoyment and utility rather than profit or refi possibilities. "Putting people into homes... shouldn't be our country's primary objective. Keeping them in their homes should be the ambition."
- **Funding-cost distortion:** Government-guaranteed lenders had minimal funding costs while AAA Berkshire faced record spreads. "At the moment, it is much better to be a financial cripple with a government guarantee than a Gibraltar without one."

chunks.heading: Derivatives: danger, and why Berkshire still writes some
chunks.text:
- **Core warning:** Derivatives raise leverage and risk and make big banks nearly impossible to analyze. Warren points to Freddie and Fannie's years of misstatement despite 100+ regulatory staff, and to Gen Re's 23,218 contracts with 884 counterparties, which cost over $400 million and five years to unwind. His takeaway: "I liked you better before I got to know you so well."
- **Transparency won't fix it:** Auditors can't audit and regulators can't regulate such books. Counterparty claims built over years create "a frightening web of mutual dependence."
- **Why Berkshire writes them:** He believes each of its 251 contracts was mispriced at inception. Counterparties pay premiums up front, so Berkshire holds the money and carries no meaningful counterparty risk. The derivatives "float" was $8.1 billion. He initiates and monitors every position, since "the CEO of any large financial organization must be the Chief Risk Officer as well."
- **Equity puts:** $37.1 billion across the S&P 500, FTSE 100, Euro Stoxx 50 and Nikkei 225, maturing 2019-2028, with $4.9 billion of premiums received. Payment is due only if the index is below its starting level at maturity. The recorded liability was $10 billion (a $5.1 billion mark-to-market loss). Collateral posting was under 1% of the securities portfolio, a lethal risk at other institutions.
- **Credit default contracts:** High-yield index contracts brought $3.4 billion of premiums versus $542 million of losses paid. Single-name CDS were $4 billion across 42 companies ($93 million annual premium). He avoids contracts requiring collateral posting.
- **Mark-to-market swings:** He endorses the accounting but says the resulting earnings swings "neither cheer nor bother" him, and that the "downs" can offer chances to expand positions on good terms.
- **Black-Scholes critique:** For a hypothetical 100-year $1 billion S&P put at 903, the formula gives a $2.5 million premium. Warren sees a under-1% chance of decline and a likely 50% maximum loss, so expected loss is $5 million; the premium would need to earn only 0.7% a year to cover it. Even in the worst case the implied borrowing cost is 6.2%. He argues volatility from past price moves is irrelevant over long periods (like valuing a farm from a manic-depressive neighbor's daily quotes), and that the formula overstates the liability on long-term puts. He still uses it for reporting to avoid appearing to be among CEOs who invent flattering valuations.

chunks.heading: Utilities, acquisitions and being the "buyer of choice"
chunks.text:
- **Goal:** Be the "buyer of choice," especially for family-built businesses, by deserving it: keep promises, avoid leveraging acquired businesses, grant unusual autonomy, and hold through thick and thin.
- **Contrast with private equity:** Warren says such buyers treat acquisitions as "merchandise" with exit strategies, and that "private equity" is misleading because buyouts usually cut the acquiree's equity share. Acquirees bought two to three years earlier were in danger from piled-on debt, with bank debt below 70 cents on the dollar.
- **Regulated utilities:** MidAmerican (87.4% diluted ownership) reinvests all earnings. In 2008 it spent $1.8 billion on wind versus $1.1 billion pre-tax earnings at the Western and Iowa utilities, and it has paid no dividend since 2000. Iowa electric prices have been unchanged since purchase and are promised steady through 2013. Wind in Iowa went from zero to nearly 20% of capacity, and PacifiCorp wind went from 33 to 794 megawatts. In return, regulators allow a fair return on the sums invested.
- **Regulators judge history:** They call counterparts in other states, so behavior in current jurisdictions determines future welcome. Kern River moved from 9th to 1st in customer satisfaction, Northern Natural from 39th to 3rd.
- **Operating group:** The non-insurance businesses earned 17.9% on average tangible net worth with little leverage, but only 8.1% on carrying value because of premiums paid. Warren credits tuck-in acquisitions (Iscar's Tungaloy purchase, etc.) enabled by financial strength, and notes CTB earned $89 million pre-tax in 2008 versus the $140 million paid in 2002.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett restates how Berkshire measures itself, what it avoids (unknowable industries, dependence on outsiders, bureaucracy), how insurance float works, and why issuing undervalued stock is costly. He admits the GEICO credit card and NetJets blunders and urges buying big when fear is high.

chunks.heading: Berkshire measures itself against the S&P 500, using book value as a proxy
chunks.text:
- Warren picked the S&P 500 as the bogey because shareholders "at virtually no cost" can match it with an index fund. His question: "Why should they pay us for merely duplicating that result?"
- A fixed, unbending yardstick stops managers from "seeing where the arrow of performance lands and then painting the bull's eye around it."
- The ideal measure is the change in per-share intrinsic value, but it can't be calculated with precision. Per-share book value is the crude proxy. Book value understates intrinsic value at most companies, and Berkshire's insurance business shows a huge gap.
- 2009: net worth rose $21.8 billion, and per-share book value rose 19.8%. Since 1965 book value went from $19 to $84,487, which is 20.3% compounded annually.
- Market price compounded at 22% a year over the same 45 years. Market gain was 801,516% against 434,057% for book value. Berkshire shares sold at a discount to book in 1965 (underearning textile assets) and now sell at a premium to its first-class businesses.
- Market prices alone can mislead over a decade. Starting prices can be "nosebleed" levels, as Microsoft and GE found.
- Track record: in all 41 five-year periods from 1965-69 to 2005-09, Berkshire's book value gain beat the S&P's.
- Berkshire beat the S&P in all eleven years the S&P was negative. Warren says "our defense has been better than our offense."
- The downside: the advantage shrinks as size grows. "Huge sums forge their own anchor."

chunks.heading: What Berkshire doesn't do: invert, avoid, and stay liquid
chunks.text:
- Warren cites Charlie Munger: "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there." This is Jacobi's "Invert, always invert."
- **Avoid businesses whose futures can't be evaluated, however exciting the product.**
  - Autos (1910), aircraft (1930) and TV sets (1950) had obvious growth. Competition then decimated almost all entrants, and survivors "tended to come away bleeding."
  - Seeing growth doesn't tell you the profit margins and returns on capital once competitors battle.
  - Berkshire sticks with businesses whose profit picture for decades is reasonably predictable. He still expects mistakes.
- **Never depend on "the kindness of strangers."**
  - Too-big-to-fail isn't a fallback. Cash needs should be "dwarfed by our own liquidity," refreshed by earnings from many businesses.
  - At the peak of the September 2008 crisis Berkshire put in $15.5 billion. $9 billion bolstered capital at three American businesses. $6.5 billion funded the Wrigley purchase.
  - The cost is steep: $20 billion-plus of cash equivalents earns "a pittance." But "we sleep well."
- **Don't woo Wall Street.** He wants partners who buy a business they understand and agree with its policies. Common goals make a good owner-manager "marriage."
- Berkshire posts financials early on weekends so owners can digest them in a non-trading period.
- Warren prefers direct, unabridged communication. A 2008 letter line ("the economy will be in shambles... but that conclusion does not tell us whether the market will rise or fall") was reported with only the first half. The Dow was 7,063 that day and 10,428 at year-end.

chunks.heading: Decentralized management: pay the visible cost of bad decisions, avoid bureaucracy
chunks.text:
- Subsidiaries run on their own with little supervision or monitoring.
- The cost: Berkshire is sometimes late spotting management problems, and some decisions would have been made differently.
- The gain: an owner-oriented attitude "invaluable and too seldom found in huge organizations."
- "We would rather suffer the visible costs of a few bad decisions than incur the many invisible costs that come from decisions made too slowly – or not at all – because of a stifling bureaucracy."
- After BNSF, Berkshire has about 257,000 employees and hundreds of operating units. It will not become a monolith with committees, budget presentations and layers of management.
- Warren and Charlie limit themselves to four jobs: allocating capital, controlling enterprise risk, choosing managers and setting their compensation.
- Risk control is never delegated. Warren personally initiates and monitors every derivatives contract (with small exceptions at a few subsidiaries). "If Berkshire ever gets in trouble, it will be my fault. It will not be because of misjudgments made by a Risk Committee or Chief Risk Officer."

chunks.heading: Insurance float and the economics of property-casualty
chunks.text:
- P/C insurance has been Berkshire's growth engine. The P/C companies are carried at $15.5 billion above net tangible assets, but are worth far more.
- Insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later (sometimes over decades). The held money is "float" that is invested for Berkshire. Float stays stable relative to premium volume, so it grows as business grows.
- With an underwriting profit, Berkshire gets "the use of free money" and is "paid for holding it."
- Competition usually pushes the industry to an underwriting loss, which is what it pays to hold float. Catastrophe-heavy years can wipe out float income.
- The industry's return on tangible equity has lagged the S&P 500 for decades. Berkshire's results come from outstanding managers running unusual businesses.
- Float grew from $16 million in 1967 to $62 billion at the end of 2009 ($61.9 billion). Berkshire has had seven straight years of underwriting profit. He expects profit in most, but not all, future years, which would make the float cost-free.
- Underwriting profit and year-end float in 2009 (2008 in brackets):
  - General Re: $477M profit (342), float $21.0B
  - BH Reinsurance: $349M (1,324), float $26.2B
  - GEICO: $649M (916), float $9.6B
  - Other primary: $84M (210), float $5.1B
  - Total: $1,559M (2,792)
- **GEICO:**
  - Run by Tony Nicely, who joined at 18.
  - Advertising budget is $800 million, close to twice the runner-up.
  - Market share rose from 2.5% to 8.1% since the 1996 control purchase, a net seven million policyholders.
  - Berkshire bought about one-third for $47 million in 1976-80, then the remaining 50% for $2.3 billion in January 1996, "about 50 times the cost of our original purchase."
  - GEICO went from sixth to third largest auto insurer, with float from $2.7 billion to $9.6 billion. It had an underwriting profit in 13 of 14 years.
  - Its edge is "low-cost producer" status. Customers stay for service and price.
- **Ajit Jain** (joined 1985) built the reinsurance operation with just 30 people.
  - He writes billion-dollar limits and keeps every dime of the risk.
  - He took over Lloyds liabilities with a single $7.1 billion premium.
  - In 2009 he negotiated a life reinsurance contract that could bring $50 billion of premium over about 50 years.
  - "If Charlie, I and Ajit are ever in a sinking boat... swim to Ajit."
- **General Re** (Tad Montross) had an outstanding underwriting year and large float per dollar of premium. It reached 100% ownership of Cologne Re.

chunks.heading: Mistakes and own-the-error examples
chunks.text:
- **GEICO credit card.**
  - Warren thought GEICO policyholders would be good credit risks.
  - They got business "of the wrong type."
  - Pre-tax losses were about $6.3 million. The $98 million receivables portfolio sold for 55 cents on the dollar, an additional $44 million loss.
  - GEICO's managers had warned him. He wrote: "I was just older."
- **NetJets.**
  - In eleven years of ownership the company had an aggregate pre-tax loss of $157 million.
  - Debt rose from $102 million to $1.9 billion in April 2009. Without Berkshire's guarantee it "would have been out of business."
  - Warren: "I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition."
  - Dave Sokol became CEO in August. Debt fell to $1.4 billion, and the company turned solidly profitable after a $711 million loss in 2009.
  - Safety and service standards stay at the top. Warren and his family fly NetJets on the same terms as other owners: "we eat our own cooking."
- **Bond opportunity missed.** Corporate and municipal bonds were "ridiculously cheap" relative to Treasuries in the crisis. Warren bought some but "should have done far more." His lesson: "Big opportunities come infrequently. When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble."

chunks.heading: Capital-intensive businesses: utilities, railroads, and the shift in appetite
chunks.text:
- Berkshire owns 89.5% of MidAmerican Energy Holdings (Dave Sokol, Greg Abel; Walter Scott family is a major owner). 2009 net earnings were $1,157 million ($1,071 million applicable to Berkshire).
- It owns UK utilities, Iowa and western US utilities, and pipelines carrying about 8% of US gas.
- MidAmerican has paid no dividend in ten years. In the last three years the Iowa and Western utilities earned $2.5 billion and spent $3 billion on wind.
- Regulated utilities and BNSF share traits:
  - Essential services.
  - Heavy investment far above depreciation for decades.
  - Long planning horizons.
  - Dependence on regulators who allow a fair return.
  - Warren calls the arrangement a "social compact." If either side shirks, both suffer.
- BNSF results will be reported in this regulated utility section. Both businesses use substantial debt not guaranteed by Berkshire and retain most earnings.
- Warren's view shifted: "In earlier days, Charlie and I shunned capital-intensive businesses." Still, "the best businesses by far for owners continue to be those that have high returns on capital and that require little incremental investment to grow."
- Because Berkshire will generate ever more cash, it is now willing to buy businesses that need large capital spending, provided they can reasonably earn decent returns on incremental capital. He expects "above-average, though certainly not spectacular, returns."

chunks.heading: Stock as currency: why undervalued shares make bad acquisition currency
chunks.text:
- Issuing about 95,000 shares (6.1% of shares outstanding) for BNSF was distasteful. "If we wouldn't dream of selling Berkshire in its entirety at the current market price, why in the world should we 'sell' a significant part of the company at that same inadequate price?"
- Buying with undervalued stock hurts your shareholders. Example:
  - Companies A and B are both worth $100 per share but trade at $80.
  - A's CEO offers 1.25 A shares per B share.
  - B's holders end up with 55.6% of the combined company and A's holders with 44.4%.
  - The CEO still gains a bigger company, "where size tends to correlate with both prestige and compensation."
- If the acquirer's stock is overvalued, using it works to its advantage. Bubbles lead to serial stock issuance by promoters spending "counterfeit money" in "air-for-assets" deals, as in the late 1960s.
- BNSF: sellers valued the offer at $100 per share. 40% was paid in Berkshire stock, but only about 30% of the total cost counted Berkshire's earlier cash purchases of BNSF shares.
- It was a close decision, justified by deploying $22 billion of cash in a business he understood and liked for the long term, run by Matt Rose. More stock would have made it senseless.
- Board advice: bankers detail why the target is worth more than its market price, but never value what is given up when stock pays. Warren suggests directors hire a second advisor, paid only if the deal fails, to argue against it. Otherwise: "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut."
- Anecdote:
  - A well-run bank trading near book value at a very low P/E bought a much smaller bank for nearly three times book value in stock.
  - The excuse was "we need to show that we are in the hunt."
  - Charlie's reply: "Are we supposed to applaud because the dog that fouls our lawn is a Chihuahua rather than a Saint Bernard?"

chunks.heading: Investing in fear, derivatives, and CEO accountability
chunks.text:
- Cash equivalents fell from $44.3 billion entering 2008 to $30.6 billion at year-end 2009 ($8 billion earmarked for BNSF), after $17 billion of retained operating earnings.
- Warren: "A climate of fear is their best friend. Those who invest only when commentators are upbeat end up paying a heavy price for meaningless reassurance."
- "What counts in investing is what you pay for a business – through the purchase of a small piece of it in the stock market – and what that business earns in the succeeding decade or two."
- Preferred-style positions bought in 18 months: Dow, GE, Goldman Sachs, Swiss Re and Wrigley, cost $21.1 billion, carried at $26.0 billion, paying about $2.1 billion a year in dividends and interest.
- Big 2009 stock sales: ConocoPhillips, Moody's, Procter & Gamble and Johnson & Johnson. He still expected those stocks to rise.
- Biggest holdings by market value: Coca-Cola $11.4B (cost $1,299M), Wells Fargo $9.0B (cost $7,394M), American Express $6.1B (cost $1,287M), Procter & Gamble $5.0B (cost $533M).
- Derivatives: Berkshire holds contracts it thinks are mispriced, as it does with stocks and bonds.
  - Derivatives float was about $6.3 billion.
  - Only a few contracts require collateral. At the low point the posting requirement was $1.7 billion.
  - Valuation swings are large (2009 quarterly: -1.517, +2.357, +1.732, +1.052 billion) but "neither cheer nor bother" him, since they don't affect cash or investment holdings.
  - Danger comes from extreme leverage or counterparty risk, which Berkshire avoids.
- CEO accountability:
  - Boards of huge financial institutions are "derelict" if CEOs don't bear full responsibility for risk control.
  - Shareholders lost 90% or more in failures, over $500 billion in the four biggest fiascos.
  - CEOs and directors "still live in grand style."
  - He argues they should pay "a heavy price" not reimbursable by the company or insurance. "Some meaningful sticks now need to be part of their employment picture."

chunks.heading: Operating businesses, housing, and Warren's view of his own luck
chunks.text:
- **McLane:** pre-tax earnings of $344 million on $31.2 billion sales, slightly over one cent per dollar. Warren says its "prime asset... is Grady" Rosier.
- Several businesses grew profits as sales shrank, "always an exceptional managerial achievement." Among them were See's, Benjamin Moore, Borsheims and Nebraska Furniture Mart.
- **Marmon** had a record 13.5% pre-tax margin on sales down 27%. **Iscar** stayed profitable while competitors lost money.
- Construction-linked businesses (Shaw, Johns Manville, Acme Brick, MiTek) earned $227 million combined, down 82.5% from $1.295 billion in 2006.
- **Housing:**
  - US starts were 554,000 in 2009, the lowest in 50 years of data. Warren calls this "good news" for clearing the overhang.
  - Starts had run about 2 million a year against household formations of about 1.2 million.
  - Clayton's industry output fell from 382,000 units (1999) to 60,000 (2009). Fleetwood, Champion and Oakwood went bankrupt.
  - Conventional site-built buyers get about 5¼% mortgages through agency guarantees. Factory-built buyers pay about 9%. Warren flags that Berkshire has "a dog in this fight."
  - Clayton buyers performed well because they intended to live in the home, not resell or refinance. Loans were based on verified incomes ("we weren't making 'liar's loans'").
  - Berkshire uses its credit to support Clayton's mortgages and charges Clayton a fee ($116 million in 2009).
- Berkshire became a 50% owner of Berkadia Commercial Mortgage, a servicer of a $235 billion portfolio, with Leucadia's Joe Steinberg and Ian Cumming.
- Closing note: Warren and Charlie are "lucky beyond our dreams" and "would gladly pay substantial sums to have our jobs."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2010 letter explains how to judge intrinsic value (investments, operating earnings, and how retained earnings get deployed), why capital-allocation flexibility and an owner-minded culture are Berkshire's edge, and how GEICO's goodwill far exceeds book value. It also covers insurance discipline and float, ignoring net income, and avoiding leverage.

chunks.heading: Book value record and what Warren treats as the right performance yardstick
chunks.text:
- Per-share book value rose 13% in 2010. Over 46 years it grew from $19 to $95,453, a 20.2% compounded annual rate.
- Warren says managers of other people's money should set performance goals at the start. Otherwise they "shoot the arrow of performance and then paint the bull's-eye around wherever it lands."
- Berkshire's stated goal: grow per-share intrinsic value faster than the S&P 500 including dividends. If it can't over time, "we have done nothing for our investors," who could have owned an index fund.
- Intrinsic value can't be calculated precisely. He and Charlie, asked separately, would give two different answers. So Berkshire tracks book value, an understated proxy whose premium to true value seldom swings wildly year to year.
- Size caps returns. "The bountiful years... will never return." Going forward he hopes to beat the S&P by "several points," which would mean better relative results in bad markets and poorer ones in strong markets.
- Yearly figures are "neither to be ignored nor viewed as all-important." Investment and operating decisions don't run on the earth's orbit. GEICO spent $900 million on advertising in 2010 to win policyholders who bring no immediate profit, and he would spend twice that if it could be done productively, even at the cost of short-term results.

chunks.heading: The three pillars of intrinsic value, and the "what will they do with the money" test
chunks.text:
- **Investments:** stocks, bonds and cash equivalents totaled $158 billion at market value at yearend 2010. Insurance float funds $66 billion of that. Float is "free" if underwriting breaks even. Per-share investments grew 19.9% a year over 40 years, but only 6.6% a year in 2000-2010 as capital shifted to buying operating businesses.
- **Operating earnings from non-insurance, non-investment businesses (68 companies):** per-share pre-tax earnings went from $2.87 in 1970 to $5,926.04 in 2010, 21.0% compounded. Berkshire's stock price rose 22.1% a year over the same span.
- **Normal earning power** (no mega-catastrophe, a business climate better than 2010 but weaker than 2005-06): about $17 billion pre-tax and $12 billion after-tax, excluding capital gains.
- **Third, subjective element:** how well retained earnings will be redeployed. "Some companies will turn these retained dollars into fifty-cent pieces, others into two-dollar bills."
- An outside investor "stands by helplessly" while management reinvests his share of earnings. If the CEO is good, reinvestment prospects add to value. If the CEO's talents or motives are suspect, today's value must be discounted.
- His example: a dollar in the hands of the CEOs of Sears Roebuck or Montgomery Ward in the late 1960s had a very different destiny from a dollar entrusted to Sam Walton.
- Market price and intrinsic value "often follow very different paths – sometimes for extended periods – but eventually they meet."

chunks.heading: Why Berkshire's capital allocation is an advantage, and the textile mistake
chunks.text:
- Most companies reinvest only within their own industry, a universe that is "tiny and quite inferior" to what the wider world offers. Competition for the few opportunities makes the seller king.
- Berkshire faces no institutional restraints. Warren and Charlie are "limited only by our ability to understand the likely future of a possible acquisition." Once that hurdle is cleared, they can compare any opportunity against many others.
- They also compare businesses against marketable securities, which most managements don't. "Often, businesses are priced ridiculously high against what can likely be earned from investments in stocks or bonds. At such moments, we buy securities and bide our time."
- Cash from low-reinvestment businesses such as See's Candies and Business Wire was used as part of the stake to buy BNSF.
- His own error in 1965: Berkshire was a money-losing textile business. "The dumbest thing I could have done was to pursue 'opportunities' to improve and expand the existing textile operation – so for years that's exactly what I did," culminating in buying another textile company. He eventually moved into insurance and then other industries.
- Some businesses earn 25% after tax to over 100% on unleveraged net tangible assets, others 12-20%, and a few very poor returns because he "misjudged either the competitive strength of the business I was purchasing or the future economics of the industry." He tries to look out ten or twenty years, "but sometimes my eyesight has been poor."

chunks.heading: Management model and culture: volunteers, owners, and a tiny headquarters
chunks.text:
- "Hire well, manage little." Managers get a letter from Warren every two years and call when they wish. They have no headquarters meetings, financing worries or Wall Street harassment. "Our trust is in people rather than process."
- Many CEOs are independently wealthy and work because they love it. "They are volunteers, not mercenaries," and no one can offer them a more enjoyable job. Styles vary widely (MBAs and non-graduates, budget-driven and seat-of-the-pants), like an all-star team with different batting styles.
- Directors act like owners. They get token pay, no options or restricted stock, and no D&O insurance. They and their families own over $3 billion of stock. "If they mess up with your money, they will lose their money as well."
- Many managers sought out Berkshire as the buyer of a family-owned business and arrive with an owner's mindset.
- Cultures self-propagate. He quotes Churchill: "You shape your houses and then they shape you." Bureaucratic procedures beget bureaucracy and "imperial corporate palaces induce imperious behavior."
- Headquarters rent is $270,212 a year, and the home-office investment in furniture, art, equipment and a Coke dispenser totals $301,363. Twenty people work on one floor.
- Compensation, the annual meeting and the annual report are designed to reinforce a culture that will "repel and expel managers of a different bent."
- Reputation memo to managers: "We can afford to lose money – even a lot of money. But we can't afford to lose reputation – even a shred of reputation." Test every act against what an unfriendly but intelligent reporter could write on a newspaper front page. "Everybody else is doing it" signals the lack of a good reason. If an action evokes hesitation, "it's too close to the line and should be abandoned. There's plenty of money to be made in the center of the court."
- He wants bad news promptly. Delay turned a Salomon problem "that could have easily been disposed of into one that almost caused the demise of a firm with 8,000 employees." Culture, "more than rule books, determines how an organization behaves."
- He asks managers for a written succession recommendation (who takes over if they are incapacitated overnight), marked "Personal for Warren."

chunks.heading: GEICO: how goodwill can far exceed book value
chunks.text:
- Warren, then a 20-year-old Columbia student, found that his teacher Ben Graham chaired GEICO. He took a train to Washington on a Saturday, found the building closed, banged on a door until a janitor let him in, and spent four hours learning insurance from Lorimer "Davy" Davidson.
- He put 75% of his $9,800 portfolio into GEICO soon after, though he "felt over-diversified."
- In the mid-1970s the stock fell over 95%. Berkshire bought about one-third in the market, rising to 50% through GEICO's buybacks, at a cost of $46 million, then bought the other 50% in 1996 for about $2.3 billion.
- The 1996 price implied $4.6 billion for 100% against tangible net worth of $1.9 billion. The $2.7 billion excess was goodwill, about 97% of the $2.8 billion in premiums paid in 1995. That is a very high price by industry standards, but justified by low costs and consistently profitable, unusually loyal policyholders.
- Today premium volume is $14.3 billion, while goodwill is carried at only $1.4 billion because accounting rules write goodwill down but never up. Using the same 97% yardstick, economic goodwill is about $14 billion.
- Under Tony Nicely (CEO from 1993), market share rose from 2.0% (stuck for over a decade) to 8.8%, with underwriting discipline and low costs. The guiding goal: "get the policyholder's business by deserving his business."

chunks.heading: Insurance float and the four underwriting disciplines
chunks.text:
- P/C insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later, holding float that stays stable relative to premium volume. Berkshire's float: $39 million (1970), $237 million (1980), $1.6 billion (1990), $27.9 billion (2000), $65.8 billion (2010).
- The industry generally operates at an underwriting loss, which is what it pays to hold float. State Farm had an underwriting loss in seven of ten years, totaling over $20 billion. Berkshire has had eight straight years of underwriting profit, totaling $17 billion, so its float is better than cost-free, "as if some party deposited $66 billion with us, paid us a fee for holding its money."
- The industry's return on tangible equity has fallen short of average American industry for decades.
- Four disciplines of sound insurance:
  1. Understand all exposures that might cause losses.
  2. Conservatively evaluate the likelihood of a loss and its probable cost.
  3. Set a premium that earns a profit after loss costs and expenses.
  4. Be willing to walk away if the right premium can't be obtained.
- "Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth," driven by Wall Street, agents and brokers, or a "testosterone-driven CEO." "The other guy is doing it so we must as well" spells trouble in any business, most of all insurance.
- Ajit Jain's reinsurance unit insures risks no one else wants or has the capital for, without exposing Berkshire inappropriately. From 1985 it grew to $30 billion of float, and Warren says Berkshire is far more conservative than most large insurers.
- 2010 underwriting profits: GEICO $1,117 million, General Re $452 million, BH Reinsurance $176 million, other primary $268 million, for $2,013 million total.

chunks.heading: Derivatives as insurance, Black-Scholes, and ignoring net income
chunks.text:
- Warren treats Berkshire's derivatives (203 contracts) as insurance-like activity, taking premiums to assume risks others want to shed. Premiums are received upfront, so there is no counterparty risk.
- High-yield credit contracts (2004-2008): $3.4 billion of premiums, $2.5 billion of losses through the crisis, now almost certain to be an underwriting profit, plus about $2 billion of average interest-free float. "We charged the right premium."
- Equity puts: $4.8 billion of premiums on 47 contracts, most 15-year, payable only on the termination date. 39 remain with $4.2 billion of original premiums. Carried at $6.7 billion on the balance sheet versus a $3.8 billion settlement value if index levels are unchanged.
- Almost all contracts require no collateral posting. That cut the premiums Berkshire could charge but gave comfort in the crisis and let it commit to advantageous purchases.
- He and Charlie believe Black-Scholes gives "wildly inappropriate values" for long-dated options, but Berkshire uses it because auditors and counterparties do. "We would rather be approximately right than precisely wrong." A Black-Scholes liability change cut one quarter's net income by $455 million even as index prices rose.
- He urges schools to stop teaching Black-Scholes as revealed truth: "You can be highly successful as an investor without having the slightest ability to value an option. What students should be learning is how to value a business."
- Net income is "almost always meaningless at Berkshire" because realized gains count and unrealized gains don't, so it can be steered at will. He says they never sell a security to affect reported net income. Watch book value and operating earnings instead.

chunks.heading: Leverage, liquidity, temperament and the American outlook
chunks.text:
- "To finish first, you must first finish." Leverage is addictive, and "any series of positive numbers... evaporates when multiplied by a single zero." Credit is like oxygen: unnoticed when abundant, all that matters when absent.
- Berkshire pledges at least $10 billion of cash (excluding utility and railroad cash) and customarily keeps $20 billion or more to survive record insurance losses (about $3 billion from Katrina) and seize opportunities. The idea comes from his grandfather Ernest's $1,000 letters to his children.
- Cash is held largely in Treasury bills. He quotes Ray DeVoe: "More money has been lost reaching for yield than at the point of a gun." Berkshire relies on no bank lines and avoids contracts with sizeable collateral calls.
- No cash has gone to dividends or buybacks in 40 years. Retained earnings run about $1 billion a month, and net worth grew from $48 million to $157 billion. The cost of caution is "a minor amount" of return, and it lets Berkshire "play offense while others scramble for survival," including investing $15.6 billion in 25 days after Lehman's bankruptcy.
- On uncertainty: tomorrow is always uncertain (December 6, 1941, October 18, 1987, September 10, 2001). Americans live "six times better" than when he was born, and "America's best days lie ahead."
- On housing: Clayton keeps its own mortgages, requires meaningful down payments and sets fixed payments at a sensible share of income. Borrowers with an average 648 FICO score had annual losses of 1.17%-1.86% from 2006 to 2010. A home can be "a nightmare if the buyer's eyes are bigger than his wallet." The goal should be a house people can afford, not "the house of their dreams."
- Owning a quality business: Coke's dividend to Berkshire was $88 million in 1995 and will be about $376 million in 2011, likely doubling within ten years. "Time is the friend of the wonderful business."

chunks.heading: Regulated capital-intensive businesses (BNSF, MidAmerican) and investment manager selection
chunks.text:
- BNSF cost $22 billion of cash and 6% more shares, and should lift normal earning power by nearly 40% pre-tax. Rail moves each ton 500 miles on a gallon of diesel, three times as efficiently as trucking. BNSF carries about 11% of all U.S. inter-city ton-miles and will spend about $2 billion more than depreciation in 2011.
- Both BNSF and MidAmerican rely on a "social compact": they invest continually and, if they serve well, regulators allow reasonable returns. Their long-term debt isn't guaranteed by Berkshire, and BNSF's 2010 interest coverage was 6:1 even in a recession.
- MidAmerican retains all earnings, unlike most utilities, and has invested or committed $5.4 billion to wind. Iowa rates are unchanged since 1999, while the other major Iowa utility raised prices over 70%.
- Choosing investment managers: past results matter but don't suffice. What counts is how the record was achieved and understanding of risk (not beta), including the ability to anticipate "economic scenarios not previously observed," plus someone for whom Berkshire is "far more than a job."
- Pay for Todd Combs: salary plus a payout based on performance versus the S&P, with deferrals and carryforwards to prevent undeserved payments after see-saw results. He criticizes hedge-fund general partners who take upside and walk away after losses. "Our only style box is 'smart.'" The aim was "a 2-year-old Secretariat, not a 10-year-old Seabiscuit."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2011 letter covers insurance float, price-disciplined share repurchases, intrinsic value, admitted mistakes (Energy Future Holdings, the housing call), succession, and a framework ranking currency, gold, and productive assets as investments. He argues low stock prices help net buyers and that fluctuation is not risk.

chunks.heading: How Warren views his investing record and succession at Berkshire (2011)
chunks.text:
- Warren measures himself by the per-share rate of gain in intrinsic business value versus the S&P 500: "If it doesn't, we are overpaid at any price."
- Per-share book value rose 4.6% in 2011. Since 1964 it has grown from $19 to $99,860, a 19.8% compounded annual rate.
- Book value is a useful but "considerably understated" proxy for intrinsic value. It tracks business value roughly because the gap between the two does not swing wildly year to year.
- Book value should beat the S&P in a bad market year and lag in a strong one. Berkshire beat the S&P in all 42 five-year periods from 1965 on, and the 2007-11 period held. He expects the streak to snap if the S&P strings together five good years.
- Operating earnings matter most. Per-share investments rose 4% to $98,366, and pre-tax earnings outside insurance and investments rose 18% to $6,990 per share.
- Succession: the board's main job is to make sure the right people run the business and the next generation is identified. Warren says Berkshire's directors are the best he has seen on succession among the 19 boards he has served on.
- Todd Combs and Ted Weschler each handle a few billion dollars and have the "brains, judgment and character" to run the whole portfolio later. Each gets 80% of performance pay from his own results and 20% from his partner's.
- More than 98% of Warren's net worth is in Berkshire stock, all earmarked for philanthropy. He is comfortable with that concentration given the quality and diversity of the businesses.
- Warren's 2011 mistakes:
  - About $2 billion of Energy Future Holdings bonds, written down $1 billion in 2010 and $390 million in 2011. He "totally miscalculated the gain/loss probabilities," calling it "a major unforced error."
