  - He predicted a housing recovery within a year and was "dead wrong."
  - He bought some small businesses that have poor returns. Charlie told him long ago, "If something's not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well."

chunks.heading: Share repurchases and why Warren wants low stock prices
chunks.text:
- Warren favors repurchases only when two conditions hold:
  - The company has ample funds for operating and liquidity needs.
  - The stock trades at a material discount to conservatively calculated intrinsic value.
- Offsetting dilution or having excess cash is not a justification. "Continuing shareholders are hurt unless shares are purchased below intrinsic value."
- "The first law of capital allocation – whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases – is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another." He recommends Jamie Dimon's J.P. Morgan letters for their focus on price versus value.
- Berkshire announced a buyback up to 110% of book value in September 2011 and bought only $67 million before the price moved above the limit. Warren says it will buy aggressively at or below that limit.
  - It will not "support" the stock, and bids fade in weak markets.
  - It will not buy if cash equivalents are below $20 billion.
  - He wants exiting partners fully informed of the value of what they sell.
- Buying a stock worth at least x for .9x or .8x is a sure way to make money for continuing holders. A director likens it to "shooting fish in a barrel, after the barrel has been drained."
- A net buyer of stock, directly or through an investee that repurchases shares, wants prices low. Warren compares those who cheer rising prices to a commuter who rejoices when gas rises because his tank holds a day's supply.
- IBM example:
  - IBM has 1.16 billion shares outstanding, of which Berkshire owns 63.9 million (5.5%). IBM will likely spend about $50 billion on buybacks over five years.
  - At an average price of $200, IBM retires 250 million shares, leaving 910 million, and Berkshire owns about 7%.
  - At an average price of $300, IBM retires 167 million shares, leaving about 990 million, and Berkshire owns 6.5%.
  - On $20 billion of fifth-year earnings, Berkshire's share is $100 million larger under the low-price scenario, and its stake might be worth about $1.5 billion more later.
- Warren says he once rejoiced when the market rose, until he read Chapter Eight of Graham's *The Intelligent Investor* on price fluctuations. "Immediately the scales fell from my eyes, and low prices became my friend."
- He admires IBM's financial management under Gerstner and Palmisano: debt used wisely, acquisitions made almost exclusively for cash, and aggressive buybacks.

chunks.heading: The big holdings as partnership interests in wonderful businesses
chunks.text:
- Warren views holdings such as American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo as partnership interests in wonderful businesses, not securities to trade on near-term prospects.
- Ownership stakes at year-end 2011: American Express 13.0%, Coca-Cola 8.8%, IBM 5.5%, Wells Fargo 7.6%.
- Only dividends show in Berkshire's income statement. Had Berkshire held the 2011 positions all year:
  - Dividends from the "Big Four" would have been $862 million.
  - Berkshire's share of their earnings would have been $3.3 billion.
  - He believes the $2.4 billion not reported creates at least that much value by fueling future earnings gains and repurchases.
- He expects a decade from now the four could earn $7 billion attributable to Berkshire, with $2 billion in dividends.
- 2011 deals:
  - IBM: 63.9 million shares costing $10.9 billion.
  - Bank of America: $5 billion of 6% preferred with warrants to buy 700 million common shares at $7.14 before September 2, 2021.
  - He added $1 billion to Wells Fargo.
- On IBM he was "late to the party," as he was with Coca-Cola in 1988 and railroads in 2006. He had read IBM's annual report for over 50 years, but his thinking "crystallized" on a Saturday in March 2011. He quotes Thoreau: "It's not what you look at that matters, it's what you see."
- Bank of America: prior management made huge mistakes, but Brian Moynihan is cleaning them up and nurturing a large, attractive underlying business.
- Wells Fargo: earnings strong, assets solid, capital at record levels.
- Derivatives: Berkshire will not start major new positions because it shuns any contract that could require instant collateral posting. That conflicts with "redundant liquidity and unquestioned financial strength."
- The high-yield index default contracts brought in $3.4 billion of premiums against $2.6 billion paid, with about $2 billion of average float over their five years. Warren credits getting a premium commensurate with the risk.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and the four insurance disciplines
chunks.text:
- Property-casualty insurers collect premiums now and pay claims later. The money held in between is "float," which Berkshire invests for its own benefit.
- Float history ($ millions): 1970: 39; 1980: 237; 1990: 1,632; 2000: 27,871; 2010: 65,832; 2011: 70,571. He doesn't expect it to grow much from here.
- If premiums exceed expenses and eventual losses, there is an underwriting profit and the float costs less than nothing.
- Berkshire had nine straight years of underwriting profit totaling about $17 billion.
- The industry usually loses on underwriting because of intense competition. State Farm lost on underwriting in eight of eleven years, and industry return on tangible equity has long trailed American industry.
- Valuation of float:
  - Book value deducts float in full as a liability, as if it had to be paid tomorrow. Warren says it should be viewed as a revolving fund, so true value is far lower than the accounting liability.
  - The $15.5 billion of insurance goodwill is the price paid for float-generating ability. Its value depends on sustained underwriting profit, not on cost.
  - This is a huge reason intrinsic value substantially exceeds book value.
- Four disciplines of insurance (General Re, under Tad Montross, follows them):
  1. Understand all exposures that might cause a policy to incur losses.
  2. Conservatively evaluate the likelihood of a loss and its probable cost.
  3. Set a premium that delivers a profit on average after loss costs and expenses.
  4. Be willing to walk away if the right premium can't be obtained.
- Many insurers pass the first three and fail the fourth. "The other guy is doing it so we must as well" spells trouble, especially in insurance. He illustrates independence with the joke about Albert, who says of the wrong-way car on the highway, "It's not just one car, there are hundreds of them."
- Risk posture: if the industry suffered a $250 billion mega-catastrophe loss (about triple anything it has faced), Berkshire would likely still record a moderate profit.
- Units:
  - BH Reinsurance (Ajit Jain): insures risks others lack the desire or capital to take. Started in 1985, it now has $34 billion of float. 2011 underwriting was a $714 million loss, and Charlie "would gladly trade me for a second Ajit."
  - General Re: float $19.7 billion, underwriting profit $144 million.
  - GEICO (Tony Nicely, 50 years of service): market share rose from 2.0% to 9.3% in 18 years. Premiums were $15.4 billion in 2011 versus $3.3 billion had share stayed flat. Low costs permit low prices.
  - Other primary insurers had $242 million of underwriting profit. Princeton Insurance, a med-mal writer, was acquired at yearend with over $600 million of float.
  - Total 2011 underwriting profit was $248 million, and total float $70.6 billion.

chunks.heading: Regulated capital-intensive businesses and the operating companies
chunks.text:
- BNSF and MidAmerican Energy hold long-lived regulated assets funded partly by long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire. Earnings cover interest amply even in terrible conditions (BNSF interest coverage was 9.5x in 2011).
- BNSF carries about 15% of all U.S. inter-city freight ton-miles and is the largest "artery" of the economy's "circulatory system." It maintains 23,000 miles of track, 13,000 bridges and 80 tunnels. It invested $1.8 billion more than depreciation in 2011. BNSF 2011 revenue was $19.5 billion and net earnings $2.97 billion.
- Warren frames a "social compact": he quotes Franklin, "Keep thy shop, and thy shop will keep thee," and restates it as "Take care of your customer, and the regulator – your customer's representative – will take care of you."
- MidAmerican (89.8% owned) serves 2.5 million customers. It retains all earnings, unlike utilities that pay out most, and so funds about $6 billion in wind investment (3,316 MW by end of 2012) plus about $3 billion of solar projects. Net earnings were $1,331 million in 2011.
- Turnarounds: Northern Natural Gas was ranked last (43 of 43) when bought in 2002 and was second most recently.
- Goodwill of $20 billion is carried for BNSF and MidAmerican, but Warren thinks intrinsic value is far greater than book value.
- Non-insurance operating group: 2011 revenues were $72.4 billion and pre-tax earnings $5.04 billion. Returns on unleveraged net tangible assets range from 25% after-tax to over 100% at the best businesses, and 12-20% at good ones, with a few poor.
- Capital allocation mistakes he made: he "misjudged either the competitive strength of the business being purchased or the future economics of the industry."
  - He tries to look ahead ten or twenty years when acquiring a business, but "sometimes my eyesight has been poor."
  - He holds poor performers because of a commitment to sellers that Berkshire will keep their businesses "through thick and thin." He believes the goodwill this builds among prospective sellers offsets the cost. He will act promptly if a business is a long-term cash drain or labor strife is endemic.
- Housing-related companies earned $513 million pre-tax in 2011 versus $1.8 billion in 2006, and employment fell from 58,769 to 43,315. Warren expects a housing recovery because household formation now exceeds housing starts (about 600,000 annually) and sees unemployment dropping when it returns.
- Manager and business examples:
  - See's Candy: bought for $25 million, earned a record $83 million pre-tax in 2011, with $1.65 billion cumulative since purchase. Warren cites "buy commodities, sell brands" as a long-standing formula (Coca-Cola, Wrigley, See's).
  - Nebraska Furniture Mart: bought a 433-acre tract north of Dallas for what should be the highest-volume home-furnishings store in the country. The Omaha and Kansas City stores each exceeded $400 million of sales.
  - McLane: bought for $1.5 billion in 2003, with $2.4 billion of pre-tax earnings since.
  - NetJets: pre-tax earnings of $227 million after being his "number one worry" a few years earlier. Its focus on safety and service widens its "moat."
  - CTB: bought for $139 million in 2002, distributed $180 million, and earned $124 million pre-tax in 2011.
  - Iscar, Marmon (bolt-on acquisitions) and TTI also set records.
  - Lubrizol, bought September 16, 2011: CEO James Hambrick lifted pre-tax profits from $147 million to $1,085 million since 2004. Three bolt-ons cost $493 million.
- Berkshire's five largest non-insurance companies (BNSF, Iscar, Lubrizol, Marmon, MidAmerican) earned over $9 billion pre-tax in 2011 versus MidAmerican's $393 million seven years earlier. They should again set records in 2012, comfortably topping $10 billion if the economy doesn't weaken.
- Operating companies spent $8.2 billion on property, plant and equipment, about 95% in the U.S.
- Warren notes the Marmon accounting oddity (a $614 million GAAP write-off with no connection to economic reality), which widens the gap between intrinsic value and carrying value.
- Clayton Homes has stayed profitable through the housing depression by sticking to old-fashioned loan policies: "meaningful down payments and monthly payments with a sensible relationship to regular income."

chunks.heading: The three kinds of investments and why productive assets win
chunks.text:
- Investing, as Berkshire defines it, is "the transfer to others of purchasing power now with the reasoned expectation of receiving more purchasing power – after taxes have been paid on nominal gains – in the future." More simply, it is forgoing consumption now to consume more later.
- Risk is not beta. It is "the reasoned probability of that investment causing its owner a loss of purchasing-power over his contemplated holding period." Assets can fluctuate widely without being risky, and a non-fluctuating asset can be laden with risk.
- Category 1: currency-based investments (money funds, bonds, mortgages, deposits)
  - Seen as safe, but "among the most dangerous of assets." Beta may be zero but risk is huge.
  - The dollar lost 86% of its value from 1965 to 2011, so $7 buys what $1 did. A tax-free institution needed 4.3% a year just to keep purchasing power.
  - For a taxpayer, rolling T-bills returned 5.7% a year over 47 years. At a 25% average tax rate, income tax took 1.4 points and the "invisible inflation tax" took the other 4.3 points, so real income was nothing.
  - "Right now bonds should come with a warning label," and he quotes Shelby Cullom Davis: "Bonds promoted as offering risk-free returns are now priced to deliver return-free risk."
  - Berkshire still holds T-bills for liquidity: a working level of $20 billion, absolute minimum of $10 billion. Unquestioned financial strength comes first.
- Category 2: assets that never produce anything (gold)
  - Value rests on an expanding pool of buyers who believe others will pay more later. Warren notes tulips in the 17th century, Internet stocks and houses. "What the wise man does in the beginning, the fool does in the end."
  - World gold stock is about 170,000 metric tons, a cube about 68 feet per side. At $1,750 an ounce it is worth $9.6 trillion ("pile A").
  - Pile B at the same cost: all 400 million acres of U.S. cropland (about $200 billion annual output), 16 Exxon Mobils (each earning over $40 billion a year), and about $1 trillion left over. "Can you imagine an investor with $9.6 trillion selecting pile A over pile B?"
  - "If you own one ounce of gold for an eternity, you will still own one ounce at its end."
- Category 3: productive assets (businesses, farms, real estate), which he prefers
  - Ideal assets deliver output that holds purchasing power in inflation while needing little new capital. Coca-Cola, IBM and See's Candy pass this double-barreled test.
  - Regulated utilities fail it because inflation forces owners to invest more to earn more, but they still beat nonproductive or currency-based assets.
  - He compares businesses to "cows" that give ever more "milk." Their value comes from capacity to deliver milk, not the medium of exchange. The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century, plus dividends.
  - The first two categories peak in popularity at maximum fear. "Cash is king" was heard in late 2008, just when cash should have been deployed. "Cash is trash" was heard in the early 1980s, just when fixed-dollar investments were most attractive. "Investors who required a supportive crowd paid dearly for that comfort."
  - Berkshire's goal is to own more first-class businesses, preferably entire companies, otherwise via marketable stocks. Warren believes this category will be the runaway winner and by far the safest.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett reviews 2012 and explains why Berkshire measures itself on intrinsic value against the S&P. He covers insurance float as a revolving fund, price discipline in buybacks, why a sell-off policy beats dividends, and why timing the market is a mistake. He also admits capital-allocation errors.

chunks.heading: Insurance float is Berkshire's core engine, and Warren values it far above book
chunks.text:
- Property-casualty insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later. That "float" is money Berkshire holds and invests for its own benefit.
- Float grew from $39 million (1970) to $237 million (1980), $1.6 billion (1990), $27.9 billion (2000), $65.8 billion (2010) and $73.1 billion (2012).
- If premiums exceed expenses plus eventual losses, the underwriting profit means "free money" and "you get paid for holding it". Warren compares it to "taking out a loan and having the bank pay you interest."
- Berkshire had a $1.6 billion underwriting gain in 2012, its tenth straight profitable year, totaling $18.6 billion pre-tax over the decade.
- Competition pushes the industry as a whole to underwrite at a loss, which is what it pays to hold float. State Farm had underwriting losses in 8 of the 11 years to 2011. The industry's premiums were inadequate in 37 of the 45 years ending 2011, so its return on tangible equity falls well short of American industry's.
- Accounting deducts the full float as a liability, as if it had to be paid tomorrow. Warren says it should be viewed as a "revolving fund". If float is costless and long-enduring, its true liability value is dramatically lower.
- $15.5 billion of insurance goodwill sits on the books as the price paid for float-generating ability. Its cost has no bearing on its value: goodwill from prolonged underwriting losses is worthless, but Berkshire's is worth far more than carrying value.
- The value of float is "a huge reason" intrinsic value exceeds book value.
- Insurers' earnings are propped up by "legacy" bond portfolios whose high yields won't be available at reinvestment. Today's bond portfolios are "wasting assets".

chunks.heading: Four disciplines of sound insurance underwriting
chunks.text:
Warren says a sound insurer must:
1. Understand all exposures that might cause a policy to incur losses.
2. Conservatively assess the likelihood of a loss and its probable cost.
3. Set a premium that on average delivers a profit after loss costs and operating expenses.
4. Be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can't be obtained.

- Many insurers pass the first three and flunk the fourth because they can't turn away business competitors are eagerly writing. "The other guy is doing it, so we must as well" spells trouble in any business, "but none more so than insurance."
- Berkshire is far more conservative about risk than most large insurers. In a $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe (about triple any past loss), Berkshire would likely still record a profit because of its many earnings streams, while other major insurers would be far in the red.
- At GEICO, one percentage point of sustained improvement in persistency (policy renewals) adds more than $1 billion of intrinsic value. GEICO's market share rose from 2.5% to 9.7% since 1995 and premiums from $2.8 billion to $16.7 billion, without sacrificing underwriting discipline.
- Ajit Jain built a reinsurance business from scratch in 1985 to $35 billion of float with cumulative underwriting profit by insuring risks others lack the desire or capital to take.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation order: reinvest, acquire, repurchase, then dividends
chunks.text:
Warren's priority for deploying earnings:
1. **Reinvest in current businesses.** Managers should seek ways to widen the moat: efficiency, territory, product lines. Berkshire spent a record $12.1 billion on fixed assets and bolt-ons in 2012, including $9.8 billion on plant and equipment. A conglomerate can "water the flowers and skip over the weeds."
2. **Acquisitions.** The test is whether Charlie and Warren can do a deal likely to leave shareholders wealthier per share. Warren admits "plenty of mistakes" and expects more, but the record is satisfactory.
3. **Repurchases.** These make sense only when the shares trade at a meaningful discount to conservatively calculated intrinsic value: "It's hard to go wrong when you're buying dollar bills for 80¢ or less." Berkshire raised its buyback limit from 110% to 120% of book in December 2012 after a large block became available at about 116%. "In repurchase decisions, price is all-important. Value is destroyed when purchases are made above intrinsic value."
4. **Dividends** come last.

- Capital allocation can be undermined by subconscious motivated reasoning: managers start with the answer they want and work backwards. Warren admits he did this in the textile business: "wishing makes dreams come true only in Disney movies; it's poison in business."
- Berkshire's building blocks for per-share value: improve subsidiaries' earning power, bolt-on acquisitions, participate in investees' growth, buy back stock at a meaningful discount, and an occasional large acquisition. It rarely, if ever, issues shares.
- Warren explains that the $4 billion Heinz common equity and $8 billion 9% preferred (with redemption premium and warrants for 5% of the common) shows he structures for downside protection and upside.

chunks.heading: Why Berkshire pays no dividend: the sell-off math
chunks.text:
Warren's worked example: two equal owners of a business with $2 million net worth, earning 12% on tangible net worth and able to reinvest at 12%, with outsiders willing to buy at 125% of net worth.
- **Dividend plan** (pay out one-third of earnings): value and dividends grow 8% a year. After ten years, net worth is $4,317,850, each owner's shares are worth $2,698,656, and the next dividend is $86,357.
- **Sell-off plan** (retain everything, each sells 3.2% of shares a year for the same initial $40,000): net worth reaches $6,211,696, each owns 36.12%, and each stake is worth $2,804,425. That is about 4% more value and about 4% more annual cash than the dividend plan.
- Two further arguments:
  - Dividends impose one cash-out policy on all shareholders. With about 600,000 holders, many are net savers who prefer none. Selling lets each holder choose.
  - Taxes are worse for dividends, since all cash received is taxed, versus tax only on the gain portion of sales. Reinvesting dividends also means paying the 125% premium to buy shares back.
- Warren's own case: he gives away about 4.25% of his Berkshire shares a year, yet the book value of his holdings rose from $28.2 billion (2005) to $40.2 billion (2012).
- Dividend policy should be "clear, consistent and rational." Quoting Phil Fisher, you can run a hamburger restaurant or a Chinese one, but you can't switch capriciously and keep the fans of either.
- The approach holds only while the book-value buildup and market premium assumptions are reasonable. If they worsen materially, Berkshire will reexamine it.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value, yardsticks, and what Berkshire's results should look like
chunks.text:
- Warren can't give an exact intrinsic value. Book value is "a significantly understated proxy." Per-share investments rose 15.7% to $113,786 and per-share pre-tax non-insurance earnings rose 15.7% to $8,085. Since 1970 they have compounded at 19.4% and 20.8%, and the share price has tracked them. The emphasis is on building operating earnings.
- Book value grew 14.4% in 2012 and 19.7% a year over 48 years (from $19 to $114,214), but lagged the S&P in 9 of 48 years. In 8 of those 9, the S&P gained 15% or more. "We do better when the wind is in our face."
- Charlie and Warren won't change yardsticks. If they fail to outpace the S&P, management brings no value, since investors can buy a low-cost index fund.
- They expect to beat the S&P only by a small margin over time, doing relatively better in flat or down markets and worse in strong ones.
- Per-share results matter, not just growth. The five largest non-insurance businesses added $9.7 billion of annual earnings with only 6.1% dilution, from the BNSF share issuance.

chunks.heading: Owning wonderful businesses, accounting reality, and mistakes
chunks.text:
- Charlie told Warren over 50 years ago that it's "far better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price." Warren still sometimes reverts to bargain-hunting with "tolerable to terrible" results, usually on smaller purchases. Large acquisitions have generally worked out well.
- Berkshire "much prefer[s] owning a non-controlling but substantial portion of a wonderful business to owning 100% of a so-so business." It can do this because it isn't limited to businesses it can operate. The Big Four (American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM, Wells Fargo) produced about $3.9 billion of Berkshire's look-through share of earnings in 2012, but only about $1.1 billion of dividends are reported. The other $2.8 billion of retained earnings is "every bit as valuable," funding buybacks and growth. Unrealized gains on the four were $26.7 billion.
- The manufacturing, service and retail group earned 16.3% after-tax on $22.6 billion of net tangible assets. Returns range from 25% to over 100% at the best units, 12-20% at good ones, and poor at a few owing to capital-allocation errors by Warren.
- Not all amortization is a real expense. Software amortization is real. Amortization of customer relationships under purchase accounting is not, and about 80% of the group's $600 million of amortization was treated as not real. Wells Fargo's roughly $1.5 billion "core deposit amortization" charge is not an expense in any sense except GAAP, since core deposits grow.
- Interest coverage should use pre-tax earnings/interest, not EBITDA/interest, "a commonly-used measure we view as deeply flawed." BNSF's 2012 coverage was 9.6x.
- GAAP forced a $700 million write-down on buying more of Marmon, even though the price implies about $12.6 billion for 90% against $8 billion carrying value, so intrinsic value exceeds book by at least $4.6 billion.

chunks.heading: Temperament, liquidity and optimism about American business
chunks.text:
- Warren calls it a "terrible mistake" to dance in and out of stocks based on tarot cards, "experts" or business activity. "The risks of being out of the game are huge compared to the risks of being in it."
- The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century (17,320%) despite four costly wars, a depression and many recessions. His first stock purchase was in spring 1942, amid Pacific war setbacks. Real GDP per capita more than quadrupled from 1941 to 2012.
- Berkshire didn't join CEOs crying "uncertainty": it invested a record amount and says "America's destiny has always been clear: ever-increasing abundance." He offers to take large, profitable projects CEOs have shelved out of short-term worries.
- Berkshire keeps "many redundant layers of liquidity" and avoids obligations that could drain cash, such as derivatives requiring collateral. That "reduces our returns in 99 years out of 100. But we will survive in the 100th while many others fail. And we will sleep well in all 100."
- Berkshire's long index put options (written 2004-2008, expiring 2018-2026) brought in $4.2 billion of premium to invest as float, with only index value at expiry counting and minimal collateral. Credit-default derivatives earned about $1 billion pre-tax.

chunks.heading: Buying local newspapers, and when to shut a business
chunks.text:
- Warren still believes newspaper circulation, advertising and profits are certain to decline overall. Berkshire bought 28 dailies for $344 million anyway, because at that price the papers should meet its economic test.
- Newspapers once had primacy through a "virtuous circle" of readers drawing ads and ads drawing readers, and local monopolies made management quality nearly irrelevant. Help-wanted classifieds are down over 90% in 12 years.
- Local news in tightly-bound communities remains indispensable. Papers with comprehensive local content and a sensible Internet strategy should stay viable.
- Giving the paper away online while charging for print is a self-destructive strategy. Walter Hussman's Arkansas Democrat-Gazette adopted pay early and held circulation best. Cutting news content or publication frequency leads to "skimpy readership."
- Berkshire's six small dailies had flat 2012 revenue, and its two large papers lost 3%.
- Buy such papers only at "a very low multiple of current earnings." Berkshire will not continue "any business doomed to unending losses": it shut down one significantly unprofitable paper from the Media General bulk purchase after finding no remedy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2013 letter explains float, GEICO's cost-advantage moat, and Berkshire's flexible capital allocation. Its centerpiece is a lesson on investing: buy productive assets using future earnings, ignore market noise and price swings, and use a low-cost index fund if you are not an expert.

chunks.heading: Float: the insurance engine and revolving fund
chunks.text:
- Warren calls property-casualty float "money that doesn't belong to us but that we can invest for Berkshire's benefit." Insurers receive premiums upfront and pay claims later, sometimes decades later (certain workers' compensation accidents).
- Berkshire's float grew from $39 million (1970) to $237 million (1980), $1,632 million (1990), $27,871 million (2000), $65,832 million (2010) and $77,240 million (2013). It began with the 1967 purchase of National Indemnity for $8.6 million.
- Berkshire underwrote at a profit for 11 straight years, totaling $22 billion pre-tax ($3 billion in 2013), while float rose from $41 billion to $77 billion over that stretch.
- If premiums exceed expenses plus eventual losses, "we enjoy the use of free money – and, better yet, get paid for holding it." Competition usually pushes the industry as a whole into underwriting losses, which is "what the industry pays to hold its float." State Farm had an underwriting loss in nine of twelve years through 2012. Warren expects the industry to keep earning subnormal returns.
- Float "can be drowned by poor underwriting results," so daily focus is underwriting profit.
- Book value deducts float as a liability as if payable tomorrow. Warren says it should be viewed as a "revolving fund": about $17 billion was paid to more than five million claimants in 2013, while new business adds new float. If it is costless and long-enduring, the true value of the liability is "dramatically less than the accounting liability."
- Insurance goodwill of $15.5 billion on the books mostly reflects the price paid for float-generating ability. Its book cost has no bearing on true value; large, prolonged underwriting losses would make it worthless. Warren believes the economic value is far above carrying value, and it is a "huge reason" intrinsic value exceeds book value.
- Float may decline, but gradually (at most 3% a year), and Berkshire can never face immediate demands large relative to its cash. Property-casualty differs from certain life insurance in this respect.

chunks.heading: Four insurance disciplines and insurance as the sale of promises
chunks.text:
- A sound insurer must (1) understand all exposures that might cause losses; (2) conservatively assess the likelihood and probable cost of loss; (3) set a premium that on average yields a profit after loss costs and operating expenses; (4) be willing to walk away if the right premium can't be obtained.
- Many insurers pass the first three and flunk the fourth. "The other guy is doing it, so we must as well" spells trouble in any business, "but in none more so than insurance." Tad Montross at General Re observes all four, and its float has been better than cost-free. General Re, which looked like a huge mistake soon after its 1998 purchase, "is now a gem."
- Warren defines insurance as "the sale of promises." Ability and willingness to pay, even in economic chaos, is all-important. Large insurers wanting to cede long-tail liabilities (asbestos) came to Berkshire; in 2007 Lloyd's transferred pre-1993 claims, with Berkshire's payments capped at a $15 billion policy limit.
- Ajit Jain's reinsurance unit insures risks others lack the desire or capital to take, yet Berkshire is "far more conservative in avoiding risk than most large insurers." If the industry suffered a $250 billion mega-catastrophe (about triple any prior loss), Berkshire would likely still show a significant profit and remain "awash in cash." Ajit built float of $37 billion from a standing start in 1985.
- Underwriting profit and float by unit, 2013: BH Reinsurance $1,294 million / $37,231 million; General Re $283 million / $20,013 million; GEICO $1,127 million / $12,566 million; Other Primary $385 million / $7,430 million. Total $3,089 million / $77,240 million.

chunks.heading: GEICO's cost-advantage moat
chunks.text:
- Warren first encountered GEICO in January 1951 and was "blown away by the huge cost advantage" versus the giants. That efficiency persists and "is an all-important asset."
- "No one likes to buy auto insurance. But almost everyone likes to drive." The expense is major for families, savings matter, and "only a low-cost operation can deliver these."
- The cost advantage "creates a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross" and let GEICO gain share every year. GEICO ranked seventh in 1996 and was number two in 2013, passing Allstate, because of "low prices and reliable service."
- Berkshire paid $1.4 billion over net tangible assets for the second half of GEICO in 1995. That goodwill stays fixed on the books, but Warren believes true economic goodwill is approaching $20 billion.
- Tony Nicely joined at 18, completed 52 years in 2013, and has been CEO since 1993.

chunks.heading: Intrinsic value, book value and buybacks
chunks.text:
- Book value rose $34.2 billion in 2013 (18.2% per share), from $19 to $134,973 over 49 years, a 19.7% compounded rate. Per-share intrinsic value is what counts, but it is subjective; book value is "a rough tracking indicator."
- Intrinsic value "far exceeds" book value and the gap has widened, which is why the 2012 buyback authorization at 120% of book value makes sense: purchases benefit continuing holders when intrinsic value exceeds that level by a meaningful amount. No shares were bought in 2013 because the price never fell to 120%; "If it does, we will be aggressive."
- Two quantitative measures: per-share investments rose 13.6% to $129,253, and pre-tax earnings from non-insurance, non-investment businesses rose 12.8% to $9,116 per share. Since 1970 these grew 19.3% and 20.6% a year, closely matching the stock price over 43 years. Operating earnings get the strongest focus.
- Buying out minorities in Marmon and Iscar cost $3.5 billion and added about $300 million pre-tax earning power plus $800 million cash. Accounting booked it $1.8 billion below price paid, reducing book value, but that "instantly increased Berkshire's excess of intrinsic value over book value by the same $1.8 billion." He calls it "the surest sort of bolt-on."
- Expected underperformance: Berkshire should beat the S&P in down or modestly up years and fall short in strong years. It has underperformed in ten of 49 years, all but one when the S&P gained over 15%. "If we fail to do so [outperform over full cycles], we will not have earned our pay. After all, you could always own an index fund."
- Five building blocks: improving subsidiary earning power; bolt-on acquisitions; investee growth; repurchases at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value; an occasional large acquisition. Berkshire will rarely, if ever, issue shares, and will always hold at least $20 billion of cash equivalents and no material short-term obligations.
- Per-share growth over mere growth: the Powerhouse Five lifted annual earnings by $10.4 billion over nine years with only 6.1% dilution (from the BNSF share issuance).

chunks.heading: Capital allocation, acquisitions and the Heinz template
chunks.text:
- 2013 deals: almost $18 billion for all of NV Energy ($5.6 billion via MidAmerican) and a major interest in H. J. Heinz. Both "will be prospering a century from now."
- Heinz structure with 3G Capital (Jorge Paulo Lemann): Berkshire is financing partner, buying $8 billion of preferred with a 9% coupon and features lifting returns to roughly 12%. Berkshire and 3G each bought half the common for $4.25 billion. 3G executives run operations. Unlike private equity, "Berkshire never intends to sell a share." One-time purchase and restructuring charges were $1.3 billion in 2013; 2014 earnings are expected to be substantial.
- Bolt-ons: subsidiaries contracted 25 deals costing $3.1 billion total (from $1.9 million to $1.1 billion). They "deploy capital in activities that fit with our existing businesses" and are run by existing managers: "no more work for us and more earnings for you."
- Subsidiaries spent a record $11 billion on plant and equipment, roughly twice depreciation; 89% in the U.S. BNSF spent $4 billion, double depreciation.
- Flexibility is an edge: willingness to buy either whole businesses or large passive stakes doubles the chances of finding uses for cash, whereas firms limited to acquisitions they can operate have fewer options.
- Partial ownership: "it's better to have a partial interest in the Hope diamond than to own all of a rhinestone." Warren prefers a substantial non-controlling stake in a wonderful company to 100% of a so-so one. Holdings in American Express (14.2%), Coca-Cola (9.1%), IBM (6.3%) and Wells Fargo (9.2%) were raised; each extra tenth of a percent in the four adds $50 million to Berkshire's share of annual earnings. Their 2013 earnings share was $4.4 billion, but only about $1.4 billion in dividends is reported; the $3 billion retained is "every bit as valuable." Unrealized gains in the four were $39 billion.
- Warren admits mistakes: some small acquisitions earn poor returns because he was "simply wrong in my evaluation of the economic dynamics." He expects more mistakes in buying businesses and stocks. In Energy Future Holdings bonds he bought about $2 billion without consulting Charlie, then sold for $259 million after $837 million of interest, a $873 million pre-tax loss: "Next time I'll call Charlie."
- Bank of America warrants (700 million shares for $5 billion, worth $10.9 billion at yearend, expiring September 2021) are effectively the fifth largest equity position.

chunks.heading: Accounting realism: amortization, depreciation, EBITDA and coverage
chunks.text:
- Non-insurance units earned 16.7% after tax on about $25 billion of average net tangible assets with little leverage. Individual businesses range from 25% to well over 100% after tax on unleveraged net tangible assets, down to a few poor performers.
- GAAP treats all intangible amortization alike, but some intangibles truly deplete (software) while others (customer relationships from purchase accounting) "are clearly not real costs." Of $648 million of amortization, roughly 20% are "real." Warren tells investors to add back most reported amortization.
- "Every dime of depreciation expense we report... is a real cost." Of EBITDA as a valuation guide: "button your wallet." Interest coverage is measured as pre-tax earnings/interest, not EBITDA/interest, "a commonly-used measure we view as seriously flawed." BNSF's coverage was 9:1.
- Great businesses can be bad investments at excessive prices; Berkshire paid large premiums over net tangible assets but gets decent returns.

chunks.heading: Regulated, capital-intensive businesses: BNSF and MidAmerican
chunks.text:
- Both carry heavy long-lived regulated assets partly financed by long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire; earnings far exceed interest needs even in terrible economies.
- BNSF carries about 15% of U.S. inter-city freight by ton-miles; a ton moves about 500 miles per gallon of diesel, with trucks using about four times as much fuel. 2013 revenue $22,014 million, pre-tax operating earnings $6,657 million, net earnings $3,793 million.
- MidAmerican serves retail customers in eleven states, holds 7% of U.S. wind capacity, and retained more earnings than any other U.S. electric utility. Renewables will have cost $15 billion when current projects finish. Net earnings were $1,636 million (Berkshire share $1,470 million). It ranked number one in a customer-satisfaction survey of 101 utilities (95.3% "very satisfied" versus 34.5% at the bottom).
- Warren relishes such commitments "as long as they promise reasonable returns" and trusts future regulation because governments need capital to keep flowing to essential projects.
- Powerhouse Five (MidAmerican, BNSF, Iscar, Lubrizol, Marmon) earned a record $10.8 billion pre-tax; smaller non-insurance units earned $4.7 billion (up from $3.9 billion).

chunks.heading: Investing fundamentals: the farm, NYU property and the know-nothing investor
chunks.text:
- 1986 farm: bought 400 acres near Omaha from the FDIC for $280,000 after a farm-price bubble burst (price declines of 50% or more; five times as many Iowa and Nebraska banks failed as in the Great Recession). His son's estimates implied a normalized return of about 10% with no downside and upside from productivity. Twenty-eight years later earnings tripled and value is five times or more. He has visited twice.
- 1993 NYU-adjacent retail property bought from the RTC with Larry Silverstein and Fred Rose: roughly 10% unleveraged yield, undermanaged, and a tenant on a bargain lease paying about $5 a foot versus $70 for others, expiring in nine years. Earnings tripled; annual distributions exceed 35% of original equity, plus refinancing distributions of over 150%. He has never seen it.
- Lessons: you needn't be an expert, but recognize limitations, "keep things simple and don't swing for the fences," and answer quick-profit promises with a "quick 'no.'" Focus on future productivity of the asset; if you can't roughly estimate future earnings, "forget it and move on." Focusing on price change is speculation; "the fact that a given asset has appreciated in the recent past is never a reason to buy it." "Games are won by players who focus on the playing field – not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard." Macro opinions and market predictions are "a waste of time" and "dangerous."
- Mr. Market lesson: if a moody neighbor shouted daily farm prices, you could only benefit. But stock owners let others' irrational behavior make them irrational; liquidity becomes "a curse." "A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy." In 2008 he never considered selling the farm or real estate, nor stocks, which are small participations in wonderful businesses.
- Charlie and Warren's stock process mirrors buying whole businesses: estimate an earnings range five or more years out; buy if the price is reasonable relative to the bottom of that range; otherwise move on. In 54 years they have never skipped a purchase because of the macro or political environment. Stay inside the "circle of competence."
- For non-professionals: "The goal... should not be to pick winners" but to own a cross-section of businesses via a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. The Dow went from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th Century. Accumulate over a long period and never sell when news is bad. Frictional costs from advisers and trading are "devoid of benefit" in aggregate: "ignore the chatter, keep your costs minimal, and invest in stocks as you would in a farm."
- His will directs the trustee for his wife to put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund (he suggests Vanguard's). Berkshire shares go to philanthropy over ten years after his estate closes.
- Ben Graham: Warren bought The Intelligent Investor in 1949; the key chapters are 8 and 20. Before that he tried charting and tape watching. Graham's adage: "Price is what you pay, value is what you get." The book's postscript mystery stock bought in 1948 was GEICO.

chunks.heading: Optimism about America and public pension warnings
chunks.text:
- Warren calls betting on U.S. prosperity "very close to a sure thing." "Who has ever benefited during the past 237 years by betting against America?" and "America's best days lie ahead." The BNSF purchase in 2009 was an "all-in wager on the economic future of the United States."
- Public pension problems stem from promised pensions that can't be funded, a "gigantic financial tapeworm." Investment policy matters; he points to his 1975 memo to Katharine Graham on pension promises, and expects mostly bad news on public pensions in the next decade.

chunks.heading: Nebraska Furniture Mart and Mrs. B
chunks.text:
- Warren bought NFM on August 30, 1983 with a 1¼-page proposal, accepted by Rose Blumkin without changes, with no investment bankers or lawyers; unaudited statements didn't worry him because "her word was good enough."
- Mrs. B never went to school, emigrated from Russia without English, and worked until 103. From a 1946 net worth of $72,264 and $50 cash, plus the talents of the family, NFM grew to the two highest-volume U.S. home furnishings stores (about $450 million each yearly in Omaha and Kansas City, Kansas). The Texas store at The Colony will have 1.8 million square feet on 433 acres.
- Warren has visiting students start the day at NFM: if they absorb Mrs. B's lessons, "they need none from me."

chunks.heading: Managers, compensation of focus and shareholder treatment
chunks.text:
- Operating managers run their businesses "as if they were the only asset owned by their families"; most have no financial need to work, and the joy of hitting business "home runs" means as much as a paycheck.
- Todd Combs and Ted Weschler each manage over $7 billion and outperformed the S&P 500 in 2013 and Warren's own picks; they have "Berkshire blood in their veins."
- Corporate office: 24 people handle regulatory filings, a 23,000-page federal tax return, shareholder inquiries and the annual meeting. Berkshire employed a record 330,745 people at yearend.
- Fair disclosure: financial information is issued late Fridays or early Saturdays so all shareholders get it simultaneously with time to analyze; Charlie and Warren do not talk one-on-one with large institutions or analysts. Meeting questions come from journalists, analysts (including a credentialed bear), and the audience, with no advance notice to Warren and Charlie.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 50th-anniversary letter covers Berkshire's origins in a failed textile business, Munger's shift from cigar butts to wonderful businesses, insurance float economics, why the conglomerate form allocates capital efficiently, stock-acquisition discipline, a fortress balance sheet, and why diversified stocks beat dollar assets over decades.

chunks.heading: Fifty-year record and what book value misses
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's net worth rose $18.3 billion in 2014, lifting per-share book value of both share classes by 8.3%.
- Over 50 years under present management, per-share book value grew from $19 to $146,186, a 19.4% compounded annual rate.
- Warren calls book value "a crude, but useful, tracking device" for intrinsic business value, the number that really counts.
- The gap between the two has widened because Berkshire now mostly owns and operates large businesses. Those are carried at cost-based values and never revalued upward, however much they have grown.
- He added the stock price record to the performance table. Short-term price moves are erratic, but "over time, however, stock prices and intrinsic value almost invariably converge."
- He and Charlie think the 50-year rise in per-share intrinsic value roughly equals the 1,826,163% gain in the share price.
- His quantitative intrinsic value markers:
  - 2014 per-share investments rose 8.4% to $140,123.
  - Earnings from non-insurance, non-investment businesses rose 19% to $10,847 per share.
  - Since 1970, investments have compounded at 19% and that earnings figure at 20.6%.
- His main focus is building operating earnings, which is why he was pleased to swap Phillips 66 and Graham Holdings stock for operating businesses.

chunks.heading: How Berkshire builds per-share value: five levers and a capital-allocation edge
chunks.text:
His five building blocks:
1. Improve the earning power of the subsidiaries.
2. Add earnings through bolt-on acquisitions.
3. Benefit from the growth of investees.
4. Repurchase shares when they trade at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value.
5. Make an occasional large acquisition.

He adds that Berkshire will rarely, if ever, issue shares.

- Per-share discipline: the "Powerhouse Five" lifted pre-tax earnings by about $12 billion in ten years. Three were bought for cash and BNSF about 70% cash, with a 6.1% share issuance. Warren says the goal is increasing per-share results, not just earnings.
- Bolt-ons: in 2014 subsidiaries contracted 31 bolt-ons costing $7.8 billion, ranging from $400,000 to $2.9 billion (Duracell, to sit under Marmon). He likes them because they deploy capital into fitting businesses run by existing managers, "no more work for us, yet more earnings." He wants them only if "sensibly-priced (Most deals offered us aren't.)"
- Capex: subsidiaries spent a record $15 billion on plant and equipment, well over twice depreciation, about 90% in the U.S.
- Flexibility: Berkshire will invest large sums passively in non-controlled companies or buy whole operating businesses. This "doubles our chances of finding sensible uses" for its cash. The stock market often offers pieces of wonderful businesses that are more attractive than whole businesses on offer.
- Experience: running businesses makes him a better investor, and investing makes him a better businessman. He had Todd Combs and Ted Weschler each chair a small subsidiary (together earning $100 million on about $125 million of net tangible assets) to deepen both skills.
- A bet on America: he calls a bet on ever-rising U.S. prosperity "very close to a sure thing." Real per-capita output has sextupled in his lifetime. "America's best days lie ahead."

chunks.heading: Partial ownership of wonderful companies, and the "Big Four"
chunks.text:
- Principle: "It's better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone." Berkshire prefers a non-controlling stake in a wonderful company to 100% of a so-so business.
- Berkshire raised its stake in American Express (14.8%), Coca-Cola (9.2%), IBM (7.8%) and Wells Fargo (9.4%).
- Each 0.1% of ownership across the four adds $50 million to Berkshire's share of annual earnings.
- Berkshire's share of their 2014 earnings was $4.7 billion (vs $3.3 billion three years earlier). Only about $1.6 billion in dividends is reported. The other $3.1 billion "are every bit as valuable to us."
- Retained earnings fund buybacks, which raise Berkshire's share of future earnings "without requiring us to lay out a dime," and fund opportunities that usually prove advantageous. Unrealized gains on the four were $42 billion.
- Bank of America: the option to buy 700 million shares for $5 billion before September 2021 (worth $12.5 billion at yearend) makes it effectively the fourth largest holding.
- Tesco mistake:
  - Berkshire owned 415 million shares (cost $2.3 billion).
  - Warren soured on management in 2013 but sold only 114 million shares.
  - Problems then worsened: market share fell, margins contracted, accounting issues surfaced.
  - "In the world of business, bad news often surfaces serially: You see a cockroach in your kitchen; as the days go by, you meet his relatives."
  - After-tax loss was $444 million, about 1/5 of 1% of net worth.
  - He admits "dawdling" and Charlie calls it "thumb-sucking."

chunks.heading: Insurance float: how it works and why it is worth more than book value says
chunks.text:
- Mechanics: property-casualty insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later, holding "float" that will eventually go to others but can be invested meanwhile. Float stays fairly stable relative to premium volume, so it grows as the business grows.
- Float history ($ millions): 1970: 39; 1980: 237; 1990: 1,632; 2000: 27,871; 2010: 65,832; 2014: 83,921. It started with the 1967 purchase of National Indemnity for $8.6 million.
- Underwriting: Berkshire had an underwriting profit for 12 years in a row, $24 billion in total, $2.7 billion in 2014. If premiums exceed expenses and losses, "we enjoy the use of free money – and, better yet, get paid for holding it."
- Industry economics: intense competition often produces an industry-wide underwriting loss, which is what the industry pays to hold float. He expects subnormal returns on tangible net worth for the industry, worsened by low interest rates.
- Warren says avoiding poor underwriting is "lip service" elsewhere and "a religion" at Berkshire.
- Float as a revolving fund:
  - GAAP deducts all float as a liability, as if it were payable tomorrow and never replenished.
  - Berkshire paid $22.7 billion to more than six million claimants in 2014, yet new business adds float daily.
  - If float is costless and long-enduring, "the true value of this liability is dramatically less than the accounting liability."
  - Owing $1 that will never leave is "worlds different" from owing $1 that goes out tomorrow.
- Goodwill: the $15.5 billion insurance goodwill asset largely represents the price paid for float-generating capability. Its cost has no bearing on its value, and prolonged underwriting losses would make it worthless. He believes its true value is far above carrying value, "a huge reason" intrinsic value exceeds book value.
- Float safety: float can drift down slowly, at most about 3% a year. Berkshire's contracts cannot create sudden large demands relative to its cash. No policyholder can cash out at will, unlike many life insurance products that are susceptible to a "run."
- Four underwriting disciplines:
  1. Understand all exposures.
  2. Conservatively assess likelihood and probable cost.
  3. Set a premium that profits after loss costs and expenses.
  4. Be willing to walk away if the right premium isn't available.
  - "Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth." "The other guy is doing it, so we must as well" spells trouble, "in none more so than insurance."
- Operations:
  - Ajit Jain's reinsurance group (float $42.5 billion) insures risks no one else wants or has the capital for, without overexposing Berkshire. A new commercial unit, BHSI, led by Peter Eastwood, is expected to reach billions in volume.
  - General Re (Tad Montross) has float "considerably better than cost-free." Soon after the 1998 acquisition it was beset by problems that made Warren believe he had made a huge mistake. It is "now a gem."
  - GEICO (Tony Nicely) gained share from 2.5% in 1995 to 10.8% at 2014. Warren says its low cost "creates a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross." He saw the cost advantage when he first met GEICO in January 1951.
- Mega-cat resilience: a $250 billion industry loss (about triple anything ever experienced) would likely still leave Berkshire with a significant profit that year, awash in cash while other insurers face red ink or insolvency.
- Sale of promises: insurance is the sale of promises, so ability and willingness to pay matter most. Berkshire wrote a $3 billion single-premium policy in 2014 (the largest ever was the $7.1 billion Lloyd's deal in 2007). Only eight P/C policies in history have had premiums over $1 billion, all written by Berkshire.
- The 1967 National Indemnity deal was done in 15 minutes with no audit and a 1½-page homemade contract with no lawyers. NICO now has GAAP net worth of $111 billion.

chunks.heading: Regulated capital-intensive businesses, accounting reality, and the manufacturing group
chunks.text:
- BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy:
  - Both hold large long-lived regulated assets, partly funded with long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire.
  - BNSF's interest coverage was over 8:1. Warren defines coverage as pre-tax earnings/interest and calls EBITDA/interest "seriously flawed."
  - BHE's utilities have recession-resistant earnings from exclusive essential services, and diversified earnings across regulators, which lowers its cost of debt.
  - BHE retains 100% of earnings, more than any other American electric utility.
  - BHE has 6% of U.S. wind and 7% of solar capacity. It is spending $15 billion on renewables and bought AltaLink for C$3 billion.
  - Warren trusts that governments will treat capital providers so funding for essential projects keeps flowing.
- BNSF problem:
  - It disappointed customers in 2014 and lost share to Union Pacific.
  - Warren says "we have a lot of work to do." Berkshire will spend $6 billion in 2015, about 26% of estimated revenue, vs BNSF's 18% average for 2009-2013 and UP's projected 16-17%.
  - BNSF carries about 15% of U.S. inter-city freight by ton-miles. Its fuel efficiency is about 500 miles per ton per gallon, with trucks using about four times as much fuel.
- EBITDA and amortization:
  - "Every dime of depreciation expense we report is a real cost." "When CEOs tout EBITDA as a valuation guide, wire them up for a polygraph test."
  - Amortization of intangibles like customer relationships arises from purchase accounting and does not reflect reality. Software amortization is real.
  - Of $1.15 billion of amortization, he calls about 20% "real." Investors should add back the rest.
- Manufacturing, service and retailing group:
  - Employed $24 billion of net tangible assets and earned 18.7% after tax, despite excess cash and little leverage.
  - Individual businesses range from 25% to well over 100% after tax on unleveraged net tangible assets, to 12-20%, to a few very poor ones. Warren says the poor ones came from his own capital-allocation mistakes: "I simply was wrong in my evaluation of the economic dynamics."
  - Even terrific businesses "can be a bad investment if it is bought for too high a price."
  - The biggest winners' value over carrying value is in insurance and regulated businesses.
- Other businesses:
  - Clayton Homes sold 30,871 homes, about 45% of U.S. manufactured homes (vs 14% when bought in 2003 for $1.7 billion).
  - Clayton kept lending in 2008-2009 with Berkshire's backing, and its blue-collar borrowers proved better credit risks than many higher-income ones.
  - Marmon builds its own tank cars and books no profit on transfer to leasing, so the fleet is carried below retail value.
- Van Tuyl Automotive: 78 dealerships with local managers as owner-partners, and $9 billion of sales. Warren sees room to build multiples of that, if dealerships can be bought at sensible prices and manufacturers approve.
- 3G Partnership: Warren says Heinz "is run far better" by 3G's Alex Behring and Bernardo Hees "than would be the case if I were in charge." Berkshire expects more partnerships with 3G, Mars and Leucadia, only on friendly transactions.

chunks.heading: Risk, volatility and why stocks beat dollars over decades
chunks.text:
- Volatility is not risk. Business schools treat the two as equal, which Warren calls "dead wrong."
- Over 1964-2014 the S&P 500 went from 84 to 2,059 (11,196% with dividends) while the dollar lost 87% of its purchasing power. It now takes $1 to buy what 13¢ bought in 1965.
- His definition of investing: "the transfer to others of purchasing power now with the reasoned expectation of receiving more purchasing power – after taxes have been paid on nominal gains – in the future."
- Conclusion: for multi-decade investors, a diversified portfolio of American businesses bought over time is far safer than Treasuries or other dollar-based securities, which are "far riskier." Holding stocks for a day, week or year is riskier than cash, and anyone with near-term needs should hold Treasuries or insured deposits.
- Fear of volatility can lead to risky behavior. In 2009 pundits pushed T-bills and CDs when the S&P 500 was below 700. By 2015 it was about 2,100, and savers earned "a pittance."
- Ways investors make stocks risky:
  - active trading and market timing
  - inadequate diversification
  - high fees to managers and advisors
  - borrowed money
- "Borrowed money has no place in the investor's tool kit." "Market forecasters will fill your ear but will never fill your wallet."
- Institutions as a group have underperformed the patient index-fund investor, partly because consultants steer them to high-fee managers: "a fool's game."
- Most advisors are better at generating fees than returns, and their core competence is salesmanship. He recommends Jack Bogle's *The Little Book of Common Sense Investing*.
- Ben Graham quote on the cause of investment failure: "The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves."

chunks.heading: Mistakes and lessons: cigar butts, Charlie's blueprint, and See's
chunks.text:
- Textile origin:
  - BPL bought Berkshire in December 1962 at $7.50 (working capital $10.25, book $20.20). Warren compares it to a "discarded cigar butt that had one puff remaining."
  - Seabury Stanton verbally agreed to $11.50, then tendered at $11.375. Irritated by the eighth of a point, Warren didn't tender and bought more.
  - He took control in 1965 and later called not tendering "a monumentally stupid decision."
  - He struggled with textiles for 18 years before closing the operation in 1985.
  - Had BPL tendered, its weighted annual return on Berkshire would have been about 40%.
- Second mistake: he bought National Indemnity (in 1967) through Berkshire instead of BPL. Its partners would have owned 100% of the insurer and avoided the unproductive textile funds. Instead of marrying a 61%-owned terrible business to an excellent one, this diverted about $100 billion from BPL partners to strangers.
- Another one: the 1975 Waumbec Mills purchase looked like a "bargain" on assets and "projected synergies" but was a disaster.
- Cigar-butt limits: the approach worked while he managed small sums and was a great success in the 1950s. It is "scalable only to a point" and marginal businesses are the wrong foundation for an enduring enterprise. "Selecting a marriage partner clearly requires more demanding criteria than does dating."
- Charlie's blueprint: "Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices." Warren says Berkshire was built to it, with him as general contractor and subsidiary CEOs as sub-contractors.
- See's Candy (1972):
  - Earned about $4 million pre-tax on $8 million of net tangible assets, with a durable competitive advantage and pricing power.
  - The family wanted $30 million. Warren wouldn't pay more than $25 million (three times net tangible assets made him "gulp"), and the sellers accepted.
  - See's has earned $1.9 billion pre-tax on only $40 million of added investment, cash that bought other businesses ("Envision rabbits breeding").
  - Lesson: it also taught him the value of powerful brands.
- Dexter Shoe (1993):
  - Berkshire paid $433 million, in Berkshire stock, and the business went to zero because of foreign competition he didn't foresee.
  - The shares are now worth about $5.7 billion.
- Paying with stock: "Trading shares of a wonderful business ... for ownership of a so-so business irreparably destroys value." The intrinsic value of shares given must not exceed the intrinsic value of the business received. "You can't get rich trading a hundred-dollar bill for eight tens."
- On acquisitions at other companies:
  - Bankers focus on "customary" premiums and EPS accretion, not intrinsic value math, and CEOs conjure "synergies" (he says he never heard "dis-synergies" mentioned in 19 boardrooms).
  - Post mortems comparing reality to the original projections should be standard practice.
- Losses: only three investment losses cost 1% or more of net worth at sale, all in 1974-1975 (one 2%).

chunks.heading: Conglomerate advantages, capital allocation, and why Berkshire is the "home of choice"
chunks.text:
- Why conglomerates have a terrible reputation:
  - In the 1960s, ITT, Litton, Gulf & Western and LTV drove their stock to about 20x earnings and then issued shares to buy businesses at about 10x.
  - Pooling accounting automatically raised per-share earnings, presented as managerial genius.
  - This forced them to bottom-fish for mediocre businesses.
  - Such serial issuance of overpriced shares, like a chain letter, "redistribute[s] wealth, but in no way create[s] it."
- Warren says neither BPL nor Berkshire has invested in companies "hell-bent on issuing shares," which he calls a sign of promotion-minded management, weak accounting, an overpriced stock and often dishonesty.
- Jimmy Ling's LTV: its split-up of Wilson & Co. made "Meatball, Golf Ball and Goof Ball." Charlie's maxim: "never underestimate the man who overestimates himself." Warren's rule: "2+2 will always equal 4." When someone says that math is old-fashioned, "zip up your wallet, take a vacation and come back in a few years to buy stocks at cheap prices."
- Why the form works for Berkshire:
  - It can move huge sums between businesses "without incurring taxes or much in the way of other costs."
  - It has no industry bias or colleagues defending the status quo: "If horses had controlled investment decisions, there would have been no auto industry."
  - It can buy pieces of wonderful businesses (common stocks).
  - It avoids the taxes, intermediaries and agency costs that stand-alone companies face when redeploying capital.
  - See's excess cash funded other purchases rather than being distributed.
  - Limit: Warren and Charlie can only evaluate businesses whose economics they understand.
- Home of choice for owners:
  - Sellers who sell to competitors expect cuts to staff, and private-equity buyers pile debt onto businesses ("'equity' is a dirty word for many private-equity buyers; what they love is debt"), then re-leverage and flip them.
  - Berkshire offers a permanent home that keeps people and culture, adds financial strength and ends dealings with banks and analysts.
  - On spin-offs: they would lose control value, capital-allocation flexibility and tax advantages (utility tax credits depend on Berkshire's taxable income elsewhere) and add duplicate costs. He mocks bankers urging 20-50% premiums to buy and later spin-offs to "unlock shareholder value."

chunks.heading: Financial strength, CEO selection, culture, and the next 50 years
chunks.text:
- Permanent loss risk: the chance of permanent capital loss for patient Berkshire shareholders is "as low as can be found among single-company investments." Warning: buying at about double book value can turn a sound investment into a rash speculation. Repurchases will only occur well below intrinsic value.
- Holding period: buy Berkshire only with a horizon of at least five years, never with borrowed money. The stock has fallen about 50% from highs three times since 1965. Ben Graham: "In the short-term the market is a voting machine; in the long-run it acts as a weighing machine."
- Fortress balance sheet:
  - Requires a large reliable earnings stream, massive liquid assets, and no significant near-term cash requirements.
  - "Cash... is to a business as oxygen is to an individual: never thought about when it is present, the only thing in mind when it is absent."
  - Berkshire keeps at least $20 billion in Treasury bills, and supplied $15.6 billion to American businesses in three weeks of late 2008.
  - No short-term debt maturities of size and no derivatives or arrangements with large collateral calls (it stopped writing derivatives once they required full collateral).
  - "We will never play financial Russian roulette," even with 100 chambers and one bullet. "It is madness to risk losing what you need in pursuing what you simply desire."
  - They prepare for the "thousand-year flood": "tomorrow is always uncertain."
- Return outlook: percentage gains will not come close to the past 50 years because "the numbers have become too big." In 10-20 years Berkshire may be unable to reinvest all earnings, and directors will choose dividends and/or buybacks. If shares are below intrinsic value, "massive repurchases will almost certainly be the best choice."
- Delegation: no committees, budgets required of subsidiaries, legal office, or HR/PR/IR/strategy/acquisition departments at headquarters. About 25 people work at HQ. Managers get trust, with an active audit function ("no sense being a damned fool").
- Fighting the "ABCs of business decay" (arrogance, bureaucracy, complacency): General Motors, IBM, Sears and U.S. Steel fell despite once-unassailable strengths. Charlie: "Tell me where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there."
- Choosing a CEO:
  - Capital allocation plus selecting managers.
  - Rational, calm, decisive with insight into human behavior, and aware of his limits ("I'm no genius, but I'm smart in spots and I stay around those spots").
  - Character is crucial: "all in" for the company, with neither ego nor avarice driving pay to match the most lavish peers. His behavior sets the tone for managers.
  - Candidates are young internal people the board knows, so the CEO can serve well over ten years. The board and Warren believe they have the right successor.
  - Howard Buffett would be a non-executive Chairman, a "safety valve" for directors if a CEO needs replacing, since a mediocre CEO who is also Chairman is hard to replace.
- Governance and alignment:
  - "Although our form is corporate, our attitude is partnership."
  - Directors are paid token fees, buy shares in the market, and the company carries no directors and officers liability insurance ("directors walk in your shoes").
- Managers: operating managers run businesses "as if they were the only asset owned by their families." Most don't need the money. "The joy of hitting business 'home runs' means as much to them as their paycheck."
- Shareholders: a proxy resolution for a dividend lost by 89 to 1 among A shares and about 47 to 1 among B shares, with 98% of voting shares saying reinvest earnings.
- Fair disclosure: new information goes to all shareholders simultaneously, usually late Friday or Saturday. They don't talk one-on-one with large institutions or analysts.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's acquisition criteria
chunks.text:
- Size: at least $75 million of pre-tax earnings (unless the business fits an existing unit); the preference is a $5-20 billion deal.
- Track record: consistent earning power, not future projections, and no turnarounds.
- Good returns on equity with little or no debt.
- Management in place ("we can't supply it").
- A simple business ("if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it").
- An offering price known upfront.
- No unfriendly takeovers and no auctions. Cash preferred; stock only if Berkshire receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
- Complete confidentiality and an answer within about five minutes.
- Tone: "if you advertise an interest in buying collies, a lot of people will call hoping to sell you their cocker spaniels." On turnarounds and auctions: "When the phone don't ring, you'll know it's me."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2015 letter explains why Berkshire's intrinsic value outruns book value, how insurance float and underwriting discipline create value, and why a partial stake in a wonderful company beats owning all of a mediocre one. It also covers honest accounting (stock comp, EBITDA, amortization), productivity and the long-run case for America.

chunks.heading: Book value, intrinsic value and buybacks
chunks.text:
- Per-share book value grew from $19 to $155,501 over 51 years, "a rate of 19.2% compounded annually." Net worth rose $15.4 billion (6.4%) in 2015.
- Early on, net worth roughly equaled intrinsic value because most assets were marketable securities marked to market. By the early 1990s Warren had shifted to owning whole businesses, where accounting writes down "losers" but never writes up "winners." Book value therefore understates intrinsic value, and the gap keeps widening.
- He says Berkshire would be "delighted to repurchase our shares should they sell as low as 120% of book value," because that would instantly raise per-share intrinsic value for continuing shareholders.
- Market-value gains should over time exceed book-value gains, though the two diverge erratically in short periods.
- Intrinsic value can't be stated precisely, but it can be sensibly estimated from per-share cash and investments plus pre-tax per-share earnings from the businesses.
  - 2015 cash and investments: $159,794 per share (up 8.3%).
  - 2015 business earnings: $12,304 per share (up 2.1%), after deducting overhead, interest, depreciation, amortization and minority interests, but before income taxes.
  - Investment dividends and interest are excluded from earnings to avoid double-counting.
  - Insurance underwriting income ($1,118 per share in 2015; $1,434 average over a decade) is now included for the first time, because Berkshire has de-emphasized catastrophe coverage and grown bread-and-butter lines.
- Since 1970, per-share investments compounded at 18.9% and earnings at 23.7%, and the stock price tracked those measures. The main goal is to build operating earnings.
- Successors' blueprint:
  1. Improve subsidiaries' earning power.
  2. Add bolt-on acquisitions.
  3. Benefit from investees' growth.
  4. Repurchase shares at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value.
  5. Make an occasional large acquisition.
  - Berkshire rarely, if ever, issues shares.

chunks.heading: Buying and holding businesses: Precision Castparts, bolt-ons and partnerships
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought Precision Castparts (PCC) for more than $32 billion cash. It supplies aerospace components, has 30,466 employees in 162 plants across 13 countries, and was brought to Warren by Todd Combs. Warren says it "fits perfectly into the Berkshire model" and will substantially raise normalized per-share earning power.
- The "Powerhouse Five" (BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, Marmon, Lubrizol, IMC) earned $13.1 billion in 2015, up $650 million. Their earnings rose $12.7 billion since 2003 with minor dilution; BNSF was about 70% cash and the rest stock, adding 6.1% to shares outstanding. The goal is per-share growth, not just higher earnings.
- Smaller non-insurance businesses earned $5.7 billion, up from $5.1 billion.
- 29 bolt-on deals were contracted for $634 million total, ranging from $300,000 to $143 million. Warren encourages them "if they are sensibly-priced," since they fit existing businesses and are run by existing managers, meaning no extra work for him.
- Style: buy businesses already run by cost-conscious managers, avoid bloat, and create an environment where CEOs and their successors can thrive. Warren cites Munger: "If you want to guarantee yourself a lifetime of misery, be sure to marry someone with the intent of changing their behavior."
- Berkshire runs "extreme – indeed, almost unheard of – decentralization."
- The Kraft Heinz partnership with 3G (Jorge Paulo Lemann and partners) takes a different path: quickly cutting unnecessary costs after purchase. Berkshire owns about 27% (325.4 million shares, cost $9.8 billion), plus preferred paying $720 million a year that will likely be redeemed for $8.32 billion. Warren calls the redemption "good news for Kraft Heinz and bad news for Berkshire." GAAP forced a $6.8 billion write-up, leaving the carrying value far above cost and far below market.
- Berkshire joins only friendly deals: "At Berkshire, we go only where we are welcome." Hostile bids are left to others.

chunks.heading: Passive stakes in great companies
chunks.text:
- Berkshire raised its ownership in all four big holdings: IBM to 8.4%, Wells Fargo to 9.8%, Coca-Cola to 9.3% and American Express to 15.6% (the last two via the companies' buybacks).
- Each extra percentage point across the four raises Berkshire's share of annual earnings by about $500 million.
- The four earned Berkshire's share of $4.7 billion in 2015, but only about $1.8 billion in dividends is reported. The roughly $3 billion retained is "every bit as valuable," funding buybacks and good opportunities.
- "It's better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone." Warren prefers a non-controlling stake in a wonderful company over 100% of a so-so business.
- The willingness to invest passively or buy whole businesses doubles the chances of finding uses for cash. A large securities portfolio also provides funds for an elephant-sized acquisition.
- Berkshire holds an option to buy 700 million Bank of America shares for $5 billion before September 2021 (worth $11.8 billion at yearend) and is likely to exercise it just before expiry.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- Property-casualty insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later, holding "float." Berkshire's float grew from $39 million (1970) to $87.7 billion (2015). Underwriting was profitable 13 straight years, totaling $26.2 billion pre-tax, with $1.8 billion in 2015.
- Float should be viewed as a "revolving fund," not strictly a liability. If it is costless and long-enduring, its true cost is far below the accounting liability. Berkshire paid $24.5 billion to over six million claimants in 2015, yet new business replaces the float.
- Contracts are structured so there are never immediate or near-term demands on cash significant to Berkshire. Float may decline at most 3% a year.
- The $15.5 billion of insurance goodwill represents the price paid for float-generating capability, and Warren thinks its true value far exceeds carrying value. It was largely on the books in 2000, and float has since tripled. Goodwill is worthless if an insurer suffers prolonged underwriting losses.
- The four disciplines of a sound insurer:
  1. Understand all exposures.
  2. Conservatively assess likelihood and cost of loss.
  3. Set a premium that yields a profit after loss costs and expenses.
  4. Be willing to walk away if the right premium can't be obtained.
  - Many insurers fail the fourth: "The other guy is doing it, so we must as well" spells trouble. Underwriting discipline is "a religion, Old Testament style."
- Industry competition and low interest rates mean the industry will keep earning subnormal returns on tangible net worth, and results over the next decade will likely trail the last.
- A $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe would likely still leave Berkshire with a significant profit for the year, with ample cash to write business in a disrupted market.
- Units:
  - Ajit Jain's reinsurance group insures risks others won't take, without overexposing Berkshire. Warren notes Ajit had no insurance experience when handed the reinsurance keys in 1986.
  - General Re (Tad Montross), once thought a huge mistake, is now "a gem."
  - GEICO (Tony Nicely) has a cost advantage that is "an enduring" moat: market share went from 2.5% in 1995 to 11.4% in 2015, and underwriting expenses were 14.7% of premiums.
  - Smaller commercial insurers earned $4 billion underwriting over 13 years (about 13% of premium volume), growing float from $943 million to $9.9 billion.
  - Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance (Peter Eastwood) reached $1 billion of premiums in under three years.

chunks.heading: Accounting, earnings quality and mistakes
chunks.text:
- Amortization is not uniformly a real cost. Software amortization is a real expense; amortization of customer relationships from purchase accounting is not. Warren calls about 20% of the $1.1 billion amortization "real" and says to add back the rest.
- Stock-based compensation is "the most egregious example" of managers asking owners to ignore real costs: "If compensation isn't an expense, what is it?" Analysts parroting such figures may not know better, fear losing access, or go along cynically.
