- Depreciation is almost always a true cost. BNSF's depreciation charge falls short of the capital outlay needed to keep the railroad running, so GAAP earnings overstate economic earnings. EBITDA as a valuation guide makes noses lengthen.
- Interest coverage should be measured as EBIT to interest, not EBITDA to interest, which Warren calls "seriously flawed." BNSF's coverage was over 8:1 in a weak year.
- The manufacturing, service and retail group earned 18.4% after tax on $25.6 billion of average net tangible assets, with excess cash and almost no leverage. Some units earn 25% to over 100%, others 12% to 20%, and a few have very poor returns.
- Warren admits "serious mistakes I made in my job of capital allocation": misjudging a company's or industry's economics, or the fidelity or ability of managers. He expects more and hopes they occur in smaller operations.
- A great business can be a bad investment at too high a price, and Berkshire has paid substantial premiums to net tangible assets, shown as goodwill.
- SEC "risk factor" lists haven't helped him evaluate a business; they rarely give probability, cost range or timing. A threat 50 years out isn't a financial problem for today's investor.
- Warren expects a few risks to hit: BNSF losing coal volume, driverless cars shrinking GEICO's premiums, print newspapers declining, online retail, and cheaper electricity storage. None is crucial to Berkshire's long-term well-being, as it adapted when its original textile business was doomed. A diversified company can redeploy funds more freely than one-industry firms.
- He says the clear, present, enduring danger is a "successful" cyber, biological, nuclear or chemical attack on the U.S. Small annual probabilities compound: a 1-in-30 yearly chance gives a 96.6% chance over a century.

chunks.heading: Capital-intensive regulated businesses and Clayton Homes
chunks.text:
- BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy together produced 37% of after-tax operating earnings. They hold long-lived regulated assets funded partly by long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire. They invested $11.6 billion in plant and equipment in 2015; BNSF alone spent about $5.8 billion, nearly three times its depreciation.
- Warren says low prices keep regulators and customers happy. BHE's Iowa rate was 6.8¢ per kWh versus 10.4¢ nationally. BNSF's revenue was just under 3¢ per ton-mile versus 4.2¢ to 5.3¢ for rivals.
- BNSF pre-tax income hit a record $6.8 billion; BHE earned $2.37 billion net.
- Clayton Homes sold 34,397 homes (about 45% of manufactured homes bought in the U.S.), up from number three with a 14% share when Berkshire bought it in 2003.
  - It keeps 100% of the mortgages it originates ($12.8 billion portfolio), unlike the 2008-era originate-and-sell chain. Warren notes "no skin in the game" drove reckless lending then, and says "When Wall Street gets 'innovative,' watch out!"
  - 2015 foreclosures: 8,444 mortgages, costing $157 million. Average loan: $59,942, with monthly payments averaging $522. 95.4% of borrowers were current at yearend.
  - Regulators reviewed Clayton 65 times in two years, with fines of $38,200 and customer refunds of $704,678.
  - Clayton funds long fixed-rate mortgages with short-term debt. The risk is offset because Berkshire always holds at least $20 billion of cash-equivalents (often $40-60 billion), which would earn more if rates rose, making Berkshire "heavily asset-sensitive."

chunks.heading: Productivity, America's prospects and temperament
chunks.text:
- Warren says "babies being born in America today are the luckiest crop in history." U.S. GDP per capita is about $56,000, six times (in real terms) the 1930 level. At 2% real growth and 0.8% population growth, per capita output rises about 1.2% a year, or 34.4% over 25 years, roughly $19,000 more per person.
- "For 240 years it's been a terrible mistake to bet against America, and now is no time to start."
- Productivity is the engine of prosperity:
  - Farming employed 40% of the workforce in 1900 versus about 2% today. Corn yield rose from 30 to over 150 bushels per acre.
  - Class I railroads moved 182% more ton-miles from 1947 to 2014 with 86% fewer workers. Real freight prices fell 55%.
  - BNSF carried 71% more ton-miles from 1996 to 2015 with only 4% more staff.
  - GEICO has about 34,000 employees for 14 million policyholders, and Warren guesses the agency model would need at least 60,000. Direct distribution pioneers (State Farm, USAA, GEICO) cut the roughly 40¢ of premium dollar agency models consumed.
  - BHE's Iowa utility produced 29 million MWh with 3,500 staff versus 19 million with 3,700 in 1998, with no rate increase for 16 years while industry rates rose 44%.
- Warren acknowledges the costs: recent gains mostly helped the wealthy, and disruption can destroy workers' livelihoods, as at the Dexter shoe and New England textile operations. Investors who risked capital can fend for themselves, but he favors safety nets, including an expanded Earned Income Tax Credit, rather than blocking productivity gains.
- Diversified investors who sit tight are certain to prosper: the Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century.

chunks.heading: Insurance and climate change, and the Berkshire culture
chunks.text:
- On the climate proposal, Warren says climate change is "highly likely" a major problem and applies a Pascal's Wager logic ("Noah's Law": build the ark if it may be essential). But policies reprice annually, so higher loss costs translate quickly into higher premiums. GEICO's loss cost per policy rose from about $30 (1951) to about $1,000, which made the business more valuable, not less. For a shareholder of an insurer, climate change "should not be on your list of worries."
- Home office: 25 people (24 plus Warren) oversee a company of 361,270 employees, with no hires or departures in 2015. Because "no one is hired unless he or she is truly needed," Berkshire never books restructuring charges.
- Managers run businesses "as if they were the only asset owned by their families." Many have no financial need to work, and the joy of hitting business "home runs" matters as much as pay.
- Disclosure: all shareholders get information at the same time (late Friday or Saturday releases), with no one-on-one talks with institutions or analysts. "There is no one more important to us than the shareholder of limited means who trusts us with a substantial portion of his savings."
- Warren advises: "Much of what you become in life depends on whom you choose to admire and copy," calling Tom Murphy of Capital Cities the best exemplar he and Charlie saw.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why book value understates Berkshire's intrinsic value, how to judge buybacks by price versus value, how insurance float works, why "adjusted earnings" mislead, and why low-cost index funds beat high-fee managers. He also owns up to his Dexter Shoe and General Re mistakes.

chunks.heading: How Warren reads Berkshire's book value versus intrinsic value
chunks.text:
- Per-share book value rose 10.7% in 2016 (net worth up $27.5 billion). Over 52 years it grew from $19 to $172,108, a 19% compounded annual rate.
- Early on, book value roughly equaled intrinsic value because most assets were marketable securities marked to market.
- By the early 1990s the focus shifted to owning whole businesses. GAAP requires writing down "losers" but never writing up "winners", so intrinsic value now "far exceeds" book value, especially in property/casualty insurance.
- Warren has "no quarrel with the asymmetrical accounting", but it necessarily widens the gap over time.
- "Over time, stock prices gravitate toward intrinsic value." That is why Berkshire's 52-year market-price gain exceeds its book-value gain.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation, retained earnings and acquisition mistakes
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie expect normalized earning power per share to rise every year, even if actual earnings dip with the economy or insurance catastrophes.
- Berkshire retains all earnings. It ranked first among US businesses in dollars retained in 2015 and 2016, and "those reinvested dollars must earn their keep."
- No magic plan: "dream big" and be ready to act fast. "Every decade or so, dark clouds will fill the economic skies, and they will briefly rain gold... rush outdoors carrying washtubs, not teaspoons."
- Mistakes he names:
  - Dexter Shoe (1993): $434 million, paid in 25,203 Berkshire shares worth over $6 billion at yearend 2016. Its value "promptly went to zero".
  - General Re (1998): issued 272,200 shares, a 21.8% increase in shares outstanding. Berkshire holders "give far more than they received".
- Course-correcting deals:
  - 1996: bought the other half of GEICO for cash.
  - 2000: bought 76% of MidAmerican Energy for cash (now 90%).
- Resulting strategy: build insurance, buy large diversified non-insurance businesses, fund deals mostly from internal cash. "Today, I would rather prep for a colonoscopy than issue Berkshire shares."
- Berkshire's shares outstanding grew only 8.3% from 1999 to 2016, mostly from the BNSF purchase, which he calls an issuance that "made good sense".
- After-tax operating earnings grew from $0.67 billion (1999) to $17.57 billion (2016). Investment gains are expected to stay substantial but random in timing, and they help finance business purchases.
- Blunders in the manufacturing, service and retailing group:
  - Some businesses produce "very poor returns".
  - He misjudged economics or industries, and sometimes the fidelity or ability of managers.
  - "I will commit more errors"; Charlie "is around to say 'no' to my worst ideas."

chunks.heading: Share repurchases: price is everything
chunks.text:
- Exiting shareholders always benefit from repurchases. For continuing shareholders, repurchases make sense only below intrinsic value.
- His arithmetic: three equal partners in a $3,000 business. Buying one out for $900 gives each remaining partner a $50 gain. Paying $1,100 costs each $50.
- Whether a buyback creates or destroys value is "entirely purchase-price dependent."
- It is puzzling that announcements almost never name a price ceiling. Managers would never ignore price buying an outside business.
- Two exceptions even when shares are cheap:
  - The business needs all its cash to protect or expand operations and is uncomfortable adding debt (assuming it has a decent future).
  - A business acquisition or other investment offers far greater value than the undervalued shares.
- His line for CEOs and boards: "What is smart at one price is stupid at another."
- Berkshire policy:
  - He may buy large amounts at 120% of book value or less, a deliberate discount to intrinsic value because estimates can't be precise.
  - Berkshire will not "prop" the price at 120%.
  - Buybacks have been hard to do, likely because the clear policy signals intrinsic value is well above 120%.
  - Warren prefers the stock to trade in a narrow range around intrinsic value. Overpriced shares disappoint owners, and buying out "partners" at a discount isn't gratifying.
- Warren rejects calling buybacks "un-American". Capital is plentiful, and he knows of no enticing project that died for lack of capital.
- Berkshire likes investees' buybacks when shares are underpriced.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- P/C insurance has propelled Berkshire since 1967 (National Indemnity and National Fire & Marine bought for $8.6 million). Premiums come in upfront and claims are paid later, creating "float".
- Float grew from $39 million (1970) to $91.6 billion (2016), and passed $100 billion after a huge policy. It may drift down, but no more than about 3% a year. Contracts are structured so no near-term demands threaten cash, "by design" and "never compromised".
- Underwriting profit makes float "free money", and Warren says you get "paid for holding it". Competition often pushes the industry into underwriting losses, which is what it pays to hold float. Falling bond yields will further hurt the industry's float income.
- Berkshire's edge:
  - Underwriting profit for 14 straight years, totaling $28 billion pre-tax.
  - Disciplined risk evaluation is "a religion, Old Testament style."
  - Unmatched financial strength gives investment flexibility: "When others are constrained, our choices expand."
- Float on the balance sheet is a full liability under GAAP. Warren says it is better seen as a "revolving fund": about $27 billion was paid to over six million claimants in 2016, while new business replaces it.
  - If float is costless and long-lasting, its true value as a liability is "dramatically less" than the accounting figure.
  - The $15.5 billion of insurance goodwill was almost all on the books in 2000, when float was $28 billion. Float has since grown $64 billion with no book-value credit, a "huge reason" intrinsic value exceeds book.
- The four disciplines of insurance:
  1. Understand all exposures.
  2. Conservatively assess likelihood and cost of loss.
  3. Set a premium that profits after losses and expenses.
  4. Be willing to walk away if the right premium isn't available.
  - Many insurers fail the fourth. "The other guy is doing it, so we must as well" spells trouble, especially in insurance.
- Catastrophe resilience: in a $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe (about triple any prior loss), Berkshire would likely still record a large profit, and would be ready to write business in a disrupted market.
- Units:
  - Ajit Jain (reinsurance) insures risks others won't or can't take. Warren says he has created tens of billions of value; he'd swap himself for another Ajit.
  - Tad Montross retired after 39 years at General Re, succeeded by Kara Raiguel.
  - Tony Nicely runs GEICO. Charlie's line: "it's great to have a manager with a 160 IQ – unless he thinks it's 180."
  - Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance, led by Peter Eastwood, grew volume 40% to $1.3 billion in 2016 and was profitable during startup.
- 2016 pre-tax underwriting profit $2,131 million (2015: $1,837 million); yearend float $91,577 million.

chunks.heading: GEICO's low-cost moat
chunks.text:
- Warren first visited GEICO in 1951 and was "blown away" by its cost advantage over industry giants. "GEICO would succeed because it deserved to succeed."
- Sales were $8 million in 1951. In 2016 GEICO did that much business every three hours.
- Auto insurance is a major family expense, so "only a low-cost operation" can deliver savings. Low costs create "a moat – an enduring one."
- Share rose from 2.5% (1995) to about 12% (2016). Employment grew from 8,575 to 36,085.
- In late 2016, auto loss costs rose and competitors pulled back from new customers. GEICO accelerated new-business efforts: "We like to make hay while the sun sets."
- "When insurance prices increase, people shop more. And when they shop, GEICO wins."

chunks.heading: Regulated capital-intensive businesses: BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy
chunks.text:
- BNSF and BHE (90% owned) had huge long-lived regulated assets and long-term debt not guaranteed by Berkshire. They produced 33% of 2016 after-tax operating earnings and invested $8.9 billion in plant and equipment.
- Debt is safe because earning power far exceeds interest. BNSF's interest coverage was above 6:1 in a weak railroad year.
- He measures coverage as EBIT/interest, not EBITDA/interest, which he calls "seriously flawed."
- BHE's debt safety rests on recession-resistant utility demand and diverse earnings streams across regulators.
- Warren trusts regulation: governments have a self-interest in ensuring capital flows to essential projects, and Berkshire should earn regulators' approval with low prices.
  - Iowa: BHE averages 7.1¢/kWh versus a 10.3¢ national average. Base rates are frozen until 2029 at the earliest.
  - BNSF revenue is about 3¢ per ton-mile versus 4¢ to 5¢ at the other four major railroads (a crude comparison).
  - Iowa wind generation equaled 55% of retail sales in 2016, heading to 89% by 2020.
  - Railroads move a ton almost 500 miles on a gallon of diesel, about four times as fuel-efficient as trucks.
- 2016 net earnings: BNSF $3,569 million; BHE $2,542 million ($2,287 million to Berkshire).
- HomeServices (from the MidAmerican purchase) owns 38 realty companies with over 29,000 agents. Berkshire expects to buy more realtors.

chunks.heading: Operating businesses, accounting distortions and "adjusted earnings"
chunks.text:
- The manufacturing, service and retail group (44 businesses reporting to headquarters) earned 24% after tax on about $24 billion of net tangible assets in 2016, with excess cash and little debt.
  - Returns vary: a couple exceed 100%, most are 12% to 20%, a few are poor.
  - Warren notes that "a business with terrific economics can be a bad investment if it is bought at too high a price." Berkshire has paid substantial premiums to net tangible assets, hence large goodwill.
  - "It's the growth of the Berkshire forest that counts." Don't over-focus on any single tree.
- He shows segment results off GAAP because amortization of purchase intangibles (about 19-year average life) is mostly not a true economic cost. He judges about 20% of the $1.5 billion 2016 charge to be "real". Once assets are fully written off, GAAP earnings rise with no real improvement ("my gift to my successor").
- GAAP depreciation can understate true economic cost. At BNSF, depreciation was $2.1 billion, but holding its own requires spending "far more." Reported railroad earnings exceed economic earnings. Even so: "Charlie and I love our railroad, which was one of our better purchases."
- On "adjusted earnings":
  - He dislikes managements that feature figures above GAAP by dropping "restructuring costs" and "stock-based compensation."
  - "Bad behavior is contagious": it can lead to practices like insurers underestimating loss reserves.
  - Berkshire restructures every year and has never told shareholders to ignore it. One-time costs should be explained when truly major, such as the Kraft Heinz merger.
  - Stock compensation is an expense. Berkshire pays similar executives in cash and counts it all as expense. Executives should have to explain why valuable pay items are not a cost, or why a payroll cost should be excluded.
  - He cringes at praise for managements who always "make the numbers". Business is too unpredictable, and a CEO focused on Wall Street is tempted to "make up the numbers."

chunks.heading: Finance businesses, investments, cash and taxes
chunks.text:
- Clayton Homes:
  - Became America's largest home builder in 2016 (42,075 units, 5% of new US homes). It makes close to half of the manufactured homes in the US, which are about 70% of new homes under $150,000.
  - Its earnings benefited from very low rates, since it lends fixed-rate long and borrows short. Warren normally shuns that, but Berkshire as a whole is asset-sensitive.
  - It foreclosed on 8,304 loans (about 2.5% of the portfolio). It offers extensions (about 11,000 borrowers) and payment forgiveness (3,800 borrowers, $3.4 million). Of borrowers helped in the last two years, 93% remain in their homes. Foreclosure losses were $150 million.
  - Berkshire provided staying power in the Great Recession, when other lenders vanished. "We never count on synergies when we acquire companies," yet important ones appeared here.
- Marmon railcars: utilization fell to 91% from 97%. Warren expects earnings to drop in 2017 but likes the business.
- Pre-tax finance earnings: $2,130 million (2016).
- Top holdings at yearend 2016 included Wells Fargo (cost $12.7 billion, market $27.6 billion), Coca-Cola (cost $1.3 billion, market $16.6 billion), IBM and Apple. Kraft Heinz was carried at $15.3 billion against $28.4 billion market value (cost $9.8 billion).
- Todd Combs and Ted Weschler each independently manage over $10 billion. Warren usually learns of their decisions from monthly trade sheets.
- Bank of America preferred: $5 billion paying $300 million a year, with a warrant for 700 million shares at $5 billion before September 2, 2021. Yearend profit on the warrant would have been $10.5 billion.
- Cash:
  - Of $86 billion in cash and equivalents, 95% is held in the US, so repatriation taxes are not an issue. Offshore cash is "simply not worth as much."
  - Cash in insurers is slightly less valuable than parent-level cash.
- Stocks are not held "forever": no commitment that Berkshire holds marketable securities permanently. Economic Principle 11 covers controlled businesses only.
- Dividend taxes beat capital gains for corporations: gains carry about 35 cents per $1. Dividends cost about 10.5 cents per $1 for non-insurance parents, 7 cents above 20% ownership, and about 14% (11% above 20% ownership) for P/C insurers.

chunks.heading: The index-fund bet and why active management loses
chunks.text:
- The 2005 argument: in aggregate, professional active managers underperform a low-cost index fund after fees. Warren offered $500,000 that no pro could pick at least five hedge funds to match an S&P 500 index fund over ten years. Only Ted Seides of Protégé Partners accepted.
- Results through 2016 (nine years):
  - Index fund: 85.4% total gain, 7.1% compounded annually.
  - Five funds-of-funds averaged 2.2% compounded. $1 million would have gained $220,000, versus $854,000 for the index fund.
  - Individual gains: 8.7%, 28.3%, 62.8%, 2.9%, 7.5%.
- The environment was "neutral", not stacked either way. Fees: roughly "2 and 20" at the hedge fund level plus about 1% on top at the fund-of-funds level. He estimates about 60% of gains went to the two layers of managers. "Fees never sleep."
- His reasoning:
  - Passive investors earn market average, so active investors in aggregate also earn average before costs. Whichever group has lower costs wins.
  - Smart people's efforts are "self-neutralizing."
  - In his lifetime he identified only about ten professionals early whom he expected to beat the S&P over long stretches.
  - Bill Ruane: "In investment management, the progression is from the innovators to the imitators to the swarming incompetents."
  - Luck: with 1,000 managers predicting, at least one will probably be right nine years running. The lucky monkey, however, "would not find people standing in line to invest with him."
  - Success breeds failure: good records attract money, size anchors returns ("What is easy with millions, struggles with billions"), and managers still seek assets since fees scale with AUM. His 1966 partnership letter, when managing $44 million, argued bigger size is more likely to hurt results than help.
- Advice: both large and small investors should "stick with low-cost index funds." Warren recommends a low-cost S&P 500 fund. Modest-means friends followed it. Mega-rich individuals, institutions and pension funds did not.
  - Consultants can't tell clients to keep adding to an index fund year after year; that would be "career suicide."
  - The wealthy want something superior, and he estimates the elite wasted more than $100 billion in a decade. Public pension funds have been hit especially hard.
  - "When a person with money meets a person with experience, the one with experience ends up with the money and the one with money leaves with experience."
- Jack Bogle deserves a statue; he is "a hero" to Warren.
- Warren does not oppose all fees: Berkshire cheerfully pays investment bankers who bring acquisitions and pays in-house investment managers for over-performance.

chunks.heading: Temperament, America's economic prospects and shareholder philosophy
chunks.text:
- America's progress is "miraculous": wealth of about $90 trillion from a standing start 240 years ago. Credit goes to ingenuity, the market system, talented immigrants and rule of law. Debt defaults don't destroy wealth: "Money is always there, but the pockets change" (Gertrude Stein).
- "Babies born in America today are the luckiest crop in history."
- The Dow rose from 66 to 11,497 in the 20th century and a further 72% to 19,763 by yearend 2016. Naysayers prosper selling gloom, "But heaven help them if they act on the nonsense they peddle."
- On panics:
  - No one can predict them. Meg McConnell: systemic risk "tends to find us."
  - "Widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases. Personal fear is your enemy," and it is unwarranted.
  - Investors who avoid high, unnecessary costs and hold a collection of large, conservatively financed American businesses for a long time "will almost certainly do well."
- Berkshire's size precludes a brilliant result ("prospective returns fall as assets increase"), but a collection of good businesses, financial strength and owner-oriented culture should deliver "decent results."
- Disclosure and treatment of owners:
  - All shareholders should get new information simultaneously and have time to digest it. Berkshire releases data late Friday or early Saturday and holds its meeting on Saturday.
  - It does not talk one-on-one with large institutions or analysts. The shareholder "of limited means" who entrusts a substantial part of savings is the person Warren pictures when running the company and writing the letter.
- Managers are "All-Stars" who run businesses "as if they were the only asset owned by their families." Most have no financial need to work, and the joy of business "home runs" means as much as pay.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett reviews 2017, warning about distorting GAAP rules and frenzied acquisition pricing, explaining insurance float and mega-cat preparedness, and settling his ten-year S&P 500 index fund bet against hedge funds. Core lessons: avoid leverage, ignore short-term price noise, favor big easy decisions, and bonds can be riskier than stocks over long horizons.

chunks.heading: Berkshire's 2017 scorecard: net worth, the new GAAP rule, and how Warren measures progress
chunks.text:
- Berkshire's net worth rose $65.3 billion in 2017, lifting per-share book value of both Class A and Class B by 23%. Over 53 years, per-share book value grew from $19 to $211,750, a 19.1% compounded annual rate.
- Only $36 billion came from Berkshire's operations. The other $29 billion came from the December rewrite of the U.S. Tax Code.
- A new GAAP rule requires net income to include unrealized gains and losses on stocks held. Berkshire owns $170 billion of marketable stocks (excluding Kraft Heinz), which can swing $10 billion or more in a quarter. Warren says this makes Berkshire's GAAP "bottom-line" "useless" for analysis.
- Realized gains are also random, "largely because we sell securities when that seems the intelligent thing to do, not because we are trying to influence earnings." He warns shareholders to ignore them.
- Warren and Charlie Munger focus on increases in "normalized per-share earning power." Berkshire publishes financials late Friday or early Saturday so owners have time to analyze before markets open Monday.
- Berkshire's four building blocks of value: sizable stand-alone acquisitions, bolt-on acquisitions, internal sales growth and margin improvement, and investment earnings from stocks and bonds.

chunks.heading: Buying businesses in a frenzy: criteria, why CEOs overpay, and aversion to leverage
chunks.text:
- Criteria for stand-alone acquisitions: durable competitive strengths, able and high-grade management, good returns on net tangible assets, opportunities for internal growth at attractive returns, and a sensible price.
- Price blocked nearly every deal in 2017, as prices for "decent, but far from spectacular, businesses hit an all-time high."
- Why others overpay:
  - The CEO job self-selects for "can-do" types, and urging such a CEO to consider acquisitions is "a bit like telling your ripening teenager to be sure to have a normal sex life."
  - Subordinates cheer the bigger domain and pay that rises with company size.
  - Investment bankers smell fees ("Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut").
  - If history doesn't justify the deal, large "synergies" get forecast: "Spreadsheets never disappoint."
  - Cheap debt makes even a high-priced deal boost per-share earnings.
- Berkshire evaluates acquisitions on an all-equity basis and never factors in synergies, "nor do we often find" them. Exceptions to assigning debt to a business: Clayton's lending portfolio and the regulated utilities' fixed-asset commitments.
- On leverage: its aversion "has dampened our returns over the years. But Charlie and I sleep well. Both of us believe it is insane to risk what you have and need in order to obtain what you don't need." Both held this view 50 years ago running their partnerships.
- Guideline: "The less the prudence with which others conduct their affairs, the greater the prudence with which we must conduct our own."
- Warren expects occasional chances for very large purchases despite the drought.

chunks.heading: 2017 deals: Pilot Flying J and the bolt-ons
chunks.text:
- **Pilot Flying J (PFJ):** Berkshire bought a 38.6% partnership interest. PFJ does about $20 billion in annual volume, is the nation's leading travel-center operator, and is run by the Haslam family (Jimmy Haslam manages 27,000 associates at about 750 locations). Berkshire contractually increases its stake to 80% in 2023; the family keeps 20%. Kevin Clayton's praise of the Haslams helped cement the deal.
- **Clayton Homes:**
  - Bought two conventional-home builders (Oakwood Homes, Harris Doyle); Warren expects 2018 site-built volume above $1 billion.
  - 2017 sales: 19,168 units through its own retail and 26,706 wholesaled.
  - Its 49% share of manufactured homes is about three times the nearest competitor, versus 13% in 2003.
- **Shaw Industries:** Acquired U.S. Floors, a luxury vinyl tile distributor. Sales grew 40% in 2017; Shaw's sales reached $5.7 billion with 22,000 employees.
- **HomeServices:**
  - Added Long and Foster, Houlihan Lawrence and Gloria Nilson, bringing agents to 40,950 (up 12,300).
  - It took part in $127 billion of "sides" in 2017 and is on track for only about 3% of U.S. home brokerage.
- **Precision Castparts:** Bought Wilhelm Schulz GmbH. Warren admits he doesn't understand manufacturing as well as brokerage, home building or truck stops, but trusts CEO Mark Donegan: "Betting on people can sometimes be more certain than betting on physical assets."

chunks.heading: Insurance float: how it works and how Berkshire got it
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought National Indemnity and a sister company in early 1967 for $8.6 million. It received $6.7 million of tangible net worth (invested in securities Berkshire would have owned anyway, "trading dollars"), paid a $1.9 million premium over net worth, and gained $19.4 million of "float."
- Float is money that belongs to others but that Berkshire holds and invests. Dividends, interest and gains belong to Berkshire, and so do investment losses.
- Float arises because premiums are paid upfront while losses emerge over the policy and often long after. Some claims (asbestos) surface and settle over many years, and some payments (lifetime workers' comp care) stretch over decades.
- "Long-tail" lines such as medical malpractice and product liability generate far more float than auto collision or homeowners. Berkshire specializes in jumbo reinsurance that assumes long-tail losses already incurred by other insurers.
- Growth of float ($ millions):
  - 1970: $39
  - 1980: $237
  - 1990: $1,632
  - 2000: $27,871
  - 2010: $65,832
  - 2017: $114,500
- Premiums reached $60,597 million in 2017, boosted by reinsuring up to $20 billion of AIG's long-tail losses for a $10.2 billion premium, "a world's record and one we won't come close to repeating."
- Berkshire is the country's second-largest p/c company by premiums and the leader in float. Float will probably grow slowly, and any decline would be at most about 3% in a year.
- Unlike bank deposits or life policies with surrender options, p/c float can't be withdrawn. That means no runs, which Warren factors into investment decisions.
- When underwriting profits occur, "our cost of float was less than zero."

chunks.heading: Catastrophe risk, financial strength, and liquidity
chunks.text:
- Hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria (Texas, Florida, Puerto Rico): Warren guessed industry insured losses at about $100 billion and Berkshire's loss at $3 billion ($2 billion after tax), about 3% of the industry. He expects roughly that share of future U.S. mega-cats.
- The $2 billion net cost cut GAAP net worth by under 1%. Other reinsurers lost 7% to more than 15% of net worth. A slightly more easterly Irma path might have added another $100 billion of insured losses.
- Mega-cat odds: he puts the annual probability of a U.S. event causing $400 billion or more of insured losses at about 2%, rising over time with more and costlier structures in vulnerable areas. Berkshire's share might be about $12 billion, far below its non-insurance annual earnings, while "much – indeed, perhaps most – of the p/c world would be out of business."
- Reserves are "similar to a self-graded exam" (V.J. Dowling), and early loss estimates for mega-cats usually run low.
- After 14 straight years of underwriting profit ($28.3 billion pre-tax), 2017 had a $3.2 billion pre-tax underwriting loss.
- In insurance "there are no trade secrets, patents, or locational advantages. What counts are brains and capital."
- Liquidity: year-end cash and Treasury Bills were $116.0 billion (average maturity 88 days), up from $86.4 billion. In 2008-2009 Warren liked having "loads of Treasury Bills" so Berkshire never had to rely on bank lines or commercial paper. "Charlie and I never will operate Berkshire in a manner that depends on the kindness of strangers." This excess cash earns "only a pittance" and is above the level they want.

chunks.heading: Non-insurance operations and capital spending
chunks.text:
- Excluding investment income, non-insurance businesses earned $20 billion pre-tax in 2017, up $950 million. BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy (90.2% owned) produced about 44%.
- Next five by earnings (Clayton, International Metalworking, Lubrizol, Marmon, Precision Castparts): $5.5 billion, versus $5.4 billion.
- Next five (Forest River, Johns Manville, MiTek, Shaw, TTI): $2.1 billion, versus $1.7 billion. All others: $3.7 billion, versus $3.5 billion.
- Depreciation was $7.6 billion against capital expenditures of $11.5 billion. Almost 90% of investment is in the U.S.: "America's economic soil remains fertile."
- Amortization of $1.3 billion is largely not a true economic cost, while BNSF (like all railroads) records depreciation well short of what upkeep requires.
- To substantially raise non-insurance earnings Berkshire needs "one or more huge acquisitions" and has the resources.

chunks.heading: Owning stocks as businesses: retained earnings and the voting/weighing machine
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie view marketable stocks "as interests in businesses, not as ticker symbols to be bought or sold based on their 'chart' patterns, the 'target' prices of analysts or the opinions of media pundits." If the businesses succeed, the investments will, though he admits "I will make expensive mistakes." "In America, equity investors have the wind at their back."
- Dividends of $3.7 billion in 2017 understate true earnings. Under Principle 6, undistributed investee earnings should deliver at least equivalent capital gains over time, though the link is invisible short term.
- Quoting Ben Graham: "In the short run, the market is a voting machine; in the long run, however, it becomes a weighing machine."
- Biggest holdings by market value at 12/31/17 (cost basis in parentheses): Wells Fargo $29.3 billion ($11.8 billion), Apple $28.2 billion ($21.0 billion), Bank of America $20.7 billion, Coca-Cola $18.4 billion ($1.3 billion), American Express $15.1 billion ($1.3 billion). Total common stocks carried at market: $170.5 billion on a $74.7 billion cost.
- Kraft Heinz (325,442,152 shares) is carried at a GAAP $17.6 billion, with a market value of $25.3 billion and a cost basis of $9.8 billion.
- Todd Combs and Ted Weschler each manage over $12 billion independently of Warren (about $25 billion together, including over $8 billion of pension assets).

chunks.heading: Temperament, debt, and surviving the drawdowns
chunks.text:
- Berkshire shares fell hard four times in 53 years:
  - March 1973 to January 1975: from $93 to $38 (-59.1%)
  - 10/2/87 to 10/27/87: from $4,250 to $2,675 (-37.1%)
  - 6/19/98 to 3/10/2000: from $80,900 to $41,300 (-48.9%)
  - 9/19/08 to 3/5/09: from $147,000 to $72,400 (-50.7%)
- This is "the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks." Even modest borrowing risks a rattled mind, and "an unsettled mind will not make good decisions."
- No one can say when declines come: "The light can at any time go from green to red without pausing at yellow." Such drops offer extraordinary opportunities to those without debt. He cites Kipling's "If": "If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs…"

chunks.heading: The ten-year bet against hedge funds: index funds, fees, and the real meaning of risk
chunks.text:
- Warren bet Protégé Partners on December 19, 2007 that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a group of five funds-of-funds (holding 200+ hedge funds) over ten years. Each side funded $318,250 of zero-coupon Treasuries, worth $500,000 at maturity. The prize went to Girls Inc. of Omaha.
- Results: the S&P 500 index fund returned 125.8% (8.5% a year). The funds-of-funds returned 21.7%, 42.3%, 87.7%, 2.8% and 27.0% (average annual 2.0%, 3.6%, 6.5%, 0.3%, 2.4%). The funds-of-funds trailed in each of the nine years after 2008.
- The expert side had every advantage: elite managers, freedom to switch managers, heavy incentives, and market behavior that was ordinary (about the 8.5% experts would have predicted). Fees averaging about 2½% of assets were paid every year. "Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter."
- In 100% of 43 ten-year periods since taking control of Berkshire, S&P gain years outnumbered loss years.
- The switch: by November 2012 the bonds sold at 95.7% of face with a yield of only .88%. Both sides sold them and bought 11,200 Berkshire "B" shares. Warren expected Berkshire to grow at least 8% a year even in a so-so economy, and agreed to cover any shortfall below $1 million. Girls Inc. received $2,222,279.
- Selling at over 100 times "earnings" (95.7/.88) was "a dumb – a really dumb – investment" relative to equities, which earn far more than 10% on equity, with S&P dividends of 2½% (about triple the bond yield) plus retained earnings and buybacks.
- Lessons:
  - Markets are generally rational but "occasionally do crazy things." Exploiting them needs no genius, only ignoring mob fears and enthusiasms, focusing on a few fundamentals, and "a willingness to look unimaginative for a sustained period – or even to look foolish."
  - Risk is the possibility that the goal of greater future consumption isn't attained. By that standard "risk-free" long bonds in 2012 were riskier than long-term stocks, since even 1% inflation erodes their purchasing power.
  - Stocks are far riskier than short-term bonds over a day, week or year, but a diversified U.S. equity portfolio gets less risky than bonds as the horizon lengthens, if bought at a sensible multiple of earnings relative to interest rates. Measuring risk by a portfolio's bond-to-stock ratio is "a terrible mistake" for long-horizon investors, and high-grade bonds "often" raise risk.
  - "Stick with big, 'easy' decisions and eschew activity." The 200+ hedge fund managers made tens of thousands of decisions, while Warren and Protégé made one.

chunks.heading: Shareholder relations, managers, and succession
chunks.text:
- Warren treats all shareholders equally, with no one-on-one talks with large institutions or analysts. The image in his mind is "the shareholder of limited means who trusts us with a substantial portion of his or her savings."
- Financial data is released late Friday or early Saturday, and the annual meeting is on Saturday. Meeting questions come from three journalists, three analysts and the audience, with no multi-part questions and no advance notice to Warren and Charlie.
- The 2017 meeting webcast drew about 3.1 million real-time viewers, up 72%.
- Operating managers run their businesses "as if they were the only asset owned by their families." Most don't need the money, and the joy of "business 'home runs'" matters as much as pay. Any shares managers and directors hold came from open-market purchases or sales of their businesses to Berkshire, so they "stand in your shoes" with downside as well as upside.
- Headquarters is small but handles a 32,700-page federal tax return and 3,935 state returns.
- Succession: in early 2018 the board elected Ajit Jain (insurance operations) and Greg Abel (all other businesses) as directors and Vice Chairmen. Warren and Charlie focus on investments and capital allocation. Both men have been with Berkshire for decades, and "the character of each man matches his talents."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains how to value Berkshire as a forest of five asset groves rather than trees, why GAAP mark-to-market and book value mislead, how float and retained earnings fund growth, and why disciplined buybacks, minimal debt and a cash fortress matter. He closes with faith in American business.

chunks.heading: Why GAAP earnings and book value mislead at Berkshire
chunks.text:
- Warren's 2018 GAAP earnings were $4.0 billion: $24.8 billion operating earnings, a $3.0 billion intangible impairment (mostly Kraft Heinz), $2.8 billion realized gains, and a $20.6 billion unrealized loss.
- A new GAAP rule forces unrealized gains and losses on stocks into earnings. Warren and Charlie think it is not sensible and predicted "wild and capricious swings in our bottom line."
- Quarterly GAAP results swung from a $1.1 billion loss, to $12 billion and $18.5 billion profits, to a $25.4 billion loss, while operating businesses were steady. Operating earnings for the year beat the 2016 high of $17.6 billion by 41%.
- His advice: "Focus on operating earnings, paying little attention to gains or losses of any variety."
- He dropped per-share book value from the letter's opening because:
  - Berkshire's value has shifted from marketable stocks to operating businesses.
  - Accounting carries those businesses in book value far below their true value.
  - Buybacks below intrinsic value but above book raise per-share intrinsic value while lowering per-share book value.
- He will instead emphasize Berkshire's market price, which over time is the best measure of business performance.

chunks.heading: Valuing Berkshire by "groves" rather than trees
chunks.text:
- Warren says investors need not analyze every business ("trees"). Berkshire's intrinsic value can be approximated by appraising five "groves": non-insurance subsidiaries, marketable equities, shared-control businesses, cash and fixed income, and insurance.
- Intrinsic value is roughly the sum of the four asset groves, minus taxes eventually payable on selling marketable securities.
- No deduction for taxes on selling wholly owned businesses: "It would be foolish for us to sell any of our wonderful companies even if no tax would be payable... Truly good businesses are exceptionally hard to find."
- Insurance float funds much of the other four groves, and interest on debt is already deducted from subsidiary earnings.
- Combining the groves in one entity lets Berkshire allocate capital objectively, eliminate enterprise risk, avoid insularity, fund assets cheaply, use tax efficiencies and minimize overhead. "The whole is greater – considerably greater – than the sum of the parts."
- Prime goal: buy ably managed businesses, in whole or part, with favorable and durable economics, at sensible prices. He buys control sometimes, but far more often finds the attributes in public companies, where Berkshire takes 5% to 10%.
- In 2018 stocks offered far more value than whole-business purchases, so Berkshire bought about $43 billion of equities and sold $19 billion.

chunks.heading: What counts as real earnings
chunks.text:
- Non-insurance subsidiaries earned $16.8 billion after tax, interest, managerial compensation (cash or stock), restructuring, depreciation, amortization and home-office overhead.
- He criticizes "adjusted EBITDA." On stock-based compensation not counting as an expense: "What else could it be – a gift from shareholders?" Restructurings are common in business and shareholders always bear the cost.
- Quoting Lincoln: calling a dog's tail a leg doesn't make it one. "Abe would have felt lonely on Wall Street."
- He adds back $1.4 billion of acquisition-related amortization as not a true economic cost, both for private businesses and stocks.
- The $8.4 billion depreciation charge understates true cost: Berkshire must spend more than that just to stay competitive. It invested a record $14.5 billion in fixed assets in 2018, 89% in America.

chunks.heading: Owning stocks as owning businesses
chunks.text:
- Warren and Charlie do not see the $172.8 billion portfolio as ticker symbols to sell on downgrades, Fed actions, politics or forecasts. They see companies earning about 20% on net tangible equity without excessive debt, versus 3% or less on 30-year Treasuries.
- Retained earnings matter more than dividends. For the five largest holdings (American Express, Apple, Bank of America, Coca-Cola, Wells Fargo), Berkshire's share of dividends was $2,966 million and of retained earnings $6,837 million. Historically, retained earnings of investees have delivered more than one dollar of capital gain for each dollar reinvested.
- He welcomes investee buybacks when the stock is underpriced. Berkshire's American Express holdings were unchanged for eight years while ownership rose from 12.6% to 17.9%. Its $1.2 billion share of 2018 earnings was about 96% of the $1.3 billion cost.
- Overpaying can turn a splendid business into a poor investment for a painfully long time, but "investment performance converges with business performance."
- Deployment: he expects more stock purchases in 2019 because business prices are "sky-high," while still hoping for an "elephant-sized acquisition." This is not a market call: "Charlie and I have no idea as to how stocks will behave next week or next year."
- The test is whether part of an attractive business is worth more than its market price.

chunks.heading: Buybacks, transparency and avoiding Wall Street games
chunks.text:
- Buybacks below intrinsic value benefit continuing shareholders: if a departing partner is priced at 90 cents on the dollar, per-share value rises with each repurchase. "Blindly buying an overpriced stock is value-destructive."
- Shareholders must get the information to estimate value so no seller is misled; the letter exists to do that.
- Decisions are made for the shareholders who are staying, not those leaving, so he ignores current-quarter results.
- Berkshire prepares no monthly company-wide earnings reports or balance sheets, has no company-wide budget and no quarterly "number" to hit.
- He warns that meeting Wall Street expectations breeds bad behavior: quarter-end trade-loading, ignoring rising insurance losses, cookie-jar reserves. "Playing with the numbers 'just this once'" can become fraud, and subordinates copy the boss.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and funding
chunks.text:
- Float is premiums collected upfront and claims paid later, invested meanwhile. Berkshire's grew from $39 million (1970) to $237 million (1980), $1,632 million (1990), $27,871 million (2000), $65,832 million (2010) and $122,732 million (2018).
- Any decline should be very gradual, at most 3% a year, and contracts can't create immediate demands on cash. If premiums exceed expenses and losses, Berkshire enjoys free money and gets paid to hold it.
- Competition often pushes the industry into underwriting losses and subnormal returns. Berkshire's financial strength gives it more investment flexibility. It had an underwriting profit in 15 of 16 years (the exception being a $3.2 billion pre-tax loss in 2017); the 16-year gain was $27 billion.
- Underwriting discipline: "All insurers give that message lip service. At Berkshire it is a religion, Old Testament style."
- A mega-catastrophe will come, possibly a cyber attack; Berkshire will take big losses but "will be looking to add business the next day."
- Debt: used sparingly. "Rational people don't risk what they have and need for what they don't have and don't need." Debt becomes fatal when credit vanishes. Most debt sits at railroad and energy subsidiaries, not guaranteed by Berkshire.
- Equity of $349 billion came from retaining all earnings; a 100% payout would have left the original $22 million.
- Other funding: deferred taxes ($50.5 billion), including $14.7 billion on unrealized stock gains and $28.3 billion from accelerated depreciation, both effectively interest-free loans.
- Financial fortress: $112 billion in T-bills and cash equivalents, plus $20 billion in other fixed income. Berkshire pledges to always hold at least $20 billion in cash equivalents. "I will never risk getting caught short of cash."

chunks.heading: GEICO, Tony Nicely and management
chunks.text:
- In the mid-1970s GEICO nearly went bankrupt after underpricing its policies. Warren backed new CEO Jack Byrne and bought about a third of the company, later about half through GEICO's buybacks "without our spending a dime." The half cost $47 million.
- In 1995 Berkshire paid $2.3 billion for the other half, about 50 times the cost of the first half.
- Under Tony Nicely, GEICO became the No. 2 US auto insurer with sales up 1,200%, $15.5 billion in pre-tax underwriting profit, and float from $2.5 billion to $22.1 billion. Warren estimates Tony added more than $50 billion to intrinsic value.
- He praises Tony as a model manager who helps 40,000 associates find abilities they didn't know they had. He succeeded with Bill Roberts, whom Warren has watched for decades.
- Early 2018: Ajit Jain took over insurance and Greg Abel all other operations. Berkshire is "far better managed" than when Warren alone supervised. He says Berkshire blood flows through their veins.

chunks.heading: The American Tailwind and temperament
chunks.text:
- Warren's first investment was in March 1942, age 11: three shares of Cities Service preferred for $114.75. Over 77 years, a no-fee S&P 500 fund with dividends reinvested would have turned it into $606,811 pre-tax (5,288 for 1). A tax-free $1 million would be about $5.3 billion.
- Paying 1% a year to helpers would cut that to $2.65 billion: the 11.8% annual return becomes 10.8%.
- The national debt rose roughly 400-fold in that period. Buying 3¼ ounces of gold with $114.75 would be worth about $4,200 now, under 1% of the stock outcome. "The magical metal was no match for the American mettle."
- Growth came through wars, a 21% prime rate, a presidential resignation, collapsing home values and financial panic, across seven Republican and seven Democratic presidents. All the scary headlines are now history.
- Saving and retained earnings drive prosperity for nations as for Berkshire. Berkshire's success is largely "The American Tailwind," and boasting of doing it alone is "beyond arrogance." He hopes to invest across borders too, but expects America to supply most gains over the next 77 years.
- He and Charlie love their jobs: they do what they find interesting with people they like and trust.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains why GAAP's unrealized-gain rule distorts results and urges focus on operating earnings. He champions retained earnings and compounding, acquisition criteria, insurance float and underwriting discipline, buybacks only below intrinsic value, and critiques board independence and deal-hungry CEOs.

chunks.heading: Retained earnings: why stocks compound (Edgar Lawrence Smith, Keynes)
chunks.text:
- Warren credits Edgar Lawrence Smith's 1924 book *Common Stocks as Long Term Investments* with changing how investors think. Smith began by trying to prove stocks beat bonds in inflation and bonds beat stocks in deflation, and his facts failed to sustain that theory ("the record of a failure").
- Keynes's review, which Warren quotes, is the key insight: well-managed industrial companies retain part of their profits and put them back into the business, so "there is an element of compound interest operating in favour of a sound industrial investment."
- Before Smith, buyers of shares treated them as short-term gambles on market movements, and "gentlemen preferred bonds." This was odd, since Carnegie, Rockefeller and Ford had built vast wealth by retaining huge portions of earnings.
- Warren's conclusion: "Mr. Smith got it right." Retained earnings of investees are "certain to be of major importance in the growth of Berkshire's value."

chunks.heading: Berkshire's 2019 results and why GAAP net income misleads
chunks.text:
- GAAP earnings were $81.4 billion: $24 billion operating earnings, $3.7 billion realized gains and $53.7 billion from higher net unrealized gains (all after tax).
- A GAAP rule imposed in 2018 requires unrealized gains and losses on equity holdings to flow through earnings. Warren and Charlie Munger disagree with it. Before 2018, unrealized gains were excluded and unrealized losses counted only if "other than temporary."
- 2018 showed the problem: unrealized gains fell $20.6 billion and GAAP earnings were about $4 billion. Going to $81.4 billion in 2019 was a "crazy 1,900% increase in GAAP earnings," while equity holdings averaged about $200 billion and intrinsic value grew steadily.
- His advice: focus on operating earnings (little changed in 2019) and ignore quarterly and annual investment gains or losses, realized or unrealized. He still expects the equity holdings to deliver major gains "in an unpredictable and highly irregular manner."

chunks.heading: Capital allocation: reinvest first, then buy good businesses
chunks.text:
- Top priority is reinvesting in businesses already owned. Over the past decade depreciation charges totaled $65 billion versus $121 billion of internal investment in property, plant and equipment.
- Acquisition criteria: (1) good returns on the net tangible capital required, (2) able and honest managers, (3) a sensible price.
- He prefers buying 100% of a business, but major acquisitions meeting the criteria are rare. More often "a fickle stock market" offers large non-controlling stakes in qualifying public companies.
- Accounting difference: earnings of controlled companies (over 50%) flow straight into reported operating earnings. For non-controlled stocks only dividends count; retained earnings "are working hard and creating much added value" but are not recognized.
- Top 10 holdings: Berkshire's share of dividends was $3,798 million versus $8,332 million of retained earnings. Examples: Apple 5.7% owned, $773M dividends vs $2,519M retained; Bank of America 10.7%, $682M vs $2,167M; American Express 18.7%, $261M vs $998M; Coca-Cola 9.3%, $640M vs $194M.
- He expects realized gains from the group to at least equal, and probably beat, the earnings retained, though "sometimes, alas, retentions produce nothing." Realized gains are taxed at the then-current rate (21% federal at the time).
- Buybacks matter because they enlarge Berkshire's share of an investee's future earnings.

chunks.heading: Acquisition lessons: Tom Murphy's advice and the marriage analogy
chunks.text:
- Tom Murphy's advice: "To achieve a reputation as a good manager, just be sure you buy good businesses."
- Warren's record is uneven: some acquisitions disappointed, more than a few were disasters, a reasonable number exceeded hopes.
- Acquisitions are like marriage: a joyful wedding, then reality diverges from expectations. It is "usually the buyer who encounters unpleasant surprises," and it is "easy to get dreamy-eyed during corporate courtships."
- Mitigating dynamic: poor businesses tend to stagnate and need an ever-smaller share of capital, while good businesses grow and absorb more capital at attractive rates. Winners become a growing share of total assets.
- Extreme example: the original textile business, which in 1965 required nearly all of Berkshire's capital and was a huge drag on returns, but by the early 1980s used only a tiny portion after Berkshire acquired a spread of good businesses.
- Today most capital sits in controlled businesses earning good-to-excellent returns on net tangible assets.
- Earnings are assessed after interest, depreciation, taxes, non-cash compensation and restructuring charges, "all of those pesky, but very real, costs that CEOs and Wall Street sometimes urge investors to ignore."

chunks.heading: Non-insurance earnings by tier (2019)
chunks.text:
- BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy (91% share): $8.3 billion combined, up 6%.
- Clayton Homes, International Metalworking, Lubrizol, Marmon, Precision Castparts: $4.8 billion, little changed.
- Berkshire Hathaway Automotive, Johns Manville, NetJets, Shaw, TTI: $1.9 billion, up from $1.7 billion.
- All other non-insurance businesses: $2.7 billion, down from $2.8 billion.
- Total: $17.7 billion, up 3% from $17.2 billion.
- Lubrizol's French plant was damaged by a fire on September 26, 2019; insurance recoveries cover much of the loss, and one of its largest insurers was a Berkshire company.

chunks.heading: Insurance float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- Property/casualty insurance has been the engine of Berkshire's growth since 1967, when it bought National Indemnity and National Fire & Marine for $8.6 million. National Indemnity is now the largest P/C company in the world by net worth.
- Model: premiums arrive upfront and claims are paid later (sometimes over decades), creating "float" that insurers invest for their own benefit.
- Float: $39M (1970), $237M (1980), $1,632M (1990), $27,871M (2000), $65,832M (2010), $122,732M (2018), $129,423M (2019).
- Any future decline would be gradual, at most 3% a year, and Berkshire's contracts can never produce immediate demands on cash that matter. If premiums exceed expenses and eventual losses, Berkshire enjoys "free money" and gets "paid for holding it."
- Industry float is worth far less than it was: insurers hold mostly high-grade bonds, and yields on float fell from roughly 5-6 cents per dollar to 2-3 cents (or less). Reaching for lower-quality bonds or illiquid "alternatives" is "dangerous."
- Berkshire has more flexibility thanks to its capital, cash and non-insurance earnings.
- Underwriting profit in 16 of the last 17 years; the exception was 2017 (pre-tax loss $3.2 billion). Cumulative pre-tax gain over the 17 years was $27.5 billion, $400 million of it in 2019. Underwriting discipline is "a religion, Old Testament style."
- He warns that such a streak will not repeat: risks can take decades to surface (asbestos), and a mega-catastrophe, possibly a cyber attack, will come. Berkshire will take big losses but it "will not come close to straining our resources" and will want to add business the next day.
- GUARD Insurance (Wilkes-Barre, PA): bought in late 2012 for $221 million, roughly net worth. By 2019 premiums were $1.9 billion, up 379%, and float was up 265%, with a satisfactory underwriting profit.

chunks.heading: Berkshire Hathaway Energy and reinvesting everything
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought 76% of BHE in 2000 and now owns 91% with Walter Scott Jr. and Greg Abel. BHE has never paid Berkshire a dividend and has retained $28 billion, unlike utilities that often pay out as much as 80% or more of earnings. "The more we can invest, the more we like it."
- Iowa residential rates were 8.8 cents/kWh in 2000 and have risen under 1% a year, with no base rate increases promised through 2028. Rival investor-owned utility rates were 61% higher (soon 70%).
- By 2021 BHE expects about 25.2 million MWh of wind generation in Iowa versus customer needs of about 24.6 million MWh, i.e. wind self-sufficiency. Three of its five largest customers are now high-tech giants.
- BHE could handle utility projects needing $100 billion or more of investment.

chunks.heading: Equities versus bonds, and temperament
chunks.text:
- Fifteen largest holdings: $248 billion market value on $110 billion cost (Apple $73.7B, Bank of America $33.4B, Coca-Cola $22.1B, American Express $18.9B, Wells Fargo $18.6B). Kraft Heinz is excluded because it is equity-accounted: carried at $13.8 billion versus $10.5 billion market value.
- He views these holdings not as "stock market wagers" to be dropped over analyst downgrades, earnings misses, Fed actions, politics or economists' forecasts, but as partly owned companies earning more than 20% on net tangible equity, weighted, without excessive debt.
- By contrast, 30-year Treasuries yielded 2.5% or less. Forecasting rates "has never been our game," and pundits "reveal, by that very behavior, far more about themselves than they reveal about the future."
- If current rates and low corporate tax rates persist, equities will almost certainly beat long-term fixed-rate debt.
- Warning: anything can happen tomorrow, including market drops of 50% or more. Still, "The American Tailwind" plus compounding make equities the better long-term choice "for the individual who does not use borrowed money and who can control his or her emotions. Others? Beware!"

chunks.heading: Boards, acquisitions bias and director independence
chunks.text:
- Warren has served on 21 public company boards over 62 years. The core board job is unchanged: find and retain a talented, honest CEO devoted to the company for a business lifetime. "When directors get it right, though, they need to do little else."
- Audit committees "remain no match for managers who wish to game numbers," encouraged by earnings "guidance" and the urge to "hit the number." In his limited experience, number-gaming came from ego more than money.
- Compensation committees rely on consultants, making pay plans complex and proxies "mind-numbing."
- Executive sessions without the CEO are a real improvement.
- Acquisitions: he has never seen a CEO who craves a deal bring in an informed critic, himself included. He suggests a board hire two advisors, one pro and one con, paying the winner ten times a token sum. Wall Street benefits from deals: "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut."
- Independence: director pay of $250,000-300,000 for about six meetings a year is 3-4 times median household income, which subtly shapes behavior. Non-wealthy directors seeking a second board need their CEO's endorsement, and CEOs "don't look for pit bulls. It's the cocker spaniel that gets taken home."
- Directors with fortunes tied to the company are often called not independent, while fee-dependent ones are. He prefers directors who bought shares with their own money; one laggard company had eight directors who never had.
- Berkshire seeks business-savvy, owner-oriented directors with a strong specific interest in the company, guided by "thought and principles, not robot-like 'process.'" Competence is narrow: "if you are Bobby Fischer, you must play only chess for money."

chunks.heading: Buybacks, taxes, succession and Berkshire's durability
chunks.text:
- Buyback rule: only if (a) Charlie and Warren think the stock sells below intrinsic value and (b) ample cash remains afterward. Intrinsic value is imprecise, so they feel no urgency to buy "$1 of value for a very real 95 cents." In 2019 they spent $5 billion to repurchase about 1% of the company. They want share count to fall over time, but "will not prop the stock at any level."
- Berkshire paid $3.6 billion of current federal income tax in 2019, about 1.5% of the $243 billion corporate total. Fifty-five years earlier it paid nothing, and retaining nearly all earnings benefitted both shareholders and the government.
- Five reasons for confidence about life after Warren and Charlie: (1) assets spread over varied businesses earning attractive returns, (2) controlled businesses housed in one entity with lasting economic advantages, (3) finances managed to withstand extreme external shocks, (4) skilled, devoted top managers for whom the job is more than pay or prestige, (5) directors focused on owners and on a rare culture.
- Warren holds 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, has never sold shares (apart from a 1980 exchange for Illinois bank shares, plus gifts and donations), and has no plans to. His will tells executors and trustees not to sell, and absolves them of liability for the concentration. Each year they convert A shares to B and distribute them to foundations that must deploy grants promptly, a process he estimates will take 12 to 15 years.
- He holds that this beats the "safe" fiduciary course of selling into Treasuries, and relies on directors being tested by "Wall Streeters bearing fees."
- Going forward, Ajit Jain and Greg Abel get more exposure at the May 2, 2020 annual meeting and can be asked questions directly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2020 letter owns up to overpaying for Precision Castparts, explains why non-controlling stakes in great businesses beat controlling marginal ones, and shows how disciplined buybacks and retained earnings compound value. It also covers float, ultra-low bond yields, and treating shareholders as partners.

chunks.heading: Earnings, GAAP, and why operating earnings count most
chunks.text:
- Berkshire earned $42.5 billion under GAAP in 2020: $21.9 billion operating earnings, $4.9 billion realized capital gains, a $26.7 billion rise in unrealized gains, and an $11 billion write-down of a few subsidiaries and affiliates (all after tax).
- Warren says "Operating earnings are what count most," even when they are not the largest GAAP item. Berkshire's goals are to grow operating earnings and to acquire large, favorably-situated businesses. In 2020 it met neither: no sizable acquisitions, and operating earnings fell 9%.
- Per-share intrinsic value still rose through retained earnings and repurchasing about 5% of shares.
- Realized and unrealized capital gains "fluctuate capriciously" with the stock market. He and Charlie Munger still expect substantial capital gains from the holdings over time.
- Stock holdings ($281 billion at yearend) are treated as a collection of businesses. Under GAAP only dividends received count as income, so the earnings investees retain on Berkshire's behalf are invisible. Warren says "What's out of sight... should not be out of mind": those retained earnings fund expansion, acquisitions, debt paydown and buybacks, which raise Berkshire's share of future earnings.
- Some investees will disappoint and a few will over-deliver spectacularly. He expects the retained earnings of non-controlled businesses to produce equal or greater capital gains in aggregate, and over 56 years that has held.

chunks.heading: The Precision Castparts mistake
chunks.text:
- The $11 billion write-down is "almost entirely the quantification of a mistake I made in 2016": he paid too much for Precision Castparts (PCC).
- No one misled him. He was too optimistic about PCC's normalized profit potential, and aerospace industry problems exposed the miscalculation in 2020.
- He still believes PCC is a fine company, the best in its business, and that it will earn good returns on its net tangible assets. His error was in the average amount of future earnings, and therefore the proper price.
- He calls it a big error and notes it is "far from my first error of that sort." CEO Mark Donegan is praised as a passionate manager.

chunks.heading: Why Berkshire is not a typical conglomerate
chunks.text:
- Conventional conglomerates bought businesses only in their entirety. Problem one: most truly great businesses did not want to be taken over, so acquirers fished among so-so companies without durable competitive strengths.
- Problem two: they paid steep "control" premiums, then tried to solve overpayment by manufacturing an overvalued stock to use as currency. His illustration: "I'll pay you $10,000 for your dog by giving you two of my $5,000 cats."
- Promotion and "imaginative" accounting, sometimes crossing into fraud, pushed a stock to say 3x business value so it could offer a target 2x its value. He notes that illusions can last a long time, since Wall Street loves deal fees, the press loves colorful promoters, and a soaring price becomes its own "proof."
- Warren and Charlie want to own all or part of a diverse group of businesses with good economics and good managers, and whether Berkshire controls them is unimportant.
- A 20-year struggle with the textile operation he inherited, plus Charlie's influence, convinced him that a non-controlling stake in a wonderful business is "more profitable, more enjoyable and far less work than struggling with 100% of a marginal enterprise."
- Capital is deployed on three criteria: durable competitive strengths, the capabilities and character of management, and price. There are no points for "degree of difficulty" in business.

chunks.heading: The Big Four, insurance float and bonds
chunks.text:
- Most of Berkshire's value sits in four businesses: property/casualty insurance (the largest, the core for 53 years, run by Ajit Jain, who joined in 1986), BNSF (100%), Apple (5.4%), and Berkshire Hathaway Energy (91%).
- The insurers operate with far more capital than any competitor worldwide. Together with cash flowing in from non-insurance businesses, this lets them follow an equity-heavy strategy that most insurers cannot, because regulators and rating agencies push them into bonds.
- Bonds are "not the place to be": the 10-year Treasury yielded 0.93% at yearend 2020, down 94% from 15.8% in September 1981. Germany and Japan have trillions of dollars of sovereign debt at negative yields. Reaching for yield through shaky borrowers is not the answer, and savings and loans destroyed themselves partly that way.
- Float is $138 billion: money that is not Berkshire's but is its to deploy in bonds, stocks or T-bills. It works like bank deposits (cash flows in and out, the total changes little), is likely to stay near this level for years, and on a cumulative basis has been costless. He adds that could change, but "over time, I like our odds."

chunks.heading: Buybacks and the Apple example
chunks.text:
- In 2020 Berkshire repurchased the equivalent of 80,998 A shares for $24.7 billion, raising every shareholder's ownership of all businesses by 5.2%.
- Criteria: buy only when it raises intrinsic value per share for continuing holders and leaves ample funds for opportunities or problems. Repurchases are not appropriate "at simply any price."
- He criticizes American CEOs for spending more on buybacks when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Berkshire does the reverse.
- Apple: Berkshire bought from late 2016 to mid-2018, ending with just over one billion split-adjusted shares and 5.2% of Apple, at a cost of $36 billion. Since then it has received dividends averaging about $775 million a year and took in $11 billion by selling a small part in 2020.
- Despite that sale, Berkshire's stake rose to 5.4% at no cost, because Apple kept shrinking its share count. Combined with Berkshire's own buybacks, shareholders indirectly own 10% more of Apple's assets and earnings than in July 2018.
- "The math of repurchases grinds away slowly, but can be powerful over time."

chunks.heading: Entrepreneurs, small starts and "Never bet against America"
chunks.text:
- Warren's examples of businesses started with little capital:
  - See's Candy (bought 1972): a century old. Rule: do not meddle, since for a non-essential consumer product "the customer is the boss."
  - GEICO: Leo and Lillian Goodwin started it in 1936 with $100,000 to sell auto insurance directly at lower prices. First full-year business was $238,288 in 1937; $35 billion in 2020. He was exposed to it 70 years ago and it was his first investment love.
  - National Indemnity: Jack Ringwalt started it in 1940 with $125,000, focusing on "odd-ball" risks the big insurers ignored. Berkshire bought it in 1967 on a handshake in 15 minutes, with no audit. It is now the only company willing to insure certain giant risks.
  - Nebraska Furniture Mart: Mrs. B started it in 1936 with $2,500. Net worth at end of 1946 was $72,264, with $50 in cash. By 1983 it was worth $60 million, when Berkshire bought 80%, again without an audit. It now owns the three largest US home-furnishings stores, each setting a sales record in 2020 despite six-plus weeks of closure.
  - Clayton Homes (founded 1956) and Pilot Travel Centers (founded 1958, bought a $6,000 service station): each now earns over $1 billion pre-tax. Berkshire owns 38% of Pilot, headed to 80% in 2023.
- Pattern he praises: owner-families who stay on to run the business, with satisfied sellers referring other sellers.
- His conclusion: "Never bet against America." American prosperity, though uneven in its progress toward "a more perfect union," has been "breathtaking."

chunks.heading: The Berkshire partnership and shareholder philosophy
chunks.text:
- Directors must act in the best interest of the corporation and its stockholders. Customers, employees (360,000), lenders and communities are valued but have no vote on dividends, strategy, CEO selection or deals.
- Warren and Charlie ran partnerships from 1956 and 1962 respectively. Warren charged no fees or salary and took his share only above a 6% annual hurdle, with shortfalls carried forward. His own money and his family's were invested alongside. Investors correctly sensed "an extreme aversion to permanent loss of capital."
- Berkshire's 1983 first business principle: "Although our form is corporate, our attitude is partnership."
- He describes five ownership "buckets": himself (which will empty through philanthropy), index funds (automatic pilot), active institutional managers, individual traders, and over a million individuals who trust them with no intent to sell. Charlie and Warren feel special kinship with the last group.
- Berkshire does not court Wall Street analysts or institutions: "We already have the investors we want." He quotes Phil Fisher's restaurant analogy: a company must consistently serve either hamburgers and Coke or French cuisine, and Berkshire has served hamburgers and Coke for 56 years.
- Pledge: "We can and do... pledge to treat you as partners."

chunks.heading: Passive investing advice, fixed assets, BNSF and BHE
chunks.text:
- Stock ownership is a positive-sum game. A monkey throwing 50 darts at the S&P 500 would do well if it never changed its picks. Wealth comes from productive assets, requiring "the passage of time, an inner calm, ample diversification and a minimization of transactions and fees." Investors' expenses are Wall Street's income.
- Berkshire owns $154 billion of depreciated US property, plant and equipment, more than any other US company (AT&T is next at $127 billion). He says this is not itself a triumph: the best returns come from businesses needing minimal assets, high margins and little capital to grow, though asset-heavy companies can still be good investments.
- BNSF and BHE earned a combined $4.2 billion in 2011 and $8.3 billion in 2020.
- BNSF: carries about 15% of US non-local ton-miles and owns 23,000 miles of track across 28 states. Since 2010 it has invested $41 billion, $20 billion more than depreciation. It has paid Berkshire $41.8 billion in dividends, keeping about $2 billion cash so it can borrow cheaply without a Berkshire guarantee. In 2020, despite a 7% volume decline, margin rose 2.9 points under Carl Ice; Katie Farmer became CEO.
- BHE: earnings grew from $122 million to $3.4 billion over 21 years, and it pays no common dividend, unusual for a utility. It is investing $18 billion (started 2006, completion 2030) to rebuild the western transmission grid for renewable power. Warren says the decision rested on trust in America's political, economic and judicial systems, and BHE is looking for other projects of similar size.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2021 letter explains that Berkshire picks businesses with durable advantages and first-class CEOs rather than stocks, values insurance float as a sticky source of investable money, and buys back shares only when price is right. It also covers holding huge cash until opportunities meet criteria, and why owners like Paul Andrews choose Berkshire as a permanent home.

chunks.heading: How Warren Defines What Berkshire Owns and Why He Picks Businesses, Not Stocks
chunks.text:
- Warren says he and Charlie have the job of managing a portion of shareholders' savings, and he reports what he would want to know "if we were the absentee owner and you were the manager."
- He treats all shareholders equally: no discussions with analysts or large institutions, and important news is released on Saturday mornings so everyone can absorb it before markets open Monday.
- His primary duty for 57 years has been increasing the intrinsic value of Berkshire shares.
- The goal is "meaningful investments in businesses with both durable economic advantages and a first-class CEO."
- Stocks are owned for expected long-term business performance, not as vehicles for timely market moves. His line: "Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers."
- He admits "I make many mistakes." The portfolio holds some extraordinary businesses, many good ones and a few marginal ones.
- Advantage of marketable stocks: occasionally it is easy to buy pieces of wonderful businesses at wonderful prices. That "shooting-fish-in-a-barrel" experience is very rare in negotiated deals and never happens en masse. It is also far easier to exit a mistake in the marketable arena.

chunks.heading: Honest Earnings, Taxes, and the Partnership With America
chunks.text:
- Warren favors "old-fashioned" earnings: calculated after interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and all forms of compensation. BNSF's record $6 billion in 2021 was measured this way.
- He warns that deceptive "adjustments" to earnings have become more frequent and more fanciful as stocks have risen: "bull markets breed bloviated bull."
- Berkshire owns and operates more U.S. infrastructure assets (property, plant and equipment) than any other American corporation: $158 billion at yearend 2021. This was never a goal, and "Berkshire always will be building."
- Berkshire paid $3.3 billion in federal income tax in 2021, against $402 billion of total U.S. corporate receipts, plus state and foreign taxes.
- Berkshire's textile history: after the 1955 merger of Berkshire Fine Spinning and Hathaway Manufacturing, net worth fell from $51.4 million to $22.1 million in nine years, partly from repurchases, ill-advised dividends and plant shutdowns. The company paid only $337,359 in income tax in that period, about $100 per day. The New England textile industry was in an "extended and non-reversible death march."
- In 1965 new management redeployed cash and steered essentially all earnings into good businesses. Reinvestment plus compounding "worked its magic." Berkshire now pays roughly $9 million daily in income tax.
- Warren credits operating in America for the result: "When you see the flag, say thanks." On March 11, 1942, he bought three Cities Service preferred shares for $114.75 (all his savings) when the Dow closed at 99: "Never bet against America."

chunks.heading: Insurance Float and Why It Is Berkshire's Core Advantage
chunks.text:
