- Berkshire bought National Indemnity in 1967 for $8.6 million. Float, money held and invested but not owned, grew from $19 million to $147 billion, including a small sum from life insurance. It rose $9 billion in 2021.
- Over 55 years the float has cost less than nothing: despite some years where losses plus expenses exceeded premiums, Berkshire earned a modest overall underwriting profit.
- Float is "very sticky." Individual funds come and go daily, but the total is immune from precipitous decline, so it can be invested for the long term.
- Float value is not reflected in GAAP earnings or net worth.
- Hiring Ajit Jain in 1986: asked about insurance experience, Ajit said "None." Warren replied "Nobody's perfect" and hired him. He calls it a lucky day and credits Ajit for much of the insurance value creation, 35 years on.
- Outlook: likely, but far from assured, that float can be maintained without a long-term underwriting loss. Warren is certain there will be some loss years, perhaps very large. Berkshire is built to handle catastrophes "as no other insurer," and will stay so after he and Charlie are gone.
- Why insurance suits Berkshire: the product never becomes obsolete, volume grows with economic growth and inflation, and integrity and capital always matter. Replicating Berkshire's operation would be almost impossible.

chunks.heading: The Four Giants: Insurance, Apple, BNSF and BHE
chunks.text:
- Insurance: Berkshire effectively owns 100% of the insurers, with invested assets enlarged by the large capital backing their promises.
- Apple: Berkshire owns 5.55%, up from 5.39%, at no cost to Berkshire because Apple's buybacks shrank the share count. Each 0.1% of Apple's 2021 earnings equaled $100 million. GAAP counts only dividends ($785 million), while Berkshire's look-through share of earnings was $5.6 billion. Warren applauds Apple using retained earnings for repurchases and calls Tim Cook a "brilliant CEO."
- BNSF: "number one artery of American commerce," record $6 billion earnings, 143 million miles and 535 million tons carried in 2021. Moving that cargo by truck would sharply raise emissions. He predicts it will be a key asset a century from now.
- BHE: earned a record $4 billion in 2021, up over 30-fold from $122 million in 2000, when Berkshire first bought a stake. Berkshire owns 91.1%. It had no wind or solar in 2000 and is now a leader in wind, solar and transmission under David Sokol and Greg Abel. Warren notes it has reported its renewables plans every year since 2007 and has the management, capital and appetite for the large power projects the country needs.

chunks.heading: The Cash Pile, Interest Rates and Share Repurchases
chunks.text:
- Berkshire held $144 billion in cash and equivalents (excluding BNSF and BHE), $120 billion of it in T-bills maturing within a year, financing about 1/2 of 1% of the public debt.
- Pledge: Berkshire (apart from BNSF and BHE) will always hold more than $30 billion in cash. The aim is to be "financially impregnable and never dependent on the kindness of strangers (or even that of friends)." Warren and Charlie "like to sleep soundly."
- The cash is not patriotism or a loss of preference for ownership. Warren has kept at least 80% of his net worth in equities since 1942, and 100% is his favorite. Berkshire's roughly 80% is due to failing to find companies meeting its long-term criteria. Cash-heavy periods "are never pleasant; they are also never permanent."
- Three ways to increase value: (1) raise earning power of controlled businesses by internal growth or acquisitions (internal opportunities now beat acquisitions on returns but are small relative to resources); (2) buy non-controlling stakes in good public businesses (little excites him now); (3) repurchase Berkshire shares.
- Interest rates: "Long-term interest rates that are low push the prices of all productive investments upward, whether these are stocks, apartments, farms, oil wells, whatever." Rates always matter for valuation.
- Buybacks: when price/value is right, this is "the easiest and most certain way" to increase shareholders' wealth. Over two years Berkshire repurchased 9% of shares outstanding at yearend 2019 for $51.7 billion, leaving continuing holders owning about 10% more of every business. Another $1.2 billion was bought by February 23, 2022.
- Buybacks only make sense at appropriate value: overpaying for Berkshire would destroy value just as overpaying for others would. Appetite is "price-dependent."
- Buybacks also raise float per share, which rose 25% in two years, from $79,387 to $99,497 per A share.
- A high-class, buy-and-keep investor base limits buyback opportunities (short-term speculators would create more volatility and more chances), but Warren and Charlie prefer these owners.

chunks.heading: Holdings Snapshot at Yearend 2021
chunks.text:
- Total equity investments carried at market: $350.7 billion (cost $104.6 billion).
- Largest positions: Apple $161.2 billion (cost $31.1 billion); Bank of America $46.0 billion (cost $14.6 billion); American Express $24.8 billion (cost $1.3 billion); Coca-Cola $23.7 billion (cost $1.3 billion); Moody's $9.6 billion (cost $248 million); US Bancorp $8.1 billion; Verizon $8.3 billion; BYD $7.7 billion (cost $232 million, held by BHE).
- Others include BNY Mellon, Charter, Chevron, GM and the Japanese trading houses Itochu, Mitsubishi and Mitsui.
- Also: $10 billion Occidental preferred and warrants (valued at $10.7 billion), a 26.6% Kraft Heinz stake carried at $13.1 billion on the equity method, and 38.6% of Pilot ($45 billion revenue), with Berkshire to raise its stake to 80% in early 2023.
- Todd Combs and Ted Weschler had authority over $34 billion.

chunks.heading: The TTI and BNSF Story: Selling to the Right Home
chunks.text:
- Paul Andrews founded Tex-Tronics (TTI) in 1971 with $500 after being fired by General Dynamics; first-year sales were $112,000. Today TTI sells over one million items, with $7.7 billion annual volume.
- In 2006, at 63, Paul worried about what would happen to those who depended on him if he died. He rejected a competitor sale (best "synergies" economics, but the buyer would cut TTI's CFO, legal and HR people and favor its own city) and a leveraged buyout (focused on an "exit strategy," ending in a reseller). He told Warren: "you are the only guy left." One meeting, one lunch, one deal.
- Results: employees grew from 2,387 to 8,043, earnings up 673%. Each year Warren suggested a raise and Paul replied "We can talk about that next year."
- Luck chain: John Roach's friendship led Paul to Omaha. In the fall of 2009 Berkshire's directors met in Fort Worth to visit TTI. Warren met BNSF CEO Matt Rose on October 22, 2009, the day BNSF reported weak third-quarter results during the Great Recession. The next day he suggested Berkshire was a better long-term home than being public and named his maximum price. Eleven days later the deal was announced. "The BNSF acquisition would never have happened if Paul Andrews hadn't sized up Berkshire as the right home for TTI."
- Lesson: Berkshire's appeal to founders is permanence and keeping people and places intact, not the highest bid.

chunks.heading: Work, Teaching and Choosing Your Shareholders
chunks.text:
- Advice to students: seek employment in (1) the field and (2) with the kind of people you would select if you had no need for money. Find that and "you will no longer be 'working.'"
- Warren and Charlie started at his grandfather's grocery store and found job satisfaction only at Berkshire. They work with people they like and trust; the home office has "no jerks" and about one departure per year.
- Teaching clarifies thinking. Charlie's "orangutan effect": explain a cherished idea to an orangutan and you may leave behind a puzzled primate but exit thinking more clearly.
- Shareholders: Berkshire cannot select owners as a partnership could, but has an unusual corps of individuals and families with a "til death do us part" attitude. People comfortable with their investments "will, on average, achieve better results than those who are motivated by ever-changing headlines, chatter and promises."
- Long-term individual owners are the "partners" he and Charlie have in mind in every decision.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett explains that Berkshire's results came from about a dozen good decisions compounding over decades, not constant activity. He covers owning businesses rather than stocks, buyback math, float, honest accounting, avoiding forecasts, and Charlie Munger's wisdom.

chunks.heading: Who he and Charlie work for
chunks.text:
- Warren says he and Charlie manage "the savings of a great number of individuals," often held for much of their adult lives. Those dedicated savers are foremost in his mind.
- He calls Berkshire holders "once-a-saver, always-a-saver." They live well but eventually give most of their money to philanthropy.
- He notes how rarely they choose "look-at-me assets and dynasty-building." His line: "The disposition of money unmasks humans."

chunks.heading: What Berkshire does: business-pickers, not stock-pickers
chunks.text:
- Capital is allocated across two forms of ownership.
  - Controlled businesses, usually bought 100%. Berkshire directs capital allocation and picks the CEOs who run day-to-day operations.
  - Passive holdings of publicly-traded stocks, with no say in management.
- The goal in both is meaningful investments in businesses with long-lasting favorable economics and trustworthy managers.
- Public stocks are owned for expected long-term business performance, not as trading vehicles. "Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers."
- On management, Berkshire emphasizes trust over rules "to an unusual – some would say extreme – degree." Warren says: "We are understanding about business mistakes; our tolerance for personal misconduct is zero."
- Warren admits his mistakes. The portfolio holds a few businesses with truly extraordinary economics, many with very good economics, and a large marginal group. Some businesses he invested in died.
- He cites Schumpeter's "creative destruction": capitalism builds a pile of losers while delivering a gusher of improved goods and services.

chunks.heading: Public stocks vs controlled businesses: pricing
chunks.text:
- Stocks often trade at "truly foolish prices, both high and low." "'Efficient' markets exist only in textbooks."
- Marketable stocks and bonds are baffling, and their behavior is usually understandable only in retrospect.
- Episodically, it becomes easy to buy pieces of wonderful businesses at wonderful prices.
- Controlled businesses are different. They sometimes command ridiculously high prices but are almost never available at bargain valuations. Owners do not sell at a panic valuation unless under duress.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation report card and the "secret sauce"
chunks.text:
- In 58 years, most of Warren's capital-allocation decisions were "no better than so-so." Some bad moves were rescued by luck (USAir and Salomon).
- Satisfactory results came from about a dozen truly good decisions, roughly one every five years, plus the advantage of long-term holding.
- Coca-Cola:
  - Berkshire completed the purchase of 400 million shares in August 1994 over seven years, for $1.3 billion.
  - The annual dividend rose from $75 million in 1994 to $704 million in 2022, growing every year.
  - The stake was worth $25 billion at yearend 2022.
- American Express:
  - Purchases were essentially complete in 1995, also costing $1.3 billion.
  - Annual dividends grew from $41 million to $302 million.
  - The stake was recorded at $22 billion.
- Each holding is roughly 5% of Berkshire's net worth, about its weighting long ago.
- Compare a $1.3 billion mistake that flat-lined, such as a high-grade 30-year bond. It would now be 0.3% of net worth and deliver about $80 million a year.
- Lesson: "The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom." A few winners work wonders over time, and it helps to start early and live into your 90s.

chunks.heading: Operating earnings, GAAP noise and accounting manipulation
chunks.text:
- Warren urges focusing on operating earnings (GAAP income excluding gains or losses on equity holdings). 2022 operating earnings were a record $30.8 billion.
- GAAP quarterly swings in 2022 (in $ billions):

| Quarter | Operating | GAAP |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 7.0 | 5.5 |
| Q2 | 9.3 | (43.8) |
| Q3 | 7.8 | (2.7) |
| Q4 | 6.7 | 18.2 |

- He calls quarterly or annual GAAP earnings "100% misleading" and says the media's headlines on them "totally misinform investors." Capital gains remain hugely important over decades.
- Even operating earnings can be manipulated. Warren calls "beating expectations" games "disgusting": "It requires no talent to manipulate numbers: Only a deep desire to deceive is required."
- He cites a CEO's phrase, "Bold imaginative accounting," as "one of the shames of capitalism."

chunks.heading: Insurance float, Alleghany and share repurchases
chunks.text:
- Berkshire bought Alleghany, a property-casualty insurer run by Joe Brandon. Berkshire's financial strength lets its insurers follow investment strategies unavailable to virtually all competitors.
- Float grew from $147 billion to $164 billion in 2022. With disciplined underwriting, it has a decent chance of being cost-free over time.
- Float has grown 8,000-fold since the first property-casualty insurer was bought in 1967. It is an extraordinary asset not recognized in the financial statements.
- Berkshire bought back 1.2% of its shares in 2022. Apple and American Express repurchases raised Berkshire's ownership at no cost to it.
- The math: fewer shares means a larger interest in the businesses. This works only at value-accretive prices. Overpaying benefits only the selling shareholders "and the friendly, but expensive, investment banker."
- Warren's local auto dealership example: three informed owners, one managing, and one passive owner sells back at a price attractive to the other two. No one is harmed, the manager is not favored, and the public is not hurt.
- Anyone saying all repurchases are harmful is "either an economic illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue."

chunks.heading: Berkshire's structure, staying power and the American Tailwind
chunks.text:
- Berkshire was a "one-trick pony" in 1965, a doomed New England textile operation. National Indemnity became available in 1967, shifting resources to insurance.
- The drivers of results: retained earnings, compounding, avoiding major mistakes, and "most important of all" the American Tailwind. "America would have done fine without Berkshire. The reverse is not true."
- Scale facts, using 2021 earnings:
  - The S&P 500 earned $1.8 trillion.
  - Only 128 of the 500 (including Berkshire) earned $3 billion or more, and 23 lost money.
- At yearend 2022, Berkshire was the largest owner of eight S&P 500 companies:
  - American Express
  - Bank of America
  - Chevron
  - Coca-Cola
  - HP Inc.
  - Moody's
  - Occidental Petroleum
  - Paramount Global
- Berkshire also owns 100% of BNSF ($5.9 billion earnings) and 92% of BH Energy ($4.3 billion).
- Permanent policies:
  - Hold a "boatload of cash and U.S. Treasury bills."
  - Avoid any behavior that could cause uncomfortable cash needs in panics or unprecedented insurance losses.
  - The CEO is always the Chief Risk Officer, which is irresponsible to delegate.
  - Future CEOs must hold a significant part of their net worth in Berkshire shares, bought with their own money.
- Warren says near-term economic and market forecasts are "worse than useless." He plans for acceptable results over time and for staying power in panics and severe recessions.
- Berkshire offers modest but imperfect protection from runaway inflation. "Huge and entrenched fiscal deficits have consequences."
- On America: after 80 years of investing, "I have yet to see a time when it made sense to make a long-term bet against America."

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text:
- In the decade through 2021, the Treasury collected about $32.3 trillion and spent $43.9 trillion.
- Berkshire paid $32 billion of corporate income tax over 2012-21, almost exactly 0.1% of all collections.
- About 1,000 taxpayers matching that payment would have covered all federal taxes, with no other business or household paying anything.
- Warren expects and hopes Berkshire pays much more in the next decade.

chunks.heading: Charlie Munger's lessons and the value of a partner
chunks.text:
Warren shares Charlie's thoughts from a recent podcast:

- "The world is full of foolish gamblers, and they will not do as well as the patient investor."
- "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there." Also: write your desired obituary early, then behave accordingly.
- Rationality must be worked on, or you stay irrational and get lousy results.
- Patience can be learned. A long attention span is a huge advantage.
- Learn from dead people, both the admired and the detested.
- "Don't bail away in a sinking boat if you can swim to one that is seaworthy."
- "A great company keeps working after you are not; a mediocre company won't do that."
- Seek good long-term investments and hold them stubbornly. Ignore market froth.
- Graham: the market is a voting machine day to day and a weighing machine long term.
- No investment is a 100% sure thing, so leverage is dangerous: "A string of wonderful numbers times zero will always equal zero. Don't count on getting rich twice."
- You don't need to own a lot of things to get rich.
- Keep learning as the world changes. Warren and Charlie hated railroad stocks for decades, then recognized that four huge railroads had become vital. "Better late than never."
- Charlie's decision-clincher: "Warren, think more about it. You're smart and I'm right."

Warren's own rule: find a very smart, high-grade partner, preferably slightly older, and listen very carefully.

chunks.heading: See's Candies and the 2022 annual meeting
chunks.text:
- At the first in-person meeting in three years, See's sold 2,690 transactions on Friday (noon to 5 p.m.) and 3,931 on Saturday.
- Volume was $400,309 over the two days, about 10 sales per minute in prime time. The kiosk sold eleven tons of candy.
- The products "haven't been materially altered in 101 years." "What worked for See's in the days of Henry Ford's model T works now."
- Warren was 92 and Charlie 99. The next meeting is May 5-6, 2023 in Omaha.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2023 shareholder letter, written after Munger's death, covers why Berkshire reports operating rather than GAAP earnings, why it buys wonderful businesses at fair prices, and why it never risks permanent loss of capital. It also covers the capital-intensity of BNSF, his utility mistake, insurance underwriting discipline, and why he trusts patient owners like his sister Bertie.

chunks.heading: Charlie Munger and the shift from Graham to "wonderful businesses"
chunks.text:
- Charlie Munger died November 28, 2023, 33 days before his 100th birthday. Warren first met him in 1959.
- In 1965, Charlie told Warren: "forget about ever buying another company like Berkshire. But now that you control Berkshire, add to it wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices and give up buying fair businesses at wonderful prices."
- Charlie also said: "abandon everything you learned from your hero, Ben Graham. It works but only when practiced at small scale."
- Warren followed this "with much back-sliding"; Charlie later partnered with him and "jerked me back to sanity when my old habits surfaced."
- Warren calls Charlie the "architect" of present Berkshire and himself the "general contractor" who carried out the day-by-day construction.
- Charlie never took credit and never reminded Warren of his mistakes.

chunks.heading: Who Berkshire writes for, and what "earnings" should mean
chunks.text:
- Berkshire targets "lifetime" shareholders: investors who save to buy a farm or rental property, not those who buy lottery tickets or "hot" stocks.
- Warren pictures his sister Bertie as the reader. She is sensible, understands incentives and human weakness, and knows pundits should be ignored: "if she could reliably predict tomorrow's winners, would she freely share her valuable insights?"
- Shareholders are owed good and bad news directly from the CEO, not from an investor-relations officer serving "optimism and syrupy mush."
- GAAP net earnings were $90 billion (2021), ($23 billion) (2022) and $96 billion (2023). Warren calls this "worse-than-useless."
- The cause is the 2018 mandate to include unrealized capital gains and losses, which can exceed $5 billion a day.
- Berkshire prefers operating earnings, which exclude them: $27.6 billion (2021), $30.9 billion (2022), $37.4 billion (2023).
- Warren still expects capital gains to be a very important part of value accretion over decades. He says it is "more than silly" to judge investment value on earnings that include short-term market swings.
- Graham's line: "In the short run the market acts as a voting machine; in the long run it becomes a weighing machine."
- He has held a majority of his net worth in U.S. equities since his first stock purchase on March 11, 1942, when the Dow was below 100 (now about 38,000). Investors "need only sit quietly, listening to no one."

chunks.heading: What Berkshire buys, and why size now limits it
chunks.text:
- The goal: own all or part of businesses with "good economics that are fundamental and enduring."
- Warren particularly favors the rare enterprise that can deploy additional capital at high returns in the future. Owning one and sitting tight can deliver wealth "almost beyond measure."
- Predicting winners is harder than it looks; those who claim to know are "self-delusional or snake-oil salesmen."
- He wants able, trustworthy managers but admits this judgment is hard. Quoting Hugh McCulloch (1863): "Never deal with a rascal under the expectation that you can prevent him from cheating you." Sincerity and empathy can be faked.
- Berkshire's GAAP net worth is $561 billion, versus $8.9 trillion for the other 499 S&P companies in 2022. That is nearly 6% of its universe.
- Doubling within five years is not possible, partly because Berkshire is highly averse to issuing shares.
- Only a handful of U.S. companies can move the needle, and they are picked over. Outside the U.S. there are essentially no meaningful candidates. "We have no possibility of eye-popping performance."
- Realistic aim: do a bit better than the average American corporation with materially less risk of permanent capital loss.
- Allegiance is to the country and shareholders: "your money is comingled with ours, it does not belong to us."

chunks.heading: Fortress balance sheet and the "not-so-secret weapon"
chunks.text:
- Markets can seize up unpredictably (four months in 1914, a few days in 2001, September 2008). Berkshire can respond with huge sums and certainty of performance.
- Today's market participants are no more stable than before; markets show "far more casino-like behavior," and "the casino now resides in many homes."
- Wall Street's juices flow from feverish activity; "whatever foolishness can be marketed will be vigorously marketed."
- The rule that will not change: "Never risk permanent loss of capital." A couple of good decisions in a lifetime plus avoiding serious mistakes is enough, given the American tailwind and compounding.
- Berkshire pays no dividend, repurchases are 100% discretionary, annual debt maturities are never material, and it holds cash and T-bills far above conventional need.
- It relied on no commercial paper, bank lines or debt markets in 2008. "EBITDA" is a banned measurement; earnings are judged after interest, taxes and depreciation.
- Extreme conservatism is likely unneeded in most decades, like insurance on a fireproof-seeming building. Quotational shrinkage can't be avoided, but permanent damage can.
- "Berkshire is built to last."

chunks.heading: Patience in Coke, AmEx, Occidental and Japan
chunks.text:
- Coca-Cola (1886) and American Express (1850) are each 4-5% of GAAP net worth. Both failed at unrelated expansion but succeeded in the base business, and their products "traveled" worldwide.
- Berkshire has not bought or sold either in over two decades. Its share of 2023 AmEx earnings exceeded the $1.3 billion cost. AmEx's dividend is expected up about 16% in 2024.
- Lesson: "When you find a truly wonderful business, stick with it. Patience pays, and one wonderful business can offset the many mediocre decisions."
- Buybacks raise ownership in everything Berkshire owns, but "All stock repurchases should be price-dependent. What is sensible at a discount to business-value becomes stupid if done at a premium."
- Occidental: 27.8% owned plus warrants giving the option to raise ownership at a fixed price for over five years. No interest in buying or managing it. Warren values its U.S. oil and gas holdings and says Vicki Hollub "knows how to separate oil from rock."
- U.S. output went from 8 million BOEPD (1975) to 5 million (2007) to over 13 million today after shale became feasible in 2011.
- Japan: stakes of about 9% in Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, with a pledge not to exceed 9.9%. Purchases began July 4, 2019. Cost ¥1.6 trillion; yearend value ¥2.9 trillion; unrealized gain 61% or $8 billion in dollars.
- Berkshire financed most of it with ¥1.3 trillion of yen bonds, since neither he nor Greg Abel can forecast currencies. The yen gain was $1.9 billion.
- Warren likes that all five cut share counts at attractive prices, pay modest executive compensation, pay out only about 1/3 of earnings as dividends, and are reluctant to issue shares.
- Building positions at Berkshire's size is "like turning a battleship."

chunks.heading: BNSF and BHE: candid mistakes in capital-intensive businesses
chunks.text:
- BNSF: 23,759 miles of main track, carried at $70 billion; Warren guesses replication would cost at least $500 billion. Capital spending above depreciation since the purchase 14 years ago totals $22 billion or more, over $1.5 billion a year.
- That gap means dividends to Berkshire fall short of reported earnings unless debt rises, which Berkshire won't do. Hence the return is acceptable but "a pittance on the replacement value," which is why BNSF was bought at a small fraction of replacement value in 2010.
- 2023 earnings fell more than expected as revenue dropped and Washington-set wage increases outran inflation goals. Margins have slipped relative to the five other major railroads, though he thinks the territory is second to none.
- BHE: Warren erred in expectations. Regulatory climate in a few states raises "the specter of zero profitability or even bankruptcy" (California's largest utility, Hawaii). Wildfire losses are estimated, final tally years away.
- The century-old pact of a fixed return on equity has been broken in some states. He calls failing to anticipate this "a costly mistake," shared with BHE's two partners.
- "Berkshire can sustain financial surprises but we will not knowingly throw good money after bad."

chunks.heading: Insurance float and underwriting discipline
chunks.text:
- 2023 insurance underwriting earned $5.4 billion (vs. a $30 million loss) and insurance investment income $9.6 billion (vs. $6.5 billion). Records were set in sales, float and underwriting profit.
- P/C insurance is the core of Berkshire's well-being. Volume grew nearly 5,000-fold in 57 years, from $17 million to $83 billion.
- Key lesson: underwriters can be any type, "But they can't be optimists at the office." Surprises, even decades after short policies expire, are almost always negative.
- Inflation, monetary and "legal," is a wild card; charlatans make detection slow and costly.
- Ajit Jain, who joined in 1986, built the operation; before that Warren was "wandering in the wilderness." GEICO, from 1951, was an "unbelievably wonderful" experience.
- T-bill income finally paid well in 2023, boosting investment income, and P/C prices strengthened.

chunks.heading: The "Omaha Effect" and Bertie's example
chunks.text:
- Greg Abel (non-insurance, ready to be CEO "tomorrow"), Ajit Jain and Charlie Munger all had Omaha ties; Berkshire itself moved to Omaha in 1970.
- Bertie was active (bonds, one-third in a mutual fund, frequent trading) for 20 years from 1956. In 1980, aged 46, she kept only the mutual fund and Berkshire and made no new trades for 43 years.
- She became very rich even after giving nine-figure philanthropic gifts, using only common sense. Warren's message: sit still with good holdings.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's 2024 annual letter covers owning up to capital allocation and personnel mistakes, judging managers by character rather than schooling, the discipline of P/C insurance and float, and Berkshire's permanent preference for businesses over cash. It also celebrates 60 years of reinvestment, which produced record tax payments.

chunks.heading: How Warren treats mistakes, honesty and reporting to owners
chunks.text:
- Warren frames the annual letter as a "report," which implies more responsibility than mandated data. The goal is to communicate the way he would want a CEO to communicate if he were a passive investor trusting someone with his savings.
- He follows advice Tom Murphy gave him 60 years ago: "praise by name, criticize by category."
- He admits mistakes openly: misjudging the future economics of a business (a capital allocation error, in either marketable stocks or 100% acquisitions) and misjudging the ability or fidelity of managers. Fidelity disappointments hurt beyond the money, "a pain that can approach that of a failed marriage."
- A decent batting average in personnel decisions is all that can be hoped for. The cardinal sin is delaying correction of mistakes, what Charlie Munger called "thumb-sucking." Problems "cannot be wished away. They require action, however uncomfortable."
- He used "mistake" or "error" 16 times in his 2019-23 letters, while many huge companies never use either word. He is wary of boards where "mistake" or "wrong" are forbidden words, since that taboo implies managerial perfection.
- If you start fooling your shareholders, "you will soon believe your own baloney and be fooling yourself as well." Greg Abel shares this creed.

chunks.heading: Pete Liegl and Forest River: buying a business and choosing a manager
chunks.text:
- On June 21, 2005, Warren got a letter from an intermediary about Forest River, an Indiana RV maker 100% owned by Pete Liegl. It gave the data and the price Pete expected, and said Pete specifically wanted to sell to Berkshire. Warren liked the "no-nonsense approach."
- He checked with RV dealers, liked what he learned, and met Pete in Omaha on June 28.
- Pete wanted to keep running the business but wanted financial security for his family. Warren accepted Pete's valuation of leased real estate without appraisal.
- Compensation: Warren told Pete to name it and he would accept (an approach he says he does not recommend for general use). Pete asked for $100,000 a year ("I wouldn't want to make more than my boss") plus 10% of earnings above the company's current level.
- Warren added that significant acquisitions would bring an adjustment for the additional capital employed. He never defined "appropriate" or "significant," and the vague terms never caused a problem.
- Over the next 19 years Pete "shot the lights out" and no competitor came close. Pete died in November 2024, still working at 80, and contributed many billions to Berkshire shareholders' wealth.
- Takeaways: not every business is easy to understand, and few owners are like Pete. Warren has had many pleasant surprises in both business potential and manager ability and fidelity. A single winning decision (GEICO as a business, Ajit Jain as a manager, finding Charlie Munger as a partner) can make a "breathtaking difference over time." "Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom."

chunks.heading: Hiring CEOs: schooling doesn't matter, talent is innate
chunks.text:
- Warren never looks at where a CEO candidate went to school. "Never!"
- Great managers come from famous schools, but plenty (like Pete) benefited from less prestigious schools or not finishing. Bill Gates left to get underway in an exploding industry.
- Ben Rosner, a retailing genius who ran a business for Warren and Charlie, never went past 6th grade.
- Warren believes in lifelong learning but observes that "a very large portion of business talent is innate with nature swamping nurture." "Pete Liegl was a natural."

chunks.heading: 2024 performance and how Warren measures earnings
chunks.text:
- Berkshire did better than Warren expected in 2024 even though 53% of its 189 operating businesses reported lower earnings. A large gain in investment income came from higher Treasury Bill yields and a much larger T-bill position.
- Insurance earnings rose sharply, led by GEICO. Todd Combs spent five years reshaping GEICO, improving efficiency and modernizing underwriting. Warren calls it "a long-held gem that needed major repolishing."
- Railroad (BNSF) and utility (Berkshire Hathaway Energy) earnings improved in aggregate, but "much left to accomplish." Berkshire raised its utility ownership from about 92% to 100% for roughly $3.9 billion ($2.9 billion cash, the rest in B shares).
- Operating earnings were $47.4 billion in 2024 versus $37.35 billion in 2023. Components for 2024: insurance underwriting $9.02 billion, insurance investment income $13.67 billion, BNSF $5.03 billion, BHE $3.73 billion, other controlled businesses $13.07 billion, non-controlled businesses $1.52 billion, other $1.4 billion.
- Warren emphasizes operating earnings over GAAP earnings because they exclude realized and unrealized gains and losses on stocks and bonds, which swing wildly year to year. Berkshire's horizon for such holdings is "almost always far longer than a single year," often decades, and long-term holdings "sometimes make the cash register ring like church bells."
- Figures are after depreciation, amortization and tax. "EBITDA, a flawed favorite of Wall Street, is not for us."

chunks.heading: Reinvestment and the record tax payment
chunks.text:
- Warren took control of Berkshire 60 years ago and calls it his mistake: the price looked cheap, but the northern textile business was headed for extinction. Charlie spotted the error immediately. In 1965 Berkshire paid no income tax, a "blinking yellow light."
- In 2024 Berkshire made four payments to the IRS totaling $26.8 billion, about 5% of all corporate income tax paid by corporate America, plus sizable payments to foreign governments and 44 states. Cumulative federal income tax paid exceeds $101 billion.
- This was possible because shareholders took only one dividend in 1965-2024: $101,755, or 10¢ per A share, on January 3, 1967. Warren says he cannot remember why he suggested it and it "now seems like a bad dream."
- Sixty years of continuous reinvestment built taxable income. Illustration: a $1 million check to the Treasury every 20 minutes through leap-year 2024 would still have left a balance owed at yearend.
- Berkshire is far more "youthful" than in 1965, since old age itself is not lethal to companies. Berkshire could only have achieved its results in America, whereas America would have succeeded without Berkshire.

chunks.heading: Where the money is: controlled businesses versus marketable stocks
chunks.text:
- Berkshire owns equities "in both hands." One hand: control (at least 80%, generally 100%) of 189 subsidiaries, worth many hundreds of billions, including a few rare gems, many good-but-not-fabulous businesses and some laggards. "We own nothing that is a major drag, but we have a number that I should not have purchased."
- Other hand: small stakes in about a dozen very large, highly profitable businesses such as Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola and Moody's, many earning very high returns on the net tangible equity needed to operate. These were valued at $272 billion at yearend (down from $354 billion). Outstanding businesses are rarely sold whole, but fractions can be bought on Wall Street and occasionally at bargain prices.
- Berkshire is impartial between the two and deploys capital where it can do best. Often nothing looks compelling; very rarely it is "knee-deep in opportunities," and Greg has shown he can act then, as Charlie did.
- Trade-offs: marketable stocks are easier to exit after a mistake, but Berkshire's size means a year or more to build or sell a position, and minority holders cannot change management or control capital allocation. Controlled companies allow those decisions, but mistakes are harder to dispose of. Berkshire almost never sells controlled businesses unless facing "unending problems," and some owners seek Berkshire for that steadfastness.

chunks.heading: Why Berkshire stays in equities, not cash
chunks.text:
- Despite a large cash pile that commentators noted, the great majority of shareholders' money remains in equities, and "that preference won't change." The non-quoted controlled businesses are worth far more than the marketable portfolio.
- Berkshire will forever deploy a substantial majority of money in equities, mostly American (many with significant international operations), and "will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses."
- Reason: paper money can lose its value if fiscal folly prevails, and fixed-coupon bonds give no protection against runaway currency. Businesses and people with desired talents usually find a way to cope with monetary instability. Lacking special talents, Warren has relied on equities and American business success throughout his life.
- On capitalism: it requires citizens to save and then deploy savings wisely and imaginatively. It has faults and abuses (scoundrels and promoters, failed capital deployed against competition or disruption), but American savings delivered output beyond any colonist's dreams. He urges the government to keep a stable currency and look after those who got "the short straws in life."

chunks.heading: Property-casualty insurance and float
chunks.text:
- P/C is Berkshire's core business and has a rare model: payment comes upfront and the true cost emerges later, sometimes 30+ years (asbestos exposures from 50+ years ago are still being paid). Most companies know their product cost before selling.
- Risk: an insurer can lose mountains of money before the CEO and directors notice. In long-tail lines (medical malpractice, product liability) it can report large but fictitious profits for decades, especially if the CEO is "an optimist or a crook." Short-tail lines such as crop or hail insurance report losses quickly.
- Berkshire invests the "float" while generally delivering a small underwriting profit, estimating for "surprises." It prices to absorb rising losses (think wildfires), takes lumps unemotionally and contests runaway verdicts, spurious litigation and fraud.
- Pricing discipline: "We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide." Berkshire must shrink when prices are inadequate. It is "not a business for optimists." Mike Goldberg's line: "We want our underwriters to daily come to work nervous, but not paralyzed."
- Contract length: writing ten-year policies for hurricane, tornado and wildfire risk would be "madness," but one-year terms are generally manageable. Auto insurers moved from one-year to six-month policies, which reduced float but allowed smarter underwriting. Insurance growth depends on rising economic risk (300 million US vehicles versus none 135 years ago).
- Advantages: no private insurer can take on as much risk as Berkshire, it can absorb extreme losses financially and psychologically, and it does not depend on reinsurers, giving a durable cost advantage.
- Numbers: over two decades, $32 billion of after-tax underwriting profit, about 3.3 cents per dollar of sales after tax, while float grew from $46 billion to $171 billion. Float has a reasonable prospect of being costless.
- Incentives: Greg, the directors and Warren have very large investments in Berkshire relative to compensation, and Berkshire uses no options or other one-sided compensation. "If you lose money, so do we." This encourages caution but does not ensure foresight.

chunks.heading: Japan: five trading houses and yen financing
chunks.text:
- Berkshire began buying ITOCHU, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo in July 2019, after looking at their financials and being "amazed at the low prices of their stocks." Admiration has grown since.
- Warren and Greg like their capital deployment, managements and attitude to investors: they raise dividends when appropriate, buy back shares when sensible, and their top managers are far less aggressive in pay than US counterparts.
- Holdings are for the very long term, with Berkshire committed to supporting boards. Berkshire originally agreed to stay below 10% of each; the companies agreed to moderately relax the ceiling, so ownership will likely rise somewhat.
- At yearend, aggregate cost was $13.8 billion and market value $23.5 billion.
- Berkshire funds this partly with fixed-rate yen borrowings (no floaters), seeking roughly currency-neutral exposure with no view on exchange rates. GAAP requires recognizing yen gains and losses in earnings: $2.3 billion cumulative after-tax gains at yearend, $850 million in 2024.
- Expected 2025 dividend income from the Japanese holdings is about $812 million versus about $135 million of yen interest cost.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's early partnership letters lay out his method: buy undervalued securities with a margin of safety, split capital among generals, work-outs and control situations, and judge results against the Dow over years, not months. They show his temperament toward bull markets, the Sanborn Map and Dempster control cases, and his view of true conservatism.

chunks.heading: Early Letters: Market Stance and Not Forecasting the Market
chunks.text:
- Warren makes "no attempt to forecast either business or the stock market"; his effort goes to "finding undervalued securities."
- In 1957 he judged blue-chip stocks priced above intrinsic value and thought it very unlikely today's levels would "be thought of as cheap five years from now."
- Policy by market level: when the market is cheap, put capital in general issues (possibly with some borrowed money). When it rises, trim general issues as profits appear and increase work-outs.
- He warns that "widespread public belief in the inevitability of profits from investment in stocks will lead to eventual trouble," and that the longer such speculators stay, "the greater the reaction from it."
- In 1959 he wrote he would "rather sustain the penalties resulting from over-conservatism than face the consequences of error, perhaps with permanent capital loss, resulting from the adoption of a 'New Era' philosophy where trees really do grow to the sky."
- On long-run expectations (1961): over a long period the Dow will likely produce about 5% to 7% a year compounded from dividends plus price gain. Over the next ten years there will be a few years of +20-25%, a few of the same size negative, and a majority in between. He does not think the sequence matters to a long-term investor.

chunks.heading: The Three Categories: Generals, Work-Outs and Control Situations
chunks.text:
**Generals (undervalued securities)**
- No say in corporate policy and no timetable for the undervaluation to correct.
- Historically the largest category, and "more money has been made here than in either of the other categories."
- Typically 5-10% of total assets in each of five or six generals, with smaller positions in another ten or fifteen.
- They are cheap because they lack glamour or an immediate catalyst, which gives "a comfortable margin of safety in each transaction," reinforced by diversification.
- They move with the Dow in a downturn; being cheap does not stop a stock falling.
- His timing of purchases was "considerably better than our timing of sales." He is content selling "at some intermediate level between our purchase price and what we regard as fair value to a private owner."

**Work-outs**
- A work-out depends on a specific corporate action (sale, merger, liquidation, tender, reorganization, spin-off) rather than a general rise in the stock. The risk is that "something will upset the applecart," not that markets fall.
- Typically 10-15 work-outs at once, at different stages. Returns, excluding borrowed money, usually fall in the 10% to 20% range.
- He uses borrowed money to offset a portion of the work-out book because of its safety, with a self-imposed borrowing cap of 25% of partnership net worth, used only against work-outs.
- Share of portfolio shifted from about 70-30 generals to work-outs at end 1956 to about 85-15 at end 1957. When work-outs were hard to find on good terms, he tried "to create my own work-outs" by building large positions in several undervalued securities.

**Control situations**
- Either control the company or take a very large position and influence policy. Measure them over several years; in a given year they may produce nothing.
- It helps for the stock to stay stagnant while being accumulated, and such holdings have little in common with Dow behavior.
- Sometimes a general is bought hoping it becomes a control situation. If the price jumps before a large stake is built, he sells at a profit instead.

chunks.heading: Accumulating a Position: Commonwealth Trust Example (1958)
chunks.text:
- Commonwealth Trust Co. of Union City, NJ: intrinsic value about $125 per share on a conservative basis, earnings about $10 per share, no cash dividend (for good reasons), price about $50. Assets about $50 million.
- A larger bank owned 25.5% and had long wanted a merger. That was blocked for personal reasons, but evidence suggested it would not last forever.
- He listed three attractions: strong defensive characteristics, solid value building at a satisfactory pace, and evidence the value would eventually be unlocked, "although it might be one year or ten years." If ten, value might reach about $250 per share.
- Over about a year the partnership bought roughly 12% of the bank at an average of about $51, becoming the second-largest holder.
- "Obviously it was definitely to our advantage to have the stock remain dormant in price." During acquisition he wants the stock to do nothing or fall, so a fair proportion of the portfolio is always in a "sterile stage" that holds back relative results in a rising market.
- With about 300 holders and roughly two trades a month, general market activity barely affected the price. Competing buyers pushed it to about $65, where he stopped buying. Small orders move inactive stocks, which is why "leakage" about holdings must be avoided.
- He sold at $80 (market quote about 20% lower) because another situation offered a better price-to-value gap: at $80 vs. intrinsic value of $135 was not the same as $50 vs. $125.
- The replacement was about 25% of assets, and being the largest holder shortens the time to correct the undervaluation.
- He cautions that the year a situation like this realizes a profit is "to a great extent, fortuitous," so a single year is a poor basis for judging long-term results.

chunks.heading: Sanborn Map: A Control Investment Case Study (1960-61)
chunks.text:
**The business and the mispricing**
- Sanborn published and continuously revised detailed city maps for fire insurers. Roughly 75 years of near-monopoly: profit every year, almost no recession sensitivity, no need for selling.
- Competition from "carding" cut after-tax map profits from over $500,000 a year in the late 1930s to under $100,000 in 1958 and 1959.
- Since the early 1930s retained earnings built an investment portfolio of about $2.5 million cost (roughly half bonds, half stocks); it was worth about $7 million against sales of about $2 million a year.
- In 1938 (Dow 100-120) Sanborn traded at $110 with about $20 per share of investments, implying $90 for the map business. In 1958 (Dow about 550) it traded at $45 with about $65 of investments, so the map business was valued at minus $20 and the portfolio at about 70 cents on the dollar.
- Reproducing the map information would have cost "tens of millions of dollars," and over $500 million of fire premiums were still written by mapping companies.

**Why it was stuck**
- Board problems: of 14 directors, nine were insurance-industry men who together held 46 of 105,000 shares (largest holding ten shares). Dividends were cut five times in eight years with no sign anyone proposed cutting salaries or director and committee fees.
- The strong portfolio masked the need to rejuvenate the map business.

**What the partnership did**
- Bought the widow's 15,000-share block, then built holdings (with associates) to about 24,000 shares. Together with two other dissatisfied holders the group had about 46,000 shares.
- Goal: separate the investment portfolio from the map business, realize its fair value, and rebuild map earnings (Booz, Allen & Hamilton recommended a similar plan).
- To avoid a proxy fight and time delay, a plan took out every stockholder who wanted out at fair value, paid in portfolio securities. The SEC ruled favorably on its fairness. About 72% of the stock (50% of 1,600 holders) was exchanged.
- Result: the map business kept over $1.25 million in government and municipal bonds, a potential corporate capital gains tax of over $1 million was eliminated, and remaining holders had slightly higher asset value, higher earnings per share and a higher dividend.
- At its peak this was 35% of partnership net assets, "an unusually large percentage," justified because the holding was partly an investment trust bought at a discount to asset value, with the partnership the largest holder.
- Takeaways: secrecy about portfolio operations matters, and control situations "may occur very infrequently."

chunks.heading: Dempster Mill: Valuing a Controlled Private Holding (1961)
chunks.text:
- First bought five years earlier as a generally undervalued security; a block became available, he joined the board about four years in, and got majority control in August 1961. "Many of our operations are not exactly of the 'overnight' variety."
- Partnership owned 70%, associates about 10%, about 150 other holders; no real market for the stock.
- Business: farm implements and water systems, sales about $9 million in 1961, only nominal profits against capital because of poor management and a tough industry.
- Book value about $75 per share, working capital about $50 per share, controlling interest acquired at an average of about $28, valued at year end at $35. It was 21% of partnership net assets.
- Valuation principle: the year-end value should not be "what we hope it would be worth, or what it might be worth to an eager buyer," but what the interest would bring "if sold under current conditions in a reasonably short period of time." This matters because new partners buy in and old partners sell on that price.
- Control positions will not rise just because large blue chips do, and in a raging bull market they feel like a hard way to make money. He valued the insulation they provide more at high market levels.

chunks.heading: Performance Yardstick: Par, Time Horizon and the Dow
chunks.text:
**Yardstick**
- The benchmark is the Dow-Jones Industrial Average including dividends. "I believe in establishing yardsticks prior to the act; retrospectively, almost anything can be made to look good."
- Three years is "a very minimal test," with the best test a period where the Dow ends near where it began. One year, and especially six months, is too short; his own thinking is "much more geared to five year performance."
- If performance is poor, partners should withdraw; he would look for another place for his own money.
- Target: average about ten percentage points per year over the Dow. With the Dow at 5-7% a year, he hoped for 15-17% a year.

**Relative performance by market type**
- Expected: better in declining or flat markets, average to lagging in strong bull markets. "A year in which we declined 15% and the Average 30% [is] much superior to a year when both we and the Average advanced 20%."
- "The important thing is to be beating par; a four on a par three hole is not as good as a five on a par five hole."
- Illustrative expectations: market down 35-40%, partnership down 15-20%; market flat, up about ten points; market up 20% or more, "struggle to be up as much." He wants partners to agree "down in the pit of your stomach."
- As the market rises, holdings become more conservative: a growing portion is kept at least partly insulated from market behavior.

**Results (partnership gain before limited-partner split vs. Dow with dividends)**
- 1957: 10.4% vs. -8.4%
- 1958: 40.9% vs. 38.5%
- 1959: 25.9% vs. 19.9%
- 1960: 22.8% vs. -6.3%
- 1961: 45.9% vs. 22.2%
- Cumulative 1957-61: 251.0% vs. 74.3%. Pro-forma limited partners' gain over the same period: 181.6%.

**Why the Dow is a tough competitor**
- Of 38 comparable mutual funds from Wiesenberger's survey for 1946-60, 32 did worse than the Dow and 6 better, none by more than a few points a year.
- Warren says this is not an indictment of fund managers; his own results on huge sums with activity restrictions would likely be no better. The point is that beating the Dow is no pushover.

**Luck in the short run**
- In 1957 three partnerships gained about 6.2%, 7.8% and 25% purely because of when money arrived. This "emphasizes the importance of luck in the short run."

chunks.heading: Conservatism, Risk and Size
chunks.text:
**True conservatism**
- Buying long bonds was thought conservative and produced market depreciation and lost buying power. Buying blue chips "almost regardless of price-earnings ratios, dividend yields" is, to him, "fraught with danger."
- "There is nothing at all conservative... about speculating as to just how high a multiplier a greedy and capricious public will put on earnings."
- "You will not be right simply because a large number of people momentarily agree with you. You will not be right simply because important people agree with you."
- "You will be right, over the course of many transactions, if your hypotheses are correct, your facts are correct, and your reasoning is correct. True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason."
- Conservatism is tested by performance in down markets, not by whether a portfolio looks conventional. Through 1961 the partnership never had a realized loss over 0.5% of 1% (one half of one percent) of net assets, with realized gains to realized losses roughly 100 to 1 (noting this reflected a mostly rising market).

**Size**
- For passive positions in thin markets, larger funds hurt (buying 10,000 shares is much harder than 100); for broad-market stocks the penalty is slight.
- For control situations, larger funds help: "A 'Sanborn Map' cannot be accomplished without the wherewithal." Competition thins as the price of entry rises, and bigger companies tend to have less concentrated ownership.
- He saw the two effects as roughly offsetting, and said 1960 and 1961 results would not have been better on 1956-57 sums.

chunks.heading: Partnership Structure and Incentives
chunks.text:
- Profit split in the 1961 merger plan: the first 6% a year to limited partners on beginning capital at market, then any excess one-fourth to Warren and three-fourths to partners. Shortfalls below 6% carry forward against future earnings but not back, and no clawback of amounts previously credited to him.
- Alignment: the merged partnership would hold his entire marketable-securities investing. He and his family were barred from buying other marketable securities, so "my results will have to be directly proportional to yours." His family's stake was about $1.8 million of $7.18 million in net assets at the start of 1962 (Susie and he $1,025,000; other relatives $782,600).
- Earlier arrangements had three versions (6% interest with 1/3 to him, 4% with 1/4, none with 1/6).
- Practical terms: monthly payments at 6% a year with an option to reinvest, borrowing up to 20% of an interest at 6%, year-end add or withdraw in round $100s, minimum for new partners $25,000, overhead expected under 0.5% of net assets excluding interest and the Nebraska Intangibles Tax (0.4% of market value of securities).
- Results are measured market to market (liquidation value), not on realized or tax results.
- Secrecy: no discussion of individual holdings, because small buying orders move thinly traded stocks and leakage hurts accumulation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's partnership letters from 1962 to mid-1964 explain his three investing categories (generals, workouts, controls), why results should be judged against the Dow over three years or more, and how a wide margin of safety drove returns. Dempster Mill shows value buying and capital reallocation in practice. He also covers compounding, taxes, and alignment with partners.

chunks.heading: 1962 results and the case for a relative yardstick
chunks.text:
- Warren measures the partnership against the Dow, not against zero. A year of -15% with the Dow at -25% is "much superior" to a year when both the partnership and the Dow advance 20%.
- First half of 1962: the Dow fell from 731.14 to 561.28, about -21.7% with roughly $11.00 of dividends. The partnership was -7.5%, a 14.2 point edge.
- Target: about a 1/2% decline for each 1% decline in the Dow. He calls that "a considerably more conservative vehicle for investment in stocks than practically any alternative."
- Full-year 1962: the Dow returned -7.6% and the partnership +13.9% (limited partners +11.9%).
- He warns that the 1962 edge was "distinctly abnormal." It came mostly from holding controlled assets and work-outs while the Dow fell. Had the Dow soared, "we would have been low man on the totem pole."
- His expectation: "much smaller advantages on average over the Dow."

chunks.heading: The Ground Rules (January 1963)
chunks.text:
- No rate of return is guaranteed. Monthly withdrawals of one-half of 1% are just withdrawals; if earnings run under 6%, they are partly a return of capital.
- Gains and losses are market values, which may bear little relation to taxable realized results.
- Good or bad is measured against the Dow and leading investment companies, not by whether the year is plus or minus. "If we do poorer, we deserve the tomatoes."
- Three years is "an absolute minimum" for judging performance; he prefers five. If a three-year or longer period is poor, partners should look elsewhere, unless it covered a speculative bull-market explosion.
- He does not predict the stock market or business cycles. Anyone who thinks that is essential "should not be in the partnership."
- He promises three things:
  - Investments chosen on value, not popularity.
  - Permanent capital loss (not short-term quotational loss) kept to an absolute minimum through a wide margin of safety in each commitment plus diversification.
  - His wife, children and he have virtually their entire net worth in the partnership.
- By 1964 he asks every partner to reread the Ground Rules yearly and not to sign unless they agree "mentally and viscerally."

chunks.heading: Expectations: how the partnership should behave across market types
chunks.text:
- Dow expectation: about 5% a year compounded (5-7% in the 1962 letter) from dividends plus price gains. "Anyone expecting substantially better than that from the general market probably faces disappointment."
- Yearly swings: a few years of +20-25%, a few of the same size negative, most in between. The sequence is "of no great importance for the long-term investor." Compounded results are the same however the years are shuffled.
- Target by market type:
  - Dow down 35-40%: the partnership down only 15-20%.
  - Dow roughly flat: up about 10 points.
  - Dow up 20%+: "we would struggle to be up as much."
- Goal: a ten-point annual edge over the Dow. With the Dow at 5%, he hopes for 15% a year. Ten points is "the very maximum" achievable over a long period.
- By 1964 he says his actual 17.7-point margin (22.3% a year versus the Dow's 10.0%, 1957-63) "is unattainable over any long period." He expects prolonged stretches of narrow margins and some years worse than the Dow.
- Size has not hurt: assets grew from $303,726 (1957) to $7.18 million (start of 1962) to $17.45 million (start of 1964). He says the portfolio could not be improved with $1 million or $5 million, and "our idea inventory has always seemed to be 10% ahead of our bank account."

chunks.heading: The three investment categories
chunks.text:
**Generals (undervalued securities)**
- Bought at a large discount to value to a private owner, with no say in policy and no timetable.
- Typical positions are 5-10% of assets in each of five or six generals, with smaller stakes in 10-15 others.
- Selection is quantitative first, but "the qualitative is important": good management, a decent industry, some "ferment" among a dormant management or shareholders. "But we demand value."
- They move with the Dow. Cheap does not mean it cannot fall. They should be the star in sharply rising markets and lag in falls.
- Warren is content to sell at a level between cost and fair value rather than "the last nickel."
- He often rides the coattails of a dominant holder planning to redeploy assets, but is "careful whose coat we are holding."
- Where the company improves earnings and assets while the stock goes nowhere, he keeps buying week after week, perhaps for years. Either the market catches up or BPL gets control at a bargain.
- He is largest single holder in three companies by mid-1964. He calls the buying end "about 90% of this business."
- Borrowing against generals is "a very dangerous practice."

**Work-outs (corporate events with a timetable)**
- Mergers, liquidations, reorganizations, spin-offs and sell-outs, especially oil producers selling to majors. He acts only on publicly announced deals: "We wait until we can read it in the paper."
- Risk is that the deal falls through (antitrust, stockholder rejection, withheld tax rulings), not market direction.
- Typical returns are 10-20% a year before leverage, steady regardless of the Dow. They are a drag in bull markets and a cushion in bear ones.
- He holds five to ten at a time. Borrowing is acceptable against work-outs, with a self-imposed cap of 25% of partnership net worth. In 1962 he paid $75,000 of interest at about 5%, implying roughly $1.5 million borrowed.
- Short sales on a late-1962 deal removed market risk and locked in a 10%+ gross profit for a few months of tied-up money.
- Pattern: "the deals take longer than originally projected" and "the payouts tend to average a little better than estimates."

**Controls**
- Arise when a cheap general sits long enough that BPL accumulates a large stake, or via a large initial block. Measure over several years.
- Activism only when needed: "We do not want to get active merely for the sake of being active." Otherwise he lets others do the work.
- Built-in profit comes from the purchase price. Once control is achieved, value depends on the enterprise, not market irrationality.
- Willingness to take control gives "two-way stretch": price rises, or BPL keeps buying until the business itself vindicates the judgment. "If it looks at all close, we pass."
- Category mix is largely accident of availability, which is why a single year says little.

chunks.heading: Dempster Mill: buying below liquidation value and the asset-conversion case study
chunks.text:
- Started as a general in 1956 at $18 with about $72 book value, $50 per share of it net current assets. Industry was tough and management unimpressive, but the numbers were attractive.
- His rule of thumb: buy 100 situations like this and perhaps 70 or 80 work out to reasonable profits in one to three years.
- BPL bought for five years at $16-25, then at $30.25 in August-September 1961 plus a tender offer at the same price, reaching over 71.7% (cost $1,262,577.27).
- Year-end 1961 valuation applied haircuts to a prompt-sale basis: inventory 60% of book (a 40% discount), receivables 85%, prepaid 25%, plant at estimated auction value. That gave about $35.25 per share.
- Old management did nothing in about six months. On April 17, 1962 he met Harry Bottle, offered pay tied to hitting goals, and Bottle was president six days later.
- Results by November 1962: inventory cut from $4.2 million to $1.6 million (about $550,000 written off), notes payable from $1.23 million to zero, adjusted value about $51.26 per share. By July 1963 inventory was under $1 million.
- Bottle's actions:
  - Administration and selling expense cut from $150,000 to $75,000 a month.
  - Factory overhead per direct labor hour cut from $6 to $4.50.
  - Five unprofitable branches closed and replaced with distributors.
  - Money-losing jobbed lines dropped.
  - Repair-part prices raised for roughly $200,000 of extra profit with almost no volume loss.
  - Freed capital put into marketable securities, a gain of over $400,000.
- At June 30, 1963 Dempster held securities worth $2,028,415.25; BPL's 71.7% share was $1,454,373.70 against a $1,262,577.27 cost. "Everything above ground (and part of it underground) is profit." He prefers this "fingers and toes method" to "any prayerful reliance that someone will pay me 35 times next year's earnings."
- Operating assets were sold in late 1963 at about book value; with the securities gain, realization was about $80 per share. Warren sold rather than keep paying corporate tax on a business that no longer needed its capital.
- Principle: "Never count on making a good sale. Have the purchase price be so attractive that even a mediocre sale gives good results. The better sales will be the frosting on the cake." And: "Our business is making excellent purchases, not making extraordinary sales."
- He values assets in controlled businesses on what a prompt sale would produce, not on potential. Management is paid with "big carrots" tied to results; he wants someone not "trying to figure how to get the fixtures in the executive washroom gold-plated."

chunks.heading: Texas National Petroleum: a typical work-out
chunks.text:
- Union Oil of California bought TNP, announced April 1962. Warren ignored earlier rumors; he never acts on rumor, though entering at the rumor stage would have paid more.
- BPL bought $264,000 of 6.5% debentures (callable at 104.25), 64,035 shares (liquidation estimate $7.42 per share) and 83,200 warrants (about 13% of the issue, exercisable at $3.50, implying a $3.92 work-out).
- Risks assessed: stockholder disapproval nil (controlling holders negotiated it), title and legal risk near nil, no antitrust problem. The one risk was the IRS ruling on the production-payment financing, delayed because the University of Southern California was the payment holder.
- Company officials predicted closing in August or September; it closed October 31, 1962 after repeated delays.
- Returns: bonds about 20% annualized on $260,773 held under five months (capital gain $14,446 plus 6.5% interest); stock and warrants about 22% annualized (gain $89,304, positions up to $731,000). Both on all-equity capital.
- Warren says it is "bread-and-butter," not a triumph. A failed work-out causes a large market-value shrink, so errors must be few.
- BPL does not discuss current holdings, even with partners: "we must plead the 5th Amendment."

chunks.heading: Why institutions can't beat the Dow, and why conservatism is judged by results
chunks.text:
- Each letter benchmarks BPL against the two largest mutual funds (Massachusetts Investors Trust, Investors Stock Fund) and two largest closed-end funds (Lehman, Tri-Continental). Together they managed over $4 billion of a roughly $28 billion industry.
- Through mid-1964 these funds compounded 9.4-10.1% a year versus 10.8% for the Dow. In the 1962 first half, all 17 large common stock funds studied by the Wall Street Journal trailed the Dow from its peak. Annual fees for the four exceeded $7 million.
- His point is not criticism. Within their institutional framework, "to behave unconventionally... is extremely difficult." Their value is convenience, diversification and insulation from bad techniques, not superior results.
- The duck analogy: "When the water (the market) rises, the duck rises; when it falls, back goes the duck."
- Hot "growth" funds that led in 1959-61 fell about 32.3% in the 1962 first half after attracting a rush of new money. Many more holders suffered the loss than had enjoyed the gains.
- Money managers meticulously grade companies' managements but not themselves. Standards should be chosen a priori, not retrospectively: "We started out with a 36-inch yardstick and we'll keep it that way."
- Conservatism is not blue chips at any price. Many who bought long bonds saw market depreciation and lost buying power. Buying blue chips regardless of price-earnings ratios is also dangerous: "There is nothing at all conservative... about speculating as to just how high a multiplier a greedy and capricious public will put on earnings."
- On independent thinking: "You will not be right simply because a large number of people momentarily agree with you. You will not be right simply because important people agree with you." Rather, "if your hypotheses are correct, your facts are correct, and your reasoning is correct. True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason."
- His test of conservatism is performance in down markets. In 1962 BPL had one realized loss of about 1.0% of assets; historically no realized loss above 0.5% of net assets and about 100 to 1 realized gains over losses (about 3 to 1 in 1962).

chunks.heading: Compounding and taxes
chunks.text:
- Compounding illustrations: $100,000 grows to $259,374 / $672,748 / $1,744,930 at 10% over 10 / 20 / 30 years; at 15% it grows to $404,553 / $1,636,640 / $6,621,140. At 16% for 30 years it reaches $8,484,940, against $224,337 at 4%.
- Small rate differences "mushroom" over time, so a few points of edge over the Dow is "a very worthwhile achievement." Isabella's $30,000 at 4% would be about $2 trillion by 1962. Francis I's roughly $20,000 for the Mona Lisa at 6% would exceed $1 quadrillion.
- He cautions that sustaining very high rates is absurd. Realistic planning includes a -30% year and a Dow -40% year.
- Taxes: he is "an outspoken advocate of paying large amounts of income taxes, at low rates." Decisions should aim at "the most probable compounding of after-tax net worth with minimum risk."
- Low-basis stocks should not be held out of tax fear. "Any isolation of low-basis securities merely freezes a portion of net worth" at the Dow's compounding rate, which he calls "a nullification of investment management." A deferred tax liability "is just as real as the asset."
- BPL makes no moves to defer or accelerate taxes; the large realized gains in 1964 reflect positions sold, not performance.

chunks.heading: Partnership structure and alignment
chunks.text:
- Limited partners receive the first 6% of annual profit; the general partner takes 25% of gains above 6%, with shortfalls carried forward. So a 14% gross year gives limited partners 12%.
- Partners can withdraw 20% before year-end at 6% interest and make advance payments at 6%. Warren pays 6% on advance payments even when bank loans cost 4% because he expects over 6% long term and sees it as future equity.
- His own stake: $1,377,400 (1963) and $2,392,900 (1964), with family adding $893,600 and $1,247,190. Associate Bill Scott and wife held $167,400, then $237,400. Warren says "we are all eating our own cooking."
- Auditors Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. make two surprise securities checks a year.
- His position is "I can't promise results but I can promise a common destiny."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's partnership letters from 1965-67 explain why he measures against the Dow, concentrates up to 40% in his best ideas, defines conservatism by facts and reasoning rather than convention, and values controlled businesses on assets and earning power. They also cover compounding, ignoring market forecasts, taxes, and the limits of size.

chunks.heading: Why Warren measures himself against the Dow, and what the comparison shows
chunks.text:
- Warren sets one yardstick in advance: the Dow including dividends, judged over at least a three-year window. His stated long-term goal is an average of ten percentage points a year ahead of the Dow, before the general partner's allocation. He calls it "Our Goal", not "Our Promise".
- He says anyone who manages money should have a standard of measurement, and that manager and client should agree on it beforehand.
- Fixed yardsticks keep "past successes" from clouding "judgment of current results" and reduce "ingenious rationalizations of inept performance". They also mean he gets blamed only for the right reason (doing worse than the Dow), not for having losing years.
- Partners who reject the standard "should not be in the Partnership".
- Partnership results (before the general partner's allocation), 1957-1966, with the Dow in brackets: 1957 +10.4% (-8.4%), 1958 +40.9% (+38.5%), 1960 +22.8% (-6.2%), 1961 +45.9% (+22.4%), 1962 +13.9% (-7.6%), 1963 +38.7% (+20.6%), 1964 +27.8% (+18.7%), 1965 +47.2% (+14.2%), 1966 +20.4% (-15.6%).
- Limited partners' compounded rate over 1957-1966 was 23.9% a year, against 11.4% for the Dow. Cumulatively that is 704.2% against 122.9%.
- He reports that his own and his family's money is almost entirely in the Partnership. In 1966 that was over 90% of net worth for his family.

chunks.heading: Why the big funds trail the Dow, and what conservatism means
chunks.text:
- Warren tracks four big funds: Massachusetts Investors Trust, Investors Stock Fund, Lehman and Tri-Continental. They manage over $5 billion and roughly 600,000 shareholders own them. He treats their record as typical of most professional managers.
- Their annual compounded rates for 1957-1966 were 8.6%, 7.9%, 9.8% and 9.0%, against 9.7% for the Dow. The Dow is "no pushover as an index".
- He blames five causes:
  - group decisions ("close to impossible for outstanding investment management to come from a group of any size")
  - a desire to conform to other large organizations
  - an institutional setup where average is "safe" and independent action isn't rewarded
  - irrational diversification
  - inertia
- He calls his own pledge of consistent measurement the first job of any investment organization.
- Warren says neither conventional nor unconventional is conservative per se. "Truly conservative actions arise from intelligent hypotheses, correct facts and sound reasoning." "A public opinion poll is no substitute for thought."
- He draws a distinction. Funds meet one definition of conservatism, results that vary only slightly from average. He prefers the other: "subject to substantially less temporary or permanent shrinkage in value than total experience". The first he'd call "conventionalism".
- His test of conservatism is performance in down markets. Over the three down years 1957, 1960 and 1962, the Dow fell 20.6%, the funds fell 9.7% to 24.6%, and the limited partners gained 45.0%.
- Even Samson gets clipped. In H1 1966 an equal split of $100,000 across eight giants (GM, Standard of New Jersey, Sears, DuPont, U.S. Steel, Aetna, AT&T, Bank of America) lost 16.6%.

chunks.heading: Concentration and diversification
chunks.text:
- Ground Rule 7 (from November 1965): "We diversify substantially less than most investment operations. We might invest up to 40% of our net worth in a single security under conditions coupling an extremely high probability that our facts and reasoning are correct with a very low probability that anything could drastically change the underlying value of the investment."
- His ideal would be 50 uncorrelated opportunities, each with an expected edge of 15 points over the Dow, 2% in each. Reality is that he has to work very hard to find a very few.
- A qualifying idea is one he expects to beat the Dow by at least ten points a year. Sizing between idea number one and number eight depends on the gap in expectation and on the chance of a poor relative result. Two ideas with equal expectation can warrant different sizes if one has a 5% chance of badly lagging and the other 1%.
- He sizes the limit so that the chance a single investment (or correlated group) makes the whole portfolio more than ten points worse than the Dow is tiny.
- He says a 100-stock portfolio "is not being operated logically". The hundredth stock can't reduce variance enough to offset the damage to expected return. He calls this the "Noah School of Investing - two of everything". Billy Rose: "You've got a harem of seventy girls; you don't get to know any of them very well."
- He accepts bumpier year-to-year results for better long-term performance, but not "substantial permanent capital loss".
- Only five or six situations in nine years went above 25% of the portfolio. In 1966 he had two over 25%, one a controlled company and one a large company he'd never take an active part in.
- 1965 was driven by five investments, with gains from about $800,000 to about $3.5 million. His five smallest general holdings were "lackluster".
- Borrowing stays small. Bank borrowings averaged well under 10% of net worth in 1966. A partner's line: "even five minutes is a long time if one's head is being held under water."

chunks.heading: The four investment categories
chunks.text:
1. Generals - Private Owner Basis
   - Undervalued stocks, found on quantitative standards, trading well below value to a private owner.
   - He also likes good management, a decent industry and some "ferment", but "we demand value".
   - It's a "two strings to our bow" situation: market price can rise, or he can buy control at a bargain. Example: a 1965 tender offer paid $3,188,000 realized on one holding, of which $2,737,000 was economic gain for 1965 after $451,000 of unrealized gain in 1964.
2. Generals - Relatively Undervalued
   - Securities cheap relative to similar-quality securities, where private-owner value isn't meaningful (usually because of size).
   - He compares apples to apples and passes when he doesn't know the industry.
   - A hedging technique introduced in 1964-65 cuts the risk of a broad revaluation. Example risk: buying at 12 times earnings when peers trade at 20, then peers fall to 10.
   - The category is less solid for projection. In 1965-66 results rested on one or two holdings, one of which became his largest position and met the 40% rule.
3. Workouts
   - Securities with a timetable (mergers, sell-outs, reorganizations, spin-offs). He acts only on publicly announced events: "We wait until we can read it in the paper."
   - Risk is the deal failing (antitrust, stockholder disapproval, tax rulings). Gross profits look small, "like looking for parking meters with some time left on them".
   - Predictable returns and short holding periods give decent annual rates. Workouts cushion down years and lag in bull markets.
   - They returned 14.6% in 1962, 30.6% in 1963, 10.3% in 1964 and about 22.4% in 1966 on average capital of $7.67 million. This was once 30-40% of net worth but is unlikely to be again.
4. Controls
   - These come from the private-owner category, when a stock stays cheap long enough to build a big stake. He is active only when needed to optimize capital use.
