   - Must have a built-in profit from the purchase price. Value then follows the business, not market quotes. He looks for wide margins and measures results over several years.
   - Dempster Mill's buyers are doing well, which he values. He rejects the "Bigger Fool Theory".

chunks.heading: Berkshire Hathaway and Hochschild, Kohn
chunks.text:
- Buying of Berkshire began in November 1962 at $7.60 a share. Average cost was $14.86 after heavy early-1965 buying, which gave control in spring 1965.
- Net working capital alone was about $19 a share at end of 1965, before valuing plant and equipment. The company had slid from a 1948 peak of $29.5 million pretax earnings, 11 mills and about 11,000 workers to two mills and about 2,300 employees.
- He found excellent existing managers, notably Ken Chace, and brought in no outsiders. "It is well to have a diet consisting of oatmeal as well as cream puffs."
- Controlled holdings are valued as businesses, not at market. At end of 1965 he valued Berkshire halfway between net current asset value and book value, which meant current assets at 100 cents on the dollar and fixed assets at 50.
- In H1 1966 the Partnership, with two 10% partners, bought all of Hochschild, Kohn, a privately owned Baltimore department store. It was the first entire business bought by negotiation. About 10% of the Partnership's $50 million-plus is in HK, against more than three times that in one marketable security.
- He values HK at cost plus retained earnings, and says management quality mattered: he wouldn't have bought it with run-of-the-mill managers even at a lower price.
- He prefers the "iceberg approach" to disclosure.

chunks.heading: Temperament, forecasting, and staying in your lane
chunks.text:
- Ground Rule 6: "I am not in the business of predicting general stock market or business fluctuations." He buys on what a company should do, not when. The market sets when he is right, his business analysis sets whether.
- He asks two questions of callers predicting declines. If they knew in February the Dow would hit 865 in May, why not say so then? And if not, how do they know in May?
- A private business is never bought or sold on a stock market guess. Market quotes should be used when they get silly in either direction, never allowed to dictate judgment. He points to chapter two of Graham's *The Intelligent Investor* as the most investment-relevant writing he knows.
- He expects poor years. If a 20-30% drop in equity value would cause distress, avoid stocks. He also warns that years of -20% or worse "should definitely be expected".
- He will not buy what he doesn't understand. He knows nothing of semiconductors or integrated circuits, and avoids deals where technology is crucial to the decision. His stance is "If you can't join 'em, lick 'em" and he will not follow fashion investing, where market action overrides business value.
- He also avoids deals where major human problems appear likely.
- He doesn't trust prophecy: it "reveals far more of the frailties of the prophet than it reveals of the future".
- He says short-term results under three years mean little, and that reporting more often than annually is foolish in a long-term business.

chunks.heading: Expectations, size, and the end of the easy years
chunks.text:
- In January 1965 he expected the Dow to return about 7% a year over 20-30 years (versus 11.1% to that date), a ten-point average edge, and so about 17% before allocation and about 14% for limited partners. He labels this "conjecture".
- He says the 1957-1966 results can't be repeated: "They may well be achieved by some hungry twenty-five year old working with $105,100". Not by a thirty-six-year-old with $54,065,345.
- He now finds perhaps one-fifth to one-tenth as many good ideas as before, only two or three new ideas a year meeting his ten-point yardstick. Causes: a changed market, his increased size and more competition. Earlier, "a lesser effort produced literally dozens".
- Capital was about $43.6 million entering 1966. He decided to admit no new partners unless they brought something other than capital, while allowing existing partners to add.
- If the stream of ideas dries up, he promises to tell partners "honestly and promptly".

chunks.heading: Taxes, compounding, and the cost of fees and managers
chunks.text:
- The goal is the largest after-tax compound rate, not the lowest taxes. "Means and end should not be confused."
- A portfolio should hold the most attractive securities at current prices, which means change and realized gains. Past performance, getting even, and the warm glow of a winner are irrelevant.
- The only ways to avoid tax are to die with the asset, give it away, or lose the gain. He maximizes gains and pays the tax.
- Swap funds (a tax-deferral pitch) did badly, he notes. Federal Street and Westminster, managed by advisers overseeing $2 billion-plus, returned 2.6% and 1.1% a year for 1962-64, against 9.8% for the Dow.
- Compounding: $100,000 at 4% / 8% / 12% / 16% becomes about $224,337 / $906,260 / $2,895,970 / $8,484,940 over 30 years. Small gains in annual rate matter a lot, so "every percentage point of investment return above average" has real meaning.
- Peter Minuit's $24 for Manhattan in 1626, compounded at 6.5%, would be about $42 billion today and about $205 billion at 7%.
- Advance payments from partners earn 6% to year-end, and advance withdrawals (up to 20%) cost 6%. He expects to earn better than 6% over the long term, since the general partner earns nothing unless returns exceed 6%.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buffett's letters track BPL's results, then explain why he cut his goals in 1967 and liquidated in 1969 as bargains vanished and speculation grew. He covers quantitative versus qualitative investing, ignoring market price for controlled businesses, and a plain-spoken guide to tax-free bonds.

chunks.heading: Why Warren changed his goal to the lesser of 9% or 5 points over the Dow (October 1967)
chunks.text:
Warren had pursued an average edge of ten percentage points a year over the Dow for eleven years. In October 1967 he lowered it to "the lesser of 9% per annum or a five percentage point advantage over the Dow." If the Dow averages -2% over five years, he hoped for +3%; if it averages +12%, he would hope for only +9%.

He gave four reasons:
- **Bargains disappeared.** Obvious quantitative bargains had dwindled sharply.
- **Hyper-reactive markets.** Intense interest in performance made markets hyper-reactive, and his analytical techniques had limited value against that.
- **Too much capital.** The base had grown to about $65 million against "a diminishing trickle of good investment ideas." He called this the least significant factor. He thought performance with one-tenth the capital "would be little better."
- **Personal motivation.** He wanted "a less compulsive approach" than when he was "younger and leaner."

He also said limited objectives should mean limited effort, and that the long-term downside risk would not be lower, only the upside potential. He told partners with better alternatives to take their money elsewhere, and about $1.6 million withdrew at yearend. Candor mattered to him: he disliked those who announce "phony proclamations" while pursuing other motives.

chunks.heading: Quantitative vs. qualitative investing
chunks.text:
Warren described two schools:
- **Qualitative:** "Buy the right company... and the price will take care of itself."
- **Quantitative:** "Buy at the right price and the company (and stock) will take care of itself."

Money can be made either way, and every analyst blends the two. He placed himself mainly in the quantitative school.

His most sensational ideas, though, leaned qualitative, where he had a "high-probability insight." That "causes the cash register to really sing," but it is infrequent. On the quantitative side no insight is needed: "the figures should hit you over the head with a baseball bat." Big money comes from right qualitative calls; "the more sure money" comes from obvious quantitative ones.

He offered three possible causes of the disappearing statistical bargains:
- Constant combing of investments for twenty years, with no 1930s-style convulsion to spawn new bargains.
- Takeover bids becoming socially accepted, which focuses attention on bargain issues.
- Exploding ranks of security analysts.

Much of the 1964-66 performance came from a single idea. He noted that qualitative ideas are rare, like insights generally.

chunks.heading: Speculation, short time horizons, and refusing to change approach
chunks.text:
Warren had long preached measuring performance, with three years as the minimum. The public shortened this to yearly, quarterly and monthly. He saw a self-generating cycle in which superior short-term results attract new money, which demands shorter time spans. The stock itself becomes "virtually incidental." He called the result "speculation on an increasing scale."

His commitments:
- He makes no attempt to guess the market and had "not the foggiest notion" whether the Dow would be at 600, 900 or 1200 a year later. Timing estimates are meaningless.
- He would not follow "fashion" investing, where anticipating market action overrides business valuations: "I will not invest my own money based upon such an approach – hence, I will most certainly not do so with your money."
- He would not abandon an approach whose logic he understands, even if it means "foregoing large and apparently easy, profits to embrace an approach which I don't understand... and which, possibly, could lead to substantial permanent loss of capital."
- He quoted Ben Graham: "Speculation is neither illegal, immoral nor fattening (financially)." In 1967 it was possible to get "fiscally flabby through a steady diet of speculative bonbons," while BPL "continue[d] to eat oatmeal."

In the July 1967 letter he wrote, "The tide continues to be far more important than the swimmers." In 1968 he criticized chain-letter stock promotions that relied on "bold, imaginative accounting," and "the hopeful, credulous and greedy, grasping for an excuse to believe." He mocked a manager's claim that securities "must be studied in a minute-by-minute program."

chunks.heading: BPL results and how the portfolio categories behaved
chunks.text:
Overall results: 1967 BPL +35.9% (limited partners +28.4%) vs. Dow +19.0%. 1968 BPL +58.8% (limited partners +45.6%) vs. Dow +7.7%. Through 1968, BPL cumulative was 2610.6% (25.3% annually for limited partners) vs. 185.7% (9.1%) for the Dow. He called 1968 "a freak like picking up thirteen spades in a bridge game."

The four mutual and closed-end funds he tracked averaged only a fraction of a point a year better than the Dow over twelve years.

1967 categories:
- **Workouts** (securities with a timetable from announced sell-outs, mergers, reorganizations and spin-offs): worst year ever. $153,273 on $17,246,879 average investment, or 0.89%. "The streets were filled with upset applecarts."
- **Controls:** $2,894,571 on $20,192,776.
- **Generals, relatively undervalued:** $14,096,593 on $19,487,996, or 72%, driven largely by one security.
- **Generals, private owner:** $1,297,215 on $5,141,710.

1968 categories:
- **Controls:** $5,886,109 on $24,996,998.
- **Generals, private owner:** $21,994,736 on $16,363,100. His best category historically, with total profits "fifty times or more" total losses over twelve years. It came from one industry idea implemented several ways.
- **Generals, relatively undervalued:** $4,271,825.
- **Workouts:** $7,317,128 on $18,980,602. Warren concentrates workouts in a few situations a year, so yearly results vary more than with an across-the-board approach.

Caveats he gave: category returns are calculated on average investment, understating returns versus beginning-base methods, and each category is dominated by one or two investments, so conclusions are only tentative.

chunks.heading: Controlled businesses: valuation and why he kept them
chunks.text:
- **Valuing controls.** Market price is irrelevant to valuing controlled companies. Berkshire was valued at 25 at yearend 1967 (market about 20) and 31 at yearend 1968 (market about 37). He would have done the same at market prices of 15 and 50. "Price is what you pay, value is what you get."
- **Why hold them.** He would keep up to 40% of capital in controlled businesses, limited by partnership liquidity needs, at an expected return below an aggressive stock operation. His reasoning: with people he likes, businesses he finds stimulating, and returns of 10-12%, it is foolish "to rush from situation to situation to earn a few more percentage points," or to trade pleasant relationships for "possible irritation, aggravation or worse."
- **Return on capital.** In 1967 Associated Cotton Shops (Ben Rosner) and National Indemnity (Jack Ringwalt) each earned about 20% on capital employed. Only 37 of the Fortune 500 manufacturers reached that figure.
- **Textiles.** The textile business earned too little, and he saw "no prospect of a good return" on those assets. Yet he declined to liquidate it: "I have no desire to trade severe human dislocations for a few percentage points additional return per annum." The business employed 1,100 people and needed no substantial new capital.
- **Reinvestment.** Capital from weaker segments was redeployed into insurance and banking. He valued Berkshire at about $43 tangible net assets per share. In 1969 he expected 10% annual intrinsic value growth for DRC and Berkshire.
- **Dividends.** Berkshire and DRC paid no dividends because of debt, policyholder and depositor protection, and good uses for capital.
- **Management.** He liked and praised the three excellent operating managers, all over sixty and "extraordinarily good," and judged the "second men" only partly knowable until they actually run a company.

chunks.heading: Closing the partnership (May-December 1969)
chunks.text:
In May 1969 he announced his retirement. He had "flunked" the goal of lighter effort: "If I am going to participate publicly, I can't help being competitive." He would not "grope around, hoping to 'get lucky' with other people's money," nor "play a game I don't understand just so I can go out a hero." He expected breakeven for 1969, and the year ended slightly over 6%.

His reasons:
- Quantitative opportunities had "virtually disappeared."
- $100 million of assets meant commitments under about $3 million could not move results, which ruled out companies with less than about $100 million of stock at market value.
- The market was more short-term and speculative.

His workouts that year were "atrocious." He took full blame: "Our poor experience this year is 100% my fault," a misjudgment of a fast-developing government trend. He also refused to let what should happen socially color what he thinks will happen: "I never believe in mixing what I think should happen (socially) with what I think will happen."

Partner options at liquidation:
- Take cash.
- Keep proportional shares in Diversified Retailing and Berkshire Hathaway, valued unilaterally by him at fair value.
- Hold residual items (Blue Chip Stamps, small workout stubs).

He chose not to register the stock for a public distribution, so that sophisticated partners would have no edge over less sophisticated ones in a thin market. He expected private sales near yearend valuations. When Blue Chip's offering collapsed (the stock fell from 24 to 16-1/2 after announcement), he kept the block, preferring a better disposal.

On Berkshire and DRC he said: "I'm going to [hold]... and I plan to buy more." He called the risk of loss low "compared to most stocks" and said he thought about them "as businesses, not 'stocks'." He hoped their prices would follow business results rather than speculative enthusiasm, and said he would not "promote" the stocks.

chunks.heading: Bonds vs. stocks in 1969, and picking a manager
chunks.text:
In October 1969 he judged that for the first time in his career there was "little choice for the average investor between professionally managed money in stocks and passive investment in bonds." His assumptions, for a 40% tax-bracket investor over ten years:
- **Tax-free bonds:** about 6-1/2% yield.
- **Stocks as a group:** about 9% pre-tax (3% dividends plus 6% gain), roughly 6-1/2% after tax. GNP growth of about 6%, stable profit share of GNP and stable earnings multiples cap long-term growth in aggregate valuation at about 6%.
- **Professional managers:** about half of stock money is professionally managed, so average results are the group average. Less than 10% might average 2 points a year over the group. Even the top 1-2% likely add no more than about 4 points, or about 9-1/2% after tax.
- **Conclusion:** passive tax-free bonds roughly equal professionally managed stocks and are only modestly inferior to extremely well-managed equity money. "Aggressively run" money (about $50 billion, perhaps 100 times a decade earlier) "just can't 'perform'."
- **Inflation:** it matters little to the comparison. "The best expectable after-tax rate of return makes the most sense."
- **Time horizon:** "In the long run, the market is a weighing machine – in the short run, a voting machine" (Ben Graham). He finds weights easier to judge than votes.

The decision should also reflect temperament: need for regular income, tolerance for principal swings, and the psychic pull of "juicy results."

On choosing Bill Ruane, he cited integrity, ability and availability to small partners. He noted Ruane's volatility (about -50% in 1962 and -15% in 1969 to date) and warned that any manager's results moderate as assets grow. The likely drawbacks lead to average results, "and average performance is just not that terrible a risk."

chunks.heading: Buying tax-free bonds: his practical rules (February 1970)
chunks.text:
He offered to help partners buy bonds in March 1970, with no financial interest, then stop advising after March 31.

**What he buys:**
- Large revenue-producing public entities (toll roads, power and water districts).
- Industrial Development Authority bonds, e.g. a project leased to U.S. Steel, only as good as the lessee. Prejudice against them had kept yields above their credit quality.
- Public Housing Authority issues, effectively U.S.-guaranteed and AAA.
- State obligations.

**What he avoids:**
- Large-city bonds. "If I can't understand something, I tend to forget it." He wants to be paid for things he can handle and to be right on affirmative decisions.
- Illiquid issues with bid-ask spreads up to 15%. His targets had 2-5% spreads, acceptable only for long-term holders.
- Lots under $25,000.
- Corporate, convertible and short-term bonds.

**Call provisions.** He rejected bonds the issuer can call at a small premium: it is a long deal if it favors the issuer and a short one if it favors you. He said such bonds yield about the same as non-callable ones and called this "the height of foolishness," citing a 1969 Los Angeles Department of Water and Power issue. Deep-discount bonds callable at far above cost are fine.

**Maturity.** Maturity depends on:
- the shape of the yield curve;
- expectations for rates;
- tolerance for price swings.

He had been wrong on rates the year before. His reasoning: with a strongly positive curve and a 50-50 view on rates, long non-callable bonds have better odds than short ones. He chose 10-25 years. Illustration: a 5% bond falls to $791.60 if rates go to 7% with 19 years left, and rises to $1,288.10 if rates go to 3%.

**Discount vs. full coupon.** Discount bonds yield more gross but incur capital gains tax at maturity. He expected them to pay off after tax for most holders. The 1969 Tax Reform Act pushed banks out of discount tax-free bonds, which helps individuals. Expected after-tax yield on 20-year bonds was about 6-1/2%.

**Tax and borrowing:** do not own tax-free bonds while carrying general bank loans, because the interest deduction is at risk.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2026 CNBC interview Buffett explains his giving plans, the Greg Abel succession, and why he initiated Berkshire's Alphabet stake. The core investing lesson: a good business earns far more than Treasuries, sustains high returns on capital for a long time, and must be bought on the right terms with the right manager.

chunks.heading: Alphabet as a business bet: capital intensity, returns, and who made the call
chunks.text:
- Warren says he "initiated" the Alphabet position. Greg Abel approves it and "is the decider"; the two "talk all the time, every day."
- Berkshire's stake is over $31 billion including a $10 billion private placement. Warren ranks it "probably number five or six" among holdings, counting wholly owned businesses such as Burlington Northern.
- He does not like it "as well as at least four or five other businesses that we own."
- He says Berkshire chooses between marketable securities and whole companies "the same way." The only differences are minor ones, such as not being able to set dividend policy.
- His rule: "the important thing is to buy a good business, and to buy it on the right terms, and then get the right person to run it."
- On Alphabet's AI spending, he says the hyperscalers are "laying out hundreds of billions." That kind of capex is comparable to what a railroad does.
- He thinks a company that spends heavily is "more likely to be a winner, based on their record, than probably 90% or 95% of what will get merchandised through Wall Street."
- He says the other hyperscalers "don't have any choice." They are "playing a game, in many cases, that they don't want to play."
- On the idea that he never buys technology: "There are all kinds of games I don't understand, sure. Why should I expect to make money in all kinds of things I don't understand?"

chunks.heading: What makes a "good business": returns on capital versus the riskless rate
chunks.text:
- Warren defines a good business as one where you can expect "high returns on capital over a long period of time."
- The benchmark is Treasuries. He can put huge sums in government bonds and collect "20 or 30 or 40 billion dollars a year," and he gets 5% on Treasury bills. A good business has to earn "a lot more than the returns on essentially riskless investments."
- His example is American Express. Most banks earn 13% or 14% on capital, while American Express earns "30% plus" without taking more risk.
- "The trick in investing is to find businesses that are going to earn high returns on capital for an extended period of time."
- The long period matters because "those doubles later on are the payoff of very good numbers."
- He ties this to Charlie Munger, who "pounded the idea" that a business isn't good because it does sexy things. It has to earn real cash that it could distribute within a short period.
- Better still are businesses that can reinvest that cash at high returns inside the business. He notes the harder case is businesses that earn high returns but can't deploy the excess capital.
- Coca-Cola is his example of a very good business. Berkshire has owned it about 45 years and has "not a thing to do with running" it.

chunks.heading: Durability, competition, and why moats get attacked
chunks.text:
- "If you have a wonderful business, you are going to be subject to attack. So it's not a question of whether it was wonderful yesterday, it's the question of how long it is going to be wonderful."
- Data Documents, from 1958: his group started it after reading that IBM had been ordered in an antitrust suit to divest 50% of the capacity of its best business. He says it was among his most successful ventures and the opportunity "ran out after ten or fifteen years."
- A&P was the number one grocer in the 1930s and a top target of trust busters. "They had a very, very good hand, and that hand disappeared."
- Henry Ford owned the car business for 20 or 25 years with a vertically integrated model, got the Model T down to about $285, and kept cutting prices while raising wages. When he turned over to the Model A, General Motors "came racing by." Warren says "you've always got somebody shooting at you."
- On IBM: customers are "either happy customers or you don't have customers." Someone eventually offers a better way to meet the customer's objective.
- He prefers slow-changing product businesses to ones with fast technical competition: "If somebody came along with a better candy, that would have more predictive value to me" than a rival finding a better process that "a hundred of their competitors would sneak in the plant at night" to copy.
- People play for keeps in business. He recounts a Sinclair filling station he half-owned in Omaha in his early 20s. They set out to wipe out the competitor next door, which pumped 30,000 gallons a month to their 15,000. Two years later the numbers were the same and they closed.

chunks.heading: Apple, key-person risk, and trade secrets
chunks.text:
- Warren still likes Apple, his largest position. He says he knows "more about Apple than I knew many years ago."
- On Tim Cook: "There was no move they could make that would replace Tim that I would have liked." His analogy is that if you have a Stradivarius playing for you, don't spend 300 years looking for another one.
- He says Apple has "very smart people all over the world trying to figure out how to make sure that Apple's future is as bright as its past."
- On Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI over trade secrets, he says most companies would love to steal trade secrets, though "they wouldn't love getting caught."

chunks.heading: Wall Street, quarterly thinking, and the gambling culture
chunks.text:
- Wall Street "is only selling something." He can't recall a Wall Street report that gets into the internal rates of return a business is actually earning, and they ask "what will happen next quarter, and it's ridiculous."
- Compounding gets harder with size. The best long-term compounder was probably Rockefeller (oil and gas over 150 to 200 years), but Geico compounded faster in its early years: "it's easier to do when you're small."
- Opportunities arrive unevenly. Some times they are "thrown at you so fast you can't believe it," and at other times "you're very, very lucky if you find one thing in a couple of years."
- He thinks the latter should be normal, but humans love to gamble, so "there's more money in actually cultivating gamblers than there is in cultivating investors."
- Someone who bought Berkshire 40 or 50 years ago generated one commission, and the broker "should have spent the rest of his time telling the client don't do anything with it."
- Values are harder to find when everybody prefers gambling. He calls state lotteries "selling them a payout with a payout ratio of 60% or something like that" and "a cynical sort of activity."
- On the Dow: his first stock purchase came when it had just crossed 100, and it is now around 52,000. America has been a wonderful place to invest, and "the village idiot could have made it from that point forward."
- On the Fed: interest rates are gravity for asset prices in his past framing. He doesn't predict what Kevin Warsh will do but thinks he was "a good choice." He notes the Fed chair, unlike a president, is "not supposed to be looking at the next election."

chunks.heading: Succession, Greg Abel, and managing the end of control
chunks.text:
- Warren says Berkshire is "my painting," and he can name fewer than ten people, perhaps fewer than five, he would trust to hand it to. With Greg Abel, "we've found him, and that becomes more evident by the day."
- He is "one hundred percent" confident in Abel, having "seen him in a lot of situations." He felt the same way about Munger and Tom Murphy.
- The remaining risk is mortality ("he is not immortal either"), and Warren has no list of backups. Berkshire's directors "like the concept of Berkshire Hathaway" and "would like to keep it going."
- Finding even one successor is hard: "nobody expects you to pick up 25 partners and have them all work out."
- The Class A shares he still holds were worth about $140 billion at the prior close. He now wants them disbursed to charity by the end of 2034, instead of ten years after his death, partly because he has faith in Abel and partly because of age and mortality, both his own and his children's.
- He says he wrote his will a couple of years ago and will not change it except for very important reasons, because he knew he "had my marbles when I wrote it." He has seen managers of Berkshire companies decline while assistants covered for them.
- Berkshire's head office has run with about 25 people, and he says it grew "ten for one" before the last few additions.

chunks.heading: Giving, luck, and passing wealth to the next generation
chunks.text:
- Warren and Susie planned early that he would compound money at a better rate than society and she would give it away well. He did "wholesale" and she did "retail." He now says he may be "one of the ten luckiest" of 8 billion people, helped by the accident of being exposed early to what he was good at.
- He is increasing gifts to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and to his three children's foundations. Each child's foundation rises about 50%, and the STB Foundation's payout is $4.5 billion this year. He gives nothing for now to the Gates Foundation, which he says received about $47 billion from him in total. He called Gates a friend since 1991 who remains in touch.
- He has never looked at his children's Form 990s and does not judge each action. He notes philanthropic bets can have "10% or 20% probability of success. It's not like investments."
- His children's foundations employ 11 to 25 people each, with expense ratios "far below that of institutions that are much better known."
- A rule he credits to someone else: give children "enough to do something, but not enough to do nothing."
- On the Giving Pledge: encourage giving, and let people choose what and when. He sees philanthropy as appealing to people's better instincts.
